Iran offers seven-day peace plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz, but Trump is in no rush
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:28:36 UTC
07:28:36 KST

Iran is pushing a fast-track agreement that it says could end the war, halt fighting in Lebanon and reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, before immediately launching negotiations over its nuclear program.
But U.S. President Donald Trump, who has said an agreement will come “eventually,” either before or after the November midterm elections, appears in no hurry to surrender the naval blockade that has become one of Washington’s most powerful sources of leverage over Tehran. Iran, meanwhile, is maintaining its own hard line.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday that Tehran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program and would reopen the Strait of Hormuz only after “all of its conditions are met.”
The official did not spell out those conditions, but Iranian officials have previously demanded an end to the U.S. naval blockade, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil sales, the release of at least $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets and an end to the war “on all fronts,” including Lebanon.
The comments came as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi remained in New York, where his spokesman said indirect contacts with Trump representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff could continue.
Araghchi held three hours of talks with Witkoff and Kushner on Tuesday, mediated by Qatar on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The New York Times reported that he was expected to remain in the city through Monday.
At a briefing for international reporters on Thursday, Araghchi outlined Iran’s latest proposal. According to reports, it is essentially an accelerated version of the memorandum of understanding reached in June, an agreement widely seen as giving Tehran significant gains, including a role in managing traffic through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian officials told the Times that Tehran now wants to implement the agreement’s complicated series of steps far more quickly than the original 60-day timetable.
Araghchi said the entire process could be completed within a week, after which negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program would begin immediately.
But Tehran is demanding significant concessions first: an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon; the release of frozen Iranian funds; the lifting of the blockade on Iranian ports; and sanctions relief allowing Iran to resume oil sales.
If those conditions are met, Araghchi said, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen “by the end of the seventh day.”
He added that it would be “better” to reach an agreement before the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Trump has an incentive, but also leverage
On paper, Trump has a powerful political incentive to secure a deal before the elections.
Even the announcement of an agreement could drive down oil and gasoline prices, which have surged since the war began and amid Iranian attacks on tankers using the Strait of Hormuz. Polls have shown deep frustration among U.S. voters over rising prices, an issue Republicans fear could hurt them in the battle for control of Congress.
Yet Trump has repeatedly said he is in no rush to strike a deal.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that Washington had informed Tehran, through Qatar, that Trump did not intend to lift the naval blockade, as he did following the June agreement before reinstating it in July.
A White House official told the Journal that the blockade, combined with tougher sanctions that this week severely disrupted Iran’s aviation sector, had put Washington in a “strong position” against Tehran.
“President Trump is open to talks with Iran under the right circumstances, but he has no need to negotiate with the Iranians,” the official said.
Trump also remains deeply suspicious after several previous understandings with Tehran unraveled soon after they were reached, whether because of disputes over implementation or divisions inside Iran’s ruling establishment.
Hard-line elements in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been accused of carrying out attacks on ships after previous understandings were reached.
That has also raised questions over how much authority Araghchi, regarded as a more moderate figure within the Iranian establishment, actually has to conclude an agreement. Hard-liners inside Iran have already criticized the renewed contacts with Washington.
Iranian official: Chances of diplomacy are ‘extremely low’
Ali Vaez, director of the Iran program at the International Crisis Group, told the New York Times that Tehran’s proposal was a “smart move.”
“They know this is very tempting for President Trump, because it ends an unpopular war and lowers energy prices ahead of the midterms,” he said.
At the same time, Vaez noted, the proposal would revive an agreement that was largely favorable to Iran, while the compressed timetable for reaching nuclear negotiations could appeal to a president eager for rapid results.
Iran has its own reasons to want an agreement before the U.S. elections.
Beyond Tehran’s urgent desire to lift the blockade and sanctions as its domestic economic crisis worsens, many analysts believe Trump could face fewer political constraints after the midterms and could become more willing to resume an intensive military campaign against Iran.
Trump himself threatened during his address to the UN General Assembly this week to “destroy” Iran if it failed to reach an agreement with him.
Reuters described both sides as confronting essentially the same dilemma: Washington and Tehran each want an agreement, but neither wants to surrender its main source of leverage without receiving something tangible in return.
For Trump, that leverage is the blockade. For Iran, it is the severe disruption of traffic through Hormuz. The United States maintains that the strait is not technically closed, although shipping remains drastically reduced.
If Washington and Tehran cannot turn that leverage into an agreement before the elections, the diplomatic window could narrow as the risk of escalation rises.
A senior Iranian official quoted in the same report warned that Tehran would respond forcefully to any American escalation.
“Our finger is on the trigger,” he said. “The Americans know what they need to do, but because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this crisis are extremely low.”
According to regional sources who spoke to Reuters, Tehran is prepared to drop its demand that ships pay transit fees to pass through Hormuz from the main agreement.
Iran, however, still wants the demand included in a separate annex. The sources said Tehran would regard any arrangement as temporary and would not formally abandon its claim to authority over the strait, which is an international waterway and was open to unrestricted commercial traffic before the war.
This time, Saudi Arabia is pushing against concessions
Another obstacle has emerged from the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states are now opposing an agreement with Iran, at least one resembling the June memorandum of understanding, according to reports by the Associated Press and Wall Street Journal.
Saudi Arabia had supported renewed diplomatic efforts during the summer and opposed a return to war. Its position has now shifted.
People familiar with the discussions told the Journal that both Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were urging Washington not to make concessions to Tehran, including lifting the blockade on Iranian ports or easing economic pressure.
Another official told AP that the change was driven by the escalating confrontation with the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen.
The Houthis have attacked Saudi oil facilities and, during their latest territorial advances in Yemen, seized areas commanding the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the strategic passage linking Europe and Asia through the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Its importance has grown further as traffic through Hormuz has been severely disrupted.
The official said Saudi Arabia had previously been able to “live with” an agreement that granted Iran some degree of control over Hormuz.
That calculation changed, he said, after the Houthi advances and an attack by militias in Iraq on Saudi Arabia’s strategic East-West Pipeline, which allows the kingdom to export oil through the Red Sea while bypassing Hormuz.
The Wall Street Journal reported that a similar shift had taken place in the UAE, which previously supported diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.
Emirati officials are now playing down expectations for talks with Tehran following recent confrontations with Iran and continued attacks on vessels in Hormuz.
Gulf states, the Emirati officials were quoted as saying, should not accept a settlement that gives Iran permanent control over the strait.
Meanwhile, sources described as knowledgeable told Iran’s Fars news agency on Friday that reports of a new round of negotiations and the dispatch of Iranian experts to New York were false.
“The reports about new talks are intended to influence the market and oil prices,” they said.

Storm alert forces broadcasters to take down outdoor tents at UN General Assembly high-level week
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
06:28:07 CST
07:28:07 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- To "fold one's tent" became a command at UN Headquarters on Friday when UN officials ordered outdoor broadcasters covering the General Assembly high-level week to take down tents and canopies because of an approaching Nor'easter.
"Due to a wind advisory issued by the National Weather Service, and for everyone's safety, the (outdoor) Media Centre and 47th Street entrance will close ... and will not be open tomorrow (Saturday)," the UN Media Accreditation and Liaison Unit (MALU) told radio and television crews in a late afternoon email alert. "Broadcasters should take down canopies and tents set up outdoors by the end of Friday."
The weather service warned a Nor'easter will have a significant impact in the New York area through the weekend with heavy rain and winds gusting to more than 80 kph.
The United Nations traditionally installs two large tents on the North Lawn inside the 47th Street gate for security screening and to house visiting radio and television correspondents and crews during the annual General Assembly high-level week.
Several broadcasters set up their own smaller tents and canopies in the adjacent Rose Garden and along the East River.
MALU said broadcasters could set up in the main cafeteria space on the first floor of the Secretariat Building on Saturday, but cautioned there would be no catering or audiovisual services, as provided in the Media Centre tent.
"Fold one's tent" stems from Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's 1844 poem, The Day Is Done: "And the night shall be filled with music, And the cares, that infest the day, Shall fold their tents, like the Arabs, And as silently steal away." ■

The seven-day timeline will start as soon as Washington accepts it, he said.
Under the plan, the United States would need to take certain actions that Iran believes may take four or five days, said Araghchi, adding that on day six, the strait would be open. "And on day seven, the talks with the U.S. will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects."

"I can tell you if there is seriousness in the U.S. side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," said Araghchi.
"The choice now rests with the United States," he said. "Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure."

Under the MoU, they were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, which ended on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement, but the fate of the talks remains unclear following a series of recent escalations between the two countries. ■

Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:21:15 UTC
07:21:15 KST

The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.
In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.
Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to say Lake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.
Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will.”
The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.
Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.
Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.
As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.
“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.
“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.
“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”
Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.
“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said a statement from the organization shared on social media.
After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.
“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”
Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.
“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote on X.
Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.
The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.
Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

Air Force Injects $87M into IVEWS F-16 Electronic Warfare Upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:18:06 UTC
07:18:06 KST

The Air Force has invested $87.4 million to upgrade the F-16 Fighting Falcon‘s electronic warfare capabilities, bolstering the fighter’s self-protection against increasingly advanced threats.
Bringing the total program value to $1.92 billion, the move is expected to jump-start fielding by funding low-rate initial production of the AN/ALQ-257 Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, which is integrated into the fighter’s airframe.
This money is intended to produce an upgraded Viper for use in the Middle East, as part of an effort pushed by the U.S. military’s Central Command.
Work on the low-rate initial production batch at the company’s Illinois facility is expected to conclude by the end of 2029. The Air Force Lifecycle Management Center, Wright-Patterson, Ohio, oversees the contract.
The Need
The company says the new EW system is sorely needed for the F-16’s future fights.
“You cannot defeat what you cannot see,” said Shalini Gupta, vice president of electronic warfare and targeting at Northrop Grumman, in a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine. “A modern EW suite is essential for operations in contested airspace. We are producing fully functional, flight-proven systems now. From day one, our customers gain the ability to geolocate threats with a single aircraft, and the confidence that comes with having a U.S. program of record system on board.”
The F-16 has seen a lot of action in Operation Epic Fury, and while its existing capabilities have handled Iranian air defenses and electronic warfare capabilities, peer adversaries such as the Chinese military have more sophisticated means to foil the jet fighter’s aims.
The Air Force issued an urgent operational need statement in 2025 that triggered a congressionally supplied $187 million in its fiscal 2026 reconciliation bill, which sped up system qualification and flight testing.
After CENTCOM’s operational need statement, Northrop and the Air Force made the effort a priority.
“This is one of many efforts to keep our fourth-gen platforms competitive as the adversary advances,” Lt. Gen. Derek France, then-commander of Air Forces Central, said in September 2025 about IVEWS. “That’s the bumper sticker, if you will.”
The recently announced additional $87.4 million LRIP modification fuels the initial production of the Viper suites. Full-rate production of the suites for the full 450-aircraft fleet is scheduled to follow this initial batch.
The initial production tranche for the Air Force was to outfit 72 Block 50 F-16s with IVEWS, with more likely to arrive as production ramps up, the company’s vice president of targeting and survivability Jim Conroy told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a 2025 interview.
Iran operates radar-guided and electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) air defense systems. Non-traditional Houthi air defense systems proved a particular challenge for U.S. aircraft, including F-16s, during last year’s Operation Rough Rider against the group in Yemen.
During Operation Epic Fury, the Air Force used its Block 50 F-16s in a suppression of enemy air defenses role, U.S. officials have said, and deployed most of its Wild Weasel SEAD F-16 units to support operations against Iran. Those units’ F-16s can carry AGM-88 anti-radiation missiles and are equipped with HARM Targeting System, or HTS, pods—a capability the Air Force’s other fourth-generation fighter, the F-15E Strike Eagle, lacks.
The System
IVEWS is an ultra-wideband, sophisticated EW system capable of radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying, and locating threats, suited for fifth- and sixth-generation aircraft.
It can also conduct single-aircraft autonomous geolocation, meaning one aircraft can find an enemy radar and map a threat while actively using the aircraft’s jammer. Older systems required multiple aircraft to triangulate a radar location and required pilots to shut off jammers when mapping threats.
Under the USAF “Big Iron” software compliance standard, teams will be able to quickly update IVEWS system software files without hardware modifications or grounding the aircraft for days, weeks, or months.
IVEWS began flight tests in 2024 and has undergone more than 550 hours of effective testing across 300 sorties during operational assessments, Northrop Vice President for Mission Systems Mike Minahan said in a July call with reporters.
The system works in conjunction with the AN/AG-83 Scalable Agile Beam Radar. The radar uses an Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) to enable faster target tracking.
As of mid-May, Northrop had delivered 1,000 SABR radars to its F-16 customers. The new radar uses digital tracking as opposed to the legacy AN/APG-66 and AN-APG-68 radars that it is replacing.
IVEWS, the SABR, and the upgraded LITENING LA pod, which gives the aircraft a 50 percent increase in the range of its targeting system, are crucial to keeping the aging F-16 combat-worthy. The pod is also used on the F-15E Strike Eagle, A-10 Thunderbolt II, B-52 Stratofortress, and the Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet.
IVEWS would likely be equipped on possible future Air Force new-build “F-16G” purchases the service will consider, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
The LITENING LA, an upgrade from the current LITENING pod, entered flight testing in December, according to Northrop officials.

- list 1 of 3Ebola fight in DRC ‘far from over,’ warns WHO chief
- list 2 of 3DR Congo rolls out Ebola vaccine for health workers as death toll rises
- list 3 of 3DR Congo begins Ebola vaccination trials for frontline health workers
The additional cases bring the number of health zones affected to 63 across seven provinces as authorities struggle to control the outbreak.
As of September 23, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, or DRC, has reported 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, according to the WHO. That means that almost half the people who contracted the infection have died.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said conflict and population displacement were making it more difficult for health workers to reach affected communities and trace people who may have been exposed to the virus.
“It’s very difficult to see Ebola in isolation because even our response to Ebola is affected by the conflict, because there is displacement and there is an access problem to some areas,” Tedros said.
The Bundibugyo strain is difficult to treat because there are no approved vaccines, Tedros said, adding that the WHO is accelerating clinical trials of vaccines and treatments.
Contact tracing falling short
Meanwhile, health workers looking for people who may have been exposed to the Bundibugyo strain are falling short of their targets.
According to Dr Jean Kaseya, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), the more than 7,000 confirmed cases should translate to about 420,000 contacts.
“But currently, we have just 30,000 people in the contact list,” Kaseya said.
“When the outbreak is at community level, we cannot talk about control,” he added.
Ituri province in northeastern DRC continues to be the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 6,032 confirmed cases since the start of the epidemic in May, including 868 new confirmed cases reported in the last 21 days.
North Kivu is the second most affected province, with 1,480 new cases, including 567 reported in the last 21 days. The province now accounts for around a third of newly confirmed cases and deaths, the WHO said in a report on Sunday.
Nearly 60 percent of people diagnosed in North Kivu died, significantly higher than the national average of 48 percent, the data show.
Medical staff say patients are avoiding health facilities until it is too late.
“Patients think that if they arrive at the hospital, they will be immediately sent to the treatment centre to die,” said Dr Michel Paluku Mukuloli, who works at a hospital in North Kivu’s Butembo.
That complicates efforts to identify cases and start treatment before the disease reaches its most dangerous stages.
North Kivu was the epicentre of three previous Ebola outbreaks, including one in 2018-2020, which until this year was the DRC’s largest and deadliest. Those outbreaks, however, were caused by a different type of Ebola virus, known as the Zaire strain.
Much less is known about the Bundibugyo strain. But responders say in the early stages of infection, patients often experience milder symptoms easily mistaken for more common diseases such as malaria and typhoid fever.

Iran warns regional air travel could be halted because of ban on its airlines

Mohammad Sio
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
Iran warned on Friday that air travel across the region could be disrupted if Iranian airlines continue to be denied access to flights and airport services.
Tehran will not accept regional countries “aligning themselves with hostile US policies against Iran,” Mohammad Mokhber, a senior adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said in a post on US social media company X.
“Our strategy on this matter is clear: Either air travel in the region is available to everyone or to no one,” said Mokhber.
“If Iran cannot travel by air and receive airport services, no country in the region will be able to do so either,” he added in a thinly veiled threat.
Mokhber said the decision by regional countries to align with Washington in implementing “hostile policies” will remain in the memory of the Iranian people.
His comments came after restrictions on Iranian airlines expanded this week amid US sanctions targeting Tehran’s international operations.
Iraq's Najaf International Airport suspended all flights to and from Iran on Friday until further notice, citing directives from authorities.
 
The United Arab Emirates also suspended flights by Iranian airlines to and from Iran on Thursday until further notice, with its General Civil Aviation Authority citing US restrictions imposed on Iranian carriers.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that Iranian airlines’ operations worldwide will come to a halt as of Sept. 23 as part of new sanctions, as efforts to end the US-Israeli war on Iran continue.
 
Talks have stalled despite a June memorandum to reach a final peace because of disagreements concerning navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important strategic routes for energy and goods supplies.

Trump tells Zelensky to meet Putin in Moscow – Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:13:21 UTC
07:13:21 KST

Trump tells Zelensky to meet Putin in Moscow – Bloomberg
US President Donald Trump has reportedly called on Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to travel to Moscow for peace talks with President Vladimir Putin, Bloomberg has reported, citing sources close to the Ukrainian leader. Russia has previously repeatedly said that Zelensky could visit Moscow at any time.
The American president made the suggestion during his meeting with Zelensky on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week, the outlet reported. The Ukrainian leader rejected the idea, people familiar with the conversation told Bloomberg, adding that Trump’s proposal had “upset him.”
Zelensky was visibly irritated by journalists outside the UN headquarters on Wednesday. Pressed about when he would visit Moscow, the Ukrainian leader replied: “On a f***king missile!”
Zelensky DOES answer reporters asking when he’ll be heading to Moscow for talks
He COMPLETELY loses his temper as he walks away:
'On a f*cking missile' https://t.co/poqL8qA9Ffpic.twitter.com/f01pupjrnG
Earlier this week, Ukraine and 51 of its backers released a statement demanding that Russia accept an “immediate and unconditional ceasefire” so that peace talks between Moscow and Kiev can take place. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow will not halt its military operation, accusing Kiev’s European sponsors of seeking a pause only “to pump the Kiev regime with weapons.”
Trump has recently renewed efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict, with his special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner traveling to both Moscow and Kiev earlier this month. Witkoff said afterward that he felt “good” about the discussions in both capitals and that Washington hopes diplomacy can bring an end to the conflict.
Moscow has repeatedly said it is ready to settle the Ukraine conflict as long as its root causes are addressed and the realities on the ground are taken into account. Russia’s demands include Ukraine abandoning its plans to join NATO and adopting neutral status, accepting restrictions on its armed forces, and formally recognizing Crimea and four other former Ukrainian regions as Russian territory. Crimea voted to join Russia shortly after the 2014 Western-backed coup in Kiev. Donetsk, Lugansk, Zaporozhye and Kherson regions held similar referendums in September 2022.
Kiev has consistently rejected Moscow’s conditions, insisting on restoring control over all territories it lays claim to and joining NATO. At the same time, Zelensky has repeatedly stated that he wants to meet Putin in person to settle the conflict, even though he legally barred himself from such talks.
Moscow has repeatedly cited Kiev’s aggressive posture and the hostile position of its European backers as major obstacles to a peace settlement. The Kremlin has nevertheless maintained that it is ready to welcome Zelensky to Moscow at any time if he truly wishes to reach a deal rather than stage a PR stunt, even though Russia considers him “illegitimate,” as his presidential term expired more than two years ago and he has not called a new vote.
On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stated that Russia was ready to “provide security guarantees” to Zelensky if he decided to travel to Moscow.

Trump and Chinese president Xi end summit without major agreement on AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:11:52 UTC
07:11:52 KST

Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping wrapped up their Washington summit on Friday, facing criticism that they had squandered an opportunity to pause their countries’ artificial intelligence (AI) arms race.
The three-day state visit emphasised pageantry and personal rapport rather than substantial agreements. The US president and Xi discussed the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the status of Taiwan. Their biggest policy announcement was a modest two-month extension of a trade truce.
But despite the presence of top tech executives at a White House state dinner on Thursday night, Trump and Xi failed to deliver the AI breakthrough that some experts and foreign governments had hoped for amid warnings that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.
“It was such a layup,” said Ro Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China. “If [Trump] had just said, look, we have established technical working groups and we’ve agreed to a framework that has called for DeepSeek and Moonshot and Alibaba to sit down with Anthropic and OpenAI and Gemini and with technical experts and they’re going to commit to at least a pause on any self-improving AI, he could have looked like he was a statesman taking the lead.
“I believe Xi Jinping would have agreed to some of at least the technical working groups. But he [Trump] didn’t want to; he has no interest in doing that.”
It was the first visit to the White House by a Chinese president in more than a decade and Xi’s second state visit to the US. Three days of pomp and circumstance culminated on Friday with Trump and Xi drinking tea. Trump said the summit had produced great strides and that “our farmers are going to be happy,” but did not provide details.
The pair then went to the National Archives, where Trump and Xi looked at the original Declaration of Independence, the constitution and Bill of Rights. Trump told reporters they were comparing China’s documents to America’s founding documents. “Ours goes 250 years, which is great, and we’re proud of. Theirs goes 6,000 years. So there’s a little difference between 6,000 and 250. But we’re very proud of our 250.”
On Thursday, Xi acknowledged that the US and China have the “responsibility to develop and manage AI for good” and “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”. China aims to have next-generation smart terminals and AI agents reach more than 90% penetration by 2030.
But Trump – who has repeatedly said the US must forge ahead to maintain its lead over China – appeared more focused on his push to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”, later claiming on social media that Xi “seems to like” the term without divulging the substance of their discussions.
Later Trump hosted a black-tie state dinner attended by titans of the tech industry. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator of Vermont, used social media to label a photo of Trump and Xi’s table with guests’ net worth: Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla ($928bn), Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ($3.5bn), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ($186bn) and Tim Cook of Apple ($3.1bn). Sanders commented: “A government of, by and for the billionaire class.”
But their counterparts in the Chinese tech industry were not present and there was little sign of either country making even a symbolic gesture to apply the brakes.
Khanna commented: “Trump didn’t have to have some groundbreaking treaty like Reagan and Gorbachev did [on nuclear weapons]. He could have at least said, look, we’re going to have a working group of Chinese and American technologists working together to make recommendations and enforcement and verification of the labs.”
Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, agrees that an opportunity was missed. “We are in this potentially transformative moment for both countries and for the world and for technology and, instead of having a meeting that would meet the moment, you got theatre of the absurd in lieu of that,” he said.
“Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders. The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.”
The state visit underlined the contrast between Trump’s treatment of democratic allies such as Canada and authoritarian rivals such as China. He broke from tradition to give Xi a red carpet welcome when he landed at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
He also found time to show Xi around the White House, including a gallery wall of presidents where Joe Biden is mockingly depicted as an autopen, a construction site for his White House ballroom and a new helicopter landing pad. “He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite,” Trump said.
But the summit was somewhat overshadowed by Trump’s decision last week to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, sparking a legal fight. On Thursday, Chinese state media were welcomed into the White House grounds even as members of America’s free press were frozen out, though later they gained entry. As in May, when Trump visited Beijing, the leaders did not hold a press conference.
Czin of the Brookings Institution added: “I had very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations. We went from the mezzanine down into the basement. In terms of the substance, it’s not clear to me what the US got out of this.”
Senate Democrats also criticised the summit, arguing that Trump failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, human rights or AI.
Chuck Schumer, the minority leader in the Senate, said: “As usual, Trump acts based solely on who flatters him at the moment, where the nearest photo op is, and what headline he covets. If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll greet you plane-side.”
Trump and Xi are on track to meet twice more this year. In November, Xi will host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and in December the Group of 20 summit will be held at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.

Illegal Negev camel race intercepted by Southern District Police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:09:01 UTC
07:09:01 KST

An illegal camel race set to take place in a firing range in Israel’s Negev was prevented by Southern District Police, Israel Police said on Friday.
Forces were deployed to the area near Route 222 in Bir Hadaj, a Bedouin agricultural town, after intelligence indicated preparations were underway for the race.
Upon arrival, police identified vehicles, carts, and participants arriving at the site.
Officers from the Shagiv Shalom station, in cooperation with fighters from the Yoav unit, Border Police, and the National Guard of the Southern District of the Israel Police, raided the site with the assistance and guidance of the air unit, according to police.
Two minors attempting to flee and hide in nearby bushes were detained for further questioning at the Shagiv Shalom station.
Police also seized the camel found near the individuals.
Camel racing a tradition in Middle East, Bedouin communities
Camel racing is a popular sport across the Middle East and a tradition in Bedouin communities.
In Israel, Bedouins from different tribes travel to attend the event alongside Jewish residents from nearby communities.
The first legal camel race was held in the Negev in 2024 and was attended by thousands of spectators.
The Israel Police Southern District promoted and arranged the event to encourage lawfulness following warnings from police that illegal races were accompanied by other crimes, such as shooting incidents and animal cruelty.
"For years, the camel races in the Negev were a symbol of the loss of governance and lawlessness," Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli had said.
The first legal race, he said, was a reflection of the uniqueness of the Bedouin culture and "an important step to strengthen governance in the Negev and the integration of Bedouin society into Israel.

Netanyahu did not discuss UAE's October 7 warning at Gaza security meeting week of attack - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:08:58 UTC
07:08:58 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did not disclose an alleged warning from the UAE president that Hamas was planning a major attack during a Gaza security meeting held on October 1, 2023, six days before the October 7 massacre, The New York Times reported on Friday.
The report cited five former Israeli security officials, who further told the NYT that Netanyahu rejected suggestions from his security chiefs to strike Hamas leaders in Gaza who were directing terror attacks in the West Bank, saying instead that Israel should maintain calm amid a potential diplomatic agreement with Saudi Arabia.
According to the report, Netanyahu believed the Saudi-Israeli deal to be imminent, worrying that any IDF operations in Gaza would derail such a deal.
The NYT report follows an investigation published by Haaretz on September 8 alleging that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ) warned Netanyahu that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel in the days prior to the October 7 attack, with three foreign sources saying that the prime minister dismissed the threat.
Netanyahu denies claims, intends to file lawsuit
Netanyahu has denied the allegations, with the prime minister saying on September 9 that he instructed his lawyers to issue a libel lawsuit against Haaretz and the journalist who covered the story, Shlomi Eldar, according to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).
“A thorough examination not only of the prime minister’s call log, but also of the records of entries into the Prime Minister’s Office during this period, does not show any entry of the Emirati representative into the Prime Minister’s Office,” the PMO said of the allegations, accusing it of being part of a “sinister plot with clear political timing, as part of the Left’s election campaign,” adding at the time that there would be “more such false plots.”
UAE rejects allegations, says country 'does not discuss' such matters directly with leaders
The UAE also rejected the claims made in the Haaretz report, with an official UAE source told the state-owned Abu Dhabi English-language newspaper The National on Sunday that "the UAE discusses security matters with other countries through the relevant bodies, and does not discuss details of this kind at the level of the leaders of the countries."
Two sources from the United States have also weighed in on the Haaretz investigation, telling The Jerusalem Post on September 9 that the Biden administration was unaware of any specific warning from the UAE before October 7 that Hamas was planning a major attack.
Shir Perets, Tzvi Jasper, Idan Kweller, and Amichai Stein contributed to this report.

Gantz: Post-Oct. 7, Israel’s future depends on a broad, moderate, Zionist government - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:08:44 UTC
07:08:44 KST

In the shadow-filled days that followed Oct. 7, 2023, few things were as clear as the solemn understanding that what was cannot be again, and that things must change.
Three years on, and ahead of the first elections since that day, with polls pointing toward yet another political deadlock, that realization has still not produced a clear collective answer to the question of how.
Israel stands at an extraordinary moment, rapidly approaching Election Day on Oct. 27. We face serious threats, among the most troubling since our nation’s modern rebirth: a decline in our global standing, rising antisemitism, a weakening connection with Jewish communities abroad and, above all, a paralyzing internal divide over the questions that define who we are.
The leaders facing this moment cannot be those who deepen that divide. Israel now needs a broad, moderate Zionist government – stretching from the responsible right to the responsible left, and strong enough to govern without dependence on political radicals.
This is not simply an argument about coalition politics. It is a strategic necessity.
When it comes to Israel-US relations, Israelis should take California Congressman Brad Sherman’s recent warning about the erosion of support for Israel in America seriously, particularly because it comes from one of Israel’s longstanding Democratic friends. The rhetoric and radical positions of figures such as Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, can cause damage to Israel’s standing even when they do not become government policy or are executed on the ground.
US-Israel alliance must transcend partisan politics
Israel does not have to agree with every criticism coming from Washington. We are a sovereign country and must make our own security decisions while working to reduce unnecessary dependence on external support. But when friends who have defended Israel for decades tell us that something is going wrong, we should listen. The US-Israel alliance cannot be held hostage to partisan politics. Presidents change, congressional majorities change, and political generations change. The alliance must be strong enough to endure all of them.
The same is true of Israel’s relationship with American Jewry. American Jews should never have to support every Israeli minister or government to demonstrate their support for Israel. Criticism of a political vision is not a rejection of the Jewish state. American Jews remain outside Israel’s democratic arena, but Israel is the nation-state of the Jewish people, and we must protect the dialogue over our shared future. Governments come and go; Jewish peoplehood does not.
That responsibility also has a religious dimension. The Western Wall should symbolize the shared history and destiny of the Jewish people. Instead, narrow coalition politics have allowed the question of how Jews can pray there to become another source of division between Israel and Jews abroad. I have said before that the Western Wall is large enough to accommodate everyone. It still is.
The consequences of disproportionate leverage for radicals do not stop at Israel’s borders. The Abraham Accords demonstrated what the alternative can look like. They shattered the assumption that Israel was condemned to isolation from much of our region.
The next chapter could be even more consequential. A regional architecture connecting Israel, the United States, and moderate Arab and Muslim countries through security, technology, trade, and shared strategic interests could reshape Israel’s position for generations.
But Israel needs the political room to pursue it.
We cannot make regional normalization a strategic priority while allowing political factions fundamentally opposed to compromise to exercise disproportionate influence over national policy.
Radical minority factions have gained outsized influence beyond their public support
Israel’s problem is not that the majority of Israelis have become radical. It is that our political system repeatedly gives radical minorities power far beyond their public support.
After a decade of political struggles, I have concluded that this model cannot provide the broad base required to make and effectively implement decisions on Israel’s fundamental national challenges.
That is why I believe Israel needs a broad Zionist government anchored by moderate forces. The purpose is to create enough political strength across the responsible Zionist center that extremists are no longer indispensable and no longer possess veto power over Israel’s national direction.
A broad coalition can embrace political diversity while being built on core, shared principles
Broad does not mean without principles. Such a government can and should contain serious disagreements between right, center and left. Zionism has never required political uniformity. But its members must share basic responsibilities: defending the country and sharing its burdens; preserving Israel as Jewish and democratic; respecting the rule of law; rejecting racism and political violence; and understanding that decisions made in Jerusalem affect Israel’s alliances and the Jewish people as a whole.
For the sake of Israel’s future and Jewish unity, we must restore political power to the broad moderate majority and ensure that narrow political interests do not outweigh the wider national interest.
Decisions made in Jerusalem do not stop at the doors of the Knesset. The political leaders who make them can and will determine how they echo in Washington, in synagogues, on campuses, in Jewish organizations and in families throughout the Diaspora.
Never has that responsibility mattered more.
Former defense minister Benny Gantz is the chairman of the Blue & White Party.

Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, US intelligence warns - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:08:33 UTC
07:08:33 KST

US intelligence assessments said Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons program, according to classified documents provided to Congress and reviewed by officials who spoke to The Washington Post.
The assessment was included in classified documents submitted to Congress as part of a review of a US-Saudi agreement to expand civilian nuclear cooperation.
The intelligence assessment raised concerns among some US lawmakers over the agreement reached by US President Donald Trump’s administration, which would allow American companies to pursue tens of billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia.
The agreement has also drawn scrutiny because it could eventually allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium to 20%, according to The Washington Post. The deal initially limits enrichment to below 5%, but allows the limit to rise to 20% after an additional study and written agreement.
The Washington Post did note that uranium enriched to 20% is still below weapons-grade levels.
US Senators warn the agreement could give Saudi Arabia the ability to develop a bomb
The agreement is currently subject to a 90-day congressional review period, during which lawmakers can seek to block it.
A group of Democratic senators led by Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Jeff Merkley of Oregon said in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the agreement could give Saudi Arabia the ability to enrich uranium and potentially develop nuclear weapons.
“The Trump administration is departing from precedent, adopting looser restrictions, and caving to Saudi demands,” the senators wrote.
Merkley told The Washington Post that the United States should not rely on assurances from the Saudi government regarding its nuclear intentions. He also questioned why Riyadh would seek the ability to enrich uranium domestically if its nuclear program were intended solely for civilian purposes.
The Saudi government did not respond directly to questions from The Washington Post but referred the newspaper to an earlier statement by Saudi Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman, who said the program would be “peaceful” and developed with “the highest levels of responsibility and transparency.”
The State Department also defended the agreement, telling The Washington Post that the United States “does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapon program.”
The department said the agreement would expand nuclear energy cooperation while maintaining what it described as the strongest nonproliferation standards that could be achieved diplomatically.
The intelligence community's assessment was included alongside input from the State Department, according to US officials who spoke to The Washington Post on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified information. The State Department's assessment was described as more confident in the agreement's safeguards and Saudi assurances.
The CIA declined to comment.
Another concern was that the agreement did not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol, which gives the agency broader access to nuclear facilities and research sites.
Twenty nuclear nonproliferation experts, including former IAEA director general Hans Blix, warned in a letter to Congress this week that the inspection arrangements could make it difficult to determine whether Saudi Arabia was secretly developing nuclear weapons at undeclared facilities.
Saudi Arabia will develop a nuclear weapon if Iran does
Concerns over Saudi Arabia's nuclear ambitions have also been linked to comments by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in 2018 that Riyadh would develop a nuclear weapon if Iran did so.
The Trump administration conducted joint Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and in 2026, but Iran's enriched uranium is believed to have survived the attacks under the rubble of the damaged facilities, according to The Washington Post.
The possibility of Saudi Arabia developing nuclear weapons has raised concerns among some US lawmakers that nuclear activity in the kingdom could contribute to a broader regional arms race.
The Trump administration has said the nuclear agreement is intended to strengthen US-Saudi ties and prevent Riyadh from deepening cooperation with countries including Russia and China.
The agreement could also have implications for US efforts to secure Saudi normalization of relations with Israel.
Trump has said normalization remains a requirement for the nuclear deal, although Saudi Arabia has not agreed to establish diplomatic relations with Israel while the Israeli government continues to oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state.

Report: Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons program, US intelligence assesses
Trump’s civilian nuclear deal with Riyadh faces scrutiny over safeguards and remains conditional on normalization with Israel
US intelligence assessed that Saudi Arabia had not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons program, The Washington Post reported, citing US officials familiar with classified documents submitted to Congress.
The assessment deepened concerns among some US lawmakers over President Donald Trump’s agreement to help the kingdom establish a civilian nuclear program. They feared the deal could enable weapons development and trigger a regional arms race.
Trump’s requirement that Riyadh normalize relations with Israel remained a firm condition for the agreement, a senior administration official told the newspaper. Analysts said the kingdom was unlikely to agree while Israel’s government continued to rule out a Palestinian state.
The nuclear deal would initially cap Saudi uranium enrichment at below 5 percent but allow an increase to 20 percent following an additional study and written agreement, according to the report.
It did not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which provides for broader inspections. Nonproliferation experts warned that this would hamper efforts to detect weapons development at undeclared facilities.
Democratic senators led by Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley criticized the agreement’s safeguards in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Some Democratic lawmakers sought to block the deal during a 90-day congressional review period, though overriding a presidential veto would require two-thirds support.
The State Department defended the agreement and said Washington would not support a Saudi nuclear weapons program. The Saudi government referred the newspaper to an earlier statement by its energy minister describing the planned program as peaceful.

Venezuela’s promised elections face long delays, sources say

2026-09-25

Venezuela’s promised elections face long delays, sources say
- Venezuela’s promised elections face delays until late 2027 or beyond due to complex reforms of the Supreme Court and National Electoral Council, crucial for credible voting.
- US officials demand economic and social stability alongside political changes, slowing election urgency and prioritising oil and investment deals with the interim government.
- Opposition participation remains limited, with key figures excluded from talks, while the political transition is treated as a long-term, open-ended process without a clear election timeline.
AI generated
CARACAS – Venezuela’s long-awaited vote may not happen for a year or more due to planned overhauls of the courts and electoral authorities, according to five political sources and analysts, despite Acting President Delcy Rodriguez’s promise of a transition to “full democracy”.
Rodriguez, who took power after an American raid captured then President Nicolas Maduro in January, told the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 23 that state institutions were preparing for elections. She said her government had opened talks with the opposition and would guarantee full participation, but gave no timetable.
Five sources – including from parties close to the government and opposition, as well as analysts – said that major obstacles remain, such as difficult institutional reforms and little apparent urgency in Washington for a prompt vote.
Two of the sources told Reuters that an election was unlikely before the end of 2027.
Tricky reforms
At the centre of the delay is the planned replacement of all 32 Supreme Court judges and the five directors of the National Electoral Council, the top electoral body.
Opposition groups and international rights observers have long said that both bodies lack independence, and that Maduro’s 2018 and 2024 re-elections were fraudulent.
Institutional reform is under discussion in United States-backed talks between Rodriguez’s interim government and a faction of the opposition.
But even after a new electoral council is installed, the authorities would still need to update voter rolls, ensure that all parties can compete and resolve basic operational questions such as whether voting would be manual or electronic, said Oswaldo Martinez of the Caracas-based consultancy ORC.
That process alone could take up to a year, according to two of the sources close to the talks.
US call for stability
US officials have also said that any political transition must be accompanied by economic and social stability, raising more potential questions on the electoral timeline.
“What would threaten an enduring republic in Venezuela would be that someone is elected and they inherit a complete catastrophe, economic and social, and then the whole project is endangered,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week.
Some critics of this position say Washington has sidelined the country’s opposition and reduced the urgency for free elections in favour of oil and investment deals with the interim government.
In August, US President Donald Trump announced an unprecedented US push to take control of a fifth of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves.
“The Trump administration is currently prioritising economic stability and oil-related deals under Delcy, with little apparent urgency to move towards a fresh vote,” said Risa Grais-Targow, Latin America director at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group.
“That, along with some of the required institutional changes, suggests new elections won’t be held until late 2027 at the earliest, with a possibility that it takes longer.”
Competing priorities
Maria Corina Machado, Venezuela’s best-known opposition leader and exiled Nobel Peace Prize laureate, has been notably absent from the talks with the interim government as her efforts to re-enter the country have been stymied.
Some US lawmakers have called for elections and say that Washington has not secured meaningful democratic concessions from Rodriguez’s government.
“Stability and economic normalisation centred heavily on US commercial participation remain the priorities,” said Nicholas Watson of consultancy Teneo, adding that Washington and Caracas are treating the need for political transition as a “longer-term” and “open-ended” process.
“Neither is taking decisive steps towards an electoral process,” Watson said. REUTERS

Moldova declares state of energy and hydrology emergency for 60 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:02:02 UTC
07:02:02 KST

CHISINAU, September 26. /TASS/. Moldova has declared a state of energy and hydrology emergency for 60 days over the threat of disruptions in the supply of electricity and fuel, rising gas prices, and the critical shallowing of the Dniester River, which supplies Chisinau and other cities.
Under a parliament resolution, the National Crisis Management Commission can make decisions deviating from the existing regulations to ensure an uninterrupted supply of energy during this period. It can change prices, tariffs, excise duties and other fees, as well as the rules regulating the energy market. The government will have the right to restrict energy consumption.
The special regime was introduced by the ruling Action and Solidarity Party. The opposition voted against it, calling the current government a state of emergency government. Since 2021, the republic has resorted to it many times after the decision to abandon Russia’s energy, which was made at an inopportune time. However, back then, the state of emergency allowed the government to ban opposition protests. This time, the special regime was introduced in individual sectors and will not apply to mass gatherings or other public activities. Nevertheless, it allows the government to classify contracts and the cost of energy supplies, and the opposition accuses the authorities of corruption. The government promised the regime will not affect the November 15 elections in the Gagauz autonomy.
The situation in the country
The republic faces a severe energy crisis, which has already led to the resignation of three governments. In 2021, the gas prices increased sevenfold, which spurred inflation to over 30% year·on·year and triggered mass protests. Starting from September 1 of this year, the gas prices rose by 41%, to about 1 euro per cubic meter, and this week energy companies have requested another increase -- by 30%.
As for fuel, this year the authorities tried to conceal the diesel fuel shortage, which was absent at about half of the country’s gas stations, using media outlets under their control. The problem was only acknowledged in the summer, when it could no longer be hidden. In September, the price of diesel fuel came very close to 2 euros per liter, which should become a new psychological threshold. This week Prime Minister Vasile Tofan warned the people about the upcoming difficult winter and urged them to "pray" that it would be mild.
The situation is exacerbated by an unprecedented shallowing of the Dniester River due to low precipitation. The government says the level of the Dniester reservoir in Ukraine dropped by half. Only about eight meters are left to the point where water discharge will stop. In the area around the Moldovan capital, the water level fell below what is planned for the water intake station designed to supply the city, and now floating pumps are operating there.
The authorities’ attempts to explain the crisis by citing the regional situation do not satisfy the people who are tired of the galloping prices, as well as the opposition, which accuses the government of incompetence. Earlier this week, farmer protests began in disagreement with the government’s plans to replenish the budget at their expense. As leader of Moldova’s largest opposition Party of Socialists Igor Dodon said the opposition is also discussing joint protests, which, according to him, should be large·scale and begin in October-November.

Why sex differences in throwing cannot be explained by socialization alone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:00:34 UTC
07:00:34 KST

Sex differences in overhand throwing cannot be explained by socialization alone, according to a commentary published in Evolutionary Psychological Science that argues biological predispositions and experience work together across development.
Scientists generally reject a simple choice between nature and nurture. Research in evolutionary biology, behavioral genetics, and psychology instead treats behavior as the product of ongoing interactions among genes, hormones, development, learning, and the social environment. Nevertheless, explanations attributing differences between women and men entirely to socialization remain influential in some areas of sex and gender research.
Robert O. Deaner and Michael P. Lombardo examine this tension through a debate about the pronounced sex difference in overhand throwing. This difference is exceptionally large—reaching roughly two standard deviations or more by adulthood, a gap comparable in magnitude to the adult sex difference in height. Their commentary responds to developmental biologist Anne Fausto-Sterling’s critique of their earlier proposal that throwing ability partly reflects adaptations shaped by stronger ancestral selection on males.
Fausto-Sterling argues that differences in children’s early social experiences and opportunities for ball play can account for the development of the throwing gap. Deaner and Lombardo contend that this explanation overlooks relevant evolutionary, anatomical, hormonal, cross-cultural, and performance evidence.
The authors adopt an interactionist framework in which evolved predispositions and environmental influences are complementary rather than competing explanations. Their central hypothesis is that ancestral males experienced stronger selection for forceful and accurate overhand throwing, particularly because males were more frequently involved in violent conflict and warfare.
Hunting and confrontational scavenging (stealing kills from other predators) may have provided additional selection pressures. Over many generations, these recurring demands could have favored anatomical, physiological, and behavioral traits that support throwing performance.
These evolved differences would not need to be fully formed at birth. Like walking or language, throwing develops through the interaction of biological capacities with experience, practice, and social input. Children may receive different levels of encouragement to play with balls, while preexisting differences in interests or physical capacities may also influence the activities they seek out and the responses they receive from caregivers. Socialization can therefore cultivate or amplify an evolved predisposition without having created it entirely.
The authors first dispute the claim that their evolutionary account depends principally on the traditional image of “Man the Hunter.” They say their primary proposed selection pressure is conflict between ancestral groups, especially warfare, with hunting serving as a complementary influence. They also argue that the anthropological evidence continues to show a substantial sexual division of hunting labor. Although women hunt in some societies, quantitative data indicate that men generally hunt more often, pursue larger animals, and obtain considerably more meat. In the authors’ view, such patterns make it plausible that males faced stronger selection for throwing-related abilities.
The authors next argue that the evidence extends well beyond childhood throwing studies. They point to an unusually large performance difference between male and female javelin throwers; differences in throwing accuracy and targeting; research connecting prenatal androgen exposure (levels of male sex hormones experienced in the womb) with male-typical propulsive behavior; and anatomical differences in the shoulder and arm that generally favor male throwing performance.
Large differences have also been observed among children in societies where both sexes receive substantial throwing opportunities or where neither receives much practice, while training improves girls’ performance without consistently eliminating the gap.
Finally, Deaner and Lombardo maintain that Fausto-Sterling’s observations of ten infants (five boys and five girls) cannot establish that maternal interaction caused the children’s differing engagement with balls, particularly because the study did not examine the mature, forceful overhand throw addressed by their hypothesis. More broadly, they argue that presenting developmental experience as an alternative to evolution misunderstand evolutionary theory: adaptations must emerge through developmental processes, and evidence that social experience contributes to a trait does not demonstrate that experience fully accounts for it.
The authors acknowledge that some lines of evidence supporting their account, including evidence concerning targeting, come from only one or a few studies. They also note that available quantitative hunting data may not represent all foraging societies.
By applying an interactionist framework to overhand throwing, the commentary argues that a complete explanation of behavioral sex differences must examine how biological predispositions and social experience jointly shape development.
The paper, “Sex Differences in Overhand Throwing are Completely Due to Socialization: A Blank Slate ‘Hypothesis’ Unconstrained by Evidence,” was authored by Robert O. Deaner and Michael P. Lombardo.

Details
It is noted that Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed the attack on an industrial facility but did not name it. Meanwhile, the owner of the refinery, "Lukoil," did not respond to a request for comment.

Former far-right group member found guilty of murdering Argentina rugby star
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:52:02 UTC
06:52:02 KST

Former far-right group member found guilty of murdering Argentina rugby star
PARIS, Sept 25 - A former member of a violent far-right group was found guilty on Friday of murdering former Argentina rugby international Federico Aramburu four years ago in Paris, following an altercation near the Boulevard Saint-Germain.
Loik Le Priol, 32, whom the court said was "animated by the will to kill", was sentenced to 26 years in prison.
"The narcissistic, intrusive and uncontrollable rage of Loik Le Priol ultimately led to the gratuitous killing of Mr. Aramburu," the presiding judge said.
In his closing statement to the court earlier on Friday, Le Priol asked Aramburu's family for forgiveness.
"I'm Christian like you, the pope is here today, I don't know if it's a sign -- hope one day you can find the strength to forgive me."
His associate Romain Bouvier, 35, also a former member of the now-banned GUD group (Groupe Union Defense), was found guilty of attempted murder and sentenced to 19 years in prison.
The court said that Le Priol and Bouvier formed "a deadly pair, united by a shared fascination with weapons and violence."
Both men are already serving prison sentences for aggravated assault in a separate case. They have 10 days to appeal the ruling.
Aramburu was having a late drink with friend and fellow former rugby player Shaun Hegarty on the terrace of the Mabillon cafe on March 19, 2022. At a nearby table were Le Priol, Bouvier and Le Priol's then-girlfriend, Lyson Rochemir, 29. She was also on trial and was found guilty of lesser charges that included obstructing the course of justice.
An altercation broke out between the two groups. CCTV footage reviewed during the investigation showed a confrontation involving Hegarty and Le Priol. The argument escalated into a fight involving Aramburu, Hegarty, Le Priol and Bouvier before security staff intervened.
The confrontation spilled onto the Boulevard Saint-Germain. Bouvier fired shots at Aramburu before Le Priol opened fire. Aramburu died at the scene.
The three defendants fled. Le Priol was arrested in Hungary, while attempting to cross the border into Ukraine.
Aramburu won 22 caps for Argentina and played for French clubs including Biarritz and Perpignan. REUTERS

Saadet Gokce and Diyar Guldogan

Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed currency movements on Friday amid US President Donald Trump’s “concern” over the weak Japanese yen, reaffirming that an “undervalued yen is a problem.”
The two finance chiefs discussed the issue in an online meeting, according to Kyodo News.
Katayama said she expects excessive yen selling to ease, suggesting there may have been some “misunderstanding” in the market and that the trend could reverse.
Bessent has called on Tokyo to strengthen the yen, as a weaker yen could fuel inflation in Japan, while rising Japanese government bond yields could push US Treasury yields higher.
Bessent said he had "a productive call" with his Japanese counterpart.
"Our conversation built on President Trump’s discussion with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi earlier this week and reflected the strength of the U.S.–Japan partnership," Bessent said on US social media company X.
He added that they discussed the desirability of a strong yen that reflects Japan’s strong economic fundamentals, and the importance of staying in close communication on currency markets.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met Trump on Tuesday, and the latter expressed concern about the yen’s weakness, Katayama said.

UN says Israel’s 942 checkpoints, barriers in occupied West Bank restrict Palestinian movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:40:45 UTC
06:40:45 KST

An extensive network of Israeli military checkpoints, gates and barriers stretches across the occupied West Bank, restricting Palestinian movement between cities, towns and villages, and separating communities from one another and their agricultural land.
The network has reached 942 checkpoints, closure points and other barriers, according to updated data from the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
The system includes 824 fixed checkpoints and closure points, as well as 118 linear barriers, including earth mounds, trenches and roadblocks, spanning a combined 107.7 kilometers (70 miles).
Hebron tops list
The Hebron governorate has the highest number of fixed checkpoints and closure points at 221, followed by Ramallah and Al-Bireh 160, Nablus 120, Bethlehem 78, Jerusalem 62, Qalqilya 41 and Salfit 40.
Jericho and the Jordan Valley have 27 checkpoints and closure points, while Jenin and Tulkarem each have 26, and Tubas 23.
Thirteen new fixed checkpoints and gates were added in the last two months, including 10 in the Jenin governorate, raising the number of fixed closure points there from 16 to 26.
The new locations in Jenin include gates and checkpoints at Al-Jalama, Arrana, the industrial zone, Deir Abu Daif, the entrance to Jenin city, Qabatiya, Umm al-Tut, the area surrounding the Arab American University, and the Zababdeh junction, among others.
A new gate was also installed on Al-Jariyout road west of Ramallah, along with gates on rural roads west and northwest of the governorate, further restricting residents’ movement between villages and surrounding areas.
Network of closures
The system is not limited to checkpoints and fixed barriers, but includes iron gates blocking entrances to towns and villages and agricultural roads, as well as earth mounds, trenches and roadblocks cutting off major and secondary routes.
The network allows Israeli forces to control Palestinian movement between cities, towns, workplaces, agricultural land and service centers.
The closure of a single gate can force residents to take much longer alternative routes or isolate villages and areas from their surroundings for hours or days.
As the network of barriers has expanded, Palestinian movement within the West Bank has become divided into separate routes and areas resembling “cantons,” with travel between neighboring communities dependent on the opening and closing of specific gates and checkpoints.
Israeli forces are not the only ones establishing barriers.
The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission documented cases in which Israeli occupiers installed gates on Palestinian roads and land, including one in Wadi Hamad on land belonging to Kafr Ni’ma and another east of Umm Safa on a road leading to a Palestinian family’s home, restricting the family’s access to the area.
Continued increase
The data shows that the system represents an expansion of a network that began developing more than two decades ago.
Around 757 barriers were recorded across the West Bank in 2003, including 464 earth mounds. The number stood at 630 in 2008 and 705 in 2018.
OCHA recorded 793 barriers in March 2024, before the number rose to 925 in December 2025 and reached 942 in the latest figures.
The barriers at the time included 89 checkpoints operating around the clock, 218 partial checkpoints, 232 road gates, 114 linear closures, 167 earth mounds and 105 roadblocks, according to OCHA data for 2025.
The figures indicate a gradual shift from temporary earth barriers toward more permanent gates and checkpoints, increasing Israeli forces’ ability to control Palestinian movement.
The restrictions affect Palestinians’ access to agricultural land and livelihoods, as well as the ability of students, patients and workers to reach schools, hospitals and workplaces, depending on the location, duration and nature of the closure.
As the checkpoint and gate network expands, military restrictions increasingly intersect with the Palestinian road network, lengthening travel distances between geographically close communities and deepening their separation.
The data indicates that the barriers do not operate independently but as part of an interconnected network of checkpoints, gates and closures capable of isolating one area from another or turning a direct route between two towns into a longer journey through several control points.

AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ – Bill Gates
Artificial intelligence is powerful enough to cause a billion deaths if used by people with malicious intent, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told NBC News’ ‘Meet the Press’ in an interview on Friday.
Governments should not rely on tech companies to police themselves, the billionaire stressed, urging Washington to pass legislation regulating AI development.
“AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that… cause a billion deaths,” he said. “Even though it’s pretty hard to get to 100%, there’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people of ill intent using the latest AI tools.”
Gates’ warning came just days after OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei renewed calls for stronger government guardrails on the technology following multiple incidents involving AI agents breaking containment in recent months.
Last month, Gates warned that “AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice.” He also argued that the risk of a rogue group using “open source AI tools to design a bioterrorism weapon” is greater than that of “a naturally caused pandemic.”
It is not the first time Gates has warned of a looming global epidemic. In a widely viewed 2015 TED talk, he said the world was poorly prepared for the next major pandemic.
His warning drew renewed attention after the Covid-19 pandemic emerged in late 2019. Gates subsequently became a magnet for conspiracy theories because of his prominent role in global public health. His earlier warnings and the Gates Foundation’s involvement in a 2019 pandemic preparedness exercise were incorporated into claims that he had planned the outbreak and intended to profit from vaccines.
His earlier remarks linking vaccines and health care to slower population growth also drew controversy. In a 2010 TED talk, Gates said the world’s population was heading from 6.8 billion toward 9 billion before adding: “Now, if we do a really great job on new vaccines, health care, reproductive health services, we could lower that by, perhaps, 10% or 15%.”
Gates has dismissed vaccine- and pandemic-related accusations against him as “crazy” and “evil.”
The billionaire’s ties to late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein have also fueled public scrutiny and conspiracy theories, although Gates has repeatedly said that meeting Epstein was a mistake and denied any improper relationship with him.
