What if AI’s greatest threat is what it reveals about us?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:33:23 UTC
06:33:23 KST

What if AI’s greatest threat is what it reveals about us?
The debate over artificial intelligence provides an opportunity to think about something more important than the latest arguments among American politicians and technology oligarchs because AI occupies a unique place in the history of humanity’s relationship with its inventions.
AI isn’t really a mind, but more a mirror, as it doesn’t exist independently of us but reflects human thought, including all the good and bad we have accumulated. Unlike the wheel, the printing press, the internal combustion engine or the nuclear reactor, AI can’t be separated from humanity, so to borrow Marxist terminology, it isn’t “alienated” from its creator.
The enormous quantity of data we produce every second undoubtedly falls increasingly into the hands of technology monopolies and this has helped create the persistent fear that AI will somehow abolish humanity, stripping people of their identities and eventually making them redundant.
But the machine, or more precisely its creators and owners, still requires human beings to produce the data on which it depends, meaning the texts, images and solutions generated by AI remain intimately connected with human thoughts and feelings and with the accumulated knowledge through which humanity has interpreted the world. So therefore there’s little reason to conclude that AI will abolish humanity as the principal creator of the reality around us.
The same applies to international politics where we should be skeptical of claims that weaker countries will inevitably fall under the control of those possessing the most powerful data centers and computing infrastructure, because politics still takes precedence over technology and the decision to become dependent on another power is ultimately political.
The Gulf monarchies, for example, are developing American AI infrastructure partly because their relationship with Washington is already based on security, so they increasingly see such infrastructure as another form of American presence, comparable in some respects to US military bases.
Likewise, a government in the former Soviet Union first decides whether its political orientation lies with the West, Russia, or China and decisions about whose technology and data infrastructure it permits generally follow.
What makes AI genuinely revolutionary is therefore something different in that its scale and pervasiveness allow humanity to see problems that have accumulated for decades and AI may be the first major technology whose rapid development has so vividly exposed a crisis of values and cultural reference points.
The printing press multiplied humanity’s capacity to distribute nonsense as well as wisdom, but the internal combustion engine told us very little about ourselves and neither did the nuclear reactor.
Even nuclear weapons initially revealed surprisingly little about humanity’s moral condition. At first they were treated largely as conventional weapons of extraordinary destructive power and later, the possibility of mutual annihilation created a system of deterrence and even encouraged the comforting illusion that political leaders possessed moral principles that would prevent another global catastrophe.
AI is different, given it has become something resembling humanity’s man-made collective conscience so through what it produces, we constantly encounter the depths of moral and cultural degradation of which human beings are capable. Donald Trump’s innocent AI “coloring pages,” fake images of catastrophes designed to attract clicks, fabricated tragedies circulating through social media and the endless torrent of meaningless content all demonstrate how easily images and opinions can lose their value.
Of course, AI didn’t create these instincts, but it merely made them impossible to ignore, and that’s why artificial intelligence is simultaneously poison and antidote.
For the first time, technological progress itself is forcing us to confront its human dimension, as obviously a car engine never spoke to us, a nuclear reactor never offered an opinion. Books did, but publishing traditionally imposed at least some barriers against false information and material of exceptionally poor quality.
AI removes many of those barriers, as it confronts us every day with the question of whether technological progress is necessarily an unqualified good and because AI is a mirror of civilization, its proliferation allows us to see an ethical crisis that exists, to varying degrees, in virtually every modern society.
For objective reasons, the West is currently at the forefront of many of these developments, but other societies are hardly immune and what has become known as “AI slop,” the endless production of low-quality visual and written material, has creators everywhere. Russia is no exception.
Many supposed debates about artificial intelligence are therefore really arguments about problems that existed long before neural networks arrived. In the creative industries, AI has exposed longstanding problems surrounding copyright and the overwhelming quantity of low-quality material, and in education and science, it has revealed the steady deterioration in the quality of work produced by everyone from ordinary students to distinguished academics. In the social sciences in particular, the ability to generate genuinely new ideas has been approaching exhaustion for years.
And in international politics, AI has destroyed another comforting illusion, as American attempts to use technological leadership to preserve geopolitical dominance demonstrate that the supposed independence of the internet was always conditional.
This is one reason governments increasingly speak about “digital sovereignty,” which is the ability to control their own technology and infrastructure rather than relying entirely on foreign corporations or states.
AI has consequently become another arena of international competition and, paradoxically, this may be useful as political competition encourages governments and societies to debate who controls these technologies, how they should be regulated, and what purposes they should serve.
In the middle of the 20th century, humanity acquired nuclear weapons and their destructive power eventually produced a system in which the strongest military powers generally avoid direct war with one another.
International politics remains unjust and violent and wars continue, but the enormous nuclear arsenals of Russia, the United States and China mean that a direct conflict between them is most likely to emerge through uncontrolled escalation rather than a deliberate decision to repeat the great-power wars of earlier centuries.
Now humanity has acquired another transformative technology, but the flood of AI-generated rubbish reveals processes that have been gathering strength for perhaps a century in the erosion of shared values and meanings, the declining authority of expertise, the fragmentation of cultural space and the replacement of creativity by consumption.
This is uncomfortable, but it may ultimately prove useful because AI hasn’t created our cultural and ethical crisis, just made that crisis visible on a scale that can no longer easily be ignored.
And precisely because artificial intelligence forces societies to confront what they have become, there are grounds for cautious optimism, where the age of AI may eventually produce not the disappearance of humanity or human morality, but the beginning of a gradual restoration of the ethical dimension of life.
That may prove true both within societies and in relations between states.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

Turning Point USA knew of security concerns yet insisted Charlie Kirk speak outdoors, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:32:45 UTC
06:32:45 KST

A new report says that Turning Point USA insisted the conservative political group’s leader Charlie Kirk speak outdoors at Utah Valley University – where he was ultimately assassinated – despite security concerns raised with his team by the school’s leaders and its police chief.
The independent report with those findings was commissioned by UVU and released on Friday. The report examined security procedures leading up to the 31-year-old’s fatal shooting on 10 September 2025 during a talk at the university’s campus in Orem, Utah.
According to the 158-page report, school staff recommended Turning Point USA (TPUSA) move its event to a more secure location weeks before Kirk’s slaying. However, TPUSA “insisted upon” an outdoor location which “created significant protective operations considerations”, the report said.
It added that a face-to-face, pre-event briefing and walkthrough with UVU police chief Jeff Long and the TPUSA protection detail – including the organization’s security supervisor Dan Flood – “should also have occurred” on UVU’s campus hours prior to the event.
“Chief Long texted Dan Flood to meet on the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway at 11[am], however, this face-to-face meeting did not occur,” the report said.
Kirk was shot and killed by a sniper that day in the early afternoon.
According to the report, the university also asked TPUSA for an estimated attendance figure. But the organization never provided one, despite saying it would control ticketing for the event, Utah’s Salt Lake Tribune newspaper reported.
“Based on our review of all available information, that at no time during the events leading up to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, or in its aftermath, did any employee or agent of UVU act in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” the report said.
However, it also noted UVU’s having deferred to TPUSA on various event logistics. “Several key event security decisions were deferred to the TPUSA field representative even though UVU staff members raised concerns, including concerns related to holding the event in the outdoor fountain courtyard area and using TPUSA’s ticketing process,” the university’s report said.
“Those decisions placed the event in an area that was more difficult to control and limited UVU’s ability to obtain reliable, real-time information regarding anticipated attendance and crowd size.”
The report added: “UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control and other conditions necessary to support campus safety.”
In response to the report, Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said: “UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie. The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement.
“Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.”
Meanwhile, a statement from Jon Anderson, UVU’s president, said the university had a responsibility to “learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations”.
“This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn,” Anderson’s statement also said.
Anderson, who became the university’s president in August, also said in his statement that UVU had made “meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year”.
Kirk’s family is planning to sue the university. His family alleged in a 16 September legal notice presaging wrongful death litigation that UVU had placed “a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event … surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms” – and that the setup was like “walking him into a fishbowl”.
UVU said it was aware of the notice and said it “addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes”, according to the Tribune.
Utah resident Tyler Robinson has been charged with aggravated murder in connection with Kirk’s killing. He has pleaded not guilty, and no trial date had been set for him as of Friday.

Brazil's Lula bans online betting, unveils debt relief plan as reelection race tightens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:32:08 UTC
06:32:08 KST

Brazil's Lula bans online betting, unveils debt relief plan as reelection race tightens
SAO PAULO, Sept 25 - Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Friday announced a ban on online betting operations in Latin America's largest economy and unveiled a new debt relief program aimed at households, the latest in a series of measures introduced ahead of next month's election.
Opinion polls have shown Lula locked in a tight race with right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, ahead of the October 4 first-round vote.
The executive order bans online betting operations in Brazil, less than two years after the government kicked off a legal framework allowing the industry to operate. It takes immediate effect but must be approved by Congress within 120 days to remain in force.
The crackdown reflects growing concern within the government that rising spending on gambling has drained household budgets and contributed to record levels of indebtedness. Recent surveys showed roughly three-quarters of Brazilians support a complete ban on online betting.
"We are facing a public health issue involving online betting. It is a serious problem," said Finance Minister Dario Durigan during the announcement.
Durigan said that betting firms' websites will remain available for users to claim remaining funds until October 5. App stores and network providers will be required to block these websites on October 6, he added.
Senator Bolsonaro called the measure "populist, hypocritical and politically motivated" during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday.
Online betting was legalized in Brazil in 2018 under former President Michel Temer but remained largely unregulated throughout Jair Bolsonaro's administration. Lula signed legislation in 2023 establishing rules and explicitly authorizing online casino games in addition to sports betting.
Licensed operators have been allowed to offer services nationwide since January 2025 after paying concession fees and meeting regulatory requirements.
Officials have argued that betting losses have fueled public dissatisfaction with the economy, despite record-low unemployment and relatively subdued inflation in the country.
The Finance Ministry estimates Brazilian households spend around 60 billion reais ($11.57 billion) annually on online betting, generating roughly 10 billion reais in tax revenue.
JPMorgan said listed companies most exposed to Brazil include Evolution, which derives about 9% of sales from the country, Allwyn, whose Betano business contributes 6% to 7% of EBITDA, Entain and Flutter.
ANJL, an association representing the betting sector, said in a statement that the measure would push more than 30 million gamblers into illegal websites, adding it disrespects investments made in compliance with the law.
DEBT RELIEF PROGRAM
Lula also announced a new initiative aimed at reducing the burden of household debt, only months after relaunching a broad federally backed consumer debt renegotiation program known as "Desenrola," which was unveiled in 2023.
The government said it will hold an auction in November to buy and restructure household debt, spending 15 billion reais to acquire up to 150 billion reais of delinquent loans at discounts of at least 90%. The program is expected to cover about half of the debt stock deemed eligible.
Households would then be able to clear overdue obligations at the discounted value, with the full benefit of the write-down passed through to borrowers.
The initiative targets debts that have been overdue for two to 4.5 years, mainly credit card balances and unsecured personal loans. Planning Minister Bruno Moretti said the auction will cover debts of up to 10,000 reais.
"This is a better Desenrola than the previous versions," Lula said. "In the earlier Desenrola, people had to approach banks individually. Now the government will purchase the debt and settle it on behalf of borrowers."
The measure had already been flagged by the government last week as part of Lula's election-year economic agenda. REUTERS

China and the US can make nice, if not peace

Alex Lo has been an SCMP columnist since 2012, commenting on China and international affairs. 
Washington and Beijing have spent nearly a decade trading tariffs, export controls and blacklists, with each round threatening rupture. Yet they keep recovering from the brink.
Tensions soared before summits and plunged immediately after. For example, in 2019 at Osaka, Trump walked back threats to impose tariffs on US$300 billion of Chinese goods and eased curbs on Huawei after Beijing reportedly agreed to buy American farm goods. In Busan last October, he lowered tariffs and shelved export controls on thousands of Chinese companies after Xi Jinping suspended some rare earth restrictions and resumed soybean purchases.
As the two presidents met at the White House this week, that pattern was repeating. Simply put, decoupling is proving ruinously expensive on both sides: two-way goods and services trade fell 25.1 per cent last year to an estimated US$494.6 billion, with American goods exports to China down 26 per cent.

What would a US diesel export ban mean for global fuel prices?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:28:56 UTC
06:28:56 KST

What would a US diesel export ban mean for global fuel prices?
Energy experts warn US diesel export ban could increase fuel costs domestically and internationally.
Diesel prices have hit record highs as the tensions between the United States and Iran, along with the war between Russia and Ukraine, disrupt key oil and fuel trade routes.
On Friday, the average price for a gallon (3.79 litres) of diesel was $6.50, up from $5.61 a month earlier, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks fuel prices daily.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Could the oil shock push fuel prices even higher?
- list 2 of 4Oil prices jump after Yemen’s Houthis claim attacks on Saudi facilities
- list 3 of 4Iran pitches seven-day roadmap to end conflict with US
- list 4 of 4What’s in Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
The spike has prompted the administration of US President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers to consider restricting US diesel exports ahead of upcoming midterm elections.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in August found that 47 percent of voters said the cost of living was the single most important factor in deciding how they would vote in the midterms — more than twice the share who cited the next-most important issue, “democratic values and norms”.
A new Marist poll also found that Americans have more confidence in Democrats than Republicans to handle the economy, with 42 percent choosing Democrats compared with 34 percent for Republicans.
Amid that voter sentiment, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Thursday that he was in touch with major oil refiners to gauge interest in a potential voluntary restriction on diesel exports, according to the Reuters news agency.
That followed remarks by Trump on Tuesday that he supported restricting diesel exports from the US, the world’s largest diesel exporter.
Energy analysts and industry groups have warned that an export ban could have unintended consequences, potentially pushing up fuel prices in the US and abroad.
Why are diesel prices so high?
Even though the US is the world’s largest diesel exporter, diesel is traded on a global market.
Disruptions to refineries in Russia and the Middle East have reduced the amount of fuel available worldwide, putting more pressure on US producers to fill the gap. In Russia, for example, drone attacks have damaged major refineries, forcing a cutback or halt in production.
“While US refineries are running at full tilt and higher than normal, the global gaps remain,” Rachel Ziemba, senior adjunct fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
It comes as US diesel supplies are also shrinking. As of September 11, inventories had fallen to 107.9 million barrels, the lowest in more than four decades, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
With global supplies tightening, diesel prices have risen around the world — including in the US. Because American producers can sell their fuel into the global market, they are drawn to the soaring global prices rather than simply setting a lower price for domestic consumers.
Why is the US considering an export ban?
In Washington, DC, leaders have flirted with the idea of pushing US companies to stop or slow exporting diesel.
Republicans have been pushing for a slowdown or outright ban of exports in an effort to lower costs for consumers ahead of the pivotal midterm elections, where cost of living is becoming a critical issue.
Such a move, they hope, would reduce local diesel prices, which is significant as diesel is used in trucks to haul food and most products, Ziemba said, adding that US diesel exports are equivalent to about 40 percent of domestic consumption.
On Tuesday, Chuck Grassley, a Republican from Iowa, called on the president to put in place a temporary halt on exports.
“I encourage President Trump to put a temporary embargo on diesel exports through executive action,” Grassley said.
Republican Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska made a similar call: “The cost of diesel is just too damn high. I’m calling for a temporary pause of American diesel exports so that we can rebuild our reserves ahead of winter,” Sullivan said in a statement on Tuesday.
In the House of Representatives, Congressman Tim Burchett of Tennessee introduced two bills that would restrict US diesel exports: One would impose a ban through January 2027, while the other would restrict exports if the national average price reaches $5 a gallon.
The administration has not made any official policy announcements, and the White House told Al Jazeera that the president is evaluating all options.
Oil and gas industry experts say that a ban could drive up prices rather than bringing them down.
“Diesel trades on a world market, just like corn. farmers don’t sell cheaper to Americans, and refiners can’t either since they buy crude at global prices. force a lower price and they’ll make less diesel. less supply means higher prices, not lower,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X.
How would an export ban work?
A ban would prevent or restrict US refiners from selling diesel to buyers overseas, theoretically leaving more fuel available in the domestic market.
Analysts at Wood Mackenzie, a research and consulting firm, say that keeping more diesel stateside would ultimately fill up US storage tanks but also force refineries to cut production. That could affect other markets that rely heavily on US fuel, including Latin America and Europe, forcing them to compete with other global buyers for supplies and driving up prices for the global market.
Wood Mackenzie says China is the only major producer with enough spare refining capacity to potentially make up much of the shortfall.
“China is currently the only country with material spare refining capacity that could cover the loss of US refinery throughputs. However, China may well decide it is not in its interest to intercede,” analysts said.
Wood Mackenzie has warned that a ban could quickly fill US diesel inventories, forcing refiners to cut crude runs and potentially increasing US petrol imports.
That was also the view of an S&P Global analysis, which found that a complete ban could also mean that production would be reduced as storage capacity is filled up with unsold diesel. According to the analysis, that could lead to production cuts of as much as 750,000 barrels a day, which could put the US into being a net importer of petrol in the fourth quarter of this year.
Who would an export ban affect?
An export ban would affect US refiners and consumers, as well as countries that rely on US diesel.
“They [export bans] may provide temporary relief, but diesel is a global commodity. Treat one part of the system, and the effects travel elsewhere. Trade-offs are inevitable. Refiners are unlikely to cheer a blanket ban. Voluntary, controlled export reductions would generally be less disruptive in the short term,” Maksim Sonin, visiting scholar at Stanford University’s Precourt Institute for Energy, told Al Jazeera.
Disruptions to US exports could reduce the amount of fuel available on the global market. Wood Mackenzie analysts say countries in Europe and Latin America that rely heavily on US fuel could be forced to compete with other producers for supplies.
“If implemented, it would lead to European and Asian product prices increasing as the buyers of US fuel, mostly in Latin America, scramble to find new supplies, bidding up supplies. European crack spreads could widen, and overall we might see more disruptions,” Ziemba added.
“Given these issues, the US may opt for a mixture of carrots and sticks aiming to incentivise refineries to keep producing, perhaps including penalties if they cut production. There may be voluntary export quotas rather than a formal ban, and there may be exemptions for countries that provide crude oil to the US, like Mexico,” Ziemba said.
That could put pressure on consumers not only at the petrol pump but in the skies as well.
Airlines for America, an airline industry trade group, has also warned that an export ban could lead to higher prices for airlines and travellers, according to the Reuters news agency. The trade group did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
The broader concern from analysts is that restricting exports could reduce US refinery production rather than simply redirecting diesel to US consumers, potentially putting upward pressure on fuel prices both domestically and internationally.
“It’s unlikely to help US consumers much given how it fails to solve underlying problems and could backfire if refineries hold on to production. The best way to address this is to end the conflicts prompting the shortages,” Ziemba said.

Global displacement challenge to international peace, security: UN refugee chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:28:39 UTC
06:28:39 KST

Yasin Gungor
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih said on Friday that mounting forced displacement poses a fundamental threat to international stability.
He urged the UN Security Council to prioritize political solutions over indefinite humanitarian assistance.
"This is not only a humanitarian challenge; it is fundamentally a challenge to international peace and security, and that is why this discussion belongs here," Salih told a Security Council briefing on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly session, stressing that displacement is "rapidly" outpacing durable solutions across proliferating and protracted conflicts.
Salih said that more than 117 million people have fled violence, persecution and conflict, maintaining that managing displacement indefinitely cannot serve as the measure of collective ambition. Under the "50 by 35" vision launched earlier this year, UNHCR aims to halve by 2035 the number of long-term displaced refugees who remain dependent on humanitarian assistance.
Political horizons needed in Sudan, Sahel, regional crises
Addressing the crisis in Sudan, Salih affirmed that "humanitarian assistance can keep people alive" but cannot deliver the peace citizens need to rebuild, calling for a truce and "serious" dialogue. In the Sahel, he argued that security and humanitarian protection must reinforce each other rather than operate as competing goals.
Salih said the "real test" of a peace process is to see whether it leads people to return to their homes in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and urged the Security Council to "help sustain that momentum."
Salih termed the half-century displacement of Sahrawi refugees in Western Sahara "untenable, unsustainable and genuinely truly inhumane" amid deteriorating conditions and severe funding shortages.
Salih demanded the unconditional release of all UN and humanitarian staff arbitrarily detained by Houthi authorities in Yemen, where UNHCR declared an initial Level 1 emergency alongside Djibouti and Somalia to scale up cash assistance and shelter.
Sustainable returns in Syria, Afghanistan
Turning to post-conflict reconstruction, Salih noted that 3.8 million Syrians displaced internally or abroad have returned home since December 2024. But he emphasized that determination alone cannot rebuild the country without international engagement and recovery investment.
He added that nearly 8 million Afghans are expected to return by the year's end, often under adverse and involuntary conditions.
"Return, I want to say, is an event; a solution is what comes after," said Salih, concluding that international success must mean creating circumstances where displaced people no longer require aid.
Gaza displacement, unhindered aid
Council members voiced alarm about conditions in the Gaza Strip, and Denmark highlighted that the enclave's population of 2.1 million people faces displacement and urgent shelter needs due to continued Israeli attacks.
Somalia's delegation argued that the prolonged Israeli occupation remains a "central cause" of Palestinian displacement. 
 
China, meanwhile, urged the international community to guarantee basic supplies, oppose forced displacement and reject land annexation in Gaza or the occupied West Bank. 
 
Russia insisted on "maintaining and wholeheartedly supporting the work of the UN Palestine refugee agency, UNRWA" amid a “humanitarian catastrophe.”
Addressing root drivers of displacement
Delegates stressed that relief supplies cannot substitute for political progress, with Panama maintaining that the ultimate objective "cannot be to eternally administer suffering" but to eliminate conditions producing it. 
 
The Democratic Republic of the Congo described humanitarian assistance as vital but "no substitute for political action," while Pakistan affirmed that relief mitigates fallout while only political accords sustainably prevent conflict.
Liberia said a return without reintegration constitutes "displacement by another name," cautioning against sending refugees back to battlefields lacking schools or hospitals, while Colombia urged cross-cutting action against organized crime syndicates that exploit and amplify forced migration flows.

"Today I'm calling for the release of Marwan Barghouti from Israeli prison. Palestinians must choose their own leaders," Khanna said. He described Barghouti as having "a unique standing among all Palestinian factions" and said he is viewed as "non-corrupt, a strong leader, and secular."
Khanna went further, arguing that "Barghouti could deliver a Palestinian state living in peace with Israel," and noted that some former senior Israeli security officials have also supported his release.
The remarks come as Khanna, a progressive Democrat representing California's 17th Congressional District in Silicon Valley, seeks to elevate his foreign-policy profile while openly weighing a possible 2028 presidential run.
During a visit to the West Bank in July, Khanna told Reuters that he was "strongly considering" a presidential bid. He also sharply criticized Israeli policy toward Palestinians during the trip, including using the term "apartheid" to describe conditions in the West Bank — a characterization Israel rejects.
US rep. says Fatah member Barghouti can help with Israel-Palestinian conflict
Khanna stressed that he was not seeking to erase Barghouti's past or absolve him of responsibility.
"Releasing Barghouti does not provide him with a pardon or moral absolution of crimes he may have committed," he said, while adding that some human-rights organizations have challenged the fairness of Barghouti's trial.
He argued, however, that Barghouti's release could be necessary to advance diplomacy, drawing comparisons to past peace processes involving former adversaries.

He said Barghouti had repeatedly expressed a similar vision.
"If we're lucky enough to have a just peace in Israel-Palestine, we will need a truth and reconciliation commission," Khanna said. "But for now, we must begin to give Palestinians a voice in their sovereignty and the peace process. Release Barghouti."
Barghouti, a senior Fatah figure, has been imprisoned in Israel since the Second Intifada. An Israeli court sentenced him in 2004 to five life terms over his role in attacks that killed Israelis. Barghouti rejected the authority of the Israeli court and has long denied responsibility for attacks on civilians.
Despite nearly a quarter-century behind bars, he remains one of the most prominent figures in Palestinian politics and is frequently discussed as a possible successor to Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. President Donald Trump himself said last year that he was considering whether to urge Israel to release Barghouti as Washington examined possible postwar Palestinian leadership arrangements.
Recent Palestinian polling underscores Barghouti's political weight. An August survey by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research found that, in a hypothetical presidential race among likely voters, Barghouti would receive 54% support, compared with 26% for Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya and 14% for Abbas. Palestinian presidential elections are currently expected in early 2027.
Khanna issued the call during the week of the UN General Assembly in New York, as the Palestinian issue again features prominently in international diplomacy and debate intensifies over the shape of future Palestinian political leadership.
Khanna has increasingly positioned himself among Democrats calling for a reassessment of longstanding US policy toward Israel and the Palestinians. His latest statement places him among the most prominent American lawmakers to explicitly call for Barghouti's release.

Ukraine–UK AI Partnership Targets Drone Swarms That Could Independently Identify Enemy Targets
The United Kingdom has become the first international partner whose defense companies will gain access to Avengers Labs, Ukraine's AI-training platform for unmanned systems.
This was reported by Ukraine's Ministry of Defense on its official website on September 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The platform trains AI models for drones and other unmanned systems using an annotated dataset built from real combat footage, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense noted.
Up to 12 British defense companies will join the program, the ministry added.
They will work within a secure perimeter that prevents them from downloading the underlying dataset, the ministry explained. Companies will instead test and train their own AI models inside that perimeter, the ministry confirmed.
The partnership became possible under a joint declaration of intent between the two governments, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense stated. To implement it, Ukraine and the UK signed a separate agreement on cooperation in artificial intelligence, the ministry noted.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed that agreement, according to the ministry. Priority development under the partnership will focus on AI models for swarms of unmanned systems, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense indicated.
Such models would let drones cooperate with one another and independently identify enemy threats and targets, the ministry explained.
Remote control of large numbers of autonomous drones is also expected to simplify logistics support and enable high-precision targeting of enemy positions, the ministry added. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense reported that the UK Ministry of Defense will select participating companies on a competitive basis.
The first competition under the partnership calls for AI models that let unmanned systems operate effectively with limited communication to human operators or satellite navigation, the ministry noted.
Those constraints reflect the difficult battlefield conditions in which the systems are meant to operate, according to the ministry. Up to 12 companies will ultimately be chosen, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense added, based on how well their proposals meet requirements set by both defense ministries.
Selection is expected to conclude within a few weeks, the ministry stated. Companies will gain access to the platform once Ukraine completes its export control procedures, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Defense.
The UK Ministry of Defense's Rapid AI Delivery Task Force, known as RAID, is leading the selection process, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense noted. The unit was created to give British forces faster access to technologies that support decision-making and reduce risk in dangerous missions, the ministry explained.
It is also meant to help the military keep pace with adversaries as they develop their own AI capabilities, according to the ministry.
Avengers Labs is built around an annotated dataset of more than 5 million battlefield frames, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense reported. Most of the material comes from unmanned systems through Ukraine's DELTA combat management system, the ministry described.
The data arrives anonymized and delayed, a step meant to avoid creating risks for personnel still fighting, according to the ministry.
The dataset spans a range of targets, including enemy tanks, artillery, air defense systems and infantry, the ministry noted, as well as aerial threats such as Shahed-type drones and reconnaissance UAVs.
More than 30 Ukrainian defense companies are already training their own AI models on Avengers Labs, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense confirmed.
Three of those products are already used on the battlefield, the ministry added.
The ministry described the dataset's scale and quality as difficult for any private company to replicate, noting that only a country with experience of a modern full-scale war could gather comparable material.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defense emphasized that the AI cooperation is part of the broader 100-year partnership between Ukraine and the UK. It added that the initiative would deepen cooperation between the two countries and strengthen Ukraine's ability to defend against Russian aggression.
The push to embed artificial intelligence deeper into Ukraine's defenses has drawn in more partners in recent weeks.
Earlier this week, Ukraine gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak program, a cyber-defense tool aimed at protecting hospitals, power plants and other critical infrastructure from attack.
The same initiative extended access to GPT-5.6 Sol, an advanced OpenAI model, as Ukraine's CERT-UA team works through nearly 6,000 cyber incidents logged in 2025 alone.

Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis
September 25, 2026
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country.
"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address.
The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint.
What else did Yemen's leader say?
In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014.
He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty.
Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas, urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis.
"The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said.
Houthis escalate conflict
For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports.
The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend, marking a major escalation.

ArcelorMittal Shuts Plant in Kryvy Rih Due to Russian Strikes, Expects $1B Impairment Charge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:07:04 UTC
06:07:04 KST

One of Ukraine’s largest foreign manufacturers of steel products, ArcelorMittal, completely halted operations at a plant in Kryvyi Rih after facing persistent Russian missile and drone strikes.
The company expects to record a non-cash impairment charge worth about $1 billion, according to a statement published on its official website.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The strength and resilience shown by ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih’s workforce throughout the conflict has been extraordinary,” the company’s CEO, Mauro Longobardo said, adding that “it is with deep regret that we have concluded that we are no longer able to safely operate ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih.”
The future of the plant is being discussed with Ukraine’s government, with focus on preserving the infrastructure so that the future operations can continue when Russia’s war is over.
$1 billion impairment charge
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, ArcelorMittal provided roughly $700 million in financial support to keep the subsidiary – located in President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown – running.
The impairment mainly reflects the loss in value of the unit’s property, plant and equipment.
Reuters, citing analysts at J.P. Morgan, said the impairment was not expected to affect the company’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), despite possible sectoral losses in third and fourth quarters.
Russia Is Breaking in Ways Moscow Can’t Hide Anymore
Supply disruptions at Ukrainian sites could tighten Europe’s supply of hot-rolled coil steel and support prices, the analysts added.
ArcelorMittal, Europe’s largest steel producer, operates in 60 countries and generated revenues of $61.4 billion in 2025, according to the company.
A pillar of Ukrainian steelmaking
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih is one of Ukraine’s largest steelmakers and a major foreign investment in the country. As a full-cycle producer, it mines iron ore and turns it into finished steel, specializing in long products such as rebar and wire rod.
The complex can produce more than 6 million tons (roughly 12 billion lbs) of steel, over 5 million tons (about 10 billion lbs) of rolled products and 5.5 million tons (approximately 11 billion lbs) of cast iron per year, according to Forbes Ukraine.
In 2025, the plant produced 1.7 million tons (3.4 billion lbs) of steel and 1.6 million tons (3.2 billion lbs) of rolled products, accounting for 23% of Ukraine’s steel output and 24% of its rolled steel.
That made it the country’s second-largest plant after Zaporizhstal, Forbes Ukraine reported.
The company exports mainly to the EU, the Middle East, North Africa and the US.
Last year, it generated Hr. 70.6 billion ($1.6 billion) in revenue but recorded a net loss of Hr. 8.9 billion ($199 million).
Russia’s ongoing campaign against Ukrainian industry
The company’s shutdown follows a sharp escalation of Russian attacks on Ukraine’s metallurgical sector in August.
According to Forbes Ukraine, Ukraine’s three main steel plants, which together accounted for about 90% of national steel production, have now halted operations after repeated Russian missile strikes.
In 2022, the Kryvy Rih facility suffered a major Russian missile strike that killed one employee and destroyed a section of the plant.
Overnight on Aug. 16, a Russian missile strike killed two workers and injured 13 others, while also damaging key energy and blast furnace units, forcing the plant to partially halt production.
The most recent attack, according to the company’s official website, happened on Monday, Sept. 21.
Ukrainska Pravda separately reported that Russian forces launched ballistic missiles on the Dnipropetrovsk region overnight on Sept. 21-22, with industrial facilities reportedly struck in the cities of Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad.

A grand display for Xi reveals the limits of Trump's summitry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:04:47 UTC
06:04:47 KST

A grand display for Xi reveals the limits of Trump’s summitry
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Calls for Trump to negotiate a meaningful framework on artificial intelligence fell on deaf ears.
- Trump repeatedly patted Xi on the back, a gesture considered highly inappropriate in Chinese political culture.
WASHINGTON — Expectations were low entering President Trump’s meetings with China’s leader, Xi Jinping, this week, after officials on both sides tempered hopes for a breakthrough. Yet the summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
It was a visual affair designed to project a new phase of managed competition between a prevailing superpower and a rising one — a message that Washington and Beijing are ultimately capable of responsible leadership. But even a cursory look beneath the surface revealed the challenges ahead for the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship.
Industry pleas and bipartisan calls for Trump to negotiate a meaningful framework on artificial intelligence fell on deaf ears. A trade truce between the two sides was extended for a mere two months. And Trump again warned Xi not to assist Iran as the U.S. war there continues — a warning that, so far, has gone unheeded, with millions of dollars’ worth of crucial Chinese parts reportedly arriving in Tehran by the planeload.
“The U.S.-China relationship has settled into a managed stalemate. It has stabilized at the top without stabilizing underneath,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow on China at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
Xi Jinping, president of China, issued a call from the White House on Thursday that artificial intelligence remain “under human control” as the world’s two superpowers race for technological supremacy.
“The elaborate pageantry matters precisely because there is still relatively little substantive progress to showcase,” Singleton said. “Trump appears to value the personal relationship as an end in itself. Xi treats his relationship with Trump as a means to shape U.S. choices and forestall future competitive actions.”
The summit followed a playbook from Trump that has become familiar over the last decade, placing his direct relationships at the center of diplomacy and reducing the complexities of statecraft to blunt attempts at charm.
As he did during his lavish state visit to Beijing this spring, Trump repeatedly patted Xi on the back, a gesture considered highly inappropriate in Chinese political culture that nevertheless reflected Trump’s strategic focus on personal friendship.
He toured Xi around a series of controversial renovations to the White House, including the South Lawn — now paved over with a massive helipad designed as the presidential seal — and the Rose Garden, also paved over in order for Trump to host al fresco dinner parties.
Before entering a heavily gilded Oval Office, Trump walked Xi along a renovated colonnade now adorned with gold-framed portraits of U.S. presidents. He paused at one for his predecessor, President Biden, replaced with a mocking image of an autopen, suggesting the former president was incapable of signing documents himself.
Trump patted Xi on the back once more, and the two men laughed, in a moment that generated outrage online.
“Let’s be very clear on this one point,” John Delaney, a former Democratic member of Congress, wrote on social media. “The President mocking a former President in front of the communist leader of China is the most un-American thing an American president has ever done.”
Part of the state visit included a dinner at the White House that was attended by some of the country’s most prominent tech executives, such as Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg. The tech giants’ presence at the event was notable given that there was heightened public interest in knowing how China and the United States are planning to regulate artificial intelligence.
During the visit, Xi called for artificial intelligence to remain “under human control” as the two countries race for technological advancement in the industry. Lawmakers and AI industry leaders have also called for guardrails on the nascent technology, which experts warn could soon surpass human understanding. Trump, however, has been reluctant to embrace limits on the industry, and it is unclear how much the topic was discussed while Xi was in Washington.
Xi Jinping’s remarks reflect growing concern within China over whether governments in Washington or Beijing will be able to contain a technology with potentially transformative capabilities, according to a U.S. official.
President Trump’s rare welcome of Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the airport, as well as the bilateral and cultural events the leaders attended were closely covered — and praised — by Chinese state media. Those who watched at home saw a China elevated in status.
But the visit showed a surprising alignment of visions between the U.S. and Chinese presidents, embracing fierce competition that avoids miscalculation and conflict. Both stressed the importance of dialogue, with Xi invoking the concept of the Thucydides trap, a historical paradigm that holds that rising powers inevitably clash with established ones.
“I don’t think anyone will be surprised if there are no significant agreements,” said David Ochmanek, a senior researcher at Rand. “My sense is that Xi sees little reason to compromise with us on anything right now.”
The two men are expected to meet twice more this year, alongside other world leaders, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and the Group of 20 summit in Miami.
“We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one, and should be kept within bounds,” the Chinese president said Thursday from the Cross Hall of the White House. “It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses. China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict, and no confrontation between us.
“Our two militaries should maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention,” he continued. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome.”

Britain’s rhetorical war, Zelensky’s UN crashout, deep state media exposed: RT stories that shaped the week

Britain’s rhetorical war, Zelensky’s UN crashout, deep state media exposed: RT stories that shaped the week
Britain turns up the war rhetoric
Anyone paying the slightest attention to the news this week could be convinced that the UK is preparing for a direct and imminent war with Russia. Retired generals are telling the public to get “psychologically prepared” for conflict; Labour Party thought leaders are suggesting that dissidents and Russia sympathizers be “locked up;” and former Brexit Minister Jacob Rees-Mogg is openly telling British men and women that they “may have to die” – right after calling the English a “mongrel race” with no historic claim to their own homeland.
Meanwhile, Sky News premiered the first episode of ‘The Wargame’ on Monday – a bizarre reality show in which real politicians and military chiefs game out a hypothetical Russian invasion for the cameras.
With the threat from Russia rising in the real world, a new series from Sky brings together former ministers and military chiefs to test what might happen if the UK faced an attack.
Watch the new TV Show 'Wargame' on Sky and NOW from 21 September pic.twitter.com/b9RcuqLHwF
“Britain’s elites,” RT columnist Tarik Cyril Amar concluded, “want you ready to die for a war they keep imagining.”
Talking heads on the continent were equally hysterical, with Spain’s El Mundo claiming that Russia could launch drones at France, Italy, or Spain from ships in the Mediterranean. The fact that the report cited Lithuania’s fanatically anti-Russian government – which in turn cited the CIA – should have been the first sign something was amiss.
It took Finnish President Alexander Stubb to step in as the voice of reason, stating on Wednesday that there is “no imminent military threat right now” from Russia. French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto followed suit on Thursday, with Crosetto declaring that El Mundo’s story “serves no one” and only adds “fuel on the fire.”
President Vladimir Putin has stressed that Russia has no interest in war with NATO. The UK’s escalation remains rhetorical for now: The British military is in no way prepared to wage war, and nobody in London has ordered extra forces to Eastern Europe. If war were to break out, however, it’s not clear whether the UK could count on the US to join in. As RT explored on the weekend, Europe takes on all the risks and costs of fighting Russia under NATO’s new ‘NATO 3.0’ doctrine.
UN-diplomatic behavior
For Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, this week’s UN General Assembly was an opportunity to demand more from his Western backers: more money, more weapons, and more sanctions on Russia.
Asked whether he’d travel to Moscow for peace talks, however, Zelensky said he’d only visit the Russian capital “on a f**king missile.”

In what’s become a familiar pattern, Ukrainian forces hammered Moscow with waves of attack drones on Sunday morning, before Zelensky arrived in New York to plead for a ceasefire ahead of Russia’s inevitable retaliation. Backed by 51 of its allies, Kiev demanded an “immediate and unconditional ceasefire,” which Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promptly refused.
“We are not going to have a pause in our special military operation,” Lavrov told the UN Security Council. “Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause and it wants to use it to pump the Kiev regime with weapons.”
A tale of two elections in Russia and Germany
Zelensky’s weekend drone attack, deemed “unprecedented” by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, tageted voting in Russia’s State Duma election, but it did little to suppress turnout, which hit a one-decade high of 57%. Putin’s pre-election appeal to patriotism translated into a bump in support for his United Russia party, which went from 49% to 58% of the vote, followed by the Communists and Liberal Democrats.
Curiously, as political scientist Vladimir Kornilov noted for RT, Kremlin-watchers in the West called the election “rigged,” but only after the wave of protest votes against United Russia which they had promised never materialized.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, however, suffered the full wrath of the German electorate over the weekend, as his Christian Democrats (CDU) suffered a historic loss to the right-wing AfD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and trailed the Left Party in Berlin. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a former CDU stronghold and home of ex-Chancellor Angela Merkel’s district, Merz’s party failed to meet the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
“The CDU will never again win a federal election,” AfD co-leader Alice Weidel vowed after the results came in, declaring the AfD “the new people’s party in Germany.”
Exposing the deep state media
Germany’s mainstream parties – the CDU and Social Democrats – have dominated the country’s postwar political landscape. Meanwhile, one name has dominated German media: Axel Springer.
The company bearing Springer’s name stirred some controversy on Thursday when it presented its annual award to Palantir founder Peter Thiel, a name synonymous with the rise of the Silicon Valley military-tech industrial complex. However, as RT explored in our ‘Wired for War’ series, Axel Springer and Palantir are cogs in the same machine: Both took funding from the CIA, and both serve the same globalist order.
The connections between the Western deep state and the mainstream media run deep, and it’s this murky world that RT America’s Ben Swann and independent investigative journalist Elizabeth Lane expose in their brand new series, ‘America Now: Exposing The Deep State of Media.’
Across four episodes, Swann and Lane lift the lid on NATO’s online propaganda machine, the UK’s efforts to frame dissent as disinformation, and the Ukrainian government operation recruiting US military veterans as propaganda agents.
Propaganda goes hand-in-hand with censorship, and it’s the latter field that the EU excels in. While Springer and the covert campaigns uncovered by Swann and Lane shape pro-Western narratives, Brussels uses its Digital Services Act (DSA) to force online platforms to stifle alternate viewpoints. This week, the European Commission published dozens of reports by tech firms including Meta and TikTok, detailing the censorship measures these companies are adopting in order to comply with the DSA. The reports lay bare persistent election interference, collaboration with EU-approved ‘fact-checkers’, and the removal of millions of politically-inconvenient posts.
‘Russia’s Starlink’
Ukraine’s use of SpaceX Starlink broadband service has been instrumental in keeping its forces in the fight for four years. Elon Musk’s portable Starlink terminals allow Ukrainian forces to guide drones to their targets, connect to NATO headquarters, and receive real-time updates from Palantir’s battlefield management software.
It’s an advantage that Russia has worked hard to neutralize with its own Rassvet satellite network. This week, Russian journalist Evgeny Balakin took a deep dive into the Rassvet project and discovered why the Ukrainians are desperate to destroy these satellites on the ground, before they change the balance of power in space.
What we didn’t cover: Negotiating the deepfake
Stories of corruption and graft from Ukraine are legion and unsurprising – we’ve covered a series implicating Zelensky’s inner circle in depth here – but when a video emerged purportedly showing agents with Ukraine’s Western-funded anti-corruption body, NABU, apparently seizing $140 million in cash from former defense procurement chief Arsen Zhumadilov, we took a closer look.
The video was posted on Wednesday, on what initially appeared to be the New Voice of Ukraine’s English-language website. It showed refrigerator boxes stuffed with $100 bills, with an attached note stating that they were for “the servant of the people” – a reference to Zelensky’s political party.
The New Voice of Ukraine was founded by Dragon Capital, whose CEO, Thomas Fiala, is a majority shareholder in Ukrainska Pravda. The latter publication has reported extensively on corruption in the corridors of power in Kiev, and it is believed that Fiala’s position on the board of the Association of European Business (AEB) in Ukraine offers his publications cover to run these controversial stories.
However, the website to which we traced the article carrying the cash claims was dressed-up to look like New Voice of Ukraine, but used a different URL to the actual English-language New Voice of Ukraine site. We held off, correctly, and NABU confirmed on Friday that it had not raided Zhumadilov’s office. “This video is a fake, created using AI,” the agency stated. The New Voice of Ukraine said that the video had been published on an imposter site, attributing the fake to unnamed “Russians.”
There are and will be many “State of Corruption” stories to report on, factually, as the veil is lifted on Zelensky’s regime. But as we’ve learned from the Ukrainian Defense Ministry using video game footage to fake combat victories, and from the Western politicians who fell for the ‘Ghost of Kiev’ hoax, in an era of escalating rhetoric, deep state and deep fake, always double-check your sources.

What is killing whale calves in Patagonia? bacteria under suspicion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:00:14 UTC
06:00:14 KST

Dozens of southern right whale calves have been found dead on Argentina's Patagonian coast. Scientists are probing a possible bacterial infection after an unusually deadly season.
Hundreds of southern right whale calves have died in recent months in Argentine Patagonia, in an episode that has put scientists and authorities on alert. Initial investigations point to a bacterial infection as a possible cause of an exceptionally high mortality rate this season.
Just this week, dozens of dead whale calves have appeared on beaches in the province of Chubut, in southern Argentina. Cases have been recorded since June, affecting one of this species' main breeding grounds in the South Atlantic.
"The mortality rate among calves is quite high, especially this season," explained Mariano Coscarella, a researcher at the Marine Mammals Laboratory of the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet), speaking to AFP.
Bacteria among the main hypotheses
Veterinarians are now investigating whether erysipelas, an infectious disease caused by bacteria that are often present on the skin of these mammals, could be behind the deaths.
Authorities in Chubut have indicated that initial analyses point specifically to a common marine bacterium, although the investigation remains open to establish with certainty what is causing the fatalities.
Coscarella believes that for the moment the evidence points to a natural cause, but warns that a possible influence of human activity still cannot be completely ruled out.
The provincial government says it is working together with the scientific community to determine the origin of the episode.
One of the southern right whale's main calving grounds
Puerto Madryn and the nearby Valdés Peninsula form one of the major breeding refuges for the southern right whale. Every year, large numbers of whales arrive in these waters to mate and raise their young. These cetaceans can reach around 17 metres in length and weigh about 40 tonnes as adults.
In 2025, a record 2,110 whales were counted in the area, around 800 of them juveniles. This year, the tally stands at 1,375 animals, including nearly 400 calves, according to data provided by Coscarella.
Despite the high number of deaths recorded this season, the researcher notes that the episode does not, for now, pose a medium-term threat to the region's whale population.
The species' longevity is one of the factors behind that assessment. Local authorities estimate that a southern right whale can live for around 60 years.

Houthi attack on Mecca, Medina would cross ‘red line’, Pakistan PM tells UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:59:43 UTC
05:59:43 KST

Houthi attack on Mecca, Medina would cross ‘red line’, Pakistan PM tells UN
Shehbaz Sharif speaks as Islamabad, Riyadh and Ankara army chiefs meet to discuss Mecca pact, closer military ties.
Pakistan’s prime minister has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, warning that any “threat to the sanctity” of the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina is a “red line that must never be crossed”.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Friday, Shehbaz Sharif denounced recent Houthi attacks as “deplorable”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Pakistan PM calls Houthi threats to Saudi holy sites a ‘red line’
- list 2 of 3Oil prices jump after Yemen’s Houthis claim attacks on Saudi facilities
- list 3 of 3Netanyahu’s UN belligerence wins cheers at home as world walks out
He added that an attack by the Iran-aligned Yemeni group, which Riyadh says targeted Mecca, “outraged Muslims across the globe”. The Houthis have dismissed the accusations as a “heinous lie”.
Last month, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed a trilateral defence pact, formally known as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. The pact states that an attack on any member will be treated as an attack on all. However, Islamabad and Ankara have refrained from getting involved in Riyadh’s ongoing fight with the Houthis.
The military chiefs of all three countries met in Riyadh on Friday and discussed enhancing intelligence sharing and military coordination, the Pakistani military said. The chiefs reviewed the security situation and threats facing Saudi Arabia, affirmed a commitment to collective defence and pledged to turn Mecca Agreement commitments into effective cooperation, the army added.
It is not clear what, if any, support Ankara and Islamabad may provide to Riyadh. In a written interview published by the US media outlet Newsweek on Friday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said support could include “intelligence, logistics or ammunition, with more extensive military assistance possible depending on the scale of the threat”.
Iran and Palestine
In Sharif’s UN address, he also referenced the US-Israeli war that was launched against Iran in late February, as well as Islamabad’s role as a co-mediator.
Pakistan’s efforts culminated in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, signed by Washington and Tehran, which was intended to help end the conflict.
The accord has since unravelled while regional countries push for a conclusive end to the war, which has caused a global energy crisis and exacerbated tensions across the Middle East.
“Yet amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voice for diplomacy must echo even louder and stronger,” Sharif said.
He added that the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively blockaded, and the Bab al-Mandeb waterway, which is now largely under Houthi control, are “arteries of the global economy” that should remain free and safe.
The Pakistani prime minister also denounced what he described as Israel’s “genocidal agenda” in Palestine, while condemning “Israeli aggression against Lebanon and Syria”. These were sentiments echoed earlier in the day by Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam in his UN General Assembly address.
India, Kashmir, Afghanistan
Closer to home, Sharif’s speech touched on tensions with Pakistan’s neighbours.
Criticising India, he accused New Delhi of weaponising the Indus waters, which both countries have jointly managed for more than six decades. The two neighbours heavily rely on the Himalayan river network.
Sharif warned that “any attempt to stop, impede or divert Pakistan’s share of the waters will be treated as an act of war”.
He also called for what he described as a “just and fair solution” to the Kashmir dispute, which both Pakistan and India claim in its entirety. Sharif alleged that there have been attempts to “alter the legal status” of Kashmir through demographic engineering.
Another pressing issue for Islamabad is the threat posed by the Tehrik-e-Taliban (TTP), or Pakistani Taliban. Sharif said groups operate from “sanctuaries inside Afghanistan, with the aim of destabilising Pakistan”, insisting that attacks launched from Afghanistan “must come to a grinding halt”.
This comes as the latest cross-border fighting left several Afghan Taliban fighters dead on Friday.

US Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use database to check voter citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:54:45 UTC
05:54:45 KST

The US Supreme Court has granted a Trump administration request to allow the use of a federal database to weed out potential non-citizens from the voter rolls.
A majority of the nine justices on the top court joined the unsigned opinion, providing a victory to President Donald Trump ahead of the November mid-term elections.
The three liberal justices on the conservative-dominated court dissented.
Trump has stated for years that many non-citizens vote in US elections and that mail-in ballots are vulnerable to fraud.
Friday's Supreme Court decision lifted a lower court order that had blocked the use of a Department of Homeland Security program known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) to verify the citizenship of individuals on the voter rolls.
SAVE is used to identify citizenship status to determine whether someone is eligible for benefits.
Ruling against the Trump administration in June, the lower court said, "States have partnered with the federal government to access the database and are actively removing United States citizens from voter rolls based on inaccurate information.
In its ruling, the Supreme Court said the federal government "has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters."
The lower court order blocking the use of SAVE "prevents the Federal Government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task."
“Victory for election integrity”
US Attorney General Todd Blanche welcomed the Supreme Court ruling as a "huge victory for election integrity," saying it will "allow states to clear the voter rolls of illegal voters."
Election experts, however, said the ruling is unlikely to have a major impact on the November elections because most US states ban purges of voters 90 days ahead of an election.
"Both the majority and dissent agree that this case is likely to have limited impact on the midterms," Rick Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said in a blog post.
"Compared to the recent mail-in voting case, this one is not very important substantively."
Hasen was referring to a Supreme Court decision earlier this month that blocked a Trump plan that would have restricted the use of mail-in ballots.
Trump reacted furiously to that ruling, calling it "horrible" in a Truth Social post.

Unknown

Adel Abdelrheem, Rania Abushamala
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
The Sudanese army said Friday it had seized control of Sodiri in North Kordofan state after fierce clashes with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
“Our forces liberated the city of Sodiri in North Kordofan state today after fierce battles that inflicted heavy losses in personnel and equipment on the terrorist militia,” the army said in a statement, referring to the RSF.
The announcement followed accounts from military sources who told Anadolu earlier Friday that army troops and allied forces had entered Sodiri and taken control after intense fighting with the RSF.
Sodiri has been a key RSF stronghold in northern North Kordofan. It lies near Hamrat al-Sheikh and Umm Badr, close to the borders with North Darfur to the west and West Kordofan to the south.
Army personnel and members of allied armed movements also posted videos on social media that they said were filmed inside Sodiri after its capture. The footage showed destroyed combat vehicles they said belonged to the RSF.
The RSF had not commented on the developments as of 1845GMT.
The army’s reported capture of Sodiri follows a series of advances elsewhere in North Kordofan that have increased pressure on RSF forces in the state’s far northwest, particularly around Al-Mazrub, Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Badr.
It also comes days after the army announced that it had captured 11 areas in North Kordofan, one of its largest reported advances in the state in recent weeks. On Sept. 6, the army said it had taken Hamrat al-Waz in Jabra al-Sheikh locality.
Since late July, the army has reported gaining extensive territory in North Kordofan, including the city of Bara and areas around Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Sayala. It also said it had secured the main road linking Bara to Omdurman, west of the capital, Khartoum.
Sudan’s three Kordofan states — North, West and South — have witnessed continued clashes between the army and the RSF since last October.
The war between the two sides began in April 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Tedros made the appeal at a high-level meeting on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly General Debate.
"So today, I leave you with just one request -- just one: get PABS done, as soon as possible. Please conclude the negotiation as soon as possible," he said.

Tedros said the adoption of the Pandemic Agreement was historic. "In a divided and divisive world, countries found common ground for a common purpose. You showed that multilateralism still works, and it's alive and well."
Tedros said that the Pandemic Agreement and the International Health Regulations do not infringe on national sovereignty in any way. "Although differences remain, I am confident that countries will find common ground, just as they did with the Agreement itself," he said. ■

Bahrain commits to joining US-led Falcon Strike task force, buying more air defense systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:42:50 UTC
05:42:50 KST

Rania R.a. Abushamala
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Bahrain has committed to joining the US Central Command’s Task Force Falcon Strike and purchasing additional US munitions and air defense systems, the US Embassy in Manama said Friday.
The commitment was made during a Military Consultative Committee meeting held Wednesday and Thursday co-chaired by US Deputy Assistant Defense Secretary Michael DiMino and Bahraini Defense Minister Lt. Gen. Abdullah bin Hassan Al-Nuaimi, the embassy said on US social media company X.
“Bahrain committed to join USCENTCOM’S Task Force Falcon Strike and purchase more U.S. munitions and air defense systems,” the embassy said.
The steps would strengthen Bahrain’s efforts to become “stronger, more interoperable, and more capable of providing for its own defense,” it added.
The US military’s CENTCOM announced the creation of Falcon Strike in August, describing it as the first multinational, multidomain task force for attack drones. On Aug. 13, it said US and allied personnel would operate one-way attack drones and unmanned systems in the air, on the sea surface and underwater.
Bahrain’s commitment comes amid efforts by the US and regional partners to strengthen defense coordination in the Gulf as tensions in the region rise.
Manama hosted a security dialogue involving 12 countries in July that addressed defense cooperation and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Yemen's president calls on his people to mobilise against Iran-backed Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:41:29 UTC
05:41:29 KST

Yemen's president calls on his people to mobilise against Iran-backed Houthis
Yemen’s Riyadh-based President Rashid al-Alimi on Friday called on his people to mobilise and join the armed forces while offering a general amnesty to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels who have seized swaths of Yemen's Red Sea coast and imposed a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.
The head of Yemen's governing body on Friday called for a general mobilisation to counter the Iran-backed Houthis, as the group ramps up attacks on government forces and their Saudi backer.
His call comes weeks after Yemen's fragmented government was dealt a major blow by the Houthis, who seized control of the country's entire Red Sea coast and are still fighting its forces in Yemen and attacking Saudi ships and territory.
"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilisation and national mobilisation, to rally around their armed and security forces," Rashid al-Alimi, who heads the Presidential Leadership Council and is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a speech.
Read moreSaudi Arabia says air defences intercepted Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh
Anyone defecting from the Houthis to the government side will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty, he added.
Alimi heads Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, whose forces are fighting the Houthis with air support from the kingdom.
Over the week-end, the Houthis attacked Riyadh for the first time in years, marking a major escalation.
Earlier on Friday, the military chiefs of staff of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks on how to support Riyadh as Yemen's Houthis ramp up attacks on the world's top crude exporter.
Yemen and its Saudi backer have been seeking international help to counter the Houthis, with a source from Alimi's office telling AFP earlier this week that he requested American support in a call with US President Donald Trump against the Iran-backed Houthis. But Trump did not promise military help.
The New York Times said the crown prince called Trump on Sunday "to implore him, again" to help counter the group's advances, and Axios has previously said that Trump rebuffed a similar request last week.
The Iran-backed group has escalated its attacks on the government's Saudi backer since July, ending a years-long truce and declaring a maritime blockade, hitting Saudi targets and seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast as they seek to stifle Saudi oil exports.
Yemen's civil war began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, with a Saudi-led coalition stepping in the following year to shore up the government.
The Houthis now control much of the north, Yemen's most populated areas, while the government was exiled to Aden, its self-proclaimed temporary capital.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
