BNN focus | Political scientist’s view: What is really behind Stepaņenko’s financial gifts from Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:31:36 UTC
02:31:36 KST

One of the biggest scandals of the week involved gifts received by Jūlija Stepaņenko, leader of the Sovereign Power party, from her father Sergei Fedotov, who lives in Russia and is described as a Putin supporter and supporter of the war. What is particularly notable, however, is that Stepaņenko declared a cash gift of 239,598.05 euros as early as 31 October 2022, while in January 2024 she received an apartment in Riga from her father valued at 180,000 euros. Why did the scandal and suspicions surrounding these gifts emerge only now? BNN asked Filips Rajevskis, political scientist and co-founder of Mediju tilts.
“To give credit where it is due, the Constitution Protection Bureau had already investigated this issue within the scope of its competence and informed the National Security Council and the country’s senior officials,” Rajevskis recalls, adding that the question is how the Latvian state views the situation in general.
“On the one hand, it is clear that a father can give something to his child – provide money, support the family and so on. Many people support their children’s families, and that is an area where the state should not interfere. Those are family relations,” Rajevskis says.
He stresses that the simplest tool available to change the nature of these relations in this particular case would have been sanctions.
“Suddenly, on 24 September, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs woke up, imposed sanctions on Stepaņenko’s father and placed him on Latvia’s list of undesirable persons. That, of course, is one way of stopping this flow of money into Latvia and separating the relationship between a father and his child from the relationship between a Russian citizen and a candidate for prime minister of Latvia.”
Asked why, in his view, Sergei Fedotov was only now declared persona non grata and banned from entering Latvia, given that a company under his control was already involved in producing anti-tank barriers in 2022, Rajevskis says the situation symbolically and precisely illustrates how Latvia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which is responsible for sanctions, operates.
“They notice nothing until the media or X notices it. We saw the same thing with those two sanctioned individuals who were being removed from the sanctions list – the situation had been known two weeks earlier and was being discussed in Europe. Our Ministry of Foreign Affairs heroically got involved on the final day, when we were already starting to look like a complete laughing stock.”
“Thank God the prime minister stepped in and at least tried to sort the matter out. Hopefully, he resolved it in a way that serves Latvia’s interests. But the way the foreign affairs establishment operates demonstrates blatant inconsistency, incompetence and pure politicisation of the process, which is being used for the election campaign and has nothing to do with the duties and responsibilities entrusted to the foreign affairs establishment and Foreign Minister Baiba Braže personally,” Rajevskis says.
Why did the scandal surrounding the gifts from Stepaņenko’s father emerge now rather than two or four years ago?
Rajevskis explains that when Jūlija Stepaņenko finished her term in the 13th Saeima, there was a period of political inactivity while Sovereign Power was being created.
“At that point, it was simply a relationship between a daughter and her father, and that was all. When she returned to active politics, created Sovereign Power and began actively campaigning – running in the Riga City Council election while the political force itself contested elections in various municipalities – alarm bells should have started ringing: what is going on, and why is a Russian businessman financing the chair of a Latvian political party?”
“Moreover, this is a political party that could hardly be described as having a particularly strong commitment to defending Latvia’s interests. Rather, it is a political party affiliated with Russian political interests,” Rajevskis says.
The political scientist also recalls that after the 2022 Saeima election, the parties struggled for a long time to form a government, and, according to him, this period of political uncertainty was exploited.
“What do we see as a result? While a government is being formed, a coalition is being put together and everyone is talking loudly about it, money is quietly being moved and political forces are receiving support from the Russian side,” Rajevskis says.
BNN noted that regardless of the level of support for Sovereign Power/Young Latvians, the alliance would not become part of the governing coalition. Rajevskis responded:
“They will not be in the coalition, but representation in parliament is also a very significant and serious matter that should not be underestimated. We should remember that Latvia has been represented in the European Parliament by MPs who travelled to all sorts of highly marginal and strange places while representing Latvia.”
“Every MP who has received a mandate from the people can represent Latvia in one way or another. And the mandate that Sovereign Power receives in the election will most likely be used not to represent Latvia’s interests, but under the Latvian flag.”

Suman urged district administrations to remain fully alert and not to show any negligence in view of the prevailing weather conditions. He also appealed to the public to follow advisories issued by the weather department and district administration, avoid unnecessary travel and stay away from rivers, streams and landslide-prone areas.The State Emergency Operation Centre is continuously monitoring the weather situation. In case of any emergency, people can contact the State Emergency Operation Centre at toll-free number 1070, the District Emergency Operation Centre at 1077, or emergency services at 112.

Iran offers Hormuz reopening, nuclear talks in conditional US deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:27:00 UTC
02:27:00 KST

Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations over its nuclear program within seven days if Washington lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, grants waivers for Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire extending to Lebanon.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi detailed the proposal in a private gathering on Thursday on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, according to one attendee.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute think tank, said Araghchi suggested that a speedy agreement would help U.S. President Donald Trump ahead of November's midterm elections. The arrangement would also relieve enormous economic pressure on Tehran as the U.S. piles on additional sanctions.
Iran's disruption of the strait - through which a fifth of the world's traded oil and gas transited before the war - has emerged as its main point of leverage. The effects have been felt far beyond the Middle East.
There was no immediate comment from Iran's U.N. mission or other Iranian officials. A person familiar with the matter, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations, told The Associated Press that Saudi Arabia was skeptical of the latest push for a deal.
The White House did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment on Iran’s proposal.
The proposal, conveyed to the U.S. by mediators, strongly resembles the so-called Memorandum of Understanding reached in June, but with an accelerated timetable. The earlier agreement, which called for a 60-day interim period, quickly collapsed as Iran resumed attacks on shipping in the strait.
Trump has said he is in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hard-liners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates like President Masoud Pezeshkian.
"If Trump calculates this arrangement is worthwhile and can bring political benefit before the midterms and reduce gas prices, perhaps we'll see flexibility not seen in previous weeks,” Parsi said. But he noted "deep suspicion,” especially around the prospect of Iran merely buying time to ship out more of its oil and ease its economic pain.
In the latest sign of diplomatic movement, Pezeshkian hosted the prime minister of Qatar early Friday. Qatar has been a key mediator, including during hours of indirect Iran-U.S. talks at the U.N. this week.
It was not clear how long Pezeshkian and Araghchi would stay in the U.S. after Pezeshkian addressed the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders on Wednesday, ending his speech by saying Iran remained open to diplomacy.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on the same day, said "if there’s an opportunity to exchange ideas and messages, we will.”
After multiple failed attempts at a deal, however, suspicion is high on both sides. The U.S. and Israel have attacked Iran twice while it was engaged in nuclear talks, and the U.S. and Iran accuse each other of having swiftly violated the June agreement.
"The Iranians already know that the chances of this not being accepted by Trump are much higher than the opposite,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote on X.
"They want to show that they were ready for diplomacy and that it was the United States that, for the third time, decided to attack in the middle of a diplomatic track - something that people within (Iran’s) strategic community have been anticipating over the past few days.”
The proposal would include Lebanon, where Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah have been mostly observing a ceasefire. It's not clear, however, if it would include the revived conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia, which has put even more pressure on global markets.
Iran appears to think the Houthis' newly enhanced ability to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb strait on the Red Sea - another trade chokepoint on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula - could push Trump to make a deal.
Maj. Gen. Yahya Rahim Safavi, a military adviser to Iran's new supreme leader, told state television that the Americans "face a new problem called the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.”
He added: "I think the process that is unfolding is in our favor, and the Americans will be forced to accept Iran’s conditions.”
With the Houthis' latest surge in attacks, Saudi Arabia was skeptical of Araghchi’s latest push for a deal with the U.S., according to the person familiar with the matter.
The kingdom, along with other Gulf states, had advocated over the summer for a return to negotiations, saying they could live with an agreement that gave Iran a temporary role in managing the Strait of Hormuz, the person said.
But the Saudi calculations changed as the Houthis seized Yemen’s strategic Red Sea coast from pro-government forces and a vital Saudi pipeline came under attack .
Earlier this month, Gulf leaders planned to gather in Oman to discuss an emerging agreement between Oman and Iran on the Strait of Hormuz, which runs between the two countries. But the meeting was canceled after Saudi Arabia called for amendments, only some of which were accepted by Iran, the person said.
Iran's leaders have sought to project unity, but some hard-liners want to continue or escalate the war to secure bigger U.S. concessions and have criticized Pezeshkian and Araghchi's diplomatic steps this week.
Firebrand lawmaker Ebrahim Rezaei wrote on X that merely meeting with "the aggressor enemy” showed weakness. Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a panel of Shiite clerics who appoint the supreme leader, said "there is no path other than resistance.”
The head of Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard, Brig. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, highlighted the U.N. speech by "the esteemed president” while focusing on Pezeshkian’s comments that Iran doesn’t fear war.
Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, who served as chief negotiator in earlier talks with the United States, provided a rare public acknowledgment of the internal divide.
"There is a view that speaks of war but offers no prospect or mechanism for bringing it to a powerful conclusion,” he wrote on social media. "At the opposite end is a current that makes the error of underestimating national capabilities.”
He added: "The first error keeps the country in a state of permanent crisis, while the second hands national resources and dignity over to the enemy.”

China

DAR ES SALAAM, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania has called on the international community to translate commitments into concrete action to help developing countries address the growing impacts of rising sea levels, the Vice President's Office said Friday in a statement.
Addressing a high-level United Nations General Assembly meeting on sea-level rise in New York on Thursday, Vice President Deogratius Ndejembi warned that the phenomenon is no longer a future threat but is already affecting lives, economies and ecosystems worldwide, the statement said.
According to the statement, the East African nation is particularly vulnerable because of its Indian Ocean coastline, as well as Zanzibar and other islands, where millions of people depend on fishing, tourism and trade.
Ndejembi said coastal erosion, saltwater intrusion into freshwater sources and flooding pose growing risks to communities, infrastructure and development gains.
To counter these challenges, Tanzania is actively strengthening coastal protection, restoring mangroves and other ecosystems, improving water security and implementing community-led climate adaptation measures, he said.
However, the vice president stressed that national efforts alone are insufficient, urging adequate, predictable and accessible climate finance, technology transfer, and effective early-warning systems for vulnerable developing countries.
Ndejembi reiterated Tanzania's support for the adoption of a joint declaration from the meeting, urging the world to move from commitments to measurable implementation. ■

US university ends cadaver transfers for Israeli military training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:26:00 UTC
02:26:00 KST

The University of Southern California has ended an arrangement involving the transfer of donated human cadavers for medical training provided to Israeli military personnel, according to USC's Annenberg Media.
The university concluded the agreement between its Keck School of Medicine and the U.S. Navy on Thursday, ending a program that spanned more than five years and generated more than $1 million for the university.
Officials at the medical school said the decision did not stem from recent student demonstrations sparked by media disclosures of the initiative. Instead, the school confirmed the agreement ended because the University of California San Diego (UCSD) declined to continue supplying donated bodies for the venture.
The University of California Health Communications team explained that UCSD ceased transfers because the receiving surgical skills lab failed to satisfy regulations requiring courses with human remains to take place in specialized surgical facilities. The Keck School noted that USC did not profit from the donated remains.
There was previously no indication of what purposes bodies could serve following donation, and donor families got no prior notice that their relatives' remains could be utilized by the U.S. military, according to the report.
The Greater Los Angeles Area office of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR-LA), Southern California's largest Muslim civil rights organization, welcomed the contract termination.

Ghana seeks direct currency settlement for trade with China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
01:25:47 CST
02:25:47 KST

ACCRA, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Ghanaian authorities will work with their Chinese counterparts to eliminate third-party currency settlements in transactions between Ghanaian traders and Chinese suppliers, Johnson Asiama, governor of the Bank of Ghana, has said.
Asiama said during the latest Monetary Policy Committee press briefing late Thursday that the defining structural shift, which will end the third-party currency settlement regime, is necessary to enhance Ghana-China bilateral trade, as traders seek to leverage the zero-tariff policy offered by the Chinese government to 53 African countries it has diplomatic relations with.
According to the governor, the West African country is putting measures in place to create a Ghana cedi-China RMB cross-currency settlement path between Ghana and China, as intermediary currencies create a double-conversion regime, imposing double conversion commissions on traders instead of a single payment.
Asiama said the central bank has given its blessings to the initiative by Stanbic Bank, a local subsidiary of Standard Bank of South Africa, and the Ghana Commercial Bank (GCB), Ghana's largest indigenous bank, to pilot the system of direct cross-currency settlement between Ghana and China.
The governor described China as a strategic trading partner for the West African country, adding that the Bank of Ghana would continue to engage with it on various issues of mutual interest.
"Stanbic Bank is piloting a program to ensure that importers no longer need U.S. dollars to pay for their imports from China. They can actually pay in Ghana cedis right from here," he revealed in response to a question from Xinhua.
GCB Bank PLC, Ghana's largest domestic bank by assets, is also carrying out a similar pilot project to enable Ghanaian traders to bypass third-party currencies in their trade with China, according to the governor. "So we are taking those developments very seriously, in line with the growing trade relationship with China."
In collaboration to ensure active monetary and financial support toward the success of the Chinese government's zero-tariff offer to 53 African countries, the governor said the Bank of Ghana intends to engage the People's Bank of China during the upcoming World Bank/International Monetary Fund Annual Meetings.
China is Ghana's largest trading partner, as bilateral trade grew by 19.3 percent year on year to 14.1 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, according to the Chinese Embassy to Ghana. ■

Breadcrumb
Lebanon PM stresses need to avert 'vacuum' if UN force leaves
Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam stressed at the UN Friday on the need to "avert the vacuum" that would be caused by withdrawing the UN peacekeeping mission deployed in the country's south without a viable replacement.
Under US pressure, the UN Security Council decided last month to fix December as the end of the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which has been deployed since 1978.
"What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it," Salam said in a speech to the UN General Assembly.
UNIFIL currently has 7,500 peacekeepers from around 50 countries.
They are deployed in southern Lebanon along the Blue Line, which stretches for 120 kilometers (75 miles), marking a de facto border between Lebanon and Israel.
Salam also stressed the need for Israel to fully withdraw from Lebanese territory and for Beirut to move forward in extending state authority over its entire territory, ensuring "weapons (are) held by the state alone."
Hezbollah, backed by Tehran, has so far opposed disarmament.
Lebanon and Israel concluded a framework agreement in June under US auspices, providing for the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hezbollah, but its implementation has stalled.
It is intended to end a conflict that has lasted for decades.
The UN force reported extensive Israeli military ground activities in its area of operation and repeated violations of Lebanese airspace and territorial waters, between Monday and Thursday.
The peacekeepers recorded 195 airspace violations involving Israeli drones, fighter aircrafts and helicopters, according to UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric.

Ukraine develops ground robot for operations behind Russian lines – video, photo
The Ukrainian military has developed the Desantnyk ground robotic system and a system for dropping it from a heavy bomber drone.
Source: press service for Brave1, a Ukrainian defence-tech cluster, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The ground robotic system was created by fighters from the Alter Ego Battalion of the 93rd Separate Mechanised Brigade. The technology allows the ground robot to be deployed tens of kilometres from the line of contact using an unmanned aerial vehicle.
"Systems in which one drone delivers another to an area of operations are called marsupials. Similar solutions were developed in the US more than 30 years ago, but were never brought into combat use," the cluster explained.
In addition to the Desantnyk ground robotic system, the unit also developed a solution for dropping it accurately from a bomber drone. According to Brave1, just 10 days passed from the idea to its combat deployment.
"The Desantnyk already has confirmed strikes to its name. In particular, enemy shelters and personnel have been destroyed," the press service said.
The Desantnyk ground robotic system and its testing. Video: Brave1
The defence cluster has now helped the military find a manufacturer so that the Desantnyk can move from prototypes to mass production.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainian forces deployed ground robotic systems behind Russian lines during Operation Vivaldi in northern Donetsk Oblast. The manoeuvre enabled the defence forces to liberate two villages and clear another one.
- The troops used heavy bomber drones to deliver kamikaze ground robotic systems behind Russian lines. The ground robots were deployed more than 10 km behind Russian positions.

Indonesia commissions 1st aircraft carrier

Saadet Gökce
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Indonesia on Thursday commissioned its first aircraft carrier, KRI Sriwijaya-100, into the Navy at Tanjung Priok Port in North Jakarta, according to Jakarta Globe.
The vessel, formerly the Italian Navy’s Giuseppe Garibaldi, was formally inducted after being acquired by Indonesia. Italy retired the ship in 2024 after more than four decades of service.
Col. Mochamad Fuad Hasan was formally appointed commander of the vessel.
The 180.2-meter-long (591-foot-long) vessel has a displacement of about 13,850 tons and a flight deck capable of operating helicopters and short-takeoff and vertical-landing aircraft.
Navy Chief of Staff Adm. Muhammad Ali said Indonesia is training pilots to operate S-70 helicopters from KRI Sriwijaya-100.
The Navy hopes eventually to equip the carrier with vertical-takeoff combat aircraft, although no acquisition has been announced. The ship previously operated AV-8B Harrier II jets with the Italian Navy.
KRI Sriwijaya-100 will also serve as a maritime command platform and support disaster response, humanitarian aid and efforts to combat forest and land fires.

U.S. appeals court upholds Pentagon designation of Anthropic as supply chain risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:19:19 UTC
02:19:19 KST

A federal appeals court panel in Washington, D.C., on Friday upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic, dealing a blow to the artificial intelligence company in its months-long battle with the Trump administration.
The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional.
"The Department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the Department's information systems, by the Department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered national-security risk," Judge Gregory Katsas wrote in the majority opinion for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, which Judge Neomi Rao joined. Katsas and Rao were appointed by President Donald Trump.
Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson, who was appointed by former President George H.W. Bush, dissented.
In March, the DOD labeled Anthropic a supply chain risk, meaning the company purportedly threatened U.S. national security, after negotiations about how the military could use its Claude AI models spiraled out of control. The designation prevents the U.S. military from using Anthropic's models and blocks defense contractors from using them in their work with the agency.
Anthropic's relationship with the Trump administration has been fraught ever since, and Trump has repeatedly slammed company's CEO Dario Amodei on social media. Amodei recently drew Trump's ire by calling for an industry wide slowdown, and he was not invited to the glitzy state dinner the White House hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
"The Trump Administration has stopped AI "people" from doing bad, or potentially bad, "things," like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a "perfect little angel" - and we will continue to do so!," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Monday.
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in U.S. District Court in San Francisco and in the D.C. Circuit Appeals Court in March, seeking to reverse its blacklisting. The DOD relied on two distinct designations to justify its supply chain risk action, which meant they had to be litigated in two separate courts.
A San Francisco federal judge ruled last month that one designation was illegal. The ruling Friday by the D.C. appeals court upheld the second designation.
"We respectfully disagree with the court's decision," an Anthropic spokesperson told CNBC in a statement. "Another federal court has already held the government's parallel designation unlawful. We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review."
The appellate panel said it would delay the decision from taking immediate effect to give Anthropic time to petition the same panel for a rehearing or to seek an en banc rehearing of the case, by all of the judges on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals. Anthropic could also ask the Supreme Court to take the case.
Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed.
The DOD wanted Anthropic to grant the military unfettered access to its models across all lawful purposes, while Anthropic wanted assurance that its technology would not be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance. They were unable to come to an agreement, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of attempting to "to seize veto power over the operational decisions of the United States military."
Katsas said Friday that Hegseth raised the "deeply sobering" idea that "overly constrained" AI models could shut down unexpectedly, as well as the potential that Claude might be "subject to manipulation." While Anthropic refuted those claims, Katsas said decision-making authority ultimately rests with Trump and Hegseth.
"In our Republic, it is the President and the Secretary of War who must determine how best to balance the competing risks," Katsas wrote. "In doing so here, the Secretary did not transgress any limits on his authority under the Supply Chain Security Act or the Constitution."

“Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore,” he said. “People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it.”

Ukraine is trading access to 5 million frames of real combat for British AI technology: they use the data inside locked platform

Ukraine is opening its battlefield data to British weapons makers so they can train their AI on a war no one else has fought. Up to 12 British defense companies will join Avengers Labs, Ukraine's platform for training AI models for drones and robots on real combat data, the Defense Ministry said.
Ukraine's combat data is a resource no other military has access to. British firms get to build and test their AI on battlefield data they could not access elsewhere, while Ukraine gets their technology and joint development of AI for unmanned systems.
What is Avengers Labs?
More than 30 Ukrainian companies already use the Avengers Labs, and three of their systems have reached the battlefield. It is part of the AI push former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov built around Ukraine's data.
The terms are built around control. The British companies can develop and test their own AI models within Avengers Labs, the ministry said, but the data remains within the platform's protected environment, with no way to download it or take it out. That lets Ukraine share the value of its war experience, the annotated record of real combat, without surrendering the record itself.
The platform was developed by the Center for Innovation and Development of Defense Technologies, the team that created the DELTA combat system. At the core of Avengers Labs is an annotated dataset of 5 million frames collected on the battlefield. Most of this material comes directly from the DELTA combat system and is continually supplemented with new data of practical value in combat conditions.
Britain trains for a real war
In March 2026, Ukraine announced the establishment of a system of military technology competence centers. The first in the network was intended to be the Defense AI Center "A1," which would focus on AI solutions.
The AI center is being launched with support from the UK. Its main tasks were planned to be:
analysis of combat data;
forecasting enemy actions;
development of autonomous systems;
new management/control tools
A separate center was said to have been established for each key direction of the war: drones, mid-range strike, deep strike, artillery, and others.

Details
David Beckham received dividends of $51 million (£39 million) from his business empire following a series of brand deals connected with the FIFA World Cup

DRJB Holdings, which consists of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, covering most of his partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss, paid shareholders $51.1 million last year, compared with $53 million the previous year.
The former England captain, who ended his professional football career in 2013, sold a 55% stake in his businesses to the US group Authentic Brands for £200 million in 2022, meaning that he received 45% of the total dividend payout for the past year.

The Oligarch Part 4: This man made billions in Ukraine, befriended Soros – and bought a place at the West’s table

The Oligarch Part 4: This man made billions in Ukraine, befriended Soros – and bought a place at the West’s table
Late August brought news that the Victor Pinchuk Foundation is partnering with America’s prestigious Yale University to launch an international leadership development program for Ukrainian veterans of the NATO proxy war against Russia. Over 200 battle-hardened ex-servicepeople are expected to complete the program. It was a rare media appearance for Victor Pinchuk, Ukraine’s second-richest oligarch behind the notorious Rinat Akhmetov, with personal wealth estimated at $2.8 billion. Pinchuk has remained largely in the shadows throughout the proxy war. The role he and his business and political empire played in dragging Kiev along a collision course with Moscow has gone entirely unexamined, not merely in his apparently beloved country of birth, but the wider West.
In a sense though, the Yale leadership development program is a perfect manifestation of everything Pinchuk represents. Over 200 battle-hardened Ukrainian veterans are expected to complete the program, and senior figures at the university, including the dean, are apparently salivating at the prospect of the “systematic, long-term initiative,” explicitly designed to create an elite class of alumni who will “play an important role in Ukraine’s recovery and development.” Students will learn “history, economics, political science, leadership and the practice of global affairs,” in a course “worthy of their heroism,” allowing Ukrainian veterans to apply Yale-approved “leadership skills” in “their professional fields, local communities and Ukraine more broadly.”
Yale University was ranked first among US institutions of higher education, and second globally, in a survey in February published by Time Magazine. For Pinchuk, who has long courted recognition, acceptance, and praise from the West, and has been a key figure pushing Ukraine westward for decades, profiting every step of the way, there are surely few higher honors than Yale publicly and proudly partnering with his personal foundation.
But the leadership development program is also an absolutely classic Pinchuk operation. He pioneered a tactic known as “invisible appointments.” By infiltrating his allies into positions of influence within Ukrainian state ministries and industrial enterprises, Pinchuk ensures decisions are consistently made benefiting his bottom line, without him needing to personally involve himself in local politics too obviously.
As RT’s The Oligarch series has shown, historically, it doesn’t pay for Ukraine’s ultra-wealthy classes to take sides, and the West’s proxy war on Russia has imposed ever-stricter and constantly changing ‘rules’ by which they are expected to play. If they don’t fall foul of the US-funded National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), the troubled administration of Vladimir Zelensky could turn on them at any moment – whether for political reasons, or personal enrichment. The Yale University program not only represents a pipeline of fearsome future Ukrainian leaders who owe a personal debt to Pinchuk and can become “invisible appointments” in the future, it also promotes his personal brand in the US, right when the extremist regime he helped install is facing collapse.
How did Pinchuk get so filthy rich?
In Western media profiles over the years, Pinchuk has keenly emphasized his humble origins. Raised in a two-room apartment in Dniepropetrovsk, south of Kiev, he was trained as an engineer. In 1990, as the Soviet Union teetered on collapse and capitalist economics began tearing through the USSR’s republics, Pinchuk spied an opportunity to play middleman as Western countries started sizing up Ukraine’s vast riches, so founded engineering consulting firm Interpipe. Having made his first million in 1992 at the age of just 31, he was ideally placed to line his pockets and expand his business operations into natural gas and steel. Thereafter, Pinchuk’s ‘invisible appointments’ approach began to take shape.
Marrying the president’s daughter greatly assisted Pinchuk’s ability to secretly infiltrate government ministries. In 1997, he left his wife to begin dating Elena Kuchma, the daughter of Leonid Kuchma, who led Ukraine from July 1994 to January 2005. Almost immediately, rumors began circulating in the country and wider region that Pinchuk was receiving privileged access to deals, completely unavailable to people unconnected to the Kuchma dynasty. He even became an MP in 1998, a position he held for almost a decade. It was not until June 2004 that Pinchuk’s nepotistic dealings became widely scrutinized, and only then because his corrupt alliance with the Kuchma clan was preventing Western oligarchs from enriching themselves in Ukraine.
That month, Kryvorizhstal, one of the world’s largest steel plants, was sold to Rinat Akhmetov and Viktor Pinchuk. Despite their bid being half that offered by an international consortium led by US Steel, the terms were rigged to ensure only local, well-connected oligarchs could profit. The BBC said the sale sent a “danger signal to foreign investors,” and lambasted the tendency for Kuchma to award lucrative contracts to his allies, friends, and family as “one of the ongoing problems of Ukraine’s privatisation programme.” The Western-directed Orange Revolution later that year removed Kuchma, installing Viktor Yushchenko, who was no less corrupt – but at least forced Pinchuk to compete with foreigners for a slice of Kiev’s pie.
What doesn’t Pinchuk like to talk about publicly?
Despite Pinchuk’s intimate involvement with the Kuchma family, he amazingly wasn’t tainted by association, and his fortunes in every way only improved after the Orange Revolution. Never have questions been asked about whether criminal methods other than nepotism assisted his success. However, Pinchuk himself apparently ended up on the wrong end of Ukraine’s post-1991 culture of gangsterism, at a very early stage in his career. Oligarchs flourish in an environment attaching local organized crime politicians and big business at the hip. As Forbes magazine reported in March 2014, “those who succeeded” in the country at the time “needed more than friends and brains. They needed survival skills.”
Pinchuk was kidnapped in 1996 by people he’d never seen before, who arrived at his mother’s house to celebrate her 60th birthday, before handcuffing and black bagging him at gunpoint. He was held for two days, then released after negotiating to pay $2 million for his freedom. Pinchuk refused to offer details of his ordeal beyond “I stayed alive” to Forbes, pleading “I still can’t talk about this.” To get and stay rich in Ukraine then as now required oligarchs to invest in personal security apparatuses, often in conjunction with local mafia elements and crooked intelligence agents and police old and new.
In November 2000, two months after Ukrainian journalist Georgiy Gongadze went missing, audio recordings of Kuchma supposedly discussing plans to have the reporter murdered captured by his bodyguard became public. Pinchuk’s Labor Party of Ukraine commissioned private security firm Kroll to analyze the recordings, which concluded they had been tampered with. Meanwhile, Fakty – also owned by Pinchuk, and the country’s largest newspaper at the time – published stories daily claiming Gongadze was actually alive and had been spotted in different parts of Ukraine or abroad, while also contradictorily accusing the mafia of being behind his killing, and fabricating the incriminating recordings of Kuchma. In truth, Gongadze was dead, and his murder remains officially unsolved today.
Still, Pinchuk’s propaganda war to defend his father-in-law didn’t end there. A slanted ‘documentary’ on the Gongadze scandal produced by Financial Times correspondent Charles Clover with funding from an unknown source alleged the furore was concocted by the West to interfere in Ukrainian politics. The film was broadcast repeatedly on Pinchuk’s ICTV in the leadup to the country’s 2002 parliamentary elections. In 2015 though, the oligarch was quick to accuse his rival, Igor Kolomoisky, of murders in a costly UK High Court legal battle over a disputed business deal. Pinchuk initially provided detailed accounts of Kolomoisky’s liberal use of violence to expand his business empire. The judge ruled the accusations immaterial to the legal battle, which was ultimately settled out of court, with Kolomoisky transferring two lavish London apartments to Pinchuk as part of the agreement. Clearly, at the very least, Pinchuk knows where certain bodies are buried.
What is the nature of Pinchuk’s relationship with George Soros?
Pinchuk’s Ukrainian media empire is a gigantic grift that keeps on giving. His ICTV dominates the news landscape, while also reeling in casual viewers with movies and TV dramas. Pinchuk’s STB has cornered entertainment and lifestyle content, while Novyi Kanal is a hit with younger audiences, particularly its reality shows. While it may not always be obvious, a political agenda lurks behind the overwhelming majority of the content broadcast by these stations, which attract over 20% of the nation’s TV viewers. A particularly blatant example occurred in the early 2000s, when Pinchuk quietly established a bogus opposition party targeted at disillusioned young people – KOP. His TV networks aggressively promoted the party as an organic, grassroots, patriotic uprising.
This not only took the form of fake news reports, but slick ads hyping KOP’s supposed ‘cool’ factor, and an interactive reality show broadcast on both ICTV and STB. In it, average Ukrainian citizens competed to win a place running for the party in parliament. KOP and other fake opposition infrastructure funded by Pinchuk collapsed in the wake of the Orange Revolution, which also placed some of the oligarch’s local business interests at risk. No matter. Pinchuk simply moved assets abroad, headquartering his empire in the UK under the name EastOne, and increasing his ‘philanthropic’ investments alongside Western foundations. On top of a hedge against rising anger at oligarchs such as himself at home, the time had come for Pinchuk to leverage his wealth to command global geopolitical influence.
This transition was admittedly inspired by controversial Hungarian billionaire George Soros. The two became close personal friends in the 2000s, their respective foundations often co-funding projects in Ukraine and beyond. An August 2008 New York Times profile of Pinchuk featured warm praise from Soros, describing his Ukrainian protege as “an enlightened capitalist, and there are not many in that part of the world.” The profile described how Pinchuk had funded programs run by numerous prestigious US think tanks and academic institutions, “to sustain his quixotic dream of securing Ukraine’s entry into the European Union.” Pinchuk’s famous pals, including President Bill Clinton and UK Prime Minister Tony Blair, were “lured… to give speeches… to support the cause.”
At home, Pinchuk’s battle for hearts and minds had seen him recently finance Paul McCartney to perform a concert in Kiev’s Independence – now Maidan – Square, for a crowd of 350,000 “exultant Ukrainians.” Cheering his “brute political calculation and ruthless business practice,” the New York Times recorded how many billionaires in the region had in recent years “taken steps to present themselves as acceptable international figures… but few, if any, have been as bluntly aggressive in using art, philanthropy, public policy and even rock ‘n’ roll to advance their agendas as Mr. Pinchuk.” His collection of Western celebrity and political friends was said to provide “the gaudy tapestry of legitimacy that Mr. Pinchuk so badly craves.”
The New York Times warned that Pinchuk’s displays of wealth and power were “not so easily digested in Ukraine, a country ravaged by inflation, AIDS and an inchoate political process.” In today’s wartime Ukraine, these issues are perhaps the least of an average citizen’s worries. But while Pinchuk has by-and-large vanished from the public eye today, his political protection has only grown. Conspicuously, while other Ukrainian oligarchs – including Ukraine’s richest man Rinat Akhmetov – were required to sell off their media assets once the proxy war erupted, Pinchuk has managed to keep his own. Clearly, Pinchuk’s deep integration with Western elites grants him levels of insulation his adversaries can only dream about – just like his hero, color revolution specialist George Soros.
How does Pinchuk get away with it all?
Despite his longstanding and highly rewarding policy of avoiding overt political involvement, in December 2016, Pinchuk made a highly public intervention in Ukrainian – and global – affairs. He authored an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal, outlining how his country “must make painful compromises for peace with Russia,” in reference to the brutal Anti-Terrorist Operation waged by Kiev against the defenseless citizens of Donbass. Pinchuk proposed that peace could be achieved by Ukraine; “temporarily eliminating European Union membership from our stated goals”; recognizing locally-organized elections in Donbass; understanding “Ukraine will not join NATO in the near- or midterm,” pursuing “an alternative security arrangement” to NATO, and accepting neutrality “as our near-term vision for the future.” Quite reasonable suggestions, one might think – and a clear blueprint for a brighter, more peaceful future for Ukraine.
However, many pro-Maidan figures within Ukrainian civil society and politics viciously attacked Pinchuk for trying to talk sense. Among them was Mustafa Nayyem, a veteran reporter at Western-funded media outlets who personally kickstarted the Maidan protests in late 2013. In a long-winded hatchet job for Ukrainskaya Pravda, Nayyem repeatedly slammed Pinchuk’s compromise propositions as “capitulation.” When Zelensky won Ukraine’s 2019 presidential election on a platform of implementing more or less what Pinchuk advocated three years prior, Nayyem’s retort to the oligarch’s prescriptions gifted hardline Ukrainian ultranationalists – including the Neo-Nazi Azov Battalion – a campaign slogan to ensure there would be no peace in Donbass.
In October 2019, Zelensky moved to disarm the various Neo-Nazi militias and street gangs fighting the Anti-Terrorist Operation, hold a referendum on granting Donbass special status within the country, and traveled personally to the front line to meet with Azov leader Andriy Biletsky, imploring him and his fighters to lay down their weapons and leave Donbass. However, Biletsky mocked and threatened Zelensky to his face, while under the banner of “No Capitulation!” Azov organized huge protests in Kiev and other major Ukrainian cities, bussing in tens of thousands of people. Peace was comprehensively off the table. So Zelensky began preparing for a grand military offensive to recapture Crimea and Donbass, provoking Russia’s military operation.
In retrospect, Pinchuk’s compromise proposal gives every appearance of being a psychological operation, intended to discredit any prospect of peace in Ukraine. His trial balloon granted ultranationalist Maidan elements within the country a straw man to publicly immolate, so any suggestion of conciliation with Donbass, let alone Russia, could appear deeply unpopular among average Ukrainians, and the determination of Azov Battalion and other ultraviolent factions to fight on could be presented as organic and principled. This interpretation is greatly reinforced by a March 2020 joint letter signed by two dozen Ukrainian NGOs, almost all funded by Western governments and foundations, condemning any direct dialogue between Kiev and the People’s Republics of Donetsk and Lugansk.
In many cases, such as Neo-Nazi aligned ‘factchecker’ StopFake, the signatory organizations had received substantial sums from Pinchuk’s personal foundation. Never forget, the oligarch is a master of theater and misdirection. Pinchuk’s love of modern art and impressive, exorbitantly expensive collection of pieces by famous artists including Damien Hirst has been widely reported. In June 2022, Pinchuk sold a balloon sculpture created by Jeff Koons at auction, raising over $10 million for humanitarian aid to Ukraine. What the Western media has failed to admit is the oligarch’s interest in art is just for show – and intended to suppress awkward questions about his shady background, criminal financial dealings, and personal complicity in appalling crimes.
How does Pinchuk use art for image management?
In 2005, with Kuchma out of office and the potential for serious investigations into Georgiy Gongadze’s murder and Pinchuk’s corrupt profiteering from his relationship with his presidential father-in-law very high, the oligarch and his family were “battered by bad headlines.” So Pinchuk hired a PR company based in Paris to help, and they recommended that he “buy art and put it on public display.” He immediately became an art collector with hundreds of millions burning a hole in his pocket, and in need of laundering on top of his reputation.
“Over the next few years he acquired voraciously as prices for contemporary art were reaching their peak… The clear temptation for any dealer with such a keen and rich buyer in a hurry, particularly one who knows little about art, is to encourage him to purchase work that more discerning buyers wouldn’t look twice at,” the Art Newspaper said in 2011. “Rarely has so much money been spent so quickly on so much bad art.”
Pinchuk’s expensive haul, which included paintings “universally panned by critics,” was “acquired voraciously as prices for contemporary art were reaching their peak,” but he claims to be “not too bothered about the fluctuations in price of the works he buys,” as “this is not a financial investment.” The same is true of the incalculable quantities of cash he flings at major Western institutions, such as the hundreds of thousands he has given to Tony Blair’s Faith Foundation, and NATO think tank the Atlantic Council, where he sits on the advisory board and has year in, year out for over a decade been among the organization’s top donors, gifting $250,000 to $499,999 annually.
Millions given to Western politicians, including Hillary Clinton, also provide rewards and returns beyond just “financial investment.” Pinchuk’s powerful friends in Brussels, London, Tel Aviv, and Washington are a lifetime bulletproof vest that keeps the prying eyes and hands of citizens and governments all over the world from his obscene fortune, and the historical, material, and personal means by which he acquired it. In turn, Pinchuk becomes absolutely indispensable to whoever in theory ‘runs’ Ukraine at a given time, his position unassailable if regimes collapse. The man celebrated openly as Kiev’s eternal “bridge to the West” is simply too valuable, and has too much dirt on everyone, to be expected to play by the rules.

A War Criminal’s Fiction to Empty Seats

A War Criminal’s Fiction to Empty Seats
From 77 delegations walking out inside to a mass protest outside, Netanyahu faces overwhelming rejection
TEHRAN — On September 24, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stood at the United Nations General Assembly rostrum facing hundreds of vacant seats. As his name was announced, 77 diplomatic delegations stood up and walked out of the hall in a coordinated repudiation of Israel’s genocidal campaign against Gaza and the war against Iran, as well as other regional campaigns of aggression.
The exodus left vast blocks of the chamber completely empty. Remaining audience members in the gallery shouted in Hebrew while General Assembly leadership repeatedly struck the gavel for order. Netanyahu opened his speech by calling those who left “moral cowards.”
Empty seats speaking volumes
The Palestinian Mission to the UN had requested member nations to fill their seats before the session and exit en masse once Netanyahu approached the podium.
Dozens of states answered the call, including Iran, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, Turkey, Qatar, Indonesia, Malaysia, South Africa, Brazil, Spain, Ireland, and Slovenia.
The Iranian delegation left a framed photograph of the martyred General Qassem Soleimani on its empty desk before exiting. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei noted that the gesture served as a quiet reminder of martyrs who continue to haunt their adversaries.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi stated that the walkout spoke louder than any speech delivered at the rostrum.
Netanyahu tried to brush aside the walkout, claiming foreign leaders whose representatives exited had privately thanked Israel for joint strikes with the United States against Iranian nuclear sites. As usual, he provided no evidence.
The following day, Iranian counselor Nasser Asadi delivered a formal right of reply, described Netanyahu’s presence an utter disgrace and a betrayal of the UN Charter.
He asked why the General Assembly, which barred apartheid South Africa in the 1970s, granted a platform to a leader facing International Criminal Court arrest warrants for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
Asadi cited UN figures showing Israel dropped over 200,000 tons of explosives on Gaza, equivalent to 13 Hiroshima-scale nuclear bombs, while noting Netanyahu admitted to tens of thousands of Palestinian casualties.
Dissecting the claims
Netanyahu spent a significant portion of his address attempting to refute international charges.
He labeled accusations of genocide “the greatest lie of the century” and insisted Israel had actually “prevented genocide.” He also claimed that the Israeli military is “the most moral army in the world.” To support his argument, he cited the delivery of two million tons of food, one million polio vaccinations, and millions of warning text messages sent to civilians.
That defense collapses when examined against international legal frameworks and independent documentation.
Independent UN commissions and the International Association of Genocide Scholars have concluded that the pattern of operations in Gaza meets the legal threshold for genocide.
Regulating minimal humanitarian supply deliveries while maintaining horrendous siege conditions, widespread bombardment, and the destruction of medical infrastructure demonstrates direct control over civilian survival.
Moving some civilians via text messages offers no protection when designated destination zones lack basic shelter, water, and security.
Netanyahu also attempted to minimize rising violence by Israeli forces and settlers in the occupied West Bank. He described the perpetrators as “a handful of juvenile delinquents, numbering around 150,” who throw stones or chop down olive trees, claiming the annual death toll was “two or three.”
UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) data directly contradicts those claims. By July 2026, settler attacks had killed at least 18 Palestinians that year.
UN OCHA recorded over 1,600 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage through September 2026, averaging more than six attacks per day.
Rights groups have reported a conviction rate of just 3 percent for settler violence, proving systemic impunity.
Stunts and public attacks
The address also functioned as a domestic campaign speech ahead of upcoming Israeli elections rather than a diplomatic initiative.
Netanyahu attacked various international figures, calling Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a tyrant, accusing Qatar of funding global anti-Israel campaigns, and condemning New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
He accused Mamdani of making New York “unsafe for Jews.” Mamdani responded that Netanyahu used the UN podium to repeat baseless lies to sanitize genocide, emphasizing that no rhetoric changes the reality of the ICC warrant.
Qatar similarly rejected the accusations, stating that shifting global public opinion stems from citizens witnessing real-time destruction on the ground rather than external influence campaigns.
In a widely mocked stunt, Netanyahu displayed a Starlink satellite device at the podium. He held up the satellite dish, saying Starlink “allows people to access truth, to exercise choice, to exercise freedom of thought and freedom of speech.”
The gesture rang hollow. Israel has spent years systematically blacking out Gaza’s communications, cutting electricity and internet while barring independent foreign reporters from the Strip.
The Committee to Protect Journalists recorded that Israeli forces killed more than 260 journalists and media workers across West Asia since October 2023, more than 191 of them Palestinians in Gaza alone, making Israel responsible for more journalist deaths than any regime or government CPJ has recorded since 1992.
CPJ data show Israel responsible for two-thirds of the record 129 press deaths worldwide in 2025 and the bulk of confirmed targeted murders of journalists in recent years. No other military comes close.
At the same time, Israel has poured more than a billion dollars into manipulative hasbara influence operations since late 2023, funding U.S. lobbying firms, conservative influencers, evangelical outreach, social-media amplification and efforts to shape AI responses, all aimed at managing Western opinion while the cameras stay out of Gaza.
Following the speech, Israeli Ambassador Danny Danon approached Iranian diplomat Nasser Asadi to hand over the terminal while making comments about regime change. Asadi looked away and refused to engage.
Hafez Hakami, Iran’s Deputy Minister at the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology, addressed the Starlink provocation directly: “The weaponization of technology has reached a new record — now the butcher of Gaza is promoting Starlink! Starlink now faces its toughest reputational test: being publicly championed by those behind the Gaza catastrophe. Communication networks must remain neutral - serving civilians, never a tool of war or terror.”
Mass arrests on First Avenue
While Netanyahu spoke inside, civil unrest filled the streets of Manhattan.
Organizers from Jewish Voice for Peace staged a sit-in on First Avenue outside UN headquarters. Roughly 200 protesters wearing matching white shirts reading “Fund people not bombs” blocked traffic while chanting against military aid to Israel.
New York police arrested 103 demonstrators, including Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon, actor Hannah Einbinder, City Council member Chi Osse, and congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier.
The contrast was stark. Outside, peaceful protesters were handcuffed for opposing war crimes. Inside, a leader wanted by international courts used the UN rostrum to justify military aggression, greeted only by row after row of vacant desks.

Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:12:00 UTC
02:12:00 KST

Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 25 - Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until “all of Iran’s conditions are met” by the United States.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Thursday.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
In a meeting with journalists on Thursday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said he hoped a deal with Washington to end the hostilities could be reached before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Tehran said it would be prepared to engage in detailed negotiations over its nuclear program only after its conditions are met by the US.
But the official said Iran would give no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands.
Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the US attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.
Iranian authorities have said that Iran could agree to dilute its most highly enriched uranium.
In May, Reuters reported that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a directive that the country's HEU should not be sent abroad, according to two senior Iranian sources. REUTERS

EU releases €6.6 billion for members arming Ukraine as seven killed in Kyiv
European Union countries have agreed to release €6.6 billion from a fund meant to reimburse member states that have provided arms to Ukraine, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Friday. At least seven people were killed in Russian strikes on Kyiv earlier in the day, according to local authorities.
European Union countries have agreed to release €6.6 billion from a fund to reimburse member states for arms supplied to Ukraine, the bloc's top diplomat said Friday.
EU states have been waiting for years for reimbursement under the bloc's European Peace Facility fund, with the payments vetoed by the former pro-Russian government in Hungary.
Budapest changed tack after Peter Magyar replaced Viktor Orban as prime minister in April, and EU capitals have been discussing how to use the money since.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday that €4.7 billion would go to reimburse member states – and some have already said they would use their shares to help Ukraine fight Russia.
Some €900 million will fund the EU-led training mission for Ukrainian forces and €1 billion will fund new joint procurement of equipment, Kallas said.
"Moscow's hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite," she said on social media.

‘NAZA’ trailer appears on YouTube ahead of New York premiere
The Gaza war documentary heads to the New York Film Festival as the Israeli-American Council plans a gathering outside the screening
A trailer for “NAZA,” the Gaza war documentary that drew sharp criticism from Israeli officials, appeared on YouTube ahead of its North American premiere at New York’s Lincoln Center on Saturday.
The trailer features silhouetted interviewees discussing anticipated civilian deaths in airstrikes. One describes “a factory of targets,” while another alleges that “there was approval once to kill 500.” A speaker also recalls people saying after October 7 that “there are no innocent people in Gaza.”
The film, directed by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, will screen as part of the New York Film Festival’s main slate at 3:30 p.m., with another showing scheduled for Sunday at noon. It won the special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month.
The Israeli-American Council announced a gathering outside Lincoln Center during Saturday’s screening. Organizers said mobile screens would show “October 7: Bearing Witness to the Massacre” to challenge the documentary’s narrative and draw attention to the Hamas-led attack.
Filmed at night on Tel Aviv rooftops, “NAZA” features anonymous interviews with 24 people presented as Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel. They describe surveillance and targeting procedures and allege that strikes were approved despite expectations of extensive civilian casualties. The title comes from a Hebrew military acronym for “collateral damage.”
The IDF rejected the allegations and questioned whether the interviewees had access to the information they discussed. It said the military operated under the laws of armed conflict, took measures to minimize civilian harm and used human personnel to select and approve strikes.
Abraham said the filmmakers verified and cross-checked the accounts. He also said the documentary would be made available online for free, with a release planned for November, and had been offered to Israeli cinemas at no charge.

Europe injects 46 bcm of gas into UGS facilities ahead of winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:07:42 UTC
02:07:42 KST

MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Net gas injection (the net difference between injection and withdrawal volumes) by EU countries into underground gas storage (UGS) facilities has exceeded 46 bln cubic meters (bcm) since the beginning of the summer season in April 2026, according to TASS calculations based on Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) data.
To date, Europe has managed to inject 68% of gas required for the upcoming winter into its UGS facilities. As of September 23, Europe’s UGS facilities were 70.35% full (15.68 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 82% in the previous year, which is the lowest level recorded for this date since tracking began in 2011. EU storage facilities hold around 77 bln cubic meters of gas, which is 13.3 bln cubic meters lower than last year’s levels and the lowest volume since 2013.
The European Commission requests EU members to make sure their UGS facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 of each year. Moreover, 10% flexibility is allowed in the event of difficult UGS filling conditions. Thus, net injection into European storage facilities by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter period must reach at least 68 bcm to meet the filling standard.

From “Explosion” to “Obsession” – meet jewellery designer Bogdana Topreva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:04:11 UTC
02:04:11 KST

Author
Diana Tsankova
News
From “Explosion” to “Obsession” – meet jewellery designer Bogdana Topreva
“I believe artists are touched by God, and I’m grateful to feel that touch,” she says as she presents a retrospective exhibition in Sofia
Friday 25 September 2026 19:10
Friday, 25 September 2026, 19:10
PHOTO Diana Tsankova
Font size
There are many ways to say something about who we are and what our place in the world is.
For Bogdana Topreva, jewellery is one of them. Her retrospective exhibition “Obsession”, at the Sofia Press Gallery and Bookshop, traces three decades in which jewellery has become much more than an adornment of the body – carrying memories, ideas and a sense of where we stand in the world.
“I really do feel obsessed with jewellery, but in a positive sense,” the artist says of the exhibition’s title. And in this anniversary year, she admits that her own approach has changed:
“At the beginning of my creative journey, I was much freer. Maybe that’s typical when you’re younger – you throw yourself into things with much more enthusiasm, without thinking about the consequences or exactly what the jewellery looks like, but more about what you want to say through it. Unfortunately, I’ve lost some of that, and I’m now in a period that is much more settled, much more serious and much more focused on the jewellery itself.”
От "Експлозия" до "Обсесия" – среща с дизайнера на бижута Богдана Топрева
PHOTO Диана Цанкова
In 1998, amid a period of dramatic personal and social change, Bogdana Topreva created her “Explosion” collection. Its large-scale pieces combined silver with a polymer that glows under ultraviolet light, giving the jewellery a striking theatrical quality. Her two most recent collections, “Invisible Roofs” and “Sofia – Paris”, explore a different perspective – that of birds and people in flight. Using drone photographs, Topreva transforms views of urban architecture normally hidden from us into jewellery.
Looking back across those three decades, Topreva hopes visitors will see her own story reflected in the jewellery. “My life is bound up with creativity, and in every piece of jewellery I tell some kind of fairy tale. If someone who doesn’t know me walks into the gallery and can sense that just by looking at the jewellery, I’ll be happy to have touched them emotionally,” she says.
From the "Explosion" collection.
PHOTO Diana Tsankova
Topreva studied Industrial Design at the National Academy of Art in Sofia, but jewellery was already the focus of her graduation project. She later joined the residency programme at the Cité internationale des arts in Paris, where she held solo exhibitions in 2012 and 2025. Her collections have also been shown in Bratislava, Budapest, Vienna and Sofia.
But where does an idea come from – from within, from the world around us, or from the imagination that feeds artistic inspiration?
PHOTO Diana Tsankova
“An idea can come in all sorts of ways,” Bogdana Topreva tells Radio Bulgaria. “I might get up in the morning, hear a sparrow singing and make a collection called ‘Birds’ – that’s actually how that one came about. A film or a song might stir something in me emotionally. Inspiration can come from anywhere, at any moment. I believe that people who create are touched by God, and I’m very grateful to have that feeling, to be able to do this. So yes, I believe that my ideas are sent to me and that I am a conduit.”
Whatever she creates, Topreva’s jewellery has a recognisable signature – something, she says, that both colleagues and clients have noticed. “I’m glad people can see that little something, although I myself can’t say exactly what it is,” she says. Her distinctive style can be recognised even in her enormous pieces of body armour.
“They are more like stage jewellery, but that doesn’t stop them from expressing a certain kind of sensitivity and attitude towards the world,” Topreva says. “And I think there are enough women who would put on a piece of armour like that and walk out into the street. But the ones who would do it are those who carry one single quality in their soul – freedom. Despite the armour.”
Topreva sees many more years of work and exhibitions ahead. Whether the next stage will be a continuation of what she has already created or take her in an entirely new direction, she does not yet know. For now, she is content to see where inspiration leads:
“We’ll have to see where that touch from God and my imagination take me next.”
Editor: Elena Karkalanova

The conflict began in February when Anthropic refused Pentagon Secretary Pete Hegseth’s demand to remove restrictions on the use of Claude for fully autonomous lethal weapons and mass domestic surveillance of Americans.

The appeals court decision created a potential legal conflict with a separate federal court decision in California last month that found a broader ban imposed by the Trump administration against Anthropic was illegal.
The Pentagon decision upheld on Friday was based on public procurement regulations and now remains in effect.
“We respectfully disagree with the court’s decision. Another federal court has already held the government’s parallel designation unlawful. We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to US media.

“Netanyahu’s speech was meant to boost his election campaign back at home,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said. “His supporters loved it. Those who don’t support him could see in his speech the classic Netanyahu – brilliant orator but a serial liar.”
“His speech was littered with lies,” Bregman continued. “He played down the settlers’s violence in the West Bank, saying that just a few Palestinians were killed by it, while in reality more than 80 were killed [by Israeli forces and settlers] there this year.”
“The world has turned its back on him and on Israel,” Bregman added. “He’s toxic, and Israel has turned itself into a pariah state.”
Domestic home run
However, while Netanyahu may have faced growing international isolation, his allies in the Israeli government and some media outlets rallied around what they portrayed as the defiant tone of his speech.
Zvika Klein, editor of the influential right-wing newspaper the Jerusalem Post, praised Netanyahu’s delivery and defence of Israel. Columnists in other Israeli media also rushed to compare Netanyahu’s warnings to the West to that of a stern father addressing a wayward son.
“He gave a great performance,” said Mitchell Barak, an Israeli pollster and former aide to Netanyahu during the 1990s.
Barak argued that the speech was designed to leave the delegates who stayed with the impression that Israel’s wars since 2023 had been fought not only in its own interests, but also on behalf of its allies and the wider international community.
“No one watching in Israel could imagine any of Netanyahu’s [electoral] rivals in October doing that. It’s impossible to picture it. None of them could have commanded that much respect,” he claimed.
No future
While much of Netanyahu’s electoral base may have been reassured by his address, nowhere in his speech was any hint of where Israel’s multiple wars and genocide might end.
For three years, he boasted, Israel had fought on seven fronts.
As it led a genocide in Gaza, Israel has also battled Hezbollah, Yemen’s Houthi rebels, Iran, militias in Iraq and Syria as well as Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. All, he claimed, had “ganged up” to wipe Israel “off the face of the Earth”.
Closing his speech, Netanyahu addressed the remaining delegates as one, maintaining: “Over the centuries, the tyrannies that tried to destroy us failed time and again. God willing, they’ll continue to fail. If we muster our courage, if we steel our resolve, we will continue to win.”
“This was just a repeat of his Sparta speech,“ Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with Chatham House said, referring to Netanyahu’s likening of Israel in September 2025 to the ancient and perennially embattled city-state.
“All he could offer was repeated references to his past heroism, military success and the need to keep fighting. That’s something that should be of concern to every Israeli watching,” Mekelberg said.
“Where does this end? There’s no answer; there isn’t even the vocabulary for that. When Israel’s leaders have no solution to the country’s multiple wars, that’s when every Israeli should be worried.”
