The US Supreme Court on Friday ruled the Trump administration can use a controversial new federal database that would ostensibly verify voter citizenship in November’s elections. Critics argue the administration is exaggerating the threat of non-citizen voters – an extreme rarity in US elections – to implement policies that would disenfranchise likely Democratic voters.
The US Supreme Court on Friday revived an expanded immigration database that US President Donald Trump's administration says aims to combat voting by noncitizens but that critics say will disenfranchise eligible voters.
The justices granted a Justice Department request to block a judge's order that would have prevented state officials from using Social Security numbers and other information to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records.
The administration's data-sharing arrangement is one of a series of actions the federal government has taken to increase its involvement in voting ahead of November's midterm elections.
The US Constitution gives individual states the primary authority to run and administer elections.
The Department of Homeland Security last year redesigned a federal database known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, used to verify a person's citizenship and immigration status. The revamp allowed users to search many records at a time and to conduct searches using Social Security numbers.
Several Republican-led states have compared their voter lists to the database, and some voters flagged as potential non-citizens have had their registrations cancelled.
Critics say such election-related actions by Republicans are driven less by concerns over election security than by an attempt to gain political advantage by narrowing the electorate, risking the disenfranchisement of eligible, often Democratic-leaning voters.
In a June ruling blocking the revamped database, US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan in Washington, DC, said the system was haphazardly assembled and contained unreliable citizenship data.
"All in all, the federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," Sooknanan wrote.
"This court cannot stand idly by while that happens."
Read moreTrump reviving election fraud claims to contest midterm results, say Democrats
The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in a 2-1 ruling on September 4 declined to halt Sooknanan's ruling, prompting the administration's request to the Supreme Court.
In a Supreme Court filing, Justice Department lawyers called the judge's order "indefensible", arguing that it "threatens the integrity" of the midterm elections.
False claims, real fears
Trump has repeatedly made false claims of widespread voting fraud, including in his 2020 election loss to Democratic former president Joe Biden.
Even according to data from the pro-Trump Heritage Foundation, which campaigns against “voter fraud”, cases of noncitizen voting are very rare – and most involve mistakes rather than fraud.
A 2024 review of Heritage Foundation data by the American Immigration Council found the group had found "just 68 cases of proven noncitizen voting dating back to 2000, amounting to less than 0.0001% of total votes”. The Heritage Foundation’s database has grown since 2024, adding an additional 21 cases.
Advocacy groups that sued to block the revised SAVE system said the new approach has resulted in people who were wrongfully identified as noncitizens being kicked off voter rolls. They argued that SAVE information can be outdated, and immigrants who have since become naturalised US citizens and are thus eligible to vote are sometimes labelled as noncitizens.
The modified system's overall error rate is not publicly known. The Department of Homeland Security and Justice Department did not provide that information when asked.

In their Supreme Court filing, the voter advocacy groups cited a Travis County, Texas, election official who said 25 percent of the system's noncitizen matches involved people who had already proven their US citizenship, as well as news reports finding that at least 81 percent of the system's responses in St. Louis County, Missouri, were erroneous.
The voting rights group League of Women Voters and privacy rights group Electronic Privacy Information Center sued in September 2025 to block the Trump administration's modified system. They said that the revamp violated federal privacy and other US laws.
Texas, which intervened in the case in support of the administration, has disputed claims that the system is unreliable.
Due to separate litigation in Florida, the Trump administration has been able to continue using its modified SAVE system in the Republican-led states of Florida, Iowa, Indiana and Ohio.

Trump administration to meet Ukraine assistance deadline
WASHINGTON, Sept 25 - The Trump administration has made legally binding commitments to spend almost all of the $400 million Congress approved for military aid to Ukraine late last year, ensuring that the money will not expire on September 30, according to three sources familiar with the plan.
As of early this week, $307 million of the $400 million of the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI) funding had been obligated, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, and the administration plans to lock in the remaining $93 million before the fiscal year ends on September 30.
The Pentagon, which oversees the USAI program, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
FIRST DELIVERIES INCLUDE WEAPONS, SPARE PARTS
The money has been a source of contention with Congress, as Democrats and some of US President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans have criticized the Pentagon for sitting on the aid for Kyiv, which members of both parties voted for last December.
Trump has in recent months taken a more positive tone toward Ukraine, signing off on a proposal to give a license for Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptor missiles and signing a Russia sanctions bill.
He met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy this week at UN headquarters in New York, after which Zelenskiy said they had discussed efforts to end the war with Russia, including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets.
The first deliveries, which will include offensive weapons and equipment such as spare parts for armored vehicles, began this month. The rest are expected to be delivered before October 2029, the sources said. Trump's White House term ends in January of that year.
The remaining $93 million in the package approved by Congress does not have to be spent by the end of the year, but it will expire if it is not formally placed under contract by then.
PATRIOT MISSILES NOT INCLUDED
One of the sources said the military equipment did not include Patriot missiles, despite Russia bombarding Ukraine's cities with drones and ballistic missiles.
The US war in Iran and the Ukraine war have depleted global supplies of Patriots, and Kyiv has been pleading for more.
Reuters reported in July that the administration had told Congress it could take years for the equipment to reach Ukrainian forces. The Pentagon has held up shipments of weapons to Ukraine several times out of concern that US weapons supplies were too low.
Lawmakers said then they were unhappy with the Pentagon's timeline, considered unusually slow for an ongoing conflict, and the issue has come up repeatedly at congressional hearings.
Ukraine has been by far the top recipient of US foreign aid since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, but the US commitment to Kyiv has been called into question since Trump took office and his Republicans took control of both houses of Congress in January 2025. REUTERS

Malaysia’s new ambassador to Türkiye, Adlan Mohd Shaffieq, has likened the country to a big open museum, praising its rich cultural heritage and the warm hospitality he has received since arriving in Ankara.
“Your country is like a big open museum. All of the cities that I go to are like free, open museums where you can go and watch the culture,” Shaffieq told Anadolu in an interview.
“It has a very deep culture. So, it's very interesting for me to discover your country,” he added.
Shaffieq, who recently began his tenure in Ankara, shared his first impressions of Türkiye, his family life and his views on relations between the two countries.
The diplomat said he was delighted to be appointed to Türkiye for his first ambassadorial posting, particularly because he believed his four children, aged between five and 11, would enjoy living in Ankara.
“Malaysia and Türkiye are like brothers and sisters,” he said, describing the warm hospitality he has experienced since his arrival.
Shared family values and historical ties
Shaffieq highlighted similarities between Malaysian and Turkish cultures, particularly their strong family ties and respect for parents.
“I think the similarities between Malaysian and Turkish families is that we are very close-knit,” he said.
Shaffieq said families in both countries enjoy gathering during religious holidays and other occasions to celebrate, cook and share meals.
The ambassador noted that Turkish television series and films have helped Malaysians become more familiar with Türkiye, while emphasising that relations between the two countries stretch back for centuries.
“Our history has the linkage not only recently, but during the Ottoman Empire,” he said, pointing to historical contacts between the Ottoman Empire and the Sultanate of Melaka.
‘Your ice cream is the best ice cream in the world’
Touching on Turkish cuisine, Shaffieq said Malaysian food differs considerably from Turkish dishes, with Malaysians generally preferring spicier meals.
However, he was particularly enthusiastic about Turkish ice cream.
“Your ice cream is the best ice cream in the world. My kids love it,” he said.
“I think food is also one of the areas that we should focus on when it comes to cultural exchanges,” he added.
The ambassador also expressed his fondness for menemen, a traditional Turkish breakfast dish made with eggs, tomatoes and peppers.
Shaffieq said he had been learning Turkish for approximately three months and intended to learn as much of the language as possible during his posting.
Unique cultural experiences
The ambassador said he had already visited several destinations in Türkiye, including Cappadocia, Kastamonu and Konya, in addition to the capital Ankara, each of which he described as having its own distinctive character.
He mentioned that he had also recently attended tomato and carrot festivals, held separately in different parts of Ankara in late September, describing both experiences as immensely unique.
Shaffieq said the opportunity to experience different local traditions and explore the country’s cultural heritage had made his time in Türkiye particularly rewarding.
Trade, defence cooperation and tourism
On bilateral relations, Shaffieq said Malaysia and Türkiye are making significant progress, pointing to growing cooperation in trade and defence.
He said bilateral trade reached approximately $5.6 billion in 2025, while the two countries have set a bilateral trade target of $10 billion.
Although ambitious, the target is achievable, he said.
The ambassador identified defence as another important area for expanding bilateral cooperation. He said Malaysia had received or commissioned three littoral mission ships this year and hoped to procure additional vessels in the future.
Malaysia has also received three ANKA unmanned aerial vehicles, which have begun operating in the South China Sea, he said, adding that further defence procurement opportunities were under consideration.
Shaffieq also highlighted tourism as an increasingly important component of bilateral relations.
Approximately 40,000 Turkish tourists visited Malaysia in 2025, he said, noting that the figure had increased compared with the year prior.

Soviet jazz-rock pioneer Alexey Kozlov dies at 90
Jazz saxophonist Alexey Kozlov has died in Moscow at 90.
His jazz club reported his death on its Telegram channel.
Kozlov was a pioneer of Soviet jazz rock. Born in Moscow on October 13, 1935, he founded Arsenal in 1973. The band became one of the Soviet Union’s best-known groups.
Arsenal released several records and CDs. One of its albums, “Svoimi Rukami” (“With Our Own Hands”), was reissued in the U.S. The band performed in France, Germany, and the U.S. over the years, including at Carnegie Hall in New York during a joint tour with Georgian singer Tamara Gverdtsiteli.
Kozlov also hosted jazz programs on Russian television and wrote a book on the history of rock music.
Kozlov’s music is mentioned in numerous books, jazz encyclopedias, and dictionaries. Vasily Aksyonov wrote about him in his novel “Ozhog” (“The Burn”), as did American journalist Hedrick Smith in “The Russians” and historian Frederick Starr in “Red and Hot,” a study of jazz in the Soviet Union.

Marking 13 years since the murder of Greek rapper Pavlos Fyssas by a member of the neo-Nazi Golden Dawn party, MEPs at the European Parliament in Brussels were invited to a performance to pay tribute to the musician's life.
A theatrical monologue about murdered Greek rapper Pavlos Fyssas at the European Parliament. Actress Dora Chrysikou portrays a young woman who was an eyewitness to a far-right crime.
The performance unfolds the story of the murder of Fyssas, while also taking us into the Golden Dawn trial. Maria Louka wrote the text, which is based on real witness statements. Korais Damatis directed the piece.

We have to provide solutions without entering into dialogue with those who want to overturn democracy. For the first time in the European Parliament a message of democracy and peace is heard so clearly. After all, weren't these also the founding causes of the European Union?"
The heroine is neither invincible nor glossy. She is transparent and fragile. She is someone from our own world - a neighbour, a friend, a sister - struggling with her fears just hours before giving her testimony at the trial. An ordinary person who becomes a subject of history.
The monologue, presented with subtitles in English and French, coincided with the dramatic rise of the far right in the recent elections in Germany and in other European countries. It also coincided with the release of Kasidiaris and his announcement that he intends to return to the political stage.

Araghchi holds a series of talks in NY on regional security, Hormuz and Iran-EU ties
TEHRAN– Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held a series of meetings with foreign counterparts on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, engaging Russian, British, Portuguese, Bruneian, Kyrgyz, Polish, Spanish, Egyptian, Jordanian, Cypriot, Pakistani and Austrian officials on regional security, the Strait of Hormuz, the war in West Asia, Palestine, Iran-Europe relations and bilateral cooperation.
Hormuz and Regional Security
The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the future of maritime navigation emerged as a recurring issue in Araghchi’s meetings with European and regional officials.
In talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Araghchi briefed his counterpart on Iran-Oman discussions concerning arrangements for a safe maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz. He also outlined diplomatic efforts by mediators to establish conditions for a return to negotiations.
In separate talks with Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel and Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger, Araghchi attributed the disruption of maritime traffic and insecurity in the Strait to US and Israeli military actions. He said, from Iran’s perspective, restoring maritime security would require an end to 'destabilizing US measures and economic pressure.'
Araghchi also raised regional security with Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, criticizing the use of the territory of regional states in military operations. He said Iran was prepared to work with neighboring countries on security arrangements based on regional cooperation rather than external military involvement.
The Iranian foreign minister’s discussions with Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also touched on the wider regional crisis. With Sikorski, Araghchi warned against linking the Ukraine conflict to developments in West Asia, urging European governments to address security challenges on their own continent while taking positions on regional developments based on international law.
Iran-Europe relations
Relations with European governments formed another major thread of Araghchi’s meetings.
During talks with British Foreign Secretary Edward Miliband, Araghchi criticized Britain’s political and military support for Israel and called on London and other European governments to reconsider policies contributing to instability in West Asia.
The two sides also discussed Iran’s nuclear program. Araghchi reiterated Tehran’s stated preference for resolving outstanding issues through diplomacy and criticized Britain, France and Germany over their positions concerning the so-called snapback mechanism and the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Similar concerns were raised in Araghchi’s meetings with the foreign ministers of Spain and Cyprus. He called on European governments to base their policies toward Iran and the region on international law and avoid 'alignment with parties responsible for aggression.'
Palestine and wider regional conflict
The Palestinian issue was central to Araghchi’s discussions with Brunei’s Foreign Minister Abdul Mateen ibni Hassanal Bolkiah, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi.
Araghchi called for greater coordination among Islamic countries and a more active role for the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in addressing the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and Al-Quds. He also emphasized the need to support Palestinian self-determination and efforts toward establishing an independent Palestinian state.
With Abdelatty, Araghchi discussed strengthening bilateral coordination alongside regional developments, while his meeting with Safadi focused on regional security and cooperation between Iran and Jordan.
Russia, Pakistan and regional diplomacy
Araghchi and Lavrov also reviewed political, economic, trade, transportation and energy cooperation between Iran and Russia, as well as coordination within international organizations. Lavrov reiterated Moscow’s opposition to 'US and Israeli military aggression against Iran' and emphasized adherence to international law and the UN Charter.
In New York, Araghchi also held talks with Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar on bilateral relations and regional developments. The meeting came as Pakistan was pursuing a mediating role between Iran and the United States.

Dr Nighat Arif on navigating health advice in the TikTok era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:47:26 UTC
01:47:26 KST

Breadcrumb
'The danger is acting on half-truths': Dr Nighat Arif on BBC's Clickbait Clinic navigating health advice in the TikTok era
As one in three Brits reportedly turn to social media for health advice, a new series aims to educate viewers about trends that have gone viral across their social media feeds.
Whether people are using TikTok to explain unexplained symptoms or scrolling through Instagram for advice on how to live longer, social media has quickly become an influential source of health information.
But when advice is marketed as 90-second clips designed to gain views, how can people tell whether it is actually evidence-based or just made to go viral?
This is the question to be tackled in the new season of BBC’s Clickbait Clinic, which sees Stacey Dooley, Dr Alex George and Dr Nighat Arif as they investigate health trends circulating online and challenge the misinformation behind them.
As a visibly Muslim woman who appears regularly on TV and works in medicine, Dr Nighat is a representation in a space that has historically lacked people who look like her.
For Dr Nighat, the word ‘clickbait’ makes her think of "bold promises that outrun the evidence headlines," headlines designed to stop your scroll, not protect your health.
"In medicine, that gap between hype and reality can cost people time, money and sometimes even safety," she tells The New Arab.
Health advice in the age of TikTok
Dr Nighat’s decision to join Clickbait Clinic originally stemmed from her firsthand experience of patients coming in with information they had found online.
"Because this is where my patients already are: scrolling, searching, and trying. I wanted to bring calm, evidence-based clarity to the noise and do it in a way that actually sticks," she says.
Almost every consultation now involves something a patient has either "read or watched online," says Dr Nighat. She explains that while some of this information can be helpful, it can also be ‘alarming or misleading’, so she chooses to unpack it during her consultation.
The appeal of social media is hard to resist.
"Access, anonymity, and algorithmic comfort" means people find answers quickly and without judgment, especially when asking questions that may feel uncomfortable.
"The danger is acting on half-truths," Dr Nighat explains, warning that viral health trends can contribute to delaying diagnosis, wasting money or people trying risky interventions.
Her advice is to look beyond the post on your screen and instead check the creator’s credentials, look for consensus, and avoid relying on a single viral post.
Ultimately, hoping that viewers will learn to pause before trying something.
"Ask ‘who benefits?’, ‘what’s the evidence?’, and ‘does it fit my situation?’" she says before encouraging people to speak to a healthcare professional as their next step.
When misinformation goes viral
Dr Nighat believes social media platforms can play an important role in sharing accurate information, particularly because they can reach a wide range of audiences, including those who may not engage with traditional health-related messaging.
"Social media can be powerful for accurate health information if creators cite sources, show uncertainty, and signpost proper care," she says.
The difficulty with social media often lies with the fact that algorithms are not designed to prioritise medical nuance.
Social media does get some things right, says Dr Nighat. "It can normalise conversations, reach underserved communities and can democratise knowledge."
But it also ‘rewards certainty over nuance’, with algorithms prioritising engagement over safety.
This can help to explain why some people might trust a stranger on TikTok more easily than a medical professional.
"Relatability can feel like expertise," she adds.
Someone who may look like you, speaks confidently and explains "what worked for them" can quite easily become emotionally persuasive.
The use of artificial intelligence could also make this problem even more complicated.
Dr Nighat says AI can be used to amplify health trends often through "slick scripts, convincing visuals, and endless variations of the same claim," creating content so quickly that it outpaces fact-checking.
She believes that platform labels, creator accountability and teaching audiences to spot AI-polished persuasion are what is needed to address this.
"If it makes someone pause and ask, ‘Is this right for me? That’s a win," she says.
Why Muslim representation matters
For Dr Nighat, the conversation doesn’t stop at misinformation. As a visibly Muslim woman and GP appearing on mainstream television, she has become a recognisable medical voice for those who may not always see themselves represented elsewhere.
"It means patients see themselves in the room before they even walk in," she says.
"Visibility builds trust, reduces stigma, and tells communities: your health matters here too."
Dr Nighat believes representation can shift who we consider "credible" and hopes it will "make it easier for women to seek help without fear of judgment or cultural misunderstanding."
But representation cannot stop at putting diverse faces on screen.
Language, cultural context, and health literacy can all become barriers to accessing reliable information, while long appointment wait times can push people towards ‘quick online fixes.’
"When the system feels distant, TikTok feels close," Dr Nighat says.
Making health content accessible
Working alongside Stacey Dooley and Dr Alex George, Dr Nighat says the programme aims to challenge health trends without shaming the people who believed them.
"Stacey asks the questions people really have, and Alex bridges clinical rigour with real empathy," she explains. "Together, we could challenge trends without shaming people who have been sold them."
Dr Nighat’s approach to sharing health information is rooted in making information engaging without sacrificing accuracy.
"Hook with empathy, not fear," she says. "State the evidence level, show uncertainty, and end with a clear ‘when to seek help’ signpost."
Her goal is not to make people think twice about what they see online, but to not to distrust everything they encounter.
Ultimately, Dr Nighat believes social media can still be part of the solution. It can reach people quickly and open up conversations that may have previously been stigmatised.
For Muslim women watching Clickbait Clinic, Dr Nighat’s presence represents more than just another doctor on TV.

The Israeli army has halted arrests of ultra-Orthodox Haredi Jews wanted for failing to comply with military draft orders amid concerns that the arrests could trigger protests, according to Israeli media.
Haaretz reported Friday that the army had decided to suspend arrests of Haredi draft dodgers over fears of unrest and protests across the country as Israeli elections approach.
The army attributed the move to “operational needs,” without providing further details, according to the newspaper.
Haaretz said arrests had been extremely limited even before the decision was taken.
According to figures cited in an Israeli Supreme Court ruling, only 16 Haredi draft dodgers were arrested during the first half of 2026, the newspaper said.
Haaretz cited unnamed police sources as saying that “there are no plans to resume them in the near future.”
The sources said arresting wanted individuals requires the deployment of large police forces and that the suspension was initiated by the military police.
According to Haaretz, the decision on whether to carry out arrests rests with the army, while the police are responsible only for implementing them.
“The suspension has coincided with a halt in ultra-Orthodox protests against the military,” the newspaper noted.
Haredi Jews continue to protest against military service following a Supreme Court ruling on June 25, 2024, requiring them to enlist and barring financial support for religious institutions whose students refuse military service.
Haredim make up around 13% of Israel’s population of 10 million and oppose military service on the grounds that they devote their lives to studying the Torah.
Senior rabbis, whose followers view their rulings as religious directives, have called on Haredi men to refuse enlistment and even to “tear up” draft orders.
They also argue that integration into secular society threatens their religious identity and the continuity of their community.
For decades, members of the Haredi community were able to avoid military service after turning 18 by repeatedly obtaining deferments on the grounds that they were studying at religious seminaries until reaching the exemption age, currently 26.
The decision came about 33 days before Israeli elections scheduled for October amid sharp domestic political debate over Netanyahu government policies.

NHS boss says staff suspected of snooping on patients’ records should be suspended immediately
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:45:48 UTC
01:45:48 KST

NHS staff suspected of snooping on patients’ medical records should be suspended immediately and barred from using health service computers, the head of NHS England has said.
Jim Mackey urged NHS England’s 205 health trusts to pursue a “zero tolerance” approach to staff who are suspected of inappropriately accessing records.
He called for a “hardline” stance towards anyone found to have accessed patients’ notes or medical histories without a clinical justification.
His intervention comes amid growing concern that staff sometimes use their position to view medical records but rarely face any meaningful penalty for doing so.
Mackey said on Friday: “Patient records contain some of the most private information people will ever share. We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust and enough is enough.”
He wrote to all trusts demanding that they routinely implement what NHS England called a “crackdown” on breaching patients’ confidential data.
The problem has gained attention after reports that NHS staff illicitly accessed medical records of victims of the attacks by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023 and stabbings by Axel Rudakubana in Southport in 2024, among other high-profile incidents.
Mackey said: “If someone is suspected of snooping we cannot leave them in post with access to patients’ records while an investigation takes days or weeks. From now on we will expect them to be suspended and have their access to NHS systems cut off immediately, while the facts are established.”
That should happen already, but rarely does so in practice.
He added: “Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient’s record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record.”
Since 2020, more than 200 NHS staff in England have been dismissed and 2,000 others sanctioned for snooping on patients’ records, an investigation by Sky News and the Health Service Journal found this month.
One employee was sacked after viewing up to 179 people’s records, another had accessed their spouse’s details in a “potential domestic violence situation”, and others had shared information they had gathered in WhatsApp groups.
Responses by 140 trusts to freedom of information requests by the media outlets showed that 214 staff were dismissed, three suspended and 540 given a final written warning over the last five years.
The Liberal Democrat MP Layla Moran, who chairs the health and social care select committee, has warned that official numbers for staff accessing patients’ records illegally under the Data Protection Act were likely to be “canaries in the coal mine”.
However, Paul Arnold, the chief executive of the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), the data watchdog, said in June that “inappropriate access is rare and does not represent the behaviour of the vast majority of healthcare staff who take their duty of confidentiality extremely seriously”.
Bristol NHS foundation trust has apologised to Paula and Tom McGowan for staff snooping on the medical records of their son Oliver, who died in 2016 aged 18. At least five members of staff, including three nurses and a doctor, accessed his records without permission.
Gillian Merron, a health minister, disclosed in July that health service bodies reported 1,445 cases of inappropriate access to the ICO between 2019 and 2025.

China’s Visibility Gap Around the Trump-Xi Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:44:00 UTC
01:44:00 KST

Beijing formally confirmed Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 23-25 visit to the United States on September 21, just two days before the trip began. The news had barely registered among many of the Chinese people I spoke with the following day. Official coverage began appearing online following the announcement, but visible discussion among ordinary users on platforms such as Weibo, WeChat, and Xiaohongshu (RedNote) remained scarce.
That changed once Xi’s visit was underway. Chinese social media filled with reports about the summit, with much of the visible content coming from official outlets and accounts, emphasizing the diplomatic significance and choreography of the visit, including Trump’s reception of Xi and calls for “constructive strategic stability.” The shift from limited information to abundant official coverage raised a different question: How much did ordinary Chinese people know about the summit before official coverage moved into full gear?
On September 22, the day after Beijing’s formal announcement and one day before Xi’s visit began, I conducted informal interviews with a dozen individuals across China and the diaspora, including overseas students and professionals, domestic public-sector workers, private-sector employees, and an older relative. Awareness varied considerably by location and occupation.
Overseas students and professionals had generally learned of the trip earlier through foreign news outlets or private messaging groups. Some public-sector employees in China learned about it only after the official announcement, noting that senior leaders’ schedules are typically kept confidential until the last minute. Meanwhile, many of the private-sector employees I spoke with in China remained unaware of the visit even after the announcement.
Yet when asked about it, many responded by searching for the news themselves. What they found was a remarkably uniform information environment. On Weibo, Douyin, and Xiaohongshu, searches related to Xi’s U.S. visit were dominated by official and state-media content. On Xiaohongshu, some targeted searches produced either zero visible results or unrelated posts concerning personal travel and visas. Under some official media posts, comment sections were restricted or turned off. The interviews suggested that curiosity could exist even when little of it was publicly visible.
It is tempting to attribute this lack of visible discussion solely to censorship, but the interviews pointed to a more complicated picture. One respondent pointed to self-censorship: “Some of what people might say in private wouldn’t feel appropriate to post publicly.” Others suggested that interest might increase only after the meetings produced concrete outcomes.
The searches themselves could not reveal whether the lack of visible discussion reflected content controls, platform ranking, self-censorship, limited public interest, or some combination of these factors.
The summit itself added another layer to this ambiguity. Once Xi arrived in the United States, information about the visit was no longer difficult to find. Official reports and accounts circulated extensive coverage of the meetings and their diplomatic symbolism. Yet the greater volume of information did not necessarily make public opinion easier to observe: Much of what was readily visible still came from official sources rather than ordinary users.
However, in specialized, interest-driven spaces, discussion was easier to find. On WeChat financial blogs like “Liu Xiaobo Talk Finance” and their commentary threads, retail investors and market watchers debated the summit’s possible implications for tariffs, stock prices, and exchange rates. According to the CGCC-USA 2026 Business Survey Report, 79 percent of surveyed Chinese companies operating in the United States reported negative impacts from tariffs, while 36 percent anticipated a slight improvement in bilateral trade relations, underscoring the concrete economic stakes surrounding the summit.
The Trump-Xi summit thus exposed a broader “visibility gap” in China’s information environment. On September 22, even after the visit had been officially announced, many of the people I interviewed had not heard about it, although they often became curious enough to search once asked. Days later, information about the summit was everywhere, but the most visible narratives remained overwhelmingly official.
For outside observers trying to gauge public sentiment in China, the difficulty is not simply that Chinese people are silent. It is that the Chinese internet makes a lack of discussion unusually difficult to interpret.

In principle, no flights should be canceled because of National Day activities, it said, adding that airlines should consider adjusting flight arrival and departure times or increasing aircraft fuel loads.
People who have booked tickets on the dates should monitor flight changes on the airlines’ official Web sites and apps before leaving for the airport, the CAA said.

Why Russia’s Potemkin election actually matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:43 UTC
01:43:43 KST

In what must be the world’s least surprising election result, parties loyal to Russian President Vladimir Putin have made a clean sweep in elections to Russia’s parliament, the State Duma. There is little purpose to parsing who won what share of the vote; the point is that opponents of Putin and his war were either jailed, dead, in exile or banned from running. As a democratic exercise, this signified nothing — but it was an important moment nonetheless.
Putin’s approach to this conflict has changed. Where he once felt he had time to wait until Ukraine and its backers faltered, he now wants the war over quickly and on his terms. So what mattered to the career KGB agent and his like-minded officials this weekend was not that the election would let Russians pass judgement his plans, but rather that it should help ensure public acquiescence to the demands for greater sacrifice he will soon make.
For one thing, the vote and its result will allow Putin to push harder on the claim that neither Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy nor his government are legitimate, and that they are therefore inadequate negotiating partners. After all, unlike Russia, they have refused to hold wartime elections. Never mind that Russia is not being invaded, meaning that what is possible for Moscow is not necessarily viable for Kyiv.
Illustration: Louise Ting
But more critical: Despite Putin’s denials, Russians have been speculating that a further troop mobilization is coming. This could be formally announced or take place under the radar, but in either case the Kremlin needs to raise hundreds of thousands more troops to replace those who are wounded or dying — and high salaries are no longer drawing enough recruits. That is easier to do when the government can make the argument, supported by a fresh (if fake) electoral mandate, that the public supports the war.
Indeed, in an address last week, Putin made it clear that this was what the elections were about.
“Your choice and determination will show once again that millions of people are backing our fighters and that we stand together,” he told his fellow Russians. “Nobody can divide or intimidate us, undermine our statehood, our public and political system.”
By the same token, if continuing the war brings hardships in the form of higher taxes, cuts to social spending or regular Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian energy output and cities, this too is easier — even for an autocrat such as Putin — if he can portray the war as a nationally endorsed endeavor. That approval has often been real, but many Russians want the conflict to end.
Perhaps most important, though, is to lock down the home front before escalating not just in Ukraine, but also in Europe. That is where Putin appears to be shifting emphasis now, as the inevitable winter slowdown follows a summer fighting season marked by Russian frustration. For if the strategy of Ukraine and its allies is to inflict enough pain for Putin to conclude that his war of choice is no longer worth the pursuit, the Kremlin’s is to persuade Europeans that they cannot afford to push him to that point.
French President Emmanuel Macron last week became the latest European leader to warn his people that Russia’s hybrid war against the West is expanding. Multiple intelligence agencies, meanwhile, have recently warned that Putin may test NATO sooner rather than later. Russia’s escalating air war is driving up the cost of Ukraine’s defense, the vast majority of which now falls to Europe. The shortfall on the tens of billions already allocated this year, according to Kyiv, is a further US$27 billion.
So, with far-right, pro-Russian parties making inroads ahead of a slew of (real) elections in Europe next year, Putin has every reason to feel confident that Ukraine and its Western backers will reach their pain threshold before he does. Russia’s leaders have not even tried to conceal their glee at German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s drubbing in a string of recent regional elections in Germany.
University of Chicagopolitical science professor John Mearsheimer, perhaps the purest US exponent of the so-called realist school of foreign policy, is one of very few Western academics still welcomed to Moscow. His recent YouTube interview with the Norwegian academic, Putin apologist and alt-right fan Glenn Diesen makes it clear why it rolls out the red carpet for the US professor — and why Russians are so certain of winning.
Much of Mearsheimer’s analysis is right on the money. He notes that whatever troubles the Russian economy is having, they are nascent compared with the potential catastrophe unfolding in Ukraine. Likewise, he says Putin’s escalation since June is already having an impact and (as I’ve written before) has a worryingly high chance of success this winter. This is largely due to the mismatch between expanding Russian missile production and Ukraine’s fast-shrinking air defenses.
He accurately describes Russia’s goal as to seize all territory that it considers historically Russian — including Odesa, the Black Sea coast and Kharkiv to the north — ensuring that a landlocked, rump Ukraine is so destroyed as to be dysfunctional.
Where he, Diesen and many others are deluded is in their embrace of the Kremlin’s portrayal of the war as an act of self-defense against Europe, which in this telling has sought for decades to use Ukraine as a “battering ram” to destroy Russia.
This is the story Putin tells to Russians and his sympathizers in the West, from academics such as Mearsheimer and Diesen, to populist political parties including Germany’s AfD and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France. Promoting it matters deeply, because if Russia is simply defending itself, there is little for Europe to fear in a Ukrainian defeat. If, by contrast, Putin has led a revisionist power to war, then Europe has a great deal to fear.
Having put that argument to bed at home, Putin can now move on to persuading voters in the West. There elections do have the power to throw leaders out — and with that to divide Europe, destroy Ukraine and win the war for Russia.
Marc Champion is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Europe, Russia and the Middle East. He was previously Istanbul bureau chief for the Wall Street Journal. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

A thaw in India-China relations?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:43 UTC
01:43:43 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) visit to India to attend the BRICS — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — summit earlier this month, followed by his meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has generated expectations of a possible normalization of India-China relations.
The renewed high-level engagement is significant after years of political and military tensions following the Galwan clash of 2020. Indian and Chinese media have portrayed the resumption of summit-level engagement positively. Yet, the current thaw needs to be assessed within the broader strategic environment in which New Delhi and Beijing are attempting to manage their relationship.
A major catalyst for this convergence has been the changing international environment. US President Donald Trump’s policies have generated uncertainty for both India and China and, paradoxically, created incentives for greater bilateral engagement. For New Delhi, the concern extends beyond continuing US-China rivalry to the changing nature of US relations with Pakistan, particularly during and after Operation Sindoor. India already confronts a major security challenge from Pakistan and a territorial and strategic challenge from China. The prospect of closer US-Pakistan engagement alongside the enduring China-Pakistan strategic relationship has added another layer of uncertainty to India’s security calculations. Reducing India-China tensions can lessen the possibility of simultaneous pressure on India’s northern and western fronts while providing New Delhi with greater diplomatic flexibility. It also signals to Washington that India retains alternative strategic options.
China has developed its own incentives to seek greater stability with India, particularly given its changing economic circumstances. China’s export-oriented growth model faces mounting pressures from domestic overcapacity, weaker external demand, and increasing restrictions on Chinese products and investments in several major Western markets. Intensifying US-China trade tensions and the diversification of global supply chains have consequently increased the importance of alternative markets.
India is particularly significant because of its enormous population, expanding consumer demand, rising purchasing power and long-term economic growth potential. A more stable political relationship can create greater opportunities for Chinese enterprises in India and provide Beijing with an additional incentive to prevent bilateral tensions from disrupting economic engagement again.
China’s geopolitical calculations provide another incentive for rapprochement. For Beijing, stability along its western frontier has strategic value because China simultaneously faces challenges in the Taiwan Strait and intensifying competition with the US. Chinese strategic discussions have at times viewed the India-China border and Taiwan as potentially interconnected elements of a broader two-front challenge. Reducing tensions with India can provide Beijing with greater strategic flexibility. The objective need not be a comprehensive resolution of differences with New Delhi. Rather, it can prevent the India-China relationship from becoming a sustained source of military and diplomatic pressure while Beijing concentrates on other strategic priorities.
India’s position in the global south adds a further dimension to China’s calculations. India possesses considerable diplomatic influence among developing countries and has sought to strengthen its role as a voice of the global south. China has similarly attempted to expand its influence among developing states and strengthen its role in reshaping global governance. A less confrontational relationship with India could facilitate Chinese diplomacy within BRICS and other multilateral institutions.
These convergences do not imply strategic alignment; the limits of the rapprochement remain substantial. The two countries’ readouts of the bilateral meeting between Xi and Modi highlighted sharp differences. India emphasized that peace and tranquillity in the border areas remain an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations, while Beijing mentioned its usual position of separating the boundary dispute from broader ties.
Second, China remains attentive to India’s expanding strategic partnerships in the Indo-Pacific region, particularly its growing security ties with Southeast Asian countries such as the Philippines and Vietnam. Indian and Japanese air forces are also conducting a joint military exercise to boost their defense ties. It is also highly unlikely that China will take concrete measures to address the trade imbalance India faces in its bilateral ties. Moreover, China will continue to support Pakistan’s use of terrorism as an instrument of state policy against India, thereby threatening regional security in South Asia.
Although the BRICS countries have sought to project their collective strength in driving the world toward a multipolar order, there are deep divisions between China and India on this issue as well. While Beijing wants a China-dominated system devoid of democratic values and openness, India seeks to promote an international order in which developing countries have a strong say. These challenges are far too wide and structural to be resolved in the near future.
The current phase of thaw between India and China should be seen as a strategic compromise rather than the foundation for an enduring bilateral peace and prosperity.
Sumit Kumar is a Ministry of Foreign Affairs visiting fellow at National Chengchi University and an assistant professor in Delhi University’s Department of Political Science.

EU urges Britain to raise tariffs on Chinese vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:42 UTC
01:43:42 KST

Brussels has told British Prime Minister Andy Burnham that Britain needs to raise tariffs on Chinese cars and align more closely align with EU trade policy to avoid “made in Europe” barriers on key exports, the **Financial Times** said yesterday.
In response to lobbying for equal treatment for British products, the bloc told London its best solution would be to join the EU’s customs union, the newspaper said, citing two people familiar with the matter.
“A customs union would solve most of the problems of ‘made in Europe,’” an EU official told the paper. “And also the question of tariff differences, which leads to fears the Chinese could avoid our tariffs by routing through the UK.”
Photo: AFP
Burnham said this week he would make the case for Britain to be considered a “trusted partner” under the bloc’s proposed “Made in EU” rules, warning that the UK’s exclusion could damage its car industry.
The “Made in Europe” policy aims to curb reliance on Chinese components by prioritizing European-made goods — a worry for the British auto industry which feeds parts into EU supply chains and sells cars across the bloc.
The bloc would use every available tool to reduce its “unsustainable” trade deficit with China, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament in her “State of the Union” address this month.
The EU and the British Foreign Office did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside business hours.
Separately, German industry association BDI yesterday called for a more determined effort to reduce economic risks linked to China, arguing that Europe must diversify supply chains and forge new partnerships while avoiding broad-based protectionism.
The BDI, representing major German manufacturers, said in a policy paper that “de-risking” should be pursued more consistently, though it stopped short of spelling out specific measures.
German industry has been increasing pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz to take a tougher line towards Beijing, with companies calling for stronger action to address what they describe as unfair competition from Chinese rivals.
“Systemic competition with China’s economy is increasingly challenging the open social market economy and requires an appropriate industrial and trade policy response,” BDI chief executive Tanja Goenner said.
The EU should have tools to respond rapidly to unfair competition, such as anti-dumping and anti-subsidy measures, Goenner said, while warning that any new trade defense measures must be carefully calibrated.
The BDI also urged Germany and the EU to broaden ties with other regions based on economic and security interests.

Netanyahu, who arrived in New York on Thursday, was to meet with only a handful of leaders before giving his speech.
Photo: AFP
Many in Washington associate Netanyahu with the increasingly unpopular fight with Iran, and Trump has labored to avoid the appearance that the Israeli leader forced him into a war that Trump said would be a “little excursion” lasting only weeks.
Netanyahu’s brief visit also demonstrated how isolated he is globally. He faces re-election next month in polls widely seen as a referendum on his responsibility for security failures and ability to defend Israel’s reputation on the world stage.
Still, Netanyahu was unfazed when scores of diplomats marched out when he took the stage on Thursday.

Experts said that without the usual high-profile meetings, the trip could hurt Netanyahu’s image at home.

US President Donald Trump yesterday took Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) to visit the National Archives, showing off the texts of US democracy to the leader of the world’s most powerful communist country to cap off a three-day state visit criticized for being heavy on pomp and light on substance.
Xi was expected to depart Washington after touring the nation’s vault of records, where the Declaration of Independence, the constitution and the Bill of Rights are held.
The two leaders have made a show of working to preserve harmony between the world’s two largest economies, although there were no major breakthroughs on issues such as trade or the safety of artificial intelligence.
Photo: AFP
Trump has been seeking to demonize Democrats as communists during the run-up to the November midterm elections, a message that has been muddied by the red-carpet treatment he has given Xi this week.
The visit comes as the US celebrates the 250th anniversary of its founding, and Trump on Thursday said he wanted to show Xi “some of the greatest treasures of that proud history.”
The archives has a special exhibition marking the semiquincentennial, titled “The American Story,” which highlights the country’s accomplishments and advances, along with images depicting its darker moments.
Trump showed Xi one copy of the Declaration of Independence on Thursday — a wall-mounted copy he keeps in the Oval Office.
The US president also said he wanted to show Xi artifacts about the relationship between the two countries.
“Just as our ancestors reached across the ocean centuries ago to trade, to learn, and to build a better world, our two countries do really the same thing, and we’re very proud of it,” he said.
Xi’s day began at the White House, where Trump and first lady Melania Trump hosted the Chinese leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan (彭?媛), for tea. Their visit falls during the Mid-Autumn Festival, a national holiday when families traditionally gather to celebrate the end of harvest, sharing mooncakes — round pastries filled with a sweet paste — over tea.
The Trumps feted their guests on Thursday night with a black-tie state dinner attended by technology industry titans. Earlier in the day, Trump gave Xi a personal tour of his White House flourishes, including a gallery wall of presidents and a new 30m-long granite helicopter landing pad.
Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan toured the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art.
The two leaders met behind closed doors for 90 minutes on Thursday, when they discussed issues such as the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to the official Chinese government readout of the meeting.
The White House has not provided any information about the private talks.

Taiwan boosts measures to prevent avian flu spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:37 UTC
01:43:37 KST

Taiwan has implemented enhanced measures to prevent an outbreak of the H5N1 virus strain ahead of an expected avian flu spike in winter, the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency said yesterday, as officials in Taoyuan worked to contain the first incident detected on Taiwan proper since 2018.
Patterns in global epidemic data, the combined effects of temperature variances and distress from overcrowded pens on poultry health, and virus-carrying migratory birds suggest a higher risk of a surge in avian flu this winter, the agency said in a news release.
Enhanced H5N1 prevention mechanisms have been instituted, consisting of biosecurity standard compliance inspections, surveillance of poultry farms and tracking migratory bird movements, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Taoyuan Department of Agriculture
The measures, implemented at the beginning of this month, would remain in effect until the end of March next year, it said.
The agency is engaged in itemizing inventories, disseminating information and training foreign workers in the poultry industry as part of preparatory work for the main effort, it said.
Officials are additionally identifying potential infection hot zones and monitoring domesticated birds with high susceptibility to the virus, including quails, egg-laying hens and free-range chickens, it said.
The measures include increasing the frequency of inspections, migratory bird movement alerts, sterilization of potential infection hot zones, and working with industry associations to facilitate monitoring and sanitizing of facilities at private farms, it said.
The Animal Disease Prevention and Prevention Act (動物傳染病防治條例) requires poultry farms to conduct daily health inspections and promptly report abnormalities to the authorities, it said.
A sudden rise in deaths among the fowls or a notable drop in their appetite are signs of avian flu and should be reported immediately, it said.
Failure to comply would result in a fine of up to NT$1 million (US$31,466) and disqualify the farm from government compensation for livestock for disease containment, the agency said.
The agency on Thursday completed the culling of 2,616 guinea fowl at a farm in Taoyuan’s Dayuan District (大園), a day after local authorities reported a confirmed case of H5N1.
It also restricted access to the farm and roads in the area, which have been sterilized.
The affected farm had reported suspicious deaths of its stock on Wednesday, prompting a government response, the agency said.
The agency is inspecting poultry farms within a 3km radius of the affected farm and has not found any evidence of an outbreak, it said.
The incident marked the first H5N1 case in Taiwan proper since 2018, the agency said.

The San Diego Padres are back in the MLB post-season for a franchise-record third consecutive year after a 4-2 win over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday.
Now, they want to win a World Series for the first time, having been there twice only to lose.
Manny Machado fielded Mookie Betts’ groundout to third base for the final out in the victory over the Dodgers that clinched a playoffs berth and the celebration was on.
Photo: AP
“I was feeling nice,” Machado said in the cramped visitors’ clubhouse, his bare chest soaked with a mix of beer and Champagne. “We’re clinching.”
The Padres (89-70) partied inside and then went out on the Dodger Stadium field in matching black T-shirts to pose for photographs.
It is to be their third straight post-season as a wild-card team.
“I’ve never won a championship,” Machado said. “I know what winning looks like. It takes a whole village to do it and we’ve been showing it this year. There’s been a lot of guys contributing in so many ways. It’s awesome to see it being done.”
Fernando Tatis Jr stole two bases for the fourth time this season and extended his on-base streak to 18 games with a walk in the fourth against the Dodgers. He was two for three with an RBI.
“Let’s celebrate,” he screamed above the din in the darkened clubhouse. “We’re here for a reason. We’re ready to compete. We’re here for the long run.”
Photo: William Liang / Imagn Images Warning: Excessive consumption of alcohol can damage your health
The Padres made franchise history under rookie manager Craig Stammen, a surprise pick by general manager A.J. Preller to replace Mike Shildt, who suddenly retired less than two weeks after the Padres were eliminated by the Chicago Cubs 2-1 in the wild-card round last season.
The 42-year-old Stammen was hired less than three years after retiring as a player despite having no coaching or managerial experience at any level. He has been with the organization since 2017 and is best known for starting the deciding Game 3 of the 2020 Wild Card Series against the St Louis Cardinals, who at the time were managed by Shildt. He pitched 1-2/3 innings as the first of nine pitchers the Padres used in the 4-0 win, which clinched their first post-season series victory since 1998.
The Padres popped half a game ahead of the Los Angeles Dodgers on May 18 after Michael King struck out nine and Miguel Andujar hit a solo homer off Yoshinobu Yamamoto in a 1-0 win at Petco Park on May 18, but they lost the next night and fell behind the two-time defending World Series champions by double digits by late June.
They were 48-48 at the All-Star break and in third place in the division and have gone 41-22 since then. They came up with a “pitching chaos” game plan to get them through a difficult period with their rotation, which is still thin without Yu Darvish and Joe Musgrove, who have missed the whole season. Nick Pivetta only recently returned from a long stint on the injured list.
Pivetta fired 4-2/3 scoreless innings on Thursday in his eighth career start against the Dodgers, allowing four hits and striking out seven.
Perhaps the biggest pickup of the off-season was first baseman Ty France, who was signed to a minor-league free-agent deal and made the team out of spring training, his second stint with the Padres. He is from West Covina, California, and played for Tony Gwynn at San Diego State. He has hit a career-high 21 homers and played solid defense.
“I still felt like I had a lot left in the tank and a lot to offer to a team,” France said. “Very grateful and fortunate that it’s here.”

Chicago are back in the post-season for the first time since 2021 after enduring three straight 100-loss seasons. The White Sox remained a game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians.
Chicago hold the head-to-head tiebreaker over Cleveland. Whichever one of those two teams fails to win the division will wind up as the third AL wild-card team.
In Boston, Angel Martinez’s second-inning home run was all visiting Cleveland needed for a 1-0 win over the Red Sox to clinch their third consecutive playoffs berth.
In Chicago, Nico Hoerner ripped a go-ahead RBI single in the sixth inning, while Matthew Boyd tossed seven strong innings to help the Cubs clinch a playoff berth with a 2-1 victory over the Miami Marlins.
Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong walked to lead off the first inning and promptly stole second base to become the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in a single season.
Seiya Suzuki belted a solo homer in the fifth inning to highlight his two-hit performance for the Cubs, who salvaged the finale of their three-game series with Miami.
Chicago are in the second NL wild-card spot, one game behind San Diego.
In Philadelphia, Jake Bauers’ RBI single in the eighth inning plated the go-ahead run for the Milwaukee Brewers, who reached the 100-win mark for the first time in franchise history with a 5-1 win against the Phillies.
When the Dodgers fell to the Padres later, the Brewers clinched the top record in the major leagues.
Philadelphia remained in an NL wild-card spot, but the Phillies could not drop their magic number to clinch from two.

Donovan’s Deep Dives: The Changhua race gets stranger: Wang, Cheng and the mystery of Wei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

The Changhua County commissioner race is the most exciting and dramatic in this election cycle, with surprises within the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) popping up every week or two. Most recently, County Commissioner Wang Huei-mei (王惠美), who is about to term limit out, alleges that KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) pushed for unknown entity Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政) to be the party’s candidate for the position far earlier than was previously known.
If true, Wang’s accusations raise a lot of questions about Cheng and the party leadership’s motives.
Many local factions and power brokers in Changhua are in open revolt against Cheng, and now two of the few powerful local allies she had have been arrested and are being held incommunicado.
Photo courtesy of Wei Ping-cheng’s campaign office
Adding to the KMT’s woes, Changhua County Councilor Chen Chung-chia (陳重嘉), an independent candidate with pan-blue leanings (ideologically closer to the KMT), has joined the race. Chen surprised everyone, including his father, who was a legislator and formerly of the People’s First Party and KMT. Chen had been a TPP member briefly, but quit.
Though not as dramatic and messy, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) had a revolt of their own, splitting the pan-green (DPP-leaning) vote. A former DPP Changhua City mayor, Chiu Chien-fu (邱建富), a party member since 1987, came in third in the party primary. He accused the party of bias, claimed it had lost its original spirit and quit to run as an independent.
The DPP has a solid candidate in legislator Chen Su-yueh (陳素月). Although she keeps a low profile in the press, reportedly she makes an average of around 30 campaign stops a day, starting at 5:30am and finishing late. Party bigwigs both locally and nationally have rallied around her, not Chiu.
Photo: Yen Hung-chun, Taipei Times
An ETtoday poll from last month put Chen ahead at 36.4 percent to Wei’s 19.4 percent and Chiu’s 12.7 percent. The poll, however, is not very useful; nearly a third were undecided, and Chen Chung-chia had not yet entered the race. Wei has announced that his camp will stop conducting internal polling, which was likely both depressing and costly to an underfunded campaign.
WEI’S SURPRISING NOMINATION
The previous story on how Wei became the nominee now has questions hanging over it.
Photo courtesy of Chen Su-yue
Cheng faced a conundrum where no matter what she did, she would be offending powerful local party factions. Cheng had campaigned for Wei in part by excoriating her predecessor as KMT chair, Eric Chu (朱立倫), for his heavy-handed approach of directly choosing party candidates and bypassing the more common primaries — exactly what Cheng did with Wei.
This caused outrage. Wei’s (and Cheng’s) only significant supporters in the county were KMT Changhua County Council Speaker Hsieh Dien-lin (謝典霖) and his family. But now Hsieh Dien-lin and his father are in jail, and his mother is out on bail on suspicion of vote-buying, which may have been paid for by using county council funds. This is a disaster for Wei.
Not only were some candidates still fuming, others, including powerful political figures such as former commissioner Cho Po-yuan (卓伯源), came out demanding that Wei be dumped and a primary be held to replace him. Cho has another axe to grind: he has run twice for KMT chair and lost, the last time to Cheng.
Cheng stood firm, and registration day has now passed.
WANG’S FURY
Most notably, Commissioner Wang Huei-mei absolutely refused to support Wei. Her fury extended to boycotting Cheng’s and the KMT’s events.
Wang’s support is important. She is a second-generation politician and well connected. She won in 2018 with a solid 53 percent, and won re-election in 2022 with a strong 57 percent support.
She has recently heaped praise on the president, premier and local DPP lawmakers for securing government budgets for projects, including tagging DPP candidate Chen Su-yueh on social media. They also show up at official events together.
For a local politician, this is not entirely unusual; thanking the powers that secure local interests is good form. The unusually high praise, especially for Chen, and her resolute rejection of Wei has caused some to speculate Wang may actually want Chen to win.
This is not outlandish; Wang has declared her loyalty to her party and to serving Changhua, and she may calculate that Chen would be more in Changhua’s interests. They’ve worked together before.
Cheng and Wei have been speaking to Wang via the media. Wei has been especially obsequious and fawning in trying to win Wang’s support. He even spent 15 minutes forlornly waiting outside of Wang’s office to offer him an invitation personally, but she did not meet him. He is also leaving the position of campaign manager open for her.
WANG’S BOMBSHELLS
Why is Wang so hostile to Cheng and Wei? She made clear she had wanted New Taipei City Vice Mayor Liu Ho-jan (劉和然) as a compromise candidate, not Wei. However, she made clear she wanted Liu due to his reputation, not through any personal connection — so she was not wedded to him as a candidate. Liu was not interested, though.
Then, early this month, Wang used Facebook to clarify her take on the matter. She stated that she met with Cheng and KMT Vice Chairman Lee Chien-lung (李乾龍) on Dec. 31 last year to discuss the election.
Wang said she initially spoke about the ground game involving borough chiefs and finding a clean candidate for commissioner.
Cheng, Wang said, immediately asked: “Is the attorney Wei Ping-cheng suitable?”
Caught off guard, Wang replied, “I’m not familiar with Attorney Wei.”
She also described other incidents, including Cheng ignoring her phone calls while she was on a trip to Europe to further discuss the nomination.
Wang found out it was a done deal through the news, which, if true, was a serious slight to a powerful local politician.
Then she dropped the bombshell: Looking back, she now believes that Wei had been the party’s sole candidate under consideration from the very beginning.
Why would Cheng be so adamant on picking a total unknown like Wei? There is no obvious connection between the two, and Cheng has referred to not being familiar with him before.
One possibility is that Lee Chien-lung threw his support behind Wei. Lee has held several key posts within the party and is typically tasked with internal party issues. He would likely have known Wei when he was chair of the KMT’s evaluation and discipline committee.
But that still begs the question: why Wei? He is not an obviously logical choice.
Could it be Wang making this up? And if so, why? Why would she take on the party chair and make up lies about her, when Cheng is in a position to significantly influence Wang’s future political career?

Groups react to minimum pay hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

Labor representatives expressed disappointment, while major business groups called for relief measures after a Ministry of Labor committee on Thursday approved a 4.745 percent increase to the minimum wage.
At its annual meeting, the Minimum Wage Deliberation Committee agreed to raise the monthly minimum wage to NT$30,900 from NT$29,500 and the hourly rate to NT$205 from NT$196, effective on Jan. 1 and pending Cabinet approval.
The adjustments, which include a NT$1,400 hike that would take the monthly minimum wage above NT$30,000 for the first time, are expected to benefit about 2.61 million people, including 414,400 migrant workers.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Tai Kuo-jung (戴國榮), one of the labor representatives on the committee, said after the meeting that they had pushed for a 7.77 percent increase so workers could share more fully in the benefits of economic growth, with this year’s GDP projected to rise 11.05 percent.
Employer representatives initially sought an increase of no more than 3 percent, arguing that industries had contributed to Taiwan’s economic growth to varying degrees, Tai said.
Employer representatives had argued that the NT$1,400 increase demonstrated their willingness to compromise, as monthly minimum wage increases in the past few years had not exceeded NT$1,250, he said.
However, labor representatives rejected that argument, Tai said.
“If we are going to look at the previous high of NT$1,250 for the monthly wage increase, why can’t we also look at this year’s economic growth rate?” he said.
The final result fell short of labor representatives’ expectations, Tai said.
Cheng Li-chia (鄭力嘉), another labor representative, described the result as “unsatisfactory, but acceptable.”
Meanwhile, business groups said that the increase would put additional pressure on firms that had not benefited equally from recent economic growth.
General Chamber of Commerce of the Republic of China chairman Hsu Shu-po (許舒博) said that labor-intensive and traditional industries rely heavily on migrant workers, meaning a higher minimum wage would increase their labor costs.
For small, medium-sized and micro businesses with limited ability to pass higher costs on to customers, the impact would extend beyond wages, as the increase would also raise employers’ statutory contributions to labor insurance, labor pensions and National Health Insurance, which are tied to workers’ pay, Hsu said.
The government should consider shouldering a larger share of insurance costs, as employers pay 70 percent of labor insurance premiums for employees, compared with 20 percent paid by workers and just 10 percent by the government, he said.
He also called for eligibility requirements to be relaxed and application procedures simplified for government support measures aimed at helping businesses cope with the minimum wage increase.
The Chinese National Association of Industry and Commerce, Taiwan urged the government to provide financing and other substantive support to help small and medium-sized enterprises upgrade and transform their operations as the minimum wage is raised.
Support would help businesses boost productivity and increase the added value of their products, it said.

World Vegetable Center welcomes first female leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

The World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg) welcomed its first female leader, Izabella Koziell, who pledged to boost the global food system’s climate resilience and deepening cooperation with Taiwan.
Koziell took over the post of director-general at the center from her predecessor, Marco Wopereis, becoming the center’s first female leader since it was established 55 years ago in 1971.
The seal handover ceremony was held at the center’s headquarters in Tainan on Monday last week, with Minister of Agriculture Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) attending the ceremony.
Photo: Wu Chun-feng, Taipei Times
Koziell previously served as deputy director of the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development and was responsible for various programs in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.
She said in her address that vegetables are undervalued even though they can be applied to addressing some critical challenges of our time.
WorldVeg’s scientific research and innovations can bring practical, feasible solutions and open new possibilities, particularly as the world is facing economic uncertainty, climate change and biodiversity losses, Koziell said.
HIGH-QUALITY CROPS
WorldVeg will make high-quality crop varieties accessible to more agricultural workers based on its excellent research capabilities, germplasm resources and global partner networks, she said.
People around the world would be able to obtain nutrient-rich vegetables more easily at affordable prices, Koziell said.
Future efforts would focus on improving nutrition, food security and the livelihoods of low-income farming households in developing countries, she said, adding that WorldVeg would continue to strengthen its research capacity.
Koziell said she would enhance WorldVeg’s partnership with Taiwan, including the Ministry of Agriculture, Academia Sinica, as well as the nation’s colleges and private sector.
Public-private collaborations would be stepped up in six major action areas — climate resilience, healthy diets, vegetable diversity, economic empowerment, urban food systems, and food safety and food loss, she said.
Chen said WorldVeg has achieved much under the leadership of Wopereis, adding that the organization continued growing with renewed software and hardware facilities.
WorldVeg not only shares its successful research and development with the world, but also assists Taiwan in participating in global agricultural development, he said.
That is significantly meaningful to Taiwan, Chen said.
TAIWAN SUPPORT
The government will continue to support WorldVeg’s development amid international challenges, he said, urging WorldVeg to promptly submit the headquarters’ second-phase facilities enhancement project to the ministry.
The ministry will provide related resources to maintain the close partnership with WorldVeg, he added.
Gordon Rogers, vice chair of the board of directors at WorldVeg, said Koziell has extensive experience in science, policy and implementation.
She has a deep understanding of the climate and environmental challenges facing the global food system, as well as their potential solutions, he said, adding that Koziell is an ideal person to lead WorldVeg’s next stage of growth.
WorldVeg is headquartered in Taiwan and has regional centers and offices across Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean.
It works with global partners to develop high-quality vegetable varieties and conserve vegetable diversity, dedicating itself to enhancing seed systems and value chains, it states.
It is promoting the “WorldVeg Plan for 2026-2033,” with the goal of boosting the scale and influence of the world’s vegetable research and innovations, it states.
