Experts advise healthier diets for kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:32 UTC
01:43:32 KST

Child health experts urged families to promote healthier diets to avoid obesity and fatty liver disease.
Speaking at the launch of community-based nutritional programs for children sponsored by the Mustard Seed Mission and Quaker Oat Co in Taoyuan on Aug. 22, nutritionist Chen Hsiu-wen (陳琇雯) said that a study of 440 obese children in Taiwan showed that 19.5 percent had a fatty liver.
A separate survey by the Child Welfare League Foundation showed that 30.2 percent of Taiwanese aged 10 to 12 years old were overweight or obese, higher than the 25 percent global average according to WHO statistics, she said.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
The foundation poll also found that children drink at least one bubble tea-type beverage a week, 21.3 percent eat sweet snacks or desserts daily, and 63.2 percent regularly eat dinners that are rich in carbohydrates, but low in protein, she said.
Parents should make sure their children not only eat enough food, but also that the food is nutritious and promotes health, Chen said.
Parents are too often concentrated on ensuring their children gain weight and height, without regard to the kind of foods they consume, she said.
Taiwanese children are eating too much refined sugar, fatty and ultraprocessed foods, and not enough quality protein, dietary fiber and micronutrients, such as iron, calcium and zinc, she said.
The unbalanced diet leads to increased risks of fatty liver disease, obesity and diabetes, she said, adding that the early teenage years are a key developmental stage for a person’s health later in life.
Parents should regulate their children’s consumption of cakes and sugary drinks, as surges in blood sugar could trigger insulin insensitivity that leads to diabetes, she said.
Good carbohydrates should replace refined sugar and ultraprocessed foods such as cakes to ensure stable blood sugar levels and mental concentration, Chen said.
This means eating unsalted nuts, whole-grain bread, whole-grain oats, yam and brown rice in meals, she said.
Many of these same foods are rich in dietary fiber, which boosts gut and metabolic health, and removes excess cholesterol, Chen said.
Fish, eggs, lean meat, tofu, sugarless soybean and dairy should be the main sources of protein for children, with a vegetable side dish in each meal, she said, adding that whole fruits should be served in place of juice.
Pick unsaturated fat, which strengthens cardiovascular health, Chen said.
Child development expert Wang Hung-che (王宏哲) said parents should deal with picky eaters by involving them in food preparation and offering alternative dishes, instead of forcing them to eat food they dislike.

Yodelers take their voices to underground parking lot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

No mountains to practice on? No problem. Yodeling fans in Austria have moved their practice sessions to an underground parking garage, since it produces echoes like those they can get in the landscapes of the Alps.
“It’s not too dissimilar to the high mountains,” yodeling teacher Anna Maria Gutschi said as she led a group of 30 people through an empty parking garage earlier this week. “You have wide hallways; you have walls that reflect a lot.”
Gutschi works for the Styrian Volksliedwerk, a cultural organization promoting traditional folk music in the southeastern Austrian city of Graz — which is not in the high mountains, but sits in a flat basin surrounded by hills and low mountain ranges at the edge of the Alps.
Photo: AP
The group has been holding a series of courses on yodeling in unusual places to keep the tradition alive in modern times. Whether it is an underground car park, a canal or a gas station — as long as the acoustics work, up to 30 people are allowed to join each time for a unique experience.
“It’s a form of communication from mountain to mountain — just like that, without the need for a phone,” Gutschi said, describing the art of yodeling as she let her voice wander up and down the scales. “And it’s not as boring as writing an SMS. Sounds much better, too.”
“The energy is rising, it’s rising and rising,” Gutschi said as she explained the unique melodic tradition to her students. “Ever higher and then it wants out on top and there it goes.”
For more than one hour, the yodelers walked through the city’s largest underground parking garage, practicing their yodeling skills until they had reached the deepest part of the garage — and the best conditions for a great sound.
While some participants were already experienced yodelers, newcomers to the craft also were welcome to join this subterranean class.
Jamey Sohn, from South Korea, who is studying sustainable development in Graz, decided to take the class to immerse herself in Austrian culture.
“When I actually came here, it was a lot more — well, I wouldn’t say easy per se, but it’s a lot more approachable than I first expected,” Sohn said.
Yodeling emerged centuries ago as a way of communicating in the Alps over long distances — not just between people, but also between man and animal. Cattle would recognize their owner from his voice and return to the stable from far away.
Over time, this primeval form of singing has evolved into its own musical genre first made popular internationally by the US musical film The Sound of Music.
For Thomas Button, a teacher from New York, yodeling is “like a form of meditation. Singing meditation.”
“It’s hard to describe how much power you get from yodeling together, the energy from within,” local yodeling fan Rudolf Schmidhofer said. “The togetherness, the polyphonic kind of yodeling where you must listen to each other.”
“I’m still a student when it comes to this, but I like it very much,” he added.

EDITORIAL: Adult guardianship a pressing issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

The Ministry of Health and Welfare on Wednesday asked the Taipei City Government to launch an administrative investigation after a former supervisor at the Taipei Department of Social Welfare’s Senior Citizen Welfare Division was detained on suspicion of embezzlement.
The 38-year-old social worker, surnamed Chiang (江), reportedly used her position, which she held for about one year, to misappropriate a total of NT$12 million (US$377,596) from five elderly people under guardianship in Taipei’s Wenshan District (文山). An investigation after the department noticed funds were missing and a subsequent search of her home uncovered several luxury items including handbags.
The incident raises serious questions about how Taiwan’s social welfare system protects elderly people who, because of illness, disability or cognitive decline, can no longer independently manage their finances, property and other affairs. It should also prompt a broader re-evaluation of the nation’s adult guardianship system.
Taiwan officially became a super-aged society this year, with people aged 65 or older accounting for more than 20 percent of the population. That share is expected to rise as the birthrate continues to fall, with elderly people projected to make up 37 percent of the population by 2045. As the nation ages, more people would require institutional protections and welfare support if physical illness or cognitive decline leaves them unable to live on their own or make decisions independently.
This issue is particularly pressing as the prevalence and growth rate of dementia in Taiwan are estimated to be about 1.5 times the global average. Longer life expectancy does not necessarily mean longer healthy life expectancy, and if this trend continues, more Taiwanese could spend their later years with conditions that affect their cognitive abilities.
The Chiang case becomes even more significant when viewed in this context. If the allegations against her are true, it would mean one ill-intentioned person was able to exploit her position to embezzle millions from five vulnerable people in just 13 months. For elderly people who do not have family members willing or able to monitor their finances or advocate on their behalf, safeguards against such abuse are vital. As the number of people requiring guardianship grows, so does the potential consequences of inadequate oversight.
Chou Tao-chun (周道君), director of the ministry’s Social and Family Affairs Administration, this week highlighted differences between Taiwan and Japan, where professional third parties play a much larger role in adult guardianship. In 2022, 80.9 percent of court-appointed guardians in Japan were people other than family members, such as lawyers. Taiwan’s government is discussing whether such an approach could be introduced.
Japan’s experience is worth examining, not because its system is without flaws, but because it has had considerably more time to confront the challenges that come with an aging population.
Japan became the world’s first super-aged society in 2007. Its adult guardianship system has consequently undergone significant changes in the past two decades, including what researchers describe as the “socialization” of adult guardianship, in which professional third parties have increasingly taken on roles once played by family members.
Japan is still in the process of reforming its system. In April, the Japanese government passed a bill to overhaul adult guardianship, including allowing support recipients greater flexibility to end support or replace guardians. The new system would also allow certain asset-related transactions to be revoked when support recipients are found to lack the capacity to make appropriate judgements.
These reforms reflect the crucial principle that guardianship and elder care serve to protect people’s health, safety, rights and property, rather than simply grant control over them — a principle Taiwan’s authorities must carefully consider.
Regardless of its outcome, the ongoing case is an opportunity to re-examine this portion of Taiwan’s social safety net to bolster oversight, accountability and mechanisms to prevent abuse and conflicts of interest. The primary goal should be to ensure that when social welfare services, such as professional guardianship, are needed, the procedures and professionals involved are subject to clear standards, independent supervision and regular financial review.
The topic of elder care and the protection of elderly people’s rights would only become more relevant as the structure of Taiwan’s population continues to change. The accusations against Chiang have not only highlighted the potential vulnerabilities of a system that would face growing demands in the years ahead, but also opened a window for the government to meaningfully re-evaluate and improve the existing framework before these challenges become even more difficult to address.
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from

Parties outline agendas with legislature to restart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:30 UTC
01:43:30 KST

The new legislative session is to begin on Tuesday next week, with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) prioritizing cash handouts and the central government budget, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) focusing on business support, family policies and welfare, and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) pushing measures on people’s livelihoods, transportation, childbirth and end-of-life rights.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) is scheduled to deliver a policy address on the first day of the sixth session of the 11th Legislative Yuan, expected to be accompanied by ministers and agency heads.
No question-and-answer session is planned.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
A roll-call vote on Control Yuan nominations is scheduled shortly afterward at 10am.
The new session would focus on next year’s central government budget, which includes a proposal to issue cash handouts, as well as a supplementary budget for this year, a KMT caucus member said yesterday.
If the cash handouts are to be issued in the Lunar New Year period, the Legislative Yuan could approve the funds separately, leaving lawmakers to review the rest of the government budget as usual, the KMT source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
The proposal has yet to be finalized and would need approval from the KMT caucus and coordination with the TPP caucus, they said.
KMT lawmakers are still discussing whether to include the funds in a special budget or use another approach, the source added.
The KMT has proposed cash payments of NT$20,000 to NT$30,000 per person, while the government has planned NT$10,000 payments.
DPP caucus secretary-general Fan Yun (范雲) said that the Executive Yuan has prepared more than 40 priority bills focusing on three main areas: helping businesses, supporting families and expanding welfare.
The bills include a Small, Medium and Micro Enterprise Transformation and Upgrading Development Act, as well as amendments to the Gender Equality in Employment Act (性別平等工作法) and the Employment Insurance Act (就業保險法), which are being negotiated by the caucuses in the Legislative Yuan, Fan said.
Other priorities include allowances for elderly farmers, national pensions, protections for people with disabilities, and preventing the sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, she added.
The TPP caucus said its priority bills would be centered around four themes: supporting livelihoods, improving transportation, boosting the birthrate and upholding dignity.
That would include amendments to the Income Tax Act (所得稅法) to expand tax breaks for tenants and parents, the TPP said.
Proposed amendments to the Gender Equality in Employment Act and the Employment Insurance Act would expand parental leave, add an allowance for family caregiving leave and flexible working hours, and extend maternity leave to 14 weeks, it said.
The TPP also hopes to legalize surrogacy through amendments to the Assisted Reproduction Act (人工生殖法), increase the monthly allowance for elderly farmers and amend the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法) so that the central government can fully subsidize health insurance premiums for elderly people, it said.
It would continue pushing to legalize euthanasia, it said, adding proposed amendments to the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (道路交通管理處罰條例) would ensure that traffic fines are earmarked for specific purposes.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:28 UTC
01:43:28 KST

The Ministry of Agriculture is for the first time leading a delegation of agricultural and fishery operators to participate in the Taiwan Expo USA, with the goal of building North American supply chain partnerships.
The delegation has set up a Taiwan Agricultural Products Pavilion at the exhibition at Kay Bailey Hutchison Convention Center Dallas in Texas, which runs from Thursday through today, the ministry said yesterday.
Taiwan is presenting its smart agricultural technology, cold-chain logistics and premium agricultural foods to inform local sales channels, import distributors and food and beverage industry about Taiwan’s advanced produce preservation and quality control, the ministry said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Agriculture
The pavilion showcases Taiwanese produce ranging from smart seafood products and frozen fruit and vegetables to ready-to-eat foods, tea beverages and snack foods, it said.
Taiwan’s participation in the expo was previously restricted to product sample displays, but this year Taiwanese industry representatives are attending in person for the first time, the ministry said.
The goal is to help Taiwanese produce enter North American premium food markets to counter the impact of US tariffs and global supply chain restructuring, it said.
The ministry would continue to assist the domestic agricultural and fishery industries in building long-term, stable supply chain partnerships with the North American market, it said.
Separately, Taiwanese premium agricultural products are also available at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport from this month, the Agriculture and Food Agency said yesterday.
A specialty food section has been set up at the Hsin Tung Yang store (新東陽) in Terminal 1 and the Tasa Meng duty free shop (采盟) in Terminal 2, it said.
Rice snacks made of local produce such as pineapple cakes, black soybean crunch and rice egg rolls, as well as tea drinks like organic hibiscus tea and barley tea, are available, the agency said.
Travelers could also purchase candied kumquat gift boxes cobranded with the National Palace Museum, it said.
Promotional discounts are available during the opening period running from today through Friday next week, as well as the Double Ten National Day holiday next month and the Double Eleven shopping spree festival in November, the agency said.
Customers can enjoy a 30 percent discount for purchases of any three items, it said..

Taiwan trade surplus to hit US$205.4bn on back of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:28 UTC
01:43:28 KST

The central bank forecasts Taiwan’s overall trade surplus to hit US$205.4 billion this year as it emerges as a global artificial intelligence (AI) hardware manufacturing hub.
The nation’s projected trade surplus this year is 4.2 times the US$49.2 billion surplus in 2018, when the US-China spat over tariffs started, it said in a report on structural changes to Taiwanese trade and investment since that year.
The growth of Taiwan’s AI hardware manufacturing sector was spurred by a US effort to build without Chinese supply chains, the report said.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
The US’ trade deficit is anticipated to exceed US$1.1 trillion, with Taiwan as its third-largest source at US$219.2 billion, following Vietnam at US$238 billion and Mexico at US$221 billion, it said.
China would be the fourth-largest at US$156.4 billion, the central bank said.
Taiwan is becoming a crucial manufacturing node in the global division of labor, with US-bound server exports boosting the nation’s development of semiconductor-making and advanced chip packaging technology, it said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
The nation imports South Korean memory chips and Japanese wafer fabrication equipment and materials, while outsourcing medium and low-technology manufacturing to ASEAN member states, the report said.
These industrial relationships put Taiwan at the center of global AI supply chains, it said.
The electronics industry has also moved away from the trade model of making products in China and selling them in the US market, the report said.
High-value added, tariffed, technologically advanced or cybersecurity-sensitive goods are now predominantly made in Taiwan, while medium and low-tech products are assembled in the US or ASEAN countries, it said.
The local production share in exports reached a record high of 52.9 percent last year, up 5.3 percentage points from 2018, the report said, adding that the share of orders produced in China dropped to 26.2 percent, a steep decline of 20.7 percentage points over the same period.
Production shares in ASEAN and the US rose to 11.3 percent and 5 percent respectively, a growth of 9.7 and 4.1 percentage points compared with 2018, it said.
Taiwanese investments in China this year are expected to drop further, a departure from Taiwanese enterprises’ long-standing strategy of investing in China, which had prevailed for much of the past 30 years, the report said.
The companies used to outsource manufacturing to China to keep costs down and increase efficiency, facilitating the latter’s rise as the world’s leading producer of consumer electronics, it added.
The rise in production costs and geopolitical risks in China has changed the equation, driving businesses to reorient their trade ties toward Japan, the US and Southeast Asia, it said.
Developed countries are also changing their policy stance, choosing to establish domestic chip manufacturing capabilities and strategically valuable materials, the report said.
Taiwan’s cumulative direct investment ratio in China in 2017 was 58.3 percent, but has plummeted to 18.8 percent between 2018 and last year, it said.
The US has supplanted China as Taiwan’s most important investment destination, the report said.
The nation’s cumulative direct investment ratio in the US from 2018 to last year increased to 18.7 percent, while the proportion of total outward investment directed at the US in 2023 and 2024 was 36.4 percent and 29.1 percent respectively, it added.

City mayor  boasts of discovering social fraud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:24 UTC
01:43:24 KST

A former supervisor at the Taipei Department of Social Welfare’s Senior Citizen Welfare Division, surnamed Chiang (江), allegedly used her position to embezzle more than NT$12 million (US$377,596) from the savings of five elderly people under guardianship from May last year to June this year.
The most outrageous aspect of this case is not merely the suspected criminal activity itself, but that such a substantial sum could have been misappropriated over such a lengthy period, and that the discrepancy was not detected through routine audits or standard account reconciliation. It was only after Chiang transferred to New Taipei City, and her successor reviewed the accounts and transactions, that the missing funds were discovered.
A preliminary investigation claimed that Chiang took advantage of certain opportunities — such as paying placement fees for the elderly — to overstate the required amounts and withdraw more than necessary before pocketing the difference.
The funds were withdrawn through several transactions, which raises an obvious question: Did no one reconcile the individuals’ accounts during that 13-month period? If they did, how were these discrepancies overlooked? If they did not, then the underlying problem is much more severe than an individual case of embezzlement.
The social welfare department said that there are standard operating procedures for managing such funds. It should therefore answer some fundamental questions: Who was responsible for reviewing the accounts? How often were they reviewed? And why did no one notice anything was wrong?
These elderly people needed government intervention because they were unable to manage their finances on their own, yet more than NT$12 million was allegedly withdrawn from their accounts for more than one year without being detected.
What exactly was the government monitoring? After the case came to light, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said that it was the result of the department’s “proactive discovery” of the anomaly, investigation and report to prosecutors.
However, the employee who committed the crime had left, and it was only when a colleague who took over her position reviewed the accounts that the discrepancy was discovered. Can that be called “proactively discovering” the issue?
It is akin to a homeowner hiring a security firm to guard the house, only for one of its employees to steal from the house for more than a year. The theft is discovered only after the employee leaves and their replacement takes inventory to find that things are missing. The company’s chairman then comes out and says they “proactively discovered” the theft.
In that situation, what the homeowner would probably want to know is not who eventually discovered that their belongings were missing from their home, but how, after the firm had been entrusted to watch the house for more than a year, things could repeatedly disappear right under the company’s nose.
Reporting the case was the right thing to do, and whistle-blowing was also the right thing to do. But, Mayor Chiang, this still does not qualify as a “proactive discovery.”
Chang Shang-yang is a farmer.

Changhua couple hospitalized with dengue fever: CDC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:24 UTC
01:43:24 KST

A married couple from Changhua County has been hospitalized with dengue fever after returning from a trip to Vietnam’s Phu Quoc Island, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday, classifying the cases as an imported family cluster.
The other 19 members of their tour group, who reside in Taichung, Tainan, Hsinchu and Nantou County, are being monitored by local health bureaus, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) said.
The couple traveled to Phu Quoc with relatives from Sept. 12 to Tuesday last week, and developed symptoms on Saturday and Sunday last week, with one of them also exhibiting a skin rash, Lin said.
Photo courtesy of the Changhua County Public Health Bureau
They sought medical attention at a hospital outpatient clinic on Monday and visited an emergency room the following day as their symptoms persisted, he said.
They tested positive on dengue NS1 rapid tests and on Wednesday were confirmed to be infected, with their samples sent to the CDC for retesting and gene sequencing, he added.
Epidemiological investigations showed that after returning to Taiwan, the couple mainly worked near their residence in Changhua County, dined at a local hot pot restaurant, shopped at a hardware store and delivered goods to neighboring townships before developing symptoms, Lin said.
Their residential area has reported no other confirmed dengue cases this year, and while nearby townships have seen imported cases, discrepancies in timing and distance rule out local transmission, Lin said, adding that they were likely infected in Vietnam.
While only the couple lives in their household, the CDC has notified health bureaus in the four other regions to monitor the health of the 21-member tour group.
Local health authorities on Wednesday inspected 75 households around the couple’s residence and found 38 water-filled containers, 13 of which were breeding vector mosquitoes, indicating a high mosquito density in the area.
Chemical fumigation was completed on Thursday to prevent community transmission.
As of Thursday, Taiwan had recorded 163 imported dengue cases this year, CDC data showed.
During the same period from 2022 to last year, there were 38, 164, 216 and 177 cases respectively.
The CDC reminded the public to take anti-mosquito precautions when traveling to dengue-endemic areas.
Those who develop symptoms such as a fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, muscle and joint pain, or rash within two weeks of returning to Taiwan should seek immediate medical attention and inform doctors of their travel history, it said.
As current temperatures remain conducive to mosquito breeding, the public should regularly empty stagnant water containers in and around their homes to lower the risk of disease transmission, the agency added.

Taiwan’s Wang Kuan-hung bags men’s 200m butterfly gold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:23 UTC
01:43:23 KST

Taiwanese swimmer Wang Kuan-hung (王冠閎) won the men’s 200m butterfly gold medal at the Asian Games in Japan yesterday, leading a 10-men final in 1 minute, 55.05 seconds.
Xu Fang (徐放) of China took silver in 1 minute, 55.65 seconds, while Kim Min-seop of South Korea won bronze in 1 minute, 55.94 seconds.
Wang, who finished eighth in the men’s 100m butterfly earlier in the Games, showed his medal-winning form in his strongest event, advancing from the heats before securing the gold in the final at the Tokyo Aquatics Center.
Photo: Reuters
The 24-year-old won silver in the same event at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, ending a 25-year medal drought for Taiwan’s male swimmers.
Speaking to reporters after the final, Wang said that the victory felt “unreal” to him.
He said he had been under considerable pressure and was very happy to finally win the gold medal, adding that he had been unable to sleep the night before and on Friday afternoon.
Wang also said that he had sustained a sudden back injury several days before the competition.
A doctor diagnosed him with acute tendon inflammation, which initially left him, his coach and his physical therapist worried and unsure how to proceed.
Wang said he reminded himself to stay relaxed and give it his all despite the injury, thanking his coach, physical therapist and supporters for giving him confidence.
The swimmer said his coach told him earlier in the day that he had a good chance of winning in the final, urging him to stay focused and maintain his pace.
“I just focused on my own lane,” Wang said.
He said he swam hard from the start and did not realize he was leading until the 150m mark, after which he gave it his all to reach the finish.
As Wang continues to rewrite Taiwan’s men’s swimming record at the Asian Games, he said he hopes to pass on his experience to younger swimmers and let them know that success is possible if they believe in themselves.
Asked about his next goal, Wang laughed and said he had not thought about it yet.

Two distinct Taiwan experiences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:17 UTC
01:43:17 KST

On the surface, a radio interview with Democratic Progressive Party and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) hosted by television producer Wang Wei-chung (王偉忠) on Sept. 10 came across as an old-time city resident putting questions to a candidate on the campaign trail. Beneath that, however, it was an encounter between two distinct Taiwanese experiences, two generations and two different political vocabularies.
Wang grew up in a military dependents’ village. His parents came to Taiwan with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government, carrying with them the legacy of war, displacement, the loss of a homeland, and an identification with Chinese culture and the Republic of China. The accents, food, family relationships and memories of military dependents’ villages are all part of Taiwan’s postwar history. They are deserving of preservation and should not be erased.
The question is not whether people from military dependents’ villages can tell their own stories, but what place those stories once occupied.
During the authoritarian era, the experiences of military dependents’ villages were intertwined with state education, the military establishment and mass media. They became the centerpiece of the national narrative. The displacement of mainlander communities was portrayed as a national tragedy shared by all, and Chinese history was the primary history taught to the people of Taiwan.
By contrast, the experiences of Taiwan’s local society — including the 228 Incident, the White Terror and suppression of local languages — were forced into decades of silence. Nostalgia surrounding military dependents’ villages is not just about memory; it is also about a connection to power.
Wang is a media professional who has long wielded prolific influence over the production of popular entertainment. He has allowed many people to see the everyday life, humor and family bonds of these communities, preserving a piece of history that is gradually disappearing. However, every narrative has its frame: When the camera focuses on the warmth and nostalgia within the villages, the authoritarian rule of the party-state and the scars borne by local Taiwanese society beyond their walls can recede into the background.
Democratization does not mean erasing memories of military dependents’ villages. It means giving those previously silenced an opportunity to speak as well. It did not deprive mainlanders of their rights, but ended the era in which a single group monopolized the authority to define the nation. Nevertheless, those who took their former advantages for granted may experience equality as deprivation, and those who took their own memories to be a shared history may mistake the emergence of other voices for exclusion.
Wang delivered his questions positioned as a Taipei old-timer, sharing many of his own experiences, cutting in, adding thoughts and presupposing the answers to various questions. His way of speaking to Shen carried something of the air of an elder: I have lived longer than you, seen more than you have, and am better qualified to tell you what Taipei is and how politics should be conducted.
Shen, by contrast, used a different political vocabulary: institutions, data, civic participation and methods of governance. He neither dismisses the experiences of older generations nor accepts experience itself as an answer. Democratic politics can respect seniority and credentials, but policies must still be tested against evidence, procedure and public accountability.
From the outset, the interview was bound to contain points of contention and reflect generational differences and imbalances in who gets to speak and be heard. Nonetheless, the conversation was meaningful. Understanding does not necessarily mean agreement, and dialogue alone does not dissolve prejudice. Its value lies in forcing both sides to see the complexity of the other, making it harder to reduce the other person to the image constructed in their mind.
Military dependents’ villages can continue to tell their own stories; a democratic Taiwan allows everyone to tell theirs. However, only when no one believes that their own memories to be the whole story can a dialogue begin and understanding take place.
Yu Ming is a registered architect.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:10 UTC
01:43:10 KST

Flights were suspended and Internet services disrupted across parts of northern Ethiopia as fighting spread and the government said it had killed 272 rebels, raising fears of a return to the brutal civil war that ended in 2022.
The renewed fighting comes four years after Ethiopia signed a peace deal with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) — ending a two-year war that killed more than half a million people — which said this week that it had formed an alliance with other rebel groups to take on the government. Conflict in Ethiopia risks conflagration in the wider region, with civil war in neighboring Sudan ongoing and simmering tensions with Eritrea.
The newly formed Alliance for Survival said it launched “large-scale defensive operations” on Wednesday in response to attacks by federal forces in Tigray, Afar and Amhara regions. It accused the government of cutting key public services in those areas.
Photo: AFP
The risk of renewed all-out conflict has deepened over disputed territory, the return of displaced people and the future of Tigray’s political leadership. The alliance brings together rebel groups in the Tigray, Oromia, Amhara, Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions.
“The army is currently reading the situation of the enemy and carrying out counter attacks,” Ethiopia’s army said in a statement on Thursday.
A government spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
In recent days, forces affiliated with the TPLF have taken control of several airports including in Mekele and fighting in Lalibela led to the city’s airport being closed.
US ambassador to Ethiopia Ervin J. Massinga said he was “disappointed to see the leadership of the TPLF” had launched “a large-scale offensive.”
The EU and the UK have called for immediate de-escalation.
“We condemn the attacks by the Tigray Defence Forces in Afar and southern Tigray, and the takeover of Tigray’s airports following the removal of legitimate federal authorities. All parties must refrain from further escalation,” a UK government spokesperson said in a statement on Thursday.
The northern Tigray region also faced an Internet outage.
“Network data indicate a sub national internet disruption in northern #Ethiopia corresponding to reports of a telecoms blackout in #Tigray,” Internet monitoring group NetBlocks wrote on X. “The incident comes amid escalating conflict between Tigrayan forces and the national army.”
Violence in the restive northern region resumed on Wednesday when federal troops pushed back against forces affiliated with the TPLF that has taken control of several airports in the region.
How the situation evolves depends on the number of fronts that open in the coming days and weeks, and the rebels’ capacity to successfully launch joint operations, analysts said.
“How will the government respond? With restraint or with total war? That now looks like the key question,” said Alan Boswell, project director for the Horn of Africa at the International Crisis Group.

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson on Thursday joined the chorus of policymakers saying additional interest-rate increases may be needed to ensure inflation returns to the central bank’s 2 percent goal.
“Looking ahead, if conditions evolve as I expect, some modest further tightening may be warranted,” Paulson said on Thursday at an event in Philadelphia.
Earlier on Thursday, New York Fed President John Williams said he and his colleagues “still have a lot of work to do” in dealing with lingering inflation risks.
Photo: Reuters
Several other officials have aired similar comments, in line with the signal given last week when policymakers voted unanimously to raise their benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point and issued projections pointing to at least one more rate hike this year.
Investors, reacting to solid economic data and policymaker remarks, have lifted expectations for a rate increase next month to about 65 percent from 53 percent at the end of last week. The Fed’s next policy meeting concludes on Oct. 28, six days before congressional mid-term elections.
The comments are likely to increase tensions developing between the Fed and the White House. On Wednesday National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett criticized policymakers for their views.
“A lot of the people who weren’t appointed by President Trump are giving speeches over the last couple of days, saying we need a lot more hikes,” Hassett said.
Paulson, who votes on policy decisions this year, said the move was needed because underlying measures of inflation, which strip out energy and food prices, remain “stubbornly elevated.”
“This recalibration brings policy closer to what I believe is needed to return inflation to 2 percent at a pace that balances inflation with risks to the labor market,” she said.
Paulson said the US economy has been resilient to shocks, with output growth solid and the labor market near full employment. She said she sees signs of “increased momentum.”
While tariff-related effects on consumer prices have eased, price pressures grew from the conflict in the Middle East and the build-out of data centers related to artificial intelligence. Wage growth, on the other hand, remains modest and signals that labor costs are not adding inflationary pressures, she added.
“The best I can say about underlying inflation this year is that it hasn’t gotten worse,” Paulson said.
The Philadelphia Fed chief said underlying inflation has shown little to no progress. She said measures are running in a range of 2.5 to 3 percent, showing little signs of easing to the Fed’s target.
Also speaking on Thursday, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said the US economy is facing a series of supply shocks, increasing the risk that an inflationary mindset takes hold.
Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin, in Washington, said a broad range of persistent cost pressures this summer — from tariffs and tech price increases, to rising fuel and healthcare expenses — raised the risk that inflation in the US could become entrenched, making tighter policy necessary.

The agreement builds on a previous US$1.8 billion computing deal that the two companies struck earlier this year. Anthropic has seen demand for its Claude software soar in recent months with customers flocking to its tools to streamline the process of coding and other tasks. The AI developer has been on a buying spree for the computing necessary to meet that growing demand, tapping companies from Alphabet Inc’s Google to Elon Musk’s SpaceX for access to chips.
Photo: Reuters
Akamai generates the vast majority of sales from its content delivery and cybersecurity services, but the company, in search of more growth opportunities, has been rapidly expanding into the computing space. The contract with Anthropic represents the largest deal in the firm’s history, and the company estimated that its capital spending tied to the Anthropic agreement alone will total about US$5.5 billion — more than six times what it spent in all of last year.
Shares of Akamai jumped 17 percent in late trading on Thursday to US$129.60 at about 4:10pm New York time.
Akamai’s cloud business is “growing obviously extremely fast,” Akamai chief executive officer Tom Leighton said in an interview. At this rate, the company’s revenue associated with cloud contracts could eclipse sales from its other segments “fairly soon,” he said. “We’re not looking necessarily at a long time frame for that to happen.”
Akamai said a part of the warrant issued to Anthropic, representing about 2 percent of Akamai’s common stock, vests with the computing agreement, which is expected to begin in the second half of next year. The rest is scheduled to come available over the course of the seven-year deal.
Some Wall Street investors have raised concerns about so-called circular AI deals in which cloud, hardware and AI companies that buy one another’s products are also directly investing in one another, saying the pacts make it more difficult to quantify real demand for AI.
This is the first time Akamai has agreed to such a warrant as part of a cloud deal with a customer, Leighton said. “It’s a serious step, but I think in this case it made sense to do,” he said. “It helps bring the companies together.”
Akamai expects revenue from the Anthropic business to total about US$150 million to US$300 million next year.
“By the time we’re through to 2028, it’ll be an annual run rate of about US$1.7 billion,” Leighton said.
The bulk of capital spending that Akamai is planning to fulfill the Anthropic contract will go toward hardware such as servers, chips and networking gear, and most of it will occur next year, Leighton said.
While acknowledging that it is a “big step up in capex” for the company, he said the returns are strong and the company is discussing even more business with “all the major players,” including the largest data center operators known as hyperscalers and big enterprises.

Rebellious Afghan taxi drivers defy ban on music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Taxi drivers in Afghanistan are turning on the tunes in their cars, defying a ban imposed by the Taliban government despite the fear of getting caught by morality police.
The music that used to flow constantly out of restaurants, cafes and shops in Kabul has been muted for five years, replaced only by religious or patriotic songs supported by the Taliban authorities.
However, taxi drivers such as Roeen have started playing Afghan and regional folk or pop music, which they quickly turn off when security forces might be around.
Photo: AFP
“At every checkpoint we pass, we lower the volume of the music or even turn it off completely... so I don’t get into trouble with them,” said Roeen, who gave only his first name for security reasons.
The ban on music in public places is imposed by the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice Ministry, whose morality police roam the city wearing long white coats.
Regulations state that “since music is forbidden and causes annoyance to passengers, drivers must refrain from playing or listening to it.”
The ministry did not respond when asked to comment on punishments Afghans face for playing music, but those breaching other rules risk being jailed.
Roeen said ministry officials have “a lot of authority.”
“We’re definitely too afraid of them to be able to listen to music at a higher volume,” he said, adding that he has “become 10 times more interested in music” since the ban.
“I have to make sure that even if I can’t listen in the early morning, by eight o’clock my music is on,” Roeen said.
In a country where various forms of entertainment including cinema are outlawed, listening to music constantly is a “form of protest” for the 28-year-old driver.
Another taxi driver, who requested anonymity for security reasons, said he only listens to music when he is alone in his car and surrounded by the noise of other vehicles.
“Before, whenever a person wanted, they could listen without any worry or stress. But now... personally I listen — but with some stress,” he said in his car that had a radio player with a USB slot.
He has been stopped twice at checkpoints for having a USB stick and a memory card.
“I didn’t lie — I said it has music, and they broke it,” he said. “Afghan culture should not vanish, and music is one of the cultures of our people. Personally, I don’t want this culture to disappear.”
As part of their crackdown on banned music, the ministry occasionally report burning instruments. No figures are available on how many they have seized.
Across the capital, residents use shared taxis as an affordable way to get around a city which lacks a proper public transport system.
Often, two passengers sit alongside the driver in the front, three are in the back, and sometimes someone rides in the open boot.
“I prefer to listen to music every day; whenever I go to any destination, I try to check if the taxi has a music player,” student Shamsullah Ahmad said. “I prefer music in the car, because wearing headphones would be noticed, but in the car, even with lower volume is better than nothing.”
The morality police have been known to take headphones out of Afghans’ ears to check if they are listening to music.
Roeen said he misses the days when “we could listen to songs, dance, and celebrate, and no one would stop us,” but now the city is “shrouded in darkness — a darkness devoid of any light.”

Nuclear plant restart review advances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:02 UTC
01:43:02 KST

Taiwan has approved a preliminary plan to restart an idled atomic power plant, marking a reversal of the ruling party’s anti-nuclear stance as the nation pursues greater energy security.
The Nuclear Safety Commission has cleared its review of an initial proposal to restart the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant, it said in a statement on Thursday. Taiwan Power Co (台電) will still need to carry out follow-up work including safety inspections, before submitting another report on implementation for review, the commission said.
The earliest the plant could resume operations is 2028, according to previous reports in local media, citing Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫).
Photo: CNA
Ma-anshan was the last of three Taiwanese nuclear plants to cease operations when its 40-year operating license expired in May last year. By moving to restart the facility, Taiwan is walking back a decision taken a decade ago to phase out nuclear power generation.
The rethink mirrors a wider revival of nuclear power globally, as governments shed much of the caution that followed the 2011 Fukushima disaster due to the need to reduce emissions while also dealing with surging electricity demand from data centers. Japan is restarting reactors, while China, South Korea, India and Bangladesh are among Asian countries building new atomic plants.
The war in the Middle East has also prompted Asian governments to try and reduce their dependence on imported fossil fuels, with prolonged supply disruptions driving natural gas prices to the highest in years and draining public finances.
In Taiwan — home to some of the world’s biggest chipmakers — the government has softened its stance on nuclear power. Last year, lawmakers revised a bill to allow atomic plants that could previously only operate for 40 years to renew or extend licenses.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) also signaled support for the industry earlier this year, saying that the government embraced advanced nuclear technologies from around the world and would assess whether atomic power might offer greater reassurance to industry.
Chipmakers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) are increasingly in search of clean and stable electricity supplies. Around the world, tech giants such as Meta Platforms Inc and Alphabet Inc’s Google have signed deals to tap power from nuclear reactors to feed demand from the artificial intelligence boom.
In an islandwide referendum in August 2025, about three-quarters of those who voted backed the reopening of Ma-anshan, although the result was ultimately discounted due to insufficient turnout.

Alcohol health warning stirs up Belgian brewers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

In a country famed worldwide for its beer, a proposed tweak to health warnings on adverts for alcoholic drinks has shaken Belgian brewers.
The change stirring up their discontent comes down to cutting just one crucial word.
The government wants to alter the warning from “the abuse of alcohol is harmful to your health” to “alcohol is harmful for your health.”
Photo: AFP Warning: Excessive consumption of alcohol can damage your health
Belgian Minister of Health and Social Affairs Frank Vandenbroucke said the move, announced in spring and still being debated in parliament, is justified by the need to better protect minors and inform adults over the risks of drinking.
“Alcohol is harmful. Everyone is free to decide how much they drink, but as public authorities, we want to provide young people and adults with accurate information,” he said.
However, brewers have railed against a push they said threatens to stigmatize a key sector of Belgium’s economy. Leading the charge has been AB InBev, the world’s biggest beer maker, which produces local classics such as Stella Artois, Leffe and Hoegaarden.
Together with other industry players it has launched a campaign to sway public opinion in the Belgian press. Last month, the group took out a full-page ad in local newspapers showing a smiling couple sharing a beer.
“What’s wrong with these moments?” read the strapline. An accompanying text took direct aim at the new warning, slamming it for not distinguishing between alcohol abuse and “responsible” drinking.
“Belgium has chosen to take aim at its own traditions, which are a source of national pride,” it said.
The man behind the industry pushback is Krishan Maudgal, the boss of the Belgian Brewers association representing about 130 producers.
He decried the government’s “paternalistic” approach, saying that Belgians were able to moderate their consumption without government interference.
“Market trends show this,” he said. “Over the last 25 to 30 years, beer consumption in Belgium has fallen by almost 40 percent.”
However, for some health experts in the country, the government’s latest move does not go far enough. Belgium’s Superior Health Council, which gives independent advice to the authorities, has been calling for years for a total ban on alcohol advertising. It also wants to see health warnings on bottles and cans, accusing the government of being too timid.
“Slogans used by the industry do not emphasize the dangers inherent in alcohol consumption sufficiently and even contribute to confusion,” the council wrote in 2024, quoting the WHO as saying that there is no level of alcohol consumption that is safe for one’s health.
Alcohol addiction specialist Martin de Duve agreed, lashing out at “the irresponsibility of producers.”
“They’re making a mountain out of a molehill; we’re just talking about changing a single sentence in the adverts,” said the doctor, who runs a prevention charity.
“[Beer is] deeply ingrained in Belgian society,” he said. “Yet it is by no means a harmless product.”

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

＃本文由生成式 AI 協作，本刊編輯編修。
We think. We decide. We act. It all seems simple and under our control. Yet, beneath these everyday processes lie hidden patterns that influence our behavior in surprising ways. These patterns, known as “effects,” help explain why people tend to react similarly under certain conditions, even without realizing it.
A. The Dunning–Kruger Effect
Photo: Ivy English I 照片：常春藤解析英語
Olivia learned to play the piano on her own by watching some online videos. After picking up a few simple pieces, she saw herself as naturally gifted. Feeling confident, she signed up for a piano competition. Unfortunately, she was eliminated in the first round, as the judges pointed out her lack of technique and limited musical expression. At that moment, she realized that her confidence was out of proportion with her actual ability.
B. The Bystander Effect
At a busy MRT station, an elderly man tripped and fell in front of everyone. Ethan was in the crowd, but he hesitated to help. It was only when a station staff member finally rushed over that he realized he could have stepped in. The assumption that someone else will act first can quietly prevent people from helping when it is needed most.
C. The Mandela Effect
When Gina was talking about Pikachu with her friends, they recalled that its tail had a black tip, as if it were an established fact from the original animation. However, when they checked the official images of Pikachu, they were surprised to find that its tail had always been completely yellow, with no black tip at all. This illustrates how people can collectively misremember the same details, even when the actual information has never changed.
思考、決定、行動。這一切看似簡單且在我們的控制中。然而，這些日常過程背後隱藏著以驚人的方式影響我們行為的模式。這些模式被稱為「效應」，有助於解釋為什麼人們在特定情況下往往會做出相似反應，甚至自己都沒有意識到。
A. 鄧寧-克魯格效應
奧莉維亞透過觀看一些網路影片自學鋼琴。學會幾首簡單的曲子後，她認為自己天賦異稟。她自信滿滿報名了鋼琴比賽。遺憾的是，她在第一輪就被淘汰了，因為評審指出她缺乏技巧、音樂表達不足。那一刻，她意識到她的自信與實力不成比例。
B. 旁觀者效應
在繁忙的捷運站中，一名老先生在眾人面前絆倒。伊森身處人群之中，卻猶豫要不要去幫忙。直到一名站務人員終於跑過去，他才意識到自己本來可以出手幫忙的。假設其他人會先有所行動的想法，可能會默默阻止人們在他人最需要的時候伸出援手。
C. 曼德拉效應
當吉娜與朋友在談論皮卡丘時，他們回想起他的尾巴尖端是黑色的，彷彿這是來自原始動畫的既定事實。不過當他們查看皮卡丘的官方影像時，發現其尾巴一直都是全黃色，根本沒有黑色的尖端，令他們大吃一驚。這說明了人們是如何集體記錯一樣的細節，即使真實資訊從未改變過。
What Did You Learn?
Which phrase in the passage means “lacking the appropriate relationship with the size, shape, or position of some part of the same thing”?（簡答題）
____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
答案:
out of proportion with
Words in Use
1. gifted a. 有天賦的
Although Stacy is gifted in art, she still practices every day to refine her skills.
雖然史黛西具有藝術天賦，她仍每天練習以精進技巧。
2. competition n. 比賽
The team trained for months before the competition began.
那支隊伍在比賽開始前訓練了好幾個月。
3. eliminate vt. 淘汰，剔除
One mistake was enough to eliminate the experienced singer from the contest.
一次失誤就足以讓那名有經驗的歌手從比賽中淘汰。
4. technique n. 技巧，技術
Mastering a new technique usually requires patience and consistent practice.
掌握新技巧通常需要耐心與持續練習。
5. confidence n. 信心
Despite facing a strong opponent, the young tennis player showed confidence.
儘管面對強大對手，那名年輕的網球選手仍展現信心。
Practical Phrases
1. under certain conditions 在特定情況∕條件下
This chemical reaction occurs only under certain conditions.
這種化學反應只會在特定的條件下發生。
2. be out of proportion with / to... 與……（在程度、實體大小等方面）不成比例
proportion n. 比例
Many members felt that the fee they paid was out of proportion to the services offered by the gym.
許多會員覺得他們所支付的費用與健身房提供的服務不成比例。
3. step in 介入，插手
The police stepped in before the situation became worse.
警方在情況變得更糟前介入。
4. as if. . . 彷彿∕好像……（= as though...）
本文中的 as if 為表與過去事實相反的情況，由於as if 子句的動詞與主要子句動詞的時間一致，因此用過去式。
? After the scandal, the mayor continued to work as if it didn’t affect him.
醜聞過後，那名市長繼續工作，彷彿那並未影響到他。
若此動作比主要子句動詞所表示的動作更早發生時，則 as if 子句採過去完成式。
Paul slipped and fell, but he quickly stood up and acted as if nothing had happened.
保羅滑倒了但迅速站了起來，假裝沒事一樣。

When we use phones, laptops, or wireless earbuds, we rarely pause to ask what makes these devices so light, efficient and powerful. Hidden inside them are “rare earth elements” (REEs), indispensable to modern life yet central to global controversy. REEs are a group of 17 similar metals that are difficult to tell apart. First identified in the late 18th century, they were known as rare earths because early chemists found them in unusual mineral deposits and believed them to be scarce. President William Lai (賴清德) should seek ways to resume cross-strait dialogue, because if the leaders of the US and China can negotiate, Taiwan should also prioritize communication, Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) said yesterday.
Thursday’s meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) — their second in five months — demonstrated that Washington and Beijing are maintaining dialogue and managing differences despite intense economic, technological and geopolitical competition, Cheng said.
That serves as a reminder for Taiwan, she said, adding that as major powers seek new balances for their own benefit, Taipei must chart its own course to maximize its own security and interests.
Photo: Taipei Times
Cheng cited tariffs, rare earths, artificial intelligence, Taiwan and Iran as issues at stake in the summit, all of which involve vital strategic considerations, she said.
Referencing remarks this week by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that foreign arms sales must factor in global US military needs, weapons stockpiles and defense industry capacity, Cheng said that Taiwan needs a long-term, stable and pragmatic strategy amid a rapidly changing international landscape.
The KMT fully supports improving Taiwan’s self-defense, and deepening security and economic cooperation with the US, she said.
However, a mature strategy must combine military and economic strength with the space for dialogue to lower the risk of war, allowing Taiwan to protect itself while also maintaining peace and creating prosperity, she added.
Taiwan does not need to choose between being “pro-US” or “pro-China,” Cheng said, adding that improving national defense and building dialogue to reduce hostility are not mutually exclusive.
Cheng called on Lai to provide the public with a comprehensive assessment of the latest US-China and cross-strait developments following the summit in Washington.
If Trump and Xi can negotiate for their respective national interests, Lai should also keep the safety and interests of Taiwanese in mind, propose concrete plans to reduce cross-strait risks and find a way to open the door to dialogue, she said.

Catalonia’s far-right surge divides the independence camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

Almost a decade after Catalonia’s failed independence bid, a growing number of voters are shifting their focus from secession to issues such as immigration and crime, fueling the rise of the far-right separatist Alianca Catalana.
The party, which draws much of its support from working- and middle-class voters in rural areas outside Barcelona, has surged in the polls and now trails only Spain’s ruling Socialists ahead of Catalonia’s next election in 2028.
While Alianca says it would seek to break away from Madrid unilaterally if it won power in the wealthy northeastern region, its message is focused far more on curbing immigration and improving public safety.
Its growing influence is reshaping Catalan politics. Earlier this month, riot police prevented violent clashes between Alianca supporters and left-wing separatists in Barcelona, overshadowing Catalonia’s Sept. 11 national day celebrations, which have historically drawn large pro-independence crowds.
The episode highlighted divisions within the separatist movement, potentially complicating efforts to form a coalition to unseat the region’s ruling Socialist Party. Traditional pro-independence parties have ruled out governing agreements with Alianca.
As its support has grown, other separatist parties have adopted more conservative positions, including lobbying Madrid to let the region restrict migration.
The party’s appeal cuts across Catalonia’s traditional political divides. Much of its support comes from voters who previously backed the separatist center-right Junts or the far-right, staunchly anti-independence Vox, according to a Catalan government survey published in July.
Alianca’s rise has been driven largely by its outspoken leader, Silvia Orriols, 41, who studied to become a librarian and comes from a middle-class farming family.
Orriols told Reuters her party was tapping into frustration with established politicians and concerns that immigration was diluting Catalan identity.
“People have regained hope and drive to fight for the restoration of the Catalan state, to implement policies aimed at preserving our identity,” said Orriols, who frequently invokes Catalonia’s history in her speeches.
She said far-right Alternative for Germany’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt state earlier this month showed that “Europe is awakening.”
“We Europeans are shielding ourselves in order to survive,” she said.
Alianca rose to prominence in 2023 after Orriols won a local election in Ripoll. Her anti-Muslim message gained traction in the mountainous town where most of the Moroccan-born perpetrators of the 2017 Barcelona terror attacks had lived.
The party entered Catalonia’s parliament a year later with two seats. Since then, it has grown from 3.8 percent to 16.7 percent of voter intentions for the next regional election, according to a poll published by El Mundo newspaper this month. It was 2.6 percentage points ahead of fellow separatist party ERC.
Eloi Radovan, whose family traditionally backed left-wing pro-independence parties like ERC, is among those who have shifted their support to Alianca.
“I feel betrayed,” said Radovan, 19, referring to how parties like ERC and Junts failed to follow through on the 2017 referendum in which Catalans voted in favor of independence. He also criticized their cooperation with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
He supports Alianca’s call for a total ban on migration because, he said, “Catalonia is increasingly becoming less Catalan.”
Junts is seeking to counter Alianca’s appeal by presenting itself as a more pragmatic centrist alternative while offering its own proposals on migration and security. Two senior Junts officials told Reuters they viewed Alianca’s plans as unrealistic and discriminatory.
The party’s gains have coincided with shifting priorities among Catalan voters.
Affordable housing, migration and crime topped the list of concerns in the July survey. Two years earlier, political dissatisfaction and Catalonia’s relationship with the rest of Spain ranked highest.
“The [2017] independence push was driven by economic anxiety, whereas Alianca responds to demographic anxiety,” historian Joan Esculies said.
Alianca’s rise is “an expression of frustration at the lack of a viable path towards independence and a cry born of fear as new waves of immigration pose a greater threat to [Catalan] language,” he said.
Yet support for independence has remained resilient despite divisions within the movement and the loss of the regional presidency in 2024 after a decade in power. The July survey showed 45 percent backing independence, down from a peak of 49 percent in 2017.
Critics say Alianca is exploiting those frustrations rather than offering solutions.
The party offers no real solutions and other separatists must combat its “xenophobic, racist discourse of exclusion,” left-wing separatist Hug Lucchetti, 45, said during this month’s protests.
“The independence movement is alive,” he said. “New ranks of activists continue to emerge.”

Google plans test of space chips in Project Suncatcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

Alphabet Inc’s Google said on Thursday it would launch a prototype satellite next week in its first in-orbit test of Project Suncatcher, a research effort to explore whether space could potentially host large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) computing infrastructure.
Companies including Space Exploration Technologies Corp (SpaceX) and Starcloud Inc are pursuing plans to deploy data centers in low Earth orbit, aiming to harness near-continuous sunlight to power energy-intensive AI computing and sidestep terrestrial constraints on electricity supplies.
The new mission, scheduled to fly on SpaceX’s upcoming Transporter-18 rideshare launch in partnership with satellite company Planet Labs PBC, is to assess how Google’s AI hardware withstands launch forces, radiation and extreme temperatures in low Earth orbit.
Photo: AP
After the launch, it will send a prototype satellite carrying Google’s tensor processing units (TPUs) into low Earth orbit to assess if the AI chips can operate reliably in space.
Space radiation can disrupt or degrade electronics, including by causing data errors known as bit flips.
Google aims to test its TPUs while running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California, Davis, but that orbital testing is needed to understand how the hardware performs in the real environment, the company said.
The company will also evaluate its design to cool the power-intensive chips in the vacuum of space, where conventional airflow cooling is impossible, by combining heat pipes with radiators, it said.
Experts have said that the concept remains years from being commercially viable given high launch costs, engineering constraints and satellite production bottlenecks.
The first Suncatcher mission is designed to gather in-orbit data and identify potential failure points, rather than demonstrate an operational orbital data center, Google said.
It aims to launch two satellites next year to test the high-bandwidth laser links needed to connect future computing clusters, it said.

Ex-US admiral calls for arms sales action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

The US should move ahead with arms sales notifications for Taiwan following the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) on Thursday, a retired senior US Navy officer said yesterday.
Mark Montgomery, a retired US Navy rear admiral, told reporters in Taipei that the Trump-Xi summit had delayed the announcements of proposed sales and he hoped the summit would have no further effect on them, urging Washington to avoid further delays.
“We need to make the arms sale notifications so that Taiwan can get in line, so that they can get these weapons when they’re ready,” Montgomery said.
Photo: CNA
The White House was mum on whether Taiwan was even addressed at the meeting.
The Chinese side said Xi called on the US to oppose Taiwan independence and “handle the Taiwan question with prudence,” China’s official Xinhua news agency reported.
It did not mention weapons sales being discussed.
Montgomery said that US lawmakers were concerned about delays to the sales, and drew a distinction between notifying the US Congress of a proposed deal and delivering the weapons.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has linked the delays to the US military’s need for weapons, Montgomery said.
However, delivery constraints should not hold up notifications, he added.
Some weapons proposed for Taiwan are not needed by the US military, he said.
Washington should send notifications to the Congress as soon as possible, he said, adding that a proposed US$14 billion sale, which has been stalled since early this year, could be divided into several smaller packages announced over a few weeks.
Asked about Xi’s remarks about Taiwan during the summit, Montgomery said that the Chinese leader had an interest in raising the issue.
What mattered more was how Trump responded and what the US government did afterward, he said.
Continued adherence to the Taiwan Relations Act and the “six assurances” should be reflected in US actions, including providing Taiwan with weapons for its self-defense and preparing for a potential regional crisis, Montgomery said.
However, arms sales alone would not be enough, he said, adding that the US’ and Taiwan’s militaries need to improve their ability to operate together through air and naval exercises, training and joint planning.
“It’s very hard to cooperate and fight together in wartime if you don’t work together in peacetime,” Montgomery said.

Kenting park office reports coral ‘poaching’ incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

The Kenting National Park Management Office on Thursday said it has forwarded complaints to authorities about an alleged coral poacher operating within the park a day earlier.
The office said that it received a report about the incident around the Hejie (合界) diving spot near Hengchun Township (恆春) at 9:50am on Wednesday.
A diving coach in the area recorded the incident and posted the video online, criticizing the alleged poacher’s diving techniques and lack of morals.
Photo courtesy of uncle_sam_dive
The coach also asked Internet users if they recognize the oxygen tank or equipment to help identify the poacher.
The office said it had alerted the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) and dispatched office staff to the area where the video was taken.
As it was already several hours after the incident, the officials and the CGA did not find anything in the area, it said.
Based on the video provided, the office said it was difficult to definitively determine whether the person had actually been poaching coral.
The office said it has forwarded the video and all information to the police and would comply with the police’s investigation results.
Per criminal provisions of the Fisheries Act (漁業法), if an offense involves violating specific restrictions announced by the authorities, such as restrictions on the conservation of aquatic resources under Article 44 of the act, violators could be subject to a maximum prison sentence of three years, an additional fine or an accompanying fine of up to NT$150,000, the office said.
The office said it would step up patrols in the area and work with local diving operators and enthusiasts to photograph or film suspected illegal harvesting and report it promptly to protect marine resources in the area.

Photo: Taipei Times
Taiwan in 2020 applied to export breeding pigs and boar semen to Malaysia, providing Malaysian authorities documents on animal health, disease monitoring and breeding pig management, it said.
Malaysia postponed its review following an African swine fever (ASF) outbreak in Taiwan in October last year, the APHIA said.
After Taiwan regained its ASF-free status in April, the agency urged the Malaysian Veterinary Services Department to complete the review and continued to communicate with the authorities, eventually earning the approval, it added.
The approval marks the opening of another overseas market for Taiwanese breeding pigs and boar semen, it said.
From 2023 to last year, Taiwan exported 353, 297 and 445 high-quality breeding pigs annually, mainly to Hong Kong and Vietnam, the APHIA said.
Boar semen was primarily exported to Palau, the Marshall Islands, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines over the same period, it said.
Malaysia has listed its import quarantine criteria, including pre-export quarantine and health examinations for breeding pigs, as well as health management for semen-producing boars and related artificial insemination centers, the APHIA said.
The APHIA said it would review and confirm the criteria as soon as possible and create an export quarantine certificate sample to be reviewed by Malaysian authorities.
Once the two sides agree on quarantine certification, Taiwanese pig-farming industry operators can export breeding pigs and boar semen that meet the standards, the APHIA said.

China’s purges spur doubt about its military might
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:42:47 UTC
01:42:47 KST

Purges of military leaders might have dented China’s war-fighting readiness, but are likely to have strengthened Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) grip on an institution that is a key source of power for the ruling Communist Party, diplomats and analysts say.
Regional military attaches and security analysts are watching the crackdown closely as China steps up efforts to modernize its military and boosts deployments around Taiwan, as well as hotly disputed parts of the South and East China Seas.
News this week of the ruling Politburo’s expulsion of two top military leaders, Zhang Youxia (張又俠) and Liu Zhenli (劉振立), from the Communist Party and the military, signaled the latest move in the long-running crackdown.
Zhang, the son of a close friend of Xi’s father, had long been seen as his closest military ally, serving as his deputy on China’s top defense command body, the Central Military Commission.
Analysts say dozens of second-line officers have filled key posts in the CMC, as well as theater commands and individual services, but five places are still vacant on its ruling seven-person committee.
China’s defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Xi’s hand has been further strengthened by the “defenestration” of proteges of Zhang and Miao Hua (苗華), formerly the military’s top uniformed political officer, Singapore-based Chinese security scholar James Char (蔡志祥) said.
“We can expect Xi to continue exercising decisive control and influence over China’s military affairs — and by extension, his dominance over the party-state, since whoever controls the People’s Liberation Army controls the party,” Char said.
Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has led one of the most extensive campaigns to root out corruption and indiscipline in China’s modern history.
It has, in part, prompted descriptions of him as the most powerful leader since founding figure Mao Zedong (毛澤東).
Millions within the vast bureaucracy have been investigated to varying extent, with scores of senior party, government and military officials also investigated and purged.
“Eradicating corrupt elements strengthens, rather than weakens, the political foundation, cohesion, and overall combat effectiveness of the armed forces,” said Tian Shichen (田士臣), president of the Chinese think tank Global Governance Institution.
Investigations of Zhang and Liu were first unveiled in January, though any formal punishments have yet to be revealed.
The extensive replacements of military brass mean that China maintains its current defense posture, continuing weapons tests and increasingly complex exercises.
However, question marks linger over the impact of the purges on China’s ability to wage war, particularly over Taiwan.
Zhang was the most senior officer with actual combat experience, gained in a brief but bloody border war with Vietnam in 1979, the last time China engaged in real fighting.
It “is hard to imagine upheaval on this scale wouldn’t create issues for more complex operations — including a full-scale Taiwan contingency,” China analyst Ruby Osman said, though the PLA had insulated routine operations from the turmoil.
“But Xi clearly sees short-term disruption as a price worth paying for long-term discipline and combat readiness,” added Osman, a senior policy adviser on China at London’s Tony Blair Institute.
Initially the crackdown targeted corruption, such as aspects of procurement by the PLA’s elite Rocket Force, the main body controlling China’s conventional and nuclear-armed missiles.
However, increasingly it has taken on a political edge, which some analysts see as a reminder that the PLA exists primarily to serve the Party, not the nation.
The PLA’s fundamental principle “has always been the absolute leadership of the party over the military,” said Tian, a former defense ministry official, dismissing foreign views that Xi’s “personal power” had been concentrated.
Zhang and Liu had “seriously contributed to political and corruption problems that undermine the Party’s absolute leadership over the military and endanger the Party’s foundation of governance,” the official PLA Daily said.
They had “caused enormous damage to the military’s political development, political ecosystem, and combat effectiveness,” it added in an editorial on Wednesday.
Char, of Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said he did not expect the commission’s top panel to be filled until the Communist Party’s full congress late next year.
Xi is widely expected to cement his fourth five-year term at the event, a prospects analysts see as driving an intensified need for internal security.
That delay could continue to hamper engagement between China and foreign militaries, a factor diplomats consider critical as regional tension festers.
Chinese Minister of National Defense Dong Jun (董軍) remains in place, but he is neither on the ruling Politburo nor the CMC, and is considered less powerful than many international peers.
Zhang’s meeting in 2024 with then US national security adviser Jake Sullivan in Beijing was viewed at the time as a breakthrough in US-China military ties, but it is not clear who will replace him.
In the interim, Xi might be making some decisions on his own, said Bonnie Glaser of Washington-based think tank the German Marshall Fund of the United States.
“The PLA can still execute orders, of course, through the joint staff, theatre commands, services and party apparatus,” added Glaser, who heads the Fund’s Indo-Pacific Program.

and Ben Blanchard in Taipei.

It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan.
