North Korea’s Ukraine POWs Are Now in South Korea. What Comes Next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:41:00 UTC
01:41:00 KST

The immediate fate of two North Korean prisoners-of-war captured by Ukrainian forces is no longer in question, but the saga is not yet over.
Ukraine has transferred custody of the pair to South Korea in what was perhaps a predictable outcome given their reported desire not to return to North Korea. However, the circumstances surrounding the disclosure have introduced new political dynamics to the situation. Now, both the South Korean government and the two former soldiers face an unprecedented resettlement process.
Kyiv first announced that it had captured the two North Korean soldiers in January 2025, immediately prompting questions of what would come of the pair. The legal provisions surrounding their eventual disposition were complicated. International rules pointed toward repatriating them with other POWs to Russia. Before the capture happened, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was his government’s position that all POWs in Ukrainian custody would receive the same treatment.
The two soldiers, however, reportedly expressed fear of repatriation and a desire to defect to South Korea. Given the Kim Jong Un regime’s publicized insistence that soldiers kill themselves rather than be captured, returning to North Korea could have exposed them to reprisals for allowing themselves to be taken into Ukrainian custody. Under the principle of non-refoulement, the potential risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations if the soldiers were ultimately repatriated to North Korea was a necessary consideration.
The South Korean government stepped in early with offers to take the POWs into their custody. With advocacy stretching back to the previous Yoon Suk-yeol administration, there was little doubt over Seoul’s desired outcome for the two individuals.
What is now evident is that the two governments came to a confidential agreement to transfer the custody of the POWs. The handover reportedly took place ahead of the U.N. General Assembly debates, and the two former soldiers are now in South Korean government care. Details of this arrangement first came to light via Zelenskyy himself.
During his speech at the U.N. General Assembly, the Ukrainian president captured international attention when he revealed that Ukraine had transferred custody of the two POWs to South Korea. In the speech, he noted that “these guys are not easy to capture alive,” adding that one of the soldiers, “when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself.” Zelenskyy’s disclosure came unilaterally and without warning to the South Korean government.
Kyiv’s decision to reveal information despite the confidential arrangement created a diplomatic problem with Seoul, but it also served a clear Ukrainian purpose. Kyiv’s intelligence has repeatedly claimed that the Kremlin is seeking an additional 30,000-50,000 North Korean troops to support a new offensive. Zelenskyy therefore used the U.N. General Assembly debates as a platform to highlight the Kim regime’s continued support for Russia’s war effort and to put North Korea’s military involvement back on the international agenda.
But Zelenskyy’s announcement caused a stir in South Korean domestic politics. Opposition lawmakers immediately chastised the Lee Jae-myung administration for not disclosing the transfer. Some argued that the government was withholding details out of fear of how North Korea may react.
Lee took to social media to push back against this criticism. He said that there was an agreement to keep the transfer confidential, expressing that it was “deeply regrettable” that the Ukraine side released details on the matter. He added that publicly disclosing the successful repatriation could have helped boost approval ratings, but it would not have been right to risk “someone’s life or the national interest” for one’s “own petty benefit.”
There are political reasons why some in the Lee administration may have sought to avoid disclosing information about the POW transfer. The government has been working to rekindle any form of inter-Korean engagement, and some policy groups within Seoul have warned that North Korea could react strongly to the decision.
However, such concerns may be unfounded. North Korean state media has not commented on the POWs since their reported capture, and there are much more significant sticking points between the two Koreas; namely, Pyongyang’s preconditions that Seoul must drop unification and denuclearization as policy objectives. Since Zelenskyy’s announcement, the only reporting from Pyongyang directed toward the South Korean government has been a statement attributed to Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui on a familiar issue: reiterating the Kim regime’s position that denying the reality of North Korea’s nuclear weapon status “is to give up the future.”
Meanwhile, from a security perspective, there are justifiable concerns related to the information disclosure. There have been North Korean assassination attempts against South Korea-based defectors in the past. The most prominent recent example occurred in a 2011 incident in which a North Korean agent attempted to kill prominent defector-turned-activist Park Sang-hak with a poison needle.
The two POWs could therefore present a different security challenge from the average North Korean defector. Their firsthand knowledge of North Korean involvement in the Russia-Ukraine War means that there is a reasonable risk that they could become targets of elimination efforts.
Given the confidential nature of the South Korea-Ukraine agreement, there are few details on what comes next for the two former soldiers. There may have been an understanding that they will remain in custody until the conclusion of the war, or Kyiv may have conceded that South Korea can treat the individuals as they would any other defector. This would affect how long the individuals remain in the government’s custody.
Whatever the length of their initial detention in South Korea, the eventual next step will be resettlement.
Resettlement can be difficult for any defector. New arrivals generally undergo a months-long program at the Hanawon resettlement facility under the Ministry of Unification’s remit, and it includes tasks such as teaching individuals about South Korean customs and courtesies, how to manage bank accounts and finances, and finding employment.
Upon completion of the resettlement process, they are then given relocation assistance to a new residence somewhere in the country. There, they are typically assigned a local officer – either a Ministry of Unification, Korean National Police, or National Intelligence Service (NIS) official – to continue supporting their transition process and to contact in the event of any issues.
The system is different for higher profile or high-risk defectors. They may be former senior North Korean officials like Thae Yong Ho, or figures such as Park Sang-hak who have used their newfound freedom to lead civic movements in protest of the Kim regime. In those cases, the individuals can remain in NIS protective custody until officials determine that it is safe for them to return to public life. Even then, there may be continued protection services.
The two former soldiers transferred from Ukraine will likely fall into that latter category, particularly with the amount of media coverage they have received.
Thus, the arrival of the two North Korean soldiers to South Korea resolves the most immediate question surrounding their fate, but the next steps remain dynamic. The situation has now entered a new phase where South Korean politics will continue to scrutinize the issue as the government works to navigate an unprecedented resettlement process.

Evan Gershkovich says his arrest in Russia was carefully planned FSB sting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:40:12 UTC
01:40:12 KST

US reporter Evan Gershkovich, in his first detailed published account of his arrest in Russia in 2023, says he was the victim of an elaborate sting operation by Russia's FSB federal security service.
In an extract from his book "This Cursed Beautiful Land," Gershkovich says that while working on a story for the Wall Street Journal about Russian military production, he held two meetings with the union boss of a factory in Yekaterinburg, a major defense-industry hub.
At their second encounter, in a steakhouse, the source produced papers with hand-copied tables of figures, telling the reporter that they related to the production of tanks.
As he jotted down notes, Gershkovich said, he heard the sound of marching feet and looked up to see a group of masked men approaching their table.
"A pang of guilt ripped through me: Had I compromised a source? But panic immediately replaced that thought. Instinct took over, my hands moving to hide the papers in the gap between the bench and the wall," he wrote in the book extract, published by the Journal on Friday.
"The men quickly descended on us. An arm was yanking my neck, pulling me off the couch... Someone shouted: 'You are under arrest by the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation.'"
Long sentence, then a prisoner swap
Gershkovich, then 31, became the first US reporter arrested on espionage charges in Russia since the Cold War. He was later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.
He writes that he and his editors had considered the risks of the reporting trip and agreed that the source should not bring any documents to the meeting; if he did so, Gershkovich should not accept anything from him.
But at the meeting, the source had "thrust the papers into my hands."
Although he had reported on the arrests of other Americans in Russia, and on the targeting and even murder of Russian journalists, Gershkovich writes that the "unspoken rule" was that foreign correspondents enjoyed a degree of immunity: they might be expelled, but not arrested.
Reeling with shock, he was handcuffed, had a black sack placed over his head, and was whisked into a van where he was placed in a chokehold and punched in the abdomen while being questioned, he writes.
FSB 'backup plan'
Gershkovich said that since his release he had learned of evidence that the FSB had a "backup plan" to arrest him on another of his planned reporting trips, to Siberia, if the Yekaterinburg operation had failed.
He said he believes the two meetings with the source in Yekaterinburg were designed to help the FSB persuade President Vladimir Putin that he was a spy and secure approval for his arrest at the second meeting.
"Putin, it seems to me, fully bought into this narrative," he said.
The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a February 2024 interview with US television host Tucker Carlson, Putin said Gershkovich had been "caught red-handed" while collecting confidential information.
The journalist, his newspaper, and the US government all strongly deny the allegation that Gershkovich was a spy.

Israel, US officials meet Abraham Accords partners in New York to expand regional cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:39:48 UTC
01:39:48 KST

Senior officials from Israel, the United States, and countries participating in the Abraham Accords reconvened in New York on Thursday for the group’s first multilateral meeting since January 2023, signaling renewed efforts to deepen regional cooperation and expand the normalization framework after years of regional upheaval.
The high-level roundtable, convened by the N7 Foundation and chaired by its chairman and founder Jeffrey M. Talpins, brought together US Under Secretary of State Allison Hooker and senior officials from Israel, Bahrain, Morocco, the United Arab Emirates and Kazakhstan. It marked the first official engagement of Abraham Accords countries to include Kazakhstan, which is preparing to join the framework.
The meeting came nearly three years after the October 7 Hamas attack and the outbreak of the Gaza war, which significantly reshaped the regional diplomatic landscape and slowed efforts to build on the momentum created by the Abraham Accords. The United States brokered the agreements during the Trump administration, which established diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE and Bahrain in 2020, followed by Morocco.
Rather than focusing solely on additional normalization agreements, Thursday’s meeting focused on the next stage of the framework: translating diplomatic ties into practical cooperation. Participants reaffirmed the principles of the Abraham Accords and discussed opportunities to strengthen collaboration between Israel, Arab and Muslim countries, the United States and other partners.
Abraham Accords countries seek broader regional network
“The Abraham Accords have demonstrated what is possible when countries come together around shared interests with a common vision for a more integrated and prosperous region,” Talpins said. “The next phase is about deepening the relationships that already exist and identifying practical opportunities for countries to work together.”
The N7 Foundation said discussions centered on shared priorities and tangible outcomes, with the goal of using regional cooperation to promote stability, security and economic development. Potential areas of collaboration include technology, trade and investment, energy, water and food security, and strategic and security cooperation.
“The Abraham Accords have created a foundation for a more connected region, and their full potential will be realized through the practical cooperation they make possible,” N7 President Oren Eisner said. “Today's discussion focused on the work ahead: strengthening existing relationships, welcoming new partners, and advancing initiatives that deliver tangible benefits to people and economies across the region.”
Kazakhstan’s participation was one of the most significant developments of the meeting. Kazakhstan has described its decision to join the Abraham Accords as consistent with its foreign policy and has said that its accession will not change its support for a two-state solution and relevant international resolutions. Its expected entry could give the Accords a new dimension by linking Israel and its Arab partners with a strategically important Muslim-majority country in Central Asia.
The meeting does not, however, represent a return to the diplomatic environment that existed before October 7. The Gaza war has complicated Israel’s relations with much of the Arab world, while the regional confrontation with Iran and broader security concerns have created new pressures on governments that established ties with Jerusalem.
Still, the decision by senior officials from Abraham Accords countries to return to a multilateral format is significant. For much of the period following October 7, regional diplomacy focused primarily on the Gaza war, humanitarian issues, and the broader Israeli-Palestinian question. The New York gathering placed regional integration back on the agenda alongside those challenges.
The meeting also reflects continued US interest in using the Abraham Accords as a platform for broader regional cooperation. The Trump administration played a central role in establishing the framework, and the latest gathering suggests Washington still views it as an important component of its regional strategy.
The N7 Foundation, which hosted the first multilateral convening of Abraham Accords countries in 2021, said it would continue working with participating states and aligned partners to develop “durable mechanisms” for strategic cooperation.
The long-term question is whether the Abraham Accords can evolve from a series of bilateral normalization agreements into a broader regional network. Thursday’s meeting in New York aimed to take that next step by bringing existing partners back together, adding Kazakhstan to the discussion, and focusing on cooperation beyond diplomatic recognition.

The United Nations human rights office issued a list on Friday adding 61 more companies operating in Israeli West Bank settlements, which the UN considers illegal.
The database is highly sensitive as firms could be targeted for boycotts or divestment to pressure Israel over settler expansion in the territory that is home to over 3 million Palestinians.
The database, first released in 2020, now includes 214 firms, mostly from Israel, but also from 10 other countries including France, Germany, China and the US.
Newly added firms included Israeli pesticides maker ADAMA, part of Chinese-owned Syngenta Group, Israel-based real estate investment holding company Alony Hetz and Spain's Salvat Logistica.
They joined companies such as travel agency Expedia and home-rental company Airbnb already on the list.
'An automatic majority against Israel'
Israeli officials have previously said the list unfairly vilifies companies working legally.
"This is a distorted mechanism, created by a deeply flawed body with an automatic majority against Israel," Israel's diplomatic mission said on Friday, alleging that the database was established to "persecute" the Jewish state.
There has been a surge in settler attacks against Palestinians as outposts proliferate, prompting Britain, France and Canada to block imports from settlements this month.
The UN rights office assessed companies active in sectors including energy, food, hospitality, transport and agriculture, based on confidential submissions to the UN rights office.
Another 60 or so companies were assessed but not included since they did not meet the UN criteria of involvement in activities that violate the Palestinian right to self-determination.
Examples include supplying demolition equipment to destroy Palestinian buildings, providing surveillance for settlements, and other services like transport that help maintain their existence, according to the UN website.
Other companies, including British-registered online travel company Opodo and Spanish-domiciled online travel agent eDreams, were dropped from the original list after submitting a reassessment request.
The UN found reasonable grounds to believe they were no longer involved in the activities that previously justified their inclusion.
eDreams said last year it had withdrawn and would continue to block listings of accommodation in illegal Israeli settlements, saying that some had appeared on its website automatically after owners uploaded them.
Palestinians want the West Bank to be part of a future independent homeland.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's nationalist government has largely backed settlers, with building ramped up since the militant Hamas group's attack on Israel in October 2023 and the ensuing Gaza war.
Travel firm Expedia has previously said that the listings in what it called "disputed areas" were clearly labeled, complied with international laws and sanctions, and underwent enhanced due diligence guided by UN standards.

Sohlberg issues injunction against Satmar org. accused of bribing voters to abstain from election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:39:22 UTC
01:39:22 KST

Central Elections Committee Chairman and Supreme Court Deputy Chief Justice Noam Sohlberg issued a temporary injunction on Friday prohibiting the "Shekel HaTahor" (Pure Shekel) organization, affiliated with the Satmar haredi (ultra-Orthodox) community, from granting, offering, or promising money to voters for the purpose of influencing them not to participate in the elections.
The court issued the injunction after the Movement for Quality Government filed a petition.
According to the petition, the association began providing “support payments” of NIS 200 to haredim who declared they would not vote in the upcoming 26th Knesset elections.
Sohlberg determined that, at this stage, the evidence accompanying the petition indicated “grave concern regarding a violation of the law that strikes at the very core of election laws.” The injunction will remain in effect pending further decision, and proceedings regarding the petition are ongoing.
About 12,000 new registrants recently joined the Shekel HaTahor program and signed a pledge not to participate in the elections. The expected grant for those eligible is approximately NIS 200.
While 12,000 people have newly registered, no data indicates how many individuals may have already received the funds.
Shekel HaTahor also operates similarly outside of election season. It is a support system associated with Satmar that assists institutions and communities that do not receive funding from the state.
The increase in the number of people turning to it is attributed, among other things, to the halting of funding for some Torah institutions. The petition is not directed at this assistance in itself. It was filed following the allegation that money was being given in exchange for an eligible voter’s declaration that they would not cast a ballot.
Offering or giving bribes to voters prohibited under election laws
Section 122 of the Knesset Elections Law prohibits giving or offering a bribe to influence a voter “to vote or refrain from voting.” The prohibition also applies to a bribe intended to cause a voter not to vote, and it is not conditional on the money having already changed hands: the offer of a bribe is also prohibited under the section.
The term "bribe" is also broadly defined in the law. Under Section 123, it may consist of money, something of monetary value, a service, or any other benefit or advantage, and the benefit need not be transferred directly from the giver to the voter.
Section 122 also applies to a voter who accepts or agrees to accept a bribe in exchange for voting or refraining from voting. The offenses fall under the "Corruption and Threats" section of the law and carry a penalty of up to five years in prison.
Satmar’s move is rooted in the Hasidic sect’s long-standing anti-Zionist ideology, which opposes participation in state institutions and Knesset elections.
Satmar is a central force within the anti-Zionist Ultra-Orthodox camp. Unlike Ultra-Orthodox parties that participate in elections and operate within the Knesset, the sect views participation in the state’s political system as ideologically and religiously objectionable.
The petition currently before Justice Solberg addresses the claim that, in this instance, a financial incentive was attached to this stance: $200 for anyone declaring they would not vote.
Satmar sect previously involved in voter bribery case
This is not the first time such an issue has arisen around the Satmar sect.
Ahead of the 2013 elections, sources involved in Shekel HaTahor reported that the sect intended to pay NIS 100 to anyone who pledged not to vote and handed over their ID card and driver's license on election day.
In the Pines-Paz v. Shas case, the chairman of the Elections Committee at the time, Justice Mishael Cheshin, explained that the purpose of prohibiting election bribery is to ensure that voters make their decisions freely and rationally, rather than under the influence of extraneous considerations and benefits.
The Supreme Court later quoted these remarks in the context of Section 122, emphasizing that the section is intended to protect the voter's freedom of choice.
Solberg issued the injunction under Section 17B of the Elections Law (Methods of Propaganda). The section allows the chairman of the Elections Committee to issue an order preventing the commission or continuation of an offense under Chapter 11 of the Knesset Elections Law, which includes Section 122. In other words, the Committee Chairman may intervene during the election campaign and halt the act at the center of the petition, without waiting for criminal proceedings that might take place after Election Day.
At this stage, this is a temporary injunction. Solberg did not determine that Shekel HaTahor had violated the law, but prohibited it from continuing the activity described in the petition pending further review.
At the time the injunction was issued, Shekel HaTahor had not yet responded to the petition.
As long as the injunction remains in effect, Shekel HaTahor is prohibited from granting, offering, or promising money to influence voters to abstain from voting.
The law stipulates that for purposes of enforcing the injunction, it is considered an order of a court, and its violation could trigger proceedings under the Contempt of Court Ordinance.
The question of whether Shekel HaTahor violated the law will be decided later, after the parties’ arguments have been examined.

====================================================================================================

Security complex anew: Iran's venture into a new architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:38:54 UTC
01:38:54 KST

Security complex anew: Iran's venture into a new architecture
QOM - The war that began with the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran has done more than destroy military targets and redraw the map of immediate threats. It has exposed the fragility of the security architecture that has governed the Middle East for decades.
The old order built around American military presence, Israeli military superiority, and the political alignment of several Arab states with Washington has lost much of its previous certainty. A new regional security complex is therefore emerging which is unmistakably different from the order that existed before the war and is particularly promising for Iran.
The central question for Tehran is no longer simply whether it can resist the pressure but whether Iran can transform the strategic consequences of that resistance into a durable regional order that better serves its national interests. Thus, a new security complex is viable in light of the following dimensions:
The most important transformation concerns the distribution of power. For decades, the Persian Gulf security system operated largely within an American-centered structure. Arab governments depended heavily on American military power, American bases constituted the backbone of deterrence, and Israel functioned as Washington's principal regional military partner. Even when Arab states disagreed with Washington, they generally operated within the limits of this security architecture.
The war has challenged this assumption. Iran demonstrated that American military installations in the region are proved liabilities rather than security guarantees. The very bases intended to protect the Persian Gulf states turned them into potential targets. Iran's retaliation reached Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, Jordan, and other locations hosting U.S. military assets. This meant something consequential: the political value of American protection has radically become less certain.
The Persian Gulf states are therefore looking for greater strategic autonomy. Pakistan and Turkey become more important as alternative security partners, while Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and other Arab states increasingly calculate their security according to their own national interests rather than simply according to Washington's regional preferences. This means the emergence of a more competitive and multipolar regional structure. For Iran, this is an opportunity, but only if Tehran understands that multi-polarity requires diplomacy as much as military power.
The second transformation concerns proximity. One of the principal assumptions of the previous security order was that the United States could project overwhelming power into Iran's immediate neighborhood. The war has complicated that assumption.
In the Caucasus, the strategic environment surrounding Iran appears less threatening than it did before the conflict. Turkey has demonstrated greater caution than a straightforward alignment with the U.S.-Israeli camp would have suggested, while Azerbaijan's relationship with Israel has become considerably more sensitive in the new environment.
This matters because Iran's security dilemma has historically been multidirectional. Tehran has had to watch the Persian Gulf, Iraq, the Levant, Afghanistan, and the Caucasus simultaneously. A reduction in immediate pressure along one of these fronts creates strategic breathing space.
Iran should therefore resist the temptation to treat the Caucasus merely as another battlefield of confrontation. The opportunity is to convert this reduced threat environment into a diplomatic belt of stability around its northern frontier.
Perhaps the most profound change is not military but conceptual. Before the war, regional competition was heavily organized around political influence, ideological rivalry, Iran's regional networks, the Yemen conflict, and the struggle over leadership in the Muslim world. The war has elevated another issue above many of these concerns, i.e., economic survival. For Saudi Arabia, the security of oil infrastructure, maritime routes, investment, Vision 2030, and economic diversification has become inseparable from national security. The closure and disruption of the Strait of Hormuz demonstrated precisely how vulnerable an economic transformation strategy could be when regional military competition threatens energy infrastructure and maritime trade.
This creates an unexpected opening for Iran. Iran does not need Saudi Arabia to become its ally. It needs Saudi Arabia to recognize that permanent confrontation with Iran is incompatible with Saudi economic ambitions. This distinction is crucial. A Saudi Arabia primarily concerned with protecting its economy is a Saudi Arabia with incentives to negotiate with Tehran.
The same logic helps explain the growing divergence between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi. Their differences over Yemen, oil policy, Israel, and regional security have become increasingly visible, demonstrating that the Persian Gulf is not a single strategic actor. Iran's opportunity is therefore not to divide the Persian Gulf through confrontation, but to encourage a regional security logic in which economic interdependence becomes more valuable than permanent military alignment with Washington.
The war has also altered the region's patterns of amity and enmity. At the governmental level, Iran's attacks on Arab territories hosting U.S. military assets generated anger and divergence. Tehran does not ignore this reality because any attempt to build a new security order while disregarding Arab perceptions would be strategically wrong. Iran's diplomatic endeavor amid the conflict showed its regional concern and responsibility for neighbors. Nevertheless, another process has occurred at the societal level. Iran's direct military resistance to the United States and Israel has changed perceptions among segments of Arab and Muslim public opinion.
Whatever their governments' disagreements with Tehran, many communities interpreted Iran's resistance as evidence that American and Israeli dominance over Muslims is far from correct. This creates an important ideational opportunity for Iran. The Axis of Resistance may have suffered organizational and material setbacks, particularly in Lebanon, but the broader idea of resistance has not necessarily weakened. Indeed, the war has strengthened its symbolic appeal among populations that view the existing regional order as dominated by external powers. If Tehran wants Arab governments to accept a new regional balance, it must translate the core idea of resistance into the broader proposition of regional sovereignty, strategic autonomy, economic security, and freedom from external domination. That would be much easier for Arab states to embrace.
The military balance also presents Iran with both opportunities and challenges. The war demonstrated that Iran possesses considerable capabilities for imposing costs on U.S. regional assets and disrupting the assumptions underlying the existing security architecture. At the same time, the conflict exposed some Iranian vulnerabilities, particularly in infrastructure and air defense, for each of them Iran needs to find a feasible solution to securely project its new role in the region.
Perhaps the most important question is who will manage regional security after the war. The United States has historically acted as the external custodian of the Persian Gulf security system. However, the war has undermined the proposition that American bases necessarily make their host countries safer. In fact, several Persian Gulf governments now increasingly view the U.S. military presence through a double lens: it provides protection, but it can also make them targets. This, at least, means that America's custodianship has become contestable. Iran, however, should not assume that the decline of American credibility automatically produces Iranian dominance. The emerging system may instead be characterized by multiple centers of coercive power.
Last but not least, the most consequential transformation is occurring inside Iran's own strategic thinking. For years, Iranian military strategy was largely reactive: respond to Israeli strikes, deter American intervention, support partners, and preserve strategic depth. The new environment encourages a different logic. Iran has demonstrated a willingness to strike directly at the military infrastructure supporting an attack against it. This represents a movement from deterrence by retaliation toward deterrence through proactive risk creation. Iran's strongest strategic position would be one in which its adversaries understand that aggression against Iran will impose unacceptable costs, while its neighbors simultaneously understand that Iranian power does not necessarily threaten their economic survival. Tehran must now construct that difficult balance.
In the end, the new architecture Iran should seek is not a revised version of the old order but a regional and peaceful security complex rooted in shared economic profit. It would require an Iran that is unsanctioned and able to participate fully in the region's economic life; Arab states that are unthreatened by Israel and free to pursue their own security and development; and Arab countries that are unexploited by great powers. Only such a settlement can transform the war's strategic upheaval into a durable order in which Iranian security, Arab autonomy, and regional prosperity reinforce one another rather than remain permanently opposed.

Spacecraft returns to Earth after rescue mission for ageing Nasa telescope fails
Unknown

2026-09-25
16:38:29 UTC
01:38:29 KST

A spacecraft that was launched in July on a mission to rescue a decaying Nasa space observatory plunged back to Earth on Friday, concluding a failed mission that will be followed by the telescope’s own demise in several weeks’ time.
Link, billed as “America’s first commercial space robot”, lifted off on 3 July from Kwajalein Atoll in the South Pacific islands with the objective of lifting the orbit and prolonging the life of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a satellite that has studied gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic events for the last 22 years.
It got as close as 7 to 9 miles (12km to 15km) to Swift and was able to take a series of images detailing its condition, but a series of earlier in-flight problems that hampered motion control and communications meant Link was unable to capture the observatory as planned and release it at a higher altitude.
Katalyst Space Technologies, the company based in Flagstaff, Arizona, which won a $30m Nasa contract for the salvage mission in September 2024, and put together an ambitious rescue plan inside 22 months, announced in a press release Friday morning that its three-armed spacecraft had re-entered Earth’s atmosphere after 85 days in orbit.
Without the altitude lift, Swift, a collaboration between Nasa and Penn State University that was launched in November 2004, will follow its own descent in the coming weeks, and is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere in November.
“From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of Nasa’s astrophysics division, said in a statement.
“While we’ll be sad to see Swift’s mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way – advancing US spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit.”
Jared Isaacman, Nasa’s administrator, also praised the mission in a statement.
“Nasa should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” he said.
“This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future.”
Ironically, Swift’s expected lifespan was shortened by the very intense flare-ups from the sun, which it was sent up to observe. Nasa suspended its observations earlier this year and repositioned Swift to try to minimize the atmosphere’s downward drag while preparing the rescue mission.
Electronics issues on board Link after launch rendered inactive two of its three reaction wheels required for maneuvering, and at one point the spacecraft went into a deep spin. Communication and control were restored, but mission managers abandoned the rescue effort last month when it became clear there was insufficient fuel left.

How Labour can reform Britain’s pensions triple lock | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

Gaby Hinsliff (Britain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage?, 22 September) is right that public policy should not subsidise wealth without limit, but breaking the triple lock is a poor way to target affluent pensioners. Most pensioners are not affluent. Indeed, a quarter of pensioners require benefits in addition to the state pension just to survive and keep a roof over their heads.
If the aim is to stop subsidising wealth, a more direct target is the generous tax treatment of private pension savings. A taxpayer contributing £100 to a pension can receive £40 or £45 in tax relief if they pay higher- or additional-rate tax, compared with £20 for the basic rate. Tax and national insurance contributions relief on private pensions costs the government a staggering £84bn a year.
Most of this money (almost three-quarters) goes to the wealthiest 20% taxpayers because they can afford to save the most and receive the highest rate of relief. Instead, a flat 20% rate of tax relief on private pensions would preserve the incentive for basic-rate taxpayers while reducing the additional subsidy concentrated among higher earners. It’s also fair because when pensions are drawn down, much less tax is recovered by the Treasury, making the net cost of this relief over £50bn a year.
This could raise billions more than breaking the triple lock. The triple lock’s 2.5% floor was only significant during the period when both earnings growth and inflation were close to zero. When inflation and earnings growth are above 2%, as they are now and are expected to be over the coming years, the difference between the triple lock and a conventional uprating mechanism becomes irrelevant.
The policy challenge therefore is to avoid the economically irrelevant, politically damaging and socially divisive red herring that is breaking the triple lock and instead reform the far more regressive support given to large private pension pots.
Stephen Richardson
Grange-over-Sands, Cumbria
Gaby Hinsliff makes the point that retirees of the future are likely to have smaller cushions to fall back on than baby boomers. But it is precisely this that justifies maintaining the triple lock as a bulwark against poverty. Young and middle‑aged workers do indeed face the prospect of an impoverished old age. As highlighted in the Pensions Commission interim report, according to 2025 figures, 43% of working-age people are undersaving for retirement, with just 25% of Bangladeshis and Pakistanis of working age participating in a pension scheme.
The pensions crisis is likely to grow, given the rise in the numbers of self-employed people – the group least likely to be saving for a pension. Millions of workers in their 40s and 50s face the prospect of poverty in retirement, given the rise of precarious working and continuing age discrimination in employment.
We do need a new deal to achieve generational fairness, but breaking the lock will leave millions facing poverty. The alternative must be keeping the lock, but tackling the reasons that justify its existence – low incomes, insecure employment and the high cost of housing.
Chris Phillipson
Emeritus professor of sociology and social gerontology, University of Manchester
There is a simple tweak that would improve the affordability of the triple lock. The goal of the triple lock is to ensure that the value of the pension keeps up with both price inflation and wage inflation. But the way it has been implemented allows pensioners to do much better than this.
Between 2011 and 2026, prices rose by 60% and earnings rose by 66%, but pensions rose by 89%. This happens because in some years prices rise more than wages, but in other years wages rise more. So the pension does better than both of them.
The fix is to smooth out the earnings link. Instead of looking at wages growth over the last year, we should look at growth over the past five years, for example. Pensioners would still be protected against price rises, and would maintain their current position in the wages league table. But they would no longer rise up it.
Bob Vickers
Twickenham, London
Gaby Hinsliff claims that “Every serious party needs billions of pounds to fund their promises, and everyone knows there’s an obvious place to find the money, but nobody wants to be the first to say so. And so a deferential silence shrouds the pension triple lock.” The problem is that everybody might think they know this, but that does not mean it is right.
If we do need to find money, it is within the government’s power to create it. And if it refuses to use that power, it can look elsewhere within the pension system for funds. For example, the pension tax relief given to the highest-earning people in this country, at rates above the basic level of income tax, costs at least £15bn a year – vastly more than costs attributed to the triple lock.
We have a cost of living crisis and a pension poverty crisis. So why is everyone looking at punishing some of the most vulnerable people in our society when the rich continue to have their ever-increasing wealth subsidised by the state at a cost of many billions of pounds a year?
Richard Murphy
Emeritus professor of accounting practice, Sheffield University
Along with my state pension, I receive two small pensions from the Ministry of Defence and the NHS. If my husband should die before me, I don’t know how I would survive financially. We have a small cottage and downsizing wouldn’t result in a significant profit.
My “inheritance” from my parents disappeared when my mother had to go into care with Alzheimer’s; her house had to be sold to pay for her care.
In a week when the billionaire tax avoider Jim Ratcliffe badmouths the country, Gaby Hinsliff makes no reference to the tax system and how the very rich can get away with paying very little.
She also makes no reference to why the UK is doing so badly financially or why young people are struggling – my son can’t afford a house – after a decade of Tory misrule, a decade of Brexit wilderness and the legacy of Thatcherism. Removing the triple lock won’t solve the now endemic financial challenges the UK is facing.
Ingrid Marsh
Newton Abbot, Devon
Gaby Hinsliff is right about the triple lock: it has done its work in raising the ratio between the state retirement pension and average earnings from 18% in 2010 to about 30% now. Two problems remain: what should replace it and how to stop an opportunist opposition from playing politics with the issue?
There is no need to decide this matter now. Far better to announce the end of the triple lock in the forthcoming budget and refer the question of a replacement to a time-limited, cross-party commission. The state pension should not become a political football or part of a short-term fiscal fix.
David Purdy
Causewayhead, Stirling

Pezeshkian uses UNGA meetings to press for diplomacy, and regional stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:35:36 UTC
01:35:36 KST

Pezeshkian uses UNGA meetings to press for diplomacy, and regional stability
TEHRAN– Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian held a series of meetings with senior foreign officials on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, engaging the leaders of Pakistan, Lebanon, the Netherlands, Armenia and Bangladesh, as well as the presidents of Switzerland and the European Council, on regional security, diplomacy, bilateral relations and the consequences of the recent conflict involving Iran.
Pezeshkian also met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Swiss President Guy Parmelin and European Council President Antonio Costa.
Across the meetings, the Iranian president placed particular emphasis on diplomacy as the means of resolving disputes, while arguing that pressure, unilateral measures and military force cannot provide a durable basis for regional security.
Diplomacy and search for a way out of regional tensions
The meeting with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre focused on the continuing instability in West Asia and the need to prevent further escalation. Pezeshkian called for international efforts to reduce tensions and create conditions for the restoration of regional security, stressing that disputes should be addressed through dialogue, international law and respect for national sovereignty.
Støre expressed concern about continuing instability, and particularly the potential international consequences of insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz. He also voiced support for diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions.
A similar emphasis emerged from Pezeshkian’s meeting with Swiss President Guy Parmelin. The Iranian president said recent US and Israeli military actions against Iran, including attacks on infrastructure and civilian facilities, were contrary to international law and humanitarian principles.
He nevertheless stressed Tehran’s readiness to develop relations with other countries based on mutual respect, sovereign equality and shared interests.
Parmelin highlighted Switzerland’s experience in diplomatic initiatives and its role as a protecting power for US interests in Iran, expressing his country’s readiness to maintain diplomatic contacts. The two sides agreed on the importance of political and diplomatic mechanisms to prevent another escalation.
Dialogue with Europe
Pezeshkian’s meetings with European officials also addressed the future of relations between Iran and Europe.
In his meeting with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, the Iranian president said Tehran remained open to dialogue but maintained that the United States must honor its commitments if diplomacy is to make meaningful progress. He argued that previous rounds of negotiations had repeatedly been followed by developments that disrupted the diplomatic process and ultimately contributed to war.
Jetten stressed the need for practical mechanisms to overcome existing obstacles in bilateral relations and identified maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz as one of the issues requiring diplomatic attention.
Pezeshkian took a more critical line in his meeting with European Council President Antonio Costa, arguing that European governments had diminished their ability to influence international developments by aligning themselves with US policies toward Iran.
He specifically criticized European positions on the snapback mechanism and the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), saying Tehran expected Europe to pursue a more independent approach.
On regional security, Pezeshkian argued that security should ultimately be ensured by the countries of the region, rather than through external intervention.
Relations with neighbors and regional partners
The Iranian president’s meeting with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif centered on bilateral cooperation and regional diplomacy. The two leaders reviewed the implementation of existing agreements and discussed developments affecting regional security, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Peninsula.
Pezeshkian praised Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to support regional peace and stability and called for continued consultations to prevent conflicts from widening. Sharif, for his part, reaffirmed Islamabad’s readiness to play a constructive role in regional diplomacy and highlighted the importance of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
With Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Pezeshkian discussed Lebanon’s sovereignty and stability as well as the consequences of Israeli attacks. He reaffirmed Iran’s support for an independent and stable Lebanon and said Tehran favored regional cooperation and dialogue while respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.
Salam outlined Beirut’s priorities, including an end to the Israeli occupation of Lebanese territory, the cessation of attacks and the strengthening of the Lebanese state’s authority.
Pezeshkian also met Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, with the two sides focusing on accelerating the implementation of bilateral agreements, particularly those concerning regional transit routes. Both leaders stressed the importance of translating existing understandings into practical cooperation.
Expanding economic and bilateral cooperation
Economic diplomacy was another component of Pezeshkian’s meetings. In talks with Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, the two sides discussed expanding economic relations and agreed on the importance of convening the sixth Iran-Bangladesh Joint Economic Commission.
Pezeshkian described the relationship with Bangladesh as possessing considerable potential for broader cooperation, while Rahman praised Iran’s assistance to Bangladeshi nationals during the recent crisis.
The meeting also addressed the wider regional situation. Pezeshkian reiterated that Iran would not yield to pressure but would continue engaging internationally on the basis of mutual respect and constructive relations.
A consistent diplomatic message
Taken together, Pezeshkian’s meetings in New York presented a consistent diplomatic message: Iran is seeking engagement with neighboring states, European governments and other international partners while opposing 'coercion, unilateralism and military pressure.'
The meetings also highlighted Tehran’s effort to connect regional security with diplomacy, arguing that lasting stability requires respect for national sovereignty, dialogue and regional mechanisms rather than externally imposed security arrangements.
At the same time, Pezeshkian used his encounters with European officials to press for a reassessment of Europe’s position toward Iran, particularly over the nuclear issue and its relationship with Washington, while meetings with neighboring and regional states focused more heavily on practical cooperation, transit, bilateral agreements and mechanisms for containing regional tensions.
The breadth of the meetings — spanning Europe, South and West Asia and the Caucasus — underscored the Iranian president’s effort at the UN gathering to keep diplomatic channels open while advancing Tehran’s positions on the regional conflict and the future of its international relations.

From teenage prodigy to Asian sprint star: Puripol Boonson's rise
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
00:33:22 CST
01:33:22 KST

by sportswriters Liu Yang and Wang Qinou
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- The moment the starting gun fired for the men's 100 meters at the 2026 Asian Games, Puripol Boonson turned Nagoya's Paloma Mizuho Stadium into his stage.
The 20-year-old Thai sprinter delivered an unprecedented feat, with three consecutive sub-10-second clockings across the heats, semifinals and final and two Games record-breaking results.
Boonson's performance in Nagoya was nothing short of extraordinary. The Thai star opened his Asiad campaign with 9.95 seconds in the heats on Thursday, announcing his arrival as the favorite for the title.
He carried that momentum into Friday's semifinals, where he clocked 9.91 seconds to break the Asian Games record, surpassing the previous mark set by China's Su Bingtian at the 2018 Jakarta Asian Games.
Less than three hours later came the final. Although he got off to a slower start, the Thai sprinter gradually found his rhythm and unleashed his formidable finishing speed. He surged ahead through the middle section of the race and held off a fierce late challenge to cross the finish line first.
He lowered his newly minted Games record once more to 9.90 seconds, with a mild 0.1 m/s tailwind, delivering on his mission to claim the men's 100m gold for Thailand.
Speaking after the final, Boonson revealed his next goal is to target Su's Asian record of 9.83 seconds.
The landmark performance in Nagoya is the latest chapter in a remarkable record-breaking journey stretching back to his teenage years.
Born in 2006, Boonson was eye-catching at the 2021 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games in Hanoi, Vietnam, held in May 2022, where he had his breakout international meet, winning gold medals in the sprint triple: 100m, 200m, and 4x100m relay.
Two months later, at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Cali, Colombia, the teenager clocked 10.09 seconds in the men's 100m semifinals, setting an Asian youth benchmark and drawing global attention.
His defining breakthrough came at the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Bangkok, Thailand, where Boonson became the first sprinter across Southeast Asia ever to break the 10-second barrier with a stunning 9.94 seconds in the men's 100m heats under legal wind conditions. Just two hours later, he won the 100m final in 10.00 seconds.
At the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games, Boonson made his Asian Games debut and claimed silver in the men's 100m in 10.02 seconds, finishing behind China's veteran athlete Xie Zhenye, which confirmed that the young Thai had established himself among Asia's leading sprinters.
As attention around him continues to grow, Boonson said he does not want to put too much pressure on himself.
"Instead, I regard it as a driving force to push myself to run faster. Because everyone has expectations for me, I will try my best not to put too much pressure on myself and compete in the most genuine and normal state," he said.
Still only 20 years old, Boonson is far from the end of his journey. With the men's 200m and 4x100m relay still ahead at the Asian Games, the Thai sprinter will have further opportunities to chase medals and perhaps more records. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Xi-Trump summit provides new strategic guidance for China-U.S. ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
00:33:11 CST
01:33:11 KST

* Chinese President Xi Jinping engaged intensively on Thursday with his host, U.S. President Donald Trump, at the White House during his state visit to the United States, reaching common understanding on many issues.
* Xi's visit comes less than half a year after Trump's state visit to China in May, when the two presidents agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.
* While China and the United States compete in AI, they have even more reasons to cooperate, Xi said, urging the two major countries in AI to leverage respective strengths rather than guard against each other.
* At the state dinner, both presidents looked back on the long history of exchanges between the Chinese and American peoples, underscoring the importance of people-to-people ties.
WASHINGTON, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- From a welcome ceremony and a formal meeting to a state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping engaged intensively on Thursday with his host, U.S. President Donald Trump, at the White House during his state visit to the United States.
The two leaders conducted sincere and in-depth exchanges and reached common understanding on many issues, which has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and provided new strategic guidance for China-U.S. relations.
PUTTING VISION INTO ACTION
"I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of China-U.S. relationship on a steady course toward the future," Xi said at the welcome ceremony at the White House.
Xi's visit comes less than half a year after Trump's state visit to China in May, when the two presidents agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.
Later at his White House meeting with Trump, Xi called for translating that vision into action and finding the right way for the two major countries to get along with each other.
The two sides need to work toward a relationship featuring cooperation as the mainstay, moderate competition, manageable differences, and promises of peace, Xi said.
Xi noted that China and the United States should, and fully can, achieve mutual benefit and win-win results through practical cooperation, help each other succeed through healthy competition, properly manage differences by seeking common ground while respecting differences, and build peace by fostering mutual trust, so that a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability can better benefit the two peoples and people around the world.
Trump, for his part, said he and Xi are good friends who have maintained in-depth and close communication, and expressed confidence that U.S.-China relations would be handled well under the leadership of the two heads of state.
The meticulous arrangements for Xi's state visit, down to the details and with care and consideration, reflected the importance Trump attached to Xi's trip.
After receiving Xi in person at the airport one day earlier, Trump hosted the grand welcome ceremony at the White House.
Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, watched a performance by the United States Marines in the company of the U.S. presidential couple. The ceremony also featured a military review, with U.S. honor guards from different military services performing traditional drills and playing instrumental music. Multiple combat aircraft flew over the White House in honor of the Chinese and U.S. presidents and their wives.
Following the talks, the two presidential couples met again for the state dinner. Inside, red blossoms and red linens decorated the room, a choice a White House release said reflected the color's longstanding cultural significance in China.
"In less than half a year, the Chinese and American presidents have exchanged state visits, making history in our bilateral engagement," Xi said at the state dinner hosted by Trump.
The strongest signal to the world is that the leaders of the world's two most consequential major countries, though overtly competitive, can meet in harmony and with good spirit, which is the headline achievement, commented U.S. scholar Robert Lawrence Kuhn.
COOPERATION GOES BOTH WAYS
From Beijing in May to Washington in September, practical cooperation has remained high on the agenda of China-U.S. interactions.
At the ceremony, Xi called on the two countries to "cooperate with sincerity."
Xi said the two sides share "deeply intertwined" interests and ample room for cooperation, noting that China-U.S. collaboration "may not solve every problem in the world," but many would be hard to resolve without it.
During his talks with Trump, Xi said the latest round of trade and economic consultations between the two countries had produced a new joint arrangement, calling it good news for industries and people of both countries, as well as the global economy.
Noting that cooperation is a two-way street, Xi said as long as the two sides uphold the spirit of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit, they can find a way out of problems.
The state dinner offered another glimpse of the breadth of economic ties between the two countries. Executives from major U.S. aviation, technology and financial firms were among the guests, including some who had accompanied Trump to Beijing in May, such as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
Artificial intelligence (AI) was another area discussed by the two leaders.
While China and the United States compete in AI, they have even more reasons to cooperate, Xi said, urging the two major countries in AI to leverage respective strengths rather than guard against each other.
The two sides should keep AI under human control, uphold a human-centered approach and use AI for good, ensuring that it serves human progress, Xi added.
Trump also stressed the importance of maintaining dialogue on AI, calling it the technology that bears on the future of humanity.
CARRYING ON FRIENDSHIP
At the state dinner, both presidents looked back on the long history of exchanges between the Chinese and American peoples, underscoring the importance of people-to-people ties.
Xi recalled how the two peoples stood shoulder to shoulder in the fight against Japanese militarist aggression more than 80 years ago, and how Ping-Pong Diplomacy reopened the door to bilateral exchanges more than half a century ago.
He also recounted the story of American Ronald Sakolsky, who supported Chinese desert control worker Yin Yuzhen's tree-planting efforts more than 20 years ago, calling it a shining example of friendly exchanges between the two peoples.
Such exchanges, Xi said, have promoted heart-to-heart communication between our peoples and strengthened public support for China-U.S. friendship and cooperation.
Trump, meanwhile, reviewed the long history of U.S.-China exchanges, pointing to early commercial ties and the exchange of "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said.
New steps are now being taken to carry that friendship forward.
At the welcome ceremony, Xi announced that two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will soon arrive at Zoo Atlanta and meet the American people. He also invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange and study programs over the next five years.
"The hope of the China-U.S. relationship lies in our people, and its future lies with the young," Xi said.
In 2023, during his visit to San Francisco, Xi announced a similar initiative inviting 50,000 young Americans to China over five years. That target has already been achieved.
"President Xi announced that he wants to double the number of students over the next five years. That's very positive, very significant, because I believe that those kinds of exchanges and students going back and forth are very, very important," said Kenneth Quinn, president emeritus of the World Food Prize Foundation. ■

Namibia launches climate plan requiring 14.07-bln-USD investment by 2035
China

00:32:51 CST
01:32:51 KST

WINDHOEK, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Namibia on Friday launched its Third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), outlining climate mitigation and adaptation measures requiring an estimated 14.07 billion U.S. dollars in investment through 2035.
Speaking at the launch in Windhoek, Minister of Environment, Forestry and Tourism Indileni Daniel said the plan marked a shift from climate planning to implementation, with the government seeking to turn its climate priorities into bankable projects and attract both domestic and international investment.
Of the total investment requirement, 6.42 billion dollars is earmarked for mitigation and 7.65 billion dollars for adaptation, according to the NDC 3.0 presentation.
About 12 percent of the financing is unconditional, while 88 percent is conditional on international climate finance, technology transfer and capacity-building support.
Daniel said Namibia must now move beyond discussions on climate finance and focus on mobilizing funding for implementation.
"Conditional does not mean optional," she said, adding that the conditional component represents what Namibia can achieve when international support matches its national ambition.
NDC 3.0 contains 72 measures and 216 actions across 13 sectors and priority areas. The mitigation component includes 26 measures and 106 actions covering energy, agriculture, forestry and other land use, industrial processes and waste.
The adaptation component comprises 46 measures and 110 actions covering agriculture and food security, water resources, biodiversity, fisheries and aquaculture, health, infrastructure, coastal areas, urban settlements and other cross-cutting issues.
The plan extends Namibia's climate target year from 2030 to 2035. It targets unconditional emissions reductions of 7.158 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent and conditional reductions of 15.608 million tonnes by 2035. ■

Mid-Autumn Festival brings families together across Taiwan Strait
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
00:32:40 CST
01:32:40 KST

TAIPEI, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- As the autumn air turns crisp and the full moon rises, like on the Chinese mainland, Taiwan is embracing the same Mid-Autumn Festival with a familiar mix of family gatherings, traditional foods and customs passed down through generations.
For many people on the island, the festival comes with four cherished traditions: admiring the moon, eating mooncakes, barbecuing and peeling pomelos.
Mooncakes and the full moon symbolize family reunion, while pomelos -- whose Chinese name sounds similar to the word for "blessing" -- are associated with wishes for good fortune and protection.
For Taiwan businessman Chueh Jen-tsun, the memories of Mid-Autumn Festival are inseparable from the glow of charcoal fires, the fresh scent of pomelos, fireworks by the riverside and songs at karaoke bars.
Before this year's festival, Chueh shared a video on social media introducing Taiwan's unique Mid-Autumn customs to people on the Chinese mainland.
"After dinner, we would often accompany our parents to the riverside to set off fireworks, and then the whole family would happily go singing karaoke," he recalled. "The warmth of those moments has stayed with me."
Mid-Autumn Festival is also a time to express gratitude and remember their ancestors. Families may prepare a feast to pay respects to deceased relatives, while some continue traditional practices of worshipping deities, praying for a happy and smooth life.
The ways people celebrate the festival may vary on the two sides of the Taiwan Strait, but the longing for family reunion and the affection among relatives remain familiar emotions shared across the Strait.
Reunion can take many forms.
The development of Taiwan was closely tied to waves of migration from various corners of the Chinese mainland over generations.
Deep connections with ancestral homes on the mainland led to the establishment of many townsmen associations across Taiwan. Today, dozens of them remain active, organizing events during holidays such as the Lunar New Year, Qingming Festival and Mid-Autumn Festival.
Ahead of this year's festival, people in Taipei and Jinan in east China's Shandong Province held a video gathering, allowing relatives and folks from the two cities to exchange greetings and celebrate together despite the distance. Such a gathering has become an annual Mid-Autumn tradition.
"The bridge cannot be interrupted and should continue," said Yu Mao-sheng, head of an association for Taiwan people who are from Shandong. The event has been held for nearly a decade, he said, expressing hope that people on both sides will have more opportunities to meet and maintain their ties through regular exchanges.
For some, the most meaningful reunion is a journey back to their ancestral hometown.
In early September, Taiwan resident Teng Tai-hsien, whose father moved to Taiwan more than seven decades ago from Shandong, traveled to Zaozhuang in Shandong to trace his family's origins and pay respects to his ancestors. He also visited Qingdao, Jinan and Yantai, meeting relatives and renewing old ties.
Teng's journey was driven in part by a promise to his father. "My father repeatedly told me that I should return to our hometown every year and never forget where our roots are," he recalled.
"When I arrived back in my hometown, I immediately felt a sense of familiarity. I truly felt that I was coming home," he said.
For Teng, the journey was more than a return to a place on a map. It was a way of reconnecting with his family roots and one he hopes to pass on to the next generation.
"I will also take my children back to Zaozhuang to pay respects to our ancestors, so that they can better understand where their roots lie," he said.
Under the full moon, reunion takes many forms -- a family dinner, a shared mooncake, a video call across the Strait or a journey home. Yet each carries the same simple wish: to be close to the people and places that make home feel like home. ■

Feature: Art in the shadow of war -- Middle East artists turn rubble into hope at Istanbul fair
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
00:32:35 CST
01:32:35 KST

ISTANBUL, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Syrian sculptor Safaa Alset does not sculpt rubble. She transforms it.
Born in Homs, she remembers the barrel bombs that struck civilian neighborhoods during the civil war that erupted in 2011, burying people beneath collapsed buildings.
From that jagged metal, she shaped trees and flowers.
"That means hope," Alset told Xinhua amid the polished halls and bright lights of Istanbul. "It means we are surviving, and we challenge death."
Bringing these heavy memories to Contemporary Istanbul, Türkiye's leading art fair, is for her an act of optimism and obligation.
"Our job is to document all that happened in the world, to deliver a message, and to educate," she explained. "That is the true role of an artist."
Running from Wednesday to Sunday, the 21st edition of the fair serves as a cultural crossroads, gathering over 70 galleries from across geographies. For Middle Eastern artists, it offers a rare, stable platform to use art as soft power, reaching the global stage despite the isolation of war.
Iranian artist Afsane Nangar uses that platform to issue a call for peace. A contemporary illuminator known for blending traditional Islamic tezhip, or book illumination, with modern touches, she refuses to let darkness have the final word.
"We see wars everywhere," Nangar said. "At first glance, everything seems dark. But we can also see the beautiful energy within it."
As the war between Iran and the United States deepens geopolitical tensions, Nangar deliberately incorporates American cartoon characters into her work to bridge communication.
The shadow of war reaches beyond the canvas and into the art market. Leila Heller, the Iranian-born founder of the Leila Heller Gallery, sees firsthand how conflict alters artists' creative process.
"The war somehow darkens their spirit," Heller said. "Sometimes, instead of red, they use black, because they're thinking difficult times are maybe ahead."
This anxiety is rooted in harsh market realities. Operating her gallery in Dubai, Heller noted that even relatively safe havens feel the strain as collectors leave and tourism dips.
But the struggle is far more severe for artists inside Iran, who are fighting simply to make ends meet. Refusing to let them face this crisis alone, Heller sells their works without taking a commission, sending all proceeds directly to the creators.
Like the artists she represents, Heller relies on a stubborn sense of hope to push through.
"I've been through many wars, through many revolutions, through many difficulties. I'm a survivor," she said. "I always look at the positive side of life."
The push for cultural diplomacy at Contemporary Istanbul extends beyond the Middle East. Pearl Lam, founder of the globally renowned Pearl Lam Galleries and a prominent Chinese gallerist at the fair, sees art as a crucial form of soft power to combat the growing geopolitical divide.
"It is more about communication," Lam said.
By presenting a diverse lineup ranging from traditional Chinese lacquer techniques to works by a Saudi female artist, Lam aims to break down global prejudices.
"The world is a mess right now," she said. "What we need is humanity, empathy, and understanding. Art gives us that soft power." ■

The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry the same tax rights as other married couples.
The decision follows a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) requiring Poland – whose domestic law does not allow same-sex couples to form any type of legal union – to recognise same-sex marriages contracted in other EU member states.
Podpisałem dziś interpretację ogólną, która zapewnia, że osoby, które uzyskały transkrypcję aktu małżeństwa będą miały w polskich urzędach skarbowych takie same prawa i obowiązki podatkowe jak wszyscy małżonkowie.
— Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 24, 2026
“Today, I signed a general interpretation ensuring that persons who have obtained a transcription of their marriage certificate will have the same tax rights and obligations in Polish tax offices as all other married couples,” announced finance minister Andrzej Domański in a social media post.
A general interpretation is an official position taken by the finance ministry aiming to clarify the application of tax law in a specific area.
Among the benefits that couples with a transcribed foreign marriage certificate can now receive include preferential treatment under inheritance and gift tax rules and the ability to file joint personal income tax returns.
Couples may also pay tax on behalf of a spouse and refuse to testify as a witness in proceedings involving their spouse.
“This is about basic equality, justice and fairness,” Domański told broadcaster TVN. “We want these rights to be enforceable in an effective way.”
The finance minister said that the decision would have a “negligible” impact on the state budget. He also noted that such couples would be subject to the obligations that apply to other married couples in Poland, which include liability for their spouse’s tax obligations.
Osoby, które uzyskały tak zwaną transkrypcję aktu małżeństwa, będą miały przed polskimi urzędami skarbowymi dokładnie takie same prawa i obowiązki jak pozostali małżonkowie – powiedział minister finansów Andrzej Domański w rozmowie z Grzegorzem Kajdanowiczem w @faktypofaktach w… pic.twitter.com/uVwDaD3ZDk
— tvn24 (@tvn24) September 24, 2026
The finance minister’s decision has drawn criticism from right-wing politicians, who argue that recognition of same-sex marriage violates the constitution, which states that “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland”.
Paweł Szefernaker, chief of staff to President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, said Domański’s actions were “inconsistent with the constitution” and had been carried out “without legislation, without debate, without honestly telling Poles what is really happening”.
“Everyone has the right to a private life,” he added. “However, the state has a duty to protect the legal order and provide tax support for marriage.”
Patryk Jaki, a deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party, said that the finance minister’s actions “clearly violate Polish law and will have legal implications in the future” for Domański, who is “writing additional points in the indictment against himself”.
Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) group, said the tax interpretation “will be revoked on the very first day” if his party comes to power.
To jest niezgodna z Konstytucją próba faktycznego zrównania małżeństwa ze związkami jednopłciowymi. Bez zmiany Konstytucji, bez ustawy, bez debaty, bez uczciwego powiedzenia Polakom, co naprawdę się dzieje.

The changes follow a ruling issued by the CJEU in November 2025 ordering Poland to recognise same-sex marriages contracted in other EU states. The court found that failing to do so infringes the freedom to move and reside within the EU as well as the right to respect for private and family life.
In light of that ruling, in March this year, Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA) ordered Warsaw’s registry office to recognise a marriage conducted by two Polish men in Germany by transcribing it into the Polish civil registry.
In May, the Polish government issued a regulation allowing such transcriptions of foreign same-sex marriages to take place nationwide. It went into force in August. However, even before then, some cities had begun transcribing marriage certificates, beginning with Warsaw and Wrocław in May.
At the end of August, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski reported that 84 same-sex couples had already transcribed their foreign marriages under the government’s new regulation.
Poland has begun paying benefits to same-sex couples who married abroad then entered their marriage into the Polish registry.
The EU court ordered Poland to recognise such marriages, even though domestic law does not allow for any form of same-sex union https://t.co/svnRjyBO8Q

While foreign same-sex marriages can now be entered into Poland’s civil registry, questions have remained as to what that will mean in practice for such couples, especially as domestic law does not recognise same-sex relationships.
In another development, labour minister Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk announced last week that the Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) has begun paying care allowances to qualifying same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry.
