Mpox case confirmed in northeastern Congolese city at center of Ebola outbreak
DAKAR, Sept 25 - A laboratory-confirmed case of mpox was identified in the northeastern Congolese city of Bunia, the director of a local hospital and two health officials said, raising concerns about a resurgence of the disease as the country battles its worst Ebola outbreak on record.
• The epidemic caused by the Ebola outbreak was declared on May 15 in Ituri province, where Bunia is located, and has infected 7,890 people and killed 3,799, according to government data published on Thursday.
• Mpox is a viral disease that causes fever and skin lesions and spreads through close physical contact.
• Congo declared an end to mpox as a national public health emergency in April after a three-year outbreak that resulted in more than 34,000 confirmed cases nationwide. Authorities cautioned at the time that the virus had not been eradicated and could resurge.
• The latest case involves a 21-year-old woman who was admitted to hospital on Thursday with lesions across her body consistent with mpox, hospital director Davin Ambitapio Musungufu said. She tested positive on Friday, he and two health officials told Reuters.
• A second woman, aged 32, has been identified as a suspected mpox case and is awaiting laboratory results, Musungufu said. She and the confirmed patient have been isolated and are being cared for by a dedicated medical team.
• Investigations are underway to trace contacts and identify the source of infection, Musungufu said.
• Dr. Adelard Lofungola, a health official who served as deputy incident manager for Congo's mpox response, said five suspected mpox cases in Bunia were currently under investigation.
• Health officials have reported an increase in mpox cases in several parts of the country over the past month, he said.
• Lofungola said the Ebola outbreak's impact on Congo's health system was complicating efforts to monitor other infections. REUTERS

New map projections don’t make the Mercator wrong | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:31:30 UTC
01:31:30 KST

The subject of projections is incredibly complicated and you did a good job of navigating the discussion (‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias, 18 September).
However, suggesting that transverse Mercator is inherently biased is not fair (if it is possible to be unfair to an equation) to both the projection and the cartographers.
Mercator et al just did the job of creating maps that were useful for the European sailors they were working for. The fact that everyone carried on using it was our laziness and not their bias.
The Equal Earth projection is a much better representation for what we use maps for now, but that does not make the Mercator wrong.
You say “A London-centric worldview has long dominated how world maps are presented.” But I can think of almost no maps that have London at the centre. The international coordinate system (ie latitude-longitude, which is unchanged by this resolution) is based for arbitrary historical reasons on a meridian drawn through Greenwich.
However, the “centre” of this coordinate system is not London but a point in the sea off west Africa. No map or representation has to use this as the centre and the current best practice – called UTM – has 60 different zones (thus 60 centres) to represent all parts of the globe.
Even the UK Ordnance Survey mapping system is not “centred” on London. As far as you can say it has a centre, it would be somewhere in Lancashire. 
Paul Harwood 
London

The dark art of maths and the AI revolution | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:28:05 UTC
01:28:05 KST

You report in your leader that some mathematicians feel discomfiture at the AI solution to a Navier-Stokes problem (The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that, 20 September). I fear that they have been hoist by their own petard: mathematics, after all, has been the prime mover of the AI revolution.
As a somewhat lowly mathematician, let me remind others of the famous quote of Augustine: “The good Christian should beware the mathematician and all those who make empty promises. The danger already exists that the mathematicians have made a covenant with the devil to darken the spirit and to confine man in the bonds of hell.”
While the accuracy of the quote, and Augustine’s meaning, are in some dispute, its appropriateness here is too good to waste.
Bev Littlewood
Emeritus professor of software engineering, City St George’s, University of London

Why Ed Miliband has embraced his ‘awkward dad’ image in viral TikTok video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:22:55 UTC
01:22:55 KST

It sparked delight among the diehard Milifans and a begrudging smile from those less keen on the foreign secretary, but a viral video of Ed Miliband has – possibly – confirmed his status as the internet’s awkward dad.
About 1.5 million people have viewed an interaction between Miliband and the TikTok personality Feroz Khan on the streets of New York, during which the digital content creator asks Miliband a series of questions including his name, job and his top piece of advice.
Following the same formula employed by Khan in every video, Miliband is stopped in a seemingly – though of course not at all – impromptu manner by the influencer who says: “You’re very well dressed, what do you do for a living?”
When Miliband, in New York for the UN general assembly, explains that he is the foreign secretary (adding that he is the UK equivalent of Marco Rubio when Khan claims not to know what that is), the influencer asks: “What makes your work so special?” Miliband gushes that he is “trying to make the world a better place”.
So far, so soft serve. But it is when Miliband is asked about any challenges he has faced and, with the charm of an ingenue, replies – “Oh wow! I ran to be prime minister of Britain. It didn’t go so well … but I kept going!” – that it is clear his media team have fully capitalised on social media’s love of the cringe moment.
Miliband has been on a journey since May 2014, when the then Labour leader was photographed ineptly eating a bacon roll during a campaign visit in New Malden. It was an image that launched a thousand memes and, occasionally, if daftly, was pointed to as a reason that Labour lost the 2015 general election.
Freed of the shackles of leadership – and embraced by a generation that frames mortifying incidents as unifying moments – Miliband is now free to take pleasure in the delights of a vegan fruity flapjack, safe in the knowledge that the video of him doing so will probably bolster his particular internet aura rather than damage it.
While Reform UK’s Lee Anderson wrote thunderously of the video, “Our Foreign Secretary! Putin will be quaking in his boots!”, his team were perhaps notching up the hits and watching Miliband’s expanding online presence.
The PR consultant Mark Borkowski said: “Ed Miliband has finally worked out that the awkward dad thing isn’t a reputational defect. It’s his brand. In an age of politicians desperately trying to manufacture authenticity, the slight cringe actually makes him feel human. He’s not trying to be cool, he’s letting the socials enjoy the fact that he isn’t.”
While the video nods to content consumers being in on the joke, some observers have pointed out that it is clearly staged rather than spontaneous, because Miliband’s aides do not stop when the foreign secretary starts speaking with a “stranger” and his answers seem rehearsed.
A government source agreed that it may well indeed have been a remarkable coincidence if Miliband had just bumped into an internet celebrity who also just happens to bump into famous people including Jennifer Lopez, Sydney Sweeney and Bradley Cooper.
“This isn’t Ed trying to hoodwink anyone. This is how these videos work – it’s really exciting working with content creators, but you have to outsource editorial control,” they said. “The vast majority of people who watch a video like this understand that the tone is native to the format.”
With the clock of views ticking up, the video had clearly reached a lot of people who may have been unfamiliar with Miliband’s early oeuvre. But Borkowski said there was potential for the knowing nod about Miliband’s maladroit moments to backfire.
“The danger comes when the choreography becomes visible,” he said. “Awkwardness works because it feels accidental. Once people think the ‘dad dancing’ has been Blackfriars Road focus-grouped, the joke shrivels.”

Swedish police launch probe into possible election fraud around Stockholm
STOCKHOLM, Sept 25 - Police said on Friday they had started preliminary investigations into five complaints of election fraud around Sweden's capital, days after a probe in another area, casting a further shadow over the September 13 national vote.
Sweden's parliamentary election saw the opposition narrowly defeat the incumbent right-wing government in a vote widely seen as a referendum on whether the far-right Sweden Democrats should be part of the next administration.
Stockholm police said they had started the preliminary investigations after receiving five complaints, including one about the vote in the suburb of Jarva.
Two of the cases also involved complaints of potential vote-buying, a police spokesperson added, declining to go into more detail or name the other areas.
It was not immediately clear what impact those cases might have on the result of the election in those areas if any wrongdoing was found.
On Tuesday, prosecutors said they were looking into potential fraud in the central Swedish town of Borlange, a case that could put 11 parliamentary seats in play if the Election Review Board decides to order a re-run.
In a statement on Thursday, the Prosecution Authority said no indictments had been issued in relation to the allegations of fraud in Borlange and no suspects had been formally identified.
In that case, the investigation centres on the election of Mohamed Abdukardir Ali, a Left Party candidate for parliament, who unexpectedly overtook other representatives on the ballot for the party.
The Left Party said on Tuesday Ali would take a leave of absence while the allegations were being investigated. Reuters was not immediately able to reach Ali for comment.
Sweden's Election Review Board on Friday was not immediately available to respond to requests for comment on the new investigations. REUTERS

Details on U.S.-China trade negotiations coming Monday, USTR Greer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:20:40 UTC
01:20:40 KST

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that the U.S. and China have reached agreements covering a subset of goods the two countries can trade on more favorable terms, marking fresh progress in negotiations between the world's two largest economies.
"We've actually reached agreement with the Chinese on a number of these things," Greer said on CNBC's "Squawk Box," referring to goods including U.S. agricultural products and medical devices and Chinese consumer goods considered nonsensitive.
Greer said the Trump administration plans to release "a lot more details" Monday about what the two sides have accomplished in negotiations over the past several weeks. He said the goal is to carve out areas of trade that could remain insulated from future tariff measures or broader trade disputes.
The two countries want some goods to be traded on a "more preferential basis" and potentially left aside if either country imposes new tariffs.
Greer did not specify Friday which products are covered by the agreements, how tariffs on those goods could change or when the new terms would take effect. Negotiations under the new U.S.-China "Board of Trade" mechanism are focused on "pure trade issues," Greer said, rather than U.S. national security restrictions on advanced technology.
"All those export controls that are national security issues, we take those off the table," Greer said.
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, after they met in Beijing in May, announced the establishment of the Board of Trade to manage trade between the two rivals in nonsensitive products. Businesses have been waiting for more details on what categories of trade would be set aside under the new framework for lower tariffs.
The news comes as Washington and Beijing have also agreed to extend their broader trade truce by two months, giving the two sides more time to negotiate over long-standing economic disputes.
Greer said Friday that the U.S. views those two months as "compliance periods" to assess whether China is following through on earlier commitments, including purchases of U.S. soybeans and other agricultural products and access to rare earths needed by American manufacturers.
"Whenever we have these compliance periods that roll over, it's a time for us to assess, reassess and determine whether or not to continue this period of relative peace on the economic front with the Chinese," Greer said.
Meanwhile, tariffs have sharply altered U.S. trade flows. Greer said Friday that the U.S. goods trade deficit with China has fallen nearly 40%, while acknowledging that some trade has shifted to other countries as companies adjust their supply chains.
Mexico has been one beneficiary of that shift. U.S. imports from Mexico reached a record $60.6 billion in July, according to the Census Bureau. The seasonally adjusted U.S. goods deficit with Mexico increased by $7.2 billion that month to $27.5 billion, according to the Census Bureau.
"When you impose tariffs ... you see market actors starting to do what market actors do, which is respond to new terms of trade, respond to new incentives in the market," Greer said. "We're actually seeing a lot come back to North America."
Greer's comments also provided new detail from the U.S. side following Trump's meeting with Xi at the White House on Thursday. Beijing has so far released a more detailed public account of the talks than Washington.
Xi told Trump on Thursday that artificial intelligence presents greater opportunities for U.S.-China cooperation than competition, according to a Chinese state media readout.
"The two sides can continue AI dialogue, exchange views on risks and benefits, and together guard against the misuse or malicious use of AI," Xi said, according to a CNBC translation of the readout.
Trump, in a Truth Social post Friday morning, called the meeting with Xi "very productive" and said the Chinese leader appeared receptive to Trump's preferred term of "SUPER INTELLIGENCE" for artificial intelligence.
"Tremendous things will be happening," Trump wrote.

Ukraine revises capacity calculation rules for ethanol, bioethanol plants
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

01:18:54 KST

Ukraine's Cabinet of Ministers has amended the procedure for determining the maximum capacity of equipment used to produce ethyl alcohol and bioethanol, including by providing for the actual capacity of the equipment to be taken into account in the relevant calculation.
The government adopted the relevant resolution on Sept. 23, the press service of the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food reported.
According to the statement, the updated procedure also defines which changes are considered changes in the maximum capacity of equipment, establishes a mechanism for carrying out a new calculation, and sets permissible deviations in actual capacity related to the technological specifics of production and the properties of measuring instruments.
At the same time, the procedure allows the actual capacity of technological equipment to deviate from the maximum capacity by up to and including 3%.
In addition, the government clarified the application of coefficients for equipment washing and disinfection, taking into account that these operations may be carried out during scheduled production shutdowns.
The changes will be applied when calculating the guaranteed tax liability for excise tax.

“Killing Ukraine’s internet would take nuclear or chemical weapons”—MiroHost founder whose data center Russia just destroyed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:18:11 UTC
01:18:11 KST

Russian drones and missiles struck Kyiv data centers over 23–24 September, knocking out internet and hosting providers. The Digital Transformation Ministry said about 100,000 subscribers lost service, NV Business reported.
Russia has widened its air campaign from power plants and warehouses to railways, fuel stations, and now digital infrastructure as it tries to grind down the country's ability to function before another war winter.
"You'd have to destroy 70-80% of Kyiv's buildings"
MiroHost founder and Internet Invest Group head Oleksandr Olshanskyi told NV Business the attack destroyed his own data center.
"Most critically important data and systems have been moved abroad or to the cloud," Olshanskyi said. "If an online store stops working, that's unpleasant but not a tragedy."
He called rumors about a full internet blackout or sharp service price hikes baseless.
"Destroying all internet in a simple way is impossible—you'd have to use nuclear or chemical weapons or destroy 70-80% of buildings in Kyiv," he said.
What Russia hit
The strikes damaged a Kyiv data center housing UTELS switching equipment on 23 September. Overnight into 24 September, Russia destroyed equipment of hosting provider CityHost.UA and the data center housing MiroHost. About 95% of MiroHost's clients operate outside Ukraine and were unaffected, he said. Russia also struck the Pavutyna network's data center. Crazy Network said a missile struck Kyiv's central traffic exchange hub, cutting service for its subscribers in Vinnytsia, Kyiv, and Khmelnytskyi Oblast.
Providers KIEVNET, Domonet, FAUST, and Etherlink also reported disruptions. Ukraine's telecom regulator NKEK said on 24 September that providers were completing emergency restoration, and Domonet estimated service would return by 21:00 that evening.
The 23 September strikes killed two people and injured more than 40, and hit a college building in Kyiv while students were on campus, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote that evening. Russia targeted major Ukrainian data centers "seeking to disrupt the flow of information," he said. "This is critical civilian infrastructure that ensures people can access life-saving information. It is not a military target."
"More sanctions pressure, more missile interceptors are the only way to stop this terror," Sybiha wrote. "These attacks must not become the new normal."
Panic, not military gain
Olshanskyi said Russia uses these strikes to spread fear, not achieve lasting results.
"The enemy's goal is to cause damage, inflame panic, and heighten nervousness," he said.
His data center's destruction "will not affect the situation at the front in any way," he said.

EU Agrees to Release €6.6B for Ukraine From EPF, Once Blocked by Orbán

EU member states have agreed to release €6.6 billion (about $7.5 billion) from the European Peace Facility (EPF), ending years of deadlock over a fund that Hungary kept blocked since 2023.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas announced the agreement in a statement on Friday, Sept. 25, while Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense welcomed the decision shortly after, expressing gratitude to EU member states for “turning political resolve into military capability.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“That’s good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia,” Kallas said, adding that “Moscow’s hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine.”
“Europe is doing the opposite,” she concluded.
Under the mechanism, aimed at preventing conflicts and strengthening international security, EU member states can be reimbursed for military equipment they have donated to Ukraine.
How the money will be split
Of the total, €900 million (roughly $1 billion) will be used to finance the EU Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine), through which Ukrainian soldiers are trained across the EU.
Another €1 billion (approximately $1.1 billion) will fund new joint procurement of equipment, while the remaining €4.7 billion (roughly $5.4 billion) will be reimbursed to member states, Kallas said.
Worth over €17 billion (about $19 billion), the EPF is a fund financed outside the EU budget for a period of seven years, starting March 2021.
Russian Strikes Hit Ukraine’s Leading Textile Manufacturer and Other Civilian Businesses
It is a single mechanism that finances all actions under the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) in military and defense, according to the European Council, who raised the EPF’s financial ceiling three times.
In March 2023, the ceiling was raised by €2.29 billion (roughly $2.6 billion). In June, it was raised by €4.06 billion (about $4.6 billion).
By March 2024, the Council created a dedicated Ukraine Assistance Fund within the facility, raising the financial ceiling by €5 billion (roughly $5.7 billion)
Hungary-Ukraine diplomatic relations continue turning sour
Led by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán for 16 years, Hungary opposed military aid to Ukraine and refused to unblock the use of the mechanism.
On Sept. 9, the EU General Court dismissed Hungary’s legal challenge against the use of seized Russian assets to support Ukraine’s military needs.
Although the veto has now been lifted, the diplomatic relations between Kyiv and Hungary remain strained.
On Sept. 18, Ukraine launched a new regional cooperation initiative named Carpathian Eight (C8) cooperation initiative in Bukovel, western Ukraine’s Ivano-Frankivsk region.
The format was initially presented as comprising Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia and Ukraine, as well as the EU institutions.
After announcing Budapest will not be joining the format, Hungary’s current Prime Minister Péter Magyar went a step further and linked the format to a village football team, sparking a public dispute and further straining already fragile ties between the two countries.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticized what he called Magyar’s “unnecessarily confrontational” position toward Kyiv, saying Hungary’s latest decisions reflected the obstructionism of Orbán’s policies.
Magyar rejected the criticism, while Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán added that there was “no analogy with the obstructionist policies pursued by Viktor Orbán,” as the Hungarian government has “offered quite a number of gestures” to Ukraine, since taking office.
Meanwhile, Budapest has continued to hold up Ukraine’s EU accession, citing the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia.
By Sept. 8, Hungary had blocked the start of negotiations on clusters 2 and 3 four times. The decision came despite a June agreement between Magyar and President Volodymyr Zelensky on the rights of Hungarian communities in Ukraine.
Orbán’s government had previously stalled the opening of the initial “Fundamentals” cluster for 17 months over the same issue.

Report: Netanyahu kept UAE Oct. 7 warning from security chiefs in meeting days before attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:13:26 UTC
01:13:26 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did not tell Israel’s security chiefs about an alleged warning from the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was considering a major attack when he met with them six days before the Oct. 7 massacre, The New York Times reported Friday.
The warning itself has been reported previously, but the Times added a significant new detail: Netanyahu convened senior security officials on Oct. 1, 2023, for a discussion on Gaza and did not mention it, according to minutes of the meeting reviewed by the newspaper. Five former senior Israeli officials also told the Times that the Emirati warning never reached the heads of Israel’s security establishment or appeared in the internal investigations they later examined. Previous reporting has likewise said senior security officials were not informed of the alleged warning.
According to the Times, UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan called Netanyahu in late September after receiving information that Hamas was considering a major attack. Two people familiar with the matter told the newspaper about the conversation, including one who said they later spoke directly with the Emirati leader about it.
The warning was vague. It did not specify whether Hamas was preparing a rocket attack or a ground invasion, and its original intelligence source remains unclear. Netanyahu has repeatedly denied receiving such a warning and has said no relevant phone call with bin Zayed took place during the period in question. The Prime Minister’s Office has said that any relevant Emirati intelligence would have been conveyed through established intelligence channels. An Emirati source previously confirmed to The Times of Israel that a warning was conveyed during a phone call between the two leaders.
Six days before the massacre
At the Oct. 1 meeting, Netanyahu told security officials that Israel should seek to maintain calm in Gaza, according to the minutes cited by the Times. When officials raised the possibility of military action against senior Hamas figures involved in directing attacks in the West Bank, Netanyahu warned that escalation in Gaza could damage efforts to reach a normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia.
Separate reporting on the same meeting has said then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar urged action against Hamas leaders, including the possibility of targeting Yahya Sinwar. Netanyahu did not approve such a move at the time.
The Times reported that Netanyahu made no reference during the briefing to his alleged conversation with bin Zayed. That detail is particularly significant because the earlier reports about the Emirati warning had already raised questions over whether the information was passed to Israel’s intelligence and military leadership.
The newspaper also reported that bin Zayed later discussed his September conversation with William Burns, then director of the CIA. According to a person familiar with that discussion, the Emirati president told Burns that he had spoken to Netanyahu about the possibility of Hamas violence in Gaza or the West Bank.
Warning absent from Oct. 7 investigations
Five former senior Israeli officials told the Times that the alleged warning does not appear in the internal investigations conducted by the IDF, intelligence agencies or other bodies examining the failures that preceded Oct. 7. The officials had been involved in reviewing those assessments, according to the report.
The Emirati warning was far from the only indication that later came under scrutiny. Israeli intelligence had obtained Hamas’ “Jericho Wall” attack plan in 2022, but military officials assessed that the organization lacked the ability to carry it out. In the years before the massacre, both political and security officials broadly operated under the assessment that Hamas had been deterred and was more interested in governing Gaza than in launching a major war.
The dispute over what Netanyahu knew, when he knew it and what information reached Israel’s security leadership has become increasingly prominent ahead of next month’s election. Netanyahu has argued that the military and intelligence establishment bears primary responsibility for failing to warn of the attack, while his opponents have argued that the political leadership’s decisions before Oct. 7 must also be examined. Netanyahu has rejected allegations that he ignored a specific warning of the Hamas assault.

'No longer hybrid' — As Russian sabotage grows bolder, Europe lacks red lines
Soldiers from the 16 Air Assault Brigade set up a mortar firing position after parachuting from a British Royal Air Force A400M transport aircraft onto Salisbury Plain at the Copehill Down training facility near Warminster, England, on March 30, 2026. (Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images)
Moscow's shadow war on Europe grows bolder by the day, and no one can say how far the Kremlin is ready to go.
Russia is no longer only meddling in elections or hacking networks: Germany found explosives-laden drones at its Leipzig Airport in an apparent Moscow-backed sabotage plot. Russian drone incursions in NATO airspace are now common. And a Russian warship shot flares at a Danish military helicopter.
The rhetoric in Western capitals has hardened, with some saying this campaign is "no longer hybrid at all."
For the first time, Berlin named Russia as a perpetrator of a physical attack against its infrastructure, and allies grow less fearful about downing drones and detaining shadow fleet ships.
But even as European officials warn that Moscow's campaign may yet escalate in the coming months, the question of how to deter it remains unanswered.
The response so far has ranged from symbolic ones, like shuttering Russian cultural and diplomatic centers, to fresh sanctions and arms packages for Ukraine — something that Moscow has weathered for years.
Analysts say Europe must toughen up, with some calling for novel ways of retaliation that will catch the Kremlin off guard.
"We've got to make Russia think: 'OK, s**t, they're awake,'" proposes Edward Lucas, a British journalist, security analyst, and head of the Baltic International Security Center (BISC).
read also
Testing Europe
Russian hybrid warfare — from cyberattacks and GPS jamming to disinformation campaigns and election meddling — was nothing new for NATO countries prior to 2022.
But Moscow cranked up its operations to a whole new level after the full-scale war broke out, with its suspected proxies setting warehouses on fire and its shadow fleet allegedly cutting cables and launching drones over strategic targets across Europe.
Researchers say that the number of hybrid attack incidents increased fourfold between 2023 and 2024, with one study recording 151 incidents in Europe between the start of the full-scale invasion and March 2026.
"It is Europe's slow and weak response that allows Russia to keep doing so and trying just "how far it can go."
This campaign has become increasingly kinetic since 2025, when a group of Russian drones invaded Polish airspace. Moscow's drones are now probing other countries at NATO's frontier, from the Baltic to the Black Sea.
Such attacks aim not only to sow panic and disrupt support for Ukraine, but also to test Europe's willingness to hit back, officials and experts say.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Sept. 17 that Russia might soon launch further "accidental" missile and drone strikes into NATO's territory to prove that Article 5 "is more theoretical than practical."
Moscow is testing something that Julian Pawlak, a security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), calls a "deterrence gap" — Europe's blank spot between its current response toolkit and a full-on military response against Russia.
And it is Europe's slow and weak response that allows Russia to keep doing so and trying just "how far it can go," the expert told the Kyiv Independent.
Part of the reason European nations are often slow to respond is the difficulty of finding solid evidence that allows them to publicly blame Russia.
Moscow often uses proxies; for example, vulnerable Ukrainian and Belarusian refugees recruited through the Telegram messaging app, says Anastasia Pociumban, an expert in hybrid threats at the German Council on Foreign Relations.
However, Pociumban also believes that the "states often use these delays to avoid taking costly response measures and not to create panic."
NATO made clear already in 2016 that a hybrid attack can trigger Article 5. But it doesn't define what red line the attacker would have to cross — that's up to individual states.
Pawlak raises doubt over whether "European politicians or capitals actually themselves know where this line is."
Adding to that, NATO members may be reluctant to invoke Article 5 at a moment when the alliance grapples with internal divisions, as a lackluster or absent response from allies could shake its credibility.
The U.S. under the Trump administration is shifting away from Europe, while Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico recently declared that his country would not be drawn into a war "because of some Article 5."
And German officials said it is "no coincidence" that fresh cases of sabotage in Germany came shortly before regional elections, which saw major wins for the Kremlin-friendly, NATO-skeptic Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Pociumban sees a "two-front pressure campaign" — with Russia deploying not only physical and cyber attacks but also leveraging parties that want to "normalize" ties with Moscow.
read also
Europe's response
A response to a Russian hybrid attack roughly comes in three steps — countering its impacts, identifying the culprit, and deterring the perpetrator from trying something like this again.
Europe has seen progress in the first area.
NATO air defenses are building up drone defenses along the border and are finally downing Russian drones.
"Europe should "blindside" the Kremlin by the scale and range of its responses."
European navies are stepping up protection of maritime infrastructure and are detaining suspected Russian shadow fleet vessels, and governments are bolstering protection of critical infrastructure.
Countries on the front lines of Russia's hybrid war — such as the Nordics and the Baltics — are further integrating military and civilian defenses, aiming to counter the very kind of threat Moscow's shadow war poses.
Estonia, for example, aims to expand the law enforcement role of military and allied forces to help counter threats similar to the "little green men" scenario in Crimea in 2014, when Russian troops without insignia occupied Ukraine's peninsula.
And European officials are learning not to mince words and talk about Russia's campaign more openly.
The Leipzig Airport attack marked the first time Berlin officially accused Moscow of orchestrating such an attack on its soil.
Estonian Intelligence Chief Kaupo Rosin dismissed "hybrid warfare" as a euphemism and urged European leaders to describe Moscow's campaign as "state-sponsored terrorism."
The stance was echoed by EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas, who said Moscow's campaign bears "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism."
Nevertheless, deterring this campaign is the most persistent problem.
After Germany officially blamed Russia for the Leipzig Airport attack, its response — next to promising additional support for Ukraine — was to shut down a Russian consulate and tighten visa access for Russian citizens.
"You should have done this a decade ago… after (Russia occupied) Crimea in 2014," Lucas told the Kyiv Independent.
Europe must "get on the front foot and take the initiative," he adds.
read also
Deterrence
In 2022, just a few months after the invasion, Lithuania banned the transit of EU-sanctioned goods to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
Russia's threats of "retaliation" sparked concern in Brussels, which in turn pressured Vilnius to relent.
Three years later, Estonia attempted to stop a shadow fleet tanker it said was violating sanctions — before a Russian Su-35 entered NATO airspace to shield the tanker, preventing the boarding.
Tallinn later said it would refrain from detaining shadow fleet ships due to the risk of military response.
The record shows that when smaller front-line states want to take bolder steps, they need solidarity so as not to bear the brunt of Russia's response alone.
This is what Lucas calls a lateral response — if a Russian drone violates Estonian airspace, it could be Sweden, Germany, or the U.K. that hits back.
Analysts agree that Europe must increase the costs to Russia of its hybrid war. But they propose different ways of going about it.
According to Pawlak, Europe should set a clear line and make sure the aggressor knows that if it carries out Action A, Europe will respond with Action B — for example, sending another shipment of arms to Ukraine.
Lucas proposes a different path: Europe should "blindside" the Kremlin by the scale and range of its responses.
A sabotage attack should trigger, for example, "a money-laundering investigation in one jurisdiction, an unseaworthy ship impounded in a second, a cyberattack on a Russia-related target launched from a third," he writes in his April column.
But Europe must be ready to see its response through, even if Moscow escalates, Lucas adds in comments for the Kyiv Independent.
"Because it would be disastrous if we see an initial escalation (by a European country), Russia then threatens, and the (European) country backs down again," he warns.

Trump and Xi declare harmony, no confrontation, as US state visit ends

Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington ends on a high note of pomp and less confrontation, as key details of his talks with US president Donald Trump are still to emerge
China’s president Xi Jinping was wrapping up his much-anticipated state visit to the United States on Friday, with details of his talks with US president Donald Trump still to emerge on the thorny issues that define what Xi called as the “healthy competition” between the two global powers.
The two leaders met behind closed doors for 90 minutes on Thursday, when they discussed issues such as the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to the official Chinese government readout of the meeting. The White House has not provided any information about the private talks, or if there were any major breakthroughs on issues such as trade or the safety of artificial intelligence which the two leaders identified as key points of their talks.
The US and Chinese presidents chose to show that they were working to preserve harmony between the world’s two largest economies.
In a visit full of pomp, Trump took Xi to visit the National Archives on Friday where the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights are held. Trump said Thursday that he wanted to show Xi “some of the greatest treasures of that proud history.”
The US president also said he wanted to show Xi artifacts about the relationship between the two countries, saying that “just as our ancestors reached across the ocean centuries ago to trade, to learn, and to build a better world, our two countries do really the same thing, and we’re very proud of it.”
On Thursday evening, the US president and the First Lady feted China’s leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan, with a black-tie state dinner attended by technology industry titans and top business leaders from the US, but less from China.
“President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” Trump said during his toast, adding that “together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations.”
In his toast, Xi said that “President Trump has pledged to make America great again” and that “China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation.”
Those in attendance included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Dell Technologies chairman and CEO Michael Dell, Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai.
Bernard Arnault, the CEO of French luxury goods company LVMH, was also invited to the state dinner.
The president presented Xi with an eagle statue that he said was designed “in personal collaboration with Melania and myself.”
The first lady helped craft the evening’s menu featuring sesame-crusted sea bass with braised baby bok choy, roasted garden eggplant as main course.

2026 could be the turning point on climate action, Al Gore says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:11:47 UTC
01:11:47 KST

In 2006 former vice president Al Gore sounded the alarm on climate change in the documentary An Inconvenient Truth. In the film, he implored the world to wake up and take urgent action to reduce fossil fuel use and avoid the worst outcomes of global warming. Yet in the 20 years since, carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere have risen significantly, and Earth’s temperature has warmed by about 0.7 degree Celsius (1.3 degrees Fahrenheit).
Now global temperatures hover around 1.5 degrees C (2.7 degrees F) above preindustrial levels—the limit agreed to in the landmark 2015 Paris climate agreement—and the United Nations recently warned that the world is set to overshoot that goal. With the urgency of reining in greenhouse gas emissions compounding, Gore has continued his Nobel Peace Prize–winning advocacy work. He’s still optimistic that humanity can prevent the worst harms of climate change and that this could be the year it begins to turn things around—if we choose to.
The moral case for making that choice was the topic of an event at Riverside Church in New York City on Friday, ahead of Climate Week NYC and the meeting of the U.N. General Assembly. Before Gore spoke there, he sat down to answer questions from Scientific American and a few other outlets, including APB News and Bloomberg.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
SCIENTIFIC AMERICAN: It’s been 20 years since An Inconvenient Truth came out. Have things been going better or worse, in terms of climate action, than you feared back in 2006?
Well, to quote Charles Dickens, in a way, it’s the best of times and the worst of times. “The worst of times” in the sense that the impacts of the climate crisis have been every bit as severe as the scientists have warned us they would be—in some cases, even more so.
But there are also instances of very, very good news that [have] emerged over the past 20 years. There has been a nearly miraculous development of solar energy, in the reduction of the cost to the point where it’s now the cheapest power in the history of the world by far; the development of utility-scale batteries that have come down in cost even faster than solar panels; wind energy; electric vehicles. This year was the first time that solar overtook coal, both in China and in the U.S.
And now that we have the second massive global disruption of fossil fuel availability and price in just four years, many nations around the world have awakened to the fact that this is a time to accelerate the transition. We have all the technologies we need right now to reduce emissions by half in 10 years. We know how to do it. We’re gaining momentum, but we’re not moving fast enough.
It is a moment of decision, and in spite of the current leadership in the U.S., I do believe that that there’s a real possibility that we will look back on the year 2026 as the turning point.
APB NEWS: U.N. secretary-general António Guterres said there are three urgent items facing the General Assembly: global conflict [amid inequality], AI and climate change. How important is it to keep climate change in front of world leaders?
I see one thing that all three of the secretary-general’s crises have in common. In each case, the most respected experts—whose advice has been proven correct over the years—have warned against neglect, have warned that we have to act.
In the case of the climate crisis, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has been proven to be spot-on in the warnings they’ve issued for decades, and yet their warnings are presently being ignored by the leadership of this country. The fact that they’ve been proven right in their past warnings should cause us to pay more attention to the warnings they’re giving us now.
BLOOMBERG: We’re seeing a lot of companies pull back on their climate targets. Do you think that voluntary corporate climate commitments are actual drivers of decarbonization in the economy?
It’s actually a complex question. There’s a lot of what’s called “green hushing,” where businesses now are continuing with the switch over to renewable energy but being quiet about it because they live in terror of tweets. There are many in the business community who have been cowed by Trump, not only into silence but also into reversing their policies. That is not true in most of the rest of the world, and it's not true in much of the U.S. either.
It’s true that too many investors and the 65 largest world banks continue to put trillions of dollars into more and more fossil fuels. But 10 years ago, at the time of the Paris Agreement, 65 percent of global energy investment was in fossil fuels, only 35 in renewables. Today 55 percent is in renewable energy. There is now twice as much investment in clean technology as there is in fossil fuels. So we are gaining momentum. We are just not gaining momentum quickly enough.
Too many governments in the world have been captured by the fossil fuel industry and the petrostates. Taxpayers around the world are actually subsidizing the burning of fossil fuels at the rate of $4.5 trillion per year. [Editor’s Note: Estimates of subsidies range from around $1 trillion to $7 trillion per year.] So when some say, “We’ve got to do more to accelerate renewable energy,” and someone else asks, “Well, where is the money going to come from?” Well, that’s a good place to get the money. Just stop subsidizing fossil fuels. It’s almost the exact amount the world needs to accomplish this transition at a speed that’s appropriate for the occasion.

Supreme Court upholds Trump's expanded data checks to spot noncitizens who registered to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:11:22 UTC
01:11:22 KST

Supreme Court upholds Trump’s expanded citizenship data checks, stoking fears of voter purges
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The decision will aid states that seek to scrub their voter rolls and remove those who are not citizens.
- It’s not clear if the decision will have much impact in California and other Democratic-led states.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday upheld President Trump’s expanded use of government data to search for noncitizens who are registered to vote.
The justices granted an emergency appeal from Trump administration lawyers and set aside a judge’s order that blocked use of this data on the grounds it was error-prone, particularly for naturalized citizens.
Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan dissented, citing the risk of errors.
The impact of the decision is likely to be limited, other than to highlight Trump’s distrust of elections and his unproven claims that a large number of illegal voters are casting ballots.
The administration had, for example, claimed that Nevada had more than 15,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls, only to have state election officials confirm these voters were citizens and lawful voters.
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill learned in July that because of a software error, more than 6,000 people had been wrongly registered to vote when they registered their car.
But it is rare to find noncitizens who choose to cast a vote even though they know it is illegal to do so.
The decision clears the way for states to check their voter rolls using data from Social Security and other records. Individuals could be targeted for an inquiry, but federal law forbids late purges of the voters rolls.
Voting rights advocates said they feared the flawed data will have an impact on legal voters.
“Today’s decision is profoundly disappointing, as it puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections,” said the League of Women Voters.
“As the court noted in its decision, it is flatly illegal for states to conduct mass removals of voters from the rolls within 90 days of an election,” said Common Cause President Virginia Kase Solomón. “If any state official attempts to disenfranchise eligible voters using this flawed database, we will take them to court immediately.”
But Florida State law professor Michael T. Morley contended that the ruling and the data checks “will help states bolster public confidence in the integrity of the upcoming November election.”
Several Republican-led states including Texas and Florida supported the administration’s appeal.
The use of the new database “allowed Texas to more efficiently, promptly, and economically ensure the accuracy of its voter rolls,” the state said. It was “able to run its entire list of 18 million voters” through the expanded system of checks “in bulk and for no cost.”
It’s not clear the decision will have much impact in California and other Democratic-led states.
The court, in an unsigned opinion, said the law supported use of the data.
“The federal government has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters,” the court said. “The order below prevents the federal government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task.”
The administration said the Department of Homeland Security can respond to more than 1 million requests per day to check if a person appears to be a citizen or not based on Social Security records and other data files.
If not, state or county election officials may require these suspect voters to furnish proof of their citizenship.
However, states and local election boards are not required to conduct these searches. The administration also said its data reports are not final proof of citizenship.
Upholding these data searches “would not require states, candidates, parties, or voters to do anything,” Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer told the court. “It would simply make available to states additional information. ... States that wish to use that information in the course of ensuring that only eligible citizens cast ballots this November should be free to do so.”
The justices turned down an emergency appeal from Trump’s lawyers, who argued the government needed a new and untested system of unique bar codes to track millions of mailed ballots.
In dissent, Jackson said the court’s order creates the “risk that states might cancel the voter registrations of at least some recently naturalized citizens or force such persons to provide proof of citizenship before voting.”
The new system of voter checks is based on the 40-year-old Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, that was created by Congress. Then, the goal was to check if applicants were entitled to receive federal benefits.
Last year, Trump issued an executive order directing Homeland Security to expand the reach of SAVE to provide states “access to appropriate systems for verifying the citizenship or immigration status of individuals registering to vote or who are already registered to vote.”
It is a federal crime for noncitizens to register and vote.
Trump has long maintained that noncitizens are voting, but he has had little evidence to support that claim.
Voting rights advocates sued, contending that the new “mass verification” system was not authorized by Congress and relied on data that are protected as private under the law.
In June, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, a Biden appointee, agreed and blocked use of the expanded searches. The Trump administration has “trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote,” she said.
On Sept. 4, the U.S. Court of Appeals by a 2-1 vote refused to overturn her ruling, prompting the administration’s fast-track appeal.
U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan sided with advocacy groups that argued the recent upgrades to the program, called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, aggregated Americans’ sensitive personal data in a way that could result in voters being wrongly purged from voter rolls.
The voting rights advocates, led by the League of Women Voters, had urged the court to stand aside.
“The government has recklessly created an error-laden master citizenship database that endangers millions of Americans’ privacy and voting rights,” they said.
The data searches are flawed, they argued, because they “only reflect a person’s citizenship status when they applied for a Social Security number. That status does not automatically update if the person later naturalizes.”
Texas admitted that the mass checks yield “some inaccurate information.” It said 2,724 people were cited as “potential non-citizens” among its 18 million registered voters.
In response, county officials had to check further to confirm the citizenship of these voters, the state said.
“This puts more focus on a largely nonexistent problem,” said Justin Levitt, an election law expert at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles. “The SAVE database is unreliable in its current incarnation. It gives DHS (temporary) permission to continue using unreliable systems, which will mean they’ll continue finding small numbers of people who they will claim are noncitizen voters who aren’t noncitizen voters.”
Last week, the Supreme Court dealt Trump a defeat when it blocked use of his proposed postal rules that could have prevented millions of voters from casting ballots by mail.
In a brief order, the court said Trump’s claims of power over states and their voting were “unlikely to succeed.”
But in the case of the expanded data files, the court said the law appears to favor the administration.

Ethiopia’s new rebel alliance faces an old problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:10:55 UTC
01:10:55 KST

Ethiopia’s new rebel alliance faces an old problem
Former enemies have united against Abiy Ahmed, but disputes over territory, power and command could pull them apart.
The formation of a new armed alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed follows a pattern that has plagued Ethiopia – an empire of many nations and nationalities still in the making – for decades. Those in power leave little space for peaceful political struggle; the winner takes it all, so those who feel disadvantaged take up arms to change the status quo. Actors and alliances change over time, but violence remains the only constant.
The civil war in parts of Oromia has raged since Abiy took power in 2018, while the conflict in the Amhara region has raged since 2023. In Tigray, the Pretoria agreement was never fully implemented. Although large-scale war had not resumed, the region had been under siege since a faction of the TPLF took power and escalated its confrontation with the federal government. Until the latest escalation, Abiy’s government had largely been content to control the centre of power while confronting rebels with drones and ground forces.
The government held national elections despite voting not taking place in Tigray and several other districts. It formed the Ethiopian National Dialogue Commission in 2021, which concluded a national conference of about 4,000 participants in August, despite the absence of armed groups and other key opposition organisations. At the same time, the government has continued to pursue major development projects. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was in Djibouti on September 24 for the launch of the Ethiopia-Djibouti petroleum infrastructure project. The newly elected parliament is due to open on October 5, when a new federal government will be constituted.
The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, announced on September 20, was not a surprise. It followed several months of coordination meetings among the groups, held in the presence of military and security representatives from Eritrea and Sudan. It brings together the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the Amhara Fano National Movement, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) and four movements from the Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions. Despite the OLA’s participation, Oromo organisations and elites are divided in their support for the alliance. The alliance aims to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and establish an inclusive transition. Three of the seven organisations – the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Afar National Unity Revolutionary Front (ANURF) – have particular strategic importance. All three are in northern Ethiopia, which borders Eritrea, allowing continuous logistical support from there.
Three days later, TPLF forces, allied with the ANURF, advanced into several districts in Zone 2 with little resistance. ANURF is led by Ibrahim Osman Aliyu, known as Haji Ibrahim, a respected figure from Berhale in Zone 2 and a relative of Ethiopia’s defence minister, Aisha Mohammed. He defected to Eritrea last year with a contingent of Afar Special Forces and local forces. In a message to the Afar people, he assured them that the current fighting was directed against the Prosperity Party, not the Afar people or fighter groups, and that services and public transport would continue unhindered. He advised Afar residents to join his forces or stay away from the fighting. Their next target may be the vital highway linking Ethiopia to Djibouti.
We have seen part of this story before, though this time the alliance took longer to form. In November 2021, nine opposition groups hastily announced the United Front of Ethiopian Federalist and Confederalist Forces. Tigrayan forces and the OLA advanced towards Addis Ababa, while the alliance’s leaders spoke of dismantling Abiy’s government and installing a transitional authority. By January 2022, the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front had left the united front, accusing the TPLF of killing Afar civilians. In December of the same year, the Benishangul People’s Liberation Movement signed a peace deal with the regional government. The federal army counterattacked, Tigrayan forces withdrew from neighbouring regions and the TPLF eventually signed the 2022 Pretoria agreement with the government. That pact required the TPLF to stop supporting armed groups elsewhere in Ethiopia.
The same pattern could repeat itself. The lesson is not that 2026 will mirror 2021 exactly. The new alliance includes Fano, whose fighters stood with the federal government against the TPLF during the earlier war and now fight Abiy. The government is also fighting on several fronts. But the precedent shows how quickly a common enemy can stop being enough when battlefield fortunes change.
Both Fano and the TPLF claim western Tigray, or what the Amhara call Wolgait-Tsegede. The founding statement offers no settlement. A Tigrayan leadership that abandons its claim risks alienating people displaced from their homes; a Fano leadership that concedes it risks losing the support of fighters for whom the territory is central. Calling the issue a matter for later negotiations buys time but does not create a compromise. The same problem reaches beyond the north: Oromo, Amhara and Somali movements do not share one vision of Ethiopia’s federal order, boundaries or distribution of power.
Nor does each organisation speak for everyone in the population it claims to represent. Tigray’s leaders are divided over their relationship with Addis Ababa and the Pretoria settlement. Fano is a collection of regional commands with different priorities. Even the Ogaden National Liberation Front’s participation has exposed an internal dispute: An overseas faction supports the alliance, while leaders inside Ethiopia’s Somali region deny joining it. A seven-signature declaration cannot settle these questions of mandate.
Then there is the military problem. These forces operate across distant regions and can stretch the federal army, forcing Addis Ababa to defend multiple theatres. But simultaneous fighting is not the same as a single campaign. A successful march on the capital would require reliable supply routes, coordinated command and political support in the areas through which fighters must pass. Government drones make concentrated formations and exposed supply lines more vulnerable. Air power alone cannot govern contested towns, but neither can an alliance govern them simply by capturing them.
Eritrea adds another risk. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of backing the alliance; Eritrea has repeatedly denied similar allegations, though ample evidence suggests otherwise. Relations between the two countries have deteriorated sharply amid Ethiopian calls for Red Sea access and disputes left unresolved after the Tigray war. Outside support could strengthen individual factions, but dependence on Eritrea could also make them unacceptable to other Ethiopians. If the Ethiopian government comes to see Eritrea as a direct threat, it may attack, with unpredictable consequences and the risk of drawing in other regional powers. If Abiy’s government itself comes under serious threat, the UAE may become fully involved to rescue one of its closest regional allies.
Three paths now seem possible. The most likely is prolonged, uneven conflict: Local offensives and temporary bargains weaken the government’s reach without dislodging it from Addis Ababa. A second is alliance fragmentation. If western Tigray, Afar or another disputed territory becomes the price of cooperation, some partners may leave or make separate deals. A renegotiation of the Pretoria agreement and concessions from Abiy to Tigray could also take the TPLF out of the alliance, as happened to the ambitions of the 2021 front. A less likely but far more dangerous possibility is a cascade of federal military defections and coordinated rebel advances. Even then, a rebel takeover would constitute an unconstitutional change of government under African Union rules and face regional opposition. Removing Abiy would settle none of the arguments over land, command and constitutional power. Victory could open another civil war.
Ethiopia has repeatedly watched coalitions of convenience promise a new beginning through force. What matters now is not whether an armed alliance or a government survives, but what happens to the people who will have to live with what both do next.

Malaysia’s new envoy likens Türkiye to ‘giant open-air museum’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:10:37 UTC
01:10:37 KST

Malaysia’s new ambassador to Türkiye, Adlan Mohd Shaffieq, has likened the country to a big open museum, praising its rich cultural heritage and the warm hospitality he has received since arriving in Ankara.
“Your country is like a big open museum. All of the cities that I go to are like free, open museums where you can go and watch the culture,” Shaffieq told Anadolu in an interview.
“It has a very deep culture. So, it's very interesting for me to discover your country,” he added.
Shaffieq, who recently began his tenure in Ankara, shared his first impressions of Türkiye, his family life and his views on relations between the two countries.
The diplomat said he was delighted to be appointed to Türkiye for his first ambassadorial posting, particularly because he believed his four children, aged between five and 11, would enjoy living in Ankara.
“Malaysia and Türkiye are like brothers and sisters,” he said, describing the warm hospitality he has experienced since his arrival. 
Shared family values and historical ties
Shaffieq highlighted similarities between Malaysian and Turkish cultures, particularly their strong family ties and respect for parents.
“I think the similarities between Malaysian and Turkish families is that we are very close-knit,” he said.
Shaffieq said families in both countries enjoy gathering during religious holidays and other occasions to celebrate, cook and share meals.
The ambassador noted that Turkish television series and films have helped Malaysians become more familiar with Türkiye, while emphasizing that relations between the two countries stretch back for centuries.
“Our history has the linkage not only recently, but during the Ottoman Empire,” he said, pointing to historical contacts between the Ottoman Empire and the Sultanate of Melaka. 
‘Your ice cream is the best ice cream in the world’
Touching on Turkish cuisine, Shaffieq said Malaysian food differs considerably from Turkish dishes, with Malaysians generally preferring spicier meals.
However, he was particularly enthusiastic about Turkish ice cream.
“Your ice cream is the best ice cream in the world. My kids love it,” he said.
“I think food is also one of the areas that we should focus on when it comes to cultural exchanges,” he added.
The ambassador also expressed his fondness for menemen, a traditional Turkish breakfast dish made with eggs, tomatoes and peppers.
Shaffieq said he had been learning Turkish for approximately three months but found the language challenging because of its vocabulary and sentence structure.
Nevertheless, he said he intended to learn as much of the language as possible during his posting. 
Türkiye’s cities offer unique cultural experiences
The ambassador said he had already visited several destinations in Türkiye, including Cappadocia, Kastamonu and Konya, in addition to the capital Ankara, each of which he described as having its own distinctive character.
He mentioned that he had also recently attended tomato and carrot festivals, held separately in different parts of Ankara in late September, describing both experiences as immensely unique.
Shaffieq said the opportunity to experience different local traditions and explore the country’s cultural heritage had made his time in Türkiye particularly rewarding. 
Trade, defense cooperation and tourism
On bilateral relations, Shaffieq said Malaysia and Türkiye were making significant progress, pointing to growing cooperation in trade and defense.
He said bilateral trade reached approximately $5.6 billion in 2025, while the two countries have set a target of increasing that figure to $10 billion.
Although ambitious, the target is achievable, he said.
The ambassador identified defense as another important area for expanding bilateral cooperation.
He said Malaysia had received or commissioned three littoral mission ships this year and hoped to procure additional vessels in the future.
Malaysia has also received three ANKA unmanned aerial vehicles, which have begun operating in the South China Sea, he said, adding that further defense procurement opportunities were under consideration.
Shaffieq also highlighted tourism as an increasingly important component of bilateral relations.
Approximately 40,000 Turkish tourists visited Malaysia in 2025, he said, noting that the figure had increased compared with the year prior.

Estonia Builds 1,000-Troop Military Base Near Russia’s Border—Price Tag Rises to $23 Million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:08:48 UTC
01:08:48 KST

- Category
- World
Estonia Builds 1,000-Troop Military Base Near Russia’s Border—Price Tag Rises to $23 Million
Estonia’s planned military base in the eastern border city of Narva will cost just over €20 million (around $23 million) and is now expected to be completed in summer 2028, six months later than originally planned, according to ERR on September 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The project’s estimated cost has increased by €5 million (almost $6 million), while political instability within Narva’s municipal government delayed the allocation of land needed for construction.
“The previous situation in Narva politics and the city's administration prevented us from moving forward with the development of the base. I won't comment on all of it here, but until that decision was made, the process was effectively at a standstill. That's where we lost the time,” said Ando Voogma, northern and northeastern regional manager at the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments, according to ERR.
The base is being financed largely with European Union funds. Of the project’s total cost, approximately €19 million (about $22 million) is expected to come from the EU Cohesion Fund.
Land-related issues have now been resolved, allowing the construction contract to potentially be signed as early as October. However, major construction work is not expected to begin until next year.
A temporary base will accommodate a company-sized unit while construction of the permanent facility is underway. Once completed, the new base will have indoor accommodation for up to 500 personnel, as well as tent capacity for an additional 500.
Around 200 military personnel are expected to be permanently stationed at the base after it becomes operational.
The project comes as Baltic states continue to strengthen critical infrastructure and defense facilities near their borders with Russia. In neighboring Lithuania, authorities are introducing additional security measures at a planned power substation near Russia’s Kaliningrad region to protect it against potential drone attacks and sabotage.
The future Gizai substation, located about 30 kilometers west of Kaliningrad, will feature reinforced barriers designed to withstand a vehicle carrying explosives, sensors capable of detecting potential underground tunneling, and concrete structures intended to protect transformers from drone strikes.

Bulgarian Parliament adopts new mechanism for the country's minimum wage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:07:07 UTC
01:07:07 KST

News
Bulgarian Parliament adopts new mechanism for the country's minimum wage
The minimum wage level will now take into account its purchasing power
Friday 25 September 2026 17:51
Friday, 25 September 2026, 17:51
Bulgarian Parliament sitting on 25 September 2026
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The Bulgarian Parliament has adopted a new mechanism for determining Bulgaria’s minimum wage. Its level will now take into account the purchasing power of the minimum wage, with consideration given to the cost of living, the overall level and distribution of wages, the rate of wage growth, and long-term trends in labour productivity in the country.
Every three years, the adequacy of the minimum wage will be assessed against two reference values: 60% of the gross median wage and the cost of living.
The new mechanism replaces the previous automatic link between the minimum wage and 50% of the average gross wage over the preceding 12-month period.

Jay-Z is no longer accused of rape; the plaintiff "never met" the rapper
Kyiv • UNN
The woman said she had never met Jay-Z and mistakenly identified him as the perpetrator of sexual assault. The rapper continues to sue her attorneys.
The woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has officially withdrawn her accusations, saying she had never met the rap star, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
The woman, whose name has not been disclosed, initially made the allegations in a lawsuit filed in 2024. She claimed that Jay-Z (real name Shawn Carter), together with Sean Combs (known as P Diddy), drugged and raped her. According to her, the incident occurred at a party following the 2000 MTV Video Music Awards ceremony.
Jay-Z denied the allegations, calling them an attempt at extortion; Combs also denied any involvement. Jay-Z’s lawyer emphasized that the events described took place within a time frame that made them physically impossible. The woman withdrew the lawsuit in 2025, and Jay-Z filed a countersuit.
Amid the proceedings in the case, the woman said that her previous statements were false. "Sean ‘Jay-Z’ Carter never raped me. I never met or spoke with Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me," her statement, obtained by Rolling Stone, said.
She added that there was "no truth whatsoever to my allegations against Mr. Carter. I understand that my false allegations caused Mr. Carter enormous pain, suffering, and harm that cannot be fully remedied."
The woman has now been removed from the list of defendants in Jay-Z’s lawsuit, although the rapper continues to sue her former lawyers. He claims they should have known that the allegations "contradicted publicly available information, were internally inconsistent, and were not supported by any credible account or investigation." Earlier this month, when filing a motion to dismiss the case, attorney Tony Buzbee and his colleagues called the lawsuit "malicious persecution."
Commenting on the woman’s new statement, Buzbee told Rolling Stone: "If for some reason she is now claiming that she lied to us and to the court, that is new information."
The woman’s current lawyer, James Blair Newman Jr., said: "Our client continues to maintain that she was a victim of sexual assault, but she was completely mistaken in identifying Mr. Carter as the perpetrator." Continuing her statement, the woman said that memories of sexual abuse were triggered by an advertisement calling on Combs’s victims to come forward. Combs was investigated in connection with a number of alleged sexual assault cases; ultimately—unlike in this woman’s case—he was found guilty on two charges related to transporting individuals for the purpose of prostitution and was sentenced in October 2025 to four years and two months in prison.
Controversial P. Diddy to be released early03.03.26, 15:26 • 5949 views
The woman said that she did not know a lawsuit had been filed on her behalf, and that when she expressed doubts about her claims, the lawsuit was withdrawn.
Jay-Z had previously spoken about how these allegations affected his life. When the case was dismissed, he said: "The trauma that I, my wife, my children, and my loved ones had to endure cannot simply be ignored." And in an interview with GQ magazine in March, he said: "I haven’t felt that kind of anger in a long time—it was uncontrollable anger. You can’t accuse someone of something like that unless you are completely certain."
He also said that he refused to settle the lawsuit out of court: "I can’t reach a settlement—it goes against my nature... I would rather die."

More than 55,000 Sudanese refugees flee to Chad as UN calls for funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:06:45 UTC
01:06:45 KST

More than 55,000 Sudanese refugees flee to Chad as UN calls for funding
UN refugee agency says 400 people a day, about 20 times the previous daily rate, now cross from Sudan into eastern Chad.
More than 55,000 Sudanese refugees have fled to neighbouring Chad this year, compounding a humanitarian crisis that will only deteriorate further unless there is a significant increase in funding, the United Nations has warned.
The number of Sudanese people arriving in eastern Chad has “accelerated sharply” over the past week and is outpacing the available support, the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, said on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Foreign fighters and external support fuel Sudan’s war: UN-backed probe
- list 2 of 3Sudan aid networks at risk of collapse, UN agencies warn
- list 3 of 3Outcry in Sudan as US reportedly holds army chief’s UN visa over truce plan
The number of refugees entering via Chad’s border areas of Adre and Tine has risen to 400 people a day, about 20 times the daily rate of previous months, the agency added.
Sudan has been engulfed in a civil war since April 2023, when a power struggle between Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti, turned violent.
More than three years later, in excess of 11 million Sudanese people have been displaced in what has become the world’s largest displacement and humanitarian crisis.
Approximately 6.4 million people in Sudan are internally displaced, while more than 3.5 million Sudanese refugees and asylum seekers have fled to nearby countries.
The UN warned on Friday that the transit centre in Chad’s Tine is under severe pressure and currently hosts more than 4,300 people, many of whom are in urgent need of shelter, water, sanitation and protection services.
About 31,000 families lack adequate shelter, and most refugees are living on less than half of the minimum amount of water needed daily.
The UN says it has so far received only 20 percent of the $1.6bn needed to fund response efforts. It says that the dire situation will deteriorate further unless the international community helps plug the funding shortfall of $1.28bn.
The UN warned that without additional help, more Sudanese refugees will make the perilous journey to Europe. More than 14,100 Sudanese refugees arrived on the continent last year, a 245 percent increase compared with 2024.

Bulgarian Parliament removes excise duty on LPG, natural gas amidst fuel crisis
Friday 25 September 2026 17:36
Friday, 25 September 2026, 17:36
PHOTO Pixabay
Font size
The Bulgarian Parliament has given final approval to a zero excise duty rate from October 1 to December 31, 2026, for natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) used as motor fuel. The measure was adopted with amendments to the Excise Duties and Tax Warehouses Act, which were approved at first and second reading during the same parliamentary sitting, BTA reported. The bill was tabled by Progressive Bulgaria.
The measure is prompted by the need to introduce temporary measures to mitigate the adverse economic effects of high fuel prices and disruptions to the supply chains for oil, petroleum products and natural gas, caused by the geopolitical situation in the Middle East, the bill's sponsors said.
