Trump backs Hormuz alternative but his Iran war is blocking the route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:03:40 UTC
00:03:40 KST

Trump backs Hormuz alternative but his Iran war is blocking the route
The US has put the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) back at the center of its Middle East strategy as shipping and energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain disrupted. US President Donald Trump told a meeting of Arab leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York that attacks on commercial shipping showed the need to shift the Middle East’s energy infrastructure away from “Iranian checkpoints.”  
“That’s why my administration strongly supports the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor,” Trump said earlier this week, while calling for other ways of moving oil, including pipelines. 
The corridor was jointly unveiled at the G20 summit in New Delhi in 2023 by the US, India, Saudi Arabia, UAE, EU, Italy, France, and Germany. The IMEC would combine maritime routes, railways and other infrastructure, alongside planned energy and digital links. It has two broad sections: an eastern leg connecting India to the Gulf, and a northern leg linking the Gulf to Europe. 
Cargo would sail from India to the UAE, move by rail across Saudi Arabia and Jordan to Israel’s Mediterranean coast, and then travel by sea from Haifa toward European ports. However, the IMEC is not by itself a single oil pipeline designed to replace Hormuz, as Trump’s comments seemed to imply. It is a trade and connectivity network. 
What’s the IMEC’s geopolitical significance?
When the IMEC was announced, it was seen as a challenger to another route, which has been in the making for decades – the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC). Conceived in 2000 by India, Iran, and Russia, the 7,200-km INSTC will move freight from Mumbai through Iranian ports such as Bandar Abbas and Chabahar, across Iran and Azerbaijan – or via Caspian Sea routes – into Russia and onward to Northern and Western Europe.
Its main advantage over other routes is speed: the INSTC is said to be between 20% and 67% faster than existing corridors, while also avoiding the Suez Canal and Bab al-Mandab.
Since 2022, it has become one of Moscow’s highest-priority alternative logistics routes, as it allows Russia to maintain trade links with partners in South Asia.
The corridor’s development, however, has been slow, largely because Iran, and later Russia, came under unprecedented Western sanctions. Even so, work has continued. India has invested around $120 million in Iran’s Chabahar Port, widely seen as a strategic anchor of the INSTC.
However, work at Chabahar has also been stalled by unilateral US sanctions against Iran.
Washington gave New Delhi a sanctions waiver in 2018, allowing India to develop and use the port for Afghanistan’s reconstruction and regional trade. A second six-month waiver given in October expired in April, making it harder for India to continue to work on the port.
Chabahar is more than 500 km away from the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz. However, it still came under attack from US forces, with airstrikes targeting Iran’s maritime infrastructure and surveillance facilities in July. New Delhi clarified at the time that the Indian-operated Shahid Beheshti terminal itself was not damaged.
For India, Chabahar – and INSTC – remain the best options to access the Central Asian, Russian, and European markets, even if Washington and Tehran end hostilities tomorrow and open up Hormuz. A lot of work has already been done and the impact from any regional instability or political uncertainty would be far less than in the case of IMEC.
Why Hormuz actors still matter and the full corridor cannot be built now
It is difficult to imagine that the IMEC, if and when it becomes a reality, would move trade fully away from Hormuz. Saudi and UAE ports in the Persian Gulf that are key hubs on the route would still be impacted by any tensions around the strait.
The route will have to be recalibrated to ports like Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, to make it bypass Hormuz. However, in the last few months ships have been attacked off the coast of Oman and as far west as Yemen. 
Even the land corridor may not be fully safe in a regional conflict, as shown by the many Iranian missile hits on Saudi Arabia. That is a point missed by Trump, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who in April called for advancing the IMEC to diversify export infrastructure away from the Hormuz bottleneck.
The IMEC’s viability depends on much more than physical infrastructure, such as ports and railway lines. Making the land connectivity part work requires deeper transport and political cooperation across the Middle East, and specifically Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel. 
That is no longer easy to pull together after Israeli forces invaded Gaza. The widespread public anger in the Arab world makes it nearly impossible for the Gulf monarchies to agree to such collaboration with Israel, the war with regional rival Iran notwithstanding. Finance is another issue, with no firm overall funding commitments or construction timelines in place. The corridor remains a long-term proposal rather than an operational alternative to existing energy and trade routes.
So where does IMEC stand?
India and its partners are still backing the project. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni reaffirmed their commitment to the IMEC in May and called for a first ministerial meeting on the corridor to take concrete steps toward its implementation this year.
Still, despite the urgency created by the Middle East conflict and Trump’s comments, a fully functioning IMEC is years away.

Trump sees no urgency for Canada deal as trade dispute deepens, USTR says

Trump sees no urgency for Canada deal as trade dispute deepens, USTR says
WASHINGTON, Sept 25 - President Donald Trump's administration is comfortable maintaining its trade standoff with Canada even as new US import bans on Canadian products take effect next week and Washington threatens 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, parts and steel from January, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Friday.
His comments to CNBC signal Washington sees little need to compromise despite a deepening dispute that has strained relations between the longtime allies, triggered retaliation on both sides of the border and raised fresh questions about the future of the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement.
The looming US import bans are on a broad range of Canadian goods, including alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and dairy products. The January increase on tariffs to 50% could carry significant consequences for North American auto production.
Canada's own retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect earlier this month. Canadian tariffs followed 50% tariffs that the US imposed on some $20 billion of Canadian goods last month, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.
"We're still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash, all of these things. We're shipping (agricultural products) back and forth across the border, so there's still a lot of strong trade between the two countries," Greer told CNBC. "We're comfortable with where we are. ... They call us now and then, and we have good conversations about potential deals. But it's not – there's no urgency on our side, I would say."
The Canadian Embassy in Washington did not immediately comment.
The breakdown has widened a rift between the longtime allies, who have blamed each other for the failed talks, spurred Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to urge a further shift away from Canada's biggest trading partner, and cast doubt on the viability of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
Some experts think the Trump administration wants to first reach a deal with Mexico, which could give the US more leverage to get a better agreement with Canada. The next round of talks with Mexico could occur in October, Mexican officials said this week. REUTERS

EU vows to pursue €120 million fine on X after US backs Musk's court challenge

EU vows to pursue €120 million fine on X after US backs Musk's court challenge
The European Union on Friday said it will pursue a €120 million fine against the X social network after the US Justice Department said it supported the efforts of X owner Elon Musk to have the case annulled. The bloc fined the platform in 2025 for breaching EU online transparency rules, notably with its pay-to-play blue "verification" checkmark.
Issued on: Modified:
The European Union's executive arm said Friday it is prepared to defend a €120 million ($137 million) fine against the social media platform X after the US government threw its support behind a legal effort by Elon Musk to have the case dismissed.
The European Commission fined X late last year for breaches of the bloc’s landmark digital protections, stoking tensions with Washington.
The EU fine against X, which followed a two-year investigation, was the first penalty issued under the bloc's digital regulations governing online content. Regulators said X’s paid-for blue checkmarks violate the EU's online transparency obligations.
"On X, anyone can pay to obtain the ‘verified' status without the company meaningfully verifying who is behind the account," the European Commission said in a press release at the time.
The US Justice Department said Thursday that it had filed an application to support X's bid to have the case annulled at the European Union's General Court.
Defending Musk
It was the second time in three months that the Justice Department has intervened to defend a company owned by Musk.
In July, the Justice Department filed a motion to intervene in a civil rights lawsuit that alleges Musk’s xAI is illegally running dozens of natural gas turbines to power a $20 billion AI data centre in Mississippi.
In that case, the NAACP and other rights groups said xAI failed to get a permit for its power plant – which is located near homes, schools and churches – creating health risks for families in north Mississippi and nearby Memphis, Tennessee, in violating the federal Clean Air Act.
Watch moreElon Musk loses lawsuit against OpenAI and Sam Altman
US President Donald Trump and the world's richest man appear to have dialled down a war of words that stunned Washington and Wall Street alike last year after Musk called Trump's tax breaks and spending cuts a “disgusting abomination”.
Musk on Thursday evening attended a state dinner held by Trump honouring China’s leader Xi Jinping along with other tech titans.
European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday that it is the EU’s “sovereign right” to draft legislation aimed at protecting its citizens.
“We are enforcing our legislation objectively, transparently and with a solid case,” he told reporters. “We are ready to defend our position in court. We have a lot of evidence at our disposal, and it will be for the court to decide, as always.”
The commission is the top enforcer of the 27-nation EU's Digital Services Act (DSA), which requires tech companies to increase transparency, strengthen user protections and give audiences greater control when they navigate online platforms or face hefty financial penalties.
But the rulebook has become a flashpoint with the Trump administration, and US officials have criticised it as amounting to online censorship.

The Justice Department warned that the fine, if upheld, “may have significant implications” for US online platforms and other companies providing digital services in the EU.
Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division said in Thursday's statement that the "European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction.”
“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” he said.
When asked whether the Justice Department had informed the commission that it intended to back Musk, Regnier said: “We do not need to be informed about anything.”
He said the commission doesn't expect the case to hurt broader relations between Brussels and Washington, notably in talks to mitigate the damage of Trump administration tariffs.
“From our perspective, nothing will change because of a DSA case,” he said.

Chinese satellites are providing Iran with intelligence data and imagery, which has significantly increased the accuracy of Iranian attacks on U.S. military facilities and civilian vessels in the Middle East.

Africa rejects new scramble for minerals – Ghanaian president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:30 UTC
00:00:30 KST

Africa rejects new scramble for minerals – Ghanaian president
Africa will not accept another era of colonial-style resource extraction as global demand for critical minerals grows, Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama has told the UN General Assembly (UNGA), calling for structural reforms to address historical injustices.
The remarks come as the US and EU pursue deals with African governments to secure minerals such as copper, cobalt, and lithium for electric vehicles, batteries, and power grids, while seeking to reduce their reliance on China.
African countries hold substantial deposits but often export raw minerals. A UN Trade and Development report published in June says many minerals agreements still focus heavily on extraction, warning that resource-rich African countries could miss out on the value generated by processing and manufacturing.
“Africa will not remain a passive arena for a new scramble for resources,” Mahama said on Thursday. He said African countries must process their minerals at home, build local industries, and retain more of the wealth they generate.
Several African governments have moved to tighten control over their mineral resources in recent years. DR Congo, the world’s largest cobalt producer, has banned exports of copper and cobalt concentrates to encourage local processing under an order reported in August. Zimbabwe also suspended exports of raw minerals and lithium concentrates in February.
Ghana has required licensed aggregators to refine gold locally since September 1, with Mahama pledging to end raw mineral ore exports by 2030. In July, the West African nation’s neighbor Mali created a state body to oversee artisanal gold sales and curb smuggling, while Niger nationalized the Somair uranium venture operated by French state-owned Orano last year.
Aside from critical minerals, Mahama also renewed the call for slavery reparations in his role as the African Union’s champion for the campaign. In March, Ghana secured a UN resolution recognizing the transatlantic slave trade and chattel slavery as the gravest crimes against humanity. It passed with 123 votes. The US, Israel, and Argentina voted against it, while 52 countries abstained.
Mahama welcomed what he called “positive overtures” from countries, particularly the Netherlands, Germany, and France, as well as from institutions, on reparatory justice and restitution following the passage of the “historic resolution.”
The Ghanaian leader, however, said real repair requires “structural transformation,” including “dismantling the persistent engines of exploitation: unfair global trade regimes, predatory resource extraction, discriminatory credit ratings, [and] unsustainable debt burdens.”
“Africa does not seek charity. Africa seeks equal partnership,” Mahama declared.

Diverse autism genes converge to disrupt shared biological pathways, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:18 UTC
00:00:18 KST

A new mapping of how proteins interact in the brain suggests that many different genetic mutations linked to autism spectrum disorder end up altering the same underlying biological networks. By determining how specific mutations rewire these protein connections, the research offers a potential roadmap for finding targeted treatments for neurodevelopmental conditions. The findings were published in Science.
Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by varying challenges with social communication and repetitive behaviors. The genetics underlying the condition are highly complex, with hundreds of different genes implicated. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2016 found that thousands of genes might contribute to the condition in different ways. Despite identifying so many risk factors, scientists have struggled to understand how such a wide variety of genetic changes leads to similar developmental outcomes.
“Over the past 15 years, large-scale sequencing studies have identified hundreds of genes associated with autism,” study co-author Nevan J. Krogan, a researcher at the Quantitative Biosciences Institute at the University of California, San Francisco, told PsyPost. “That progress was initially very exciting; in 2012, only a few genes had been clearly implicated, whereas today the list includes several hundred.”
“However, identifying genes and mutations has not, by itself, produced a sufficiently detailed understanding of autism biology or led to many new therapeutic strategies,” Krogan continued. “A list of genes is somewhat like a parts list for a machine. To understand how the machine works, and what happens when one part is altered, you also need to understand the proteins those genes produce and how those proteins interact inside cells. That was the gap we wanted to address.”
To bridge this gap, scientists look to proteins, which are the microscopic machines that carry out most of a cell’s functions. Proteins rarely act alone. Instead, they bind to one another to form larger complexes, much like interlocking puzzle pieces. A 2026 study showed how a single autism-linked mutation can physically disrupt the binding between two partner proteins, impairing how brain cells communicate. Similarly, a 2026 preprint study that has not been peer-reviewed indicated that turning off different autism-associated genes in human brain cells disrupts shared biological pathways.
Mapping these physical connections can be highly useful for medical research. In fact, research covered by PsyPost in 2022 used protein interaction networks to identify existing medications that might counteract the biological processes underlying autism.
Building on this concept, a research team that included Krogan and lead author Belinda Wang sought to map the physical interactions of proteins associated with autism risk genes at a massive scale. They wanted to see if different mutations might converge on the same biological complexes, selectively rewiring how these proteins connect rather than simply destroying their function altogether.
“Through this work, we generated what we believe is the largest protein-protein interaction map assembled for a neuropsychiatric disorder,” Krogan said. “The map provides a molecular framework for understanding how autism-associated mutations may disrupt cellular systems. Importantly, it has also revealed potential therapeutic directions that would not have been visible from genetic information alone.”
“We are now following up on several of those opportunities through drug-development programs,” he noted. “The broader goal is to move beyond cataloging autism-associated genes and toward understanding the underlying biology well enough to identify new strategies for treatment.”
The team focused on 100 genes identified as high-confidence risk factors for autism. They introduced the protein versions of these genes into human embryonic kidney cells. This cell type is widely used in laboratories because it is easy to grow and allows for large-scale analysis of protein interactions. Using a technique called affinity purification and mass spectrometry, which acts like a microscopic fishing hook to pull out a target protein along with everything attached to it, they identified which other proteins bound to their targets.
The resulting map uncovered 1,881 total interactions, 87 percent of which had never been reported before. On average, each autism risk protein interacted with 11 other proteins. The researchers observed a highly interconnected network, meaning that the different autism risk proteins tended to bind to the same central hubs.
To determine which proteins touched directly rather than indirectly, the team used AlphaFold, an artificial intelligence system that predicts the three-dimensional shapes of proteins. They then tested one of the central hubs, a protein complex involving the molecules DCAF7 and DYRK1A, in living systems. They edited the genes of Xenopus, a type of frog often used to study early development, as well as human neural progenitor cells, which are stem cells that develop into brain cells.
Disrupting this shared protein complex impaired the multiplication of the progenitor cells and resulted in a smaller forebrain size in the frog models. This provides evidence that different autism risk proteins work together in the same physical machinery to regulate early brain growth.
The researchers then looked at the impact of the disease-linked mutations themselves. They introduced 54 specific genetic mutations derived from autistic patients into 30 of the risk proteins. They repeated their protein-fishing experiment to see how these mutations changed the interaction network compared to the typical, unmutated proteins.
The mutations caused 253 interactions to be altered, with some connections strengthening and others weakening. The researchers found that completely different mutations often caused the exact same changes in the protein network. For example, three different mutations in a gene called FOXP1 all caused its resulting protein to lose its connection to a partner protein called FOXP4.
To see how this specific severed connection affects brain development, the team grew human forebrain organoids. These are miniature, three-dimensional bundles of brain tissue grown in a dish from stem cells, which mimic the early stages of human brain development.
In organoids carrying the FOXP1 mutations, the loss of the FOXP1 and FOXP4 connection led to the partner protein attaching to the wrong sections of DNA. This biological misstep caused the brain cells to mature too early. The premature maturation altered the proportion of specific types of neurons in the organoids and increased their overall electrical activity.
This overlap in downstream effects was exactly what the researchers were looking for. “The most surprising finding was the degree of biological convergence,” Krogan noted. “We began with roughly 100 genes associated with autism, but the corresponding proteins were not acting independently. Many were connected within a smaller number of shared biological networks.”
“That suggests we may not need a separate treatment for every individual genetic mutation,” he added. “A smaller number of therapies targeting common pathways could potentially benefit multiple groups of patients. That possibility has significant implications for future drug development.”
The findings provide independent researchers a new lens to interpret the thousands of rare mutations identified in recent years.
Lisa Bradley, a senior research associate at The Centre for Applied Genomics at The Hospital for Sick Children Research Institute who was not involved in the study, noted that the research complements existing genomic efforts. “This large-scale study of bona fide high-risk genes specifically looks at the very real possibility that ASD-associated mutations rewire specific protein-protein interactions,” she told PsyPost. “For me, the key takeaway is that this strategy provides a way to move from many different ASD-associated genes toward a smaller number of convergent molecular mechanisms, which otherwise could have remained hidden.”
Bradley found the study’s experimental validation using human forebrain organoids particularly persuasive. “For me, the FOXP1 story was the most convincing because they took an ASD-associated mutation from disruption of a specific protein interaction with FOXP4 through to downstream effects on gene expression and neuronal development in brain organoids,” she said. “Other ASD studies have implicated altered cortical layer development, so this provided an important proof of principle that altered protein interactions can translate into meaningful cellular neurodevelopmental consequences.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The initial protein mapping was conducted in kidney cells rather than brain cells. While the researchers validated key interactions in brain-specific models later, the initial environment might lack some specialized proteins found only in developing neurons.
Bradley cautioned that the findings offer early-stage evidence for molecular mechanisms, “rather than demonstrating that they are causal mechanisms.” She added, “Some of these genes and mutations could also be associated with complex ASD, including co-occurring intellectual disability, so the molecular changes identified may include broader NDD [neurodevelopmental disorder] biology rather than mechanisms unique to autism etiology.”
The study focused on 100 high-confidence autism risk genes, but hundreds more have been linked to the condition, meaning the current map represents only a fraction of the total biological picture. “In this study, we examined a small number of genes and mutations in depth using stem cells, neurons and brain organoids,” Krogan said. “We have now built a pipeline that allows us to apply the same approach more systematically and at a larger scale. Our next goal is to identify which autism-associated mutations and biological pathways are most suitable for therapeutic development.”
Before new therapies can be developed, these molecular interactions must be observed in broader behavioral contexts. “While the molecular and mechanistic evidence is very compelling and is likely to be highly relevant to complex ASD etiology, I would like to see this tested in a mammalian developmental model where social and ASD-relevant behaviors can be examined alongside learning and cognitive impairments,” Bradley said. “This would allow more direct tests of causality for the FOXP1-FOXP4 interaction and how these molecular changes ultimately translate into social behavior.”
Additionally, artificial intelligence predictions of protein structures are estimates and sometimes miss the nuance of how proteins bend and fold in a living organism. Beyond refining these models, future research could expand this network and test additional drug candidates that might stabilize these weakened protein connections. The researchers believe the principles established in this study could eventually stretch to entirely different fields of medicine.
“The concept of biological convergence may extend beyond autism,” Krogan pointed out. “We are applying these tools to other neuropsychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder, to look for shared pathways. We are also seeing overlap between some genes and proteins implicated in autism and those studied in cancer.”
“Because drugs already exist for certain cancer-related targets, there may be opportunities to investigate whether some of those compounds could be repurposed for neurological or psychiatric conditions,” he continued. “That possibility is still at an early stage, but it opens an unexpected avenue for collaboration and therapeutic research.”
Ultimately, the research team views this extensive protein map as a foundational resource for the scientific community, moving the field past simple catalogs of genetic risks.
“This is an important step between identifying a genetic change and developing a potential treatment,” Krogan concluded. “It is not the final step, and new therapies will still require years of research and testing. That said, our study provides a clearer biological framework for identifying therapeutic opportunities that were not apparent before.”
The study, “Autism mutations rewire protein interaction networks to drive neurodevelopmental pathology,” was authored by Belinda Wang, Rasika Vartak, Kelsey M. Hennick, Yefim Zaltsman, Zun Zar Chi Naing, Benjamin J. Polacco, Ali Bashir, Manon Eckhardt, Mehdi Bouhaddou, Jiewei Xu, Nawei Sun, Micaela C. Lasser, Yuan Zhou, Justin McKetney, Keelan Z. Guiley, Pawel Gniewek, Una Chan, Naufa Amirani, Owen Griffiths, Nishant Chadha, Reshmi Tognatta, Merve Cakir, Martin Gordon, Prachi Khare, Sam Drake, Vanessa Drury, David F. Burke, Silvano Gonzalez, Sahar Alkhairy, Reuben Thomas, Stephanie Lam, Montana Morris, Ethel Bader, Mélanie Dos Santos, Anastassia V. Komarova, Maxwell Bennett, Craig Ennis, Octavio Castillo, Yvonne Lim, Robert Martin, Meghan Seyler, Tierney Baum, Rebecca Krasnoff, George Wang, Sagnik Middya, Sheng Wang, Presley Pham, Juan Arbelaez, Dexter Pratt, Sofia Bali, Shivali Chag, Julia A. Kaye, Nadir Mahmood, Lee Spraggon, Thomas Rolland, Shawn Hervey-Jumper, James S. Fraser, Thomas Bourgeron, Steven Finkbeiner, Caroline Demeret, Danielle L. Swaney, Sourav Bandyopadhyay, Trey Ideker, Pedro Beltrao, Helen Rankin Willsey, Ruth Hüttenhain, Kirsten Obernier, Tomasz J. Nowakowski, Matthew W. State, A. Jeremy Willsey, and Nevan J. Krogan.

Our lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insane | Brigid Delaney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:09 UTC
00:00:09 KST

Think of your online life as a garden. At first it’s just a few seeds here or there – a Facebook profile where you created entire albums from a night at the pub, or maybe a Tumblr or a Myspace page listing your favourite bands. It is fun – something just for you and your friends to enjoy.
Then the garden grows. You get an Instagram account and document moments from each day on Stories, use LinkedIn for networking and sharing career triumphs, and check your X/Twitter hyper-vigilantly in case you wrote something that just got you cancelled.
Your online garden grows more sprawling and complex; now it’s no longer just a fun project for yourself on weekends and weeknights. As it grows, you start to view it through the eyes of others.
How will this garden be seen? Will people like it? What can I plant in this garden that will make more people like it?
A few more years pass. And now, instead of working on the garden here and there, you’re in there all the time. You have discovered if your garden is really enticing, you can make money off it. You want – then need – big numbers coming in there. You look at other people’s gardens all the time and you get jealous. They have better gardens.
When you’re not in your garden, you’re still somehow tending to it – looking at the number of people coming in, and comparing them with what it used to be, and being worried that maybe you didn’t plant the right things. But people will tell you if you’re doing it wrong. They’ll spray paint all over the garden walls how much your garden sucks, how you’re a loser, how ugly it all is.
And with all this activity going on you hardly notice how, over time, the world outside your garden has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world. The garden is your home now.
When this current moment ends and a more enlightened time kicks in, descendants looking back will see that millions (or is it billions?) of us have spent the last 10 years or more migrating our lives and identities, and our political, communal and social selves, to a digital realm that has sent many of us insane.
The (digital) signal that we are living a better life has been imbued with more energy and importance than living a better life itself.
Those descendants will see what we can’t really see now – a massive serf culture has emerged, where people have become servants to these gardens.
They’ll see how truly unfree so many of us are – allowing the rich, real, tactile world to recede, while the digital gardens have sprawled to take up all our time and energy (the average user spends about 2 hours and 39 minutes a day on social media.)
And it will become apparent that the real elite won’t be the people with the most popular digital gardens. They’ll be the people who never had gardens. Or people who had small private gardens, where they only let a few friends in.
Brand strategists and trend forecasters are saying that, in 2026, the true measure of status is privacy and a low or no digital footprint.
This is a different way of living off-grid.
You experience a rich and interesting life in the real world and don’t feel the need to post about it.
Your sense of self worth is not linked to how many people see that you’ve been somewhere, hung out with someone or worn something.
Your income, status and financial security is not dependent on your social media account.
Your attention span has not been corrupted or shortened by chronic social media consumption and AI use – and this gives you almost superhuman powers such as the ability to read long, difficult novels, think critically, and retain information in your head.
Your emotional stability is not dependent on how your content is performing.
You have not internalised the digital panopticon where everything you do is with an eye to how it is perceived.
You have a healthy social life in the real world, meaning you have less time or inclination to post.
Brand strategist Eugene Healey in his Substack wrote a recent series on “post-luxury status symbols” and said “the greatest privilege is to be chronically offline” and “in this culture of overexposure – it’s only natural that it becomes desirable to opt out”.
The ultimate flex is not needing social media, walking away from your digital garden and back into your real life.

War Bros Didn’t Always Rule Silicon Valley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

In September 2015, the Founders Fund hosted a retreat at an eco-resort in British Columbia. Most of the attendees were VCs and people from the companies the firm was backing, but they also invited a few outsiders, including computer pioneer Alan Kay, writer Neal Stephenson, and me.
One morning at breakfast I was sitting across from Kay at a long table. The man who conceived the Dynabook—basically the modern computer that we all use—was expounding on his exploits when Founders Fund leader Peter Thiel plopped down next to him. As Kay, in full raconteur mode, spun stories of optimizing the mouse and advising Steve Jobs, Thiel listened with increasingly visible incredulity. Finally, he couldn’t take it. “Who ARE you?” he demanded of Kay.
The mustachioed legend was stunned. He began stumbling out his bona fides, but quickly realized that for someone unacquainted with his résumé, it would have sounded ridiculously overblown. It was like asking Einstein or Mick Jagger to explain themselves. Kay stopped mid-sentence and sighed. “I’m just an old has-been,” he said and went back to his breakfast. Two worlds had collided, and failed to connect.
I thought back to that moment a couple of weeks ago while reading an op-ed in The New York Times headlined “Silicon Valley Was Right From the Start,” by Sharon Weinberger. The essay claimed that the portrait often painted of the Valley as driven by the counterculture and a desire to make the world better was a sham. Today’s bare-knuckled approach to accumulating massive wealth, kowtowing to an authoritarian leader, and embracing lethal military technology simply exposes the industry for what it always was. (Weinberger’s essay was promoting her new book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War.)
“Silicon Valley’s values haven’t changed, just its customers,” she wrote, calling the industry’s current love affair with military tech “less a story of political conversion than of market adaptation.” In that reading, all that hippie stuff about free expression and democratization during the 1980s PC revolution and the 1990s Internet boom was a mirage, an opportunistic feint by Big Tech to push its wares and garner the loot.
I disagree. The story as I see it is that beginning in the late 1970s, a new generation of technologists, identifying with the counterculture, operated with a set of values that unleashed innovation and ironically set the stage for the industry’s current wealth. Yes, that movement carried a torch from the field’s defense industry roots. But even as DOD funding kept fueling innovations (Darpa grants provided dough for the GUI, the internet, and Google Search), that new generation was characterized by idealism, a hackerish love of building things, and disdain for conventional practices.
That mindset changed not only the course of the computer industry, but the culture of American business. (Before Apple Computer, a CEO wouldn’t dare come to work in anything but a suit.) Denying the existence of that idealism is not only inaccurate, but it conveniently lets the new generation of defense contractors off the hook for their pivot toward deadly materiel.
When I shared my views with Weinberger, she acknowledged that I’d probably studied tech culture more than she had from her perch in Washington, DC. Still, she gamely defended her op-ed. “We’re all products of what we grow up in,” she says. “If you were growing up in the peace-dividend era, with defense tech jobs disappearing, the money from defense was less important, and you start to have different values.”
By that standard, the market shift from missile control modules to Macintoshes was driven not by values but by greed. Likewise, she says, the recent return to high-tech weaponry doesn’t represent a philosophical repositioning but a fortuitous opportunity to sell to a Pentagon eager to exploit the Valley’s innovations. “It's not like everybody in the workforce in Silicon Valley woke up and went, like, ‘Defense is cool,’” says Weinberger. That impulse to go where the money is, she argues, is the defining ethos of Silicon Valley. “Your prime directive is for your company to succeed,” she says. “Why didn't Apple work with the military? Because they didn't need to. They had the consumer marketplace.”
Actually, Apple and its cohorts invented the consumer marketplace for computers. And the shoulders that Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, and others stood on were not those of pocket-protector-wearing nerds clocking into jobs at Lockheed, but young and freaky computer scientists. My friend John Markoff’s book What the Dormouse Said is all about how the counterculture set the tone for the Valley during its tremendous growth years. When we spoke this week, Markoff noted that the Valley’s transition point from a defense-oriented industry to one shaped by counterculture values rose from three pivotal computer labs—AI pioneer John McCarthy’s Stanford lab, the Stanford Research Institute, which hosted Douglas Engelbart’s groundbreaking GUI innovations; and Kay’s Xerox PARC, which essentially set the foundation for the computers that we all use today.
These influential institutions were hippie havens. In fact, says Markoff, many of the researchers in those labs worked there in order to get draft deferments to avoid the Vietnam War. “Money was not the motivating factor for these people,” he says. “The Valley’s entrepreneurial culture emerged from a fusion of the counterculture hackers and engineers who believed that technology would change the world, and the more traditional semiconductor culture, which quickly escaped its military roots.”
While those labs were thriving, a ragtag group of engineers met at the Homebrew Computer Club, hosted by a political radical named Lee Felsenstein. That was the bunch that invented the personal computer industry, notably Apple. When I first became exposed to the computer world in the early 1980s, the countercultural nature of the enterprise blew my mind, and drew me into covering that world full-time. I saw for myself how, working within the infrastructure of big business, techno-idealists like the early Macintosh team built the products of their dreams.
No, the Valley did not turn from defense to consumer products because that’s where the money was. Well into the ’80s and ’90s, Apple in particular had to fight the image that their products were like toys, because they eschewed the macho industrial vibe of previous machines in favor of a friendlier look and feel. It took decades for the company to significantly break into the corporate market. (It’s ironic that the current War Bros that Weinberger writes about in her book are obsessed with masculinity.) Google was founded by iconoclasts who thumbed their noses at Wall Street even as their company pursued its IPO.
The most nuanced study of the relationship between the Valley’s military past and the counterculturists who built the modern industry is historian Margaret O’Mara’s book The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America. When I spoke to her this week, she agreed with me that the Valley's counterculture shift wasn’t a mercenary pivot but a genuine movement toward making the world better. The market’s move from defense tech to consumer, she says, was a reflection of a generational political shift. In the presidential elections of 1980 and 1984, the Valley voted decisively for Reagan. But as the Valley increasingly tilted toward the counterculture, that all changed, and for many recent cycles those tech-heavy zip codes have been tattooed in deep blue hues. While Trump-affiliated War Bros are currently getting attention, they represent only a small cohort of self-interested multibillionaires. Essentially, they’ve hijacked the values of the Valley.
“I feel like the wealth and the concentration of power has warped everything so profoundly,” says O’Mara. “When you’re in a bubble, whether you’re a president or a billionaire, you have a very hard time understanding how the rest of the world is receiving you.”
I’m sure that the War Bros themselves believe they are acting out of patriotism—though at least some of them have fetishized cool war movies and shoot-’em-up computer games to the point where they get a kick out of making products with spectacular kill functions. But for the past 40 years or so, Silicon Valley typically wanted nothing to do with killing, even though there was always money to be tapped from the Pentagon budget. Ignoring that history or, worse, denying it, takes the War Bros off the hook.
It’s too bad that Peter Thiel didn’t bother to understand what made Alan Kay tick or even know who he was. Thiel himself is a beneficiary of Kay’s idealism, as well as the ethos of countless hackers and founders. They strived for something more lofty than a Valley of Death. Don’t pretend otherwise.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

These are the first feathers ever found in fossilized dinosaur poop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

These are the first feathers ever found in fossilized dinosaur poop
The plumage may help explain why only some birds survived dino doomsday
Exquisitely preserved feathers, the first ever found in fossilized dinosaur poop, are providing a peek into how some ancient birds lived — and possibly went extinct.
Dense bristles suggest some of the feathers could repel water, possibly as well as those of modern pelicans, researchers report September 10 in Current Biology. And their central shafts are filled with air pockets, a trait that in modern birds keeps plumage lightweight yet stiff enough for flight. “That’s something we’re seeing for the first time in the Age of the Dinosaurs,” says vertebrate paleontologist Jingmai O’Connor of the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago.
The find also offers a clue that might explain why, among birds, there were winners and losers in the mass extinction that ended the dinosaurs’ reign about 66 million years ago. The ancestors of modern birds survived the asteroid-triggered event while many other types of birds, including the group these feathers came from, died out.
One of O’Connor’s colleagues unearthed the fossilized dung, or coprolite, in 2016 in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation. If it weren’t for a “lucky break” on the coprolite’s surface that put one feather on full display, her team might never have known it had feathers inside, O’Connor says.
The scientists used micro-CT scans to 3-D map the coprolite’s inner contents. Leg bones and fish scales suggest the bird was aquatic — a member of a group called hesperonithiforms — and that it had eaten shortly before its demise. And while some of the feathers resembled those of modern birds, others were more primitive and stringy, which could have made it difficult for the bird to maintain body heat.
Poor insulation might explain why hesperonithiforms and their close kin didn’t survive the deep chill that followed the asteroid impact, O’Connor says. But researchers need more feathers from various bird species during that time period to test the hypothesis. And fossilized feathers are incredibly rare.
Now that it’s clear poop can be an excellent guardian of plumage, O’Connor says, “people should start looking.”

Mariupol defender, 22, describes his captivity in letters
Mark Mykhailov, a 22-year-old Mariupol defender, has been held captive in Russia for four years after being captured at the Azovstal steel plant. His family and friends can communicate with him only through letters. In one of them, Mark sent a poem to his mother.
Source: Mark's friend Zlata in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)
Details: Zlata also shared the letters Mark has sent from captivity.
"I have known Mark since school. We were in the same class and also lived in the same block in Mariupol. He always brought a smile to people's faces near the drama theatre, performing card tricks – he was fascinated by them. He also loved playing football," the young woman recalled.
On 24 February 2022, 18-year-old Mark went to defend his native Mariupol, The Bridge Media reports. In April, he suffered a shrapnel wound to his neck during the fighting, as well as other injuries and concussion. A month later, after the defence of Mariupol, Mark was taken prisoner.
His loved ones managed to establish correspondence with him only four years later, in April 2026. At the time, he said he weighed just 54 kg. His family does not know his current weight.
His health has deteriorated significantly during his time in Russian captivity. Mark has been diagnosed with tuberculosis and damage to both lungs requiring urgent treatment.
On 18 March 2026, a Russian court sentenced Mark to five and a half years in prison on charges of participating in a "terrorist organisation". This is how the Russian side classifies his affiliation with the Azov Brigade.
In one of his letters, Mark described being transferred from Volgograd. On 11 September 2026, he was taken away for transfer. He later ended up in Izhevsk. Before the journey, Mark tried to take care of the most important thing – making sure his loved ones received word from him.
"Having written a letter to my mum and my friend Zlata, I was left alone with my thoughts," Mark said.
The young man said he is glad to have the opportunity to communicate, at least through correspondence, which had not been possible before.
"Reading the letters from my friends and loved ones, I realise that ordinary life is going on, with its intrigues, quarrels and life as usual. I reread a letter from my friend and realised how much he has grown up," Mark wrote.
In his letters, the young man reflects on his life after 2022.
Quote from Mark: "Reading these stories, you immediately begin to live in your mind the life that disappeared in 2022… You take your mind off things for a while, and then you become sad. That is why I try not to reread the letters.
Sitting in this place, I've begun to realise how I simply wasted my time on unnecessary things and people I did not need. Everything is now in the past, the present is here, and the future – you can try to grasp it with your hands, but if the circumstances are stronger, you can end up in trouble."
Details: In another message, the young man dreamed about how he would spend his day if he were free.
"Without bars, with a thermos and the person I love, it would make for a wonderful weekend," Mark wrote.
He also wrote a letter to his mother, urging her not to grieve for him and to stay strong. The young man dedicated a poem to her.
Background: Russia previously sentenced three teenagers from Melitopol for "terrorism". The three young men from temporarily occupied Melitopol, who were accused of "terrorism", received harsh sentences in fabricated cases. They were 16-17 years old when they were detained.

Taiwan Isn’t Giving Up, It’s Pulling Apart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

In a recent article for The Diplomat, Mor Sobol offered an even-handed assessment of the debate set off by Simon Shuster’s piece in The Atlantic, which asked whether Taiwan might simply “give up” under growing pressure from China. Sobol argued that both Shuster’s pessimistic answer and his critics’ confident rebuttals rest on thinner evidence than either side recognizes.
Sobol pointed out that telling a pollster “I would defend Taiwan” is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, and that Taiwan is not a unitary actor. The question worth asking is how the trends in public opinion, military recruitment, defense spending and other metrics move over time, not what any single snapshot shows.
I agree. As a scholar who studies Taiwanese defense attitudes with survey data, I want to add evidence showing why the much-discussed “willingness to fight” has, to some degree, misled outside observers. The problem with polling is not that attitudes can’t be measured. It’s that pollsters keep asking the most superficial question. “Would you fight?” captures a sentiment. What decides whether that sentiment translates into action is whether citizens believe the conditions for sacrifice are in place. Those conditions can be measured, tracked over time, and broken down by group.
When we do that, the picture is more troubling than either the optimists or the pessimists suggest, though for different reasons.
Citizens never accept the risks of war unconditionally. They take part in what I call a Defense Social Contract, which rests on three pillars, all of them vitally important.
The first pillar is trust in the state. People will sacrifice for a government they believe governs competently and fairly, and for a country they believe has a future worth defending. When citizens feel the state has failed them, its claim to extraordinary sacrifice loses legitimacy.
The second pillar is trust in one another. Defense is a public good, and public goods invite free-riding. I will hold the line only if I believe my neighbors will too. That means the burden must be shared, rather than some Taiwanese being expected to serve while others are exempt. Resistance must also be the common cause of all Taiwanese, not the property of one political camp.
The final pillar is trust that resistance can work. Facing a far more powerful adversary, citizens of a small democracy must believe their own military is capable and that allies will arrive in time. Sacrifice that looks futile turns into fatalism.
If any one pillar gives way, professed willingness to fight stays a sentiment and never becomes action.
What the Surveys Show
All three pillars can be measured. To do so, I used two nationally representative waves of the Taiwan National Security Survey (TNSS), fielded in June 2024 and September 2025, with 2,745 respondents in total. This makes it possible to do what Sobol recommends: track change over time and look inside the aggregate. The timing deserves emphasis. The 2024 survey was fielded about a month after President Lai Ching-te took office. The 2025 survey was fielded about a month after the final round of Taiwan’s Great Recall votes, a national effort to recall all legislators from the Kuomintang (KMT) that ultimately failed.
The TNSS directly asks respondents what they would actually do if China invaded. One option is to “let nature take its course” (shun qi zi ran). That answer is not surrender, and it is not a rejection of Taiwan. It is withdrawal: wait and see. I call it fatalistic passivity. Between the two waves, the share of Taiwanese choosing it rose from about 26 percent to nearly 37 percent.
From 2024 to 2025, the TNSS results showed that all three pillars weakened or came under strain.
On trust in the state, the share of respondents who said the national economy had gotten worse rose from 31 to 48 percent. Negative economic evaluations are strongly associated with passivity, although the association weakens once other factors are taken into account.
The share who doubt Taiwan’s military could defend the island on its own rose from 69 to 74 percent. Confidence in the military and the expectation of U.S. intervention are among the strongest and most consistent predictors of lower passivity across every model. Passivity is highest among those pessimistic on both counts.
Finally, there’s trust in fellow Taiwanese. Respondents who believe “most Taiwanese would resist” are much less likely to opt to “let nature take its course.” Predicted passivity falls from about 36 percent among those who think their compatriots definitely would not resist to about 25 percent among those who think they definitely would.
The most important finding, however, is not the numbers themselves. It’s the breakdown of the survey results along political lines. Among respondents who identified with the KMT, expressions of passivity rose from 22 percent in 2024 to 40 percent in 2025, an 18-point jump. That difference holds after controlling for national identity, unification-independence preferences, confidence in the military, expectations of U.S. assistance, economic evaluations, and demographics. Among Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) identifiers, it rose from 26 to 30.5 percent, a change statistically indistinguishable from zero. The 13.6-point gap between the two trajectories is statistically significant.
I want to stress what this does not mean, because the finding is easy to misread. On its face, it might seem to show that KMT supporters love Taiwan less or are less willing to defend it. That’s not accurate. In 2024, KMT identifiers were actually slightly less fatalistic than DPP identifiers. In other words, at the start of Lai’s presidency, KMT supporters showed no sign of giving up on Taiwan’s defense simply because the DPP had won another term.
In neither wave is the partisan gap on its own statistically significant. Both surveys took place under a DPP government, with KMT supporters in opposition throughout. The divergence between June 2024 and September 2025 therefore suggests that something changed over those 15 months in how the opposition camp relates to the DPP government.
Between the two surveys, Taiwan went through more than a year of fierce executive-legislative conflict, ending in the 2025 Great Recall. Advocates framed the campaign to remove 31 KMT legislators as a defense of national security against Chinese infiltration. Opponents saw it as an attempt to overturn an election result. All 31 recall votes failed. The September 2025 survey was fielded weeks later.
The partisan gap was already there. In both waves of the TNSS, KMT identifiers were about 20 points less likely than DPP identifiers to believe most Taiwanese would resist (roughly 61-63 percent versus 80-82 percent). In both the DPP and the KMT, the share who believe “most Taiwanese would resist” barely moved from 2024 to 2025. A substantial share of the electorate had already lost confidence that the burden would be shared.
But people’s own willingness to act did change, and it fell most among supporters of the KMT, whose political opponents had been presenting national security as a partisan cause.
Survey data cannot prove that any single event caused the shift. But when the language of national security becomes a weapon in domestic political combat, this pattern should come as no surprise.
What We Should Be Tracking
My reading is that the problem for Taiwan’s defense is not a lack of will but a lack of unity. It is very hard to ask citizens to risk their lives alongside people they already dislike and distrust in everyday politics, or to sacrifice for a government they see as a political adversary. The TNSS does not directly measure cross-partisan trust, so this interpretation needs further testing. It fits the evidence, though: a society that still sees itself as one nation but is increasingly unsure it can fight as one.
To gauge Taiwan’s willingness to fight, Sobol argued for watching behavior: recruitment, retention, reserve training, and civil defense participation. I strongly agree. I would add three sets of attitudinal indicators that come before this behavior and help explain it.
Do supporters of every party believe that the government asking for sacrifice governs fairly and competently, and that the country has a future?
Do citizens believe the burden is shared? Conscription reform, reserve obligations, and civil defense must be seen as universal, not selective. National security must stop being used against political opponents. Leaders of all parties should stop branding one another as Beijing’s proxies and should negotiate defense budgets and reforms as cross-party agreements.
Are allied signals consistent? Taiwanese must believe they can hold out until help arrives. Mixed messages from Washington or Tokyo damage the very pillar my data identify as most critical. Allies should also engage Taiwan’s major parties evenly, so that outside support is not seen as backing one camp.
These indicators should be broken down by party, age, gender, and region, and tracked across survey waves. If behavior and attitudes move together, across various segments of society, we can trust them more. If the aggregate holds steady while part of society quietly pulls back, we are looking at what I call “fragile resilience.”
So is Taiwan giving up? The evidence says no. Taiwanese still identify with their country, and most still expect their compatriots to resist. What the data show is a society pulling apart. Fatalism rose most sharply among those who identify with the KMT, whose legislators had just been targeted in a campaign that cast national security as a partisan cause.
This polarization is harder to see; the headline number on willingness to fight won’t capture it. It’s also dangerous. Beijing doesn’t need Taiwanese to embrace unification. It only needs enough of them to decide that the war belongs to someone else.
But pulling apart is also easier to fix than giving up. It is a political problem, and political problems have political remedies: a government that earns trust across party lines, a defense burden that everyone shares, and allies whose signals don’t waver. The fate of 23 million people depends on whether Taiwan’s leaders can rebuild a defense contract that citizens across the political spectrum believe in.
No one can save a small democracy that cannot stand together, however many polls say it is willing to fight.

In parcels from the United States, customs officers discovered Apple devices worth approximately UAH 1 million
Kyiv • UNN
Customs officers discovered 35 undeclared Apple devices in parcels from the United States. Their total value is approximately UAH 1 million.
At a customs post in Lviv, customs officers discovered undeclared goods worth approximately one million hryvnias in international parcels. The State Customs Service of Ukraine reports this, according to UNN.
Details
On September 24, 2026, at the Lviv-Postal customs post, customs officers discovered 35 Apple devices in international postal shipments from the United States addressed to Ukrainian citizens that had not been listed in the customs declarations. The violation was uncovered through an analysis of preliminary information on international postal shipments conducted by employees of the Coordination and Monitoring Customs Office
During the customs inspection, it was established that the information stated in the declarations did not correspond to the actual contents of the parcels.
The discovered equipment included 17 iPad tablets, 9 iPad Airs, 1 iPad mini, 2 iPad Pros, 5 MacBook Pro laptops and 1 MacBook Air. The total value of the equipment is approximately UAH 1 million. These actions show signs of a violation of customs rules предусмотреного by Part 1 of Article 473 of the Customs Code of Ukraine
Employees of the Coordination and Monitoring Customs Office are currently taking measures to document the violations that were discovered.

Kyiv customs officers seized rare bronze artifacts dating from the time of Kyivan Rus from a parcel. The items in question are seven pieces of bladed weapons and their decoration dating from the 2nd–12th centuries AD.

ORIGIN and Anduril sign memorandum on counter-drone air defence solutions for NATO’s eastern flank during LIAA trade mission to the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:58:07 UTC
23:58:07 KST

US defence technology company Anduril, which develops autonomous systems and command-and-control software, and defence technology company ORIGIN, which develops autonomous unmanned aircraft systems, have agreed to assess the integration of their technologies to strengthen deterrence on NATO’s eastern flank. Under the memorandum of understanding, the companies will explore integrating Anduril’s Lattice software platform with ORIGIN’s autonomous BLAZE interceptor drone as part of a layered counter-drone air defence solution for Latvia. The memorandum was signed during the Latvian business trade mission organised by LIAA as part of President Edgars Rinkēvičs’ official visit to the United States.
Lattice is Anduril’s software platform, which brings data from different sensors and unmanned systems into a single environment. It gives operators a real-time view of the battlefield and enables them to assign tasks to connected sensors, vehicles and other assets. Under the memorandum, ORIGIN and Anduril will assess how BLAZE, together with deployed radars and other sensors, could be integrated into this environment. They will also develop a concept of operations for counter-drone missions.
The companies have agreed to conduct joint technology testing, demonstrations and validation in Latvia. They will develop a concept of operations, enable data exchange and assess the solution’s effectiveness in different counter-drone scenarios. This cooperation could allow interceptor drones to operate as part of broader defence infrastructure rather than as standalone systems. As threats become increasingly coordinated, integration within a common command-and-control environment is becoming essential to comprehensive air defence.
Mārtiņš Mārenis, Chief Commercial Officer at ORIGIN, said: “We want to work with industry leaders and innovators to develop counter-drone systems that make a real contribution to strengthening the defence capabilities of NATO Allies. Integrating BLAZE with Anduril’s Lattice platform would allow our interceptor drones to operate within a unified system, giving allied forces better situational awareness and a faster response to evolving drone threats. These are precisely the capabilities that modern air defence and countries on NATO’s eastern flank need to protect their airspace effectively.”
The memorandum was signed during the LIAA-organised Latvian business trade mission to the United States, which is taking place alongside the President of Latvia’s official visit. The mission runs until 27 September and covers New York, Los Angeles and San Diego. It brings together representatives of companies and organisations across four sectoral tracks, including defence and dual-use technologies.
“The memorandum of understanding between ORIGIN and Anduril is a significant outcome of this trade mission. ORIGIN came to the US with defence technology developed in Latvia and a concrete proposal for cooperation, while the signing of the memorandum demonstrates Anduril’s interest in developing that cooperation. Latvian companies aim to carry out joint projects with US partners, secure orders and attract investment. LIAA will continue to help advance this cooperation,” said Ieva Jāgere, Director of LIAA.

Cheetah cubs survive powerful storms, mother's illness at zoo
Unknown

Cheetah cubs survive powerful storms, mother's illness at Prague Zoo, but curator warns "it's still a long run"
Five cheetah cubs had to survive a weather scare and the illness of their mother after their birth at the Prague Zoo. But they are doing well now, the zoo said on Friday.
The zoo said the quintuplets — four males and one female — that were born on June 18 had faced a tough time from the start.
Their mother, Daenerys, opted to give birth in an outdoor enclosure with a period of strong storms hitting Prague soon after.
Despite her inexperience, Daenerys took "exemplary" good care of her first cubs under such weather conditions, the zoo said.
Daenerys protected the five from torrential rains, licking water from their fluffy fur to keep them dry, curator Pavel Brandl said.
"Thanks to the mother's attentiveness, all five cubs survived the heavy downpours," the zoo wrote in a statement. "Soaking and subsequent pneumonia — along with predation — are common causes of mortality in cheetah cubs in the wild. It appears, however, that the mother dried her young by licking water from their fluffy coats with a characteristic dorsal mantle."
To make things worse, Daenerys suffered from an intestinal infection in August.
But despite all odds, the five looked lively and healthy on Friday.
"At this moment, everything seems fine, but it's still a long run," Brandl said. He said it might take a year before it's clear they will survive the crucial period after their birth.
"The mother of the cubs continues to surprise us," Brandl said after the cubs were born. "She arrived from France several years ago in poor physical and mental condition, and at the time, I was convinced we would never see offspring from this female."
Scientists say every cub is critical to saving the species, which is threatened with extinction.
Cheetahs, the fastest land animals in the world, can reach maximum speeds of between 70 and 75 mph. It's estimated that fewer than 7,000 of them remain in the wild.
Since 2020, the number of cheetahs in European zoos has declined by 25%, according to the zoo.
"Every successfully reared cub is therefore both an achievement and a source of hope," the zoo said.
Last October, 11 cheetah cubs were rescued from illegal trade in Somaliland in what a conservationist described as "one of the largest confiscations of the species."

Grégoire is due to present the pope with a model of Notre-Dame, a few steps away from the building.
Paris crowd praises pope for standing up to Trump
Leo's past criticism of the US president has won him points with many Parisans opposed to Trump's policies, who came out in droves to celebrate the first official state visit by a pope in 18 years.
“He dared, at his level, to oppose the American president,” said retiree Thierry Marien, who lined up hours early to grab a spot on the popemobile route to Notre-Dame cathedral, where Leo was to celebrate vespers later Friday.
“Not because he is opposed to the American president but because he’s opposed to countries where we can see there’s a risk of their political systems becoming a bit more dictatorial and there are already enough of those in the world.”
“I appreciated that he did that. He could quite easily have said to himself, ‘In my situation, I won’t criticise any heads of state,'” he said.
Leo took further distance from the Trump administration policies by making a lengthy visit to UNESCO, from which the US has withdrawn as part of its retreat from many international organisations.
Replay: Watch the pope's full UNESCO address
In his speech at UNESCO headquarters, Leo scolded world leaders who disregarded the rule of law and warned that international dialogue risked becoming a "charade".
Click on the player below to watch the full speech.
The pope has arrived at Notre-Dame Cathedral
Leo is the first pontif to visit the iconic cathedral since it reopened to the public in 2024, after years of repair following a devastating fire.
He is due to celebrate Vespers and give a homily inside the towering Gothic structure.
'We are not really religious but we know that this is a huge event'
Martin and Gabriel, 20, live in the neighbourhood and came by to check out the celebrations “out of curiosity”.
“We are not really religious but we were baptised and we know that this is a huge event, so we wanted to experience it first hand.”
They say they didn't want to join the gathering of young people at the Stade de France “to prioritise those who are religious”.
To which Laure (in the red T-shirt) responds, “Oh no! I disagree with what you say! Jesus would have wanted each and every young person present”.

Dutch opposition party votes to join European Socialist family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:55:32 UTC
23:55:32 KST

Dutch GroenLinks party leader Jesse Klaver attends the launch of the name "Progressief Nederland" for an upcoming merger of GroenLinks and PvdA parties, at the Sugar Factory in Halfweg on March 26, 2026. | Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP via Getty Images
The largest opposition party in the Netherlands has chosen to join the European Socialists rather than the Greens in an internal vote, the results of which were announced Friday.
Some 65% of votes cast by members of Progressive Netherlands (PRO), which was formed earlier this year when the Dutch GreenLeft (GroenLinks) and Labour (PvdA) parties merged, backed joining the Party of European Socialists instead of the European Green Party.
Before voting began, an advisory committee to the party recommended joining the PES, arguing that membership would give the party greater influence at the European level.
Advertisement
“There are only three European political families represented at all three levels [of the EU],” the advisory committee wrote in a report, adding that the PES has “prime ministers, the President of the European Council, European Commissioners, and leaders of national parties.”
“The Greens … have fewer ministers, no members of the European Commission, and no heads of government; consequently, their preliminary consultations carry less weight,” the report went on.
PRO leader Jesse Klaver joined a PES meeting ahead of the European Council summit in June, alongside Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
What about the MEPs?
European political parties and political groups in the European Parliament are closely linked, but they are not the same thing.
A PRO spokesperson told POLITICO that the party’s eight MEPs are likely to remain in their current parliamentary groups: four in the Socialists and Democrats and four in the Greens/European Free Alliance.
The spokesperson said PRO would likely review the arrangement ahead of the next European Parliament election in 2029.
Advertisement
The choice of European party will, however, have implications for the allocation of EU funding.
Most EU cash for European political parties is distributed according to their share of MEPs. Under the rules, the PES could count all eight PRO MEPs toward its funding share, even if four remain in the Greens.
The Dutch party told POLITICO one option would be for the four MEPs from the former GroenLinks side to technically leave PRO, allowing them to be counted separately under the funding rules.

'Moldova is the best performer in my class': EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:54:29 UTC
23:54:29 KST

'Moldova is the best performer in my class': EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
The EU has gone through seven waves of enlargement since 1973, but there has not been one since Croatia joined in 2013. Indeed, there are not likely to be any new members in the club before 2028 – some 15 years after Croatia entered. But 2026 undeniably has momentum, and is on track to be a record year in terms of opening and closing new chapters for existing applicants. That is why our guest, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, sees this as "the year of the enlargement."
"Montenegro, which is really the frontrunner, could finish technical negotiations at the end of the year, and then become a member in 2028," Kos says. "Albania is well on the way. Moldova is delivering better and better and, of course, also Ukraine. So these are the four frontrunners. But when we say that this is the year of the enlargement, I mean that in the nine months of this year, we have opened and closed more chapters than in any previous year in the last 25 years."
But there's a distinction between the frontrunner and the best student. Kos says that Moldova "is the best performer in my class," taking into account that it started the process much later than applicant countries in the Balkans.
Speaking of the Balkans, Kos admits that there is uneven implementation of reforms, which could lead to €330 million in EU funding shifting away from the weakest performers.
"We will see how much money we will reallocate," Kos says. "Montenegro, for instance, has a 91 percent implementation rate of reforms to date. But then we also have Bosnia and Herzegovina with a zero (rate), because their politicians are not able to ratify two important agreements which would enable us to pay the money," Kos explains. "You know, our European Union is not a charity. So in order to be able to help their economies and societies to develop, they have to deliver the reforms, and we only give the money if they are doing this."
We turn to Serbia, which has been an EU candidate since 2012, but which has had a turbulent relationship with Brussels. According to Kos, "the trust between EU member states and Serbia was broken even more with the glorification of the war criminal Ratko Mladic at his funeral, which is really unacceptable. And that's also why I cancelled my planned mission to Serbia. We can have different opinions on how fast a country should make reforms. But there is no space for the glorification of a war criminal, or for denying the genocide in Srebrenica. We expect all the EU candidates, especially those from the Western Balkans, to walk the way of reconciliation. But sometimes I have the feeling that, instead of healing the wounds of the past, leaders are rubbing salt into those wounds."
Of course, enlargement is not only about the EU's closest neighbours. While Georgia's EU bid has stalled, Armenia is increasingly eyeing EU membership as an attractive option – even though it has not formally applied.
"We are helping Armenia, especially now when Russia stopped importing many Armenian products. So we are helping Armenia to redirect its exports to the European Union. We are also in the process of visa liberalisation. This means that Armenians would be able to travel to the EU without a visa. So now they have to align a lot of legislation, and they are doing great work. I'm full of admiration for the people of Armenia. It is not easy but, with the result of the last parliamentary elections, they have clearly shown that they want to be on the European path."

Everyone's Still Talking About Climate Change, Actually
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:54:15 UTC
23:54:15 KST

For a brief moment last year, it seemed like the anti-climate atmosphere created by the Trump Administration might kill New York Climate Week. Ahead of the September gathering, business executives and advocates waffled. Was the U.S. still the place to get together to talk about climate? Would going put a target on their back?
This year, it felt almost as though those questions disappeared. Leaders from the world’s biggest companies hopped between panels, engaging in serious discussions about AI-driven electricity demand, geopolitical disruptions to energy markets, and the state of energy and climate policy. Protesters hit the street—as well as disrupting a panel I moderated—to point out that things were moving too slowly. Even Trump Administration officials showed up at some sessions (though they may have framed their participation around the concurrent United Nations General Assembly not Climate Week).
Take a step back from the chaotic mix of roundtables and dinners, panels and meetings, and it’s clear that the climate agenda, broadly construed, has persisted. There’s no question that anticipated Democratic victories in the fast-approaching U.S. midterm elections have created a sense that much of the administration’s barking will remain just that. But there’s perhaps an even simpler explanation for the continued engagement: the implications of climate change and the related energy issues have only become more important for companies and the economy.
The energy-market disruption that has resulted from the war in Iran featured prominently this week. So did the political backlash to data centers, the related issues of higher power prices. And the role of new energy technologies in addressing the problem came up early and often in discussions. On top of this, the effects of climate change—storms, heat waves, and fires—have begun to extract real economic damage that even the most resilient firms can no longer ignore.
“People are now looking at the things that cause volatility, and they’re putting it together,” Sarah Kapnick, head of climate advisory at JPMorgan, told me on a Climate Week panel. “They’re putting geopolitics together with sustainability, climate, and AI.”
Still, the apparent vitality of New York Climate Week comes with caveats. I shared my sense that New York Climate Week has rebounded with a European climate leader, who pointed out that American participation may be strong but the presence of leaders from outside the U.S. has diminished somewhat, particularly from Europe. Simply put, many Europeans don’t want to travel here, instead putting their efforts into London Climate Action Week and other gatherings across the Atlantic.
The climate conversation has also survived in part by shedding some of its old vocabulary. Climate action, net zero, and emissions were mostly out. Energy security, competitiveness, and affordability were in. That may represent a retreat from the sweeping ambition of earlier Climate Weeks. But it also reflects a deeper reality: even when companies stop using the language of climate action, they cannot escape the problems rising emissions have created.
To most of those I discussed the topic with, it remains an open question whether that new framing is a good or bad thing. Emissions reduction paired with economic growth should be celebrated even if climate isn’t mentioned. At the same time, a conversation that avoids getting to the heart of the matter doesn’t feel all that sustainable. For the past several decades we’ve been holding a ticking time bomb, waiting for the effect of climate change to hit. Now, how society responds to the unfolding crisis—embracing adaptation, pushing back against the sources of emissions, or simply turning to populist backlash—may be the new climate time bomb.
