They say Dobropillia is encircled, but they are actually 10+ km away: ISW publishes map disproving Russia’s claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:10:37 UTC
23:10:37 KST

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) published a map in its analytical report on 24 September that contrasts the claimed Russian encirclement with the location of Russian forces as assessed by the experts. Based on the evidence observed by ISW, the nearest area where Russian forces are present is 10.2 kilometers from the southeastern outskirts of Dobropillia.
Russia has been spreading disinformation about its successes around Dobropillia as part of what ISW calls a cognitive warfare effort to portray Ukrainian defenses as on the verge of collapse. Russia's Defense Ministry published a map claiming the city was surrounded. ISW's own map challenges it. The Ukrainian military says the city remains under its control.
Russian Defense Ministry claims it is already destroying encircled Ukrainian troops in Dobropillia and moving further
Units of Russia's Center Grouping of Forces continue combat operations against encircled Ukrainian forces in the Dobropillia area of Donetsk Oblast while simultaneously advancing toward Oleksandrivka, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed. ISW analysts, meanwhile, said they have not observed evidence supporting Russia's claim that the city is encircled. They also noted that Ukrainian officials "directly refute" the claim.
ISW observed evidence that Russian infiltrators, small groups, were operating east and northeast of Dobropillia on 19 and 20 September. The institute did not assess that these infiltrators had consolidated their positions.
Ukrainian forces maintain positions south and northeast of Dobropillia, military observer Kostiantyn Mashovets said on 20 September, according to ISW.
Russian forces have not made major gains in the Dobropillia direction, the chief of staff of an artillery reconnaissance battalion said on 22 September, according to the institute. On the same day, a Russian milblogger described the "alleged Russian encirclement of Dobropillia" as potentially meaning not the direct presence of infantry, but only the establishment of fire control over Ukrainian logistics, including roads west of Dobropillia and toward Sviatohorivka, according to ISW.
ISW noted that Russia's pervasive military culture of lying—what Russian milbloggers themselves call "beautiful reports"—has degraded the Defense Ministry's own ability to understand the battlefield and enabled inflated claims like the Dobropillia encirclement.
Russia uses this disinformation as a "diversion"
In its statement, the Russian Defense Ministry itself described Dobropillia as a "strongly fortified settlement" whose seizure would threaten key Ukrainian supply lines running from Dnipropetrovsk Oblast toward the Fortress Belt—the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk-Druzhkivka urban agglomeration.
Russia has recently renewed its attempts to break through toward Dobropillia.
Third Army Corps Commander Andrii Biletskyi said that Russian forces sought to bypass the fortified cities through Dobropillia and link up with troops advancing from north of Lyman, rather than launch a direct assault. ISW noted on 16 September that the Vivaldi operation disrupted Russia's two-pronged plan. In its 24 September report, ISW said Russia's claims about Dobropillia were partly intended to divert attention from Ukraine's elimination of the Russian salient north of Lyman, which has likely forced Russia's command to rethink its wider encirclement plans.

Trump wants to ‘colonize’ Brazil – Lula campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:09:51 UTC
23:09:51 KST

Trump wants to ‘colonize’ Brazil – Lula campaign
US President Donald Trump wants to “colonize” Brazil and gain control of its natural resources by interfering in the country’s upcoming presidential election, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign has said.
Meta blocked the advertising account used by Lula’s campaign on Facebook just days before the first round of the presidential election on October 4 in which left-wing incumbent Lula is seeking a fourth term against his main rival, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. Recent polls have put the two candidates in a tight race, with a runoff scheduled for October 25 if neither wins more than half the vote.
In a minute-long television advertisement broadcast on Thursday, Lula’s campaign accused Trump of meddling in Brazil’s election in a bid to turn the country back into a colony and seize its natural resources. The video points to US-funded political advertising targeting Brazilian voters, alleged involvement by American tech companies, and an intelligence warning that the risk of US interference had reached a “critical level.”
“Flavio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate,” the narrator says. “And what Trump wants is to colonize Brazil, to take our wealth, steal our future and leave us behind.”
Trump fiercely backed Flavio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, during his trial over an alleged plot to overturn his 2022 election defeat and remain in power.
Risk of US interference in Brazil at ‘critical level’
The ad cited a confidential assessment by the Brazilian Intelligence Agency (ABIN), which was sent to the presidency, the country’s electoral court, and the Justice Ministry. The document warned of escalating US pressure on Brazil and raised the risk of external influence or interference in the election to a “critical level.”
“According to ABIN, the pressure from the United States must increase and Trump’s goal is to defeat Lula to control our natural resources,” the campaign ad says.
Lula echoed the accusation on X, stating that Bolsonaro wants to “hand our natural resources over to the United States.” “If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,” the president wrote.
The campaign video also suggested direct links between Bolsonaro’s campaign and US political interests. “And now we know that there’s American money in Flavio’s campaign,” the narrator says, pointing to Rockbridge Network, a secretive US donor network co-founded in 2019 by Vice President JD Vance and investor Chris Buskirk. Reuters has described the Silicon Valley-backed organization as financing right-wing media, polling and voter-turnout operations to spread Trump’s brand of nationalism, with wealthy investors including Peter Thiel and Rebekah Mercer among its reported backers.
Brazilian media reported that Pedro Sang, described as a Rockbridge organizer in Brazil, helped set up Bolsonaro’s campaign headquarters in Sao Paulo and took on a leadership role there. Lula’s Workers’ Party asked the Brazil’s Supreme Court to investigate possible foreign financing, which is prohibited under Brazilian election law. Sang denied that Rockbridge provided funding to political campaigns in Brazil.
Meta blocks Lula campaign ads
Meta has meanwhile disabled the advertising account used by Lula’s campaign on Facebook, preventing it from running new ads just days before the election. The campaign said the US tech giant gave no explanation for the move and demanded that access be restored, threatening legal action and describing the restriction as another example of alleged Big Tech interference in the vote.
“The evidence of interference is all there, it keeps happening and we have already denounced it publicly,” Workers’ Party communications chief Eden Valadares said. Meta has not publicly explained why the account was disabled.
The move follows a study published last week that found Meta approved 13 of 15 test political ads paid for through a US-based account and targeting Brazilian voters, including an AI-generated video depicting Trump urging Brazilians to vote for Bolsonaro. The researchers did not actually publish the ads, while Meta said the experiment did not reflect the scale of its efforts to protect the Brazilian election.
US hits Brazil with tariffs over Big Tech
Washington has ramped up economic and diplomatic pressure on Brazil ahead of the vote, imposing 25% tariffs on Brazilian imports in a dispute that observers say centers on Big Tech regulation rather than trade imbalances. The US Trade Representative cited Brazil’s treatment of American tech companies and court orders forcing platforms to remove political content, among other policies, to justify the tariffs.
Washington also revoked the Brazilian ambassador’s visa in August as tensions escalated during the election campaign. Lula’s government called the move politically motivated interference.
Lula has cast the pressure as a threat to Brazilian sovereignty. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people,” he told the UN General Assembly this week. “Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians.”
Venezuela raid fuels fears of US intervention
The alarm has spread beyond Lula’s camp. Right-wing presidential candidate Renan Santos has also accused Trump of wanting Brazil as a “vassal state,” to secure favorable rare-earth contracts and said Brazil should not become a vassal of the US or China.
Santos pointed to the US military operation in Venezuela in January, when American forces captured President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores and brought them to the US to face drug and weapons charges. Lula condemned the raid as the first direct US military attack on South America in more than 200 years of independence, while Santos warned: “I don’t want to see Latin America become an American protectorate.”
The State Department last month shrugged off claims that the White House was meddling in Brazil’s election, declaring that “any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie.”

Deep mining for memories: Greece opens digital archive to preserve Serifos ironworks history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:07:57 UTC
23:07:57 KST

"The Living History of the Serifos Mines", a project by the Friends of Serifos funded by Cycladic Identity, has created a digital archive of Greek mineworkers' history and memories.
Serifos is one of the most beautiful islands in the Cyclades. Behind its major tourism development lies a history that most people know nothing about. The island was an important mining centre as far back as antiquity. Its subsoil is rich mainly in haematite and magnetite, with the result that to this day half of Serifos is perforated with galleries and shafts after many years of mining.
In the south-west, mainly at Mega Livadi and Koutalas, visitors can still see rusted rails, machinery, tools, wagons and loading piers. These are the visible traces of the intensive mining activity that shaped the island until the mid-20th century.
In more recent times, iron ore extraction began in 1870 and became more systematic from 1885 onwards. Annual production often reached 200,000 tonnes. Mining was not only a livelihood for locals; many others arrived from different parts of Greece to work on the island.
In 1963, the mines closed for good, forcing most workers to migrate and change profession. The mining sites were abandoned. Their story, however, remains deeply etched in the soul and identity of the islanders.
To highlight and preserve these memories, the Friends of Serifos Association launched the project "The living history of the mines of Serifos", with the support of the Cycladic Identity initiative of the Museum of Cycladic Art. The research, interviews and documentation of material lasted a year. The result is a journey into the past, a moving exploration of residents' memories and the history of the mines, captured in a printed and a digital album.
Digital underground
The digital archive (source in Greek)contains more than 250 photographs, rare documents, press clippings from the period and 10 first-hand testimonies by miners and their descendants who are still alive. This was deemed necessary because for decades the history of the Serifos mines survived mainly through the oral accounts of those who had lived and worked there.
As generations pass, these testimonies had to be recorded before they disappeared forever. At the same time, information panels with QR codes were installed at the mining sites, allowing visitors to read the miners' interviews on the spot.
Earlier this month, the Friends of the Cultural Heritage and Environment of Serifos Association presented the project to local residents, organised a round-table discussion with miners and their descendants, and held a guided tour of the mining sites at Mega Livadi, led by Thodoris G. Livanios.
Katerina Papathoma, Vice-President of the Friends of Serifos Association, was the Programme Manager. Although she is not originally from the island, she has been living here for years and has grown deeply attached to it.
_"_The aim of the Friends of Serifos Association is twofold. First, to save and preserve this living history of the mines of Serifos. This was done through recordings and live interviews given to us by the miners and their descendants on the island. The second aim is that we want to share this story. The fact is that even we who live here in Serifos do not really know this history," explained Papathoma.
"I realised this when all the material was brought together and I saw that many aspects of this place's history are completely unknown. So first we ourselves have to learn, to answer questions we may have and to understand what happened with the mines.
"The second reason is to have a structured body of information so we can pass it on to young people. It is the young who will very soon be called on to deal with Serifos's issues. They need to know these places in order to become attached to them and, if possible, to protect them."
Miners' strife
Serifos was the largest mining centre in Greece after Lavrio. The mines at Mega Livadi are a listed historic site. This was where the bloody miners' strike of 1916 took place. They demanded the introduction of the eight-hour working day and more dignified working conditions from their employers, the German company Grohmann.
The uprising was universal. It was driven by starvation wages, punishing working hours, appalling living conditions and the total lack of safety measures, which often led to deaths and crippling injuries.
The strike ended in bloodshed, during which four strikers lost their lives (Th. Kouzoupis, M. Zoilis, M. Mitrofanis, I. Protopappas) and two members of the gendarmerie were also killed (Ch. Chrysanthou and I. Triantafyllou). Konstantinos Speras (1893–1943) was the leading figure in the strike. Born in Serifos, he became a key figure in Greece's workers' and trade union movement.
The Municipality of Serifos has for several years been trying to turn the area at Mega Livadi into an open-air mining museum that will showcase the history of the mines, the area's unique identity and offer a different kind of development for this abandoned region.
Konstantinos Revintis**,** The mayor of Serifos, spoke to Euronews at the site of the strike: "We are standing in the historic place where the miners' strike for the first eight-hour working day and for better working conditions took place, on 21 August 1916. It is a historic site that we want to highlight by creating here an open-air mining museum that will tell the story without a voice, simply through traces.
"Everything that still exists here must be restored. We have formed several partnerships with various bodies of recognised standing that have the necessary technical and management expertise, such as the National Technical University of Athens, the University of the Aegean, the Hellenic Society for the Environment and Cultural Heritage, Europa Nostra, the World Monuments Fund, the World Monuments Watch and other organisations. The Mega Livadi Association is a local body that shows particular sensitivity on this issue.
"And of course, we as the Municipality are playing the leading role. If the Ministry of Culture can support us, that would be ideal, as well as the Ministry of Finance, because we are in a coastal zone here," said Revintis. "Our aim is to complete this project and return the site to public use so that people can visit it and so it can become an attraction, both for permanent residents and for visitors."
The project "The living history of the mines of Serifos" was funded by Cycladic Identity, an important initiative run by the Museum of Cycladic Art since 2022.
Its goal is to safeguard the intangible cultural heritage that has shaped the island's history over the centuries. To date, the museum has supported 26 projects in total on 15 Cycladic islands and will soon announce ten more for 2027:
"The Cycladic Identity initiative is essentially our concrete way of saying thank you to the islands. In practice, we support organisations active on the Cycladic islands in the fields of culture, biodiversity and intangible cultural heritage," explained Theano Agalloglou, Project Manager of the Cycladic Identity initiative at the Museum of Cycladic Art.
"We want to engage as many residents as possible. We want them to feel proud of their unique cultural and natural heritage, but also to raise their awareness. We believe it is extremely important that the oral testimonies of the miners, or 'Metalliotes' as they were called on the island, are documented, digitised and preserved as a legacy for the new generation," added Agalloglou.
The project and the album were presented at the Theatre of the Serifos Association in Chora. There, former miners and descendants of mining families shared their stories and memories with the audience.
The testimony of Andreas Livanios (Katsafouris)
_"_I went to work in the mines around 1956–57. I was still a child. I went because at that time everyone, the whole of Serifos, worked in the mines. The mine meant great hardship, because those from Mega Livadi and Koutalas lived nearby. I am from Kallitsos, in the north. To leave home and reach Mega Livadi, it took us three hours on foot. We had to get up at 2 in the morning, get ready and leave at about twenty to three so that we would be at the worksite at ten to six or a quarter to six. If we arrived at one minute past six, we were sent to the office and lost the day's pay.
"It was exhausting because it was night and there was no road. We walked without light, in the cold and rain, along a path through the fields. I worked on compressors that pumped air. I went in the morning because these compressors ran on dynamite. I would put a small stick of dynamite inside, tap the detonator with a hammer and the machine would start up.
"What was left from the mines was only damage and hardship. They have eaten away all the guts of Serifos. There are galleries in the mountains where, if you go in, you get lost. Even now, when I think about it, I can hardly breathe. All the wealth left this place. Nothing was left for the island, which could have become a little Paris if the resources had been used properly."
The testimony of Alexandros Livanios
"On both my mother's and my father's side, they were miners. My mother's father survived, although he was very seriously injured. He spent a couple of years in hospital but pulled through. He survived and even kept all his limbs, but for two years he had lost his mind. My other grandfather on my father's side, Alexandros Klaos, was killed. His body is still inside a mine at Aspros Kavos. My father never met his own father. My grandmother was pregnant with him when her husband was killed. There is no mining family in Serifos that does not have either someone injured or someone dead.
"The mines were both a blessing and a curse for the island. They kept people here, because mining was the main occupation and farming was a sideline. These people worked from night to night in the mines. Only Sundays were left for them to go and work their fields. Usually it was the woman who replaced the man because he was tied up with work. If you think that he had to leave from Chora and walk two hours to Mega Livadi, he had to get up in the middle of the night and return again at night.
"The school at Mega Livadi had 150 children when I was a pupil there. Gradually it was deserted and became a necropolis. In winter there are almost no residents at all. After the mines closed, there was both internal and external migration. I went to sea. I started out as a lathe operator and then went into the maritime sector because the pay was better, much better."
The testimony of Thodoris G. Livanios
"I am an amateur researcher and folklorist. I have recorded dozens of people who worked in the mines and are unfortunately no longer with us, including people who experienced the 1916 strike. These are unique testimonies that I keep in my archive.
"We are children of miners, children of workers. We are descendants of the victims, not of the German exploiters. I have countless memories, because I experienced a lot in the mines both as a child and later through recording powerful testimonies that, unfortunately, have not yet been fully used. I have made several documentaries, television and radio programmes, and I have documented the popular culture of Serifos.
"Serifos is an empty shell. It was exploited by the Grohmanns and the successive employers who extracted the ore, drank the workers' sweat, drank the workers' blood and, in the end, left them unpaid."

Why Canada is not ruling out a possible war with the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:05:41 UTC
23:05:41 KST

Why is Canada’s PM Carney not ruling out a possible war with the US
Trump’s annexation threats have prompted Carney to examine even remote risks to Canada’s sovereignty.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he has examined the possibility of a US military attack against Canada, according to The New York Times.
In an interview with the newspaper on Wednesday, Carney described an attack as an “extreme tail risk” – an event with a very low probability but potentially severe consequences.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Rising malnutrition in Nigeria as US war on Iran raises food costs
- list 2 of 4Pakistan, Turkiye edge closer towards joining Saudi war against Houthis
- list 3 of 4Humanitarian crisis worsens in Ceuta as thousands remain stranded
- list 4 of 4Fighting in northern Ethiopia spurs fears of blackout and blockade
“That’s just risk management,” said Carney, the former head of the Bank of England. “It would be irresponsible not to.”
Experts say his comments do not indicate that a war is likely or that Canada is preparing to fight one, but they do show that Carney considers it a remote possibility. Here is what that might mean.
Why are relations between Canada and the US strained?
The main bones of contention are the ongoing trade war and Trump’s jibes about Canada becoming a US state.
Trade war
Shortly after Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he imposed a 25 percent tariff on goods imported from both Canada and Mexico, saying they would not be lifted until both countries took steps to curb the flow of fentanyl, a highly addictive and lethal drug, into the US. The leaders of Mexico and Canada struck a deal pausing the impending tariffs for 30 days, but they were reimposed on Canada in early March after Trump declared that it had failed to do enough.
In July 2025, he threatened to raise that to 35 percent unless Canada backed down on a digital services tax, which it agreed to do.
Canada, the biggest foreign supplier of steel and aluminium to the US, was also badly hit by Trump’s separate 25 percent tariffs on steel and aluminium, which he imposed globally in March 2025.
Since last year, trade talks have continued but ultimately collapsed in August, and both sides have since imposed new, tit-for-tat tariffs. Trump levied 50 percent taxes on $20bn of Canadian goods, and Canada matched them for US goods.
The problem for Canada is that its economy is closely tied to that of the US, making a trade war particularly consequential. Some 72 percent of Canada’s $556bn goods exports went to the US in 2025.
Security threat
Trump has made much of this dependence. “I think Canada would be much better off being a 51st state,” the US president said in 2025.
When trade talks fell apart this year, Trump responded to Carney’s announcement by writing on his platform Truth Social: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!”
Trump also took the provocative step of renaming Lake Ontario – which sits along the border of Canada and the US – “Lake America”.
Carney is, therefore, seeking to reduce that dependence. His government is also reviewing its planned purchase of American F-35 fighter jets, while Carney said that Canada also intends to rely less on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service.
This month, he has visited the European Union and the United Kingdom in a bid to expand alliances. The EU has offered associate membership to Canada, while Canada has applied to join the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a European military coalition.
Ty Solomon, a professor of international relations at the University of Glasgow, told Al Jazeera there were “at least two issues at play” when it came to tensions with the US. The first was “the hostility that President Trump has shown towards Canada”, reflected in his threats to annex it as the “51st state”, and the tariffs both countries have imposed.
The second, Solomon said, was a changing security landscape that included US threats last year to annex Greenland, as well as “ongoing Russian and Chinese interest and activity in the Arctic”. In this “multifaceted geopolitical environment”, he said, “unexpected events in one area could trigger further unexpected dynamics in these other areas”.
Therefore, while US military action is a “vanishingly small possibility”, Eric Taylor Woods, an associate professor of political communication at the University of Leeds, told Al Jazeera that Canadians are nevertheless unsettled by Trump’s comments and want to know their prime minister is defending the country’s sovereignty.
Carney set out this new geopolitical reality at the World Economic Forum in January, when he urged countries such as Canada to work together as great powers use their influence more aggressively.
“If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu,” he said.
What would happen in a military conflict between the US and Canada?
Experts consider a US attack on Canada highly unlikely – Solomon said a US attack on Canada remained “somewhat unthinkable”.
But, Woods said, if there was one, “I would not expect Canadians simply to accept the loss of their sovereignty”, despite the “enormous disparity in military capabilities”.
“The US has a vastly larger and more powerful military than Canada,” Solomon said. “On paper, then, there would appear to be no contest.”
But, he said, the prolonged US war against Iran had cast doubt on assumptions about “overwhelming US military force and effectiveness”.
Furthermore, Solomon said, if it did happen, it would be “an unmitigated disaster for American global interests”.
“What remaining trust there is of the US would evaporate completely, and it would greatly accelerate other democracies’ efforts to forge new alliances outside of the American security and alliance system,” he added.
What happens next?
The unease between the two is likely to continue.
Carney has said he is still prepared to reach a trading deal with Trump. He told The New York Times that they had spoken “frequently” since trade talks collapsed. “We can pick up the phone and talk to each other about issues,” he said. “He’s direct. I’m direct.”
Woods noted, also, that Trump had so far avoided the “schoolyard personal insults and name-calling” he often directed at Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau.
Solomon said that “privately, I suspect that Carney and his advisers do not trust the Trump administration much at all: Trump is well known to change his mind – and American foreign policy – very quickly and seemingly on a whim”.
“As a leader, it is very difficult to trust this sort of behaviour because every agreement is built upon uncertain foundations.”

Pope Leo XIV criticizes AI, assisted dying on France arrival

Pope Leo XIV criticizes AI, assisted dying on France arrival
September 25, 2026
Pope Leo XIV arrived for a four-day visit to France on Friday, the first official papal visit to the strictly secular country in 18 years.
Leo, the spiritual leader of the some 1.4 billion Catholics worldwide, was greeted at Paris' Orly Airport by French President Emmanuel Macron and will be in the country until Monday.
What did Pope Leo say alongside Macron at the Elysee Palace?
In remarks delivered at the Elysee Palace, Leo on Friday underscored opposition to assisted dying initiatives just two months after France created a legal right to die for those with incurable illnesses.
Though he did not specifically mention France's new law, the pontiff criticized what he called "profit-driven ventures" such as surrogacy and assisted dying.
"I firmly reiterate that the protection of the right to life constitutes the indispensable foundation of every other human right," the pope said in an address to Macron and other French politicians.
"I am concerned at times by those trends in society that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one's own death," he said.
Pope Leo also delivered an urgent warning regarding the development of artificial intelligence.
"If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment," he said.
What else in on the pope's itinerary in France?
The papal itinerary has Leo meeting Macron at the Elysee Palace, speaking at UNESCO headquarters, leading Vespers at Notre Dame Cathedral and celebrating Mass for an estimated 80,000 young people at the Stade de France national stadium on Friday.
On Saturday, he is scheduled to celebrate Mass for another 600,000 at Place de la Concorde on the Avenue des Champs-Elysees before departing for Lourdes, a famous Catholic pilgrimage site located near France's Spanish border.
On Monday, Leo will travel to Metz, near the German border, where he will deliver a speech entitled: "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity." Macron will introduce Leo at the event and has invited fellow leaders across the EU to join him in attendance.
Pope speaks of press freedom, peace on flight amid White House exclusion furor
While traveling to France, US-born Leo was asked by a CNN reporter for his thoughts on US President Donald Trump's attempts to ban news outlets from covering him.
"I am very happy that here, you are all welcome," he told reporters.
Leo, who was forced to fly home alone after plane trouble on a recent trip to Spain, took the opportunity to apologize to his press pool.
Speaking to reporters at the back of his plane on Friday, Leo said, "I want to apologize personally for an incident, that I had nothing to do with, but which I know left a number of you unhappy with the fact that we couldn't have the flight back together back to Rome."
He further told reporters he was coming to France as "a pilgrim for peace" in a time of war.
Leo, a tireless critic of the wars in Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere, said "It is a message which at this time, as we all may know, is particularly important."
AI, Church sexual abuse also on the agenda
Leo had already tipped his hat on his plans to address global concerns regarding so-called artificial intelligence (AI) and the "new dangers" it presents to "security and international peace" during his discussions with Macron.
Speaking at the Vatican prior to departure on Thursday, Leo had said leaders must "govern wisely" when dealing with the new technology, which he says raises questions about the very essence of what it means to be human.
Leo has taken a keen interest in AI, writing his first papal encyclical — published this May and entitled "Magnificent Humanity" — on the issue.
The pope is also seeking to repair the Catholic Church's standing in France, where opinions grew particularly bleak in 2021 following the publication of a report documenting seven decades of abuse — impacting 330,000 French children — by clergy and lay leaders.
Leo will meet victims of church abuse during the trip.

WTO grants Russian request for CBAM dispute panel — official

GENEVA, September 25. /TASS/. The Dispute Settlement Body of the World Trade Organization (WTO) granted Russia's repeated request to establish a panel to examine its dispute with the European Union over the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), Russia’s Permanent Representative to the WTO Nikolay Platonov told TASS.
"We voiced our request to establish a panel to consider this dispute today at the meeting of the WTO Dispute Settlement Body, and it was satisfied," Platonov said. This was a repeated request; the first one had been blocked in July of this year, he noted.
In May 2026, the Russian Ministry of Economic Development announced Russia’s intention to challenge the CBAM at the WTO. According to the Russian side, this mechanism, which introduces in particular additional charges on certain goods imported into the EU from third countries, significantly restricts access to the community's market. Brussels through the CBAM is not fighting climate change "but the problem of European production shifting to third countries." the ministry said.
Over recent years, Russia consistently drew the attention of all members, including the EU, to the CBAM’s non-compliance with the WTO’s core rules in different working bodies of the organization. Russia's position has been shared by many other WTO members.

Hundreds on hunger strike in Lebanon prison as amnesty stalled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:00:48 UTC
23:00:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Hundreds on hunger strike in Lebanon prison as amnesty stalled
Hundreds of inmates in a Lebanese prison have been on hunger strike for 10 days over the stalled implementation of an amnesty law supposed to benefit them, a judicial official told AFP on Tuesday.
Lebanon's parliament last month passed the sweeping amnesty law, the first since 1991 after the country's civil war. The legislation is meant to help thousands of prisoners and wanted people, many of them Islamists.
But a group of lawmakers has since lodged an appeal with Lebanon's Constitutional Council seeking to overturn the law, leading to a suspension of its implementation on September 10.
At the overcrowded Roumieh prison near the capital Beirut, the country's largest jail, "400 mostly Islamist detainees have been on hunger strike since September 12" in protest at the suspension, the official said, requesting anonymity.
The Constitutional Council, which verifies whether laws are in line with the Lebanese constitution, is expected to announce its decision next month.
According to the official, prison administrators are monitoring the health of the striking prisoners, 80 of whom suffer from chronic illness.
For years, Lebanon's parliament had been trying to pass the amnesty law, largely as a way to reduce overcrowding in prisons, which has been exacerbated by slow-moving trials and the detention of suspects for years without judicial proceedings.
In a report last year, the country's National Human Rights Commission said the prison population had reached 300 percent of capacity, with more than 6,200 inmates by the end of March.
Some Islamist detainees have been held for years, in some cases without trial.
The prospect of granting amnesty to some of these detainees, accused of carrying out bombings and attacks against the Lebanese army, polarised the debate around the law before it was passed.
The legislation, which experts say was the result of political horse-trading, is supposed to also benefit other factions and religious communities.

The Trump-Xi summit exposes a US disadvantage in the Global South
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:00:26 UTC
23:00:26 KST

The Trump-Xi summit exposes a US disadvantage in the Global South
Washington asks for alignment while Beijing offers strategic flexibility without military entanglement.
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States came with all the choreography: a B-2 flyover, pandas, a Nixon-era toast. But for anyone watching from the Global South, the spectacle was beside the point. More important was Beijing’s emphasis on “constructive strategic stability” in its relationship with Washington. For capitals from Riyadh to New Delhi to Jakarta, the summit offered a glimpse of how they may navigate relations with the two powers over the rest of this decade.
Beijing emerged from the summit offering diplomatic cover without military entanglement. Washington, by contrast, came to the meeting already embroiled in the nearly seven-month US-Israeli war on Iran, pressing allies on trade, reasserting US dominance in Latin America, and demanding that the Global South choose sides in its effort to contain China, all while Trump himself toasted Xi and hailed the summit as a success. For governments across the Global South being urged to distance themselves from Beijing, that contrast will not go unnoticed.
The Middle East: China’s advantage
Nowhere is this clearer than in the Gulf. Trump wants China, Tehran’s largest trading partner, to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz, choked since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February. Xi backed a return to a ceasefire and eventual peace talks, but the Chinese readout offered no specifics on reopening the strait and no commitment to pressure Iran. Beijing appears determined to preserve its room for manoeuvre.
For Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Doha, that has obvious advantages. China can call Tehran, issue a UN statement, or offer to mediate, all without deploying a single soldier or demanding a military base. Meanwhile, Washington is a direct party to the war, and its credibility as a security guarantor is eroded by the very crisis it helped create. Gulf capitals are already calibrating: stay under the US umbrella for hardware, but hedge through Beijing for diplomatic crisis management and energy-market stability. China’s usefulness, in other words, lies partly in the fact that it is not fighting the wars Washington is.
That calculation extends across the wider region. For Iraq, Egypt and Algeria, all watching energy prices spike and shipping lanes choke, China’s restraint has its appeal. The Global South does not need another great power to join the war; it needs someone who can talk to all sides without shooting. Beijing is positioning itself to play that role.
Navigating Trump’s unpredictability
For governments elsewhere across the Global South, this creates a difficult set of choices. They are pressed to distance themselves from China, even as Trump himself re-engages. They are asked to absorb tariffs and supply-chain shocks, while Washington and Beijing extend their own trade truce for another two months. The result is a growing sense that other countries are expected to bear the costs of great-power rivalry while Washington and Beijing retain the freedom to negotiate with each other.
The response is already visible. India deepens its multipolar balancing, buying Russian oil while courting US tech and Chinese investment. Indonesia continues its “free and active” foreign policy, signing defence deals with both Washington and Beijing. South Africa and Brazil use BRICS platforms to hedge, not as anti-Western gestures but as insurance against a system where others write the rules. The summit did not cause this hedging, but it is likely to reinforce it.
AI and who writes the rules
Artificial intelligence raises a different problem for the Global South: who gets to set the rules. Xi’s emphasis on “human control” and Trump’s resistance to new AI guardrails represent two competing visions, but neither was designed with the interests of countries across the Global South at its centre. The two sides have agreed to continue a new AI dialogue and are discussing an incident-notification mechanism, but no binding rules exist. Many countries will remain dependent on AI systems, infrastructure and standards developed elsewhere, with little say over the norms that govern them. China’s state-led model may look more attractive than America’s corporate-led alternative, but it is still another form of dependence.
Yet the Global South is not entirely passive. India is building indigenous large language models and exporting its digital-public-infrastructure playbook; the United Arab Emirates has positioned itself as a major AI hub; the African Union is pushing data-sovereignty frameworks aimed at giving African states greater control over their data and digital infrastructure. These efforts are nascent but show a determination to avoid a simple choice between US and Chinese models. Beijing has tried to institutionalise its vision, launching a Global AI Governance Initiative and helping establish the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, whose founding agreement was signed by 29 countries in Shanghai in July. For some, this offers an alternative to Western frameworks; for others, it swaps one dependency for another. The question is whether countries across the Global South can coordinate strongly enough to shape the rules themselves.
Beyond the ceremony, the broader message from the summit is already clear. Washington secured the photographs and a temporary tariff truce; Beijing secured something more strategic: recognition of the terms on which it wants the relationship managed. For governments across the Global South, the meeting reinforced an approach many are already pursuing: avoid choosing sides where possible, maintain ties with both powers and use the competition between them to preserve room for manoeuvre.
Great-power rivalry, on Beijing’s terms, is not peace. But for capitals from Riyadh to Jakarta, the space between Washington and Beijing can also create opportunities to build leverage and pursue their own interests. The challenge is to ensure that future deals between the two powers do not leave everyone else simply absorbing the consequences.

Scientists strip down the LSD molecule to find the exact parts that trigger hallucinations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:00:17 UTC
23:00:17 KST

A recent study has successfully stripped down the complex chemical structure of LSD to pinpoint exactly which parts of the molecule cause hallucinations and which parts might be harnessed for therapy. By testing these simplified molecules, scientists identified a specific structural combination that produces antipsychotic effects in mice without triggering a hallucinogenic trip. The research was published in PNAS.
Lysergic acid diethylamide, commonly known as LSD, is a powerful psychedelic drug that alters perception, mood, and cognitive processes. It exerts its effects primarily by interacting with specific proteins on the surface of brain cells called serotonin receptors. One of these, the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor, is widely recognized as the main trigger for hallucinogenic experiences. It is also responsible for promoting neuroplasticity, which is the brain’s ability to grow and rewire itself.
Classic psychedelics tend to activate a broad array of targets in the brain and body. This wide-ranging activity was detailed in a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, which demonstrated that these compounds engage many different signaling pathways. Activating some of these pathways can lead to unwanted physical side effects. For instance, a 2011 review noted that when drugs stimulate a receptor known as 5-HT2B, it can lead to a dangerous thickening of the heart valves.
To develop safe psychiatric treatments from psychedelics, scientists aim to modify these molecules so they no longer activate the 5-HT2B receptor or cause hallucinations. To measure hallucinogenic potential in the lab, researchers observe mouse behavior. Specifically, a 2020 study demonstrated that the intensity of a rapid side-to-side head movement in mice, known as a head-twitch response, closely matches the potency of hallucinogenic effects in humans.
LSD has a highly complex, four-ring chemical skeleton known as an ergoline core. Because of this complexity, modifying its structure to isolate its therapeutic benefits has been historically challenging. A research team that included lead author Andrian G. Basargin and senior author David E. Olson sought to systematically deconstruct LSD.
“The synthesis of ergolines like LSD is quite challenging,” Olson, director of the Institute for Psychedelics and Neurotherapeutics at the University of California, Davis, told PsyPost. “By creating simpler analogues, we were able to determine which structural features of LSD were responsible for which pharmacological properties.”
By removing different rings from LSD’s four-ring core, the researchers aimed to identify the absolute minimum structural requirements needed to trigger hallucinogenic effects, and to discover simpler, safer variations of the molecule that might treat mental health conditions. “This information is critical for medicinal chemists to develop optimized medicines,” added Olson, a professor of chemistry and biochemistry who leads the Olson Lab.
The researchers used a process called function-oriented synthesis to create nine simplified versions of LSD. These new compounds were stripped down to possess only three, two, or one of the original four chemical rings found in LSD. To evaluate how these structural changes altered the drugs’ effects, the team first tested the compounds on lab-grown cells engineered to express different human serotonin receptors. They measured how tightly each compound bound to the receptors and how strongly it activated them.
Next, they tested the compounds in mice. They administered varying doses of each compound to groups of three to four female mice and used an automated magnetic system to track their head-twitch responses. In separate tests, they also placed the mice in an open-field arena and administered a dose of amphetamine, a stimulant that increases dopamine release and causes hyperactivity, to see if the new compounds could calm the animals.
The team found that the complete four-ring structure of LSD is necessary for the drug to maximally activate the 5-HT2A receptor. Every simplified molecule they tested had a weaker ability to bind to and activate this receptor compared to the original LSD molecule. By stripping the molecule down, the scientists pinpointed the exact structural components responsible for a psychedelic trip. They found that a two-ring combination corresponding to the “A” and “D” rings of the original LSD molecule was the bare minimum required to induce the characteristic head-twitch response in mice.
“If you delete certain structural elements of LSD, you can still produce psychedelic effects,” Olson explained. “This is analogous to determining that you can remove the roof of a car, windshield, doors, etc. and it can still drive.”
Removing a specific part of the molecule called the “D” ring resulted in a three-ring compound named UCD0094. This modified version showed a drastically reduced ability to activate both the hallucinogenic 5-HT2A receptor and the heart-risk 5-HT2B receptor. However, it maintained a strong ability to activate the 5-HT2C receptor, a target that is associated with antipsychotic and anti-addictive properties. The authors suggest UCD0094 could be a strong candidate for developing drugs that promote brain plasticity without causing hallucinations.
An even simpler, two-ring compound called UCD0076 demonstrated unique promise. UCD0076 showed almost no ability to activate the hallucinogenic 5-HT2A receptor, but it strongly activated the 5-HT2C receptor. When tested in mice, UCD0076 did not induce head twitches. Instead, it behaved like an antipsychotic medication. At high doses of 31 milligrams per kilogram, pretreating the mice with UCD0076 prevented them from having head twitches when they were subsequently given a known hallucinogen.
In the open-field tests, UCD0076 successfully reduced amphetamine-induced hyperactivity in a dose-dependent manner. The findings indicate that by selectively targeting the 5-HT2C receptor, this simplified molecule can suppress behaviors linked to psychosis. These findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that slightly modifying LSD’s structure can eliminate its hallucinogenic effects while producing a therapeutic, antipsychotic-like compound capable of healing damaged brain circuits.
However, not all of the new molecules behaved in live animals exactly as they did in isolated cells. For instance, a synthesized compound named UCD0179 appeared to be a potent activator of the 5-HT2A receptor in cell cultures, but it failed to trigger head twitches in mice.
“We were surprised that UCD0179 did not produce hallucinogenic effects in vivo given its in vitro profile,” Olson said. “This really speaks to the importance of a drug reaching its target in sufficiently high concentrations.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. First, the majority of the new compounds were tested as racemic mixtures, meaning they contained a blend of two mirror-image versions of the molecule. Because receptors in the brain often respond differently to exact structural shapes, testing isolated, pure versions of these molecules might yield slightly different results regarding their potency.
Additionally, the head-twitch response is a reliable indicator of hallucinogenic effects in rodents, but mice are not humans. It is always possible that a compound might affect human perception in ways that animal behavior cannot fully capture. The researchers also noted that LSD interacts with a wide variety of other targets, including dopamine and adrenergic receptors. Future studies will need to explore how these newly synthesized molecules interact with this broader array of brain targets to fully understand their safety and potential side effects.
“Our long-term goals are to use this information to develop better medicines for treating neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions,” Olson concluded.
The study, “Deconstruction of lysergic acid diethylamide,” was authored by Andrian G. Basargin, Andras Domokos, Joseph J. Hennessey, Isak K. Aarrestad, Rohini Sambyal, Yara A. Khatib, Johanna Krüger, Lee E. Dunlap, Samuel J. Carter, Isabella A. Rebek, John L. McKee, Serena S. Schalk, Min Liu, James C. Fettinger, Monica A. Gonzalez, Abhay Potluri, Dean J. Tantillo, Oliver Fiehn, John D. McCorvy, and David E. Olson.

Russell produced a lap of 1:42.526 around the Baku City Circuit to beat Ferrari's Charles Leclerc by 0.837 seconds, with McLaren's Oscar Piastri third, just 0.001 seconds further back.
Isack Hadjar took a notable fourth place on his return after missing three races with a wrist injury, outqualifying his Red Bull teammate Max Verstappen, who could manage only eighth.
Lando Norris was fifth for McLaren ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Alpine's Pierre Gasly, with Williams' Carlos Sainz and Alpine's Franco Colapinto completing the top 10.

McLaren had appeared to emerge as Russell's biggest threat after struggling for pace during practice, with Piastri and Norris occupying the top two positions with four minutes remaining. But neither was able to respond to Russell's final effort, while Leclerc jumped into second.
Russell's pole gives him an opportunity to reduce Antonelli's substantial championship lead in Saturday's race after the Italian's qualifying session ended almost as soon as it began.
Antonelli struck the inside wall at Turn 1 during Q1, damaging the front-left of his Mercedes. He initially attempted to drive slowly back to the pits before the team instructed him to stop the car.
His earlier lap was quick enough to carry him into Q2, but with the damaged car unable to take part, Antonelli was classified 16th.
Behind the top 10, Oliver Bearman, Liam Lawson, Alex Albon, Esteban Ocon and Arvid Lindblad were eliminated in Q2, along with the stricken Antonelli.
Gabriel Bortoleto, Nico Hulkenberg, Fernando Alonso, Sergio Perez, Valtteri Bottas and Lance Stroll were knocked out in Q1 and will occupy the final six places on the grid.
Sainz provided another notable result by taking Williams into Q3 for the first time this season. Both Williams cars had progressed from Q1 with a heavily revised car that has shed 28 kilograms since the start of the season.
Antonelli faces a recovery drive on Saturday, although Baku's long straights provide plenty of overtaking opportunities, while Safety Car periods and red flags have frequently shaken up races on the street circuit.
The championship leader has already demonstrated his ability to recover from the back of the grid this season, winning at Monza from 19th earlier this month.
Russell, meanwhile, will start from the ideal position to capitalize on Mercedes' strong pace and cut into his teammate's championship advantage. ■

I love a drink in the stands, but Burnham’s beer proposal feels out of step with modern football | Marva Kreel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:00:08 UTC
23:00:08 KST

Andy Burnham is right that football fans have historically been treated differently from other sports fans. But if we’re going to talk about discrimination in football, the ban on drinking at your seat feels like a strange place to start.
The rule may have its roots in a very different era of football, but for many fans today, being able to take a pint to your seat may not be top of their list of changes they’d like to see in the game. Especially at a time when discrimination is very much present elsewhere in football.
The legislation, introduced under Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s as part of a crackdown on football hooliganism, was rooted in the idea that football fans needed to be treated differently from the supposedly better-behaved crowds at rugby and cricket – which smacks of classism and the stereotyping of working-class fans. But football has changed since then, and so has drinking culture. Fans have adapted to the restrictions and built a matchday ritual around them. A good fan concourse pint is up there with an airport pint or a beer-garden pint on the first day of summer.
Fans have got used to this routine, and one of the biggest concerns of lifting this ban now seems to be the Boxpark-ification of football: the dreaded performative beer throw when anything good happens.
Even when it’s not performative, it does raise a problem of logistics. With no cup holders, when a 95th-minute winner goes in and you’re suddenly off your seat with your limbs in the air, a pint is unlikely to remain where you left it. There will be people walking back and forth from the concourse during the game for another pint or the toilet, too. It used to happen before, of course, but it would still be a new irritation that fans would have to adapt to. And, most importantly, it isn’t a change many fans seem to have been asking for.
As a fan of both men’s and women’s football, I’ve experienced the Women’s Super League’s successful trial of beer at your seats, as well as drinking at non-league games, and it was a nice change. It has even become a distinct part of the matchday experience in leagues where the atmosphere is different and the crowds are smaller. But the women’s game is not simply the men’s game with fewer people in the stands. The matchday experience is different – and that’s important when we talk about what works.
Watching Everton Women with a beer in hand can be lovely. So can spending a long day at the cricket with a pint. But I was also at the game in which Chloe Kelly scored the winner for England against Germany at Euro 2022, and was immediately swallowed up in the chaos of the celebrations, being thrown around by the people around me. Having a pint in my hand in that moment would have been less than ideal. Beer and football can clearly coexist, but what works at one level of the game, or in one kind of crowd, doesn’t necessarily translate neatly to another.
But this is where Burnham’s argument starts to feel out of step with the reality of football now. At a time when working-class fans are being priced out of their season tickets, racist, sexist, homophobic online abuse is ever-present, and figures at the very top of the game – such as Jim Ratcliffe – use their platform to push deeply divisive politics, it feels out of touch to make the right to drink a pint in your seat a headline example of football discrimination.
And that’s not to deny discrimination of working-class fans, but this is a problem that runs much deeper in the game. And if the old assumption is that football fans are uniquely likely to cause trouble when alcohol is involved, lifting the ban doesn’t automatically remove that belief. It’s possible these biases will show up in how games are policed, with a heavy pre-emptive police and security presence.
If the ban is lifted, there’ll be teething problems, there will be beer showers, complaints and no doubt a bunch of stories in the press making an example of any issues of violence held up as evidence that football fans can’t be trusted with a pint. Eventually, though, fans will adapt, security will relax and, for the most part, it will probably become normal.
But that’s precisely why Burnham’s argument feels like such an odd intervention. There are serious questions about class and access in football that deserve to be scrutinised as discrimination. If Burnham wants to tackle the ways football fans are treated unfairly, there are plenty of other places to start.
Football fans have every right to drink their beer wherever the rules allow. But sometimes a pint is just a pint – and football has bigger battles to fight.
- 
  Marva Kreel is a broadcaster and football content creator

HBO’s Billionaire Divorce Drama War Doesn’t Know What It’s Trying to Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:00:03 UTC
23:00:03 KST

In the third episode of War, a legal drama from HBO and Britain’s Sky TV, a tech billionaire played by Dominic West makes a generous and degrading offer. He’ll give Steven (Robert Daws), one of many hirelings advising him in a nasty divorce, a wristwatch worth a million dollars if he disrobes “down to your socks, right now.” Steven’s initial response is a nervous giggle. Then he’s frantically unbuttoning his shirt. His point duly made, West’s character, Morgan Henderson, quickly stops the striptease. “For people like me, the word trust loses all meaning,” Morgan says. “There are no lengths to which people won’t go, there’s nothing they won’t do to debase themselves, to humiliate themselves, and you, if they think they can get a slice.”
This is as close as the first season of War, premiering Oct. 1 on HBO, gets to a thesis statement. Created by Lupin and Hijack hitmaker George Kay, this planned anthology series set within the high-rent hallways of London’s elite law firms takes, as its debut subject, the protracted uncoupling of Morgan and his actress wife, Carla Duval (Sienna Miller). The show is everything you’d expect from a prestige-branded drama: persuasively acted, aesthetically polished, intricately plotted, and, with a few baffling exceptions, subtly scripted. It can be quite exciting. But as the season progresses, sparse character development and minimal insight into the absurdity of possessing—let alone fighting over—sums of money that could sustain hundreds of upper-middle-class Steven types add up to a frustrating lack of perspective.
From the very beginning, the Henderson-Duval split is sordid. After accepting an award with a high-minded speech, Morgan—the entrepreneur behind a socially responsible social media platform called Zephyr—allows himself to be seduced by a beautiful young woman, Flora (Rose Williams). It’s a honeytrap, set by Carla in a desperate scheme to investigate rumors of her husband’s infidelity. On a junket promoting a dire-sounding period drama called The Milliner (her declining film career fuels some of War’s wittiest moments), she wastes no time forwarding Flora’s selfie with a sleeping Morgan to her lawyers. And so the gears of the divorce machine shudder into motion, working to formalize a gradual estrangement that had been masquerading as the unavoidable byproduct of two demanding, international careers. We don’t learn much about either spouse as people; Carla’s personality is especially tough to pin down. At times, it’s implied that she’s cold or cutthroat. Her son from a previous relationship (Aran Murphy, in his second HBO troubled-teen role this fall) is barely mentioned before he pops up in Episode 3.
The show’s failure to flesh out these characters could have worked. The anthology’s overarching concept implies that it’s the lawyers, not the clients, that we’re supposed to be getting to know. In Morgan’s corner is Cathcarts & Sons, a venerable, old-school firm whose patrician pomp is telegraphed by stuffy, dark-wood interiors. Carla hires upstarts Taylor & Byrne, whose glassy, modern office space, by contrast, underscores a mission of operating on the light side of the legal arts—avoiding dirty tactics and putting clients first. (Flora’s photo, which is proof of Carla’s entrapment as well as of Morgan’s cheating, is an early ethical test.) The adversaries have history that goes beyond the prep-school-to-white-shoe-firm pipeline, and it gives both sides further ammunition for a fight they’re incentivized to draw out for as long as possible.
There are a few compelling characters among the attorneys. Married Taylor & Byrne partners Nick Taylor (James McArdle) and Serena Byrne (Phoebe Fox) are about to have their first child, and the question of whether she—the tougher but somewhat less senior and, of course, female of the two—will step back from work to focus on family meshes well with the show’s depiction of Carla as a mostly absent mother. Pip Torrens could make your skin crawl (complimentary) as St. John Smallwood, a cruel, sardonic leader of the opposite team, a constant reminder of how much ground there is between compromised and sociopathic on the moral spectrum.
But even these standouts feel underdeveloped. And most of the dozen or so colleagues of theirs we meet are either cyphers or types. Smallwood’s underling David Schill (Miles Jupp) is flop sweat personified. Shadow and Bone star Archie Renaux is very good at conveying the quiet calculations of Johnny Warren, a working-class junior lawyer who is basically the straight Tom Ripley, Esq., but the fact that his character can be summed up so concisely speaks to its limitations. Farther down the call sheet, for every inspired casting choice (Celia Imrie as a sprightly barrister), there are a couple of name actors wasted in roles that serve expository purposes (Patrick Fabian as a Morgan minion, Nick Mohammed as a Taylor & Byrne staffer).
There are so many characters, and Kay does so little to identify a protagonist within this cynical milieu, that—as the case progresses inevitably from a pantomime of mediation to a courtroom spectacle with the potential to make careers and ruin lives—it’s hard to know where to look. Ideas surface and either stall out, like the nihilism of Gabe’s superrich teen cohort in an era whose apocalyptic mood is a direct result of their parents’ actions, or linger redundantly. Well before the midpoint of the season, viewers will be trained to see lawyers as 24/7 performers, manipulating everyone around them through false sincerity and empathy, if not full fabrication. Glib flourishes like an episode that ends with both spouses saying "I do" to escalating their conflict and the occasional insertion of misplaced crime-drama clichés ("It's done," Flora tells Carla after sleeping with Morgan) undermine otherwise solid scripts.
The point may be that money destroys families and debases everyone who seeks it. But even if Succession hadn’t already eloquently made it (Morgan’s watch stunt is a milder version of Logan Roy’s viscerally disturbing Boar on the Floor), that’s not what War’s ultimate framing of Morgan and Carla suggests. While all the scheming and jockeying and betrayal can be thrilling, the resolution feels like a shrug. Kay invokes big, timely issues—extreme wealth, gender roles, the horrors of social media—without finding much to say about them. An anthology is supposed to be a collection of complete stories. War’s slick but shallow first outing is anything but.

Seven golds on debut: Zhang Zhanshuo makes Asian Games history
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:59:46 CST
22:59:46 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Moments after touching the wall in the men's 400m freestyle final on Friday, Zhang Zhanshuo surfaced, raised both hands and slowly counted from one to seven.
The 19-year-old Chinese swimmer had just completed his first Asian Games with seven gold medals. The Tokyo Aquatics Center was filled with cheers. Zhang, however, appeared remarkably calm.
"I feel much calmer than I had imagined," Zhang said after winning the 400m freestyle in an Asian Games record of 3 minutes 41.28 seconds. "Of course, I'm very happy to win these seven gold medals, and I will turn them into greater motivation going forward."
The victory made Zhang the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at a single edition of the Asian Games. More significantly, his haul equaled the Games record for most gold medals won by an athlete at a single edition, a mark set by DPRK shooter So Gil-san in 1982.
For Chinese swimming, it was also a new benchmark, as Zhang surpassed the six-gold haul of teammate Zhang Yufei at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023. His seven titles came from a demanding mix of individual and relay events: the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle, the men's 4x100m and 4x200m freestyle relays, and the mixed 4x100m medley relay.
He won gold in seven of the eight events he entered, while setting an Asian record in the 200m freestyle, Games records in the 400m and 800m, and Asian records in the two men's freestyle relays.
But the seven medals did not change the way Zhang viewed the competition. Asked what had excited him most during the Games, he did not point to the medal ceremonies or the seven-gold haul. Instead, he recalled the instant he touched the wall.
"When I touched the wall and came out of the water, I looked back at the big screen and saw my time flashing, or the 'AR' mark," he said.
Then came the quiet count from one to seven. "It was a perfect finish to the Games," Zhang said.
The calmness was not a sign that Zhang considered his work finished. Quite the opposite, when asked about his ambitions for the Los Angeles Olympics, Zhang stressed that the Asian Games was not his ultimate goal.
"I need to settle down and face the gaps between myself and the world's best. The Asian Games is not my ultimate goal," he said.
And his next target is the world record. Zhang's 3:41.28 was just 1.25 seconds outside the world record, and he said breaking that mark would be one of his next goals over the coming two years.
"I think that will be one of my next goals, and I will give my all to chase the world record," he said.
The young swimmer is also clear about what stands between him and that target.
"There are many things I need to improve," Zhang said. "That's also one of the purposes of this competition, to make a new summary and find the gaps, both technically and in terms of ability."
Zhang said his turning technique still lagged behind that of some of the world's top swimmers, making it an important focus for his next phase of training.
The same approach applies to his events. Rather than picking one as his favorite, Zhang said he wanted to continue developing across the middle and long distance free events.
"Everything is possible. I will stay humble and keep pushing forward," he said.
At 19, Zhang has already matched a record that had stood for more than four decades. He left the Tokyo Aquatics Center with seven gold medals, but also with a clear sense that there was more work to do.
Asked to rate his performance at the Games, Zhang gave himself 85 out of 100. For Zhang, the number seven therefore marks both an achievement and a starting point.
"There are still gaps between me and the world level in some events," he said. "I will turn these gold medals into greater motivation." ■

NAZA, off screen

22:59:45 KST

NAZA, off screen
BUENOS AIRES — For months, we have been living with harrowing images from Gaza, amid allegations and accusations of genocide. Images, testimonies, and an incessant flow of information—and yet nothing stops. Gaza has also become this: the repetition of unbearable scenes that we see again and again, without their accumulation seeming sufficient to interrupt the machinery that produces them.
But in recent weeks, a film burst onto the scene at the 2026 Venice International Film Festival and received an ovation lasting nearly half an hour. It is NAZA, by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two Israeli filmmakers who construct the film from a singular vantage point: testimonies emerging from within Israel’s own military and intelligence apparatus. The film brings together 24 military and intelligence sources and was made over the course of three years.
The question then shifts: what does it mean to look from the inside? Filmed at night, on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, NAZA enters what generally remains off screen: the systems, calculations, and decisions that precede the bombing of Gaza and the mass deaths of Palestinian civilians. And that calculation has a name: NAZA. But NAZA did not originate with this film. Nor did it originate with this war. To understand what it means, we have to go back in time and enter the history of a procedure developed within the Israeli military apparatus itself.
What does NAZA mean?
NAZA comes from נז״א, an acronym for nezek agavi (נזק אגבי), literally “collateral damage,” an expression incorporated into Israeli military language. In planning certain attacks, the military apparatus makes a prior estimate of the civilian casualties the operation could cause. The so-called “NAZA number” expresses that forecast: how many civilians could die as a consequence of the attack before it is authorized.
Put simply, the calculation begins with the identification of a target, intelligence about the people who are inside it or in its vicinity, and the anticipated effects of the munition. NAZA, therefore, is neither artificial intelligence nor software: it is a military concept and calculation. New technologies may play a role in identifying and assessing targets, but the term predates them. To trace its origins, we have to go back more than two decades. Ronen Bergman, an Israeli journalist specializing in intelligence, explains in Rise and Kill First: The Secret History of Israel's Targeted Assassinations that during the Second Intifada, civilian deaths caused in targeted killing operations began to be referred to as nezek agavi, “collateral damage,” an expression that over time was condensed into the acronym NAZA.
From inside the system
Retired lieutenant colonel and former Israeli Military Intelligence member Sarit Zehavi says that nearly twenty years ago she took part in developing procedures designed to warn and monitor the evacuation of civilian populations, as well as in target-approval processes. Her public intervention is particularly revealing in relation to one of the figures associated with NAZA: 500. Zehavi maintains that “NAZA 500” does not mean an automatic authorization to kill five hundred civilians, but rather a prior estimate of potential harm that should lead to measures to reduce it through evacuations, changes in munitions, or even cancellation of the attack.
But the problem posed by NAZA goes beyond the existence of the calculation itself: what happens when the number of civilians expected to die increases and the attack is nevertheless authorized? The question took on another dimension after October 7, 2023. An investigation by The New York Times said that the Israeli military loosened certain rules of engagement and, in some operations, allowed the risk of killing up to 20 civilians even when targeting lower-ranking combatants. The procedure, however, predates this period. Testimonies from Israeli soldiers collected by Breaking the Silence after the 2014 Gaza offensive describe categories of nezek agavi—collateral damage—classified into levels 0, 1, and 2. One of those testimonies makes a fundamental point: those levels did not count buildings or material damage. They counted human lives.
NAZA is not the only mechanism involved in target selection. In recent years, other tools used by Israeli intelligence have become known. Habsora (The Gospel) processes large amounts of information to help identify possible physical targets, such as buildings or infrastructure. Lavender focuses on individuals, generating assessments of their possible links to armed organizations. And Where’s Daddy? - the name attributed by intelligence sources to a tracking system - was reportedly used to locate previously identified individuals, including when they were in their homes. NAZA serves a different function: it estimates the anticipated collateral damage before an attack. It does not determine who the target is, but how many civilians could be affected by striking it. These tools do not necessarily operate together or in every operation, but they reveal different stages of the same architecture: identify, locate, calculate the damage, and decide whether to strike.
Designing death
The precedent appears in This Is How We Fought in Gaza: Soldiers’ Testimonies and Photographs from Operation “Protective Edge” (2014), a report published in 2015 by the Israeli organization Breaking the Silence (Shovrim Shtika), which brings together testimonies from more than sixty Israeli soldiers and officers who took part in Operation Protective Edge in 2014. Among them, testimony 109 is particularly revealing. At the end, the interviewer asks whether that collateral damage also included material destruction. The answer is no: the levels referred exclusively to human lives. NAZA therefore begins long before a bomb falls on Gaza. It begins in that space cinema can almost never show: a room, a screen, a set of data, a number, and someone who ultimately decides. What we will later see as an image—a destroyed building, bodies, survivors—had already existed before in another form: as a calculation. Perhaps that is where the power of the title and the film lies: bringing into the frame what had remained off screen. Behind the abstraction of “collateral damage,” behind every level and every number, lies something that technical language turns into a figure: human lives.

SUVA, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Fiji's inflation rate accelerated to 7.6 percent in August from 5.7 percent in July, driven largely by higher food, energy and kava prices, the Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF) said on Friday.
The central bank's board has maintained the overnight policy rate at 0.25 percent, saying the decision balances growing inflationary pressures with the need to support economic activity.
RBF Governor and Board Chairman Ariff Ali said inflation is expected to remain above 6 percent through the end of the year. He cited global commodity prices and the developing El Nino weather pattern as potential sources of further price pressures.
Despite the inflationary pressures, the RBF said Fiji's economy continues to perform broadly in line with expectations.
The economy expanded by 2.5 percent last year, with tourism, consumer spending and construction among the main contributors to growth.
The RBF said Fiji's foreign reserves stood at about 3.9 billion Fijian dollars (around 1.7 billion U.S. dollars) as of Wednesday, sufficient to cover around 5.5 months of retained imports, providing a buffer against external shocks.
Ali said the economic outlook has become more challenging, particularly given the expected impact of El Nino on growth next year. ■

Xi, Trump honor history of China-U.S. joint fight against Japanese aggression in WWII
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:59:26 CST
22:59:26 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- More than 80 years after Chinese and American forces stood side by side against Japanese aggression in World War II, that legacy of shared struggle came to the fore in Washington on Thursday as the two countries' leaders honored the bond forged in war.
As U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday morning, the shadow of the wartime history gave way to shared memory -- with Xi recalling how the two peoples once stood shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression.
Invoking a shared historic legacy, Xi reflected on the deep ties forged during wartime.
"During the Second World War, Chinese and Americans fought shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression. Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people," Xi said.
Trump brought back the shared wartime memory by recalling the history of the U.S. and China fighting alongside each other as allies during World War II. "Throughout history, the pursuit of those common interests has connected our people across vast oceans, those big, tremendous distances and many differences, and even made us allies in World War II," he said.
Trump praised the Flying Tigers, officially known as the American Volunteer Group of the Chinese Air Force, for those American pilots' bravery during their joint combat with Chinese soldiers and civilians against the Japanese invasion.
Trump noted that "it was the United States Marines' encounter with Chinese people that inspired the Marines to adopt a Chinese phrase they still use today, 'gung ho.'"
"The Marines use it as an expression of great enthusiasm, but in Chinese, it literally means working together," Trump said.
The term "gung ho" originated from the Chinese Industrial Cooperatives movement, also known as the "Gung Ho" movement, launched in the late 1930s to support China's war effort.
"Just as our people worked together to win that war, President Xi and I will continue working together to forge a better future for both of our nations," he added.
At a state dinner hosted by Trump on Thursday evening, Xi took a moment to recount the story of the Hump Route.
"Over 80 years ago, the Chinese and American people stood shoulder to shoulder in the fight against Japanese militarist aggressors. Together we opened the famous Hump air route over the Himalayas. During the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, Chinese soldiers and civilians rescued hundreds of American pilots at the cost of hundreds of thousands of Chinese lives," Xi said.
The Flying Tigers helped open and safeguard the Hump Route, a vital air corridor over the Himalayas that became a wartime lifeline for China. From 1942 to 1945, the route served as a key channel for Allied supplies to support China's resistance against Japanese aggression.
This focus on wartime alliance came right on the heels of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's meeting with Trump at the United Nations General Assembly in New York two days earlier. ■

The Commission also opened infringement procedures against Greece and other EU countries for failing to incorporate new rules on money laundering and human trafficking into national legislation.
The member states have two months to respond and complete the required measures, after which the Commission may proceed to the next stage by issuing a reasoned opinion.
