A HRW report shows how South Korean women face systemic barriers to climbing the career ladder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

South Korea's gender pay gap grows as women get older
September 25, 2026
At 27, a woman in South Korea earns 8% less than male peers. By her late 50s, she earns 50% less. This is according to government wage data published in a recent Human Rights Watch (HRW) report.
South Korea is a global technology and industrial powerhouse, but its gender pay gap has remained the highest in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) since comparable records began in 1992.
"The gender division of labor inside the home leads directly to a gender division of labor in the labor market," Min Hee Kim, a Korean activist for women labor struggles, told DW.
The problem, she argues, is not simply that women are paid less than men. As women age, the kinds of work available to them narrows and the consequences of lower pay, career breaks and precarious jobs accumulate.
For the report, "Too Old and a Woman," HRW interviewed 41 South Korean women aged 28 to 87 about their working lives.
Structural barriers to women's careers
Discrimination has changed form rather than disappeared, Kim said. Until the 1980s, it was legal for employers to fire women simply for getting married, a practice known as "marriage-based dismissal," where employers assumed a married woman would soon leave to raise children anyway.
Today, "it is difficult to openly say, 'We won't hire you because you're a woman,'" Kim added. But caregiving responsibilities still fall on women, pushing them into lower-paid jobs when they try to return to work.
According to the HRW report, women's university attainment has passed men's since the 1980s. Higher education would suggest equal opportunity after graduation, but the job market says otherwise.
One year after graduating, women already earn 22% less than men, according to a 2024 study.
Many women told HRW that after leaving work for marriage or children, chances of returning to the workforce were limited to a handful of jobs such as call centers, cleaning or caregiving.
Women who opt to focus on their career told HRW they hit a glass ceiling at work. Women held 18% of manager jobs in 2024, and only five of 38 senior civil servants were women.
Wages peak and drop off
Women's wages peak in their late 30s and then steadily decline, according to Labor Ministry survey data cited by HRW.
South Korea's Gender Ministry told HRW that career interruptions, along with occupational segregation and discrimination within organizations, drive the gap.
J. Mi-sook, 53, told HRW that her three years of experience weren't recognized by her next employer, so she started at entry level on a lower salary.
The longer women spend outside the workforce, the less experience they accumulate on their resumes, which results in less pay and less work stability.
Kim pointed to structural discrimination, a concept from the report that HRW describes as discrimination so embedded in social practices and institutions that even the people harmed by it may not recognize it as a problem.
"When you are alone, it is easy to think, 'It's because I'm not capable enough,' or 'It's because I'm getting older,'" she said. It's only when women who've had similar experiences meet and talk, she added, that they realize, "this wasn't just my problem."
It gets harder as you get older
Park Jae-soon, 61, was forced to retire at 60 from a utility company and now works part-time as a care worker. Her annual income fell from 55 million won ($40,500/€35,600) to 15.6 million won, a 72% drop.
HRW argues the mandatory retirement age and the "peak wage" system, which lets employers cut older workers' pay in the years before retirement, should both be abolished.
According to data cited in the report, women received 53% of men's National Old Age Pension on average in October 2025, a 47% gap.
"I think what is important here is that this is not simply a problem of middle-aged women having difficulty finding jobs," Kim said.
"The work that women have traditionally done inside the home, like cleaning, cooking, caregiving and managing other people's emotions, is classified as 'work suitable for women' when it enters the labor market, and then low wages are assigned to it," she added.
From first paycheck to pension
HRW argues the disadvantage builds stage by stage, from a woman's first paycheck up until her pension.
"Career interruption among women in their 30s is already a pension issue," Kim said. "Part-time work among women in their 40s is a pension issue, and low wages among women in their 50s are already a pension issue," she added.
South Korea's government has said it will pursue a phased increase in the statutory retirement age from 60 to 65.
"This cannot be solved with just one policy. Equal pay for equal work needs to be actually implemented, wage structures need to be transparent, and care needs to be treated as a public responsibility rather than something that is pushed onto individual families and women," Kim said.
The rights activist said the report is an important starting point, but believes its picture is incomplete.
Most interviewees were recruited through civic organizations and largely in Seoul, she noted, while disabled women, migrant workers and others may experience a different combination of age and gender discrimination.
"The important question is not simply, 'How much discrimination do women face?'" she said. "It is which women, in what positions, become increasingly distanced from which resources and rights as they grow older."
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

EU member states have agreed on the terms for allocating €6.6 billion from the European Peace Facility to Ukraine. This is good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia

-  €900 million is earmarked for the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine);

Supplement
The European Peace Facility (EPF) is an off-budget EU fund. The fund will be financed through contributions from EU member states.
The ultimate goal of the Facility is to enhance the EU's capacity to prevent conflicts, support peace, and strengthen international stability and security. The instrument is intended to contribute to this by enabling the EU to assist partner countries more effectively: either by supporting their peacekeeping operations or by helping strengthen the capacity of their armed forces to ensure peace and security on their own territory, as well as through broader military and defence measures in support of the objectives of the Common Foreign and Security Policy.

'Like Auschwitz': Nova families urge authorities to block Simchat Torah festivities at massacre site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:16:49 UTC
22:16:49 KST

Following objections from bereaved families, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund has asked Israel Police and the Fire and Rescue Authority to prevent Simchat Torah celebrations from being held at the site of the Nova music festival massacre in Re’im Forest.
“Celebrating and holding festivities at a place where a massacre took place is disrespectful, both to the sanctity of the site and to Judaism,” KKL-JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrovsky told ynet.
The memorial site for those murdered at the Nova festival has become a major destination for visitors, and for some bereaved families it has taken on a significance even greater than the cemetery. Last year, Simchat Torah celebrations were held there, with images of visitors dancing, setting up meals and camping at the site causing distress among relatives of those killed.
Dassi Aviad, whose son Aviad Halevi was murdered at Nova, said she wanted people to continue visiting the site for generations, but urged them to treat it with reverence.
“Every person who comes and stands in front of a photograph or a sign warms the heart. I hope this place will be full of visitors for generations,” she said. “But people need to understand that this ground is sacred, even if it has not been officially declared so, no less than a synagogue or other holy places.”
“People should walk here on tiptoe, thinking with every step about where they are walking and what may have happened right beneath their feet,” she added. “People can, should and must come on this day just as on any other, but they should walk around in respectful silence honoring those who were murdered with unimaginable cruelty, rather than turning the place into an overnight campsite with tents as though it were a campground on the Sea of Galilee.”
Omri Rahum, whose sister Nitzan Rahum was murdered at Nova while four months pregnant, said families were horrified by footage from last year’s holiday.
“We saw videos of people setting tables and holding meals. Seeing people dancing like that... so much filth was left behind that it had to be cleaned up afterward,” he said.
“Simchat Torah is the day our lives were turned upside down. Unfortunately, the police are hesitating and saying they have no solution. The bereaved families, as usual, are being abandoned. For us, this place is like a cemetery and Auschwitz.”
KKL-JNF Director General Ilan Shohat has asked Police Commissioner Dani Levy and Southern District Commander Haim Bublil to prevent organized gatherings and activities at the site.
“Any gathering at the site during this period could have exceptional public, safety and emotional consequences,” Shohat said.
He also asked police to help prevent overnight camping, the lighting of fires and barbecues, and to maintain public order.
Ostrovsky said the site’s importance lies in its national significance and that it should remain a place where Jews of every background can feel at home.
“Every Jew, secular or religious, should feel at home there,” he said. “Initiatives of this kind only damage the delicate fabric that this place represents in such an important way.”
“KKL-JNF will do everything in its power to prevent this, and I intend to speak with the heads of the security and rescue services so they can help us maintain public order and the sanctity of the site.”
Israel Police said it would operate during the holiday period “in cooperation and coordination with all relevant authorities, each according to its area of responsibility and based on the situational assessment, in order to maintain public safety, public order and the security of visitors.”
The Fire and Rescue Authority said that, aside from the annual Oct. 7 memorial ceremony, it had not received requests to approve any large-scale events at the Nova site in the near future.
Any requests that are submitted will be examined individually, the authority said, adding that patrols would be carried out in Re’im Forest and at the Nova site throughout the holiday.
The authority added that it “strongly opposes the holding of events without its approval and in violation of the law.”

Ukrainian EW System From Unwave Participated in Drone Dominance Tests in USA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:15:53 UTC
22:15:53 KST

Ukrainian electronic warfare (EW) manufacturer Unwave participated in trials as part of the Drone Dominance program at Fort Carson in Colorado, USA.
Following its participation, the company received a request from the U.S. side to continue supporting the program’s activities, Unwave told Militarnyi. Drone Dominance calls for the Pentagon to procure more than 200,000 drones by 2027.
The tests took place from August 24 to September 2, with the participation of 14 drone manufacturers and 3 electronic warfare system developers.
The main goal of the Ukrainian developers’ participation was to create conditions as close as possible to a real battlefield to test the drones’ resilience.
As part of the training, Unwave presented four of its own electronic warfare systems.
The first system presented was the Vikha tactical-operational complex, which operates in the 300 MHz–3.2 GHz band with a power output of over 100 W and provides a range of over 300 meters.
To protect personnel and positions from FPV drones and explosive payloads, Unwave demonstrated the Boombox system. This multi-channel portable electronic warfare system, weighing 11–25 kg, operates in the 0.4–1, 1.9–2.7, and 5.8 GHz bands, providing a protective coverage radius of 50 meters.
The company also presented the Shatro system, developed specifically for installation on vehicles and military equipment. It has a channel power of 50–100 watts and covers the 0.2–5.8 GHz frequency ranges.
The fourth model was Choven-2, which suppresses FPV drones within a radius of 70 meters and Mavic quadcopters from 50 meters.
It is worth noting that Unwave’s electronic warfare system was the only one capable of jamming a drone during the NATO Baltic Trust 26 exercises in Latvia.
The exercise marked the final stage of NATO’s program to test UAV countermeasure systems.
Thanks to its successful performance in countering drones, the Ukrainian system received a special commendation from the exercise organizers.

Estonia launches joint study to map optimal electricity mix by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

Estonia launches joint study to map optimal electricity mix by 2027
Estonia's Chamber of Commerce, major energy companies and government have launched a joint effort to determine the most cost‑efficient mix of electricity generation, storage and cross‑border connections needed to meet the country's rising power demand.
The analysis will be completed by the end of February 2027, the chamber announced.
The analysis seeks an answer to the question of which portfolio of production, storage and connection capacities is optimal for Estonia at different consumption levels and what investments this requires.
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry emphasizes that the analysis will be carried out based on the principles of intellectual honesty, freedom from ideology, impartiality and transparency. "All technologies are assessed on the same basis, and the result is not directed by predetermined technological or worldview preferences. All assumptions and constraints affecting the analysis are clearly set out and justified," the chamber's statement says.
The process is structured so that the input and decision‑making rights of companies supporting the project are clearly separated. The companies supporting the project and Elering belong to an advisory council that provides sectoral input and feedback, but does not decide on the assumptions and inputs used in the model. These decisions are made by a steering committee consisting of representatives of the state, academia and the Chamber of Commerce and Industry, which also approves the terms of reference, methodology, input data and constraints.
Public discussion expected
All core elements of the analysis — the terms of reference, methodology, inputs, results and conclusions — will be made public so that public discussion can take place.
Interim results of the project will not be commented on during the analysis. The project results will be presented to the public once the analysis is complete.
The analysis is funded by the companies participating in the project. The project is supported by Eesti Energia/Enefit, Utilitas, Alexela, VKG, Evecon, Baltic Energy Partners, Saare Wind and Fermi Energia, as well as electricity consumers Maag Food and Lemeks. Elering participates in the advisory council as the system operator.
The steering committee includes Einari Kisel (Ministry of Climate), Ahti Kuningas (Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications), Raoul Lättemäe (Ministry of Finance), Erkki Raasuke (EIS), Evelin Pärn‑Lee (Competition Authority), Jaak Aaviksoo (Estonian Academy of Sciences), Hannes Agabus (TalTech), Ivo Palu (Estonian Electrical Power Engineering Society), Uku Varblane (Foresight Centre), and Mait Palts and Raivo Vasnu (Estonian Chamber of Commerce and Industry).
The project is led by foreign‑investment consultant and former Minister of Entrepreneurship and Foreign Trade Anne Sulling.
The analysis will be completed at the end of February 2027, before the parliamentary elections, so that the results can be used by the new government in shaping energy‑policy decisions.
The initiative grew out of a report published in April 2026 by Anne Sulling and Erkki Raasuke, which examined under what conditions international investors would be willing to invest in large energy‑infrastructure projects in Estonia.
One of the report's central recommendations was to calculate the optimal portfolio of electricity production, storage and external connections for Estonia, in order to provide the state with an analytical basis and investors with the necessary foresight.
Elering is conducting a separate study
At the same time, Elering and Tallinn University of Technology have begun preparing future scenarios for Estonia's energy system, in order to assess the impact of different energy‑policy and technological choices on electricity prices and security of supply. This analysis will be completed by the end of 2027.
In the course of the work, Elering will create an electricity‑market model that compares possible development paths for Estonia's energy system up to 2050. The model should help assess how different choices affect electricity prices and system reliability. Tallinn University of Technology will prepare European energy‑system development trajectories and possible scenarios for Estonia.
The analysis will take into account network tariffs, the renewable‑energy charge, the cost of ensuring security of supply, the cost of balancing the system, and the need to reinforce electricity and gas networks up to 2050. The analysis does not include possible changes to state taxes and excise duties.
Elering is conducting the analysis as an independent system operator.
Scenario development and consultations will begin in autumn 2026. European development trajectories and Estonian scenarios will be discussed with stakeholders from September 2026 to February 2027. The scenarios to be modelled will be approved in February 2027, and the report on competitive energy prices will be completed by the end of 2027.
--
Editor: Mirjam Mäekivi, Argo Ideon

ISW connects drone crashes in Moldova and Romania, a Starlink fire in Poland, and a Berlin airport shutdown into one Russian pattern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:11:09 UTC
22:11:09 KST

Several recent incidents across Europe were conducted by Russia or are likely attributable to Russia, ISW assessed in its 24 September report, though authorities have not officially linked the Polish and German incidents to Moscow.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has expanded into a parallel campaign of provocations against European defense and logistical infrastructure. The Kremlin is using drones, arson, and undersea cable sabotage to degrade Europe's will and ability to support Ukraine, while deliberately intensifying the frequency of airspace violations to erode the boundary between hybrid and kinetic war.
Drones over Moldova and Romania
Four Russian drones flew over Bukovyna and targeted an energy facility and border crossings with Moldova and Romania, Chernivtsi Oblast Military Administration head Ruslan Osypenko reported. Ukrainian forces shot down three. The fourth flew toward Suceava County in northeastern Romania.
A drone crashed in Cernița, Florești district, Moldova—preliminarily identified as a Russian Gerbera type, the first such device found in the country. It carried an onboard camera, hit a tree, and exploded, Moldovan police said. Romania's Defense Ministry reported a second aerial vehicle entered Romanian airspace for four minutes and crashed near Solca in the same border region; geolocated footage confirmed it was also a Gerbera, ISW noted. Poland evacuated the Hrubieszów and Dorohusk border crossings for 30 minutes, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said. Three countries were put on alert by a single night of Russian strikes.
"Intentional and accidental Russian drone incursions into NATO and Moldovan airspaces are likely part of the Kremlin's efforts to normalize airspace violations by intensifying their frequency," ISW assessed.
Sabotage in Poland and Germany
A fire engulfed the power system and backup generator at a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska, central Poland, on the evening of 23 September. Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski confirmed it was sabotage aimed at cutting internet access, including for Ukraine's military. Authorities have not identified who was responsible, but the act aligns with Russia's "new" doctrine of attacks, Gawkowski said. The station is now operating normally.
German authorities suspended operations at Berlin-Brandenburg airport for 45 minutes the same evening after staff reported a drone sighting, Die Zeit reported. Federal police could not confirm it. ISW assessed both incidents fit Russia's wider pattern of sabotage against European defense assets, though neither has been officially attributed to Russia.
Western intelligence warnings
A Lithuanian Defense Ministry source reported on 23 September that Russia could launch Gerbera drones from a shipping container in the Mediterranean against Spain, France, and Italy. Danish Defense Intelligence assessed on 24 September that Russia will intensify its hybrid war in coming months, including destructive cyber attacks and sabotage carrying a high risk of casualties, and that there is a low but growing risk of a limited Russian military attack on a NATO border state. It sees no indications of an outright invasion. The CIA reportedly warned Poland that Russia may sabotage underwater cables to disrupt its banking system, according to Newsweek Polska journalists.
NATO tracked and confronted Russian submersibles rehearsing deployment of a new cable-disabling weapon near Svalbard in spring 2026—no cables were damaged, but the operation demonstrated Moscow's intent, Reuters reported. Shadow fleet vessels likely served as drone-launch platforms for incursions into NATO airspace, ISW noted.
"The increasing frequency of such warnings suggests that Western intelligence agencies are picking up indicators that the Kremlin is looking to diversify its platforms and means for conducting attacks against NATO and European states and is considering conducting such attacks," ISW assessed.
ISW said it has not yet seen evidence that Russia has conducted the attacks the warnings describe.
Denmark's assessment—that a limited Russian military strike on a NATO border state could come in the coming months—suggests the boundary between hybrid provocations and military action is narrower than European policy has assumed. ISW's synthesis reframes what governments have treated as separate incidents into one campaign.

Iran, India have huge potential for cooperation in health and tourism: Ambassador
Unknown

2026-09-25

Iran, India have huge potential for cooperation in health and tourism: Ambassador
TEHRAN – New Delhi’s Ambassador to Tehran Vishwesh Negi has highlighted the significant potential for Iran-India cooperation in traditional and modern medicine, pharmaceuticals and tourism, as well as in strengthening cultural and people-to-people ties.
He made the remarks in a brief interview with the Tehran Times on the sidelines of a ceremony hosted by the Indian Embassy in Tehran on September 23 to mark National Ayurveda Day.
Today’s ceremony to mark Ayurveda Day, brought together a number of Iranian physicians who shared views on the ancient Indian medicine system alongside views on the ancient Iranian medicine system. It was a fruitful gesture for promoting cultural heritage and exchanging ideas. Tell us about your embassy’s collaboration and efforts to promote other aspects of Indian heritage in Iran and plans for mutual cooperation.
Well, there are a lot of things we want to do with Iran at this point in time. We really want to establish Iran as one of the major centers where we can promote and practice wellness traditions such as the concept of yoga, what comes along with yoga, Ayurveda, and a very healthy way of living, I think.
And I think these systems are very relevant. They are very relevant in today’s world because our lives have become very complex. We get exposed to a lot of elements which are alien to our body and to our culture. So I think this kind of healing, or this kind of healthy lifestyle, which involves yoga, Ayurveda and homeopathy, can help moderate our body and enable us to have, at least, a mentally healthy lifestyle.
We intend to do a lot of activities in Iran in cooperation with the government of Iran, whatever the rules and regulations allow.
And I think one of my important missions out here, first of all, at this point in time, would be to look at how we can generate greater cooperation in the health sector.
You mentioned the health sector as an important area of cooperation. What are the areas where you see the greatest potential for expanding India-Iran health cooperation?
So today I was there; I went to Iran Pharma, the largest pharmaceutical exposition in Iran. There also, a lot of Indian companies had opened up their booths. So there is a lot of cooperation in the pharmaceutical sector between the two countries.
That is also something which can be scaled up a lot, given the geopolitical situation improves. InshaAllah, when things become better, I think there is huge potential for a large amount of pharmaceutical cooperation in terms of the export of APIs to Iran, training, technical expertise exchanges between health professionals in the two countries, and also looking at new forms of medicine, research and development.
You may be knowing that during the time of COVID, India had supplied 1 million doses of vaccines to Iran. That kind of cooperation suggests that there is trust between the two countries, and I think it all goes well.
So, as I said, there is huge potential in Ayurveda, in yoga and in conventional medicine.
But given the current circumstances, we are not able to realize the full potential. But inshaAllah, in time we will be able to.
What are your views on tourism relations between the two countries and ways to promote them?
Well, tourism, as I said, is something I have already spoken to a lot of Iranian policymakers about. The honorable Prime Minister of India has identified trade, tourism and technology as the three things we need to engage with friendly countries.
Tourism is an important sector for promotion. In recent years, the number of tourists going from Iran to India has come down a bit. It might be due to the geopolitical condition; it might be due to the economic condition. But we are very keen to bring it to the same level of tourism flows to India and even beyond.
So, we intend to take a lot of measures. We are looking at possibilities for relaxing the tourist visa regime, streamlining the processes, and rationalizing tourist visa fees so that Iranians have to pay less to go to India. We are also trying to familiarize them with a lot of activities.
A lot of institutions in India, like Ayurveda, can be one of the aspects that can promote tourism from Iran to India, along with modern education, arts and various art forms. And I think all these things, this whole cultural connect between the two countries, will eventually promote greater tourism flows from Iran to India, and I think similarly from India to Iran.
So, I think, as I said, there is huge potential. We are trying to understand the ecosystem of the tourism infrastructure and create infrastructure so that Iranians can travel to India as easily as possible.

Zoroastrian funerary inscription from late Sasanian era discovered in southern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:09:15 UTC
22:09:15 KST

Zoroastrian funerary inscription from late Sasanian era discovered in southern Iran
TEHRAN - A newly discovered funerary inscription dating to the late Sasanian period and associated with a Zoroastrian burial has been found in a carved frame north of the ancient city of Estakhr in Marvdasht plain of Fars province, southern Iran.
The inscription is written in Pahlavi script and is believed to be associated with one of the burials of Zoroastrian followers during the late Sasanian period, Jamaran.ir quoted archaeologist Abolhassan Atabaki as saying on Thursday.
The archaeologist explained that with the expansion of Zoroastrianism in the post-Achaemenid period and later during the Sasanian era, burial practices underwent fundamental changes. Many burials in the ground were abandoned and funerary practices were transferred to elevated and mountainous areas, a shift he attributed primarily to Zoroastrian beliefs concerning bodily resurrection and life after death.
According to Atabaki, Zoroastrians regarded the world beneath the ground as dark, stagnant and associated with evil. They therefore avoided burying the dead directly in the soil.
The corpse was also considered capable of contaminating sacred elements such as earth, vegetation and water. At the same time, Zoroastrians believed that the soul of the deceased should ascend toward the rays of the sun.
For this reason, the body was placed in elevated structures known as “sun towers” before the final funerary stage, where rituals including “khorshid-negahreshni” were performed and the bones were purified. After birds of prey and other scavenging animals removed the flesh, the cleaned bones were transferred to places among rocks and cliffs, Atabaki said.
In that regard, Najmeh Ebrahimi, a history expert, said the Sasanian period saw a variety of burial practices, depending on the social status and financial means of individuals.
These included rock-cut graves, stone cairns, grave towers, trough-shaped graves, jar burials, small “dakhmaks” and ossuaries. Such funerary structures are referred to as “dakhmak” in many Sasanian inscriptions.
Ebrahimi highlighted the archaeological importance of the Marvdasht plain, saying that the area contains the largest known concentration of Sasanian inscriptions, with more than 50 inscriptions discovered and reread to date.
The plain also ranks first in terms of Sasanian funerary inscriptions, she added.
The inscription is believed to provide further evidence for the funerary practices and religious beliefs of Zoroastrian communities in the Marvdasht region during the final centuries of the Sasanian period.

Asian Games | Feature: From the shadow of war to the Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:09:14 CST
22:09:14 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Athletes from across Asia have gathered in Japan to compete for Asian Games medals. Among them are those whose journeys to the Games began far from a training ground, in places where conflict has disrupted daily life, separated families and made the pursuit of sport uncertain.
For athletes forced from their homes, sport can offer "a sense of purpose, belonging and hope," said Vinod Kumar Tiwari, deputy director general of the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA).
Palestinian triathlete Abdelrahman Tantish left Gaza about six months after the war began. He spent nine months in Egypt, where he trained alongside local athletes, before joining the Qatar national team for training.
For Tantish, reaching the Asian Games means more than taking part in a race. Many young people in Gaza have sporting ambitions, he said, but conflict and scarce resources leave them with little opportunity to pursue them.
"I hope that by competing at the Asian Games, I can show the world that despite hardship, Palestinians still have hope and can still achieve extraordinary things," he said.
Jibril Rajoub, president of the Palestinian Olympic Committee, described the obstacles athletes face, including limited resources, restrictions on movement and the strain of worrying about their families. Sometimes, he said, the committee identifies a promising athlete but cannot arrange for that person to leave and compete.
"We compete amid the rubble and train under bombardment," Rajoub said. "Despite the restrictions imposed on us, we keep moving."
The committee seeks opportunities for Palestinians from Gaza, the West Bank, Jerusalem and communities abroad, he said. Their presence at the Games also gives them a chance to meet other athletes and share their experiences.
For Yemen's wushu athlete Mugahed Mohammed, the journey to Nagoya took more than two decades. He began practicing the sport at five, yet years of conflict at home had kept him from the Asian Games until now.
His coach, Bassam al-Sabri, said Yemen's wushu program has struggled to develop since conflict broke out in 2014. International competition became difficult to access, Chinese coaches who had previously helped develop the sport left, and local training facilities fell short of professional standards.
Mohammed and his coach spent two months preparing for the Games. Their route took them through Yemen and Oman before a 20-day training camp in Hangzhou, China, arranged with Chinese support. Mohammed scored 9.083 points in the men's changquan competition on Sept. 20. A medal remained out of reach, but he had made it to the stage he had long hoped to reach.
"I am very grateful to my coach for standing by me and helping me all these years," he said. "I will keep training and work toward becoming a champion. I also hope my experience encourages more young people in Yemen to take up wushu."
Support for athletes can also come through opportunities to train and compete across borders. Iranian cyclist Mandana Dehghan Manshadi said she spent much of the past two years in China with her team.
"Most of my preparation was done in China. I raced there and trained with my team," she said. The range of events available, including races featuring climbs and mountainous sections, allowed her to prepare for specific demands on the road. "I had some of the best times of my life in China," she added.
Afghan road cyclist Fariba Hashimi arrived in Nagoya with her own measure of how far she had come. She finished 24th in the women's road race at the Hangzhou Asian Games three years ago. On Sept. 22, the 23-year-old won silver.
The name of Chinese brand Lansheng Tianxia, which has sponsored her, appeared on her podium jacket. Her sister Yulduz, also a cyclist, received help from Chinese friends during the Hangzhou Games. Such support is part of the sisters' journey, though Fariba said the encouragement she carries also comes from people she has never met.
Speaking after the race with tears in her eyes, Hashimi said, "I'm not alone." The night before, she recalled, a woman inside Afghanistan whom she did not know had sent her a message urging her not to give up on her dream and to keep fighting for women back home.
Hashimi said messages like that gave her strength to continue. She hopes her result will help other women see that their dreams are worth pursuing.
The Aichi-Nagoya Games have also welcomed an OCA Refugee Team for the first time. Its two members, Syrian taekwondo athletes Talah Al Hassan Al Hinide and Mahmoud Al Jasem Al Mohammad Al Hussein, live in Jordan's Azraq refugee camp.
The two athletes described how taekwondo had changed their lives. For Talah, it helped restore the confidence that displacement had worn away. "Taekwondo gave me the opportunity to dream again," she wrote.
Mahmoud described how training gave structure to his days and a path forward. "I woke up every morning with a purpose," he wrote. Competing at the Asian Games carries meaning beyond their own results, offering them an opportunity to represent others who have lived through displacement.
Their stories show what it can take simply to reach the start line, and how sport can create connections and opportunities across borders. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- On the closing night of the swimming program at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, China's Zhang Zhanshuo capped a remarkable campaign by winning the men's 400m freestyle on Friday, becoming the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at a single edition of the Games.
The 19-year-old clocked 3 minutes 41.28 seconds, breaking the Asian Games record, to complete a clean sweep of seven of the eight events he entered. His haul also matched the Asian Games record for most gold medals won by an athlete at a single edition, set by DPR Korean shooter So Gil-san in 1982.
Zhang's reaction to his unprecedented achievement was strikingly calm.
"I feel much calmer than I had imagined. Of course, I'm very happy to win these seven gold medals, and I will turn them into greater motivation going forward," Zhang said after the race.
He said the most emotional moment came when he touched the wall and looked up at the scoreboard, where his time flashed with an Asian Games record. He also raised his hand and counted from one to seven in the water after the race, a simple gesture to mark his seven titles.
"It was a perfect finish to the Games," Zhang said.
Asked about his ambitions for the Los Angeles Olympics, Zhang stressed that the Asian Games was not his ultimate goal.
"I need to settle down and face the gaps between myself and the world's best. The Asian Games are not my ultimate goal," he said.
His next target is more demanding, which is the world record. Zhang's 3:41.28 was just over a second outside the men's 400m free world record, and he said he would work toward breaking it over the next two years.
"I think that will be one of my next goals, and I will give my all to chase the world record," he said.
Zhang acknowledged that plenty still needs to be improved, from technique to overall ability. He singled out his turns as one area for further work, saying there remains a significant gap between his turns and those of the world's top swimmers.
"I think there are many things I need to improve. That's also one of the purposes of this competition, to make a new summary and find the gaps, both technically and in terms of ability," he said.
Zhang's seven golds came in the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle, as well as the men's 4x200m free, 4x100m free and mixed 4x100m medley relays. He said he did not regard any single event as his favorite, preferring to continue developing across the middle and long distance free events.
"Everything is possible. I will stay humble and keep pushing forward," he said.
China won five more titles on the final day and finished the swimming program with 30 gold, 13 silver and 11 bronze medals.
China's Li Bingjie also completed a five-gold collection after winning the women's 800m free in 8:24.02, but the 24-year-old was far from satisfied with her performance.
"I'd give myself a seven out of 10," Li said. "My time was below my expectations, and I also wasn't good enough at preventing illness and injury."
Li said she caught a fever after her 400m free race and was also less content with her result in the relay the previous day, where she felt she had relied on her teammates to build the advantage.
Despite these defects, she saw the Games as an evidence that she was gradually climbing back after a difficult period following the 2025 National Games. She said changes in her training approach had been a process of trial and error, while her mindset had also improved compared with that during the national championships.
"All five gold medals were earned through great efforts," Li said, adding that she wanted to take photos with her teammates to remember the achievement. She joked that her five golds were like "five gold mooncakes" for the Mid-Autumn Festival which falls on Friday.
Zhang Yufei successfully defended her women's 50m butterfly title in 25.41 seconds, with teammate Wu Qingfeng taking silver in 25.62 and Japan's Rikako Ikee bronze in 25.97. Zhang was visibly emotional on the podium, wiping tears after the victory.
For Zhang, the Games had produced some of the strongest emotional ups and downs she had experienced in recent years.
"Winning has become something quite common for me, so now I'm more focused on the times and on pushing myself to achieve better results," Zhang said. Reflecting on her long rivalry with Ikee, she added that she hoped both could continue swimming healthily and happily.
Qin Haiyang claimed the men's 50m breaststroke title in 26.68, ahead of compatriot Liu Junjie in 26.99, while Japan's Shin Ohashi took bronze in 27.01.
Qin said he was satisfied overall with his Games' results, although he believed there was room for improvement. Asked about Ohashi breaking his world record in the men's 200m breaststroke on Thursday, Qin said the event was becoming increasingly competitive, with a growing diversity of techniques and styles among the world's top swimmers.
Japan's Kodai Nishiono won the men's 200m backstroke in 1:56.42, followed by South Korea's Lee Ju-ho in 1:56.58 and China's Xu Jiayu in 1:56.73.
Chinese Taipei's Wang Kuan-hung took the men's 200m butterfly title in 1:55.05, with China's Xu Fang second in 1:55.65 and South Korea's Kim Minseop third in 1:55.94. China's Wang Xizhe finished fourth in 1:55.95.
China also won the women's 4x100m medley relay in a Games record of 3:54.55, with Japan taking silver in 3:57.64 and South Korea bronze in 4:00.67. ■

====================================================================================================

GRS Certification for Bags: Five Mistakes Buyers Make With the Certificate  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:09:08 UTC
22:09:08 KST

The GRS certificate a supplier sends with a quotation for recycled bags is a scope certificate, because a transaction certificate cannot exist until the goods ship. A scope certificate cannot prove that the order contains a single gram of recycled material.
The Global Recycled Standard (GRS) is a voluntary, third-party verified standard owned by Textile Exchange. It certifies products with at least 20% recycled content and tracks that content through a certified chain of custody, from the recycler to the final business-to-business seller. It also sets social, environmental and chemical requirements for the sites that process the material. For retail buyers of reusable shopping bags, GRS is a check on recycled content they can verify themselves, and in Europe that check matters more from 27 September 2026, when the EU's new rules on environmental claims and sustainability labels apply.
"GRS is four audits wearing one badge," says Simmy Lin, Managing Director of Bk-bags, a Ho Chi Minh City based supplier of reusable shopping bags. "Recycled content, chain of custody, labour, chemicals. Most buyers only ask about the first one, and then they are surprised when their own compliance team asks about the other three."
Mistake 1: Treating the GRS scope certificate as a transaction certificate
GRS certification uses two documents: a scope certificate for the company and a transaction certificate for each shipment.
The scope certificate is issued to a company after an audit. It lists the certified legal entity, its sites, the standard and version, the product categories, the process categories, the materials it may handle, and a validity date. It proves the company is inside a certified chain of custody.
The transaction certificate (TC) is issued for certified goods shipped from one certified seller to one buyer. It names the products, the quantities, the buyer and the certified weight, with pre-consumer and post-consumer content recorded separately. It is the only GRS document that relates to your goods.
A GRS scope certificate says the supplier is in the certified chain. A GRS transaction certificate says your order was.
Bk-bags' full GRS certification guide reads a scope certificate field by field and lists twenty questions to send a supplier, in English, Spanish and Japanese.
Mistake 2: Asking for the transaction certificate too late
A transaction certificate does not arrive automatically. The seller applies to its certification body, and if the seller never applies, no certificate exists.
There is also a deadline. Under Textile Exchange's older certificate policy, which certification bodies can use until 1 April 2027, the certification body must issue a TC if a complete application arrives within 90 calendar days of the earliest shipment date, and may issue one up to 180 days. Under the new policy, which certification bodies may use from 1 October 2026, the "must" window is 180 days. Under both, the certification body may still issue a TC up to 365 days after the earliest shipment date when every product on it is a final product, such as a bag. That is the certification body's discretion, not the buyer's right. Once a complete application is received, the certification body has 14 calendar days to issue it.
Write the transaction certificate into the purchase order as a condition, together with a seller's scope certificate that is valid on the shipment date.
Mistake 3: Trusting the PDF instead of verifying the GRS certificate
A PDF is a file, and files can be edited. You can verify a GRS certificate yourself, without asking the supplier for anything.
1. Scope certificates: search the company name or its Textile Exchange ID on Textile Exchange's Find a Certified Company database, which Textile Exchange describes as the official source for authenticating scope certificates.
2. Transaction certificates: use Textile Exchange's Authenticate a Transaction page, which Textile Exchange names as the only official source for transaction certificates. Treat the URL or QR code printed on the certificate as a pointer, not as the check.
3. While you are there, check four things: the certificate is valid today, the certified organization matches the company on your invoice, your material is on the materials list, and the site and process categories match what you were told.
4. If anything does not reconcile, contact the certification body named on the certificate.
"Any supplier who is unhappy about you verifying their certificate has told you something useful," Lin says. "It takes five minutes and the database is public."
Mistake 4: Asking for GRS on virgin material instead of recycled PP or rPET
GRS certifies recycled content. There is no GRS route for virgin material. A quotation for "GRS certified virgin PP" bags is either a misunderstanding or a fabrication.
For reusable bags, the recycled materials most often certified to GRS are recycled polyester and rPET, recycled polypropylene, including recycled PP woven and non-woven fabric, and recycled cotton. The test is whether the material is named on the supplier's certificate. Bk-bags' own scope certificate, for example, names recycled post-consumer and pre-consumer polypropylene, polyester, polyethylene, PET and polystyrene.
GRS is not a quality standard. The standard says so in its own text. A GRS bag can still have weak handles or a print that cracks. Quality is your specification and your inspection.
GRS and RCS are different. The Recycled Claim Standard (RCS) tracks recycled content from 5% but has no social, environmental or chemical criteria. If the certificate says RCS and the sales deck says GRS, ask why.
Mistake 5: Printing a GRS claim the certificate does not support
- 20% recycled content makes a GRS product.
- 50% recycled content is the minimum for the GRS label on a consumer-facing product.
- Certification up to the brand. Under Textile Exchange's Standards Claims Policy (TE-301 V1.4), an on-product GRS claim on a final product sold to consumers requires certification up to the brand, and the certification body must approve the claim before it is used. A retailer whose own brand is on the bag needs its own GRS certification to put a GRS product claim or the GRS logo on it.
- Without that certification, a brand can still make its own specific claim, such as "made with 60% recycled polypropylene by weight", backed by the transaction certificate and without the GRS name or logo.
Regulation now sits on top of Textile Exchange's rules. Directive (EU) 2024/825 applies from 27 September 2026 and bans generic claims such as "eco-friendly" unless the trader can demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim. In the US, the FTC Green Guides (16 CFR 260.13) say that when a product is only partly made of recycled material, the claim should state the recycled share by weight.
"The safest sentence is the boring one," Lin says. "Say the material, say the percentage, say which certificate it sits on. Adjectives are what regulators read twice."
GRS is changing, but not for 2026 orders
Textile Exchange published GRS 5.0 in July 2026, and GRS itself is being replaced by the Materials Matter Standard, effective 31 December 2026 and mandatory from 31 December 2027. Existing GRS certificates stay valid until their own expiry date. For an order placed in 2026 or 2027, the checks above still apply.
A checklist for ordering GRS certified bags
1. Ask whether the document you received is a scope certificate or a transaction certificate.
2. Verify the scope certificate on Textile Exchange's Find a Certified Company database.
3. Check that the certificate will still be valid on your shipment date.
4. Confirm your material is on the certificate's materials list, and that it is a recycled grade.
5. Write the transaction certificate into the purchase order as a condition.
6. Ask what recycled percentage the TC will show, split into pre-consumer and post-consumer content.
7. Agree the exact wording on the bag, and who is certified to make it, before artwork is approved.
Read more: Your Guide to Buying a Crossbody Bag
About Bk-bags
Bk-bags is a supplier of reusable shopping bags and packaging to retailers and brands, based in Ho Chi Minh City and supplying since 2006, with production in Vietnam and China. Simmy Lin is the company's Managing Director. Its range of reusable bags covers PP woven, PP non-woven, rPET, cotton and polyester, with a minimum order of 10,000 pieces for PP, cotton and rPET and 5,000 for polyester.

Italy adopts 30-pct cap on foreign pupils, sparking debate over integration policy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:08:52 CST
22:08:52 KST

ROME, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- The Italian government has approved a decree introducing a 30-percent ceiling on certain foreign students in school classes, a measure aimed at promoting integration but already drawing criticism from education unions and school principals over its necessity and feasibility.
Under the decree approved by the Council of Ministers on Thursday, the 30-percent limit applies not simply according to citizenship, but to students with foreign citizenship who have insufficient experience in the Italian school system and inadequate Italian-language skills.
In primary schools, the rule applies to students who are not born in Italy and have not attended at least two years of kindergarten. In lower and upper secondary schools, it applies to foreign students who have not successfully completed at least three years of schooling in Italy.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said about 34,000 classes currently have a foreign-student share above 30 percent. He said first-generation foreign students have, on average, less Italian-language preparation and that the rate of "implicit dropout" -- failure to achieve required competencies -- is higher among foreign students than among Italian students.
"Our goal is to put the Italian language at the center as a major tool for integration," Valditara said.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni defended the measure as an effort to prevent so-called "ghetto classes," arguing that concentrating large numbers of students with limited Italian-language skills in the same classroom could hinder their integration and affect the learning environment for other pupils.
The decree also provides exemptions where the 30-percent limit cannot reasonably be met, including cases involving students' residence or family circumstances. Schools unable to comply will have access to dedicated funding for strengthening Italian-language education. The government has allocated 17.5 million euros for such schools, while additional funding is earmarked for extracurricular Italian-language programs.
Another controversial provision requires parents of children facing serious language and integration difficulties to attend free Italian-language courses arranged through social services. Parents who fail to attend can face fines ranging from 200 to 1,000 euros.
The package has nevertheless faced strong opposition from education-sector representatives.
The FLC CGIL teachers' union criticized the decree as a "propagandistic" intervention disconnected from the realities of Italian schools, arguing that it failed to address issues such as teachers' salaries and precarious employment. The DirigentiScuola association of school principals questioned whether the measure could be implemented in practice, particularly after the school year had already begun.
According to Ansa News Agency, the controversy also reflects a broader debate over whether language support and the redistribution of students should be the main tools for integration, or whether a numerical ceiling could create new administrative and logistical problems for schools in areas with high immigrant populations.
The decree forms part of a broader school package that also bans students from attending school activities with their faces covered, including by burqas or niqabs, with fines of 200 to 1,000 euros. When the student is a minor, the fine is imposed on the parents. ■

How a Cloud-Based LMS Can Support Corporate Training at Scale  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:08:45 UTC
22:08:45 KST

Corporate education must reach employees across offices, time zones, job functions, and experience levels. Classroom sessions can create scheduling conflicts, travel expenses, uneven instruction, and incomplete records. Moving training online solves many of these problems, but only when the platform fits the organization's actual needs. Understanding what to look for makes the selection process far more productive.
A cloud-based LMS gives training teams one central location for assigning lessons, updating materials, tracking results, and supporting continued development. The right platform helps organizations expand education programs without matching growth with administrative burden. It also connects employee learning with compliance duties, performance targets, and workforce planning. The sections below cover the key areas where a cloud-based LMS adds measurable value.
A Practical Starting Point
A cloud-based LMS provides access to lessons through an internet connection, regardless of an employee’s location. Training leaders can organize onboarding, safety education, product instruction, and professional development in one controlled environment. Course revisions reach assigned learners without separate emails or printed materials. Before choosing a platform, decision-makers can compare reporting tools, mobile access, security controls, user limits, integration options, and total cost.
One Training Standard
Large companies often deliver identical programs through separate departments or regional offices. That arrangement can produce conflicting guidance, duplicate effort, and incomplete records. A central platform establishes one approved source for policies, procedures, and role-based instruction. Managers can assign a shared curriculum across locations, while local teams add information required by law or operational practice. Employees receive consistent guidance, and administrators gain clearer control over revisions.
Faster Employee Onboarding
New hires need practical information before handling independent duties. An online platform can provide orientation lessons, policy documents, role instruction, and required assessments in a planned sequence. Human resources staff may assign education before the starting date, while supervisors review progress during initial weeks. Automated reminders limit manual follow-up. Early results can reveal where new employees need clarification, additional coaching, or access to a subject expert.
Flexible Access for Every Role
Employees rarely work under identical conditions or schedules. Sales representatives, field technicians, warehouse staff, and service workers may need employee training outside ordinary office hours. Online access allows each person to study through an approved computer, tablet, or mobile device. Short modules can fit between duties, while saved progress prevents repeated work. This arrangement supports participation without requiring every employee to attend one scheduled session.
Smarter Course Administration
Administrative effort increases sharply as enrollment numbers rise. A learning platform can automate assignments, reminders, certificates, renewal notices, and completion records. Training coordinators spend less time maintaining spreadsheets and more time reviewing instructional quality. Rules can connect requirements with departments, locations, job titles, or employment status. New staff members may receive relevant lessons automatically after their information enters the organization’s human resources system.
Clear Performance Reporting
Training decisions require more than completion totals. Useful reports can display assessment results, time spent studying, overdue activities, attendance patterns, and department comparisons. Supervisors can review individual progress without requesting separate updates from coordinators. Training leaders can identify lessons with low pass rates or frequent repeat attempts. Those findings may indicate unclear directions, unsuitable difficulty, weak reference material, or poorly written assessment questions.
Consistent Compliance Control
Regulated industries must demonstrate that employees received required instruction. A learning platform stores records in one location and connects each activity with a learner, course, date, score, and completion status. Renewal rules can help prevent expired qualifications from going unnoticed. Audit teams retrieve documentation faster, while supervisors gain earlier visibility into outstanding obligations. Reliable records reduce uncertainty during internal reviews, inspections, and certification checks.
Content Updates at Scale
Policies, products, and operating procedures may change several times each year. Printed manuals and local files make controlled revisions difficult. A cloud system allows authorized staff to replace lessons, revise assessments, and publish approved versions from one administrative area. Learners receive current material after publication. Version tracking also helps coordinators confirm which employees completed an earlier lesson and who requires the updated assignment.
Better Learning Decisions
A growing company needs evidence before expanding or replacing an education program. Platform data can be compared with business measures such as error rates, customer feedback, sales results, or safety incidents. Training teams can examine outcomes across locations and employee groups. These comparisons cannot prove that instruction caused every improvement. They do provide a stronger basis for reviewing value, identifying knowledge gaps, and setting future priorities.
Support for External Learners
Corporate education may include contractors, partners, distributors, and customers. A learning platform can create separate groups with controlled access, distinct branding, and different completion rules. External users receive relevant material without entering internal employee areas. This structure helps organizations share product guidance, service procedures, and policy information with wider audiences. It also adds reporting options for partner readiness, customer education, and required acknowledgments.
Conclusion
A cloud-based Learning Management System can help companies deliver organized, measurable, and accessible education across a large workforce. Centralized content improves consistency, automation reduces administrative effort, and reporting gives supervisors useful evidence. Flexible access also supports employees with different schedules, locations, and responsibilities. Success depends on selecting a platform that fits business goals, content requirements, user groups, reporting standards, security expectations, and budget limits. With careful planning, corporate education can expand while remaining clear, controlled, and practical.

Feature: Thai teenager Preechayan makes waves on table tennis at Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:08:41 CST
22:08:41 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Thitaphat Preechayan left the table tennis venue with a backpack slung over his shoulders, smiling as he walked away after losing to world No. 1 Wang Chuqin at the Asian Games.
The Thai high school student had spent the previous several days testing himself against some of the world's best table tennis players.
Three days earlier, the 16-year-old, ranked 275th in the world, stunned world No. 8 Lin Shidong 3-2 in the men's team quarterfinals.
Before that match, Preechayan repeatedly watched videos of Lin on social media, studying his opponent before stepping onto the court.
"I was very excited to play against them," Preechayan said. "I thought I couldn't lose. I just played point by point, and finally I won."
On Friday, the teenager took the opening game 11-3 against Wang in the men's singles round of 32 before the Chinese star settled into the match and won 4-2.
"I was fully focused during the match," Preechayan said. "I knew I was going to play against a world-class player, but I wasn't afraid."
"We had never played against each other before, and his ability to beat Lin was beyond what many people expected," Wang admitted. "I attached great importance to this match. I tried to make every point count and played very tightly."
"I feel very happy because I was able to take two games from him," Preechayan said. "But I think I still have to work harder."
Preechayan was born in Bangkok in 2010. He first picked up a table tennis racket at the age of seven after becoming fascinated in the sport by watching his older brother's practice.
His talent became apparent soon. His family decided to homeschool him between the ages of seven and 12, giving him more time to train before he returned to traditional schooling.
It was not long before Sanon Wongkaew, who was then coaching Preechayan's older brother and later joined the Thai national team's coaching staff, took notice and invited the teenager for a tryout.
Preechayan was able to hit topspin on his first attempt. Wongkaew encouraged him to train regularly and enter more competitions, where he soon found himself beating older players.
At 12, he earned a place on Thailand's under-13 national team.
"At that time, I didn't even know what it meant to be on the national team. I just knew I'd been selected," Preechayan said. "The more I competed, the more fun it became, and I loved table tennis even more."
His progress sped up in 2025. He won the U15 mixed doubles title at the ITTF World Youth Championships with Thai teammate Kulapassr Vijitviriyagul, becoming the first Thai to win gold at the event. He also won the U15 boys' singles title at the WTT Youth Contender San Francisco.
Thailand is not traditionally regarded as a table tennis powerhouse, but its national program has placed greater emphasis on developing young players and providing more opportunities for them to train overseas.
Preechayan normally trains at the Thai national team's base at a university. Ahead of the Asian Games, he also spent time training in Jinan, capital of China's Shandong province, gaining first-hand experience of training in the sport's leading nation.
His favorite player is another Chinese player, Fan Zhendong, an Olympic champion known for tenacity.
"I like his style of play," Preechayan said. "His mental strength is very strong."
For now, his ambition is simple but significant: to make his name known to Thai fans and build a career that can leave a mark for Thailand in the years ahead.
"I want to go to the Olympics," he said. "Maybe I can win a medal." ■

A Weekend in Riga Beyond the Sightseeing Checklist  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:08:24 UTC
22:08:24 KST

Riga is easy to approach as a list of landmarks: walk through the Old Town, photograph the best-known buildings and move on. But a short visit becomes more rewarding when there is time to notice how the city fits together. The market, the river, residential streets and evening venues offer a fuller picture than a hurried route between attractions.
Begin on Foot, but Leave Time to Wander
The Old Town is a practical starting point for a first visit. Its compact streets make it possible to explore without a strict itinerary. A short walk can take you from a quiet courtyard to a busy square, then towards the Daugava for a different view of the city.
Rather than trying to see every building in one morning, choose a few places that genuinely interest you. Leave time for a café stop or an unexpected detour. A flexible route is especially useful when the weather changes or a place turns out to deserve more time than planned.
Make the Central Market Part of the Day
Riga Central Market is close to the Old Town and the central transport stations, so it can be part of a walk rather than a separate excursion. It is a working market as well as a visitor attraction: people come to shop for ordinary meals, not only to show travellers local products.
Browse beyond the first stalls you see and pay attention to what is in season. Buying a small snack can make the visit more memorable than treating the market only as a place to photograph. Check current opening hours before setting out, and be considerate of traders and shoppers if you want to take pictures.
Explore a Different Side of Riga’s Architecture
Riga’s Art Nouveau district offers a change of pace from the Old Town. Alberta iela is known for its decorated façades, but the pleasure of the neighbourhood lies in looking closely. Entrances, windows and individual details are easy to miss when you are focused on reaching the next landmark.
A weekend also leaves space for a museum, a concert or a neighbourhood café. Check programmes and opening hours directly with the venue, particularly around public holidays. Having one indoor option in mind is useful if the weather does not cooperate.
Choose an Evening That Suits You
After dark, visitors might keep things simple with dinner and a walk, attend a performance or explore a venue that matches their interests and budget. Nightlife need not be a required part of a city break. The best choice is one you can enjoy without rushing or spending more than planned.
Some travellers also consider gambling among their entertainment options. If that interests you, distinguish between visiting a physical venue and using a website: rules and availability can differ. An online casino comparison can help readers identify questions to ask about licences, payment methods and terms before choosing an operator. It does not replace checking the operator’s current legal status and conditions.
It is also worth distinguishing locally licensed services from foreign online casinos. A licence issued abroad does not automatically mean an operator is authorised in Latvia or available to every visitor. Check the applicable rules and your eligibility, set a spending limit in advance, and never treat gambling as a way to pay for a trip.
Riga works well as a weekend destination because a visitor does not need to do everything. A market visit, two neighbourhood walks and one well-chosen evening activity can leave a clearer impression than an overfilled schedule. Keep some of the trip unscripted and give the city time to be more than a checklist.

The company managed to reduce its losses by almost half, reaching 10.9 million euros, as opposed to losses of 18.3 million euros a year earlier. The company continues to invest and develop its network of stores in the country.
Salary growth and “Top Employer” rating
The company’s successful results are ensured by an efficient and talented team, whose salary growth and qualification improvement are constantly invested in. In the 2025 financial year, “Lidl Latvija” increased employees’ salaries in stores and the logistics center, investing an additional 3.2 million euros, and keeping promise to pay the highest average salaries in the food retail industry.
Systematic attention to improving working conditions yields results and international recognition – this year, “Lidl Latvija” has received the prestigious “Top Employer 2026” and “Top Employer 2026 Europe” certificates for the fourth year in a row.
About “Lidl”
Lidl, part of the Schwarz Group based in Neckarsulm (Germany), is one of the largest food retailers in Germany and Europe. With more than 13,000 stores and 230 logistics centers, Lidl currently operates in 31 countries, employing around 395,000 people. Lidl's sales in the 2025 financial year reached 140.2 billion euros.
Lidl offers its customers high-quality products and goods at the best price. Everyday life in its stores, logistics centers and offices is characterized by simplicity and process orientation. In its daily operations, Lidl takes responsibility for people, society and the environment. For us, sustainability also means that we prove our promise of quality standards with our work every day.
SIA “Lidl Latvija” was established in February 2018 and opened its store network in Latvia on October 7, 2021. Currently, the Lidl Latvija network has 39 stores in 16 cities in Latvia. Microsoft abandons personal AI chatbot race with Copilot reboot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:08:00 UTC
22:08:00 KST

Microsoft abandons personal AI chatbot race with Copilot reboot
- Microsoft has merged its consumer and workplace Copilot AI assistants into one product focused on corporate customers, exiting the personal chatbot market dominated by OpenAI, Google, and Meta.
- The new Copilot app improves workplace productivity by allowing editing in Word and Excel, includes a coding assistant, and rebrands the Scout assistant as Autopilot.
- Microsoft’s shift reflects user demand for AI tools that enhance work tasks, with over 30 million subscriptions already and plans to integrate personal Copilot features into enterprise use.
AI generated
Microsoft is merging the consumer and workplace versions of its Copilot AI assistant into one product aimed at corporate customers, ceding the crowded market for personal chatbots to OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and, now, Meta Platforms.
At an event in Seattle earlier this week, Microsoft executives gave a few dozen business and technology leaders a preview of what they are calling the new Copilot. The result of a six-month engineering effort, the latest iteration of the assistant has absorbed the separate version for home use, adopting some of its slick design features, and casting aside the marketing that sought to position the company as a builder of personal AI.
People have high expectations for workplace software, informed by their experience with smartphone apps, Jacob Andreou, who leads product development of the unified Copilot app, told the audience of corporate customers on Sept 23. Importing some user experience features from the consumer app “made Copilot so much better in just the last few months”, he said.
Microsoft’s individual users, Andreou added, tend to be people who like to poke around in PowerPoint and Excel, and are more interested in “the full power that we offer to enterprise users” than a simplified chat app.
The updated software, announced on Sept 25, gives users the ability to edit Word or Excel documents within a Copilot app or browser tab, addressing a common gripe that Microsoft’s assistant had only limited reach into the company’s own productivity software.
There is also a tab for a coding assistant to enable regular users to put together dashboards or automate tasks. Microsoft’s Scout, an always-on assistant that co-workers can summon, is joining the Copilot package too, rebranded as Autopilot.
The new Copilot, which will roll out in the coming weeks, brings to a close one of Microsoft’s biggest bets of the AI era. Two years ago, executives formed separate teams to build two assistants – one for the workplace and one for home. Having helped OpenAI bring ChatGPT to the world, Microsoft bet that its own consumer assistant could win over a new set of customers and tapped AI industry veteran Mustafa Suleyman to lead the effort.
It quickly became an uphill battle when ChatGPT sprinted to a billion users and Google deployed its Gemini personal assistant to the vast Android ecosystem. Comparatively few people took Microsoft up on its offer of a personal chatbot. Suleyman in March ceded his Copilot product development responsibilities to Andreou, a former Snap executive.
Microsoft’s retreat coincides with the arrival of Meta’s Muse, a personal assistant that can act on users’ behalf and has raced to the top of the app download charts.
In interviews this week, Andreou and Charles Lamanna, an executive who oversees Microsoft teams working on some of Copilot’s core workplace features, said Muse’s success proved people were receptive to AI automation. Microsoft’s opportunity, they said, is to bring similar capabilities to office workers.
“We’re not going to build a Copilot that’s like your personal companion,” Lamanna said. (In April 2025, Suleyman had laid out Microsoft’s ambitions for Copilot in those very terms, standing in front of an enormous video screen introducing “Your AI Companion”.)
“That’s just not what people want from Microsoft,” Lamanna said. “We help you get stuff done.”
Andreou said many of the features of the personal Copilot, including specialised tools for health questions, studying or surfacing news and information, were incorporated into the rebuilt product. “In this unified Copilot, you actually still have all of these amazing consumer verticals and all of these kind of bespoke experiences,” he said.
Some other features included in the personal Copilot, including custom podcasts and an animated blob of an avatar that popped up during conversations, have been retired. Anthropomorphic touches live on in the new Autopilot bots, which appear as smiling shapes when they are invoked in a Teams chat or e-mail.
Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella compared the shift in office work brought about by automated AI services to the personal computer’s displacement of inter-office memos and faxes. “That was not just about our new digital tools,” he said at this week’s event. “It was a complete, new way to conceptualise how that business process trajectory worked. That’s what’s happening around Copilot.”
Companies were paying for more than 30 million Copilot subscriptions as at the end of June. And while individual users are free to use limited versions of Copilot’s chat experience, its most powerful tools are reserved for subscribers to the company’s M365 apps bundle, which has about 90 million paying users.
David McLaren, who leads data and AI work at GHD, a Canadian engineering and professional services firm that is part of a Microsoft programme for early adopters of AI tools, said employees were turning to Copilot for summaries of conference calls and help managing e-mail, as well as work putting together pitches and analysis for clients. “It will get you off the white, blank page,” he said.
GHD started using Copilot in late 2023 with a 300-person trial, and has since rolled out the tool to all of its 12,000 employees.
“I’m amazed by the use cases,” McLaren said. “They’re all over the place.” BLOOMBERG
