21:01:00 KST

New Air Force, Pentagon, and White House initiatives are taking a new swing at an issue that has long frustrated military families: barriers to spouse employment.
Unemployment and underemployment have plagued military spouses for years, with the unemployment rate among military spouses holding steady at around 20 percent—despite initiatives to promote spouse preferences for hiring on base, support for remote work, and advocacy for making professional licenses more portable across state borders.
Improving spouses employment is not a “charitable initiative,” but a major retention and readiness incentive, argued Lyndsey Akers, a consultant with AFA’s United Forces & Families program.
“When military spouses have greater access to meaningful and sustainable careers, we strengthen the economic stability of military families,” Akers said at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last week. “We support the conditions that enable continued service, and we connect employers with an experienced, adaptable, and often overlooked talent pool.”
Top-down interest from the White House’s new Military Spouse Commission is driving renewed interest in the topic.
Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Military Community and Family Policy Stephen Simmons said at the conference that the nation “has admired” the problem for too long; but “we haven’t done enough about it, and to get an issue the attention it needs, usually, first off, you have to elevate.”
Cindy Wilsbach, wife of Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach and a senior writer for presidential correspondence at the White House employee, said the new commission President Donald Trump’s interest.
“It was marching orders from the leader of the free world to say, ‘We see the military spouse family and we recognize there are some longstanding generational problems that we need to get after,’” Cindy Wilsbach said during a panel discussion.
Both Wilsbachs are members of the commission, as are all the service chiefs, their spouses, and their senior enlisted advisors, and their spouses, including:
- Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas A. Schiess and his wife Debbie Schiess
- Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David Wolfe and his wife, Dr. Doniel Wolfe
- Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John F. Bentivegna and his wife Cathy Bentivegna
“With the four spouses here going to be involved with the Military Spouse Commission, we’ve got an opportunity to make some real change to laws that prevent us from hiring people fast enough and putting people into jobs and places and moving positions around,” said CMSAF David Wolfe during a panel discussion.
Cindy Wilsbach said the commission won’t try to reinvent efforts already underway but instead “will add to the work that’s being done,” while raising the profile of the issue to give advocates access to the President and other high-level decision-makers.
Global Military Spouse Connection
One program that’s newly in place and starting to grow is the Air Force’s Global Military Spouse Connection, which started in June as a pilot program for just a few installations.
Officials say the program is meant to serve as a “bridge” between Active-Duty military spouses who have PCSed to a new location and local hiring managers.
“Using career field administrators, GMSC creates a structured, active pipeline to connect the military spouse talent pool with employment opportunities,” according to an Air Force release.
“We are assisting hiring managers in finding the best-qualified individual,” said career field administrator Wyteeshia McRoberts, in a statement. “We’re not contacting them to do favors. We are looking at resumes, seeing what they qualify for and making recommendations for the right jobs.”
CMSAF Wolfe highlighted the program in his Sept. 14 keynote address to the conference, noting how the program “went from idea to first action in only 60 days,” and promising rapid expansion. On Sept. 22, the Air Force announced the program was already available for spouses moving to the following locations:
- Luke Air Force Base, Ariz.
- Goodfellow Air Force Base, Texas
- Laughlin Air Force Base, Texas
- Mountain Home Air Force Base, Idaho
- Travis Air Force Base, Calif.
- Patrick Space Force Base, Fla.
- Ramstein Air Base, Germany
- RAF Croughton, U.K.
- RAF Mildenhall, U.K.
- RAF Lakenheath, U.K.
- RAF Feltwell, U.K.
- Kadena Air Base, Japan
SpouseWorks
While the Department of the Air Force has launched the new connection program, the Office of the Secretary of Defense is focused on better publicizing the programs it already has, said Simmons.
Until recently, spouses looking for Pentagon help to land jobs, scholarships, or fellowships were on their own navigating a confusing sea of acronyms: SECO, MyCAA, MSEP.
SECO stood for Spouse Education and Career Opportunities, but wasn’t visible enough to leaders or community members, Simmons said. So his team rebranded to “SpouseWorks” and changed the organization. Before, the program “was buried in one of our directorships through no fault of their own,” Simmons said. “But in my mind, … it needed to report directly to me, so we turned it from a sub-office to a directorship.”
Other programs were folded in, so that now there are also SpouseWorks Fellowship and SpouseWorks Scholarship programs. “We’re trying to make it very simple and easy to use.”
SpouseWorks offers training, education, and professional development; career coaches; and a job board. Simmons said the goal is to be a one-stop shop for military spouses and a resource for employers seeking high-quality employees.
Early returns are promising. “We’re up well over 50 to 80 percent usage year over year,” he said. “And we’re only about halfway through the first year of the SpouseWorks rebrand.”
Challenges Remain
Headwinds continue, however. “I wish we could say that we had a lot of consistency, but what happens is with every change of leadership, somebody has a bright idea and then a great program goes away,” said Sue Luangkhot Hoppin, president of the National Military Spouse Network. “We don’t dot the Is and cross the Ts and we don’t necessarily solidify the programs before we move on to the next one.”
Lack of consistency from base to base, due to different commanders’ priorities, is also a challenge, he said. Elevating the issue to department leaders can raise the profile and relieve operational commanders of an extra burden.
One policy change that had unintended consequences for families was the widespread rollback of remote work options for federal civilians. Because of frequent PCS moves, remote work is an ideal option for many military spouses. “Remote work is a lifeline for a lot of military spouses,” Luangkhot Hoppin said. “It allows them to work even if they have childcare issues. But if they have to go back to the office, all of a sudden they need to have access to affordable child care, and that’s become an issue.”
Liz O’Brien, senior vice president at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation, argued that remote work is only a piece of the equation, noting that during the COVID-19 pandemic, when remote work options surged, spouse unemployment stayed stubbornly high. Childcare is one of the biggest barriers to better spouse employment, O’Brien, Luangkhot Hoppin, and Simmons agreed. Simmons sees an “intrinsic relationship” between the two; without ready and available childcare, many spouses can’t work. If they have to wait months for childcare openings to materialize, their window for employment can begin to close down.
Simmons said the Pentagon is working multiple fronts to reduce the wait times for childcare, both through expanded capacity at its Child Development Centers as well as through partnerships with the Armed Forces YMCA, private industry, and support for informal childcare support.
“Year over year … our childcare wait lists are down 25 percent, which is phenomenal,” Simmons said. And the tie to spouse employment is clear. “As a result, you see that wait list drop, you also see the spouse employment drop.”

It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

In recent weeks, concerns about AI have forged unlikely alliances in the tech and policy worlds. Tech moguls such as Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis joined Dario Amodei, Satya Nadella and Bill Gates in sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI and called for a slowdown of the technology’s development despite years of racing for dominance. The senator Bernie Sanders teamed up with Steve Bannon to urge Congress to regulate AI, which has become one of the very few issues to unite Americans across the political spectrum.
The latest moves were sparked in part by the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s warnings on Twitter/X that AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and believe that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
The reality is, we don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing.
Bill Gates’s nearly 6,000-word essay in late August warning about AI and its potential harms to humanity doesn’t come as a surprise. One of us has been a Microsoft employee for nearly a decade, witnessing all the dangers unfold in real time. Together, we’ve spent the past two years organizing with other Microsoft employees and activists to uncover the company’s role in the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza. We have collectively called on Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military.
But it’s not just Microsoft that is involved in AI-driven destruction.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza was a testing ground for the use of AI in warfare and the results were deeply disturbing. Israel’s military used AI to identify people to kill, with 12,000 targets generated and bombed in the first month alone. This was done with little to no meaningful human oversight, as documented in an investigation by Oscar-winning Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham, whose latest film NAZA, a Guardian-produced film, includes chilling testimonials by the soldiers involved.
Earlier this year in Iran, the US military launched an AI-involved airstrike that hit Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, killing 156 children, teachers and other civilians. The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied on faulty data.
The horrors wrought by AI aren’t limited to people overseas – they’re already being felt by vulnerable communities in the US The Department of Homeland Security is using AI tools – including Microsoft’s Azure – to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants at a massive scale. Law enforcement agencies nationwide are deploying facial recognition technology despite evidence of algorithmic bias that has led to the wrongful arrest and incarceration of Latino and Black Americans. The NYPD also partnered with Microsoft to build its Domain Awareness System, using Azure to connect to 18,000 security cameras, according to the New York Daily News, creating a mass surveillance system that has expanded to Georgia and other parts of the world, including Brazil and Singapore. Datacenters that power AI are being built in rural and low-income neighborhoods throughout the US where many are living under the poverty line and are now facing significant health threats from air pollution caused by these facilities.
Though many of these harms have been documented over the years, rightwing government leaders are continuing to shut down dissent through dishonest and draconian measures. Donald Trump has called AI risks a “hoax” and said any attempts to limit the power of the technology were part of a “sick conspiracy”. House Republicans have dismissed the public’s concerns about AI, blaming Chinese government disinformation for public opposition to datacenters. Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, has threatened to revoke the citizenship of NAZA film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
One thing is clear: the dangerous future that Gates, Amodei, and others are warning us about is already here, and we must act now to prevent further harm. Those of us with families in Gaza, Lebanon, Iran and US neighborhoods terrorized by ICE already know people living through the nightmare.
In the last few weeks, we’ve seen promising efforts from US policymakers attempting to curtail the potential harms of AI technology. The House recently proposed the Frontier Act to embed third-party evaluators within tech companies to conduct safety assessments, and earlier this month, Sanders and the representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act to stop tech leaders from building and developing technologies that humans cannot control.
These bills are a good starting point. But they could take years to pass and don’t address the devastation already being caused. Frontier AI companies and governments must act now to ban the selling and use of AI technologies in military targeting, autonomous weapons systems, and mass surveillance. This is what employees from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind are calling for.
We are living through a precious and fleeting moment when we can still confront the harms AI has already caused to the most vulnerable and course-correct before they become irreversible, spreading into more communities. We need to establish clear guardrails right now and shape the future of AI so that it protects everyone, not just a privileged few.
- 
  Mohamed Hussein organizes with No Azure for Apartheid, an employee-led movement calling on Microsoft to end its involvement with the Israeli military. He is also a leader in Palestinians and Allies at Microsoft, an internal employee group.
- 
  Granate Kim works with No Azure for Apartheid and is the Campaigns Director at MPower Change, an organization that mobilizes Muslim communities in defense of human rights.

DNA database of UK dogs could help police collar criminals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

From tracking criminals to sniffing out drugs, dogs have long helped police crack cases. Now experts are hoping a database of canine DNA could offer vital leads.
While hair, saliva and other canine material may be found at crime scenes, or on individuals connected to incidents, scientists say they are often not fully investigated.
Yet such traces could provide valuable clues, from the identity of a canine perpetrator to evidence a dog’s owner was present at a crime scene.
“You might have a human case, kidnapping, for example,” said Prof Denise Syndercombe Court, a forensics expert at King’s College London who is leading the work. “Lots of us have dogs. We live with dogs all the time. And so if you can identify canine material associated with a crime like that, then that can be very powerful in being able to provide intelligence to help solve a human case where there’s no other evidence.”
As a result, researchers at King’s College London and the Royal Veterinary College have teamed up to harness the potential of canine DNA.
It is not without its challenges.
“Forensically, we don’t have loads of DNA,” said Syndercombe Court. “You have a few cells that are left at a crime scene … So you’ve got to make something useful out of that.”
One approach is similar to that employed in the forensic analysis of human DNA, which is to focus on very small segments called short tandem repeats (STRs).
This technique involves looking at the number of times these small segments are repeated in the DNA, resulting in two numbers for each STR – one inherited from each parent.
Syndercombe Court noted the set of numbers provided a virtually unique profile – be it for a human or a dog. What is more, in dogs some sets of numbers are more common in some breeds than others.
By focusing on STRs the team has built a database covering 80 different breeds – the first of its kind in the UK. For the 10 most common breeds, including labradors, cocker spaniels and miniature schnauzers, samples were taken from at least 50 dogs of each breed.
The upshot is that canine DNA from a crime scene can be analysed and the results either compared with those from a particular dog – allowing that animal to be confirmed or ruled out as being linked to a crime – or screened against the database, potentially allowing experts to identify the breed of dog from which it came.
The latter could be particularly useful where the dog thought to be linked to a crime is unknown, or where samples cannot be taken from a canine suspect, or where the sample does not match the DNA of a dog under suspicion.
Syndercombe Court said her team now hoped to expand their database to include breeds such as pitbull terriers, American XL bullies and Japanese tosas that are banned in the UK.
While the STR analysis focuses on DNA from the nucleus of a cell, the team have also created a database using another approach: sequencing DNA from within mitochondria – the tiny structures that power cells.
With many mitochondria per cell, this approach can be useful where there is very little material to work with – although it is more limited as this DNA is only passed from mother to offspring.
The focus on doggy DNA has already offered insights for police investigations. In one case, the approach shed light on whether serious injuries sustained by a man were down to another person – as he claimed – or occurred when he tripped over his own dogs as they attacked the accused.
Forensic analysis supported the latter. “We looked at the T-shirt [of the accused] and there were holes in the T-shirt,” Syndercombe Court said, adding the team also found DNA from two different dogs on the garment.
In another case, the DNA analysis shed light on a sheep attack.
“We got some decent DNA from the crime scene, and the police thought it was a particular person’s dogs,” said Syndercombe Court.
However the DNA from those dogs did not match the DNA recovered from the crime scene.
“So we were not only able to exclude his dogs, which were of a particular breed, but also say the breed of dog that [did] this attack was very likely to be [another breed],” said Syndercombe Court.
Dr Nicholas Dawnay, an expert in forensics at Liverpool John Moores University – who was not involved in the work – said research assessing how best to use canine DNA collected from crime scenes was hugely important.
“Whether it is a dog attacking a human or livestock or wildlife species, the ability to match the individual dog back to the attack is the primary goal. Obtaining breed information at the early stages of an investigation may help narrow down the pool of possible dogs, which is exciting,” he said.
But Dawnay said a big challenge remained regarding the funding of canine forensic casework: “Police budgets are stretched and without effective funding, the benefits of this research may struggle to be realised.”

Cocktail of the week: Eleanore’s apple highball – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

I adore calvados, and this highball was built off the back of a love for calvados and tonic. This refreshing aperitif expands on that idea andfeels really quite sophisticated in comparison.
Apple highball
Serves 1
For the apple syrup
250g eating apples, washed – we use braeburns
250g caster sugar
For the drink 
25ml calvados – we use Avallen
20ml Lillet Blanc 
15ml apple syrup (see above and method)
15ml fresh lemon juice
   1 dash orange bitters – we use Regans’
1 dash champagne, to taste
1 dash tonic water, to taste
1 twist lemon zest, to finish
First make the syrup. Dice the apples, core, peel and all, put them in a saucepan, and add the sugar and 100ml water. Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring, for about 10 minutes, until the apples are soft and the sugar has dissolved. Fine strain into a clean jar, seal and store in the fridge, where the syrup will keep for up to four weeks (it’s also lovely diluted with sparkling water).
To build the drink, put all the liquids bar the champagne and tonic into a cocktail tin filled with ice and give it a short shake. Strain into a small chilled highball glass filled with fresh ice and top with a dash each of champagne and tonic. Give it a quick stir, squeeze the lemon zest over the top, to express the oils (if you like, drop it into the drink afterwards), and serve.
- 
  Johanna Cole, general manager, Eleanore, Edinburgh

A baby girl appears to alter a father’s relationship priorities in one highly specific way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:07 UTC
21:00:07 KST

Having a daughter appears to shift a father’s focus toward maintaining a strong romantic relationship with the child’s mother. The research suggests that fathers of daughters show higher levels of commitment and relationship satisfaction compared to fathers of sons. These findings, published in Personality and Individual Differences, provide evidence that a child’s sex can influence a father’s psychology in ways that promote long-term family stability.
The foundation of this research rests on paternal investment theory, a framework suggesting that fathers serve as an early model of male behavior for their children. For daughters in particular, a father’s presence and level of involvement provide information about whether men in the broader social environment are reliable and likely to invest in long-term relationships. When a father is absent or uninvolved, daughters tend to adjust their expectations and sexual strategies to fit a world where male support is unpredictable.
For instance, a 2003 longitudinal study found that girls who grew up with an absent father were more likely to engage in early sexual activity and experience teenage pregnancy. Along similar lines, a study covered by PsyPost in 2016 indicated that an earlier age of father absence is linked to a higher number of casual sexual encounters during college. Another line of research, such as a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, has found that father absence during specific developmental windows is associated with accelerated physical maturation, including an earlier onset of puberty.
Because daughters bear the higher physical costs of pregnancy and childcare, their reproductive success is especially sensitive to signs of reliable male support. The researchers hypothesized that having a daughter might prompt fathers to maintain a stronger pair-bond with the mother. By demonstrating a stable relationship, fathers model reliable male investment, which might encourage daughters to delay reproduction and seek out committed partners.
“But no prior study had looked at the reverse, the impact having a daughter has on a man,” Kristina M. Durante, a professor of marketing and research fellow at the Center for Women in Business at Rutgers Business School, told PsyPost. “This was a significant gap, especially given that one of the leading theories for why father absence negatively impacts daughters is because fathers send a message to a daughter about what to expect from a future partner.” The research, led by Krystal Duarte alongside Durante, aimed to test whether fathers of daughters display stronger pair-bond motivation than fathers of sons.
To investigate this dynamic, the researchers conducted three separate studies. In the first study, the team surveyed 184 parents with a single child under the age of 18. The sample included 101 fathers and 83 mothers. Participants completed questionnaires assessing their emotional attachment to their partner and various components of their relationship quality, such as satisfaction, commitment, and trust.
The results indicated that fathers of daughters reported stronger attachment bonds to the child’s mother than fathers of sons. On a 9-point scale measuring attachment strength, fathers with daughters averaged a score of 8.04, compared to 7.37 for fathers of sons. Fathers of daughters also reported higher levels of relationship commitment, satisfaction, and trust. In contrast, mothers’ reports of relationship quality and attachment did not differ based on whether they had a son or a daughter.
For the second study, the researchers analyzed data from a large, long-term project called the Fragile Families and Child Wellbeing Study. This dataset allowed them to examine how mothers perceived their partners’ behavior over several years, from the child’s birth up to age nine. The final sample included 587 couples. The team measured both partner-directed support, such as showing affection and fairness toward the mother, and parenting-focused support, such as cooperating on childcare rules.
Mothers who had a daughter reported receiving more partner-directed support from fathers shortly after childbirth compared to mothers who had a son. This difference in romantic relationship support was specific to the parents’ dynamic as a couple, as the researchers found no differences in general parenting or co-parenting behaviors based on the child’s sex. Additionally, fathers’ perceptions of the mothers’ supportiveness did not vary depending on whether they had a boy or a girl.
“Outside of finding that daughters have an impact on dads, we were surprised and delighted to see that dads of daughters were reported to be better partners by the mother,” Durante noted. “So, this isn’t just dad ‘reporting’ that he is a more committed partner, moms are feeling that commitment through his behavior.” Over time, the gap in partner support between fathers of daughters and fathers of sons appeared to narrow as the children grew older.
The third study aimed to rule out the possibility that preexisting personality differences between men who have daughters and men who have sons were driving the results. The researchers tracked 168 first-time parent couples from their third trimester of pregnancy through the first two years of their child’s life. Participants reported on their relationship satisfaction, romantic attachment styles, and feelings about childcare at multiple points before and after the birth.
Before the babies were born, there were no differences in relationship quality or attachment between the expectant fathers of sons and those expecting daughters. After childbirth, however, fathers of daughters reported greater relationship satisfaction and provided more support to their partners. They also showed decreases in attachment anxiety, meaning they became more secure and less worried about their relationship.
Meanwhile, fathers of sons tended to become more avoidant, pulling away emotionally, and less satisfied with their relationship over time. Once again, these shifts were specific to the romantic pair-bond, as satisfaction with childcare duties did not change based on the child’s sex. By tracking these changes across the transition to parenthood, the study provides evidence that the birth of a daughter directly relates to a reconfiguration of a father’s romantic motivations.
“Having a daughter seems to shift dads toward greater investment in their relationship with the child’s mother, not just toward the kid, but toward the marriage/partnership itself,” Durante explained. “This showed up across three different methods (self-report, partner-report over time, and before-vs-after having the baby), which is what makes it compelling: it’s not just ‘dads of daughters say nice things,’ it’s that fathers’ actual relationship behavior appears to change after a daughter is born.”
“These are small-to-medium effects, which means differences of about half a standard deviation on measures like commitment and relationship satisfaction, not full standard deviations,” she added. “The effect isn’t large enough to predict any single father’s behavior, but it’s consistent enough, showing up across three independent studies using different methods, to suggest something real and biologically patterned is going on beneath the surface.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “It’s not that dads love daughters more than sons,” Durante clarified. “It’s not that fathers of sons are bad partners. Sons’ fathers didn’t get worse, so much as daughters’ fathers showed a distinctive uptick in pair-bond-focused behavior.”
“This is an effect we found in the US and may not translate to other non-Western populations,” Durante pointed out. In societies where fathers are less involved in daily family life, or in places with a strong cultural preference for sons, the effects of a child’s sex on a father’s relationship behavior might look quite different. The research also focused on heterosexual couples, leaving it an open question whether similar dynamics exist in non-heterosexual partnerships.
Future studies could explore the exact biological or social mechanisms that relate to this shift in fathers. For instance, the transition to fatherhood is known to correspond with drops in testosterone, which encourages caregiving. However, it is not yet known if having a daughter influences these hormonal changes more than having a son. Exploring how the sex of multiple siblings interacts to influence a father’s relationship behavior could also provide a more detailed picture of family dynamics.
“We are continuing to look at how a person’s early experience with mom and dad impacts their behavior in adulthood,” Durante said. “We are looking closely at how moms may differentially influence the development of sons versus daughters.”
“Becoming a father to a daughter may recalibrate a man’s relationship priorities, nudging him to be a more visibly committed partner, possibly because daughters are especially attuned to what their father’s relationship teaches them about what to expect for a future partner,” she concluded.
The study, “Daughters promote pair-bonding in fathers in modern Western cultures,” was authored by Krystal Duarte, Kristina M. Durante, Jeffrey Gassen, Americus Reed, Steven Rholes, and Jeffry A. Simpson.

Mahershala Ali Balances Tenderness and Swagger in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

No one really wants to talk about religious rage, the complex resentment when you feel your God has abandoned you: We like our faith to be tidy and count-your-blessings clean, not clouded with doubt and fury. In writer-director Bassam Tariq’s action thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, Mahershala Ali plays Latif, a Houston, Texas, hit man who’s also, ostensibly, a devout Muslim: He strives to be a man of faith even as he’s breaking bones (and more) in the name of Allah. Then his wife dies suddenly, making him a single dad with three kids to care for, teenager Fatiha (Adia), her younger brother Qadir (Jahleel Kamara), and an infant, Aziza, who can’t tolerate baby formula; only her mother’s breast milk will do, and supplies are quickly running out. That’s a workaday problem Latif has got to solve, and prayer takes a backseat to his feelings of betrayal. “You take her from me,” he rages in voiceover, “and you expect me to bow down to you?”
A crisis of faith and a desperate search for breast milk: As plot drivers go, that’s a pretty novel combination, but Tariq and Ali pull it off here. The tone is equal parts sacred, profane, and comical. Tariq opens the film with a skull-crushing action sequence in which Latif, dressed in swirling robes, beats the heck out of a baddie in a public bathroom; the sequence is exhilarating and brutal, not least because Ali, wrapped in quasi-Samurai warrior garb and wielding a menacing knife, makes such a dashing, beguiling figure. When his wife dies, he realizes his priorities must shift toward his family, but he can’t free himself from his longtime boss Mike (Laith Nakli), who has a special job for him: Mike’s porn-king nephew Hatty (Abubakr Ali) is being harassed by a (Christian) religious fanatic, Pastor Hwan Yoon (John Cho). Can Tariq take care of that? He can—but meanwhile, baby Aziza is yowling with hunger, and it turns out that a sex worker formerly in Hatty’s stable, Tiffany Boone’s Fugazi, is lactating and has a bountiful supply of what baby needs. If Latif’s life of spirituality mingled with bloody violence seemed complicated before, it has now entered the realm of the surreal.
Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is most entertaining when it indulges its tawdry side. Hatty, with his tacky sex mansion and bevy of "halal-certified" cuties, is a particularly clever invention, and Cho, decked out in spangled western shirts and sporting a row of gold teeth, appears to be having a blast as a sleazy operator who’s more interested in power than in Jesus. The action sequences are sharp and swift. In his quest for milk, his tiny daughter strapped snugly to his chest, Ali’s Latif is a new kind of action hero. (Some of the movie’s visuals echo the climactic baby-rescue scene of John Woo’s magnificent Hard Boiled, in which Chow Yun Fat descends the wall of a multi-story hospital building while fending off a hail of bullets, even as he cradles a gurgling mite with one arm.)
But Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother also tangles with complex issues of faith. It’s clear that Latif’s daughter Fatiha, who breaks fast when she shouldn’t and has a crush on one of the family’s young Mormon neighbors, is straying from the path. But the movie doesn’t judge her for it. The suggestion is that doubt is part of faith—you can’t have the second without the occasional tension of the first—and even Latif will have to face that crisis.
The Pakistani-born Tariq previously co-directed (with Omar Mullick) the 2013 documentary These Birds Walk, and he was one of the filmmakers in talks to direct the ill-fated Marvel reboot of Blade, with Ali set to star. In a world where blessings, even mixed ones, are sparse, it’s not a terrible thing that Ali was saved from potentially being chewed up by a Marvel vehicle; he’s a superb actor who deserves better, and Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother gives him plenty to work with. The movie’s title refers to a hadith in which a man approaches the Prophet Muhammad and asks, “To whom should I give the best of me?” The prophet’s answer, so emphatic he repeats it three times, is “Your mother”; only when the man asks the question for a fourth time does the prophet respond, “Your father.” As Latif, Ali captures the spirit of the movie’s title: he seems powered by a contradictory blend of male privilege and humility. Early on, he sees, as if for the first time, the little notes his wife had left all over the house, reminders for herself and the kids of all the minuscule things that need to be taken care of in a household. She had handled all these tasks quietly, and seemingly with ease. Now those things—essentially women’s work—are left to him, including sustaining an infant who needs something he can’t provide.
As Latif, always spoiling for a fight, Ali swaggers through the film. But there’s another man inside, a gentle, God-fearing one, and that’s the one you see in the somber beauty of Ali’s eyes. Out of necessity, Latif needs to reconcile with his feminine side. Suddenly, he’s both father and mother, and he finds that filling the role of the latter is the greater challenge. It’s the tenderness he carries within that makes Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother both distinctive and thought provoking. The thrills are just a fringe benefit.

Nepal PM urges climate justice after ‘Himalayan tsunami’ devastates country

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25

21:00:00 KST

Nepal PM urges climate justice after ‘Himalayan tsunami’ devastates country
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah brought a stark warning from the Himalayas to the UN General Assembly on Thursday, saying catastrophic floods that killed at least 1,400 people in his country laid bare the human cost of climate change, and the failure of the international system to protect those least responsible for it.
Addressing the general debate of the Assembly’s 81st session, Mr. Shah said the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster four weeks earlier in northern Nepal had swept through mountain communities with a ferocity described as a “Himalayan Tsunami”.
More than 6,000 people remain missing and damage is estimated at around 10 per cent of Nepal’s gross domestic product (GDP).
“The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world,” he said. “And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?”
Climate justice
Mr. Shah said a warming climate was destabilizing the Himalayan ecosystem, with melting permafrost contributing to unstable mountain slopes and increasing the risks of avalanches, floods and landslides.
The devastation, he added, extended across Nepal’s border with China and downstream towards India.
“Climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports.”
Nepal contributes less than 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions, he said, yet disasters repeatedly destroy infrastructure and livelihoods and force the country to borrow to rebuild.
“Climate Justice cannot just remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations document,” he said.
The Prime Minister proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China to share satellite data and expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, strengthen early-warning systems and coordinate cross-border disaster assistance.
He also called for greater grant-based climate financing, arguing that the Loss and Damage Fund, Global Environment Facility and other mechanisms remain “grossly inadequate”.
“When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete fifty forms. We act,” he said.
Broken logistics for food
Broadening his address, Mr. Shah noted that climate vulnerability was exposing deeper inequalities in the international system, where poorer countries face disruptions caused by conflicts and decisions beyond their control.
He contrasted shortages of fertilizer, fuel and road-building materials in Nepal with the speed at which weapons move around the world.
“We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food,” he said.
Countries like Nepal face a similar predicament, he added: “hit by the climate we did not warm and hit again by the wars we did not start.”
Yet Mr. Shah said those failures strengthened rather than diminished Nepal’s commitment to multilateralism.
“This is why we continue to believe in multilateralism,” he said. “This is why we need a United Nations in which the presence of small poor countries is felt, and we can work together towards just outcomes.”
A new generation
Mr. Shah also linked his international message to political change at home, saying Nepal had arrived at the General Assembly with a renewed democratic mandate reflecting the aspirations of a new generation.
“Our youth have demanded a politics of integrity and accountability,” he said. “This generational shift is not only a national story. It is part of a global awakening against conflicts, inequities, and lack of opportunities.”
Calling for investment in resilience, stronger infrastructure, early-warning systems and reduced dependence on fossil fuels, the Mr. Shah ended by returning to the warning from the Himalayas.
“And when the next warning comes from the rooftop of the world: Let us be ready to hear it, and ready to act.”

Africa needs its own AI solutions, not borrowed ones, says expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Africa needs its own AI solutions, not borrowed ones, says expert
Africa should focus its use of technology on solving its own real challenges rather than copying the systems and priorities of other parts of the world.
That’s the opinion of one of the expert members of the UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, Girmaw Abebe Tadesse, who leads Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab in Kenya.
In an exclusive interview with UN News in Nairobi, Mr. Tadesse said the first step for the continent is to identify key problems that need to be addressed before deciding on the type of technology, infrastructure and data needed.
The interview took place as world leaders, policy experts and top AI executives met at UN Headquarters in New York during High-Level Week where greater attention is being focused on how the frontier technology can be safely managed for the benefit of all.
Problem-solving approach
Mr. Tadesse believes that African countries should adopt an approach that takes into account the challenges their citizens face every day.
“We are trying to bring the reality of our environment and integrate AI technology with the local problems we face. It is important to ask ourselves what problems we want to solve first,” he said.
He explained that after identifying these challenges, an assessment should be made of the type of infrastructure, technology and data needed to provide solutions.
Collaboration and diversity
He stressed the importance of collaboration between governments, higher education institutions, development partners, creative communities and technology companies.
He said that stakeholders should share knowledge, experience and expertise to create solutions that meet the African environment even in a situation of limited resources.
“When we bring together diverse stakeholders, we can use existing knowledge and wisdom to produce solutions needed by our communities,” he explained.
Role for African youth
The expert added that the rapid growth of technology and the large number of young people in Africa represent an opportunity that can make the continent an important hub for AI innovation in the world.
“Many young people are already using technology to solve the challenges of their communities, while there are also investors and development partners willing to support these efforts,” he said.
In his view, this mix of passionate young people, technology innovators and development partners makes Africa an ideal place for collaboration in building development-oriented AI systems.
Cooperation is key
However, Mr. Tadesse warned that the continent needs to accelerate cooperation between countries and its institutions to avoid duplicating work already done by others.
“There is a need for African countries to collaborate more, share experiences and learn from each other's successes instead of each starting from scratch. If we work together, the future is bright. But we don't have much time to wait,” he stressed.
Mr. Tadesse's statement comes as the adoption of AI continues to grow rapidly – from education, health and agriculture to business and public services.
He said the success of AI in Africa will depend on the ability of countries to join forces, set common priorities and invest in solutions that are based on the needs of their citizens.

Lopez: All those undecided L.A. voters may actually know what they want — someone to win them over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Here’s why so many L.A. voters are undecided in mayor’s race
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- If you want to lead a world-class city, you need to have world-class answers.
- L.A. City Hall is broken, and voters want to know who can fix it.
Political polls are like weather forecasts. They’re worth passing consideration, maybe, but you’d have to be a fool to bet your house on their accuracy.
And yet there’s something that rings true about the recent poll suggesting that L.A. Mayor Karen Bass is in deep trouble among likely voters as she tries to hold on to a job that Councilmember Nithya Raman is trying to snatch away from her.
Here are the numbers, as compiled by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and co-sponsored by The Times:
Raman: 39%.
Bass: 28%.
Undecided: 33%.
Bass has naturally tried to debunk the poll. What else could she do, when her supporters are outnumbered by people who can’t make up their minds? Bass would need to dominate the undecided vote to have a chance, but given her high unfavorability rating, that’ll be hard to do.
On the other hand, Raman certainly hasn’t put things out of reach, despite the fact that Bass carries the baggage of the Palisades fire and has made only minimal progress on her signature issue — homelessness. Election day is less than two months away, and Raman has failed to convince anywhere near a majority that she’s the answer.
So what do Raman and Bass need to do between now and Nov. 3?
Some speculate that Bass may need to step up the negative attacks.
I beg to differ.
We need both candidates to be bolder, more creative, more convincing, and to tell us things we haven’t heard before.
All the recent L.A. mayors I’ve known had their faults and failures, whether the task was filling potholes, building out transit or addressing the high cost of housing. But among their best qualities, Dick Riordan was arrogantly confident, Jim Hahn had a steady hand on the tiller, Antonio Villaraigosa was tireless and passionate, Eric Garcetti was a long-range thinker on earthquakes, water and energy.
Councilmember Nithya Raman leads Mayor Karon Bass by double digits in the latest UC Berkeley/L.A. Times poll. But there is a big caveat.
L.A. needs a mayor with all of those qualities. A cheerleader. A task master. A ball buster.
Running the second-largest city in the country is no easy task, because many of the problems at street level begin well beyond local control, related in part to an economy that leaves too many people behind.
But if you want to lead a world-class city, you need to have world-class answers on the big stuff like housing and homelessness and on the basics, too, like fractured sidewalks and neglected parks. Most voters don’t give a hoot about which candidate is more of a socialist or a moderate. City Hall is broken, and they want to know who can fix it.
On Wednesday, I checked the same sadly neglected area around City Hall that I wrote about in April and found only minimal improvements. Graffiti has been washed from the Frank Putnam Flint fountain, but it remains a broken-down monument to neglect, as it has for most of the past 60 years. And all around it, most of the little placards identifying native plants are broken or missing.
The L.A. Mall is still a largely abandoned wreck, with broken planter boxes and weeds at street level. A woman with two shopping carts told me she’s been homeless for 5½ years. The restaurant next to the nearby police department is shuttered; the restaurant across the street from it is long dead, and the once-vibrant downtown — which generated revenue that benefited every neighborhood of the city — is gasping.
I drove down Hope Street, south of 12th Street, because a reader who lives in that area and has told me about repeated fires at abandoned properties. A tractor was clearing debris from a recent blaze.
I drove west on Olympic toward Alvarado, an area I visit regularly to see a friend. Streets are strewn with trash. They’re always strewn with trash. At Olympic and South Lake, where encampments line the street and a fire once spread into a church parking lot, destroying vehicles, there’s a concrete triangle that was heaped with trash. It’s always heaped with trash, like a municipal dump on a busy thoroughfare.
Next I headed west on Wilshire to the RFK Memorial I wrote about 10 months ago, near the site of the 1968 Bobby Kennedy assassination. It remainsfenced-off, with trash and graffitiand with overgrown vines covering tributes to Kennedy. The city was going to help the school district clean things up. Then the school district took on the task.
It’s still a mess. Actually, it’s more than that. It’s an indictment. And so is the fact that in Studio City, where frustrated neighbors complained for five years that an abandoned property had been taken over by squatters, it took a recent fire to get City Hall’s attention.
The property, since cleared, is in Raman’s district, and she and Bass traded accusations about who had dropped the ball.
The mayor’s camp dismissed the Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll as an outlier, but one Bass insider said the survey ‘put a pit in stomachs.’
“As far as homelessness goes, I don’t see either candidate really showing a clear vision to solve this,” said Kayt Miranda, whose home was damaged by the fire at the abandoned property. “I mean, it’s a tall order, and I wouldn’t want to be in charge of that. But I’m not hearing anything from either of them that sounds like it will work or hasn’t been tried already.”
To be fair, Bass and Raman have each had lots of success on homelessness, with thousands of people being brought indoors. That job is not easy, especially given the number of people with mental illness and addiction issues. I know this from personal experience, having spent a year trying to steer a friend in from homelessness.
But the pace is too slow and the cost too high. As my colleague David Zahniser reported earlier this year, $300 million had been spent on the mayor’s Inside Safe program since December 2022, and as of last December, 40% of the 5,800 people who had been housed were back on the street.
And that was with an estimated annual cost per person of $82,000. Raman, who had supported the program, became a critic of it and touted a less expensive strategy that itself has been criticized for its slow pace, as Times City Hall reporter Noah Goldberg wrote in August.
Not long ago, a homelessness policy expert suggested to me that if we could figure out a way to double the nearly $1,000 Social Security Disability subsidy many homeless people get, it would open some doors in a housing market they’re now priced out of. Too expensive? It’s cheaper than what we’re doing.
I’d like to hear the candidates rethink the playbook like that, double down on what works and drop what doesn’t.
I’d like to hear from a candidate with a realistic plan to get L.A. out of the cellar in park rankings nationally, to break up the 10-year logjam for a sidewalk repair and the two-year wait to fix a street light.
All those undecided voters know exactly what they want.
A mayor who says fix the busted fountain by the end of the week, or else.
They want someone to win their vote.
steve.lopez@latimes.com

Yemen violence deepens concerns over child hunger crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Yemen violence deepens concerns over child hunger crisis
Aid agencies in Yemen highlighted the growing hunger emergency sparked by renewed fighting between Houthi opposition forces and Government troops, after mobile health clinics reported that hundreds of children displaced by the violence are suffering from the most deadly form of malnutrition.
Key points
- More than one in four screened children are acutely malnourished
- Around 200 children screened have severe acute malnutrition
- At least 15 children have been killed since 3 September
Of nearly 2,900 children screened in areas where there is safe humanitarian access, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said that more than one in four was acutely malnourished, while around 200 were sick with severe acute malnutrition.
“This is only a glimpse of how devastating the situation is across Yemen; every day we are seeing more and more cases,” said Akhil Iyer, the agency’s top official in the country.
Testimonies from some of the approximately 130,000 people who have fled clashes in the southwest illustrate how civilians have been severely impacted by the fighting in recent weeks, after years of food and nutrition crises.
“We spoke to Haifa, a young mother who fled Yemen's west coast as well, and she told us that the sounds of gunfire were closing in on her house, as her house was shaking. She told us that she didn't have time to think, she just knew that she had to run and run quickly with her family,” the UNICEF official said.
Today, Haifa and her family “live in extreme heat, in [one] a side of a tent”, in AlFirdos displacement camp near Aden. They have no way of earning money and they struggle to find food and medicine, Mr. Iyer explained.
“She pointed out to us that displacement has stripped them of their dignity. This is in fact what displacement does.”
Most vulnerable at highest risk
Briefing journalists from Aden, Mr. Iyer also described the plight of four-year-old Taha, who he found receiving treatment at a UNICEF-supported mobile clinic.
“His family had just fled violence in Mokha district, some 200 kilometres (124 miles) away, leaving behind their home and belongings. His mother told us, ‘We escaped with nothing. My only fear was that I would lose my son before finding help.’ Taha’s story is sadly not unique.”
Over the past three weeks, nearly 130,000 people in Yemen have been forced from their homes. That number includes an estimated 71,000 children. The majority have been uprooted in southwestern Taiz governorate where they are unable to move to safer areas “because of fighting, blocked roads, or lack of transportation”, Mr. Iyer continued.
Since 3 September, UNICEF has verified that at least 15 children have been killed and 14 injured, primarily by shelling attacks. Three more youngsters are still missing. “Behind every one of those children is a parent living through the unimaginable – grief, fear, or the agony of not knowing,” Mr. Iyer stressed.
Before the latest uptick in fighting, more than 2.2 million children under five in Yemen were projected to be acutely malnourished this year, with more than half a million suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
Access dangers
Providing healthcare for all those exhausted by repeated displacement is vitally important, particularly amid a spread of preventable diseases, including measles, acute respiratory infections, diarrhoea and cholera. But reaching communities with the highest health needs is becoming “increasingly difficult”, according to the UN World Health Organization (WHO).
In 90 of the 105 health-cluster priority districts in northern Yemen, “UN operations have been suspended”, explained the agency’s Amna Smailbegović. “The disruption has a direct impact on essential services, including outpatient consultation, skilled deliveries and child health services.”
For its part, UNICEF and other aid agencies do not have safe and unimpeded humanitarian access to between 65-70 per cent of children because the areas where they live are controlled by Houthi opposition forces.

Sudan’s farmers are ready to return – private investment could get them there
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Sudan’s farmers are ready to return – private investment could get them there
The war in Sudan has devastated the economy and agricultural production, but a UN-backed plan aims to mobilise private sector investment to help farmers return to their fields.
The roadmap for recovery, and the potential for some $155 million in external investment, were among the outcomes of a three-day dialogue held this week in Khartoum, organized by the UN Development Programme (UNDP) and Sudan’s Ministry of Finance.
More than 300 participants from 20 countries – representing the Government, financial institutions, the national and international private sector, farmers’ and trade associations, as well as other stakeholders – registered for the event.
A ‘stepping stone’ forward
“This dialogue is a stepping stone towards moving forward in bringing more private sector engagement, which ultimately socioeconomic recovery depends on,” said Arvind Kumar, Team Leader for Recovery and Resilience at the UNDP Country Office in Sudan.
He told UN News that focusing on the private sector is critical because it provides some 98 per cent of jobs.
Speaking from the capital, Mr. Kumar described an economy that has been broken by war but not completely paralysed. Sudan’s farmers continue to grow crops, goods are still being transported, and markets still function in some areas.
But the last two years have seen yields fall by 40 to 70 per cent in some cases, he said, while the cost of agricultural inputs such as fertilisers and fuel have increased due to the crisis in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf.
“The third and most key important aspect is that there is not much injection into the economy from the private sector,” he said. “And they are willing to come back.”
Millions going hungry
Mr. Kumar stressed that “food production is obviously not close to what Sudan needs,” highlighting the immense impacts of the civil war that erupted in April 2023.
The brutal battle between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has left more than 19 million people facing hunger. Nearly 35 million require humanitarian assistance and 13 million have been displaced.
Before the war, Sudan exported gum arabic, sesame, cotton, hibiscus, sorghum and livestock, he said, and once accounted for a 12 to 13 per cent share of the global sesame market, now reduced to six per cent.
Although livestock exports continue, the share of “high-value agricultural crops” has declined because most businesses have lost assets and lack access to capital, “therefore it is very difficult for them to come and rebuild, so it is taking time.”
Meanwhile, UNDP analysis shows that 90 per cent of farmers cannot access financing, and “with the support only of aid, they will not be able to continue to improve food production.”
Recognition, recovery and potential resources
He said the dialogue in Khartoum concluded with “three key outcomes”: recognition of the need for continued engagement with the international and national private sector, adoption and endorsement of a private sector recovery roadmap for agriculture, and “an encouraging potential investment” of nearly $155 million from Pakistan, India, Türkiye, Egypt and Syria.
Participants also discussed the need to re-connect farms with markets and ultimately buyers, while business owners raised concerns about regulatory barriers and the difficulty of linking up with international investors.
Financial support for farmers
UNDP is exploring measures to bring more support to farmers through the banking system, such as credit guarantees.
It is also working with the national and international private sector to restore a warehouse receipt system – a process that would allow farmers to store produce in approved facilities and receive receipts that may be used to secure financing.
Trade facilitation is another top priority. UNDP is engaging with the Sudanese authorities responsible for customs and ports, as well as UN trade and development organization UNCTAD, “to review the reforms that are needed for ease of business.”
Mr. Kumar said people need education, healthcare, electricity and jobs to rebuild their lives, He insisted that development should begin alongside life-saving humanitarian assistance “and there is an opportunity and a space to bring development back on track.”

World News in Brief: West Bank demolitions accelerate, urgent support for Sudan, Haiti diplacement, AI hub to boost gender equality

Three more villages in Msafer Yatta have already been “almost entirely” destroyed in September 2026, OHCHR said, highlighting fears of ethnic cleansing in the occupied Palestinian territory.

Sudan needs urgent support as El Niño compounds food insecurity
Funding shortages are limiting UN efforts to aid communities in Sudan impacted by ongoing war and displacement – just as El Niño threatens to bring 30 to 40 per cent less rainfall than usual.
In an alert, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) warned of worsening food security, for farmers, pastoralists and fishing communities in regions largely reclaimed by Government forces, during the protracted war with former paramilitary allies, the RSF.
The agency has several ways of supporting the most vulnerable, such as vaccinating millions of livestock and providing goats to displaced women-headed households and mothers, so that children have a ready supply of nutritious milk.
Boosting food supply
FAO’s Rein Paulsen said the agency’s response is focused on mitigating the impacts of rainfall loss and drought on livestock to maintain healthy herds.
“This is about ensuring that the body weight of animals are retained, that they’re vaccinated against the types of diseases that will compromise their health, that they have access to animal feed concentrate.”
Another successful ongoing project that’s brought investment returns of 30 to one involves purchasing drought-resistant seed for farmers. From an initial $17 million outlay, farmers produced sorghum crops worth more than $500 million.
This year, the agency needs $193 million to support its initiatives. It is currently only 23 per cent funded.
Haiti's displacement crisis spreading beyond capital, IOM warns
Haiti's displacement crisis is spreading beyond Port-au-Prince, with some of the sharpest increases now occurring in regions once considered relatively safe, according to new data released this week by the UN International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The latest assessment recorded nearly 1.5 million internally displaced people nationwide, with almost 80 per cent now outside the capital as violence spreads into other areas.
The steepest rise was in Artibonite department, where displacement grew by 16 per cent between May and August.
Once a refuge for families fleeing violence, parts of the department are now facing escalating insecurity themselves.
Mass displacement
Recent attacks in Kenscoff, near the capital, displaced more than 4,000 people, with homes burned and reports of kidnappings and deaths.
“Violence, displacement, food insecurity, forced returns and climate risks are all unfolding at the same time, placing enormous pressure on families and communities,” said Elise Verron, IOM's Senior Emergency Coordinator in Haiti.
With the Atlantic hurricane season underway, many displaced families are living in informal settlements or host communities with little capacity to withstand further shocks.
IOM is appealing for $60 million to reach 6.4 million people under its 2026 crisis response plan.
UN Women launches digital hub dedicated to gender equality
UN Women on Friday launched a Digital, Innovation and AI Hub focused on its core remit: gender equality.
It brings together researchers, governments, technology companies and women’s rights organizations to help shape artificial intelligence (AI) in ways that benefit women and girls.
The launch comes as world leaders coalesce for the General Assembly’s 81st session, where AI is high on the agender – but women and girls remain largely absent from the debate, the UN agency said.
8 in 10 AI jobs held by men
According to UN Women, men hold nearly eight in 10 AI jobs and almost nine in 10 senior leadership positions shaping the technology.
“The artificial intelligence systems we build today will shape how we live and work tomorrow. If women are missing from their design and governance, we risk carrying the inequalities of the present into the future,” said UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous.
A global analysis of 133 AI systems by the agency, found that 44 per cent showed gender bias.
Additionally, nearly one in four women human rights defenders, activists and journalists surveyed by UN Women reported experiencing AI-assisted online violence.
The hub will generate evidence on how emerging technologies affect women and girls, support Member States in developing gender-responsible digital and AI policies and work with technology companies to embed gender equality principles into technological design and governance.
“AI can deepen gender inequality or help overcome it. That is a human choice – and those choices are being made now by engineers, companies, investors and governments,” Ms. Bahous said.
“Equality is not only about representation. It is also about power,” she added.

‘No one speaks on behalf of Lebanon’: PM Salam asserts State authority at UN

‘No one speaks on behalf of Lebanon’: PM Salam asserts State authority at UN
Lebanon’s Prime Minister, Nawaf Salam, has stressed that decisions over war and peace, and control of weapons, must rest solely with the State and its constitutional institutions.
He said this priority was reflected in recent Cabinet decisions, taken after Lebanon “found itself facing a war it did not choose, but which was imposed on it.”
Speaking during the annual debate of the UN General Assembly, Mr. Salam said the war broke out “despite our repeated warnings of the dangers of being drawn into it.”
“As the war expanded across the region and initiatives multiplied to end it, we held firm to a principle that admits no compromise: no one speaks on behalf of Lebanon, and no one negotiates for it except the Lebanese State, through its constitutional institutions.”
He rejected any return to Lebanon being used as an arena for others’ conflicts or as a bargaining chip.
“Lebanon’s future is not to be decided on its behalf, and its security and stability must not be the price of deals struck in its absence,” he said.
Ending the war
Lebanon’s position on the war has been clear from the outset, Mr. Salam said: an end to the fighting, a consolidated ceasefire, full Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, the release of all prisoners, and the return of residents to their villages and their reconstruction.
On this basis, he said, the Lebanese State has entered negotiations with Israel, under the auspices of the United States and its President, to reach arrangements aimed at ending the war and restoring full Lebanese sovereignty.
Success, he added, would not be measured by declared intentions but by implementation.
He stressed the need to translate the tripartite framework reached in the negotiations into practical steps, with a clear timetable and a verification mechanism to ensure that all its provisions are carried out.
Avoiding a vacuum after UNIFIL
Mr. Salam praised the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), including its leadership, personnel and staff, for their courage and sacrifices in maintaining stability, supporting the Lebanese army and implementing Security Council resolution 1701, the 2006 measure designed to end the war between Israel and Hezbollah.
He noted Security Council resolution 2790, which mandates the end of UNIFIL’s operations by the end of this year and the start of its gradual withdrawal, and asks the Secretary-General to explore options for continuing to support implementation of resolution 1701.
Mr. Salam stressed the need to avoid a vacuum should UNIFIL withdraw without agreement on a new international force to take its place and continue monitoring, reporting and liaison work.
Humanitarian toll
The Prime Minister described a war that has caused a widespread humanitarian crisis and extensive destruction of housing, public facilities, infrastructure and productive sectors, leaving large numbers of Lebanese without homes or livelihoods.
He thanked UN agencies and international partners for their humanitarian support and called for continued funding to meet the basic needs of those affected, particularly the displaced, alongside support for early recovery, reconstruction and development.
Lebanon is fulfilling its own responsibilities on reform and extending State authority across its territory, he said, but the international community must also shoulder its responsibilities in upholding Lebanon’s sovereignty and implementing resolutions of international legitimacy.

‘Invest with Iraq’: PM sets out vision for new economic future
Iraq’s Prime Minister, Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, said his country aims to exert its influence as an active economic power in the region, and as a bridge for dialogue and cooperation between its peoples.
He was speaking during the debate of the UN General Assembly’s high-level segment, where he set out his country’s vision for economic growth, stability, and regional cooperation.
“We are moving forward to ensure that the State alone holds decision-making power over war and peace, and that weapons and instruments of power remain in the hands of its constitutional institutions, so that the law is the arbiter and the national interest is the compass,” he said.
He explained that the executive measures being taken in this area are moving in the right direction, as they form the basis for building a State of institutions, protecting sovereignty, consolidating stability and creating the environment needed for development and investment.
With the mission of the international coalition in Iraq now over, he said, “we are moving our relationship with our strategic partners into a new phase, from military cooperation to economic and development cooperation that serves our shared interests.”
He called on everyone to secure borders, address gaps and remain constantly vigilant to prevent an environment conducive to extremism from taking hold.
Energy and development
Mr. Al-Zaidi spoke about institutional reform, saying: “Our Government is waging a battle against corruption and the protection of public funds, and we are pursuing sustainable, substantive reforms to raise the efficiency of performance and improve services.”
He said Iraq is working to draw on successful expertise and innovative practices from the world of economics, finance and business to advance its economic and financial reform, and to provide a secure environment for domestic and foreign investment.
“Our ambition is for Iraq to become a global hub for energy production, and to make use of its capabilities to sustainably strengthen regional and international security and stability,” he said.
But he added: “We view with concern the repercussions linked to freedom of transport and maritime navigation, and the crisis they have caused in the form of rising energy prices worldwide.”

He spoke of the Development Road project as Iraq’s comprehensive vision for regional integration and stability, describing it as an important gateway and strategic corridor for trade, investment, industry and energy, linking east and west from the Grand Faw Port, through Türkiye, to Europe.

From conflict to integration
Mr. Al-Zaidi stressed that his country’s vision rests on helping to move the region from conflict to integration, from rivalry to cooperation, and from depleting resources to investing them in development.
He said Iraq reaffirms its support for dialogue and diplomacy to defuse crises, and for efforts to allow trade to pass through Iraqi territory, offering major facilities as alternatives to complex trade routes.
He pointed to the challenges posed by desertification and water scarcity facing Iraq, which affect its food security.
“We affirm our commitment to our legitimate and fair water rights, and we call for the shared management of water resources based on the principles of cooperation and international law,” he said.
He concluded: “Iraq has never been on the margins. It is the heart of history and the pulse of the present, and it is worthy of partnership for the future.”

UN voices grave concern as fighting spreads across northern Ethiopia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

UN voices grave concern as fighting spreads across northern Ethiopia
The UN said on Friday it remains gravely concerned by the continued deterioration of the security situation across northern Ethiopia, as fighting spreads across multiple fronts and increasingly disrupts humanitarian operations.
Briefing reporters in New York, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the UN was “particularly troubled by reports of the use of drones as well as incidents of harm to civilians,” and again urged all parties to “exercise maximum restraint and address their differences through dialogue.”
He said Secretary-General António Guterres was following developments closely and continues to engage on the issue with leaders in New York in a bid to de-escalate the growing crisis – which threatens to return the country to the state of full-scale war in the north which erupted in Tigray in 2020.
Internet outages
According to news reports, internet and call services have been largely cut across the Tigray region. Many rely on banking and mobile transactions due to lack of access to cash and bank ATMs.
The 2020–2022 Tigray war began after political tensions between Ethiopia's federal government and the region's former ruling party, the TPLF, erupted into fighting between Government troops and Tigrayan militia in November 2020.
Eritrean forces joined on the Government's side, and the conflict spread into neighbouring regions, with the UN documenting widespread atrocities and warning of famine-like conditions before it ended two years later.
The UN welcomed the peace deal of November 2022 under African Union mediation, though it continued to flag slow progress on implementation as a risk to the peace now under threat from this week's escalation.
UN mediation
The Secretary-General’s Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa, Guang Cong, is engaging with national and regional interlocutors and coordinating closely with partners, including the AU and regional intergovernmental body IGAD, to support a resumption of dialogue under 2022 accord, Mr. Dujarric said.
On the humanitarian front, the UN aid coordination office (OCHA) said the escalation risks adding to already substantial needs, including among civilians displaced by previous fighting in Tigray, in an area also experiencing below-average rainfall linked to the El Niño weather pattern – which promises to exacerbate already extreme weather conditions worldwide.
The UN and partners are continuing regular humanitarian operations where security allows, in Tigray as well as the northern regions of Amhara and Afar, assessing emergency needs.
Fighting chokes off aid
But insecurity is already taking its toll: this past Sunday, a drone strike in northwestern Tigray hit a truck carrying food assistance for internally displaced people.
Road closures have paused or displaced planned humanitarian movements, Mr. Dujarric said, while operations in parts of Amhara face significant constraints, including the seizure of humanitarian vehicles by armed groups.
The UN stressed that all parties must ensure safe and unhindered access for humanitarian partners to reach those in need, wherever they are.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, also issued a strong statement on Friday saying he was deeply alarmed by the escalation and urged all parties to de-escalate tensions and avoid a return to full-scale war.
He said reported airstrikes hit five schools in Tigray on 22 September, and a mortar strike two days later killed civilians in Kobo, Amhara.

Tuvalu urges decisive global action as rising seas threaten its future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Tuvalu urges decisive global action as rising seas threaten its future
Climate change remains the greatest existential threat to Tuvalu, Prime Minister Feleti Teo told the UN General Assembly on Friday, warning that the pace and scale of international action are still falling far short of what vulnerable island nations need.
“For Tuvalu, sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality,” he said, describing efforts by the Pacific island nation to protect both its physical territory and its identity as the climate crisis transforms its environment.
Mr. Teo said Tuvalu had already reclaimed 15.3 hectares of elevated, flood-free land on the capital island of Funafuti through its coastal adaptation project, with another 10 hectares being reclaimed.
For a country with only around 26 square kilometres of land, he said, that constituted a significant adjustment.
At the same time, Tuvalu is using digital technologies to preserve its sovereignty, institutions and national identity, including through an initiative designed to safeguard its culture and historical heritage in digital form.
Nationhood ‘not negotiable’
The Prime Minister strongly welcomed the UN Political Declaration on Sea-Level Rise endorsed by Member States, describing it as a “monumental and gratifying achievement” for a country that had been at the forefront of efforts for such an agreement.
Among its commitments, he highlighted recognition of the continuity of statehood and sovereignty despite sea-level rise, the permanence of maritime zones and rights established under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and protection for the dignity, culture, identity and heritage of affected peoples.
“The Declaration affirms that Tuvalu’s nationhood is not negotiable, that our maritime rights are not erasable, and that our people should never be forced to choose between their homeland and their future,” he said.
‘World must act now’
Mr. Teo warned that with a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C global temperature target now inevitable, an orderly, fair and just transition away from fossil fuels had become even more urgent.
Tuvalu is calling for vigorous action to reduce both methane and carbon dioxide emissions, while championing Pacific-led initiatives such as the Tassiriki Call for a Fossil Fuel Free Pacific and the Funafuti Call for Climate Justice and Climate Action.
He also welcomed the operationalisation of the Loss and Damage Fund, calling for adequate, predictable and timely financing, provided as grants, to support countries already experiencing unavoidable climate impacts.
“The world must act now decisively, collectively, and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come,” he said.
A ‘large ocean state’
The Prime Minister also placed the ocean at the centre of Tuvalu’s development and security. While possessing just 26 square kilometres of land, the country is custodian of some 750,000 square kilometres of ocean.
“Ocean governance is not simply an environmental policy,” he said. “It is also an issue of economic security, food security and climate security.”
With the world off track on the Sustainable Development Goals, Mr. Teo urged accelerated action on SDG 14, concerning life below water, and greater international support for Pacific-led climate financing and resilience.
Concluding, he stressed that even the smallest countries could lead on adaptation, ocean stewardship and international law, while cautioning that “national leadership cannot substitute for global responsibility.”
