Pakistan’s Sharif warns any diversion of Indus waters will be ‘treated as an act of war’
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif told the UN General Assembly on Friday that any attempt by India to stop, impede or divert Pakistan’s share of the Indus River waters “will be treated as an act of war”.
Addressing the General Debate, Mr. Sharif said the shared waters of the Indus River system were the “lifeblood not only for the people of Pakistan, but for the entire region”, and that India’s unilateral decision to hold the existing treaty in abeyance had “no legal basis whatsoever”.
He said India’s claims had been rejected by UN experts and the Court of Arbitration.
“Water must never be weaponized. Rivers should nourish nations, not divide them,” he stated.
‘Voice for diplomacy’
On the conflict that has roiled the Gulf in February, Mr. Sharif said Pakistan had brought Washington and Tehran together in Islamabad.
With hostilities recently surging again, he said, “amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voice for diplomacy must echo even louder and stronger.” The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Red Sea bottleneck “must remain open”, he added.
He condemned the recent Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including the attempted drone attack on Mecca.
Kashmir and Gaza
Mr. Sharif said Pakistan had exercised its right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter when it faced “external aggression from India” a year ago, crediting US President Donald Trump’s intervention with averting all-out war between the “two nuclear armed neighbours”.
Ensuring South Asia never again reaches “that precipice”, he said, requires a just solution to the Kashmir dispute, adding that Kashmiris had waited eight decades for a UN plebiscite.
“Generations have endured illegal occupation, arbitrary detention, extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, sexual violence and collective punishment,” he said.

On Gaza, he recalled eight-year-old Wafa Akilah, killed on what should have been her first day of school.
“Does not a child born in Gaza deserve the same life and the same future and same dream as a child, anywhere else in the world?” he asked, adding that in the West Bank “the forcible eviction of Palestinians clearly reflects Israel’s genocidal agenda, which continues unabated”.
Mr. Sharif said terrorist groups were operating from sanctuaries in Afghanistan to destabilize Pakistan and called on Afghan authorities to take “verifiable, decisive action”.
‘Peace is also a far better choice’
Echoing the 81st Session’s theme of trust restoration, the Pakistani Premier maintained that trust would be restored when “guns are silenced and replaced by handshakes, embraces and smiles.”
“We have chosen dialogue over confrontation. We have chosen cooperation over coercion. We have chosen peace over war,” he said.

Haiti at ‘watershed moment’, Prime Minister tells UN, urging full backing for security force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:00 UTC

Haiti at ‘watershed moment’, Prime Minister tells UN, urging full backing for security force
Haiti is at a “watershed moment” in its struggle against gang violence and needs sustained international support alongside stronger national security institutions, Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé told the UN General Assembly on Friday.
Addressing world leaders in New York, Mr. Fils-Aimé said criminal violence was threatening communities across the country, but insisted Haiti was neither defeated nor seeking to have others determine its future.
“Haiti will resist. Haiti is standing tall,” he said, calling on the international community “not to save it, but to stand side by side with it while it takes its own destiny into its own hands.”
‘No time for half measures’
The Prime Minister said the scale of violence, including massacres, displacement and attacks against women and children, demanded decisive action.
He paid tribute to victims as well as Haitian and international security personnel who have died serving the country, stressing that the human toll must not become simply another statistic.
Haiti, he said, is strengthening its own security forces, including through a programme to train 4,000 police officers. More than 2,000 have already been trained, while over 1,500 new soldiers have completed training. The Government also plans to train 15,000 additional soldiers over the next three years.
“Our goal is not only to respond to the crisis of today,” he said, but to build the capacity for Haiti to sustainably ensure its own security.
At the same time, Mr. Fils-Aimé expressed concern that the international force intended to support those efforts was still not fully operational or at its planned strength of 5,500 personnel.
He called for renewal of the mandate of the “gang suppression force” and its full deployment with the personnel, equipment and resources required.
“A mandate is not enough,” he warned. “There’s a need for forces. Equipment is needed, and one needs to resolve to see the effort through.”
Weapons trafficking and impunity
The Prime Minister also urged stronger international action against illicit weapons and ammunition trafficking, noting that the guns fueling violence in Haiti are arriving through transnational criminal networks.
As part of efforts to combat impunity, the Government has established two specialized judicial hubs addressing financial and mass crimes and sexual violence, while reactivating the national commission for disarmament, demobilization and reintegration.
Elections and economic recovery
Mr. Fils-Aimé said restoring security must go hand in hand with economic recovery and a return to democratic government through “free, credible, inclusive and honest elections”.
Enrollment centres are open, political parties and groups have been accredited, and prospective candidates are completing formalities, he said.
The Prime Minister also called for a fundamental shift in Haiti’s economic relationship with international partners.
“We need to move from aid to investment, from assistance to production, from dependency to partnership,” he said, arguing that investment and job creation, particularly for young people and women, are essential to lasting peace.
Despite the enormity of the challenges, Mr. Fils-Aimé closed on a message of determination.
“The challenges are colossal, but our willpower is even greater,” he said. “Our generation now needs to let [the tree of liberty] bear the fruit of peace.”

‘Gamechanging’ brain tumour test reduces diagnosis from eight weeks to two hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:53:43 UTC
20:53:43 KST

A rapid new test for brain tumours can diagnose patients while they are still on the operating table.
Scientists have called the development “gamechanging” and said it could secure early treatment for those who “do not have time on their side”.
The test was developed by the Brain Tumour Research Centre of Excellence at the University of Nottingham and can diagnose forms of cancer while the patient is still undergoing surgery.
The NHS has begun using the diagnostic tool, which can cut waiting times for a diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours. It could also secure early access for clinical trials for certain patients.
Prof Frankie Swords, the NHS medical director, said the rapid test was “a huge leap forward for patients” with the “potential to completely transform how we diagnose brain tumours”.
It also means patients can start having treatment earlier, which could save lives, and also prevents uncertainty.
It is a genomic test, which means it analyses the genetic code of a sample of a tumour in a matter of hours. NHS England will be piloting the new tool in five specialist centres around the country, before rolling it out more widely.
Stuart Smith, a consultant neurosurgeon at Nottingham university hospitals NHS trust and co-lead of the university’s research centre of excellence, said: “I am very proud to have been part of this exceptional team creating this rapid genomic testing, which will save valuable waiting time for patients who potentially are being told they don’t have time on their side.
“The ability to have detailed information about the tumour at the point when decisions are being made in the operating theatre is gamechanging.”
Rather than looking down a microscope at a tumour, the test allows doctors to get faster and more accurate results. Small tissue samples are sent from the tumour to a pathology lab, where they are put into a shoebox-sized sequencing machine made by Oxford Nanopore. Inside, the molecules of DNA pass through a nanopore – a tiny hole – and this reveals the unique genome, which defines the type of tumour.
Primary brain tumours are the single biggest killer of children and adults under 40 in the UK.
The specialist centres where the test is first rolled out will be Nottingham university hospitals NHS trust, University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, Great Ormond Street hospital NHS foundation trust, King’s College hospital and Newcastle hospitals NHS foundation trust.
The test will then be brought to sites in Bristol, Oxford, Leeds and Manchester.

Ukrainian Drone Attack Hits Russian Electronics Plant Supplying Parts for Kh-59 Missiles and Pantsir-S1
A Ukrainian drone attack in Russia’s Ulyanovsk targeted the NPP Zavod Iskra electronics plant, which supplies products to the Russian defense industry, according to an OSINT analysis by independent Russian media outlet ASTRA.
An ASTRA OSINT analyst identified the affected facility as JSC NPP Zavod Iskra in Ulyanovsk. The plant is part of Russia’s Almaz-Antey aerospace and defense corporation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ulyanovsk regional Governor Alexey Russkikh confirmed that industrial and civilian infrastructure in the city had been damaged in the drone attack.
According to preliminary information provided by Russkikh, eight people were injured, including seven adults and one child. Five of the adults were reported to be in moderate condition, while the remaining two sustained minor injuries. The child was also described as being in moderate condition.
Founded in 1971, Zavod Iskra is a major Russian electronics manufacturer specializing in the development and serial production of semiconductor devices, microwave components, power electronics, medical products, and LTCC ceramic packages for electronic equipment.
According to Militarnyi, Zavod Iskra is also part of the supply chain for Kh-59M2/M2A guided air-launched missiles. The company provides the Yaroslavl Radio Plant with 3OT127A transistor pairs used to manufacture SB-1AM television transmitters for T1A-02 equipment.
It also supplies diodes used in the TVK-2 television channel of the 72V6 combat vehicle, a component of Russia’s Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile and gun system.
The reported strike in Ulyanovsk came as another major Russian industrial facility was targeted by drones. The LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez refinery, one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, was also hit in a drone attack on September 25, ASTRA reported, citing an OSINT assessment.
Perm regional Governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed a drone attack in the region and said emergency services had been deployed to the site.

Number of Sudanese fleeing to Chad surges 20-fold as aid runs dry, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:52:02 UTC
20:52:02 KST

Number of Sudanese fleeing to Chad surges 20-fold as aid runs dry, UN says
GENEVA, Sept 25 - There has been a sharp increase in the number of people fleeing from Sudan to Chad to escape fighting and dire conditions, and aid funding is failing to keep up with needs, the United Nations refugee agency said on Friday.
More than 400 people a day have been crossing into eastern Chad over the past week, a 20-fold increase from the numbers seen in recent months, UNHCR said.
They were fleeing Sudan's Darfur, Kordofan and Blue Nile regions — which have all been hit by clashes between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in a more than three-year-old civil war.
There were "people who tell us that they flee the conflict, they flee the aerial bombardments, they flee the drone attacks," Mamadou Dian Balde, UN Regional Refugee Coordinator for the Sudan Situation, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Nairobi.
Only 18% of the $1.6 billion funding it needed this year had come in, UNHCR said.
“It means less food. It means less capacity for people to be relocated to safer areas. It means less capacity to shelter themselves,” Dian Balde said.
The agency warned of potential knock-on effects if Sudanese refugees’ basic needs are not met in Chad, saying its analysis shows many move on towards Europe after repeated failed attempts to find safety.
The civil war has devastated wide swathes of Sudan, displacing up to 14 million people, ruining harvests and decimating the economy, according to UN estimates.
Drought and other harsh conditions were also forcing people to move, UNHCR said.
Almost 1 million refugees have crossed into Chad since the conflict began, more than 55,000 so far this year, according to UNHCR data.
Aid groups like UNHCR face major funding shortfalls after the administration of US President Donald Trump and other donor countries cut billions of dollars in foreign assistance over the past year. REUTERS

C8 could become regional development platform despite political differences – political scientist
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:50:30 EEST
20:50:30 KST

The Carpathian Eight (C8) format has prospects for further development as a platform for regional cooperation among all member countries in the areas of economy, security, energy and infrastructure, despite political differences among some participating countries, political scientist and head of the Center for Analysis and Strategies Ihor Chalenko said.
"The Carpathian Initiative is primarily a political platform within which economic, security, cultural and other dimensions of cooperation can develop. At the same time, the economic component was one of the key motives for its creation," Chalenko said during a discussion at the Interfax-Ukraine press center on "Carpathian Initiative (C8): From Regional Cooperation to a New Role for Ukraine in Europe" on Friday.
According to him, despite a political demarche by the Hungarian leadership, Budapest remains interested in practical economic cooperation within the new format.
Chalenko also called claims that there were no consultations with the Hungarian side on creating the initiative disinformation. According to him, consultations between the sides had been underway since at least November 2025 and intensified at the foreign ministry level in the summer of this year.
The political scientist also drew attention to the prospects for Ukrainian-Hungarian cooperation in the energy sector, particularly in the context of the future use of the Druzhba oil pipeline after the current contractual arrangements expire. "We need to demonstrate stability and a high level of reputation. Unfortunately, the political statements recently coming from the Hungarian leadership undermine this reputation," he said.
Chalenko stressed that the security component of the Carpathian Eight is not directly related to the war but is aimed at creating stable conditions for the development of the economy, energy, tourism and environmental projects in the macroregion.
In his view, the development of regional formats is in line with current trends toward strengthening the role of macroregions in Europe amid a crisis of confidence in traditional supranational mechanisms. "Developing horizontal communications among border regions, oblasts and municipalities has significant potential and makes it possible to build long-term cooperation that does not depend on electoral cycles," the expert said.
In conclusion, Chalenko said he believed that the Carpathian Eight could become one of the successful regional cooperation formats alongside the Bucharest Nine, Nordic-Baltic Eight and other international initiatives.

Police suspect militants crossed Myanmar border, killed four in Manipur
Bodies of the four men, belonging to the Tangkhul Naga community who were allegedly killed by militants, were found in Manipur's Kamjong district.The bodies of the four men, identified as Vareishim Jajo, Phami Jajo, Betterson Jajo and Ningthem Kashak, were found at an isolated spot near the Myanmar border in remote Pilong village around 1.30 am on Friday, police said. The bodies bore multiple bullet marks and were found after a prolonged search by police and locals, reported PTI.Police said the bodies were being brought to Kamjong district hospital for post-mortem examinations. Pilong village is around 34 km from the district headquarters.Locals alleged that militants from neighbouring Myanmar crossed into India and ambushed a group of five villagers on Thursday, before the bodies were found. One of the villagers managed to escape and alerted local authorities. However, the search for bodies continued till early Friday.“Villagers claimed that four persons were killed when militants from neighbouring Myanmar crossed the border and attacked five people. One of them managed to escape and reported the incident to the villagers and the local authorities. The killing has not been confirmed. A police team has been dispatched to ascertain the claim," the officer had said.
Naga Peoples' Front state president Awangbou Newmai condemned the killings and alleged that members of the Kuki National Army (Burma) were behind the attack. He appealed to all communities to "shun violence" and "co-exist as peaceful neighbours".The killings come amid a fresh escalation in Kuki-Naga violence in Manipur that has spread across parts of Ukhrul, Kamjong, Kangpokpi, Tamenglong and Noney districts since February. What began with clashes between Tangkhul Naga and Kuki communities in Ukhrul in February has developed into a wider cycle of ambushes, attacks on villages and civilian killings.In recent weeks, attacks have been reported on both communities. Four Kuki villagers were killed in separate attacks in Tamenglong and Noney on September 13, followed by attacks on Naga settlements and the killing of a Naga teenager in subsequent days.
A 36-year-old Kuki electric lineman was also killed in an attack on Kuki settlements along the IT Road corridor in Kangpokpi on September 23, while Naga villages along the Noney-Kangpokpi-Senapati borders came under attack the same day.The latest violence has occurred despite a heavy security presence in the state, with the Army, Assam Rifles, CRPF, BSF, ITBP and SSB deployed in affected areas. The violence has also increasingly involved allegations of attacks by armed groups operating along the Kuki-Naga fault line, although responsibility for individual attacks is often disputed or remains under investigation.

British companies will use battlefield data from Ukraine to develop AI-powered drones
Kyiv • UNN
Up to 12 British companies will gain access to data from Ukrainian drones. They will use it to develop AI for autonomous unmanned vehicles.
British companies will gain access to real battlefield data from Ukraine, which they will use to develop new artificial intelligence models for drones. Reuters reports this, citing the British government, writes UNN.
Details
It is noted that the agreement between British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy provides access to a database of images and videos collected by unmanned aerial vehicles in Ukraine, which includes more than 6 million instances of detecting objects such as tanks, artillery, air defense systems, infantry, and aerial targets.
Swarms of drones fly, sail, or move autonomously, using artificial intelligence to work together, detect threats and targets, and make decisions, the government said, adding that a human is always involved in such operations.
This first-in-the-world access to real battlefield data will allow British companies to continue pushing the boundaries of innovation in defense, deter our enemies, and ensure greater security in our country, as well as further strengthen Ukraine
Access to the database is being granted to a maximum of 12 British companies, which must submit proposals demonstrating how their work will meet both Ukrainian and British defense requirements.
The British government expects proposals, in particular, concerning autonomous AI-based target recognition and distributed decision-making systems, through which drone routes, priorities, and behavior can be adapted without the need to rely on a single command center.

Australia urges global cooperation on climate, AI checks and international law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:47:22 UTC
20:47:22 KST

Australia urges global cooperation on climate, AI checks and international law
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese underlined the need for countries to work together to address the climate crisis, emerging technologies such as AI, and the breakdown of international rules, at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
He said that cooperating on urgent challenges that confront every country, creating solutions that work for citizens and staying true to the UN’s founding purpose “remains the test of our time” which “we can and we must pass”.
The UN was established eight decades ago “from the ruins of war” by citizens and leaders who vowed to work together to prevent another global conflict, Mr. Albanese stressed.
Uniting nations
“We can seize and share and shape the opportunities this moment holds in the interests of our citizens. But we can only do it together,” he said.
Mr. Albanese insisted that “the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone, nor can it be subcontracted to the world’s richest companies or dictated by the pace of technology.”
He stressed that “shaping a secure, peaceful and prosperous world is a task for all of us”, which is why Australia is seeking a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for 2029-2030.
Promoting wider perspectives
If successful, “Australia will safeguard the rules that protect us all by upholding international law, including the UN Charter and the sovereignty of all States,” he said.
“We will amplify the voices of small States and middle powers to ensure a wider range of perspectives shape the Council's decisions.”
The Australian premier noted that the world is rapidly changing and new issues – including climate change, emerging technologies such as AI, and the breakdown of trust, civility and social cohesion – demand the full attention of the international community.
He also emphasized the need to “embrace” change and reform multilateralism.
Cooperation, not coercion
“As a middle power, Australia is showing leadership and working with others on fresh ideas to tackle the big issues now facing the world in our region,” the Prime Minister said.
He highlighted how his Government is “elevating relationships that help to build sovereign capability and offer nations sovereign choice free from coercion”.
That way, partners can address the “big issues” they face such as economic and energy security, development and transnational crime, among others.
Social media ban
Mr. Albanese also recalled that last year Australia instituted a social media ban for people under 16, following the campaign by grieving parents who addressed the General Assembly that turned into global action.
“Already, more than 20 countries are bringing in or have brought in age restrictions on social media,” he said, “and with the European community taking action, there are many more to come.”

IRCS holds advanced life support course for Ghanaian health staff
TEHRAN – The Iranian Red Crescent Society’s health center in Ghana has held the first advanced life support course for nurses in the African country, aimed at strengthening their capacity to respond effectively to medical emergencies.
In addition to providing medical services, the center seeks to boost educational infrastructure and improve the knowledge of the health staff through sharing expertise with them, the IRCS website reported.
The IRCS is also holding an online training program and a practical training workshop at the center to ensure the specialized training will be ongoing so that the health personnel fully benefit from the IRCS capacity and knowledge.
The initiative does not merely target health staff; it also plans to train the local community. The program focuses on first aid training and essential rescue skills to prepare individuals for unexpected emergencies and teach them how to handle the situations and respond effectively to a wide range of injuries. In case of an emergency, the trained person can help the wounded people in the first critical seconds prior to the arrival of medical teams.
Health services in Ghana
In August, the IRCS health center in Ghana organized a one-day medical camp aimed to provide free medical services to flood victims and the needy, benefiting 547 individuals.
The initiative was taken following floods in the city of Accra and a request from the Ministry of the Ministry of Inner City and Zongo Development. IRNA quoted Hamidreza Dehqan, an IRCS official, as saying.
The Iranian Red Crescent Society’s health center was deployed to provide free medical care to those seeking assistance and individuals in need, Dehqan added.
He noted that 547 people benefited from health services during the one-day medical mission. The services provided included general practitioner consultations, medication distribution, pharmacy services, mobile laboratory testing, and counseling on midwifery and hygiene.
The humanitarian activities of the IRCS are not confined by geographical boundaries, Dehqan said, adding: “The presence of the Iranian Red Crescent Society’s health centers in various countries exemplifies the organization’s humanitarian approach to addressing the needs of local communities—an approach that prioritizes human dignity, assistance to the needy, and the alleviation of human suffering.”
In such programs, providing free medical services to those in need exemplifies altruism and humanitarian responsibility, demonstrating that serving humanity—transcending geographical boundaries—is one of the Iranian Red Crescent Society’s most vital missions, Dehqan stressed.
Referring to the fundamental principles of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, he noted that humanity, impartiality, neutrality, independence, voluntary service, unity, and universality constitute seven fundamental principles; the implementation of health programs in underdeveloped areas represents the practical manifestation of these principles in the field of service.
He emphasized that a key approach of the Iranian Red Crescent Society in its overseas operations is to simultaneously focus on treatment, prevention, and the promotion of community health.
“In this context, organizing health camps—alongside the ongoing activities of Red Crescent health centers—facilitates access to medical and counseling services for vulnerable groups.”
Pointing to the operations of the Iranian Red Crescent Society’s health center in Ghana, Dehqan stated that the continued presence of IRCS health centers in African nations is part of the Society’s humanitarian mission on the international stage, a presence founded on serving humanity and helping to improve the health of local communities.

U.S. President Donald Trump has given final approval for Ukraine to receive licenses to produce interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed this in response to questions from journalists on WhatsApp, according to Forbes Ukraine.
Zelensky did not specify when production could begin or which types of missiles would be covered by the license.
According to Zelensky, Trump announced the final decision during their most recent meeting in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
“President Trump emphasized this during our latest meeting. There are specific agreements in place, and we are making progress,” Zelensky said.

According to Reuters, launching mass production of components after a licensing agreement is signed could take between three and seven years.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is not relying solely on future domestic production. Kyiv is negotiating regular deliveries of ready-made interceptors and also plans to purchase around 1,000 Patriot missiles using credit financing from the European Union.

Ukraine strikes three Russian plants involved in missile production
Ukraine's defence forces have struck three facilities in Russia's Ulyanovsk, Tula and Voronezh oblasts.
Source: The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
The targets included the Yefremov Synthetic Rubber Plant in the city of Yefremov, Tula Oblast, and Voronezhsintezkauchuk near Voronezh.
Details: The General Staff said both facilities are involved in the production of solid rocket fuel, including for ballistic missiles used by the Iskander operational-tactical missile system.
Another facility struck was NPP Zavod Iskra plant in Russia's Ulyanovsk. Ukrainska Pravda reported the attack earlier citing OSINT sources. The General Staff said the plant was struck on the night of 24-25 September.
The General Staff said Zavod Iskra is part of the Almaz-Antey air and missile defence conglomerate and produces semiconductor devices and electronic components for Russia's military-industrial complex.
The General Staff added that, as part of production cooperation, the plant is involved in manufacturing Kh-59M2/M2A guided air-launched missiles and the 72V6 combat vehicle used in the Pantsir-S surface-to-air missile and gun system and its variants.
The General Staff said Voronezh is around 180 km from the Ukrainian border, Yefremov about 300 km away and Ulyanovsk around 800 km away.
Background: It was reported earlier that Ukraine's defence forces attacked the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara Oblast. The plant supplies Russia's military-industrial complex with synthetic rubber, which, among other things, is used to produce solid rocket fuel for short-range and ballistic missiles.

Qatar Airways retires idle A330s and sends pilots to RwandAir as Iran war drags on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:33:00 UTC
20:33:00 KST

Qatar Airways retires idle A330s and sends pilots to RwandAir as Iran war drags on
- Qatar Airways has retired its last Airbus A-330 jets and seconded some pilots to RwandAir due to high fuel costs and disruptions from the ongoing Iran war.
- The airline operates fewer flights and reduced passenger capacity, but plans to resume growth and expand its fleet with 138 new aircraft over five years.
- Qatar Airways supports pilot secondments to RwandAir to maintain flying skills while continuing a major fleet renewal with 410 planes on order through the 2030s.
AI generated
LONDON – Qatar Airways has retired its last Airbus A-330 passenger jet and seconded some pilots to Rwanda’s flag carrier as the prolonged Iran war disrupts Gulf aviation and accelerates the global phase-out of older jets, according to two people with knowledge of the matter and data reviewed by Reuters.
The move is the latest sign of the impact of a doubling of jet fuel prices since the war began, ending an industry-wide scramble for older jets to meet post-Covid travel demand.
Qatar Airways leased four Airbus wide-body A-330 jets from Oman Air in 2025 and planned to keep flying them through 2026, but the aircraft never entered service, the people said. The carrier has now fully retired its A-330 fleet.
One of the A-330s was acquired earlier in 2026 by Rwandan flag carrier RwandAir. Qatar Airways has longstanding ties to the airline and the people said a group of pilots, some of whom had not flown commercially since the start of the war, have been seconded to RwandAir.
The secondments and details of the fleet retirements have not previously been reported.
A Qatar Airways spokesperson said it was normal for the airline to regularly review its fleet, “retiring older aircraft and introducing newer, more efficient aircraft as they are delivered”. In the next five years it expects to receive 138 new aircraft, the spokesperson added.
The carrier operates a mixed Airbus and Boeing fleet of 239 passenger jets and 30 freighters, according to the company. A-330s made up 7 per cent of the passenger total, as of March, according to company data.
“A group of Qatar Airways A-330 pilots are being offered a voluntary short-term secondment opportunity with RwandAir,” the Qatar Airways spokesperson said, adding the scheme offered valuable flying opportunities for pilots while supporting the operational requirements of both airlines, without saying how long the secondment would last.
Costs spike as war continues
The war has impacted airlines globally but particularly the Middle East aviation hubs of Dubai and Doha following the Feb 28 US-Israeli strikes on Iran, although flight volumes have recovered to near pre-war levels.
By grounding the less fuel-efficient and older A-330 fleet, Qatar is containing jet fuel costs. Parking the planes is substantially cheaper than flying them at current high oil prices, analysts said.
The remaining aircraft Qatar Airways leased from Oman Air are parked either in Teruel, Spain, or in Doha, according to flight tracking data, and have remained parked in recent months, as the Iran war has dragged on. Two of the A-330s parked in Doha, which Qatar is leasing from aircraft lessor Jetran, will be returned to the lessor in October.
Passenger capacity falls
Analysts said older planes like the out-of-production A-330 operated by Qatar Airways would have been phased out by now, but have remained in service longer than expected due to manufacturing delays and high post-Covid travel demand.
Now, surging oil prices have made it less attractive to operate older jets, with global A330-200 and A330-300 flight operations down by about 12 per cent from September 2025, according to seven-day averages calculated by Cirium Ascend, which tracks global fleet movements.
Cirium data shows there are overall some 801 active A330-200 and A330-300 jets globally.
A total of 1,437 of the two models were built and delivered, Airbus data show. Those early models of A330 are no longer in production.
Qatar’s operational headache has been compounded by widespread disruption to Gulf carriers since the war began and the loss of some transit passengers to competing hubs.
“Middle East carriers are not flying the aircraft as much because of restrictions on the use of airspace there,” IBA’s head of consulting Dan Taylor said earlier in September.
As of September, Qatar Airways’ seven-day average available seat kilometres – the industry’s standard measure of passenger-carrying capacity – was 10 per cent lower than a year ago, according to Cirium Ascend, compared with a similar decline at Emirates and flat global industry capacity.
Qatar Airways is on average operating 12 per cent fewer flights versus a year ago, and using 4 per cent fewer planes, although it is on track to return to capacity and network growth by 2027, Cirium said.
Fleet renewal plans
While short-term demand has weakened, Qatar still expects growth to resume once regional disruption eases and will soon start recruiting pilots for newer aircraft, it said.
The secondment of just over a dozen staff to RwandAir would ensure pilots trained to fly A-330s can continue flying, the spokesperson said. Airlines do sometimes offer secondments to their pilots based on international partnerships with other carriers.
RwandAir, which has a codeshare agreement with Qatar, did not respond to a request for comment. It said in a post on X in August that it had received the first of five expected A-330 jets.
Qatar Airways, which runs one of the world’s busiest hubs and competes mainly with Dubai-based Emirates, continues to take delivery of new jets. It has received two large wide-body jets each from Airbus and Boeing in 2026, company data shows.
The Qatar Airways spokesperson said that between September 2026 and the end of 2027, the carrier was planning six aircraft exits and 19 new plane deliveries.
To meet growth objectives stretching into the 2030s, the airline has a total of 410 planes still on order from Boeing and Airbus, including 160 announced during a visit to the emirate by US President Donald Trump in May 2025. REUTERS

Over 18 fraud cases involving deepfakes reported in Russia since 2025 — Interior Ministry
Unknown

2026-09-25
11:32:57 UTC
20:32:57 KST

MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Eighteen fraud cases involving the use of deepfakes were reported in Russia over the 18-month period starting in 2025, and this is a relatively small number compared to the overall figure, a senior Russian Interior Ministry official told TASS.
"In 2025 overall and the first half of 2026, the number of registered fraud cases (under Article 159 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation) committed with the use of voice conversion and image-shaping technologies [deepfakes] stood at 18 out of 478,831 [in total]," Sergey Kalinin, a deputy head of the Russian Interior Ministry’s Department on the Fight Against Information and Communication Technologies Crimes, said.
Kalinin added that the number of reported fraud cases involving deepfakes is insignificant compared with the overall figure of registered fraud cases during this period.
However, Kalinin pointed out that it is common for scammers to use generative models to create believable audiovisual content (deepfakes), which allows them to impersonate victims’ relatives, bank employees, representatives of government agencies or public figures.
"By using synthesized voices or video recordings, scammers can coerce their victims into financial transfers or disclosing personal data," he told TASS on the sidelines of the ‘Dialogue about Fakes 4.0’ international forum.
The Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum is a global platform for discussing methods to combat disinformation and developing fact-checking technologies. The event was held at the Russia National Center on September 22 with the participation of over 2,000 journalists, experts and businesspeople from 80 countries.
It was organized by the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN), established in 2025 by the TASS news agency, the autonomous nonprofit organization "Dialogue Regions," and the New Media Workshop. TASS was the forum’s strategic media partner.

The Trump Administration Is Trying to Get Musk and X out of a $137 Million EU Fine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:32:17 UTC
20:32:17 KST

The US government is trying to get Elon Musk and his social media platform X out of a $137 million fine by the European Union in an escalation of its criticism of the bloc’s tech rules.
The US Department of Justice said it had filed an application with the help of the Department of State to support a legal challenge by Musk to annul the case in the EU’s General Court. The Luxembourg-based court will now decide whether the US has a right to intervene.
The US government is arguing that it should be involved in the case to protect American companies. The fine is precedent-setting as the bloc’s first sanction under the Digital Services Act, which requires online platforms to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content, especially the largest sites. Many of those, which include Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, Google’s YouTube, and Microsoft’s LinkedIn, are headquartered in the US and contribute significantly to the US economy, it pointed out.
“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” said assistant attorney general Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.
The case also has “implications” for US-EU relations, it warned. The act has become a major source of tension between officials, with US President Donald Trump calling the penalties “overseas extortion.” Last year, he threatened imposing tariffs on any country implementing digital regulation, which he said were “all designed to harm, or discriminate against, American technology.” Vice President JD Vance has criticized the DS’s content moderation rules as “authoritarian censorship.”
The European Commission slapped X with the €120 million fine in December following a two-year-long investigation which found X had breached transparency obligations. Claiming users with blue checkmarks are “verified accounts” when they simply have to pay for the status is deceptive, the Commission ruled. X’s inaccessible and incomplete advertising repository and failure to provide access to public data for researchers is also hindering research into the platform’s risks, it said. In July, the Commission accepted X’s plan to fix the data access issues, which X now has six months to implement.
Both Musk and X launched appeals against the ruling on behalf of both parties in February. The EU’s investigation was “incomplete and superficial” and the interpretation of the DSA obligations “tortured,” they said. They also complained they had not been given “rights of defence … suggesting prosecutorial bias.”
Musk has also complained about the financial and administrative burden of heightened transparency requirements as governments globally try to get a better understanding of—and limit—social media platforms’ risks of harm. In July, he argued Australia’s “invasive” information-gathering powers within the country’s under-16 social media ban interfered with international law. At the time, professor of internet law at Queen Mary University of London, Julia Hörnle, told WIRED that Australian regulators were within their rights to order disclosures related to a company’s operations in that particular country.

Daniel Thomas, widely known as "Danny Tommo", has built a large online following and recently founded Patriot Platform, a group focused on people arriving in Britain across the Channel on small boats.

Thomas, 37, is charged with criminal damage by slashing at a small boat with a knife while a rescue worker was on board and a further charge of failing to provide the PIN code for his phone.

The Ghanaian president also raised the issue of reparations from former colonial powers, noting that the structural legacies of slavery continue to fuel existing global inequalities.
"But real repair demands structural transformation. It requires dismantling the persistent engines of exploitation: unfair global trade regimes, predatory resource extraction, discriminatory credit ratings, unsustainable debt burdens, and the continued export of raw materials from Africa while real value addition and job creation occur elsewhere," he said.

China and the US are racing ahead on AI. Can they manage risks together?
Beijing and Washington told to tackle rising AI threats together at Singapore forum, but some argue fears about runaway technology are overblown
The United States and China must work together to establish safety guardrails for artificial intelligence, leading scholars and industry leaders said at a Singapore forum, warning that rapid advances in the technology demand stronger risk controls.
Speaking at the FutureChina Business Forum on Friday, Jude Blanchette, managing director of consultancy Macro Advisory Partners, urged the two superpowers to find common ground despite escalating geopolitical tensions.
“If ever there was a moment for [the US and China] to feel a strong impetus to come together, it would be now … given the shared concerns about the impact of emerging technologies, not only AI but also robotics,” Blanchette said.
He argued that the world was moving from an era shaped by traditional human behaviour to a “technocene” in which exponential technological leaps would dramatically reshape global power dynamics.

====================================================================================================

Palestinians in Masafer Yatta are surviving without water after Israeli settlers cut off a lifeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Palestinians in Masafer Yatta, in the south Hebron hills, are facing repeated water cuts after Israeli settlers damaged infrastructure supplying water to families in the area. According to Hebron’s governor Khaled Dudin, this attack follows a persistent pattern of settlers directly targeting the water supply, now for the fifth time.
Masafer Yatta is a 36-square-kilometer semi-desertic hilly area in the South Hebron region of the occupied West Bank. It directly overlooks the Naqab desert and extends west to the edge of the Dead Sea Valley. The hills are adjacent to the 1949 Armistice line, known today as the Green Line and viewed internationally as the borders of Israel proper. This strategic location makes it crucial for urban and agricultural growth south of the West Bank. For Israel, Masafer Yatta is treated as a buffer zone separating Israel proper from the deeper Palestinian demographic presence — a zone that needs to be emptied of Palestinians.
Last Saturday, during a field visit to Masafer Yatta, governor Dudin told the media that 1,600 Palestinian families within these 14 Palestinian hamlets are facing difficult living conditions due to damaged water lines, with families forced to rely on water tanks. Dudin also pointed out that water lines had been previously rehabilitated with the support of international organizations.
The Israeli settlers’ attacks on Palestinians’ means of life in Masafer Yatta has been ongoing since before October 2023, but has escalated in the past three years, and particularly in the past weeks. Sami Hureini, local activist and resident, told Mondoweiss that “the villages of Masafer Yatta have come under a relentless wave of attacks by settler groups, but also of demolitions by the Israeli army itself.”
Hureini said that there is no real infrastructure for services in Masafer Yatta, because the Israeli army doesn’t allow it. “In the past years, the communities were able to extend one water line from the edge of the zone where the Israeli army imposes strict control, and reached all 14 villages,” Hureini said. “But Israeli settlers kept damaging it, and sometimes the Israeli army bulldozed it.”
The main water line in the area was extended in 2018. It was first cut by the Israeli army’s civil administration in 2019, but was fixed by the joint municipality of Masafer Yatta. It was then partially damaged by Israeli settlers and fixed again multiple times.
In January, the Israeli army cut it again, and since then, it was damaged five times by Israeli settlers or the army.
The demolition of Palestinian property in Masafer Yatta has intensified since 2023, but more particularly since the beginning of 2026.
The area under strict Israeli military control was designated as a “firing zone” (areas in the West Bank that are off-limits to civilians and controlled by the Israeli army) in 1980, and Palestinians are not allowed to build or develop infrastructure around their homes. Palestinian families have been engaged in a legal battle with the Israeli army in Israeli courts for over 20 years for their right to live in their villages. In May 2022, the Israeli court gave its definitive ruling on the case — against the Palestinian residents, hence green-lighting their expulsion. This expulsion, Hureini affirmed, has been happening in a gradual, but accelerating manner since before the ruling.
Two weeks ago, Israeli forces demolished multiple built structures in Fakhit, a hamlet that is home to 70 residents and 12 farming families, leaving 30 people without housing. According to testimonies published by the Arabic news site Alaraby Al-Jadeed, Israeli forces gave residents only 20 minutes to evacuate. In the past two days alone, Israeli forces conducted 24 demolitions in three villages: Fakhit, Tabban, and Jinba, leaving 300 people without homes.
“People did not leave,” Hureini explained.“They stay in tents and caves that they have cleaned and made into living spaces, but living conditions are very dire, and are getting worse every day.”
Hureini also pointed out that Israeli settler groups have been stealing the water from Palestinians’ water wells, and that many of the people in the area have been forced to sell part of their livestock. Palestinian families in Masafer Yatta are mostly livestock herders who depend on sheep to make a living. Nidal Younis, the mayor of Masafer Yatta, told Mondoweiss that “in addition to the human consumption of water in Masafer Yatta, there are over 4,000 livestock that need water supply.”
This is not the first time that Palestinians in Masafer Yatta have faced water shortages because of Israeli damage to water lines. In December 2023, Israeli settlers damaged a waterline that serviced the hamlets of Isfaya, Maghayer al-Abid, and Tuba. In May 2025, Israeli army forces demolished seven water wells and 10 water tanks in the hamlet of Khalet Al-Dabe’.
‘The aim is to make people leave‘
According to local mayor Nidal Younis, the joint municipality for Masafer Yatta was able to connect the main water line for all of the 14 villages in 2018 with the help of European funding, providing high-quality water at an affordable price. “In early 2019, the Israeli army’s civil administration cut the line for the first time, and later Israeli settler groups damaged it again in the same year, but we were able to fix it every time,” he said.
“This time it is more difficult, as the escalating demolitions and restrictions by the Israeli army in Masafer Yatta make new attempts to fix the water line almost futile, and people are left relying on old wells, which settlers repeatedly damage or steal water from, and on overpriced water tanks that are very difficult to get to the remote areas in Masafer Yatta.”
Masafer Yatta is not the only place where Palestinians face water restrictions by Israeli forces or settlers. Since 2025, Israeli settler groups have repeatedly damaged water pumps at the Ain Samia spring east of Ramallah, which provides running water for 20 villages. Last May, Israeli settlers took over the Ain Al-Auja spring, northeast of Jericho, depriving Palestinian farmers of a vital irrigation source. Currently, 47 Palestinian families are left without access to water as a result of Israeli military infrastructure projects in the east of Tubas, in the northern Jordan Valley.
These patterns have been denounced by Amnesty International, and by Israel’s main human rights group B’Tselem who called it a “systemic, cruel campaign to deprive the most vulnerable Palestinian communities in the hottest, most arid parts of the West Bank of their water sources.”
In September 2011, the Emergency Water, Sanitation and Hygiene group (EWASH), a coordination body consisting of 28 international and local NGOs as well as UN agencies published a joint report with the Palestinian human rights group Al-Haq, stating that Israel’s water restrictions on Palestinians were a means to displace Palestinians from their lands.
For Nidal Younis, it is a clear policy with a clear aim. “People in Masafer Yatta are holding on to their land against all odds,” he said. “But steadfastness in these conditions becomes more difficult every day. The aim is to make people leave, the Israeli occupation doesn’t want anything to do with Palestinians in this area.”
Younis explained that the water line and the water wells had been rehabilitated with funding from the European Union, and that they have been damaged repeatedly since January, either by Israeli settlers or the Israeli army. “These wells and the water line provided water to the population for six shekels [about $2] for the cubic meter, which is affordable, and in good quality, but now, access to water has become a real challenge for every family in Masafer Yatta, especially the most remote places.”
“The village of Jinba, for example, is located deep in the so-called firing zone, at 24 kilometers from the nearest town with services,” the mayor explained. “This makes it difficult even for water tanks to reach it, since the Israeli army has blocked most roads from reaching the area.”
The mayor added that the roads in question are little more than rugged dirt paths that cut through the hills, and that Israeli settlers have established 13 settler outposts throughout Masafer Yatta.
Masafer Yatta’s ‘firing zone’ is 35 square kilometers wide. Located in the southernmost tip of the West Bank, its herding communities in the 14 villages are the only Palestinian presence in the area. Israel claims that Palestinians haven’t had a “permanent presence” in Masafer Yatta prior to 1980, ignoring the fact that the seasonal relocation of families is their ancestral way of life, and that they are the owners of grazing and farming lands there, most of which have been occupied by Israeli settlers since 2023.
The ‘firing zones’ play a central role in Israel’s plans to expand settlements in the West Bank. As was revealed in the declassified minutes of a 1979 meeting between the World Zionist Organization then-Israeli agriculture minister Ariel Sharon, where he said that ‘firing zones’ in the West Bank would be used as “land reserves for settlements.” Israel declared Masafer Yatta a ‘firing zone’ the following year.

Asian Games | Wang scores in extra time as China edges Vietnam to reach women's football semis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
19:29:18 CST
20:29:18 KST

OSAKA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Wang Shuang scored in the 109th minute as China edged Vietnam 1-0 in extra time Friday to reach the semifinals of women's football at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
China will face DPR Korea in the semifinals on Tuesday as DPRK thrashed Chinese Taipei 5-1 in another quarterfinal.
China topped Group G with two wins and one draw for seven points, while Vietnam advanced as the best third-placed team after collecting one point from one draw and two defeats in Group E.
The Steel Roses put Vietnam under pressure from kickoff but failed to create clear-cut chances in the first half.
China head coach Ante Milicic fielded striker Shao Ziqin, who had just returned from Portuguese club Benfica, in the 57th minute, to increase the pace of China's attack.
In the 63rd minute, Wang dribbled past defenders before delivering a fine pass, but Xie Zongmei missed the goal from close range.
Wang Yanwen was booked in the 74th minute for pulling down a Vietnamese player and will miss the semifinal due to two yellow cards accumulated.
China had a few chances in stoppage time, but shots from Shao Ziqin and Sun Fangxin inside the penalty area were all saved by the Vietnamese goalkeeper.
China registered 24 shots, including 10 on target, during regular time, compared with two shots and one on target for Vietnam. It was the first time that Chinese women's football failed to beat Vietnam in regular time.
China dominated in extra time and broke the deadlock in the 109th minute. A long ball was played into the penalty area, where Shao Ziqin controlled it before Wang Shuang calmly placed her shot into the far corner.
Milicic admitted that China should have settled the match in 90 minutes.
"It was a frustrating day because we really should have scored a goal earlier in the 90 minutes, but we didn't. But in the end, happy to get the win," he said.
Looking ahead to DPRK, Milicic said China would face a very different tactical challenge.
"If you look at them, their U17 and U20 and senior national team all play the same way. The junior teams are all used to winning World Cups, winning Asian Cups. They're very strong and difficult to deal with," he said.
"To dominate the game against them, not many teams have that opportunity. However, in a one-off game, I'll always believe in our girls. We'll come up with a game plan."
Milicic also acknowledged that China would have to make several changes due to injuries and suspension, with Zhang Linyan was injured in the group stage, while Li Qingtong and Wang Aifang picked up injuries on Friday's match.
"So there's going to be a lot of changes that we have to do. But the first thing we need to do is recovering well, see who's available," Milicic said.
"We're playing a very strong team next, but we're not afraid. We don't want to set the target for the final. Whether we'll get there depends on the day. But one thing I can guarantee you is the girls will fight and give everything they can." ■

Israeli boy, 14, killed in Russian drone strike on Kyiv home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:29:16 UTC
20:29:16 KST

A 14-year-old Israeli boy was killed Friday when a Russian drone struck his family’s home in central Kyiv, not far from the Israeli Embassy, ynet has learned. The boy was reportedly in his room doing homework when the drone hit.
The boy belonged to a Jewish family with Israeli citizenship that had moved to Kyiv in recent years. His mother suffered an arm injury in the blast and was hospitalized in moderate condition. His younger brother was also inside the apartment but escaped without physical injury.
The boy’s family has asked for his body to be flown to Israel for burial, where his grandparents live. The Foreign Ministry has been involved in handling the case.
Kyiv’s Jewish community and the Jewish Relief Network Ukraine, or JRNU, an emergency network operated by Chabad, were assisting the family and coordinating with authorities in Israel and Ukraine.
Rabbi Simcha Levenharz, who oversees operations for JRNU, said the organization was in continuous contact with the family and representatives of ZAKA, an Israeli volunteer emergency response organization, in case arrangements were needed to bring the boy’s body to Israel.
“These are the impossible conditions of life in Kyiv right now,” Levenharz said. “Despite the terrible tragedy and the fighting, we are doing and will continue to do everything we can to support the community and bring the joy of the holiday to every Jew, together with Chabad emissaries in Kyiv and throughout Ukraine.”
The strike hit a 16-story residential building in Kyiv’s central Pecherskyi district at about 8 a.m., according to Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv police said the boy was killed and at least seven residents were wounded, while later figures from Mayor Vitali Klitschko put the number of injured across the capital at nine, eight of whom were hospitalized.
Ukrainian officials said the drone struck the upper floors of the apartment building, with reports placing the impact between roughly the seventh and 10th floors. Emergency crews, police investigators, bomb disposal experts and medical teams were dispatched to the scene.
The Israeli Embassy is located on Lesi Ukrainky Boulevard in Kyiv’s Pecherskyi district.
The deadly strike came as Russia continued an intensified campaign of drone attacks against Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine. Ukrainian officials said Friday’s assault also struck residential and nonresidential buildings elsewhere in the capital. In the southern Odesa region, authorities reported that another person was killed in Russian strikes on a residential area and logistics facilities.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces carried out overnight drone strikes targeting Ukrainian defense industry facilities, logistics centers and vessels used by the Ukrainian military. Moscow has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians.
The attack follows weeks of increasingly intense Russian drone operations. Russia has deployed faster, higher-flying jet-powered versions of its Shahed-style attack drones, which Ukrainian forces have found more difficult to intercept than their propeller-driven predecessors. Reuters reported this week that the new drones can fly at altitudes of 4 to 7 kilometers and have placed additional strain on Ukraine’s air defenses.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, beginning a war that has subjected Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities to repeated missile and drone attacks. The United Nations has warned that Russia’s sustained use of long-range missiles and drones in densely populated areas has been a major driver of civilian casualties.

China's FAST telescope marks 10th anniversary
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
19:29:04 CST
20:29:04 KST

Balloons are released to celebrate the complete installation on China's Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST) in southwest China's Guizhou Province, July 3, 2016. China's Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST) has identified more than 1,300 pulsars over the past decade, outnumbering the total pulsar discoveries made by all other international telescopes over the same period, according to an academic conference that opened on Wednesday.
FAST marks its 10th anniversary on Friday. It has driven a historic leap for China's radio astronomy over the past decade. Boasting enhanced observational capabilities, the telescope, located in southwest China's Guizhou Province, has continuously expanded humanity's understanding of the universe.
As one of the world's most vital astronomical observation facilities, FAST has achieved a series of internationally influential findings in key research fields covering pulsars, neutral hydrogen galaxies, fast radio bursts and gravitational waves. (Xinhua/Ou Dongqu)

As one of the world's most vital astronomical observation facilities, FAST has achieved a series of internationally influential findings in key research fields covering pulsars, neutral hydrogen galaxies, fast radio bursts and gravitational waves. (Xinhua/Ou Dongqu)

20:28:50 KST

ATHENS, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- A powerful explosion partially collapsed a two-story building in central Athens on Friday morning, injuring three people, Greek state broadcaster ERT reported.
The blast occurred shortly after 7:30 a.m. local time (0430 GMT) at a two-story building on Lysicratous Street in Athens' historic Plaka district, opposite the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
The ERT reported that one passer-by suffered minor injuries, while one woman was safely extracted from the ruins of the building and another from an adjacent building that also sustained extensive damage. Both women were reported to have non-life-threatening injuries.
The cause of the explosion remains under investigation. Initial indications pointed to a possible natural gas leak, according to the ERT. ■

Cambodian museum unveils unearthed Angkor-Era Buddha statues
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
19:28:49 CST
20:28:49 KST

People visit an exhibition showcasing Buddha statues and fragments at the Preah Norodom Sihanouk-Angkor Museum in Siem Reap province, Cambodia, on Sept. 15, 2026. A collection of 274 Angkor-era Buddha statue fragments is now on public display at the Preah Norodom Sihanouk-Angkor Museum in Northwest Cambodia's Siem Reap province, the APSARA National Authority (ANA) said in a news release on Friday. (ANA/Handout via Xinhua)
PHNOM PENH, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- A collection of 274 Angkor-era Buddha statue fragments is now on public display at the Preah Norodom Sihanouk-Angkor Museum in Northwest Cambodia's Siem Reap province, the APSARA National Authority (ANA) said in a news release on Friday.
The sandstone fragments, which date back to approximately the late 13th century, were unearthed during archaeological excavations at the Banteay Kdei Temple within the UNESCO-listed Angkor Archaeological Park.
The exhibition highlights three distinct artistic styles of the Angkor period: Baphuon, Angkor Wat, and Bayon.
Voeun Vibolsokhum, a technical staff member at the museum, said that conservation specialists meticulously cleaned and restored the fragments following their discovery.
"Selected intact Buddha images are now permanently exhibited, allowing visitors, students, and researchers to appreciate the diversity and development of Khmer Buddhist art," he said.
The sculptures represent Mahayana Buddhist art across three of the 10 recognized artistic styles of the Angkor era.
Vibolsokhum noted that each style carries distinct visual characteristics.
He said the Baphuon style typically depicts the Buddha seated in meditation with open eyes, sheltered beneath the hoods of a protective naga, while the Angkor Wat style features the Buddha in meditation with open eyes, adorned in a crown and intricate jewelry. In contrast, the Bayon style generally shows the Buddha seated in meditation with closed eyes.
"Together, these three artistic styles reflect the evolution, diversity, and remarkable creativity of Khmer Buddhist art during the Angkor period," Vibolsokhum said. ■
Buddha statues and fragments are exhibited at the Preah Norodom Sihanouk-Angkor Museum in Siem Reap province, Cambodia, on Sept. 15, 2026. A collection of 274 Angkor-era Buddha statue fragments is now on public display at the Preah Norodom Sihanouk-Angkor Museum in Northwest Cambodia's Siem Reap province, the APSARA National Authority (ANA) said in a news release on Friday. ====================================================================================================

Asian Games | Ice-cold behind the arc, China falls to S. Korea in women's basketball semifinal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
19:28:47 CST
20:28:47 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Defending champion China went ice-cold from beyond the arc and fell to South Korea 85-80 in the women's basketball semifinals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Friday, dashing China's bid for a third straight title.
China dominated the rebounds 52-31 thanks to its height advantage, but a scoreless night from three-point range - 0 for 13 - combined with 18 turnovers left the team without enough firepower to win.
2.23-meter center Zhang Ziyu led China with 22 points, while Luo Xinyu and Yang Shuyu added 17 and 15, respectively. South Korea was led by Lee So-hee's game-high 23 points, with Lee Haeran adding 22. China's Han Xu and Li Yueru, along with South Korea's Park Ji-su, all missed the tournament due to commitments with their WNBA clubs.
The first three quarters were tightly contested. China opened with a 7-0 run, but the team struggled to adjust to South Korea's pace once Zhang checked in and was quickly overtaken - Zhang first played just one minute and three seconds before being subbed out.
China leaned on Luo and Tang Ziting to stay in the fight, and steadied itself once Zhang returned to the floor. South Korea shot a chilly 3-for-21 behind the arc in the first half, but the shots started falling in the third quarter, when the team knocked down four three-pointers. China, relying on drives from Wang Siyu and Yang, still carried a four-point lead into the fourth.
South Korea captain Kang Lee-seul, who finished with 16 points, caught fire in the decisive final 10 minutes, putting her team back in front. With China trailing by one with 9.1 seconds left, the team fouled intentionally, but Wang Siyu picked up her second unsportsmanlike foul of the game and was ejected. South Korea later converted all four ensuing free throws, and a last-gasp three-point attempt from Tang rimmed out as time expired, sealing the five-point loss for China.
Asked about China's scoreless night from beyond the arc, head coach Gong Luming pointed to the difficulty of getting the ball back out to the perimeter once it went inside.
"We have a big edge in the paint, but we couldn't get the ball back out once it went in. We wanted to slow the pace and play to our strengths inside, but the timing between our inside and outside game wasn't there," Gong said.
He added that South Korea's aggressive defense played a role. "Their pressure created real problems for us. Everyone was fighting at their limit, and we had open looks, but we didn't have enough left in the tank to convert them."
Gong acknowledged that his team's approach ran counter to the international game's growing emphasis on perimeter shooting, calling it a matter of necessity rather than choice.
"To keep pace with that global trend, you need the right players and the skill set for it. Once you have both, you build a team with a foundation," he said. "We have to work with what we actually have on this roster - what we want to do and what we're able to do."
"Tonight isn't the full picture of this team, but we'll go back and take a hard look at why we lost," Gong added.
On the development of the towering center Zhang, Gong said she still has plenty to work on, and that experience on the floor remains the best teacher.
"This was her first Asian Games, right off her first World Cup - valuable experience that will help her work through transition speed, post positioning, physical contact and getting back on defense," Gong said. "Every bit of progress matters. We don't want to rush her - she still has a lot of room to grow."
China will play for bronze on Friday.
Looking ahead to the bronze medal game, Luo said the team would give it everything. "We want to fight for the win and finish this Asian Games with the best result we can, with what we're capable of." ■

Russia's ruling party retains "constitutional majority" in State Duma: official election results
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
19:28:37 CST
20:28:37 KST

MOSCOW, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- The results of the 9th State Duma elections show that the ruling United Russia party won 349 seats, retaining its "constitutional majority" status, Russian Central Election Commission (CEC) Chairperson Ella Pamfilova announced on Friday.
Pamfilova said that representatives of six parties and four self-nominated candidates were elected to the new State Duma, the lower house of parliament.
According to CEC statistics, United Russia won 349 seats in the lower house of parliament, followed by the Communist Party of the Russian Federation with 37 seats, the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia with 23 seats, New People with 19 seats, A Just Russia with 17 seats, and Rodina with one seat. The four remaining seats were allocated to self-nominated candidates.
The final turnout in the Sept. 18-20 State Duma election was 59.8 percent, higher than the 51.72 percent recorded in 2021, Pamfilova said.
The State Duma is Russia's permanent legislative body, with 450 deputies.
The seat allocation for this election followed the traditional model: of the 450 State Duma seats, 225 are distributed proportionally according to party lists, with participating parties required to reach a 5 percent threshold to obtain seats; the remaining 225 seats are elected through single-mandate constituencies nationwide under a relative majority voting system. ■

China Focus: No more "calorie bombs": Mooncake makes healthier, lighter comeback in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
19:28:34 CST
20:28:34 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- As the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches, mooncakes, China's time-honored festival delicacy, are taking on smaller portions, lighter recipes and simpler packaging, while increasingly finding their way into everyday consumption.
For generations of Chinese consumers, traditional mooncakes with fillings such as lotus seed paste, egg yolks and mixed nuts have been a festive staple. But as living standards rise and health awareness grows, consumers are increasingly seeking lighter, more balanced options rather than indulgence alone.
Such a shift is visible at a pastry shop in Taiyuan, capital of north China's Shanxi Province, where customers are browsing shelves stocked with low-sugar and multigrain-based mooncakes.
"I want to buy some mooncakes for the Mid-Autumn Festival, but traditional ones are often quite large and contain a lot of sugar and oil," said a customer surnamed Jia. "These new, smaller low-sugar mooncakes are just what I need."
Tan Zhenjun, who runs a mooncake factory in Shenchi County, a major mooncake-producing area in Shanxi, said Jia's choice reflects a trend that has gained momentum in recent years, prompting producers to offer more mini-sized products.
Traditional mooncakes were often larger and richer, serving not only as festive treats but also as a source of extra nourishment when food was less abundant, Tan said.
As living standards improved, mooncakes gradually shifted from a filling food to a more leisurely treat, paving the way for today's lighter, lower-calorie varieties.
Tan said the mooncakes produced by his bakery have "shrunk" from 120 grams each to 100 grams and now to 50 to 80 grams.
Sales of eight-piece boxes are also gradually overtaking those of 20-piece boxes, he said. Consumers are increasingly choosing box sizes based on family size and actual needs, rather than buying large quantities for holiday display.
Healthier recipes are following the same trajectory. At a major pastry brand's flagship store on an e-commerce platform, a low-sugar mooncake has sold more than 300,000 units, while customer service staff said sales of low-sugar varieties have quickly caught up with those of traditional ones.
"People are paying more attention to health nowadays," one consumer wrote in a review, saying the low-sugar version satisfied her cravings with fewer calories.
The trend toward healthier choices is perhaps more evident in handmade mooncakes developed by a public hospital in Zhengzhou City, central China's Henan Province, which feature fillings inspired by traditional Chinese medicine.
Developed by the hospital's clinical nutrition department, the mooncakes use Chinese yam, dried tangerine peel, powdered sesame and other traditional Chinese medicinal ingredients, drawing on the traditional concept of food as medicine. The products have become popular at the hospital restaurant, attracting consumers interested in healthier alternatives.
Low-sugar products are expected to remain a major direction for innovation in China's mooncake industry, with natural sugar substitutes, low-glycemic-index ingredients, plant-based recipes and probiotics gaining attention, according to a 2026 report by iiMedia Research.
The shift is not limited to recipes and flavors. It is also changing how mooncakes are packaged and consumed.
For years, elaborate mooncake gift boxes were closely associated with Mid-Autumn Festival gift-giving. Today, simpler paper wrapping and compact packaging are gaining traction as consumers place greater emphasis on the products themselves rather than dazzling presentation.
For younger consumers, mooncakes are no longer just a festival specialty shared by families. They can also serve as workplace snacks, afternoon treats or pop-up indulgences for their appetite and mind.
On Chinese social media platform Rednote, Gen-Z content creators posted videos of molding pies, ice cream and even cheeseburgers into mooncake forms, garnering thousands of likes and joyful comments.
"So it's the pastry pattern that matters, right?" asked a viewer in the comments.
"I don't know, but that's a perfect beef-and-cheese-flavored mooncake for me," another viewer replied.
As mooncakes take smaller, simpler and more diverse forms, the boundary between mooncakes and other pastries and snack foods is becoming less distinct.
For traditional mooncake makers, the changes mean that innovation is no longer simply about new flavors or eye-catching gift wrappings. Increasingly, it is about finding the right balance among ingredients, recipes, portion sizes, packaging and consumption scenarios.
The shift also reflects a broader effort in China to upgrade consumption and better meet people's growing needs for a better life. The country's plan to expand consumption during the 15th five-year plan period, released in July, calls for initiatives to boost consumption, upgrade goods consumption and enrich consumption scenarios, including measures to promote health-oriented consumption.
Against this backdrop, the changing mooncake market offers a glimpse into how rising living standards are reshaping Chinese consumption habits: from quantity to quality, from elaborate packaging to the product itself, and from one-off festive purchases to more casual and personalized treats. ■

LISBON, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- More than 100 heavy vehicles from Portugal's earthworks sector joined a slow-driving protest Friday morning to demand concrete measures to address rising fuel costs.
The protest began at around 7:40 a.m. local time (0640 GMT) at the Lordelo entrance to the A42 motorway in Paredes, northern Portugal, with more than 100 vehicles taking part initially, according to the official Lusa news agency.
The convoy was scheduled to travel south via the A41 motorway and then continue along the A1 toward Coimbra, where the protest was expected to end at the Coimbra Sul exit.
Miguel Machado Mendes, a representative of the protest organizers, said at the scene that nearly 500 heavy vehicles were expected to join the demonstration along the route toward Coimbra.
The protest was being monitored by the National Republican Guard, Portugal's national gendarmerie force.
The demonstration brought together companies involved in aggregate extraction, transportation, earthmoving and other activities related to the earthworks sector.
According to a statement issued by the organizers, diesel prices in Portugal rose from 1.59 euros (1.81 U.S. dollars) per liter on Feb. 27 to 2.22 euros (2.53 dollars) per liter.
The organizers described the increase as "historical" and said it was creating an "unsustainable" situation for companies in the sector. ■

ALMATY, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- The search operation for the Kazakh Naval Forces servicemen swept out to sea concluded Friday morning after the bodies of two remaining victims were found, bringing the death toll to 14, the Kazakh Defense Ministry said.
A total of 17 service members were carried off by waves during a naval exercise on the Caspian coast in Kazakhstan's southwestern Mangystau region amid sharply deteriorating weather conditions, including intensifying winds, the ministry has said in a statement.
Three of those swept to sea have been rescued, and 12 soldiers were confirmed dead earlier, according to the ministry.
A criminal case has been opened over the incident, the country's Prosecutor General's Office said.
A nationwide day of mourning was declared in Kazakhstan on Friday, according to the presidential press service. ■
