MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Russia, the US, and Ukraine are not currently preparing for a new round of talks amid ongoing discussions and bilateral meetings, the EU is considering approving a new loan to Ukraine using frozen Russian assets in light of the upcoming 2027 elections in some member states, and the likely duration and impact of the US-China trade truce on bilateral relations. These stories topped Friday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Trilateral talks on Ukraine not currently being prepared
A new trilateral round of talks involving Russia, the US, and Ukraine is not currently being prepared. The sides are discussing this issue, but only in general terms. Meanwhile, the Russia-US track remains active: earlier, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a meeting, and media reports noted that special presidential envoy and Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev had traveled to the US for talks with American officials.
"In practical terms, the issue of a trilateral meeting was not discussed here in New York. What matters here is not talk about certain formats or far-fetched schemes. What is needed here is real progress toward a serious political settlement. It seems that Zelensky and his team are not yet ready for this," Grigory Karasin, a member of the Russian delegation to the UN General Assembly and chairman of the Russian Federation Council Committee on International Affairs, told Izvestia.
The problem stems primarily from differing approaches to the settlement itself, Igor Istomin, acting head of the MGIMO Applied Analysis of International Processes Department, noted. According to him, Moscow has repeatedly stated its readiness to seek solutions through diplomatic channels, but not at the expense of its own interests. Previous attempts at reaching an agreement have been hindered by Kiev and the European countries supporting it, which have been unwilling to engage in reciprocal dialogue while duly considering Russia's position. Recent signals from the Ukrainian side do not provide sufficient reason to believe that this approach has changed significantly, the expert added.
According to Istomin, the dialogue will only be substantive if Kiev stops relying on unconditional support from European countries. The Ukrainian side is largely offsetting the ongoing difficulties in its relations with Washington by relying on assistance from the EU.
The next major forum at which the leaders could potentially meet will be the APEC summit in China's Shenzhen on November 18-19. The Kremlin previously reported that the possibility of a trilateral meeting between Putin, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping had been discussed. However, preparations have not yet begun: the Russian Foreign Ministry emphasized that the agenda and possible outcome of such a meeting must first be determined. Another opportunity will arise on December 14-15 at the G20 summit in Miami. The US has invited Putin to attend. The Kremlin welcomed this move, stating that the details are being worked out via diplomatic channels.
Izvestia: Ukraine to spend EU’s 90-billion-euro loan before end of 2027
The EU is considering approving a new loan to Ukraine using frozen Russian assets. This will be necessary if Kiev spends the previously allocated 90-billion-euro loan ahead of schedule. Earlier, Zelensky requested an additional $27 billion in funding from the EU. Brussels may allocate these funds from the already approved loan ahead of schedule, though in that case, the funds would not last until the end of 2027. In addition, 800 million euros will soon be allocated from the loan to finance civilian needs. Attempts to seize Russian assets may intensify in the coming months because opponents of funding Ukraine may gain ground during elections in Germany, Greece, Spain, and France throughout 2027.
Brussels is looking for a way out of this situation. In particular, it is considering the possibility of using Russia’s frozen assets to continue funding Kiev, Pekka Toveri, head of the EU-Ukraine Parliamentary Association Committee in the European Parliament, told Izvestia. "The EU is working on funding for the period after 2027. Either through frozen Russian assets or in some other form," he noted.
At present, according to official data, Ukraine has already received about 15 billion euros from the 90-billion-euro loan, with most of the funds earmarked for the production of drones, the purchase of interceptor missiles, and the development of the military-industrial complex. In turn, Yegor Sergeyev, a senior researcher at the Institute of International Studies of the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO), believes that while Brussels will meet Kiev’s new demands, it will not provide the full amount requested. This is necessary both to reach an agreement between the countries and to show the public that the EU has become more cautious against the backdrop of corruption scandals in Ukraine, the expert pointed out.
The EU is already beginning to divide along the lines of support for Ukraine, St. Petersburg State University professor Natalya Yeremina told Izvestia. According to her, EU member states are growing weary of supplying weapons from their own stockpiles, which consume an increasingly significant portion of their budgets. The coming year will be critical for both Ukraine and EU countries in terms of continued funding, Yeremina emphasized.
Vedomosti: Likely duration of US-China trade truce
China and the US have agreed to extend the trade truce until January 10, 2027, in the hope of reaching a more comprehensive deal during that time, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s official state visit to the US. Speaking at an official banquet at the White House, US leader Donald Trump expressed his readiness to work with Beijing to forge a better future for both countries. In response, Xi emphasized his desire to steer the "ship of US-China relations onto a calm course" toward the future.
The Chinese would like to extend the trade truce by one year, until the 21st National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party, Alexander Lomanov, head of the Center for Asia-Pacific Studies under the Russian Academy of Sciences’ World Economy and International Relations Institute, told Vedomosti. However, both Xi and the entire Chinese elite have acknowledged that the situation has changed and are ready for a different scenario. Therefore, this source of pressure is no longer as strong for Xi, as he understands that Trump’s actions cannot seriously slow down the Chinese economy and are effective only in the technology sector. However, according to the expert, even here, Beijing holds a trump card in the form of rare earth elements, on which the Americans will remain dependent until roughly the early 2030s. China is ready to respond but will not be the first to escalate the trade conflict.
Extending the truce by only two months may indicate that one of the parties wants to gain additional concessions from the other, Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin emphasized. According to him, China’s position is "in principle stronger," while the White House faces a more difficult situation. Moreover, Washington hopes for more productive relations with Beijing, which Trump has not yet achieved. Based on this, Trenin pointed out that China has given the US two months to resolve certain issues to its satisfaction. He added that, in general, time is working against the US: China’s power is growing, even though its foreign policy has not yet been particularly aggressive. However, this does not mean that China is becoming less influential or less interested in the future of the world.
According to Trenin, Russia has "no suspicions whatsoever" about any grand deals between Beijing and Washington behind its back. "I think that here we are confident not so much in China as in our interpretation of China’s interests and American policy. And this suggests that the mini-thaw currently taking place between them is, more likely than not, a short-lived phenomenon," the expert stressed.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Venezuela to complete democratizing country, hold elections
Venezuela’s authorized president Delcy Rodriguez announced during her address to the UN General Assembly plans to finish the country’s democratization process and hold elections. This was one of Washington’s demands to end the pressure on Caracas, which lasted from last summer until the January operation to capture Nicolas Maduro. However, the date of the elections remains unknown.
Viktor Heifets, director of the Ibero-American Studies Center at St. Petersburg State University, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta that Rodr·guez’s speech did not mention a specific date for the elections. "She said she is ready to ensure Venezuela’s full transition to democracy, but for this transition to be successful, it must be seamless and guarantee the right of all political forces to participate. This is an acknowledgment of the struggle for all that is good against all that is bad. In reality, I don’t think holding elections is part of the Venezuelan leadership’s immediate plans," the expert noted.
Heifets added that Rodriguez’s legitimacy as interim president is currently quite questionable in light of the Venezuelan Constitution, which is why it was necessary to emphasize that elections would take place. "Besides, Rodriguez must be aware that her approval ratings aren’t all that high. If she intends to remain in power and elections are held in the near future, it’s highly likely she won’t win, assuming there’s no election fraud. I think she and her inner circle know this," the expert pointed out. The later these elections take place, the better Rodriguez’s chances of expanding her influence are, Heifetz stressed.
"It’s important to note that Rodriguez’s main source of support is not the local military or ruling party elites, but Trump. No one can say yet how much power the US president will have after the November congressional elections. Perhaps Rodriguez decided to play it safe and declare that, of course, they intend to hold the elections," the expert noted. He recalled that not long ago, opposition politician Maria Corina Machado had stated the need to hold elections no later than 2027, and in this situation, Rodriguez could not stay silent. "But it is unlikely that the authorized president’s statement will lead to the setting of a specific and near-term election date," Heifets emphasized.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Rising tanker freight rates’ effect on oil exports
Freight rates for supertankers have surpassed $1.2 million per day, setting an all-time record, media reports say. These are VLCC and ULCC tankers, which can carry 1.5 million barrels of oil or more. This calculation is based on the Middle East-Asia route. Last year, by comparison, the freight rates for such tankers on the same route peaked at $80,000 per day.
These sky-high freight rates are one of the main reasons Russian oil costs more than Brent crude at buyers’ ports. Oil is in short supply, and buyers are unable to force Russian companies to cover all transportation costs. Buyers must shoulder part of the cost themselves. Russian National Energy Security Fund head Konstantin Simonov told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that a significant portion of the so-called discount is actually the cost of freight, plus insurance, services, and trading expenses.
According to DA Consulting CEO Daniil Tyun, record freight rates of $1.2 million per day primarily apply to specific routes. This figure cannot be automatically applied to Russian exports. Nevertheless, the global tanker market is interconnected. When carriers begin to earn exceptionally high revenues on Middle Eastern routes, part of the available fleet is redirected there. As a result, the supply of vessels for other routes, including those to Russia, decreases. Sanctions and longer voyage durations are creating additional pressure, the expert noted.
In addition, rising freight costs are indirectly affecting oil production volumes, energy expert Kirill Rodionov emphasized. Production is already 1.5 million barrels per day below OPEC+ quotas.
It is not increasing, in part due to rising freight costs. Unplanned maintenance at Russian oil refineries has reduced domestic crude processing capacity. In this situation, exporting becomes an option for oil companies to avoid cutting production. This was the case last year; however, high freight costs and shipping restrictions in the Black Sea are now constraining production.

Reasoning together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
22 minute listen
Jürgen Habermas died on 14 March 2026, in the German town of Starnberg, aged 96. Every fall, from the mid-1990s into the late-2000s, he would come to Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois to teach and give talks, a visit that a dedicated group of students looked forward to every fall term. The year that has stayed with me is 2004, when he taught what he’d spelled out in Between Facts and Norms (1992), his opus applying his theory to democratic politics. Law, philosophy, history, political science: students spanned many disciplines to come watch the famous German scholar every week, dressed in Wrangler jeans and a tweed jacket, expose his theory of deliberative politics in his unmistakable nasal voice, thick German accent, and impeccable English. Max Weber and the Frankfurt School, which were intimate to him, since he’d been Theodor Adorno’s research assistant in the 1950s, came to life in his speech and then in schemas and figures in chalk as he theorised about them.
I understood almost none of it at first: words I’d read were coming to life in the room, spoken by their author, and still not resolving into sense. After several lectures, the shape came into focus: this wasn’t just Between Facts and Norms being rebuilt in public, but decades of work arriving at a single place. Since The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), Habermas had been arguing that reason survives in modern life only as something people do together, that is, by giving each other reasons and staying open to being moved by them, rather than by force, money or tradition. Between Facts and Norms was that idea turned toward law and democracy directly: a state counts as legitimate only when its laws could in principle be justified to everyone bound by them, through exactly that kind of open exchange. I’d watched that argument take root in a decades-long intellectual history. Thinking is a practice, it involves owing each other explanations, questions, answers. It is not a fast process, and doing it in public, out loud, in front of a room, is what makes it worthwhile.
I attended all of Habermas’s seminars during my time at Northwestern with great interest and, to be honest, a sense of awe. One day, the topic of the weekly seminar was inclusion, and I had argued, with the timid conviction of a green graduate student, that deliberative publics ought to be designed for inclusion, and that entry into these publics required that members accept the terms of deliberation themselves. ‘Well, we can tell that Ms Prattico really is a Catholic in the strict, universalist sense,’ was not the answer I expected – and what took me by surprise wasn’t that he’d made a joke of my religion, but that he’d seen me as a person with a history and a set of unexamined beliefs, something he’d noticed only by teaching me.
After the seminars, the class would sometimes go out for drinks. It was on one of these occasions that I understood where the joke had come from. I’d asked him what it had been like arriving in the US as a visiting professor for the first time, at the New School for Social Research in the autumn of 1967, which decades earlier had served as a refuge for scholars fleeing the same Germany in which he’d grown up. It was the start of a long habit of crossing the Atlantic: Princeton four years later, for the Gauss Lectures where he first tried out the turn toward language that would eventually become his theory of communicative action; then, decades on, Northwestern, where I got to sit in the room.
Habermas answered my question by going back further than any of that. He’d been raised Lutheran. Visiting the US in the 1960s and ’70s, he’d been introduced to the Quakers, and something in their small meetings had stayed with him, specifically the way they sought unity with everyone present. When he came to describe the conditions under which people could reason together as equals, he said he heard an echo of those meetings: conditions that hold only when everyone who could be affected by a norm isn’t just included but has a voice, can object, and speaks with sincerity. In those conditions, which go far beyond mere inclusion, the only constraint left on discourse is ‘the unforced force of the better argument’, as he put it in Justification and Application (1993). It didn’t feel like something he’d have said at the podium.
The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962), his seminal work originally published in German, made an argument about something concrete: 18th-century coffeehouses, salons and journals, where private citizens began treating the affairs of state as something they had standing to publicly discuss and judge, rather than simply obey. That habit, Habermas argued, was where modern democratic legitimacy first took root. The book also identified tendencies that would weaken it, too. He thought that the public sphere had already started to decay, folded back into spectacle by advertising and mass media, the public reduced from participants to an audience. It took almost 30 years for an English translation to appear. By the time it did, in 1989, Habermas had gotten a great deal of mileage out of the book in its original language; indeed, it had already made him a name outside Germany. When Craig Calhoun finally gathered the English-language response into a single volume, Habermas and the Public Sphere (1992), bringing together historians and theorists who challenged the argument, closing with a long response from Habermas himself, he could have easily spent the occasion defending a book that had already proved itself. Instead, he very openly contended with these critiques.
He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story. But the warning itself never went away
Two critics stand out. Nancy Fraser argued that the public sphere was never actually open to everyone since it had excluded women and other groups from the start. She proposed replacing one public with many, arguing with each other, including publics formed by the very groups shut out of the first one. Geoff Eley made a related point from history: working-class and plebeian public spheres had existed alongside the bourgeois one all along, not before or after it. Both were extending an argument that Oskar Negt and Alexander Kluge had made back in 1972, that a whole proletarian public sphere existed, which Habermas’s book never accounted for.
Habermas answered these criticisms directly, in an essay called ‘Further Reflections on the Public Sphere’, printed as the closing chapter of Calhoun’s book. Habermas conceded that the exclusion of women was not incidental but built into how the bourgeois public sphere had worked from the start. Unlike the exclusion of underprivileged men, which was a problem of class, and in principle correctable, the exclusion of women, he now wrote, ‘has been constitutive for the political public sphere not merely in that the latter has been dominated by men as a matter of contingency but also in that its structure and relation to the private sphere has been determined in a gender-specific fashion.’ Habermas conceded that other public spheres had existed alongside the one he had taken as foundational. And he softened the warning, without abandoning it. He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story, the early stirrings of consumer society. But the warning itself never went away. Sixty years on, he was still diagnosing a public sphere being distorted by commercial and structural forces, only now the culprit was platforms and algorithms rather than advertising and mass circulation.
He did not give up everything. He still wanted to keep the public sphere as something to measure democracies against, even if the history behind it was messier than he’d first made it look. The criticism and his answer to it sit in the same book, printed one after the other. Habermas’s views were open to being challenged, and open for us all to witness his thought in process.
Early in my dissertation work, I wanted to explore the role of experts in democracies through Habermas’s theory of deliberative politics, though I didn’t yet know how – I was, by any measure, stuck. My advisor, Cristina Lafont, one of his most trusted students, arranged a meeting anyway, at the hotel where he stayed during his visits to Northwestern’s campus in Evanston. He didn’t seem to mind that I arrived without a fully formed argument. Over almost two hours at what was then the Homestead Hotel, he had me lay out the problem as it stood, half-formed, and began working through it himself, out loud, testing it against his own theory as he went. He explained the three types of discourse that characterise deliberation – moral, ethical, and pragmatic – and was clear that when it comes to the moral, there are no experts: only individuals working out, together, what’s right in a given context.
Followed to its conclusion, that seemed to leave no room for expertise anywhere in deliberative politics. But he then turned to pragmatic discourse, where expertise does real work: finding the most empirically sound way to reach a goal already agreed on. Experts have no authority over what’s right, fair or worth valuing – only over facts. This was, in miniature, an argument he’d been making since his early work on science and politics: that treating value-laden political questions as though they were merely technical ones corrodes democracy. Decades later, in Justification and Application, he’d given the same worry he’d laid out in the trichotomy that morning sharper philosophical shape.
In later meetings in his office, more routine than that first one, I pushed the distinction further: what did it mean for climate change – a problem almost always treated, in his terms, as a matter of pragmatic discourse, all graphs and targets and carbon budgets, and almost never as a moral one. Who pays? What do we owe the people who pay? How should the resources that caused the damage be used? He didn’t have a ready answer. He asked question after question, testing the case against his own framework as though it genuinely hadn’t occurred to him before.
Justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold now: those standards can be shown wrong later
I’ll never know for sure if he was being generous or if I had shown him something he had not yet thought of in applying his own distinction. What stayed with me wasn’t the answer but the manner of it: a philosopher in his 70s, decades into a settled framework, still willing to test that framework against a case he hadn’t considered, in real time, out loud, in front of a student.
By 1999, Habermas gave up a position he’d held since 1973, the year he’d argued that truth is simply whatever people would agree on if they argued it out under fair-enough conditions. By the end of the century, he’d decided this was a mistake: it confused truth with justification. A claim can meet every test we have for it, survive every objection anyone raises, be about as justified as a claim can be, and still turn out false. That’s because justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold right now, and those standards can later be shown wrong. Truth doesn’t move when our standards do. Moral claims were different, he still thought: what’s right can only ever be what a fair conversation would settle on. There’s nothing else for rightness to answer to. But facts about the world answer to the world itself, not just to our best current agreement about it.
Several people had been pushing him toward this change. The US philosopher Richard Rorty pushed from the side from which Habermas was now backing away: for Rorty, there was no need for truth to answer to anything beyond what an audience could be talked into agreeing on, and he’d been making that case to Habermas for years. Lafont, my advisor, who’d arranged the hotel meeting, pushed from the other side, drawing on the US philosopher Hilary Putnam, who had spent much of his career arguing against exactly the kind of view that made truth depend entirely on human agreement. Lafont had argued since 1994 that Habermas’s own philosophical tradition, in its turn toward language, had drifted into a position where it couldn’t say the world holds firm no matter how we talk about it. When Habermas changed his mind, he moved toward Lafont’s position, not Rorty’s.
What Habermas never spelled out is what this does to moral and political claims once people stop being able to agree at all. Truth, on his revised view, still has somewhere to go even if everyone stops talking: the world doesn’t care whether anyone’s listening. His philosophy of Rightness never had that option. So, when the people who’d need to agree on something splinter into groups that no longer talk to each other, a factual claim can still be true or false regardless. A moral claim has nothing left holding it up, once nobody’s left in the room to agree on it.
Habermas gave up a position he’d held for almost 30 years because the people around him showed him it didn’t hold. He’d spent decades arguing that claims get redeemed when someone can compel you to answer, and then was compelled himself, and answered, in print, aged 70. Those critiques were not meant to be damning objections: they were precisely what his theory called for and was built on, ultimately.
Habermas returned to the subject in ‘Reflections and Hypotheses on a Further Structural Transformation of the Political Public Sphere’ (2022). His starting point is a particular relationship between beliefs and reality. Constitutional democracy runs on citizens holding certain assumptions about their own disagreements, namely that the disagreements are real, that they’re about something, that better reasons could in principle settle them. The system holds together only as long as those assumptions stay reasonably close to how politics actually works. His argument is that a public sphere, run through social media, threatens that relationship and widens that gap.
For Habermas, there are two forces at play in this widening. Platforms drop the editorial filtering that newspapers and broadcasters used to perform, and they turn every user into someone who publishes. For Habermas the deeper problem isn’t the resulting noise; it’s that heavy platform use produces something smaller than a public: semi-public spheres, self-enclosed, silos whose members can no longer perceive the wider public sphere as inclusive at all – claims to universality beyond their own horizon become, in his words, ‘suspect of hypocrisy’. That perception is itself the damage, on his account, as much as anything actually happening out in the general public sphere. He ends by insisting that ‘maintaining a media structure that ensures the inclusive character of the public sphere and the deliberative character of the formation of public opinion and political will is not a matter of political preference but a constitutional imperative.’
A factual claim still has to get the world right, whether or not anyone’s around to check it. Moral claims never did: they answer only to discourse. And discourse is exactly what he’s just described coming apart. He doesn’t draw the conclusion for moral and political claims himself, but it follows from putting his two books next to each other: the very thing a claim about what we owe each other had to answer to is the thing he says is disappearing, in an age dominated by exchanges on social media.
People retreat into whichever group agrees with them and lose their grip on a shared standard of true and false
Around that time, I reached out to my advisor for help asking Habermas for a foreword to a collection I was editing on Habermas and democracy. He was known for guarding his time closely – very few people had his email address, and he accepted only a handful of the hundreds of such requests he received each year. A couple of months later, an email came from an address I didn’t recognise: he had accepted, and written to say so himself. Amid the logistics, he added one condition: ‘You should send me at least a substantive part of the book before I can and would sit down and settle a few ideas.’ At 92, he wanted the material in hand before he’d commit to anything.
What came back was not a review of the interviews that make up the book one by one. He says so himself in the opening lines: it isn’t his task to comment on the conversations directly. Instead, he used the occasion to answer the standing objections to his view of deliberative democracy, and to close with the digital transformation that turned out to run through nearly every interview in the book – a theme he noticed himself, and named as central to the collection. One section was on experts, common sense, and the chain of translation that carries specialised knowledge into public reasoning: the same distinction he’d first sketched over a hotel breakfast, worked out now in far more detail, at the very end of his working life.
At one point, he writes that what’s been lost, in the democracies now regressing, is ‘a conflict of opinions that remains recognisable as a dispute about which position is backed by the better reasons.’ That’s as close as he ever came, in anything he wrote for me directly, to stating my own premise in his own words. He names the same loss again later in the foreword, describing people who retreat into whichever group already agrees with them and lose their grip not just on the public sphere’s inclusiveness but on the idea of a shared standard of true and false. What he doesn’t do here, any more than he did in 1999, is follow that loss when it concerns a moral claim once the discourse behind it comes apart. And that is what I tried to explore in my philosophical work since my dissertation.
He still believed the gap between expert and layperson could always, in principle, be closed by the right chain of translation. It was the one thing he never revised: he revised his theory of the public sphere, his theory of truth, but never the conviction that under the right conditions people can still reach each other. I am not persuaded that these conditions are as anywhere close to being met today – but that’s a disagreement I never got to have with him.

Trump’s trade war with Canada adds a challenge in Senate races

- Public support for tariffs on Canada is tepid, adding to low ratings for Trump.
WASHINGTON — President Trump’s trade war with Canada could intensify the headwinds Republicans are navigating ahead of the November midterms, with its effects poised to reverberate in northern battleground states with crucial Senate races.
With the election less than six weeks away, Republicans are facing an increasingly bleak outlook, as new polls this week showed voters favoring Democrats by as much as 12 points amid widespread cost-of-living anxiety and low approval for Trump.
The escalating beef with Canada — Trump attacked the country anew on social media Wednesday — stands to heighten voters’ economic worries and add to the GOP’s political challenge in dead-heat races, analysts said.
“It doesn’t make things easier. It’s not helping,” said Rusty Hills, a University of Michigan public policy professor and onetime chair of the Michigan Republican Party.
The president’s unpopular policies on the war in Iran, the economy and data centers have already handed Republican candidates the tough task of appearing responsive to Americans’ frustration with cost-of-living issues without alienating Trump and his voter base.
The trade war, said Lance Dutson, a Maine Republican media strategist, puts “another log on the fire” of the affordability issue.
The tariffs have appeared unpopular in recent polling, including among a majority of independent voters. Though they are not expected to dramatically increase consumer prices, they could affect voters’ perception of the economy — and even small economic impacts on certain industries, such as auto manufacturing in Michigan, could have an effect in very close midterm races, experts said.
As California’s wine industry struggles, a family-owned vineyard spanning 3,500 acres is for sale after its exports to Canada dropped 35% in a year.
Trump’s new import bans on some Canadian goods are set to begin next week, a response to retaliatory tariffs Canada levied earlier this month. Trump argues that Canada has “been ripping off” the United States and that tariffs will help domestic manufacturers.
On Wednesday, the president inaccurately claimed on Truth Social that Canada is allowing “millions and millions” of immigrants into its country.
“It is a Liberal takeover that will end very badly. Already showing up in their numbers. Big unemployment. ‘Oh Canada!” the president wrote on social media Wednesday morning.
Five of the nine states most likely to decide Senate control border Canada — Alaska, Ohio, Michigan, New Hampshire and Maine. Two more, Texas and Iowa, also do substantial trade with Canada.
Democrats must retain their Senate seats including New Hampshire and Michigan and flip four of the other states to win a majority, a tall task. As the landscape worsens for Republicans, however, some are testing how much they can distance themselves from Trump.
“It’s a tightrope, there’s no question,” Hills said. “[Candidates] are looking for some wiggle room on some of these issues like the war and prices and Canada tariffs, because they need every independent and swing voter they can get.”
A majority of Americans oppose raising tariffs on Canadian goods, including 64% of independents, an Economist/YouGov poll found. Only 14% of independents said they supported additional U.S. tariffs on Canada in a late August Ipsos poll.
And in Michigan, 68% of independent voters disapprove of the tariffs, a poll this month from the Washington Post and Schar School found.
“The more we put tariffs on stuff, the more they put tariffs on stuff ... prices are just ultimately going to go up for all of us,” said one Michigan swing voter in a Sept. 9 focus group conducted by the firm Engagious, in which 11 of 13 participants said the trade war was bad for the state.
The highest costs of the tariffs will be concentrated within a few industries, including auto and other manufacturing, dairy, and alcohol and spirits, said Alex Durante, a senior economist at the Tax Foundation. The tariffs likely won’t create a major change for consumers, but the general impression that tariffs can contribute to higher prices might turn off voters who are already worried about inflation, he said.
Counter-tariffs imposed by Canada in response to U.S tariffs last year resulted in a 6% increase in the prices of affected goods, researchers found in paper published by the Journal of Monetary Economics.
“This trade war is certainly not helping the president and his party in the midterms,” Durante said. “What’s weighing on the top of people’s minds is this general affordability crisis ... and they realize that tariffs are another factor that is impacting affordability.”
The latest escalation of the trade dispute began in July, when Trump threatened new 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods, reinvigorating a conflict that began with tariffs the president imposed in 2025.
The two countries began trade talks, but the negotiations fell apart in late August, and Trump imposed tariffs on about $20-billion worth of Canadian goods. Canada retaliated with tariffs on about $20-billion worth of American goods that took effect Sept. 8. Trump then announced import bans on some Canadian goods, including certain alcohol and dairy products, which go into effect next week.
Construction and farm equipment in Illinois, aluminum and pipe products in New York, and iron and steel products in Ohio are among the goods targeted by Canada’s counter-tariffs, the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. reported. In California, about 10.5% of the state’s Canadian imports are exposed to the counter-tariffs imposed by Canada.
Democrats have seized on the issue as another way to tie Republican candidates to Trump’s policies, something that analysts said may have varying degrees of success in different swing states.
In Maine and New Hampshire, where the Republican Senate nominees have criticized Trump’s move, the tariff issue may be less likely to stick. Efforts to tie Republicans to Trump have historically been less successful in the region because of its independent streak, said Jim Merrill, a veteran Republican strategist in New Hampshire.
Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins warned the White House against imposing tariffs and successfully pushed for the administration to exempt road salt and cement this month. She told Politico that the Trump administration had “very much underestimated” the effect of the tariffs on Maine residents.
An acrimonious trade war between the United States and Canada is threatening to reinforce the resolve of Canadians who stopped visiting the U.S. last year
Republican John Sununu, a former senator who is running to retake the seat in New Hampshire, has also criticized the tariffs, saying a trade war with Canada “doesn’t make any sense.” He indicated he would support legislation in Congress to restrain the president’s tariff powers.
Elsewhere, Senate nominees have walked a careful line on tariffs. In Alaska, Sen. Dan Sullivan has largely avoided the issue, even as Democrats there have used it to ramp up attacks on his record in recent days. In Ohio, former Sen. Jon Husted told the National Review in August that the public “would like to understand the strategy behind what the president’s trying to do.”
Former Rep. Mike Rogers of Michigan, the Republican Senate nominee, told reporters over the weekend that he was in favor of “good” tariffs that would help Michigan and opposed to “bad” tariffs that would hurt the state.
Focusing on issues other than tariffs may be the right strategy on the campaign trail, Hills said.
“He’d much rather be talking about the Republican plan for affordability,” Hills suggested. “There’s interesting things we need to be talking about in order to win this election, and this isn’t one of them.”

Can Democrats flip the House? Here's the latest in key races
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Can Democrats flip the House? Here’s the latest in key races
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- All 435 House of Representatives seats are up for election; 21 are considered toss-ups.
- An Ohio incumbent is facing an ethics investigation after his ex-wife accused him of extreme physical abuse, which he denies.
WASHINGTON — After two years of struggling to slow down the Trump administration agenda under a Republican governing trifecta, Democrats are hoping to capture both chambers of Congress in the upcoming midterms.
All 435 House of Representatives seats are up for election, with 37 considered competitive, 21 of them toss-ups, by the Cook Political Report — a respected polling analysis site. Republicans currently hold a 218-214 edge over Democrats, with two seats vacant and one independent in the chamber.
To control the House, Democrats need a net gain of four seats.
Recent polls have shown Democrats creeping up on or surpassing their Republican opponents as President Trump’s approval rating hovers under 40%, which may offer an opening in unexpected places. But still, in a time when a more progressive wing has risen in popularity on the left, even some moderate Democrats are suffering from associations with the current administration.
Here is a look at five competitive races:
Ohio 7th: Miller vs. Poindexter
Incumbent Republican Max Miller, mired in controversy, will face union ironworker Brian Poindexter in a 7th Congressional District race that went from solidly Republican to a toss-up in the matter of weeks.
Miller, a second-term congressman, is facing a House Ethics Committee investigation after his ex-wife, Emily Moreno — daughter of Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno — accused Miller of extreme physical abuse, which he has denied.
Miller also faced accusations from former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham that Miller had abused her during their relationship. An Ohio judge recently ordered both parties to remove social media posts about each other that were considered disparaging.
Poindexter, a relative unknown, has surged in the meantime. According to a Co/efficient poll last month, Poindexter was leading Miller by 14 points, with 86% of respondents claiming they were aware of allegations against Miller.
Poindexter has centered his campaign on strengthening unions, retaining healthcare benefits for retirees and injured workers and raising wages.
Miller has attacked his opponent for a 1998 arrest in which Poindexter, a teenager at the time, allegedly tried to swallow a rock of crack cocaine during a traffic stop. Miller also homed in on an instance of alleged assault at a baseball game in 2013 by Poindexter.
Texas 34th: Gonzalez vs. Flores
Incumbent Democrat Vicente Gonzalez Jr. is attempting to retain his seat against challenger Eric Flores, an Army veteran endorsed by Trump.
Elected in 2016, Gonzalez held the 15th Congressional District for three terms until 2021, when a Texas redistricting shift absorbed his McAllen home into the 34th district. He is currently serving his second term under a new map, which favors Republicans and has shed many of his Latino constituents.
Flores, a political newcomer, made his first national appearance at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas, touting his commitment to border security and accusing Gonzalez of allowing migrants to make the community unsafe.
Immigration looms as an issue in the race. Gonzalez has introduced bills to prevent federal and state immigration enforcement officers from entering homes without an official warrant, and to force agents to wear clear identification. He has publicly criticized raids targeting hospitality, medical and construction workers.
Democrats need to gain at least four seats, and not lose any, to retake control of the Senate. Here are five races to watch in the final weeks before Nov. 3.
Gonzalez has scored endorsements from several progressive organizations in the state, including LUPE Votes — a subsidiary of La Unión del Pueblo Entero.
In a Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center poll from August, Gonzalez was leading Flores, 45% to 42%, with 8% undecided.
North Carolina 1st: Davis vs. Buckhout
Incumbent Democrat Rep. Donald Davis will have to contend with a district that has grown more conservative to retain his seat against Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout.
North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District was the state’s only swing seat held by a Democrat before last year’s redistricting, which made the area lean Republican. This will be a rematch of the 2024 race, which Davis won by less than 2 points, or around 6,000 total votes.
Cook Political Report ranked this race as leaning Republican, calling Davis “the most vulnerable House Democrat in the country.”
It is unclear whether the gerrymandering effort will have been effective enough to make the district flip to Republican. Trump endorsed Buckhout in March and reiterated his support last week.
New York 17th: Lawler vs. Conley
New York Republican incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler is attempting to fend off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley, a former White House director of counterterrorism on the National Security Council.
Cook Political Report rankings showed that early this year, the 17th Congressional District race went from likely Republican to a toss-up.
Pete Buttigieg went on the campaign trail last week with Conley to promote the candidate’s bid to unseat Lawler.
“Cait is as serious as it gets about keeping our country safe,” Buttigieg said on a rally stage in Tarrytown, “just like she is serious about bringing down the cost of housing, healthcare and energy.”
Lawler has presented a bipartisan image in Congress, but has come under fire in his purple district for aligning himself with the Trump administration on several issues, including his support for the Iran war.
At the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention, Lawler focused much of his speech on lambasting “socialist” Democrats and attempting to appeal to the more “common sense” wing of the opposition party.
“Radical socialists are winning Democratic primaries,” he said. “They claim to be well-meaning, but there is nothing kind-hearted about protecting criminals at the expense of American families … nothing compassionate about prioritizing illegal immigrants.”
Conley, however, has publicly refused to campaign with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani or Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — without condemning either figure — to avoid the open conflict between establishment figures and the more progressive wing of the party.
A July poll from co/efficient showed Lawler leading Conley 50% to 45%, with a nearly 3% margin of error.
Arizona 1st: Shah vs. Feely
A Democratic PAC plans to invest nearly $1 million to support Democrat state Rep. Amish Shah against Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL player with close ties to the president.
The 314 Action Fund — which seeks to elect Democrats with backgrounds in science, technology, engineering and mathematics — has made a big bet on the Democrat running in the 1st Congressional District, Arizona’s wealthiest, according to the Arizona Mirror.
Subsequent ads have brought attention to Feely’s close association with Trump and his recent attendance at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas. Trump won the state by five points in 2024.
Elon Musk has also figured in this race, with his America PAC giving $24,000 to Republican candidates Feely in the 1st District and Juan Ciscomani in the 6th District, according to the Copper Courier.
The Cook Political Report called the 1st District “one of the most competitive … in the country.”

Tax the rich? California voters are divided, according to new poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Tax the rich? California voters are divided, according to new poll
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- California voters narrowly support a proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ assets, while showing stronger support for extending a tax on high-income earners that funds schools and healthcare, a poll shows.
- Proposition 40 has lost support as opponents spend heavily on advertising, leaving 45% of likely voters in favor, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.
- Voters also reject a proposed voter ID requirement, and large numbers remain uncertain on several measures as they confront a lengthy ballot.
The slate of statewide measures on the Nov. 3 ballot provides voters two opportunities to tax the rich, which in past years has proved tantalizing to California’s left-leaning electorate.
Only one of those measures has strong voter support, however, and it’s not the proposition that’s attracted nationwide attention, ignited a nearly quarter-billion-dollar political slugfest and created a rift among top leaders in the Democratic Party.
Likely voters expressed middling support for Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets intended to compensate for an impending $100 billion in federal healthcare funding cuts. They were far more likely to back Proposition 3, a ballot measure that would make permanent a tax increase on the wealthy that funds schools and healthcare, according to a poll released Friday by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that is co-sponsored by The Times.
Proposition 3 appears to be a much less controversial endeavor, which may explain why it has more voter support. The ballot measure would extend a tax enacted in 2012 on individuals who earn at least $360,000 a year that is set to expire in 2031. Proposition 40 proposes a brand-new tax on billionaires and is opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who fears that it could hurt the state’s finances in the long run.
“When you’re going about taxing the billionaires’ assets, I mean that’s something kind of new and different, and it’s risky, and the governor’s against it, and you know a lot of people are expressing caution about it,” said Mark DiCamillo, director of the poll.
Voters are deeply concerned about income disparity but also skeptical about the unusual approach of the billionaire tax.
Proposition 40 has drawn the greatest attention and campaign spending of the 14 ballot measures voters will decide on Nov. 3.
In the poll, 45% of likely voters support the proposal, while 42% oppose it and 13% are undecided. That’s a decline in support compared with six weeks ago, when 48% of likely voters supported it while 41% opposed it, and comes after nearly $100 million of spending on television ads, social media messages and mailers, largely from opponents.
The billionaire tax was crafted by a healthcare union in response to legislation passed by congressional Republicans and signed by President Trump last year that could result in millions of Californians losing Medi-Cal coverage, rural hospitals shuttering and other healthcare services being slashed unless a new funding source is found.
The proposal would retroactively apply to billionaires who lived in California as of Jan. 1, prompting some to preemptively move out of the state. Ninety percent of the revenue would fund healthcare programs, and the remaining funds would be spent on education programs and food assistance.
Here is a list of some of the billionaires who’ve made moves to leave California.
There are two counterproposals on the ballot that would nullify the wealth tax if either receives more votes than Proposition 40, and they have raised $144 million. Voters are torn about Proposition 41, which would prohibit any new state taxes from being excluded from a voter-approved cap that restricts how much tax revenue the state can spend each year. The billionaire tax would have such an exclusion. Voters also are divided on Proposition 42, which would prohibit new taxes on personal property, intellectual property, retirement accounts and other assets and would limit situations in which a ballot measure or state lawmakers can impose or raise taxes retroactively — both of which are essential parts of the billionaire tax initiative.
Proposition 42 has greater support, with 43% backing it, 34% opposing it and the remainder undecided, according to the poll. Even more voters were uncertain about Proposition 41: 3 in 10 said they were undecided, while 37% said they supported it and 33% said they planned to vote against it.
The large number of undecided voters this close to the election points to voters being overwhelmed by the sheer number of statewide ballot measures, DiCamillo said.
“It’s confusion,” he said, adding that many voters may make a decision once they receive more ballot information.
That said, the fact that none of these proposals has the support of more than 50% of likely voters doesn’t bode well for their prospects, DiCamillo said.
Ballots will begin arriving in the mailboxes of the state’s 23.2 million voters in days.
Democratic voters outnumber Republicans by nearly 2 to 1 in California, but the party’s leaders are deeply divided about the billionaire tax, given the volatile state budget’s reliance on the wealthy. Newsom, who is pondering a 2028 presidential campaign, and the two men vying to replace him — Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton — oppose it. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont), a potential 2028 White House contender, supports it, as does the California Democratic Party.
Additionally, Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West and architect of the ballot measure, has come under scrutiny. Regan has been accused of threatening and intimidating women who worked for the union’s parent organization, and of physically assaulting one, according to reporting by The Times. He was also accused of trying to extort SEIU’s state council, suggesting that it could face an investigation over “governance issues” if it did not support Proposition 40, according to an investigation commissioned by SEIU.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West President Dave Regan denied the allegations. He said he did not attempt to extort from union officials, or assault or threaten female labor leaders.
Regan has denied these claims, describing them as a “smear” campaign orchestrated by Proposition 40 opponents.
Much less attention has been paid to Proposition 3. Californians who earn more than $360,000 now are subject to a 10.3% tax, while those who earn more than $721,000 face a 12.3% levy. The vast majority of the billions raised through this tax go to K-12 schools, while the remainder is spent on community colleges and healthcare.
The other ballot measure that is receiving national attention is Proposition 39, which would require voters to present a government-issued identification document to cast a ballot or provide a PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
The proposal comes as Trump has continued to make claims that elections, notably in California, are being rigged by Democrats. Americans are increasingly alarmed about the security and sanctity of voting, and growing fears about intimidation efforts at polling places in the midterm elections.
Fifty-two percent of likely California voters oppose the voter ID proposal, while 39% support it and 9% are undecided, according to the poll.
“It doesn’t look like it’s in a strong position,” DiCamillo said, noting that while voters have opposed it in prior polls, the opposition has grown.
Nearly one-third of voters were undecided about two other propositions:
- Likely voters were evenly split about Proposition 4, which would repeal a ban on public funding of campaigns, with 35% supporting it and 35% opposing it, and the remainder undecided.
- Four out of 10 likely voters opposed Proposition 43, which would increase the threshold necessary to pass local taxes from a simple majority to two-thirds, while 31% supported measure and 29% were undecided.
Voters will also face questions about environmental policy, housing, recall elections and other matters, as well as statewide, congressional and local elections. Californians are fatigued by the length of the ballot.
In addition to high-stakes U.S. House races, California voters in November also will weigh in on a slew of ballot measures.
The Berkeley IGS/Times poll findings are based on an online survey in English and Spanish of 6,989 registered California voters, 4,512 of whom are considered likely voters, on Sept. 15-20. The results are estimated to have a margin of error of about 2 percentage points in either direction in the overall sample, and larger numbers for subgroups.

West replacing world politics with war, using dollar as tool of sanctions — de Gaulle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:58:55 UTC
18:58:55 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, September 25. /TASS/. The West is seeking to replace world politics with war, using the dollar as a tool of sanctions to that end, Pierre de Gaulle, grandson of French President General Charles de Gaulle (1959-1969) and head of the Foundation for Peace and Friendship Among Peoples, said at the 12th St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum.
"These countries want to replace world politics with war. The dollar has become an instrument of sanctions," he said.
At the same time, de Gaulle noted that such actions stem from the unwillingness of Western countries to accept the fact that the world order, "which a few years ago was considered the developing world, now dominates."
"This is a world that unites peoples and populations, one that calmly and freely chooses its partners while respecting sovereignty," he said. "This new dynamic is taking on fresh meaning, because it is the natural dynamic of free choice, free trade, free communication."
However, de Gaulle said that the West keeps trying to "prolong the bipolar confrontational world against Russia."
About forum
The 12th St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum is being held on September 24-26. The forum features 10 thematic sections, bringing together Russian and foreign cultural figures, government officials and representatives of the professional community. In 2026, the forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Russian government, Russia’s Culture Ministry and the St. Petersburg administration.
TASS is the forum’s general information partner.

Saudi, Turkish, Pakistani military chiefs to meet over Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:58:37 UTC
18:58:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi, Turkey, Pakistan military chiefs hold talks on Houthi attacks
The military chiefs of the three countries in the Mecca Defence Pact have held talks in Saudi Arabia, as the bloc moves to strengthen coordination amid escalating fighting in Yemen and continued Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
Turkey's defence ministry earlier said that Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu was travelling to Saudi Arabia to attend a meeting of the alliance's chiefs of staff.
Later on Friday, Ankara published photographs of the three military officials in uniform, stating that the meeting had taken place, without disclosing where.
The meeting comes as Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan continue efforts to institutionalise the Mecca Defence Pact, established under an agreement signed by the three countries more than a month and a half ago.
The first meeting of the political and strategic defence committee established under the agreement was held in Istanbul at the end of August.
The Saudi meeting is expected to focus on strengthening coordination between the three countries, with the agreement covering cooperation in areas including military training and defence industries.
It comes as Yemen's Houthi movement continues attacks on Saudi Arabia amid escalating fighting in Yemen.
Foreign ministers discuss urgent meeting
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey discussed preparations for an urgent meeting of the three countries' military chiefs during talks in New York.
Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan reviewed progress towards establishing the alliance's secretariat, committees and working groups.
They also discussed preparations for those bodies to begin their work.
The ministers strongly condemned attacks targeting Mecca and civilian and economic facilities in Saudi Arabia, praising the Saudi armed forces' response.
They affirmed Riyadh's right to take measures it considers necessary to defend its security under Article 51 of the UN Charter.
The three ministers also discussed regional developments, stressing the importance of respecting international law, state sovereignty and non-interference in countries' internal affairs, as well as ensuring the security and freedom of maritime navigation.
They reiterated their commitment to working towards lasting peace and stability, de-escalation and peaceful solutions to ongoing regional crises.
Alliance moves towards formal structure
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Thursday described the Mecca Defence Agreement as a "strong step in the right direction".
"When embarking on such a highly important initiative in a difficult geographical region, it is not surprising to face some challenges," Erdogan said.
"If a new idea is put forward or a new will is demonstrated, it is natural that there will be those who do not accept it."
He added that he had "no doubt" the three countries would move forward more strongly as work to institutionalise the alliance was completed.
Pakistan's foreign ministry announced on Wednesday that retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood had been appointed the first secretary-general of the alliance.
Riyadh was previously selected as the headquarters of the alliance's secretariat, while Pakistan will hold the secretary-general position for its first three-year term before the role rotates between the three countries.
Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif had previously warned that the trilateral defence alliance could be activated if the fallout from the conflict in Yemen extended to Riyadh. His comments came as the Houthis launched attacks on oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.
The Mecca agreement is intended to strengthen defence cooperation between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan and bolster collective deterrence.
Under the pact, an armed attack against any one of the three countries is considered an attack against all three.

‘Corruption under CM’s nose in Punjab’: Congress questions why ED acted before elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:58:13 UTC
18:58:13 KST

NEW DELHI: Punjab Congress chief Amrinder Singh Raja Warring on Friday questioned the Enforcement Directorate's timing in carrying out searches in the state, alleging that corruption had taken place in several departments under the "chief minister's nose".Warring said alleged corruption in Punjab must be investigated, but questioned why central agencies had become active only ahead of elections."I have never given a clean chit to any central agency, because central agencies tend to become active only around election time. But yes, the fact remains that within Punjab, not just GMADA [Greater Mohali Area Development Authority]—there are many other departments and ministries where scams on a massive scale have occurred," Warring told reporters."Those scams must be thoroughly investigated, and this corruption was taking place right under the chief minister’s nose," he added.Taking a swipe at those allegedly involved in the irregularities, Warring said people in Punjab were aware of what had happened."Don't just take my word for it; as an opposition party chief, I am bound to say this, but ask anyone, ask the common people: it wasn't some foreign invader like Ahmad Shah Abdali who looted Delhi; the looters were specific individuals whose names are now surfacing," he further said.
Warring said the ED action was welcome but questioned why similar action had not been taken earlier."All this happened under the chief minister's watch. Yet, questions also arise regarding the ED: Why have you become active only now?" he said."It is good [that action is being taken], but during the past five years when Punjab was crying out in protest, you knew that the policies of Delhi were formulated here... that the Delhi policies were mirrored here. Gaza suffers world’s worst ever economic crisis: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:54:56 UTC
18:54:56 KST

Palestinians gather to receive bags of flour distributed by UNRWA, the U.N. agency helping Palestinian refugees, in Deir al Balah, central Gaza Strip, Nov. 2, 2024. (AP File Photo)
Gaza is suffering the world’s worst economic crisis ever recorded, with nine in 10 businesses destroyed and hundreds of thousands of people unemployed, a top U.N. development agency warned on Sept. 24.
Israel’s military offensive sparked by Hamas militants’ attack in October 2023 devastated the territory of 2 million people before a patchy ceasefire was announced in October 2025.
“The collapse of the economy of Gaza is the world’s most severe economic crisis on record,” said Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting secretary-general of the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
“It has wiped out decades of development and generated an acute economic crisis for its people,” he told reporters in Geneva as the organisation released a new report.
It said 92 percent of Gaza’s “economic establishments have been damaged or destroyed”.
The territory’s daily per capita GDP is $0.58 a day, the report said. Prices are 274 percent higher than in 2022.
Israel’s military offensive killed more than 73,000 people, according to the territory’s Health Ministry.
Before October 2023, “two out of three Gazans were poor. Today, everyone in Gaza is multidimensionally poor,” said Mutasim Elagraa, UNCTAD’s coordinator for assistance to the Palestinians.
Industrial activity and agricultural production have fallen by 94 percent, with only 1.5 percent of arable land accessible, forcing “total dependence on humanitarian food aid,” Elagraa said.

Iran pitches seven-day roadmap to end conflict with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:54:40 UTC
18:54:40 KST

Iran pitches seven-day roadmap to end conflict with US
Tehran seeks rapid implementation collapsed ceasefire deal, offering to open Hormuz if regional conflicts halted.
Iran has proposed a seven-day roadmap aimed at ending the war with the United States.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi outlined the plan to reporters in New York on Thursday, according to US media. The proposal seeks to implement the conditions in the Memorandum of Understanding agreed by Washington and Tehran in June, including a halt to hostilities and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Rubio warns of Iraq ‘Balkanisation’: Is that a real threat?
- list 2 of 4Saudi-led coalition says shot down 6 ballistic missiles launched by Houthis
- list 3 of 4Iranian-American group sues Trump over war
- list 4 of 4Benjamin Netanyahu attacks Israel’s enemies and allies in UN speech
Reportedly passed to Washington via mediators earlier this week, Iran’s proposal asks the US to meet specific conditions within seven days to restart ceasefire talks and end the blockade choking the strategically important strait.
The restrictions on maritime traffic in Hormuz have become a key issue in the conflict due to the impact on oil and gas exports and the global economy.
The proposal, which was presented to reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, comes as the war, started by US and Israeli strikes, is almost into its seventh month.
The US-Iran MoU deal expired in August as each side accused the other of violations, and there has been little sign since that they could return to the agreement, although Tehran has suggested it could happen.
Under Iran’s proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Gaza and Lebanon, within seven days, The New York Times reported.
Washington would also release Iran’s frozen assets, estimated at no less than $12bn, waive sanctions on Iranian oil and lift its naval blockade.
The Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the final day of the period. Talks on Iran’s nuclear programme, ostensibly the root cause of the conflict according to President Donald Trump, would start immediately.
The proposal closely resembles the MoU, but sets out a hugely ambitious timetable. The Pakistani and Qatari-brokered deal signed on June 17 set a 60-day window for negotiations, but still unravelled within weeks.
Vague wording led to disputes over who controlled shipping through the strait, and the two sides traded attacks before US President Donald Trump declared the deal “over” on July 7.
“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators,” Araghchi told reporters.
‘America must choose’
Separately, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a US television interview that it is for the Trump administration to choose whether to end the war, as Tehran does not wish to continue fighting.
“When we can resolve issues through dialogue, we shouldn’t resort to killing one another. But with the instigations conducted by Israel, they have imposed this war on us,” he said on Fox News’ ‘Special Report with Bret Baier’.
“But we do not wish to continue. It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not,” he said in remarks translated by the broadcaster that aired on Thursday.
Pezeshkian took a defiant stand at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, telling the world that Iran would not “bend at the knee” to Washington – even as Trump acknowledged ongoing US-Iran talks.
In the Fox interview, he said: “If the current American government, within international legal frameworks, wishes to reach an agreement, fine. If not, before the [US midterm] elections or after the elections, what difference does it make for us?”
Earlier this month, Pezeshkian said Tehran would “immediately reciprocate” if the US returned to its commitments under the MoU.
Slow-moving diplomacy
An unnamed White House official told CNN that the administration was having “positive and constructive discussions through the mediators”. The New York Times quoted an official as saying that Washington would not rush into a deal.
An Iranian security source told Al Jazeera there could be room for further diplomatic engagement if Washington met Iran’s conditions and commitments.
However, analysts said the proposal suggests that diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran are not advancing significantly.
“Basically nothing has really changed,” Cyrus Schayegh, professor of international history and politics at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told Al Jazeera.
Iran “keeps insisting that it wants to keep the additional power it gained during the war and that the June memorandum still is basically key to the roadmap moving forward,” said the professor, while the US “keeps basically refusing to accept this roadmap debate”.
No significant movement towards ending the conflict is likely before the US mid-term elections in November, he asserted.
Araghchi told reporters that “it would be better” to reach a deal before that vote. Pezeshkian said earlier that any agreements with the US would not be tied to the timing of the midterms, according to CNN.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said on Friday that top diplomat Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, one of the main mediators in the conflicts across the Middle East region, had spoken with Pezeshkian about de-escalation and conditions for dialogue.

Iran proposes reopening Hormuz within seven days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:52:18 UTC
18:52:18 KST

A gull flies overhead as a boy stands with his bicycle on a beach overlooking commercial vessels anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026. (AP File Photo)
Iran has submitted a proposal to the United States to end their war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, its foreign minister told media outlets in New York on Sept. 24.
“If certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start,” Abbas Araghchi, who is in the U.S. for the U.N. General Assembly, told media outlets including the New York Times and The Guardian.
Araghchi also met for talks on Sept. 22 with U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff.
Iran has previously set out seven conditions for ending the war and reopening the strait.
According to Araghchi, as quoted by the New York Times, the latest plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon.
It also calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iran.
On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.
Araghchi said he was waiting for a U.S. response to the plan and maintained that China supported the proposal.
During the same meeting with the media outlets, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied accusations that Iran was trying to kill the president, saying it has “never been the position [of the Iranian government], overtly or covertly, to seek to assassinate” Trump or his family members.
The Iranian president also said in the session that Iran wants a deal, but that any agreement was not related to the timing of the U.S. midterms.
During the briefing, Pezeshkian also spoke about recent meetings with Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since the war began, saying the leader was in “quite good health.”
Questions over Khamenei’s health have intensified in recent months following reports that he suffered serious injuries in the U.S.-Israeli strike that killed his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, at the start of the conflict in February.
Pezeshkian said he had observed no significant health problems or physical signs of concern during his meetings with the supreme leader. He added that their latest face-to-face meeting was held about a month ago and lasted roughly seven hours.
The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear program.
But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.

Swedish, Finnish fighter jets intercept group of Russian military aircraft

Swedish, Finnish fighter jets intercept group of Russian military aircraft
STOCKHOLM, Sept 25 - Finland and Sweden said on Friday they had scrambled fighter jets to intercept and identify Russian military aircraft in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland, in the first such joint operation by the two Nordic countries.
The Baltic Sea region, of which the Gulf of Finland is part, is on high alert after incidents involving gas pipeline outages, airspace violations and drone sightings since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said the operation, which took place on Thursday, showed how the so-called Quick Reaction Alert cooperation could monitor and safeguard both countries' airspace.
"It is a concrete expression of the readiness and trust we have built together – and an expression of the strength in the Nordic, Nordic-Baltic, and broader NATO cooperation in our part of the world," Kristersson wrote in a post on social media X.
"The Baltic Sea has never been as vulnerable as it is now – but it has also never been better protected than it is right now," he said.
The two air forces' jets tracked down and identified a group of Russian aircraft including a transport plane and several fighter jets, the Finnish Air Force said.
The Russian embassies in Stockholm and Helsinki did not immediately respond to requests for comment when contacted by Reuters.
Finland and Sweden both joined NATO following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, departing from a longstanding policy of non-alignment. Their Nordic neighbours Norway, Iceland and Denmark were already members of the Atlantic alliance, as were the three Baltic republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. REUTERS

Israel threatens to demolish Palestinian detainee's West Bank home
