Saudi Arabia allies line up support as Houthi attacks mount
France is sending its military to protect key Yanbu oil terminal; Pakistan and Turkiye to hold military talks with Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia’s allies are rallying to support the country as the Houthi rebels step up attacks.
France confirmed on Friday that it is sending troops to guard the major oil terminal at Yanbu. Meanwhile, Saudi officials are meeting with peers from Pakistan and Turkiye to discuss options under their mutual defence pact.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Yemen government forces claim control of Mount Qarfan in Taiz
- list 2 of 4Despite flurry of New York diplomacy, US-Iran deal remains elusive
- list 3 of 4How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis?
- list 4 of 4As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
French President Emmanuel Macron told broadcasters TF1 and France 2 that Paris is to send “soldiers, radars, and defence systems” to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
“Not to involve ourselves in any conflict, but to protect the site,” he said.
Yanbu hosts major oil storage and refining facilities and is connected by the East-West Pipeline, which can carry up to seven million barrels a day.
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), have repeatedly fired missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world’s largest energy exporter.
On Thursday, the rebel group said it had struck the facilities of state oil firm Aramco in Yanbu, and a “sensitive target” in Riyadh. Saudi forces said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles. Authorities have not confirmed any damage.
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye met on Thursday to arrange an “urgent meeting” of their military chiefs of staff under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which treats an attack on one member as an attack on all, the Saudi foreign ministry said in a statement.
They also condemned Houthi attacks that they claimed targeted Mecca and other civilian sites.
However, doubt persists over what action Turkiye and Pakistan might take under the pact, which is yet to be officially triggered. Both of the Saudi allies are heavily involved as mediators seeking to bring an end to the conflicts across the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia’s grand mufti called on soldiers to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis, according to the Saudi state news agency.
The Iran-aligned Houthis have been battling the Saudi-backed government of Yemen for more than a decade. That conflict has been rekindled amid Israel’s wars against the Iran-aligned Hamas group in Gaza and the Hezbollah group in Lebanon, and the United States war on Iran.
At the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Yemen’s Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al-Alimi-Bawzer warned that the Houthis were using shipping security “as a tool for blackmail”.
“It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” he said.
The US has not renewed military involvement, but Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud said the kingdom was “continuing to work with our partners in the US”.
The Houthi targeting of Yanbu adds to the pressure on Saudi Arabia’s oil exports.
Earlier this month, the Houthis seized the Yemeni port of Mocha and several Red Sea islands, giving them significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, which usually carries about 12 percent of global oil trade.
Strikes have also disrupted the operation of the East-West Pipeline linking Yanbu to export routes. Riyadh had been using it to export crude bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, which is restricted amid the Iran-US war.
However, the Houthis have now forced the Saudis to switch some exports back to Hormuz.
Brent crude rose more than 3 percent on Thursday, briefly topping $108 a barrel, before easing to $105.77 on Friday morning.
June Goh, a senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities in Singapore, said oil would likely stay above $100 a barrel as long as the war on Iran continued.
“With no clear resolution in sight, the gap in oil inventories globally is getting wider,” Goh told Al Jazeera.

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Sydney Roosters roar into NRL grand final with 36-20 win over Dolphins
Sydney Roosters are through to their first NRL grand final in seven years after Mark Nawaqanitawase genius and a miracle Sam Walker injury comeback inspired a 36-20 demolition of the Dolphins.
The Roosters shot out to a 16-0 lead inside 27 minutes in front of a sold-out preliminary final crowd of 52,286 at Lang Park on Friday night.
Their defensive grit on the tryline, a feature of their finals campaign, limited the damage from a mini-Dolphins comeback, but two-try hero Nawaqanitawase has a box of unlimited magic tricks that he unfurled with a wow factor rarely seen on a rugby league field.
The Dolphins had won eight straight games to reach their first preliminary final, a wonderful achievement, but on this occasion it was the Roosters' big-game players who stood tallest.
Walker returned in a record-equalling 27 days from a syndesmosis injury to orchestrate the backline in a masterclass to set up a decider clash with either Penrith or Newcastle.
Roosters coach Trent Robinson will be angling for his fourth premiership win in as many attempts.
An error or a moment of magic was needed to turn an early set-for-set stalemate, and the paranormal Nawaqanitawase provided it in the 18th minute.
The rugby-bound revelation's pivotal moment was pure instinct and skill backed with supreme confidence.
Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth hesitated with his pass for what would have been a Dolphins try had it hit the mark. The man known as "Marky Mark" swooped, raced 90m and the Roosters never looked back.
"Big players make big plays in big games," Billy Slater said on Channel Nine commentary.
Dolphins bench impact man Kurt Donoghoe dropped the ball when he came on and then missed a tackle for a rampant Victor Radley to score.
Walker's sublime lob for jumping Daniel Tupou had been well rehearsed and was perfectly executed.
The Roosters lost bench rake Connor Watson to a category one HIA, upgraded by the independent doctor, in the first half and the St George Illawarra-bound utility will miss the grand final.
Dolphins winger Jamayne Isaako scored tries either side of halftime, but Nawaqanitawase collected a kick and flicked it back for Robert Toia to crash over.
When Nawaqanitawase bulldozed over for his second and Walker sliced through, it was all over for the hosts.

Polish foreign minister warns Russia may be preparing ‘something big’ this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:26:59 UTC
17:26:59 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has warned that Russia may be preparing a major operation this year and could stage a false-flag attack to justify further mobilization.
“We are receiving information ... we are not revealing the sources, but there are many (of them), that Russia is preparing something big this year,” Sikorski said at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York on Thursday, according to Polish broadcaster TVP World.
“I believe that Putin needs a pretext for mobilization, so they could carry out a false-flag attack and tell the Russian people: ‘We are under attack, and therefore we need to mobilize,’ ” he added.
Sikorski did not specify what the reported operation might involve. Asked about possible scenarios, he said Belarusians were concerned about being drawn into the war in Ukraine.
He also warned that Baltic countries with Russian minorities could face escalation, saying NATO must be ready to deter potential aggression. A full-scale Russian invasion of a NATO member would be “crazy,” he said, suggesting that Moscow might instead pursue a less explicit action that would make it harder for the alliance to invoke its Article 5 mutual-defense clause.
Sikorski said Russia could sustain its war in Ukraine for another year or two despite economic pressure, unless Ukrainian strikes destroy more than half of its oil refinery capacity.

Xi’s US visit more about spectacle than substance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:26:58 UTC
17:26:58 KST

China's President Xi Jinping (L) and U.S. President Donald Trump speak through interpreters during a State Dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 24, 2026. (AFP Photo)
U.S. President Donald Trump treated Chinese leader Xi Jinping to pomp and pageantry on Sept. 24, as the leaders of the world's two superpowers met in Washington DC for talks.
Trump hailed his "great friendship" with Xi and pulled out all the stops to woo the Chinese leader, greeting him on the runway on his arrival, offering him a rare tour of the presidential helicopter, and gifting him a bald eagle statue.
The pomp, however, masked the lack of diplomatic breakthroughs.
"The pageantry was the point," according to Ryan Hass at the Brookings Institution.
"When the troop reviews and opening ceremony are taken out of the schedule, the two leaders had less than two hours of direct meetings with each other," he added.
Those meetings yielded "many new consensuses, "according to Xi, but the only concrete deals announced were a promise to invite 100,000 young Americans to China for exchanges, and lending two pandas to a zoo in Atlanta.
Instead, the meetings were meant to show that the two leaders could "effectively manage U.S.-China relations within tolerable bounds of competition", Hass said.
Xi once again urged the two sides to avoid the "Thucydides Trap" — the theory that a rising power will come into conflict with an established one — but there was little sign of progress on thorny issues like Taiwan or artificial intelligence.
Trump and Xi hinted at big differences in their approach to the regulation of Artificial Intelligence — or "super intelligence", as Trump referred to it.
While Trump has dismissed calls from tech leaders for regulations to "pace the frontier" of the technology, Xi said AI should "always be under human control."
One significant deal was the extension by two months of the countries' fragile trade truce, due to expire in November.
The detente paused a bruising trade war last year by reducing U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods and removing Beijing's export controls on rare earths vital to manufacturing.
Trump is "trying to stabilize relations for now until the U.S. can basically decrease its vulnerabilities to Beijing," according to Jared Mondschein, Director of Research at the United States Studies Centre, University of Sydney.
Trump, a self-styled dealmaker, has repeatedly called on China to purchase more U.S. goods to establish a more "balanced" economic relationship.
However, Xi's visit hasn't yet produced any commitments for Chinese purchases of, for example, Boeing planes or American farm produce.
Trump has repeatedly called on China to help extricate the U.S. from its conflict with Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz for shipping, calls Beijing has rebuffed.
China has also been accused of helping Iran target U.S. military assets in the Middle East.
Xi told the U.S. president to end the war and come to a negotiated settlement with Tehran as soon as possible, according to a Chinese readout of the talks.
"The idea that China is going to be a big power broker, appear publicly and negotiate solutions — I think that's really unlikely," said Rana Mitter, professor of U.S.-Asia relations at the Harvard Kennedy School.
"I don't think that China is going to be the magic card that gets the U.S. out of trouble in the region."
Xi also repeated his warning, given to Trump in May, that he should show "prudence" over Taiwan.
But he also went further than he had in that meeting by urging the U.S. to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence.

Trump asks Supreme Court to allow deportations to countries with troubling human rights records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:25:17 UTC
17:25:17 KST

Esra Tekin
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
US President Donald Trump’s administration asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to permit it to deport migrants to countries other than their countries of origin without first allowing them to present concerns that they could face human rights violations.
The Justice Department submitted an emergency request after the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals issued a ruling late Wednesday that effectively halted the deportations.
The removals had continued after the Supreme Court previously ruled in favor of the administration on the issue more than a year ago.
US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s chief attorney before the Supreme Court, argued that the latest ruling had caused significant practical difficulties for immigration authorities.
He said it had resulted in canceled flights, increased costs, possible diplomatic complications, and difficulties removing migrants considered dangerous criminals.
Sauer wrote that although delaying deportation could benefit some migrants, it would not serve the interests of the country.
The Supreme Court had previously considered the administration’s policy and allowed it to remain in effect despite objections from Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson.
The court later ruled in the administration’s favor again in a case involving a group of migrants who had spent several weeks detained at a US military facility in Djibouti.
The policy was introduced last year as part of the Trump administration’s broader immigration enforcement efforts.
A longstanding challenge for US administrations has been deporting migrants to countries that are unwilling to accept them, sometimes because of strained diplomatic relations with the US.
The Trump administration responded by sending some migrants to third countries, even when they had no personal or family connections there.
The policy attracted significant attention after immigrant advocacy organizations disclosed that a group of migrants who were originally supposed to be sent to South Sudan were instead being held in Djibouti.
The group included migrants from countries such as Cuba, Vietnam, and Laos, and they were reportedly detained in a converted shipping container.
Around 25,000 migrants have been deported under the policy.
The legal dispute centers on the Convention Against Torture, which the US Senate ratified in 1994.
The agreement generally prohibits deporting or extraditing people to countries where they could face torture.
However, the law does not clearly specify how the government must assess the risk of torture or what procedural protections migrants should receive before being removed.
In Thursday’s emergency filing, the administration asked the Supreme Court to immediately issue an “administrative” stay, which would allow deportation flights to resume.
The Justice Department said it had already canceled flights because of the lower court’s ruling and had removed nearly 150 migrants from flights scheduled to take them to at least four different countries.
The Supreme Court instructed the immigrant rights organizations challenging the administration’s policy to respond to the request by Monday afternoon.

US dollar reaches nearly 2-month high amid hawkish Fed expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:24:08 UTC
17:24:08 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
The US dollar index rose to 101.24, marking its highest level in nearly two months, fueling expectations that the Fed will maintain its hawkish monetary policy.
The US economy remained strong and continued inflationary pressures and forecasts that the Fed will continue rising rates drove the demand for the dollar.
Investors shifted to cash amid the ongoing geopolitical risks in the Middle East, contributing to the rise in the dollar.
The US manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) reached its 52-month highest at 57 and its services PMI hit its 59-month highest at 58.7.
Money markets expect the Fed to continue with a hawkish stance with a 70% probability to hike rates by 25 basis points next month.
Jane Foley, senior foreign exchange strategist at Rabobank, told Anadolu that the strong PMI data showed a level of economic vitality that could concern the Fed’s hawks.
“The impact of the data was magnified by yesterday’s rise in oil prices and remarks from the Fed’s (board member Michael) Barr that more rate rises might be needed —  together these factors helped accelerate market forecasts for another Fed policy tightening as soon as next month which underpinned with value of the US dollar,” she said.
 
“While (the) ECB (European Central Bank) rate hike speculation is also prevalent in the market, upside potential for the euro is likely limited by the eurozone’s status as an energy importer, (while) next year’s French Presidential election may also be a limiting factor for the euro going forward,” she added.
Kyle Chapman, a foreign exchange markets analyst at the London-based Ballinger Group, told Anadolu that the dollar appreciated due to the Fed’s shift towards a more hawkish stance, weak risk appetite, and the ongoing strength of oil prices.
“US rates have risen across the curve after Warsh reaffirmed his commitment to monetary policy discipline,” he said.
Francesco Pesole from the ING Group stated that strong US PMI data, rising oil prices, and weak risk appetite contributed to the US dollar’s rise, while the currency’s move has started to look “stretched relative to fundamentals.”
“We are cautious in calling for a bottom in the dollar just yet because any upside surprise in upcoming US data releases can easily prompt markets to fully price in an October Fed hike and prop up short-term rates even more, but if this risk doesn’t materialize, we expect a correction in DXY (US Dollar Index) in the coming weeks, with a return to the 100-100.5 area,” he said.
“USD/JPY remains another source of potential downside risk for the dollar — the rapid rally in the pair may draw Japanese authorities to intervene that could easily spill over into a weaker USD across the board,” he added.

Malaysia calls for stronger cooperation to expand global halal economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:22:47 UTC
17:22:47 KST

Sahin Demir
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Malaysia called Friday for stronger international cooperation to expand the global halal economy, urging countries and businesses to turn growing demand into greater trade, investment and market access.
Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi made the remarks at the official opening ceremony of the 22nd Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS 2026) and Global Halal Summit 2026 (GHaS 2026) at the Malaysia International Trade and Exhibition Centre (MITEC) in Kuala Lumpur.
The ceremony brought together foreign delegations, government officials, industry representatives and participants from around the world.
Calling for a more connected global halal economy, Zahid said policymakers and businesses should work together to translate the sector’s growth into concrete economic opportunities.
“Let us turn that shared ambition into trade, investment and jobs,” he said.
“Our work must continue beyond this gathering. Success will only be measured by the barriers we remove, the partnerships that endure, and the businesses that reach new markets,” he added.
“Together, we have built trust in halal, halalan tayyiban. Now let us build greater prosperity through halal,” Zahid said.
 
From certification to global markets
Zahid stressed that halal certification alone is not enough for companies seeking to expand internationally.
“Certification is only the beginning of that journey,” he said.
Companies also need consistent production, suitable packaging, working capital, reliable logistics and an understanding of their target markets, he added.
Zahid said only about 14.7% of halal-certified companies in Malaysia are exporters, stressing the need to help more businesses compete internationally.
“To realize our ambition, we must help more of these companies compete abroad,” he said.
He pointed to Malaysia’s international halal trade initiatives, saying MIHAS in Dubai generated 2.2 billion Malaysian ringgit ($540 million) in sales in 2024, followed by 3.2 billion ringgit ($785 million) at MIHAS in Shanghai in 2025.
 
Halal economy built on trust, integrity
Malaysia’s Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department for Religious Affairs Zulkifli Hasan said the development of the halal sector is a collective effort involving Malaysia’s Department of Islamic Development (JAKIM), the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, MATRADE, the Halal Development Corporation and other institutions.
“Halal is not simply a matter of standards, certification or trade,” he said.
Zulkifli said Shariah principles, integrity, ethics and responsibility provide the foundation of trust upon which the halal economy can grow while contributing to economic development and the well-being of communities around the world.
He said Malaysia’s approach to developing the halal economy extends beyond certification to trade, investment, innovation, research, talent development and international market access.
Zulkifli also highlighted the Malaysian Halal Certification System, spearheaded by JAKIM, including its recognition of foreign halal certification bodies in different regions.
He said the system has helped establish a “chain of trust” that strengthens international confidence in halal products and services.
Malaysia, he added, remains committed to strengthening its role in the global halal sector through trusted standards, innovation, technology and strategic international cooperation.
GHaS 2026 is being held under the theme “Shariah and Integrity: Empowering the Global Halal Ecosystem.”
MIHAS 2026, meanwhile, is being held at MITEC from Sept. 23-26 under the theme “Shaping Trust, Driving Resilience,” bringing together companies and industry representatives across the global halal economy.

AI generated
PARIS – Pope Leo urged the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence, opening his four-day visit to France on Sept 25 with a fervent warning that AI could create a future where “a paradise of machines” takes control of the earth.
The first US pope, who has made sounding the alarm about the risks of AI a central part of his 16-month papacy, put the issue at the heart of his visit to France, the first by a pope in nearly 20 years.
“If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a ‘paradise of machines’ invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment,” he said, speaking under the gilded ceilings of the Elysee Palace.
The Pope also strongly reiterated the Church’s pro-life teachings, criticising initiatives to allow assisted dying for those who have incurable illnesses, two months after French politicians approved such a measure.
“I am concerned... by those trends in society that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death,” he said.
Leo, on a whirlwind three-city visit to France, will also seek to repair the Church’s standing there after abuse scandals sparked nationwide shock, and is also expected to lay out a vision for the future of Europe in a speech on Sept 28.
‘Message of peace’
Leo was greeted at the Paris Orly Airport, under a clear blue sky, by French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte, and by children who sang for him and asked for autographs. Leo will also travel to a famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, in the south-west, and to Metz, on the German border.
He was due to lead a prayer service in Paris on Sept 25 at the restored Notre-Dame cathedral, in the first visit by a pope since a devastating fire nearly destroyed the Gothic masterpiece in 2019.
Telling reporters on the plane to Paris that he was coming to convey a message of peace, Leo added: “It is a message which, at this time, as we all may know, is particularly important.”
People lining the streets Leo was due to pass through on his way to the Elysee held up phones and waved flags and signs.
“He brings a message of peace and hope that is very, very positive. His visit to France sends a wonderful signal to the country,” Catholic passer-by Antoine Barxias-Casties said in front of Notre-Dame cathedral on the eve of Leo’s visit.
Next on Leo’s agenda on Sept 25 was a speech to staff at the headquarters of the UN culture and education body, UNESCO, which is facing budget shortfalls after US President Donald Trump withdrew from the agency in 2025.
Leo attracted Trump’s ire earlier in 2026 after the Pope criticised the Iran war.
Asked about Trump’s attempt to bar CNN and several other outlets from the White House, Leo, aboard the plane to Paris, reaffirmed his support for freedom of the press, saying all were welcome to cover his visit.
Secular nation
France, a secular nation where the separation of Church and state is enshrined in a 1905 law, has witnessed a steady decline in affiliation to the Catholic Church during the post-war era, mirroring a trend in other traditionally Catholic countries.
Although the French Bishops’ Conference points to an increase in baptisms of adults, a report published by the official statistics agency INSEE showed that only 25 per cent of French 18- to 49-year-olds identified as Catholic, compared with 43 per cent a decade earlier. Only 8 per cent of Catholics said they regularly attended a place of worship.
Leo’s visit comes as Catholic leaders in France have been at odds with the government over the 2024 enshrining of a right to abortion in the French Constitution – a world first – and the passage of the law legalising assisted dying.

Local Church leaders hope the Pope’s visit will repair the Church’s standing after a crushing 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.
French bishops have since introduced compensation and safeguarding measures, but survivors have continued to press Church leaders to demonstrate accountability.
Alain Esquerre, 66, a spokesman for victims at the Notre-Dame de Betharram Catholic institution, told Reuters: “Leo bears the immense responsibility of ‘declaring enough is enough’.”
The Pope will meet seven French victims of abuse by Catholic clergy on Sept 27 in Lourdes. REUTERS

Polar explorer Otto Schmidt's 135th anniversary to be celebrated in St. Petersburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:14:46 UTC
17:14:46 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, September 25. /TASS/. St. Petersburg will celebrate the 135th anniversary of legendary polar explorer Otto Schmidt. The event, dubbed Garden of Memory of the Arctic Heroes, will take place at the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute on September 25. The event's participants will plant shrubs on the institute's territory in honor of the researcher, press service of the Museum of the Arctic and Antarctic said.
"In 2026, the museum will organize planting shrubs in the area around the institute in memory of Otto Schmidt (1891 - 1956), an outstanding scientist, polar explorer, leader of many expeditions, head of the Main Directorate of the Northern Sea Route, and one of the first directors of the All-Union Arctic Institute," the press service said in a release.
Since 2022, the museum has been the initiator of a project under the Green Russia national environmental movement. The event on Friday will open the chain of events devoted to the museum's jubilee - it will turn 90 in 2027.
About Otto Schmidt
Otto Schmidt is a Soviet statesman, geophysicist, Arctic researcher and Hero of the Soviet Union. He led Arctic expeditions on icebreaking steamships the Sedov, the Sibiryakov, and the Chelyuskin in 1929-1934.
About the museum
The idea to have a museum dedicated to studies in the polar latitudes emerged in the late 1920s in the wake of the Arctic's active development. In 1930, the USSR leadership issued an order to establish the All-Union Arctic Institute, which was supposed to have a specialized museum. The museum was due to be in the building of the former St. Nicholas Church of the Same Faith on Marat Street. Leading polar researchers of that time participated actively in the work on the museum's exposition - Otto Schmidt, Rudolf Samoilovich, Yuly Shokalsky, Vladimir Wiese, and others.
The museum opened to the public on January 8, 1937, and in the same year it was awarded an Honorary Diploma from the Exposition Universelle in Paris. The museum has responded promptly to events in polar research. For example, back in 1938, they opened an exhibition about the North Pole-1 first drifting station, which presented a tent used by Papanin's team, and the expedition participants' personal belongings. In the 1950s, due to the active Soviet Antarctic expeditions, the collection received new objects. In 1958, the museum received its current name - the Museum of the Arctic and Antarctic. In 1998, it gained the status of a Russian State Museum.
Nowadays, the Russian State Museum of the Arctic and Antarctic is the world's largest polar museum with a collection of more than 100,000 objects.

Gov't warns against bringing Four Species into Israel without authorization ahead of Sukkot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:05:57 UTC
17:05:57 KST

With Sukkot just around the corner, the Agriculture and Food Security Ministry issued a warning that under the Plant Protection Law, it is prohibited to bring plant products – including the Four Species – into Israel in carry-on luggage due to concerns about the introduction of pests that could harm local flora and agriculture.
The Four Species are four specific plants – lulav (palm branch), etrog (citron), hadassim (myrtle) and aravot (willow) – that are bound together and ritually waved during Sukkot to symbolize unity and divine praise.
The warning was issued with special consideration to the situation at Ben-Gurion Airport, which has become a bustling hub, with chaos on the rise.
As in previous years, amid the High Holy Days, the Plant Protection and Inspection Services reinforce their staff at the airport, in response to the increase in attempts by individuals and merchants to bring Four Species sets, which may be infested with various pests, into Israel.
Ministry warns against bringing plant products
The ministry has reiterated that bringing in plant products without authorization violates the law. However, to prevent inconvenience to travelers, inspectors from the ministry are providing travelers with a free personal set of locally produced items as a replacement for the confiscated Four Species.
“Every border inspection, every confiscated set, and every pest intercepted at the border is part of a security system designed to prevent irreversible damage to local crops and the agricultural export sector,” said Shlomit Tzioni, director of the Plant Protection and Inspection Services at the Ministry of Agriculture.
“The Plant Protection and Inspection Services operate year-round, and with increased vigilance during the holiday season, to protect Israel’s flora and agriculture”.
While the plants are mostly confiscated when they are brought to the country inside luggage, the ministry said that it will make one exception and let people keep the product if they are bringing an individual etrog for personal use only.
Rise in plant smuggling
In recent years, the ministry said it has seen a rising trend of plant product smuggling into Israel.
According to data from the ministry’s Plant Protection and Inspection Services, since the beginning of 2026, more than 1,200 passengers have been apprehended at Ben-Gurion Airport with various types of plant material in their luggage that are prohibited from entering the country.
The total amount of plant products seized and sent for destruction stands at approximately 3 metric tons, including fruits, vegetables, seeds, and tree parts.
“Importing fruits, vegetables, seeds, flower seedlings, and the Four Species without prior approval from the Plant Protection and Inspection Services poses a serious risk,” said Tzioni, adding that he believes that it ‘may lead to the introduction of pests that do not currently exist in Israel’.
These pests could harm local crops, thereby “causing irreversible damage to vegetation and agriculture,” according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, and could even eventually wipe out entire sectors and undermine Israel’s food security.
Furthermore, Israel exports agricultural produce to many countries, such as Europe, the Far East, Russia, and the United States, and so, in addition to the immediate danger to agriculture in Israel, this could harm the export sector and the country’s economy.
Tzioni added: “We call on the citizens of Israel to help protect Israel’s flora and agriculture and to prevent a situation that could endanger local flora, agriculture, and the State of Israel’s food security. Together, we will ensure a happy and safe Sukkot for Israeli agriculture.”
The Environment and Climate Change portal is produced in cooperation with the Goldman Sonnenfeldt School of Sustainability and Climate Change at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. The Jerusalem Post maintains all editorial decisions related to the content.

Tel Aviv ranks 34th globally, highest in Middle East, in Oxford Economics’ 2026 Global Cities Index
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:05:27 UTC
17:05:27 KST

Tel Aviv ranked 34th globally in Oxford Economics’ 2026 Global Cities Index, published on September 15, which assesses major cities across five key areas: Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment, and Governance.
Tel Aviv’s strongest results were recorded in Economics, where it ranked 16th in the world, and Human Capital, where it placed 31st. The city ranked 156th in Quality of Life, 234th in Environment and 401st in Governance.
While it's still not the 2024 result, in which Tel Aviv ranked 30th worldwide, it's better than the 2025 result, where the city was placed 46th.
The index is fairly new, introduced in 2024, and ranks the top 1,000 cities worldwide. The index claims to offer insights into how cities are adapting and thriving in a rapidly changing environment.
Tel Aviv is also the highest-ranked city in the Middle East and North Africa in the 2026 index, and one of only three Middle Eastern cities included in the global top 50.
Oxford Economics highlights Tel Aviv’s technology and innovation ecosystem as one of the driving forces behind its strong overall position. The report describes the city’s ‘Silicon Wadi’ ecosystem as “home to both startups and established companies operating across sectors including defense, finance and biotechnology”.
While the scale and productivity of these industries help place Tel Aviv in the top global decile for both GDP size and GDP per person, the report states that Tel Aviv’s economy, as a microcosm of broader Israel, has “taken a significant hit since the attacks on 7 October 2023 and the subsequent war, and the conflict with Iran has only added to regional geopolitical risks”.
According to the report, Tel Aviv’s economy is valued at approximately $267 billion, with GDP per person of $86,300 and a metropolitan population of 3.1 million. Oxford Economics identifies the city’s large economic base, concentration of corporate headquarters and low emissions intensity among its principal strengths.
Security situation weighs on governance score
In addressing the effect of the regional geopolitical situation on Tel Aviv’s ranking, the report labels the Governance category as the ‘weakest’, “a reflection of Israel’s unique geopolitical situation”.
“Regional geopolitical tensions with Iran and its allies also play a significant role, particularly the recent conflict in Iran and the renewed attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon,” the report reflects.
At the same time, Oxford Economics states that “Tel Aviv remains slated to perform well in the rankings in the coming years from a structural standpoint,” pointing to the city’s underlying economic and human-capital strengths while noting that continued regional instability presents risks.
Tech and education drive economic and human capital scores
The data shows that the city’s technology sector plays a central role in its strong Human Capital performance. Oxford Economics points to the contribution of institutions including Tel Aviv University and Bar-Ilan University to research and development, particularly in fields connected to the city’s technology sector.
The report also notes that Tel Aviv has one of the highest rates of educational attainment in the Middle East and North Africa, supported by a highly skilled workforce and the concentration of high-paying technology jobs.
Quality of life and environment
On quality of life, the report states that high-paying jobs contribute to Tel Aviv’s high income per person, which ranks among the global top 100.
It also highlights the region’s highest life expectancy and the city’s healthcare system, while identifying high housing costs as an ongoing challenge.
On the environmental side, Oxford Economics points to the relatively low carbon intensity of Tel Aviv’s economy, reflecting the importance of technology and professional services in the city’s growth.

Gold medalist Yuan Jinwei of China poses during the victory ceremony of men's cross-country of cycling mountain bike at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Cen Yunpeng)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's Yuan Jinwei came from behind to win the men's mountain bike cross-country race at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Friday, finishing in one hour, 25 minutes and 15 seconds, just three seconds ahead of Japan's Tatsuumi Soejima.
Indonesia's Feri Yudoyono took bronze, 26 seconds behind Yuan. China's other rider, Lyu Xianjing, finished seventh in 1:28:09.
Fourteen riders from eight countries and regions contested the eight-lap, 29.6km race at Obata Ryokuchi Park. Yuan was fourth after the opening lap and slipped to fifth by the end of lap three, 15 seconds off the lead. He posted the fastest fourth lap in 10:22, cutting the gap to two seconds, and moved into first place by the end of lap six.
The lead changed hands again on the final lap. Yudoyono was first through the opening intermediate timing point before Soejima took the lead at the second. Yuan regained first place at the third, where he and Soejima were both shown with a cumulative time of 1:21:56. Yuan held on to cross the finish line three seconds ahead.
Yuan said the earlier exchanges had failed to create a gap, so he conserved his energy over the final two laps and waited for a chance to pass. "I had to find a slightly wider section in the final half lap and make the overtake," he said. After winning silver at the Hangzhou Asian Games, Yuan added that he had come to Japan determined to give everything and leave with no regrets.
Yuan also thanked teammate Lyu for his support. Official lap data showed that Lyu recorded the fastest times on laps three and five. Yuan said Lyu crashed after colliding with another rider while helping him and was taken to hospital for checks on a back injury. According to Yuan, the injury did not appear serious at the time.
Yuan's victory gave China its fourth consecutive Asian Games gold in the men's mountain bike cross-country event. ■

VIENTIANE, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Laos is working to address labor shortages and develop short-term and long-term plans to balance labor supply and demand.
The Lao Ministry of Labor and Social Welfare held a consultation meeting with partners and relevant stakeholders in Lao capital Vientiane on Thursday to discuss labor supply and demand and address challenges in the domestic job market. She stressed the importance of effective employment services and appropriate policies and mechanisms to regulate the labor market and better balance supply and demand. Such measures are needed to meet employers' workforce requirements, support domestic investment projects and respond to changing economic conditions.
The ministry has already strengthened its employment service system in line with relevant policies and regulations. Key measures include expanding employment service operations, promoting online services for job seekers and employers, and organizing job fairs and consultation meetings with relevant stakeholders.
The lack of accurate labor market information has made it more difficult to match job seekers with vacancies, balance labor supply and demand, and develop a workforce that meets employers' actual needs.
Anousone also emphasized the need to establish a stable and sustainable job placement system capable of addressing labor market challenges, including workforce attraction and incentives, in both the short and long term. ■

Methamphetamine harms rise in Australia: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:00:12 CST
17:00:12 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Methamphetamine-related deaths, hospitalizations and consumption in Australia have reached record levels, with researchers warning that harms from the illicit drug continue to rise, according to a report released Friday.
There were 753 overdose deaths involving amphetamine-type stimulants, primarily methamphetamine, in 2024, or a rate of 2.9 deaths per 100,000 people, which is substantially higher than in previous years, said the report released by the National Drug and Alcohol Research Center (NDARC).
Nearly 14,000 hospitalizations were due to methamphetamine use in 2023-24, accounting for 24 percent of all drug-related hospitalizations, the report said.
Wastewater drug monitoring showed an estimated 15.8 tonnes of methamphetamine was consumed across Australia in 2024-25, the highest level recorded, with consumption particularly elevated in regional areas, said Associate Professor Amy Peacock, who leads NDARC's drug trends program.
The rising harms were driven by increased global supply and strong local demand for the illicit drug, Peacock said.
The burden of methamphetamine-related harms has also shifted toward older age groups. People aged 15-24 accounted for 5 percent of amphetamine-type stimulant overdose deaths in 2024, down from one in eight in 2005, while mortality rates increased among people aged 25-54, she said.
The report also found that more than 16 tonnes of methamphetamine was seized by Australian authorities in 2024, significantly higher than in previous years, and called for coordinated efforts on prevention, harm reduction, treatment and monitoring. ■

Türkiye and the UN: The world has outgrown the top five
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:59:17 UTC
16:59:17 KST

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said last week that a serious geopolitical split has paralysed the work of the Security Council.
When superpowers resort to wars that violate international law, he pointed out, they create an atmosphere of impunity and increase the risk that other states will also consider the use of force an acceptable tool of foreign policy.
What he did not say implicitly is that this problem affects the very foundation of the international system formed after World War II.
When the UN was created, the main task was to prevent a recurrence of any global conflict.
The post-war order was built around the idea that major powers had a special responsibility for maintaining international security.
That is why the United States, the then-Soviet Union, Britain, France and China received permanent seats in the Security Council and the right of veto.
This design reflected the balance of power in 1945. However, over the following decades, the international system changed significantly.
The number of independent states grew, new economic and political centres appeared, and international politics ceased to be determined solely by relations between a few major powers.
At the same time, the institutional framework of the Security Council has remained largely unchanged. The capabilities of the permanent members themselves have also changed.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Moscow lost much of its former international influence. The US retained its leading position but increasingly had to distribute global costs and responsibilities among allies and partners.
In some cases, Washington has preferred to operate outside UN mechanisms if it sees them as restricting its own freedom of action.
China, by contrast, has significantly increased its economic and political weight, although it continues to adhere to a cautious line in most international crises.
Britain and France have retained permanent membership in the Security Council, even though their current capabilities no longer match the global influence of the mid-20th century.
Thus, the problem is not only in the composition of the Security Council.
The very environment in which it operates has changed: the distribution of economic, military, and political power has become much more complex.
One of the most important changes was the growing independence of regional powers.
The classical model, in which the decisions of the great powers almost automatically determined the behaviour of other states, no longer explains much of international politics.
The largest centres of power still retain a decisive influence, but regional states have gained more room for independent manoeuvre.
They participate in conflict resolution, form regional balances and build relations with several major powers at the same time.
Therefore, the current world order cannot be viewed solely through the rivalry of the US, China, and Russia. It is also necessary to take into account states that have sufficient political, economic and military potential to independently influence international processes.
At the same time, the expansion of the capabilities of regional powers is not accompanied by a comparable change in their position in international institutions.
States can play an important role in conflict prevention and regional security, but they lack permanent representation in bodies that make binding decisions.
It is in this context that Türkiye's approach to UN reform takes on special significance.
‘The world is bigger than five’
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's formula, ‘The world is bigger than five’, is usually perceived as a demand to reform the Security Council. However, its content is broader.
It reflects Ankara's position that the ability to influence international decisions should not remain the exclusive privilege of the five states that received special status because of the political reality of 1945.
The Turkish approach calls for a review of the Security Council's representation and decision-making system.
Ankara advocates fairer geographical representation and criticises the existing veto mechanism, which allows one permanent member to block decisions even without the support of most other participants.
It is not just about increasing the number of states represented in the Security Council. The expansion of its membership without changing the decision-making mechanism can preserve the former dependence of international security on the political will of a limited number of powers.
Therefore, the question of reform inevitably affects both representation and the distribution of powers.
It is not so much about the representation of Türkiye itself, but about the principles of the formation of international institutions and the distribution of power between states.
To what extent do global institutions today reflect the real distribution of responsibility for international security? And can states directly involved in crisis management avoid key decisions?
Türkiye's foreign policy of the last 10-15 years allows us to consider these issues with specific examples.
Ankara has become an active participant in diplomatic processes in several regions at once.
It participated in settling crises related to Syria and Libya, made diplomatic efforts in the context of the Russian-Ukrainian conflict, and pioneered in launching the Black Sea Grain Initiative.
Türkiye also participated in the processes around Karabakh and the Armenian-Azerbaijani dialogue, and took diplomatic steps to limit further escalation in the Middle East.
The significance of these processes lies not only in the expansion of Turkish diplomatic geography. Ankara can simultaneously maintain working relations with various centres of power and use these ties to solve specific regional problems.
The Black Sea Grain Initiative is one example of how a regional power can help solve an international problem while maintaining channels of interaction with the parties to the conflict.
At the same time, the grain initiative has demonstrated both the possibilities and limitations of such diplomacy.
Türkiye, together with the UN, facilitated the creation of a mechanism for exporting Ukrainian grain through the Black Sea, but the agreement's continued functioning depended on the consent of the parties to the conflict.
The Syrian direction demonstrates another feature of Turkish foreign policy. Ankara simultaneously interacts with Russia, the US and regional parties to the conflict, preserving its own regional security interests.
Türkiye acts here both as a mediator and as an independent participant in the processes on which its national security directly depends.
In such situations, regional powers do not just implement the decisions of the largest centres of power; they also help shape the conditions under which those decisions can be implemented, even though their capabilities are limited by the interests of other participants and the differences between them.
At the same time, NATO membership does not limit Turkish foreign policy to the framework of the transatlantic alliance.
The Black Sea region, Eastern Europe, the Caucasus, the Middle East, the Balkans and Turkistan (Central Asia) remain areas where Ankara is developing various forms of political, economic and military-diplomatic interaction.
Through the Organization of Turkic States, Türkiye also participates in the formation of a separate space for cooperation in the Turkic world.
Thus, Türkiye is an example of a state that maintains allied relations with one of the largest centres of power, but at the same time builds its own system of regional ties and foreign policy priorities.
A new geography of power and responsibility
The growing independence of regional powers does not mean that the great powers are losing their importance.
The US, China, Russia and other major centres of power continue to determine the key parameters of world politics. However, the modern international system is no longer reduced exclusively to their rivalry.
At the same time, another process is taking place – the redistribution of responsibility for regional security.
States located directly in the conflict zone are increasingly forced to participate independently in their containment and settlement. At the same time, their actual role does not always correspond to their ability to influence global decisions.
This is where the contradiction between current geopolitical reality and the UN's institutional architecture arises.
The Security Council retains a structure shaped by a few major powers of the mid-twentieth century, while international security increasingly depends on the interaction of a much wider range of states.
Therefore, UN reform cannot be reduced solely to changing the number of seats in the Security Council. It touches on a more fundamental question: to what extent the existing decision-making system reflects the real distribution of power, responsibility, and political influence.
However, this is where the main obstacle to reform arises. Changing the UN Charter requires broad support from the organization's member states, as well as ratification of the amendments by all five permanent members of the Security Council.
Thus, states with special powers in the current system must agree to change the rules that give them that power.
This turns Security Council reform from a matter of institutional structure into a problem of the international balance of power.
Even if a majority of states support greater representation and revised decision-making, implementing these demands depends on the position of powers, which may not want to limit their own advantages.
In such circumstances, the importance of the Turkish initiative is not limited to the possibility of achieving concrete changes in the composition of the Security Council.
The ‘world is bigger than five’ formula allows Ankara to advance the debate on the principles of the international order, seek the support of states that do not have permanent representation in the Security Council, and strengthen its own role in the discussion of global governance reform.
For Türkiye, this means changing state representation in the UN system and recognising the new role of regional powers in international politics.
At the same time, strengthening the role of regional powers does not necessarily mean weakening the largest centres of power.
On the contrary, greater state participation in decision-making can help share responsibility for international security and expand opportunities for diplomatic crisis management.
The key question is whether international institutions can adapt to these changes before the gap between their formal powers and realpolitik widens further.
For Türkiye, the answer lies both in the future of the UN and in its own place in the emerging world order.

EXPLAINER - Pope Leo XIV in France: What to know about 1st papal state visit since 2008
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:58:27 UTC
16:58:27 KST

- Meetings in Paris, Lourdes and Metz to highlight education, artificial intelligence, interreligious dialogue, peace and Europe’s future
 
Pope Leo XIV begins a four-day trip to France on Friday, becoming the first pontiff to make an official visit to the country since Benedict XVI in 2008.
The Vatican has described the Sept. 25-28 trip as an Apostolic Journey.
The trip will take the pope from the Elysee Palace and UNESCO headquarters in Paris to the Catholic pilgrimage site of Lourdes and the eastern city of Metz, close to the borders with Germany, Luxembourg and Belgium.
The itinerary includes meetings with French political leaders, young Catholics, abuse survivors, migrants, educators, representatives of other religions and a broader European audience.
The visit also comes at a sensitive moment for the Catholic Church in France, which is seeking to rebuild public trust after revelations of widespread sexual abuse and amid its strong opposition to France’s newly enacted assisted-dying law.
 
Why is the visit being described as historic?
Pope Leo’s trip is the first official papal state visit to France in 18 years.
He is traveling in response to invitations from President Emmanuel Macron, French Church authorities and UNESCO’s director-general.
Pope Francis visited Strasbourg in 2014, Marseille in 2023 and Corsica in 2024, but none of those trips was an official state visit.
The distinction makes the pontiff's trip the first state visit to France since Benedict XVI visited Paris and Lourdes in 2008.
The trip will also offer an early indication of how the first US-born pope engages with European governments and increasingly secular societies.
 
 
Where will Pope Leo go?
The pope is set to arrive at Paris-Orly Airport on Friday morning before meeting Macron at the Elysee Palace. He will then address French authorities, members of civil society and the diplomatic corps.
Later, he will speak at UNESCO headquarters, where education, cultural dialogue, heritage and peace are expected to feature prominently. He will also attend evening prayers at Notre-Dame Cathedral and a youth vigil at the Stade de France.
On Saturday, he will visit Maison Bakhita, a Paris center supporting migrants and refugees, before meeting participants in the French Church’s synodal process, catechumens and recently baptized Catholics. He will then celebrate an outdoor mass at Place de la Concorde before traveling to Lourdes.
His Sunday program includes a meeting with French bishops, Mass at the Lourdes sanctuary and visits with sick and disabled people.
The pope will conclude the trip in Metz on Monday with an interreligious gathering, a meeting focused on Europe’s roots, peace and unity, and Mass at Saint-Etienne Cathedral.
 
How will the clergy abuse crisis shape the visit?
The pope is also scheduled to meet privately with survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy in Lourdes, according to media reports.
This Lourdes meeting with abuse survivors will be among the most closely watched moments of the trip.
France’s Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Catholic Church, known as CIASE, estimated in its landmark 2021 report that about 216,000 people had been sexually abused while minors by members of the clergy or religious orders since 1950.
The estimate rose to approximately 330,000 when abuse involving lay people working in Church institutions was included.
 
Why is assisted dying likely to be a flashpoint?
The visit comes just over a month after France promulgated a law establishing a right to assisted dying for eligible adults suffering from serious and incurable medical conditions.
The legislation, enacted in August, followed an emotionally charged national debate over personal autonomy, end-of-life suffering and the availability of palliative care.
French bishops strongly opposed the measure, describing its adoption as a “grave rupture” and warning that legalizing euthanasia and assisted suicide could place vulnerable, elderly, disabled and seriously ill people under pressure.
Protection of life, care for vulnerable people and access to medical treatment are among the themes officially identified for Pope Leo’s visit, yet it remains unclear whether he will directly challenge the law during his meeting with Macron.
 
What does the trip say about religion’s place in France?
The pope will be addressing a country shaped by laicite, France’s model of state secularism, and where formal religious participation has declined substantially.
Official data from France’s national statistics institute showed that 51% of people aged 18 to 59 in metropolitan France said they had no religion in 2019-2020. Among those identifying as Catholic, only 8% reported attending a religious service at least once a month.
During his visit, he will pray at Notre-Dame Cathedral, celebrate Mass at Place de la Concorde and meet French political leaders.
The pope will also visit Metz in the Alsace-Moselle region, where the 1905 law separating churches and the state does not apply. The region retains a system in which several religions, including Catholicism, are formally recognized, reflecting its distinct historical and legal development.
 
What are the pope's wider priorities?
At UNESCO, Pope Leo is expected to connect education and culture with peace, international cooperation and the ethical challenges posed by artificial intelligence.
The pope has also called for international regulation of artificial intelligence. On Sept. 21, he called for AI systems that serve human dignity and strengthen peace.
Metz, meanwhile, has been chosen for its location in a region marked by European wars, shifting borders and Franco-German reconciliation.
Its association with Robert Schuman, one of the architects of European integration, will provide the pope with a setting to discuss war, peace and the continent’s political future.

Fact-checking Netanyahu’s lies at the UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:54:09 UTC
16:54:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Fact-checking Netanyahu’s lies at the UNGA
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed a half-empty United Nations General Assembly on Thursday after dozens of delegations walked out in protest.
His speech, lasting almost 40 minutes, came about a month before Israel’s parliamentary elections and included attacks on Iran, Qatar, Turkey and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Netanyahu defended Israel’s conduct in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, repeated accusations against Hamas and challenged international criticism of his government.
But several of his claims conflict with figures published by the United Nations, findings from US government investigations and information reported by Israeli media.
Here are eight of the principal claims and what the available evidence shows.
1. Settler violence in the West Bank
Netanyahu sought to play down settler violence in the occupied West Bank, describing it as a relatively small number of incidents involving about 150 people who threw stones, cut down olive trees and occasionally started fires. He suggested that perhaps two or three people had been killed.
Figures from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) indicate a much wider problem.
By 20 July 2026, 18 Palestinians had been killed in incidents linked to settler attacks, exceeding the 17 recorded throughout 2025. Of those killed in 2026, 12 were killed by settlers, three by Israeli forces and three in circumstances where responsibility remained disputed.
The number of recorded settler attacks reached 1,835 in 2025. During the first four months of 2026, the monthly average rose to about 190, the highest daily rate recorded by OCHA.
The consequences extend beyond deaths and injuries. Between January 2023 and July 2026, settler attacks and associated restrictions contributed to the full or partial displacement of 123 Palestinian communities, including 47 that were completely emptied.
Netanyahu’s description also omitted the political influence of the settler movement, whose leading figures hold ministerial positions in his government.
2. Hamas 'stealing' humanitarian aid
Netanyahu repeated the Israeli government’s allegation that Hamas had stolen most of the humanitarian aid entering Gaza.
Israel has used accusations of widespread aid diversion to justify restrictions on deliveries and its support for the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, a US- and Israeli-backed aid distribution operation.
But an internal review by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) found no evidence of systematic theft of US-funded humanitarian assistance by Hamas.
The review examined 156 reported incidents of theft or loss between October 2023 and May 2025.
It found no indication that Hamas had benefited from the supplies involved in those incidents.
Less than 1% of the US-funded assistance covered by the review was affected by loss, theft, diversion, fraud or waste.
Reuters also reported that Israeli military officials had found no evidence of systematic Hamas theft from UN aid distribution sites and considered UN distribution operations largely effective.
The USAID findings do not establish that no aid was ever diverted. However, they do not support the allegation that Hamas stole most of the assistance.
3. Two million tonnes of food entered Gaza
Netanyahu argued that Israel could not be committing genocide because it had allowed food and vaccines into Gaza.
He asked what genocidal government would allow two million tonnes of food into the territory, equivalent to one tonne per resident, and provide one million doses of polio vaccine.
The food aid figure comes from Israeli authorities and has not been independently verified.
It also does not establish how much food reached civilians or whether supplies were sufficient to prevent hunger.
On 22 August 2025, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) confirmed that famine was occurring in Gaza governorate, which includes Gaza City.
Netanyahu also cited the polio vaccination campaign without acknowledging the leading role of international health organisations.
The campaign was organised by the Palestinian Ministry of Health in collaboration with the World Health Organization, UNICEF, UNRWA and other partners. Israel agreed to humanitarian pauses to allow vaccinations to take place.
Netanyahu dismissed accusations of genocide as the “biggest lie”.
However, in September 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed four of the five acts defined in the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The commission also concluded that senior Israeli officials, including Netanyahu, had incited the commission of genocidal acts.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani responded to Netanyahu’s speech by pointing to the arrest warrant issued against him by the International Criminal Court.
In a statement, Mamdani said Netanyahu had again used the UN platform to repeat unfounded claims intended to improve the image of Israel’s actions against Palestinians.
He added that no such claim could change the fact that Netanyahu remained subject to an ICC arrest warrant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
4. Christians in Bethlehem
Netanyahu claimed that Bethlehem had been overwhelmingly Christian when it was under Israeli control but had become overwhelmingly Muslim after being transferred to the Palestinian Authority.
He suggested that Christians had been driven out.
However, figures from a census conducted by Israeli authorities following the occupation of Bethlehem in 1967 contradict the claim about its previous religious composition.
The census recorded 14,439 residents in the town, with Christians accounting for 46.1% and Muslims 53.9%.
Including the refugee camp within the municipal boundaries increased the Muslim proportion to about 58%.
The figures are published by the Jewish Virtual Library, which also carries the text of Netanyahu’s speech.
The city’s religious composition has changed over several decades, but the 1967 figures do not support the claim that Bethlehem was overwhelmingly Christian during Israeli rule.
Netanyahu’s account also omitted the reasons many Palestinian Christians give for emigration. These include land confiscation, the construction of Israel’s separation barrier, military checkpoints and restrictions on access to occupied East Jerusalem.
Presenting Bethlehem’s demographic changes primarily as a consequence of Muslim-Christian tensions therefore leaves out the effects of Israeli occupation.
5. Claims about children killed on 7 October
Netanyahu again referred to accounts of children being allegedly burned alive during the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.
Some of the most widely circulated accounts of atrocities against infants, including allegations that babies had been beheaded, were challenged by subsequent investigations.
Haaretz reported that some claims circulated by emergency responders and volunteers from the Israeli organisation Zaka were not supported by the available evidence.
The Israeli newspaper examined information from Israel’s National Insurance Institute, kibbutz leaders and police, among other sources. It reported that one infant, 10-month-old Mila Cohen, was killed at Kibbutz Be’eri when gunfire struck the door of the family’s safe room.
The widely circulated claims about beheaded babies were not substantiated by the evidence subsequently reported by Israeli and international media.
6. The killing of a settler near Ramallah
During his criticism of French President Emmanuel Macron, Netanyahu referred to the killing of Nathaniel Shukron, a father of six who held French citizenship.
He said Shukron had been visiting a spring with his son when a Hamas attacker shot him at point-blank range.
However, no armed organisation publicly claimed responsibility for the attack, and no official statement identified the attacker as belonging to Hamas. The group praised the attack but did not say it had carried it out.
Netanyahu also presented the spring as an ordinary recreational site. Wadi Raya spring, near the Israeli settlement of Halamish, also known as Neve Tzuf, had been taken over by settlers about a year earlier.
Palestinian landowners had been prevented from accessing the area, where settlers had established an outpost intended to attract visitors.
No formal Israeli confiscation order had been issued for the land. That background was absent from Netanyahu’s account.
7. Gaza before 7 October
Netanyahu said there had been no Israelis in Gaza, either civilians or soldiers, on 7 October 2023.
The statement is accurate in the narrow sense that Israel withdrew its permanent ground forces and settlements from the territory in 2005.
However, it omits the wider system of control Israel continued to exercise over Gaza.
Since 2007, the territory has been subject to an Israeli blockade restricting movement by land, sea and air.
Israel maintained control over key crossings, population records and the movement of people and goods.
In its July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice said Israel’s withdrawal in 2005 had not entirely ended its obligations under the law of occupation.
The court found that Israel continued to exercise important elements of authority over Gaza, including control of land, sea and air borders, restrictions on movement, import and export taxes, and the buffer zone.
It said Israel’s obligations remained proportionate to the degree of effective control it exercised.
Netanyahu’s account also omitted Israel’s previous restrictions on food entering Gaza.
Israeli government documents have shown that authorities calculated the territory’s food requirements in calories when determining permitted supplies.
8. Qatar and changing international opinion
Netanyahu accused Qatar of spending vast sums to spread false information about Israel through funding for American universities and media organisations, including Al Jazeera.
He suggested that these activities were intended to influence young people’s views. Qatar has rejected the allegation.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said Netanyahu was attempting to divert attention from the Israeli government’s actions in the occupied Palestinian territories.
He argued that attributing changing international opinion, particularly among young people, to influence campaigns dismissed the ability of a generation to form its own views based on what it had witnessed.
Polling indicates a significant shift in American attitudes towards Israel and the Palestinians.
According to a Gallup survey published in February 2026, 53% of Americans aged 18 to 34 said they sympathised more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathised more with Israelis.
It was the first time a majority of respondents in that age group had expressed greater sympathy for Palestinians. The proportion expressing greater sympathy for Israelis was also the lowest recorded for the age group.
The shift was not confined to younger adults. Among Americans aged 35 to 54, 46% expressed greater sympathy for Palestinians and 28% for Israelis.
A year earlier, the corresponding figures had been 33% for Palestinians and 45% for Israelis.

Israeli drafted into Ukrainian army receives Sukkot supplies in detention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:50:46 UTC
16:50:46 KST

Breslov Hasid Jonathan Karlinsky, a dual Israeli-Ukrainian citizen drafted into the Ukrainian military after traveling to the country for the annual Rosh Hashanah pilgrimage to Uman, received a set of the Four Species on Thursday so he can observe Sukkot while held at a military detention facility in the Odesa region.
Video obtained by ynet showed Karlinsky receiving the ritual items used during the weeklong holiday, which will begin Friday evening. The set included an etrog, or citron, brought from Kfar Chabad in central Israel.
Karlinsky, 49, a resident of Beitar Illit, was born in Ukraine and later immigrated to Israel. He was detained by Ukrainian military police during a document check at the Ukraine-Romania border after traveling to Uman for Rosh Hashanah. Authorities determined that he remained subject to Ukraine's wartime military service requirements.
Karlinsky had traveled to Uman as part of the annual pilgrimage by followers of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov, the founder of the Breslov Hasidic movement, who died in 1810 and is buried there. Tens of thousands of mostly Orthodox Jewish pilgrims travel to his grave for Rosh Hashanah each year, a tradition that has continued despite Russia's war against Ukraine and the severe restrictions on commercial air travel to the country.
His detention initially left his family and members of the Breslov community unable to determine where he had been taken. His family appealed to rabbis, community activists and Israeli officials in an effort to secure his release. The Foreign Ministry initially told the family it was working to locate him.
Last week, however, the Ukrainian military informed the Federation of Jewish Communities of Ukraine, or FJCU, that Karlinsky was being held at a detention facility for deserters in the Odesa region. The federation is an umbrella organization representing Jewish communities across Ukraine.
Efforts to obtain an exemption from military service were unsuccessful. An initial claim that Karlinsky qualified for an exemption because he was the father of six children was found to be incorrect; he has one daughter. According to the FJCU, Karlinsky had also previously served in the Ukrainian military before becoming religious and immigrating to Israel.
Because of his medical background, however, Ukrainian authorities decided not to send Karlinsky to a frontline combat position. He is expected instead to serve as a military doctor at a rear-area base near Kharkiv, several dozen miles from the combat zone. Karlinsky also asked not to carry a weapon for religious reasons, a request Ukrainian authorities agreed to accommodate, according to the FJCU.
The organization said a video provided by the military showed Karlinsky saying he was in good condition and being treated fairly. The FJCU said Ukraine's shortage of medical personnel was one reason authorities were unwilling to release him.
Since Karlinsky was located, Rabbi Avraham Wolff, the chief rabbi of Odesa and southern Ukraine and a Chabad emissary, has been working to provide for his religious needs. Wolff arranged for fellow Chabad emissary Rabbi Shneur Vigler to visit Karlinsky and provide religious and emotional support.
Wolff has also arranged for kosher food to be delivered to Karlinsky each day. The Jewish community provided him with food for Shabbat, the meal before the Yom Kippur fast and the meal breaking the fast, as well as a prayer book. Ahead of Sukkot, Wolff arranged for Karlinsky to receive a set of the Four Species so he could perform one of the holiday's central religious commandments while remaining at the military facility.
The Four Species — an etrog, a palm branch, myrtle branches and willow branches — are traditionally held together and waved during prayers on Sukkot, the Jewish harvest festival that follows Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Meir Stambler, chairman of the Federation of Jewish Communities of Ukraine, said Ukraine's continuing war with Russia had left the country with a severe shortage of personnel and made exemptions from military service increasingly difficult to obtain.
"This is truly a war of survival," Stambler said, noting that people are being killed daily and that Ukraine faces a severe manpower shortage. "Every Ukrainian citizen is needed here."
Meanwhile, Stambler praised Ukrainian authorities for accommodating Karlinsky's religious requirements, including his request not to carry a weapon. He said it might eventually be possible for Karlinsky to serve within the Ukrainian military rabbinate.
Local Jewish community officials said Karlinsky was the only ultra-Orthodox Jew detained in the current wave of stepped-up mobilization enforcement. They said Ukrainian authorities had significantly intensified checks on men of military age, with eligible Ukrainian citizens encountered inside the country increasingly being stopped and directed toward military service.
Karlinsky's case drew particular attention in Israel because he has lived in the country for years, is married, studies at a yeshiva and is part of the Breslov Hasidic community. But his Ukrainian citizenship left him subject to the country's wartime mobilization rules when he entered Ukraine.
His detention was one of several involving Breslov pilgrims traveling to or from Uman around Rosh Hashanah this year, though the other cases were unrelated to Ukrainian military service. Three other pilgrims were detained in separate incidents in Cyprus and Moldova, a major transit route for Israelis traveling to Ukraine while its airspace remains largely closed to commercial flights because of the war.

Taiwan minimum wage talks extended due to dispute over NT$400
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:48:32 UTC
16:48:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A NT$400 (US$12.59) gap prolonged minimum wage talks into Thursday evening before labor and employers agreed on NT$30,900 per month, CNA reported Friday.
The Minimum Wage Review Committee usually finishes its annual meeting around 2 p.m. or 3 p.m. This year, however, negotiations were still underway at 4 p.m., making it one of the longest sessions in recent years, per UDN.
Before the meeting, labor groups had called for a 7.77% increase. Employers supported a smaller 3% rise, arguing that economic conditions differed across industries.
Labor representatives later lowered their proposal to 6.6%, but the two sides remained divided. Academics at the meeting then suggested a 5.62% increase based on economic growth, employment data, and inflation.
Employer representatives rejected the proposal, saying some of the figures used in the calculation dated back to 2014. The two sides then held separate discussions in an effort to narrow the difference.
The gap eventually fell to NT$400. The labor side sought a monthly minimum wage of at least NT$31,100, while employers offered NT$30,700, per Liberty Times.
Employers later raised their offer by NT$200 and asked labor representatives to lower their demand by the same amount. The labor side initially resisted but eventually accepted the compromise, bringing the monthly minimum wage to NT$30,900, per Economic Daily News.
The hourly minimum wage will rise from NT$196 to NT$205. The monthly rate will increase from NT$29,500 to NT$30,900, with both changes amounting to about 4.75%.
Several labor representatives said that economic conditions supported a larger increase. They also said employers could have shown more flexibility, pointing to strong growth in artificial intelligence-related industries and continued expansion in some traditional sectors, per Newtalk.
