céleste boursier-mougenot brings his floating ceramic orchestra outdoors in athens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:45:25 UTC
16:45:25 KST

CÉLESTE BOURSIER-MOUGENOT TAKES CLINAMEN OUTDOORS in athens
After floating through the grand interiors of Paris’ Bourse de Commerce and New York’s Park Avenue Armory, Céleste Boursier-Mougenot’s clinamen is moving outside. From September 26th to December 5th, 2026, the French artist’s endlessly shifting sound installation occupies the renovatedOnassis Mandra in Athens, where hundreds of white porcelain bowls drift across three circular pools, colliding softly to create an ever-changing aquatic score.
First conceived in 1997, clinamen has never been a fixed installation. Water, porcelain bowls, circular basins, and the gentle currents set the vessels in motion, and yet every presentation produces a different configuration, sound, and rhythm. More than twenty iterations have followed the original work, each adjusted to the architecture and acoustics of its host.
For its latest version, the biggest variable is no longer simply the building around it. For the first time, clinamen is being presented outdoors, exposing the work to the particular conditions of its new setting in the center of Athens. At Onassis Mandra, the bowls share their soundscape with the city, as well as with shifting sunlight, wind, voices, surrounding sounds, and potentially rain. The move outside is also a departure for Boursier-Mougenot himself, who had previously resisted the idea. ‘People wanted to put it outside. I said no. It’s an indoor piece,’he explains during the press preview in Athens attended by designboom.
In Athens, the installation becomes an open system, set within the open-air setting of Onassis Mandra, the surviving Belle Époque outdoor theater located beside the Onassis Library and Dionysiou Areopagitou. ‘It needs to be perfectly balanced,’ Boursier-Mougenot says of the work’s relationship with its surroundings. ‘It has to be perfect when there is no wind, no rain. And then if suddenly the breeze comes, it’s going to be perfectly balanced.’ A passing gust can alter the movement of the bowls; a change in light can transform the appearance of the water; rain can introduce another layer to the composition. The title of the work refers to the Epicurean concept of the clinamen, the unpredictable deviation in the movement of atoms, and this idea of small departures is central to how the installation operates.
Each porcelain bowl has been individually selected by Boursier-Mougenot for its particular timbre, allowing every collision to contribute a slightly different sound. As the bowls approach, separate, and meet again, they produce delicate, bell-like tones without the presence of a performer. There is no score to follow and no fixed sequence to repeat. It’s the movement of the water that continuously generates the sound. ‘For Boursier-Mougenot, this interest in movement goes back to his early relationship with music. ‘I was fascinated by the movement, by the gesture, by the action, to produce sound,’ he notes. ‘The only message I want to convey is an invitation to inhabit a space that I have designed especially for them,’says Boursier-Mougenot.
The city remains audible around the pools. Traffic, voices, birds, footsteps, wind, and rain mingle with the sound of porcelain, so the installation never sounds the same twice. The weather becomes part of it too, with a sudden shower adding its own rhythm to the bowls moving across the water. The artist also sees chance as a recurring force in his wider practice. ‘Many of my works have been made by coincidence,’he shares during the preview. ‘It’s crazy. I have many, many stories to tell.’ In Athens, clinamen puts that idea to a new test, allowing an outdoor environment to introduce variables that previous presentations could largely control.

Pope Leo heads to France amid assisted dying, abuse debates

Pope Leo heads to France amid assisted dying, abuse debates
First papal state visit to country in 18 years comes as church confronts contentious issues.
Pope Leo XIV is heading to France for the first official papal visit to the country in 18 years.
The four-day visit begins in Paris on Friday, where Leo will meet President Emmanuel Macron at the Elysee Palace before addressing French officials and civil society.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What has Pope Leo warned about AI – and why that’s significant
- list 2 of 4Pope warns people smugglers they face God’s wrath
- list 3 of 4Pope says AI must be ‘disarmed’ to prevent domination, exclusion, and death
- list 4 of 4Is the Vatican standing up to Trump?
The first American pope will carry a message centred on human dignity as the Catholic Church in France confronts a newly enacted assisted dying law and the lasting fallout from clerical sexual abuse.
After meeting the president, Leo will deliver an address at UNESCO, attend a service at Notre-Dame Cathedral and join a youth vigil at the Stade de France.
Cardinal Jean-Marc Aveline, head of the French bishops’ conference, said “the defence of the dignity of human life” would be at the heart of Leo’s message.
France enacted a law in August establishing a right to assisted dying under specified conditions for adults suffering from serious and incurable illnesses. The measure had faced strong opposition from the Catholic Church, which teaches that human life should be protected from conception until natural death.
However, Martin Dumont, secretary-general of a religion research institute in France, told the AFP news agency that he would be “very surprised” if the pope adopted a confrontational stance on the issue.
Leo is expected to meet seven survivors of clerical sexual abuse in Lourdes on Sunday. A landmark independent inquiry published in 2021 estimated that about 330,000 people had been abused as minors by clergy or other people associated with the French Catholic Church over seven decades.
Retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told the Reuters news agency that the scandals had “wounded the church deeply and damaged its credibility”.
Survivors have continued to press church leaders for greater accountability despite compensation and safeguarding measures introduced in recent years.
Leo’s visit comes as the Catholic Church seeks to make its voice heard in a country with a deeply rooted tradition of secularism and declining church influence over public policy.
But his message will extend beyond France’s domestic debates. The pope is also due to visit a Paris centre supporting migrants, speak on artificial intelligence and conclude his trip in Metz with a meeting focused on Europe’s role in promoting peace and unity.

Israeli settlers deploy drones to abuse West Bank's Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:40:42 UTC
16:40:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli settlers are using drones to forcibly change Palestinian life in the occupied West Bank
Rabie Abu Na’im vividly remembers the sound of the drone that Israeli settlers would launch daily over the Al-Khalayel Bedouin community east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank to monitor residents and eventually drive them out.
This community, which settlers succeeded in emptying following a relentless wave of attacks, was one of the areas where drones played a critical role in terrorising the Palestinian population and forcing them to flee.
Since the election of the Israeli government in 2022, settlers have employed various tactics in their declared campaign to seize land in the occupied West Bank, expand settlements, and densely establish outposts between Palestinian villages and towns to redraw territorial boundaries.
Among these tactics, drones have emerged as a key tool for the round-the-clock surveillance, intimidation, and expulsion of Palestinians, particularly herders, whom the drones pursue and force to retreat while they graze their livestock.
Recent reports indicate that Israeli settlement councils have also begun distributing drones to settlers for use in photography, reconnaissance, and monitoring the areas surrounding settlement outposts.
Abu Na’im told The New Arab that drones played a major role in the forced displacement of his community; over three years, Israeli settlers launched them to track residents' movements, with the drones becoming increasingly aggressive over time.
"When herders left their homes in the morning, the drones would pursue and shadow them; if they approached certain areas, settlers would gather to attack and drive them away. Eventually, the drones began monitoring residents inside their homes around the clock, and there was nothing anyone could do to stop them," he added.
Later, Israeli settlers began equipping drones with audio devices that broadcast insults and threats to Palestinians, warning them to leave the area. Women and children were terrified, and gradually residents left, coinciding with fierce physical assaults that injured many of them.
Drones were also frequently used to drop tear gas canisters on the communities targeted by settlers.
"A few days ago, when a boy and a young man were killed in Al-Mughayyir, drones played a major role. The raid began when a drone tracked a flock of sheep; settlers then attacked the site to steal the livestock under the protection of the Israeli army, which killed the two victims in cold blood during the incident," Rabie remarked.
Killer-bots in the sky
Drones can monitor vast areas, track the movement of people and livestock, and film Palestinian farmers and herders without settlers needing to approach them. Consequently, access to the land becomes exposed and monitored even before any direct confrontation occurs.
The situation is particularly dangerous for herding communities which rely on daily movement between their homes, grazing grounds, and water sources; areas that are increasingly encroached upon by rapidly expanding settlement outposts.
When the movements of herders are monitored from the air, settlers can pinpoint the location of livestock, determine when residents leave their homes and which areas they utilize, and then intervene to block their access to those lands.
Notably, this use of technology predates the recent distribution of equipment by years. Israeli funding had previously been revealed for equipping settlement outposts with gear, including drones, as part of a security package designed to monitor the surrounding areas.
However, Palestinians are convinced that its role goes far beyond that, as it has played a part in the killing of several boys and young men.
Mohammed Abu Siyam, a shepherd from the village of Mikhmas, east of Ramallah, recounted to TNA that Israeli settlers attacked the village last February and stole a herd of livestock; some Palestinians confronted them.
His son, Nasrallah, 19, was among the group and suggested climbing the mountain peak to locate the stolen herd. At that moment, the settlers launched a drone to track them.
“Using the drone, the settlers monitored my son and the others. An armed group of them lay in wait for the youths' arrival and immediately opened fire, killing Nasrallah and wounding other young men," he added.
To this day, the drone shadows Mohammed while he grazes his sheep, as if counting his livestock and inspecting everything with him, he said.
Off-limits to Palestinians
For Palestinian residents, the drone's very presence in the sky alters people's behavior.
A shepherd aware that his movements are being watched might hesitate to approach his own land; a farmer might avoid a specific area; and a family might reconsider staying in a place where every movement is subject to surveillance.
Imad Al-Batta, from the village of Hajjah near Qalqilya, told TNA that drones are violating the privacy of homes by flying extremely close to them, so close that families feel the devices might fly right through their windows.
"We are under surveillance by settlers' drones around the clock; privacy is non-existent, and everyone feels constantly threatened. These drones have also guided several settler attacks on the village, one of which resulted in the death of a young man and the injury of five others just days ago," he explained.
Yet, while drones are distributed to Israeli settlers and used without any oversight, Palestinians are prohibited from owning them even for purely professional purposes.
The Israeli army has arrested numerous Palestinian photojournalists over the past three years on the grounds of possessing a drone for photography.
Photojournalist Abdul Rahman Hassan, from Bethlehem, told TNA that soldiers raided his home on 19 August, arrested him, and transported him to a nearby detention center.
He remained handcuffed there for hours before an Israeli police vehicle transferred him to another detention center in the "Beitar Illit" settlement, where he was interrogated for hours regarding his possession of a drone.
"I told them I had always used it without anyone stopping me, but the interrogator informed me of a military order in place since 2017 prohibiting Palestinians from possessing such devices”.
They then made him sign documents acknowledging possession of a drone, and threatened that if he was found with a drone again, he would face imprisonment for many years.
In dozens of instances, the Israeli army has raided toy shops across various occupied West Bank cities, confiscating all drones even those intended as toys for children, and warning shop owners against selling them under threat of arrest.
A tool for forced displacement
Last May, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented the use of drones by Israeli settlers to pursue residents of the Arab al-Mleihat community in the Al-Ma’arajat area.
This occurred amidst a series of attacks and violations that ultimately resulted in the community being emptied of its residents.
Salah al-Khawaja, the Central Region official for the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission, told TNA that the use of drones by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank follows two simultaneous tracks: one linked to the Israeli army, and the other to settlers, settler organisations, and settlement outposts.
He explained that the Israeli army conducts campaigns in Palestinian areas to confiscate drones, citing the pretext that they are used to monitor settler attacks and violations against Palestinians, and this occurs alongside the provision of advanced drones to settler organisations and outposts, ostensibly to ensure "security" for the settlers.
“Potential uses for these drones include filming Palestinian vehicles and recording their license plates, which allows for tracking the owners and taking legal action against them," he said.
The use of drones against Bedouin communities can extend beyond monitoring movements to surveilling residents' private lives, including filming their homes and enclosed areas within the communities.
"These practices can create a state of constant pressure on Palestinian families, particularly in Bedouin communities, leading them to feel targeted and unsafe in their own localities; given the nature and culture of Palestinian society, this can become an additional factor driving families to leave the areas where they live," he concluded.

Founding anniversary: A lens on future of our mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:34:29 UTC
16:34:29 KST

25 September: Founding Anniversary through the Lens of the Future: Innovative Vision for the Mission of Our Organization in a Changing World
Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed
Fifty-seven years have passed since the founding of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), whose journey began in Rabat, Kingdom of Morocco, on 12 Rajab 1389 AH, corresponding to Sept. 25, 1969, under the name “Organization of the Islamic Conference.”
This anniversary, which is dear to the heart of every Muslim, coincides with my assumption of office as Secretary General of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation a few weeks ago. This convergence carries a profound symbolic meaning that heightens my sense of the magnitude of the trust placed in me and the determination to fulfil the Organization’s mission and responsibility in which the peoples of our Ummah pin their hopes.
On this anniversary we recall the birth of the OIC when the arson attack on the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque shook the conscience of the Muslim Ummah and awakened its will to close its ranks and safeguard its holy sites. Our Organization has, by the Grace of Allah, and through the resolve of its founders, succeeded in keeping the flame of the Palestinian cause alight and upholding its terms of reference: to safeguard the rights of the Palestinian people and support them in achieving an independent and sovereign State within the borders of 4 June 1967, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital.
While this issue remains at the core of the OIC’s mission, the horizons of its collective responsibility have expanded to include, alongside political action, areas of economic, cultural, social and scientific cooperation.
Anyone who looks back at the history of the OIC, which began as an idea and grew through the efforts of its founders and the support of its Member States, will observe that the Organization has remained faithful to its highest purpose: deepening Islamic solidarity and maintaining a unified position on the various issues of the Muslim world, guided by its Charter, principles and objectives, relying on the justness of its demands, standing on the side of truth and equality, and its commitment to understanding and respecting others. This approach has been embodied through accomplishments recorded in many fields – supporting development, reinforcing social solidarity, fighting poverty, combating exclusion and marginalization, and promoting family values. In this context, the OIC played a pivotal role in responding to humanitarian needs, supporting dignified livelihoods for refugees and displaced persons in many parts of the Muslim world and beyond. It followed up on the affairs of Muslim communities in non-Member States and contributed to confronting the wave of extremism and radicalism that has swept through many of our countries.
In confronting Islamophobia, the OIC has established its presence as an active interlocutor in Western circles and countries. It has earned recognition for the justness of its demands, which, on many occasions, has been demonstrated in action taken in response to the Organization’s demands to create an environment more conducive to coexistence and the rejection of hatred.
For decades, these issues have given the OIC a distinctive position, making it the exclusive body and the ideal forum for coming together, addressing crises and seeking appropriate solutions within the shared identity derived from the noble teachings of Islam and its values founded on moderation.
This understanding of the OIC’s historic role deepens my awareness of the weight of the responsibility I now carry. It propels me to articulate a new vision for the Organization that will respond to the demands of its role in confronting global and regional challenges while holding fast to its sound principles and authentic points of reference. Through them, the OIC can put its capabilities and expertise to work for the good and benefit of the Muslim Ummah and foster solidarity among its Member States.
The OIC today faces a very difficult test amid international polarizations aggravated by deep regional tensions, growing economic complexities that accumulate year after year, and acute humanitarian and environmental crises whose price is paid by poorer countries and by the most vulnerable and fragile groups. The burdens of this responsibility are made greater still by the rapid and unprecedented transformations taking place around the world, as new technologies enter our daily lives and their attendant interconnected challenges that are difficult to confront by the major powers, not to talk of the Muslim world, which has been weighed down by accumulated crises that drain its resources and limit its ability to keep pace with these transformations.
The Organization of Islamic Cooperation, comprising 57 countries across four continents and representing nearly 2 billion Muslims, including Muslim communities in non-Member States, finds itself obliged to keep pace with the accelerating global transformations unfolding today. It does so carrying accumulated historical legacies that cannot be overlooked: civil wars, political fragility, unrest and weak economic structures.
The OIC, by the Grace of Allah, has the institutional, human and material wherewithal to take on this responsibility. For its work, it relies on forty-four entities operating under its umbrella, including subsidiary, affiliated, specialized and independent organizations, as well as the eight offices of the General Secretariat in New York, Geneva, Brussels, Ramallah, Baghdad, Mogadishu, Niamey and Kabul. This institutional network provides the OIC with many arms, enhancing its presence in all parts of the world. Being an overarching framework, and given the wealth of the OIC’s Member States and their vast human potential, the network constitutes a basis for confidence in the Organization’s ability to keep pace with new developments. We must, in turn, dispel the doubts in its effectiveness created by the growing crises.
Against this backdrop, the objective I aspire to realize during the next five years is defined. I seek to build a leading and influential organization that is leading in performance, grounded in efficiency, governance, transparency, innovation and initiatives, such that it can contribute in finding solutions rather than merely following events. The Organization will be influential in serving the Member States, defending their causes, enhancing their international presence and building effective partnerships that contribute to consolidating security, peace and development.
Today, we are called upon to press ahead with the implementation of the plans and directives of the Member States and their urgent demand for the reform of the Organization, building on its past successes in many fields and its proven record on several occasions. The Palestinian cause and the rights of the Palestinian people will remain one of the central pillars around which the Organization’s work will revolve. Islamophobia and hate speech, proactive diplomacy and conflict mediation, support for digital and technological transformation, leveraging the Artificial Intelligence revolution, as well as combating poverty and deprivation will also be at the top of the OIC’s priorities in the coming years.
At the core of these priorities lies investment in human capital as the most effective entry point to building a more prosperous future. This will be done by paying due attention to education, scientific research, innovation, the knowledge economy and by expanding opportunities for the youth and women to contribute to development, thereby transforming the human weight of the Muslim world to productive and influential force.
Related to this is the economic and development dimension because our collective benefit from the human, natural and financial potential of our countries is below the desired level. Hence, in consultation with Member States, we shall work to convene an OIC economic summit to articulate a practical vision for enhancing integration, trade, intra-OIC investments, and public-private sector partnerships, thereby transforming the abundant resources of our countries into opportunities that support growth and sustainable development and bring direct benefit to our peoples.
Achieving these priorities and translating the reform into practical reality requires the solidarity of Member States under the OIC umbrella. It requires adherence to the Organization’s principles and fundamental tenets, and exemplifying the spirit of unity in a common vision and coordinated positions that enhance the clout of the Islamic group at international forums and give it an audible and influential voice.
In order to support this collective action and expand its international horizons, for my part, I commit to deploying the experiences I have accumulated through a range of responsibilities in my country, at the United Nations and elsewhere to strengthen international partnerships and foster integration with counterpart organizations at the regional and global levels, through a range of diplomatic and developmental mechanisms.
This commitment stems from my firm belief that openness to others, exchange of expertise and prioritization of dialogue are essential factors for success that is not confined to the geographical boundaries of the Muslim world, but which extends beyond them to become a model of global success that can be built upon and leveraged. Such a model can demonstrate to the world that the Muslim world possesses the weight and strength needed to make a distinctive contribution to sustainable development at the global level.
There is no doubt that this commitment requires a political and media discourse that highlights the Organization’s work and message and conveys the true image of Muslims and the Muslim world, which has long faced defamation campaigns and incitement to hatred.
I cannot fail to express my gratitude to the leaders of the OIC Member States for the trust and support they have bestowed upon me, and I look forward to their further support in carrying this trust. I am determined to build on the achievements of our Organization, mobilize its energies, in loyalty to a journey spanning decades full of achievements and lessons from challenges. The greatness of a journey does not only lie in achievements recorded, but also in the ability to overcome obstacles, seize opportunities and renew determination, so that we can create for our Ummah a befitting future in a world that is being reshaped.
Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed is the secretary-general of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.

‘We’ll Meet in the Sukkah’  brings people together for face-to-face dialogue across Israeli society

The Safeguarding Our Shared Home (Shomrim al HaBayit Hameshutaf) organization is continuing its annual initiative to bring Israelis of different backgrounds and opinions under the shared s’chach of sukkahs across Israel for the fourth year in a row.
The initiative, "We'll Meet in the Sukkah," is dedicated to Moshe Ochion and his son Eliad, both of whom were murdered in the October 7 attack in Ofakim just one day after taking part in the initiative that year.
The organization invites people and groups across the country to register their sukkahs to host guests or visit other sukkahs for face-to-face dialogue and exposure to a variety of opinions, worldviews, and demographics.
"We are entering a period where we will naturally hear much more about what divides us," Eyal Gur, one of the leaders of Safeguarding Our Shared Home, said.
"Election campaigns are built on disagreement and the presentation of differing worldviews - that is part of democracy. Yet, alongside political discord, it is crucial that we do not lose the ability to speak with one another."
Face-to-face disagreement important as elections approach, Gur says
Gur explained that the goal of the "We'll Meet in the Sukkah" initiative is not to make people agree, but to allow for conversation even through disagreement.
"The Sukkah offers us a chance to step away from screens and headlines for a moment, to meet face-to-face with someone who thinks differently than we do, to listen to them, and to share our own views," he said.
"I believe this ability is more important than ever, especially as we approach the elections."
Among the sukkahs taking part in the initiative is one dedicated to Haymanot Kasau, who went missing almost three years ago. Her family will be present in the sukkah throughout the holiday.

KKL-JNF unveils archival photos showcasing Sukkot celebrations in honor of the holiday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:32:50 UTC
16:32:50 KST

In honor of the upcoming Sukkot holiday, the Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) Photo Archive on Thursday released a series of four previously unseen photographs of Israelis celebrating Sukkot across the country in the 1950s and 1960s.
The first image, from Sukkot 1959 (5720), shows a Hassidic Jew inside a Jerusalem sukkah holding the Four Species, performing the mitzvah of lulav. The sukkah walls surrounding him, according to KKL-JNF, are adorned with handmade paper chains and ornaments.
In contrast to the calm, prayerful tone of the Jerusalem sukkah picture, the next image (seen at the top of this page), from 1963, shows a large celebration in the northern town of Horshat Tal, with crowds of people watching a dance performance in honor of the harvest holiday.
Another picture, also from Jerusalem, shows children in 1964 participating in the city's "Jerusalem Flag" ceremony during Chol HaMoed. They are dressed in white, marching through a park holding the Four Species, flowers, flags, and other religious paraphernalia.
Jerusalem's annual Four Species market event
The final photograph was taken at Jerusalem's Four Species market - an event that still occurs annually in Israel's capital - in 1967, just months after the Six-Day War and reunification of Jerusalem. A child is seen holding an etrog, surrounded by countless tables piled high with lulavs, myrtle branches, and etrogs.
“These photographs allow us to encounter Sukkot once again as it was celebrated in Israel decades ago, and as it is still celebrated today: in the family sukkah, at the Jerusalem market and at large outdoor gatherings," said Efrat Sinai, Director of Archives at KKL-JNF.
"They show how tradition, Zionist education, agriculture and community came together to create the holiday's unique Israeli character. Beyond their historical value, these are vibrant, deeply human moments that remind us how much we have changed, and how the customs of the holiday continue to connect generations.”

In the days leading up to the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, the IDF is again confronting questions over the failures that preceded the attack, its relations with Israel Police, and the growing burden on reserve soldiers, as new findings and disputes emerged on Thursday.
In a few days, Israel will mark the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, an event in which the IDF failed in its primary mission of protecting the State of Israel.
Three years later, the investigation into the fighting at the Paga outpost, which was supposed to protect Kibbutz Be'eri, was released to the public on Thursday.
A total of 133 civilians, members of the kibbutz security team, police officers, and soldiers were murdered or killed in Kibbutz Be'eri on October 7. Eighteen soldiers were killed at the Paga outpost and in the sectors under its responsibility. Another 25 soldiers were wounded. Two soldiers were abducted to Gaza after they were killed.
The investigation determined that the IDF failed in the battle at the Paga outpost. The serious shortcomings within the Golani Brigade included the preparation of the troops for their mission. Operational complacency meant that troops were preparing for public disturbances rather than a raid. The failure went so far that some positions did not have machine guns or MAG machine guns.
It took the IDF three years to release the investigation, which reflects the severity of the failure. The lesson from what happened in southern Israel before October 7 is that the IDF operated like a neighborhood soccer team, without rules or procedures, in a manner that was essentially amateurish.
No sufficiently decisive command structure could recognize what was happening across the border and put the IDF on a war footing or prepare it for a raid.
Following the October 7 massacre, the IDF lost the public's trust, and it can fairly be said that it did so with good reason. Since then, it has tried to rebuild itself both operationally and in terms of its public image.
IDF criticizes police for claiming to have found tunnels
Israel Police announced on Thursday that two tunnel shafts had been uncovered in the Jaljulia area, near the seam line opposite Kfar Saba.
The IDF responded by attacking the police account, denying the announcement and arguing that the shafts were not tunnels and were not close to the seam line.
IDF Spokesperson Brig.-Gen. Effie Defrin criticized the police and, in an unusual move, wrote: "During the operation, two shafts approximately 12 meters deep were located. Weapons were found near the shafts, including an M16 rifle, a hunting rifle, a handgun, and ammunition, which were confiscated by the troops.
"Contrary to official and irresponsible statements issued on the matter, after the shafts were investigated, the existence of a tunnel route in the shafts was ruled out, and it was also determined that the shaft was not close to the seam area."
Israel Police's Judea and Samaria District commander, Dep.-Ch. Moshe Pinchi, directly confronted Defrin, effectively portraying the IDF spokesperson as a liar.
"The report is correct and sticks to the facts. You can't bury your head in the sand. I don't work for the IDF spokesperson. After October 7, you can't simply not report it," Pinchi said.
Tensions between the IDF and Israel Police are not new, particularly in the West Bank. IDF officers have repeatedly said that the police operate politically rather than operationally. Publicly, however, the IDF's senior command generally treats the police and the Judea and Samaria District with respect.
The IDF's senior command learned about the alleged tunnel near Jaljulia following an announcement by Kfar Saba Mayor Rafi Saar.
Deputy IDF Chief of Staff Maj.-Gen. Tamir Yadai received the mayor's message on his phone, like other Kfar Saba residents, saying that a tunnel had been uncovered meters from the city on the Palestinian side. Within minutes, panic spread among residents of the Sharon region, and with considerable justification.
The IDF was furious with the police command.
Police intelligence provided the information about the shafts. An operation involving the IDF, Israel Police, and Border Police was subsequently carried out. The commander of the Ephraim Brigade was at the scene when the two shafts were discovered. Four suspects were arrested at the site, and several firearms and other weapons were seized.
Under standard procedure, the Ephraim Brigade commander summoned troops from the Yahalom special engineering unit.
The complexity of the situation must be understood. Investigating a tunnel is a complicated and dangerous process. Robotic systems are first sent inside. Only after it is established that the tunnel is not booby-trapped, contains no terrorists, and poses no danger of collapse can engineering troops enter and inspect its interior.
However, before the first stage began and before the Yahalom troops prepared at the scene, police issued their announcement about tunnels near the seam line.
The police announcement was inaccurate. The shafts were more akin to pits and did not constitute an infiltration route or a passage connecting buildings.
Police disclose information about IDF terror attack victim
In fact, IDF anger toward the police began hours earlier, when the police spokesperson issued a statement about the attack at the Maccabim checkpoint and disclosed that the person wounded was an IDF soldier, before the soldier's family had been notified.
"They simply went too far in the police. They violated every procedure and every standard of professional ethics. They rush to tell the public without basic responsibility," a senior IDF officer said regarding the two incidents.
The IDF is currently in a sensitive position. On the one hand, the situation in the West Bank requires the military to flood the area with troops. That is why the headquarters of the 98th Division was sent to the West Bank.
Egoz Unit troops have already been transferred there, and additional units are expected to arrive in the coming days.
But the IDF's main problem is its shortage of soldiers and money. The political leadership's lack of responsibility has forced the IDF to prevent soldiers from taking leave ahead of their discharge and to take away their annual vacation days almost casually.
Reservists are being required to serve another round of reserve duty, in direct contradiction to remarks by Deputy Chief of Staff Yadai about seven months ago that reservists would serve a maximum of 70 reserve-duty days in 2026.
In practice, the deputy chief of staff's promise has not been borne out on the ground. Most reserve units have already exceeded 100 days of reserve duty this year, and the year is not yet over.
IDF unable to assertively confront political leadership with problems
The central problem facing the IDF General Staff is that it does not know how to "bang on the table" and confront Israel's political leadership with the complex reality.
The same problem existed exactly three years ago, on the eve of the October 7 massacre, when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu preferred to put on rose-colored glasses and sleep soundly at night. The military leadership did not sound the alarm loudly enough.
The 2026 General Staff should have been expected to be more assertive toward the political leadership than the 2023 General Staff, presenting the real challenges rather than attempting to smooth over reality according to the wishes of the political leadership.
Otherwise, it will not end with a dispute with the police. Israel could instead find itself surprised in one of its operational arenas, and that must not happen.

MDA medics finish building woman's sukkah for her after treating head injury
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:32:41 UTC
16:32:41 KST

A woman in her 60s was injured in Netanya after an iron pole fell and struck her in the head while she was building a sukkah, after which Magen David Adom medics who treated her decided to finish constructing it for her ahead of the Sukkot holiday.
The woman had begun building the sukkah beneath her home as part of preparations for the approaching holiday when an iron pole fell while the upper supports were being tied together and struck her head.
A family acquaintance who had been helping her with the construction called MDA's 101 emergency hotline, which dispatched rapid-response medics and an ambulance to the scene.
Rapid-response medics Nachman Levy and Netanel Peretz, MDA EMTs, senior EMT Ben-El Amira of MDA's motorcycle unit, and an ambulance team led by MDA EMT Shmuel Mami quickly examined the woman and provided initial medical treatment.
But their assistance did not end there.
"I was conscious when the MDA team arrived, and I told them exactly what had happened. While they were examining me and giving me medical treatment, they asked where the sukkah I had started building was," the woman recalled. "I was sure they were asking so they could understand which iron pole had hit me, but then I saw them continuing to build my sukkah."
Amira, a senior EMT with MDA-Hatzalah Sharon who was the first to arrive on a yellow emergency motorcycle, said the team decided to help once they determined that the woman's condition was stable.
"After the team and I examined her, provided medical treatment, and understood that the woman's condition was stable and that she did not require urgent evacuation to the hospital, we wanted to make her happy ahead of the holiday and build the sukkah she had not finished," he said.
The woman said she was deeply moved by the gesture.
"I have no words. This is a team of amazing people who arrived to perform one mitzvah, providing medical treatment, and performed another mitzvah by building the sukkah," she said. "I did not know how to thank them because I was so moved. You made me happy and helped me very much. I wish everyone a happy and safe holiday."
MDA issues safety guidelines ahead of Sukkot
MDA also issued safety guidelines for building and using sukkot ahead of the holiday.
Those building a sukkah in a yard should wear closed shoes and clear nearby vegetation where snakes or other dangerous reptiles could be hiding. Keep access routes to and from the sukkah clear of obstacles so occupants can leave quickly if necessary.
Position the sukkah at a safe distance from electrical installations and gas canisters, and do not use open flames near gas or electrical equipment during construction.
When building a sukkah on a high-rise balcony, take care to prevent heavy objects from falling and injuring passersby. Secure awnings, planters, wooden boards, roofing material, and other objects firmly.
Keep children away while sukkah walls are being erected so they are not struck by falling parts. Securely connect the walls to one another to prevent collapse, especially when they are made of wood or other rigid materials.
In case of injury, MDA advised calling 101 or using the "My MDA" application as quickly as possible, then following instructions from medics and paramedics at the emergency dispatch center until crews arrive.

‘Checkout’s super return, what’s up in ‘Widow’s Bay,’ Pacino's ‘Serpico’ makes a comeback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:32:10 UTC
16:32:10 KST

Sometimes a series is so consistently good that it doesn’t always get the praise it deserves, and that’s the case with 'Checkout' (Kupa Rashit), the supermarket sitcom on KAN 11 (also available on kan.org.il) and on Netflix.
Its sixth season about the travails and triumphs of the staff of the supermarket, Shefa Issachar, and its customers just started airing on KAN, and this episode has some of the funniest moments I have watched in a long, long time.
Much of the comedy in the season opener involves what Ramzi (Amir Shurush), the indefatigably upbeat employee, refers to as a “poetry slum” (he means “slam”) organized by Shira (Noa Koler), the ambitious and awkward manager, in which she takes part.
The show’s writers - who recently gave The Jerusalem Post a peek at what they have planned for this season, including the election-night episode - have been to a few pretentious poetry readings, it seems.
They have great fun with the culture clash of talentless avant-garde poets and the staff of the supermarket, who attend the “slum” at Ramzi’s urging - and he trades shifts with them, giving them the hours they want, so Shira won’t be all alone out there.
When Shira stands up to share her poetry, all the resentment that she has ever felt at her employees for ignoring and insulting her comes out and then some.
But my favorite moment was when Kochava (Keren Mor), the self-centered, lazy cashier, gives a dry, one-line put-down to a spoiled, insufferable poet who performs before Shira.
There’s also a plotline concerning Amnon (Dov Navon), a cheap, fussy customer, who takes on the last role in the world anyone would have expected of him – but it won’t be as funny if you know what it is, so no spoilers here. Let’s just say that the more things change, the more Amnon stays Amnon.
'Widow's Bay' keeps the horror horrible and comedy funny
The series 'Widow’s Bay' just won 14 Emmys, breaking the record for most wins for a comedy, but if you don’t have Apple TV+, you might not have heard of it. It’s a quirky hybrid of comedy and horror, and plays like a Stephen King novel meets 'Schitt’s Creek', with a little bit of Jaws thrown in.
The challenge in a series like this is to keep the horror horrible and the comedy funny, and 'Widow’s Bay' manages to do that, for the most part, although I like it best as a workplace comedy about the hapless mayor of a cursed town who just wants to do his job and keeps getting derailed by crazy supernatural stuff.
The series pulls that off because its lead actor Matthew Rhys is so good you might suspect he has gotten a bit of help from otherworldly powers.
Rhys gave one of the greatest performances in television history as Philip, the increasingly reluctant Soviet spy in Washington, in 'The Americans', where his character’s sarcasm and suppressed but inherent playfulness made him instantly relatable.
He has appeared in several other series since then, including 'The Beast in Me' with Claire Danes, where he played a vile businessman suspected of murder, but none of his roles since 'The Americans' has fit his skills as perfectly as 'Widow’s Bay.'
(If you haven’t seen 'The Americans' or want to rewatch it, it’s available on Disney+. I saw most of it a second time last year, and I enjoyed it even more than the first time. It’s right up there with 'The Sopranos,' 'The Wire,' and 'Mad Men' as one of the greatest series this golden age of television has produced.)
A haunted community in New England that residents can't leave
In 'Widow’s Bay,' he plays Tom Loftis, the befuddled mayor of a New England island community known for its ghost stories and myths, and he wants to turn it into a tourist destination. The twist, of course, is that the ghost stories are all true.
The pilot opens with him anxiously waiting for a visitor to arrive by ferry, a New York Times writer he hopes will crown 'Widow’s Bay' the next Martha’s Vineyard. But only the night before, a fog rolled in over the bay, which in most places would be inconvenient, but which here means that it rolls over certain people and puts them in a kind of coma, from which they awaken as murderous zombies.
The island has a few other quirks. Not only is there no cellphone reception, but there are frequent power outages. Most people who spend the night in the Captain’s Suite at the inn go insane because they see visions of evil clowns and that kind of thing.
And those who were born on the island - Loftis wasn’t - die when they leave.
But it’s also a sitcom that might remind you of 'Checkout,' and Loftis has his hands full managing his staff, who are incompetent or just weird.
There are also moments where, like in Jaws, people are telling the mayor to shut the town down because of the danger from the spirit world, just as tourists are arriving on a packed ferry.
This genre mix doesn’t always work smoothly.
Remember 'BrainDead,' the political comedy by Michelle and Robert King, the creators of 'The Good Wife,' which mixed a plotline about aliens invading the brains of Washingtonians and getting their cues from songs by The Cars, with a satire on political corruption? It sounds better than it was, and it didn’t last very long.
'Widow’s Bay,' from its first season, seems likely to have more staying power, largely because Rhys can sell the sillier aspects of the series.
'Serpico,' true story of a NYPD officer who blew the whistle on corruption
And speaking of great actors, Al Pacino starred in Serpico (1973), which just became available to stream on Netflix. It’s based on the true story of a New York cop who blew the whistle on corruption at every level of the police force.
Directed by Sidney Lumet, the movie isn’t really a great film, and almost everyone who sees it knows how it ends.
But Pacino gives an incredible, riveting performance, and without this shaggy, glowering star at its center, no one would be watching it. He shows the stubbornness that drives whistleblowers and what they sacrifice as they ignore and push away loved ones and feel contempt for anyone who urges them to compromise.
Pacino convinces you that Serpico is so deeply wounded by the major and petty corruption all around him that he would pay any price - even give his life - to see the wrongdoers brought to justice, and he nearly does.
Another interesting dimension of the film is watching this working-class guy move to Manhattan and discover a new world as he begins dressing like a hippie for his undercover work.
The cast features a who’s who of 1970s American character actors, including John Randolph, Tony Roberts, and M. Emmet Walsh, but it’s really a one-man show.
Pacino lost the Best Actor Oscar that year to Jack Lemmon for his role in the far more dated 'Save the Tiger.' The other also-rans were Robert Redford for The Sting, Jack Nicholson for The Last Detail, and Marlon Brando for Last Tango in Paris. They made some pretty good movies in the 1970s.

Light Through the Wall: Indian House Interiors Shaped by Brick Jali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

A brick façade does more than define the façade of a house. When designed as a porous screen, it becomes an intermediary between inside and outside, shaping the atmosphere and environmental conditions of the spaces behind it. Across contemporary Indian residential architecture, brick jali — a perforated or lattice brick screen — has been reinterpreted with a contemporary sensibility, drawing on vernacular architectural elements.
Porous brick envelopes mediate light, air, heat, and views. Carefully arranged openings allow sunlight to penetrate the interior in a softened, dappled manner, creating a constantly changing rhythm of light and shadow. At the same time, the screens temper solar exposure and heat gain while allowing air to move through the house. In some houses, porous brickwork works together with courtyards, voids, staircases, and other passive strategies to support natural ventilation. In some houses, perforated bricks mediate between bedrooms, an adjacent terrace, and exterior space, embracing the sanctuary of intimate moments.

Global crude steel production fell 1.2 percent from a year earlier to 144.2 million tons in August.

The U.S. produced an estimated 7.3 million tons of crude steel in August, up 3 percent from a year earlier, while Japan’s output rose 0.4 percent to 6.7 million tons. Russia’s production was estimated at 5.5 million tons, down 0.3 percent, while South Korea produced 5.4 million tons, up 2.6 percent.
Global crude steel production totaled 1.23 billion tons in the first eight months of the year, down 0.7 percent compared with the same period last year.
During the January-August period, China’s steel output declined 3.1 percent year-on-year to 651.9 million tons, while India’s production increased 6 percent to 115.9 million tons.
In the same period, U.S. crude steel production rose an estimated 5.5 percent to 57.5 million tons. Japan produced 54 million tons, down 0.2 percent, while Russia’s output fell 5.1 percent to 43.8 million tons. South Korea increased production by 2.8 percent to 42.8 million tons.

Türkiye ranked as Europe’s sixth-largest auto market in the first eight months of 2026, with 564,241 vehicle sales, according to data released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).
Europe-wide new car sales rose 5.8 percent year-on-year during the January-August period to 9.19 million units.
Despite remaining one of Europe’s largest automotive markets, Türkiye diverged from the broader regional trend. The country’s passenger market contracted 13.78 percent from a year earlier, making it the worst-performing market among Europe’s 10 largest automobile markets in terms of sales growth.
Türkiye also became Europe’s sixth-largest market for fully electric vehicles (EV), with sales totaling 105,255 units in the first eight months of the year. Electric vehicles accounted for approximately 18.7 percent of all passenger car sales in the country during the period.

Germany remained Europe’s largest automobile market with 1.97 million vehicle sales, followed by the U.K. with 1.39 million units, Italy with 1.13 million, France with 1.08 million and Spain with 818,000 units.
Germany also led Europe’s EV market with 515,545 sales, followed by the U.K. with 355,748, France with 322,099, Belgium with 108,879 and Denmark with 106,265 units.
Türkiye ranked sixth with 105,255 fully electric vehicle sales.

Trump’s new Middle East has one missing piece: Palestine

Migrants at Greek ‘model’ camp say conditions have pushed some to contemplate suicide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:14:26 UTC
16:14:26 KST

A migrant camp championed by Greece's conservative government as a “model” for Europe has been rocked by repeated protests, with asylum seekers describing conditions so desperate that some say they are contemplating suicide.
At the EU-funded Sintiki camp near Greece's border with Bulgaria, police have repeatedly clashed with incarcerated migrants trying to break out after months in detention.
In an open letter last month, some of the nearly 400 Egyptian and Bangladeshi migrants held there said they were exhausted, barely getting enough to eat, and forced to share four bathrooms.
"Many of us are contemplating suicide... we are crushed, physically, psychologically and ethically... please save us," they wrote.
AFP was unable to get access to the occupants of Sintiki.
'Time bombs'
For people from Bangladesh, the rate of acceptance for asylum applications is less than one percent, according to Greek migration ministry figures. The same goes for applications from Egypt and Pakistan.
Under the terms of the European Pact on Migration and Asylum, which came into force in June, people applying for refugee status are detained until their case has been examined. If their bid is rejected, they remain imprisoned until being sent back.
The migrants also asked for permission to work so they could support their families back home. "We have been jailed for over 12 months... people here are like time bombs," the letter read.
The unrest has taken a visible toll on the facility, with the camp now looking "bombarded", a senior police officer told AFP.
"Three of the four sectors of the facility were destroyed during the unrest", said Giannis Kounios, head of the police union in the Serres region. Damage to housing units has left many without shelter.
Community chief Spyros Leonidas of nearby village Promachonas said the location was not even fit for a camp.
"It's inside a ravine. In winter, the temperature reaches -10°C and 45°C in summer. A person cannot survive there, especially locked up for so many months," he said.
More than 50 migrants were arrested after two recent uprisings and later sent to prison.
Lawyer Iraklis Pekiaridis, who represented migrants arrested following unrest in November, said some "preferred to go to prison rather than return to this camp".
Activists who have visited the site have described conditions as "wretched".
Despite the criticism, Migration Minister Thanos Plevris has described Sintiki as a model for curbing migration. The former hard-right lawmaker has suggested the camp's harsh conditions are meant to deter future arrivals.

World leaders raged against Israel in Gaza. Will their UNGA fury translate into action?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:08:22 UTC
16:08:22 KST

World leaders have taken an unusually critical tone against Israel from the podium of the ongoing UN General Assembly session in New York.
Some of them, such as Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, have never shied away from highlighting Israel’s atrocities against Palestinians from the global platform.
He told participants of the 81st session that Gaza had become the “most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our age” and that the world was confronting a genocidal mindset that cannot get enough of killing.
Concern over Gaza has also been voiced by leaders of countries closely aligned with Israel, alongside criticism of the international community’s failure to act.
For example, French President Emmanuel Macron said the credibility of the international community is at stake as it continues to remain “inactive” on the plight of Palestinians.
Jordan’s King Abdullah II called the forced displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank a “war crime”.
Meanwhile, UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said Israeli violence in the occupied West Bank is raising the “spectre of ethnic cleansing”.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to exterminate Gaza’s Palestinian population.
But observers question whether that fury expressed through passionate speeches at the UNGA can take the shape of concrete policy and check Israeli atrocities in Palestine.
After all, Israel has killed more than 1,400 Palestinians despite the so-called ceasefire of October 2025.
Nasir Qadri, an international law practitioner and critical legal scholar at Koc University in Istanbul, says the ongoing 81st session has been the “most explicit the UN General Assembly has produced in decades” in terms of highlighting Israeli crimes against Palestinians.
“Heads of state naming genocide, indicting war crimes, and demanding the occupation’s end from the UNGA podium… are not expressing positions. They are generating a legal and political record whose consequences extend well beyond the (UN) general debate,” he tells TRT World.
He says states that have publicly named genocide and cited binding International Court of Justice (ICJ) orders cannot subsequently authorise arms transfers or block accountability mechanisms without that conduct being legally characterised as complicity in an “internationally wrongful act”.
“International law has a long memory for what states said before they chose to look away,” he notes.
Qadri says the gap between the UN podium and the policy desk is “where Palestinian lives are lost”.
What distinguishes recent UNGA proceedings from the past speeches at the same forum is that world leaders are “no longer hedging the language”.
“The question is whether their foreign ministries will follow,” he says.
Legal duty versus theatrics
Qadri draws a sharp line between legal duty and theatrics when asked about the instruments – arms embargo, sanctions, international force – that can possibly force Israel to change its policy towards Palestinians.
The ICJ’s provisional measures already require states to prevent genocide and ensure humanitarian access, he insists.
“Every arms transfer to Israel since January 2024 has occurred against that obligation, making an arms embargo not a new policy option but an existing legal duty (that) states are actively breaching,” he says.
The European Union’s Association Agreement with Israel, worth about 42 billion euros a year, contains a human rights clause, commonly known as Article 2, that has gone unused “across three decades of documented violations”.
Invoking Article 2 of the association agreement needs “no Security Council vote” and no American consent – “only the political will that Macron’s UNGA speech suggests (the European Union) is approaching”.
In contrast, deployment of an international protection force carries the “highest rhetorical frequency” and the “lowest operational prospect”, thanks to repeated US vetoes in favour of Tel Aviv.
He says the back-to-back UNGA speeches, sharply critical of Israel, have produced a documented record of states naming genocide, while choosing inaction knowingly – something that will create the “evidentiary foundation” for accountability long after the UNGA ends.
Mustafa Yetim, professor of international relations at Eskisehir Osmangazi University, tells TRT World that he is sceptical of rhetoric that stays mostly on paper and never translates into action.
“The measures taken thus far have not produced a substantial impact on Israel’s ongoing disruptive, genocidal actions in the region, as many of them have remained largely cosmetic and symbolic,” he says.
If European governments genuinely intend to isolate Israel, they will have to reconsider not only official language, but also “institutional and material support”, including military, economic and political ties.
Europe adopted far more consequential measures against Russia after launching the war with Ukraine, he says.
That contrast raises questions about the consistency, sincerity, and credibility of European responses to different wars, he adds.
“The gap between rhetorical criticism and substantive policy measures remains a central challenge to the credibility of Europe’s stated commitment to international law,” Yetim says.
The cost of being on history’s right side
Matching UN language with actual policy would not be cost-free for world leaders with newfound sympathy for Palestinians.
Qadri says the price for some Arab governments may be the security architecture that keeps them in power.
Many of these countries have defence partnerships, intelligence-sharing arrangements and US security guarantees that, in his words, flow through bilateral relationships “requiring silence on Palestine” as an unspoken condition.
According to Yetim, Israel is unlikely to alter its policies without facing tangible consequences.
Arab states, therefore, should develop new mechanisms capable of imposing meaningful costs on Israel, he says.
Without those mechanisms, these governments remain “vulnerable to continued disruptive actions” by Israel, he adds.
In Qadri’s view, European governments will have to sacrifice the domestic coalitions that depend on not being seen to act against Israel.
For example, Germany’s constitutional guilt framework has functioned as a legal argument against conditioning arms exports to Israel, he says.
Abandoning it will require acknowledging that Holocaust memory “obligates protection of civilian life universally” rather than selectively.
For France, which has recognised Palestinian statehood, the sacrifice will be invoking the EU Association Agreement’s human rights clause, a step that will fracture the consensus insulating trade from accountability, he says.
Western governments draw the line between bluster and action “precisely where the cost becomes domestic” rather than rhetorical.
“The line holds because no Western government has yet been compelled (to act) by its own legal obligations, its own courts, or its own public (on) arms transfers to a state under ICJ genocide proceedings,” he says.

U.S. Air Force gets its first uncrewed ‘fighter’ aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:07:54 UTC
16:07:54 KST

- The U.S. Air Force received its first two Collaborative Combat Aircraft, Anduril's YFQ-44A and General Atomics' YFQ-42A, at Creech Air Force Base, Nevada.
- Air Combat Command will use the uncrewed jets to test how they operate alongside crewed fighters.
The U.S. Air Force has taken delivery of its first two Collaborative Combat Aircraft, uncrewed jets built to fly alongside fighter pilots, at Creech Air Force Base in Nevada, the Department of the Air Force said Sept. 24.
Anduril delivered its YFQ-44A Fury to the base’s Experimental Operations Unit in August, and General Atomics followed with its YFQ-42A, which the Air Force called Vengeance, last week. Air Force operators are now flying the Fury on their own, Anduril said. Air Combat Command will use both aircraft to work out how the drones should fight next to crewed fighters in contested airspace.
“Putting CCA in the hands of Airmen is how we build the operational future of this program,” said Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink. “Anduril’s Fury and General Atomics’ Vengeance deliveries show we can move at incredible speed, compete, and deliver cost-effective combat power to the force.”
“We’re thrilled to welcome Fury and Vengeance to the experimental operational unit,” said Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach. “Our Airmen are excited to see what Collaborative Combat Aircraft can do.”
Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCA, are semi-autonomous drones meant to carry weapons and sensors on missions with jets such as the F-35 and the future F-47. Each is expected to cost roughly a third as much as an F-35A. Anduril’s Fury is about half the size of an F-16.
Airmen at Creech have started testing how small teams can launch and recover the aircraft from scattered, austere locations, an approach the Air Force calls Agile Combat Employment. The service ran its second such exercise with CCA at Creech in July. The same month, a YFQ-44A fired an AIM-120 air-to-air missile in a live test.
The Air Force picked Anduril and General Atomics in 2024 to build prototypes for the first round of the program, known as Increment 1. The YFQ-42A first flew in August 2025 and the YFQ-44A in October 2025. General Atomics paused flight testing earlier this year after one of its aircraft crashed, then resumed.
On June 17, the Air Force ordered both designs into production, four months ahead of schedule, rather than choosing one. Production aircraft drop the “Y” prototype prefix and become the FQ-42A and FQ-44A. The service has said it wants more than 150 CCAs by the end of the decade and has asked for $1 billion in fiscal 2027 procurement funding, plus $1.4 billion for development. It has not disclosed contract values, unit prices or how orders will be split between the two companies.
Both firms are already building production jets. On July 28, Anduril rolled out the first FQ-44A built at its Arsenal-1 factory in Pickaway County, Ohio, and General Atomics said full-scale manufacturing of the FQ-42A was underway.
The Air Force is also planning a second round of the program, Increment 2, but has not released firm requirements. Northrop Grumman’s Talon Blue design has already received the YFQ-48A designation.

In West Bank art centre, Palestinian children paint hopes beyond checkpoints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:06:57 UTC
16:06:57 KST

In West Bank art centre, Palestinian children paint hopes beyond checkpoints
JERUSALEM, Sept 25 - On the outskirts of Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian woman has transformed her home into an art centre where children use drawing to process their experiences of settler violence and Israeli military raids.
Artist Sarah Abu Madi says she founded the centre - Rommana, meaning pomegranate in Arabic - in 2020 to give local children a place to express their feelings and talk about what they had experienced.
The centre's work has taken on greater urgency as violence by Israeli settlers has surged in recent years amid a major expansion of Jewish settlements in the territory.
"If a settler or a soldier does something, we ask: 'How did that make you feel? What did it make you think about? How does that affect you?'," Abu Madi said. "If there is a raid on a home, we ask: 'What did that make you feel? What do you think? How does that affect you? What do you wish there would be?'."
This week, the children were asked to sketch the things most important to them. Talia Sabah, 10, drew a picture of birds flying from a cage, saying it represented freedom.
"I feel freedom is the most important thing in life," Sabah said.
"I wish the military would stop being in our lives and there would be freedom, and we could do what we want with life."
'ART CREATES A SPACE THAT TELLS THEM: YOU CAN DREAM'
Israel captured the West Bank in 1967 and since then the territory has been under Israeli military occupation. Hundreds of thousands of Israeli Jewish settlers have moved to the territory, with settlement expansion accelerating rapidly under the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The United Nations and most countries regard the settlements as illegal under international law governing military occupations. Israel disputes that interpretation and says the territory's status is disputed.
The Rommana studio is located in Wadi Al-Samen, a Hebron quarter isolated from the rest of the city by six military checkpoints, according to Abu Madi. The area sees frequent military raids as well as incursions from nearby Israeli settlements and settler outposts.
Children spoke about encounters with Israeli settlers and soldiers with a familiarity unusual for children their age.
"My grandfather on my mother's side owns land in the mountains, but the settlers established a settlement there, and anyone who goes up to the mountain gets arrested," said Karam Sabah, 11.
When Rommana first opened, it consisted of a few carpets laid on the floor of an old storage room. Today, children sit around low plastic tables beside colourful murals they helped paint.
Their artwork has begun travelling beyond the West Bank, with one exhibition held in Canada and another planned in Mexico, Abu Madi said.
Around 600 children attend the centre, she said. Her goal is to expand the project so that all 3,000 children living in the neighbourhood can take part.
One of the paintings by the children showed three children sitting on the back of a winged horse, representing a dream of being able to fly freely, no longer trapped behind checkpoints.
"Art also creates a space that tells them: you can dream. You can imagine and build a reality different from the one you're living in," said Abu Madi. REUTERS

Europe uses subsidies, taxes and policy pauses to offset pain of high fuel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:06:47 UTC
16:06:47 KST

Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are driving governments across Europe to craft subsidies, taxes and policy revisions that might shield their economies, companies and increasingly aggrieved citizens from record gasoline and diesel prices.
Countries around the world have intervened to limit the economic impact of diminished energy supplies and soaring fuel prices since the start of the Iran war, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Seven of the 10 nations working most actively to contain the economic damage are in the European Union, the OECD said in a report published on Sept. 23.
Lithuania cut train ticket prices in half. Greece is taxing gambling more to fund public relief efforts. Italy delayed the scheduled demolition of coal-fired power plants and slashed the required paperwork for oil and natural gas projects. The Netherlands increased funding for a program that provides free energy-saving services in homes. Poland has proposed heavily taxing the record profits of certain fuel producers and sellers.
Before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, Russia’s war in Ukraine disrupted global energy supplies and caused turmoil in Europe. The EU imports nearly all of the oil it uses and 85 percent of its natural gas. Overall, imports supply 57 percent of the bloc’s energy needs, with much of its domestically produced energy coming from renewable and nuclear sources, according to the EU’s statistical office.
Europeans are becoming more incensed as pump prices surpass the equivalent of $12 a gallon in some countries. EU citizens are spending an extra 203 million euros ($231 million) a day just for diesel fuel, according to the European advocacy organization Transport & Environment.
“It’s a cruel irony that the U.S. is the least vulnerable to a crisis of its own making, while Europe’s economy again takes the hit,” Antony Froggatt, an analyst at the organization, said.
Some European governments are spending billions to help their countries weather the current energy crisis.
EU leaders in Brussels gave member nations temporary discretion to provide state aid to households and energy-intensive industries like agriculture, transportation and fishing. They also offered limited leeway from EU spending rules for investments that strengthen energy security and reduce the bloc’s long-term reliance on imported oil and natural gas.
“The pressures from higher energy prices and borrowing costs are biting for people and for businesses,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union address last week. “We need to double down on our affordable, homegrown, clean energy, be it renewables and nuclear, or biomethane and others” to “give us independence and drive down energy prices.”
Alongside national relief programs, EU nations have tapped their strategic reserves as part of an agreement by the International Energy Agency’s 32 member countries to make 400 million barrels of oil from their emergency stockpiles available to the market.
The EU has worked to reduce its reliance on energy imported from Russia through renewable energy production and converting systems and industries to run on electricity instead of fossil fuels.
Von der Leyen said greater electrification could reduce the EU’s annual bill for imported oil, gas and other fossil fuels by 260 billion euros ($296.6 billion) by 2040.
As the EU tried to wean itself off Russian energy, it became more dependent on the United States. Von der Leyen personally struck a deal with President Donald Trump last year that included a commitment for the EU to buy $750 billion worth of American energy over three years.
The Iran war has made the relationship both more vital and more complicated for the EU, which has increasingly turned to the U.S. for diesel. The support Trump expressed this week for banning diesel exports to drive down U.S. prices worries the bloc, which would have to find alternative sources of the fuel.
Brussels is lobbying Washington to drop the idea of suspending overseas diesel sales.
“We believe this is a bad idea,” European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill said on Sept. 24. “EU-U.S. cooperation in the field of energy is strong, stable and mutually beneficial. Any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides.”

UNGA speakers call for upholding UN-centered multilateralism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:03:45 CST
16:03:45 KST

by William M. Reilly
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Member states and regional organisations called for upholding multilateralism with the United Nations at the center on Thursday, the third day of the UN General Assembly's General Debate.
"Multilateralism is a crucial equalizer. It ensures that all have an equal voice under international law and an equal role in shaping our shared future," said Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa, adding that the UN Charter remains the common compass. "The UN has a sacred duty to save succeeding generations from this scourge of war."
European Council President Antonio Costa, speaking on behalf of the European Union, said multilateralism is not an ideal of the past, but rather the only realistic way to address the problems of today. "This is why our message is clear: we need multilateralism -- multilateralism that is strong, effective, representative and capable of delivering for people."
"We share the same planet and, ultimately, the same destiny," Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi said, adding that the UN must evolve to meet the moment. "We need more effective, more representative multilateral institutions that are closer to the people and more able to respond to the challenges of our time. We need cooperation. We need solidarity and we also need to demonstrate austerity within these institutions. But above all, we need to restore trust in our collective ability to change things."
"The UN must become an instrument for the future," said President Mohamed Irfaan Ali of Guyana, adding that the Security Council must embrace the "emerging multipolarity of our world, including permanent representation from Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean."
"The world has changed and multilateralism must change with it. We need a new and invigorated multilateralism, one equal to the turbulence of our age, sufficiently courageous to confront its trials, sufficiently imaginative to navigate its transformations, and sufficiently principled to defend the rule of international law," said Ali.
Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said that in face of the challenges in the world today, "the most effective response is a multilateral response, and the UN is, and should be, and should continue to be at the heart of the multilateral system." That is why, he said, Portugal looks to the future with renewed commitment to the mission of the UN.
Jose Manuel Restrepo, vice president of Colombia, speaking on behalf of President Abelardo de la Espriella, said that multilateralism should respect the sovereign equality of states while being capable of acting effectively.
"More trust between States needs to come about," said Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye. "We need a UN that is stronger, more representative and more effective. It needs a fairer, more inclusive and more effective multilateralism. Addressing our challenges requires bridges and not walls, dialogue and not confrontation, cooperation and not isolation."
Comorian President Azali Assoumani urged the next leadership of the UN to continue to "embody unity and the renewal of a more credible multilateralism," calling for particular attention to small island and vulnerable States, including making the right to development a pillar of multilateralism by facilitating access to sustainable funding and reducing inequalities globally.
Highlighting how the world's crisis particularly affects small island developing States, Fijian President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu urged the upholding of the UN Charter and its principles, including sovereign equality, territorial integrity and peaceful settlement of disputes. "We choose dialogue over coercion, human dignity over domination and cooperation over confrontation. Fiji calls for the peaceful settlement of conflicts wherever they occur."
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said that the United Nations must remain the centrepiece of the multilateral system, while regional institutions such as ASEAN are critical for countries to translate global principles into cooperation suited to local realities.
Charnvirakul also reiterated support for Security Council reform that "gives developing countries and underrepresented regions, particularly in the Global South, a greater role in decision making." ■

Asian Games | China sweep 3 golds in canoe sprint on Mid-Autumn Festival
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
