16:03:43 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese canoeists bagged three canoe sprint gold medals in as many events as they contested, celebrating the Mid-Autumn Festival on Friday at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
As canoe sprint entered its second medal day, the Chinese crew of Yu Shimeng, Yin Mengdie, Wang Nan and Shen Siyu took the lead from the start and steadily extended their advantage to win the women's kayak four 500m final in 1:33.784, 2.777 seconds ahead of Uzbekistan.
The crew has enjoyed a dominant season, winning all three World Cup races in the event and claiming the world title in August. The victory made it the first Chinese and Asian crew to win a world title in the women's K-4 event.
"We performed quite normally today. When we crossed the finish line, I felt a sense of relief. We have achieved our goal for the major competitions this year," Yu said.
She added that she had not been in her best form recently, but her teammates had continued to support one another.
Friday also marked China's Mid-Autumn Festival and Wang's birthday. The crew said they planned to prepare a small cake that night and sing a birthday song together. "There are so many happy occasions to celebrate," they said.
In the men's canoe single 500m final, China's Ji Bowen took the lead in the first half and accelerated after the halfway point to widen the gap. He crossed the finish line first in 1:47.338, beating his Uzbekistani rival by 0.607 seconds.
Ji, the Paris Olympic champion in the men's canoe double 500m, has also enjoyed a consistent season in the C-1 event, winning the Asian Championships and two World Cup titles before taking bronze at the World Championships in late August.
In the women's canoe double 500m final, China's Sun Mengya and Ma Yanan quickly moved into the lead and controlled the race in the second half, winning in 1:54.700, 1.719 seconds ahead of the Uzbekistani pair.
Sun previously partnered with Xu Shimiao to win this event at both Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024.
Now she and Ma renewed their Asian Games partnership following their victory at the 2018 Jakarta Asian Games to again grab the gold medal.
"After going through injuries, being able to return to the national team and compete again is an honor for me. I'm also very happy to partner with Mengya again and win gold," Ma said.
"For us, today's gold medal has a special meaning because it is the Mid-Autumn Festival. The best gift we can give is to dedicate this gold medal to our country and to everyone who has supported us," Sun said.
Four gold medals were contested in canoe sprint on Friday. South Korea won the men's kayak double 500m in 1:31.859, edging Japan by 0.317 seconds. ■

Breath test shows promise for identifying cancerous lung nodules: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:03:20 CST
16:03:20 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- A simple breath test could help doctors distinguish between cancerous and non-cancerous lung nodules, supporting earlier lung cancer diagnosis and negating the need for invasive testing, Australian-led research has found.
Researchers analyzed exhaled breath using two complementary technologies: an electronic nose, or eNose, which identifies patterns in breath chemicals, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, which detects specific volatile organic compounds in breath, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's Griffith University.
"Both breath-based approaches showed substantially better discrimination between malignant and benign nodules than models using standard clinical information alone," said Chamindie Punyadeera, a professor from Griffith's Institute for Biomedicine and Glycomics, corresponding author of the study published in MedComm.
Lung nodules are currently assessed through invasive procedures including CT-guided biopsies and bronchoscopy, while some patients may undergo surgery to investigate suspicious nodules, the statement said, noting that about 2.5 million new cases of lung cancer are diagnosed worldwide each year.
Co-author Zhang Xi from Griffith University said biopsying lung nodules could be technically challenging, particularly when lesions were small or difficult to access, and could cause complications such as a collapsed lung.
While the breath test showed promise in identifying nodules most likely to be malignant, it was not intended to replace biopsies, Zhang said, but could help doctors decide which patients needed invasive intervention most urgently.
"It is hoped it could also potentially reduce unnecessary procedures for patients with benign nodules by including the non-invasive test into routine clinical care," Zhang added. ■

Chinese copy of Russia’s Tor air defense system seen in Algerian colors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:02:06 UTC
16:02:06 KST

- Photos on Chinese social media show an HQ-17 air defense system in camouflage matching Algerian equipment, with Chinese sources saying it is for Algeria.
- Neither Algeria nor China's CASIC has confirmed a sale, and the quantity and delivery date remain unknown.
A Chinese HQ-17 short-range air defense system painted in camouflage matching Algerian military vehicles has appeared in photos shared widely on Weibo, with Chinese sources claiming the system is headed to Algeria.
The photos were highlighted by an OSINT defense account, which noted that the camouflage pattern matches the paint used on a large number of Chinese-made weapons already in Algerian service. The other sources acknowledged a small possibility that the vehicles belong to an export order for a country in Africa’s Sahel region that uses similar camouflage. It also said reports that Algeria operates the HQ-17 had circulated before.
The HQ-17 is a Chinese development of the Russian Tor-M1, a mobile system that detects, tracks and fires on low-flying threats from a single vehicle. China bought 27 Tor-M1 systems from Russia in two contracts in 1996 and 1999, then developed its own version. CASIC built it to shoot down aircraft, helicopters and drones as well as cruise missiles, guided bombs and air-to-surface missiles.
Each launch vehicle carries its own radar and eight missiles, so it can fight without support from other units, though it can also take targeting data from separate surveillance radars. The Chinese version uses an electronically scanned radar designed to resist jamming. The missile reaches Mach 3 and can engage targets between 1.5 km and 20 km (1 to 12 miles) away, at altitudes up to 10 km (33,000 feet).
The People’s Liberation Army Ground Force operates the tracked HQ-17 and the wheeled HQ-17A, which rides on a 6×6 truck and can fire while moving. China first showed an export version, the FM-2000, at the 2018 Zhuhai Airshow and cleared a variant called the HQ-17AE for export in 2021. The HQ-17AE can guide four missiles against four targets at the same time. Serbia operates the HQ-17AE, and the system has also been reported in Saudi Arabia and Tajikistan.
Algeria runs one of the largest air defense networks in Africa, built on both Russian and Chinese equipment. Its long-range layer reportedly includes Russian S-300PMU-2 and S-400 systems alongside the Chinese HQ-9, with Russian Buk-M2 systems at medium range. Algeria has also fielded Chinese CHL-906 electronic warfare vehicles, which its Ministry of National Defense showed during an exercise in the country’s southwest.
A short-range system such as the HQ-17 would sit at the bottom of that network, protecting units and key sites from drones, helicopters and incoming missiles that get past the longer-range layers.

Lasvit suspends chandelier of flowers preserved in glass in Napa Valley home
Czech lighting brand Lasvit has preserved the forms of dried flowers inside hand-blown glass to create a large chandelier in a home in Napa Valley, California, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen for the brand.
Called Herbarium, the installation was made from dozens of individually crafted glass pieces suspended at different heights above the home's main living area.
Lasvit installed its Herbarium chandelier in a Napa Valley residence
Some of the glass pieces are long and slender, while others form rounded, teardrop-like shapes, creating a loose cascade that extends towards the floor.
Each piece was made by placing dried flowers and plants beneath molten glass. The heat consumes the organic material while leaving its impression embedded in the crystal.
"Our glassworks are surrounded by wild nature," said Lasvit chief designer Mária Čulenová, who led the creative team behind the installation.
"With Herbarium, we wanted to capture this wilderness so that anyone could take home a piece of this landscape – a piece of the meadow, preserved in glass."
The chandelier occupies the centre of the double-height living room, where it hangs in front of a large window overlooking the surrounding landscape.
Its clear and amber-toned pieces catch both daylight and artificial illumination, casting irregular shadows across the pale walls.
The residence sits in Napa Valley, surrounded by vineyards, wildflowers and a stream running through the property.
Inside, the Herbarium installation echoes the vegetation visible through the windows, preserving its forms in glass.
Herbarium is part of Lasvit Icons, a collection of the Czech glassmaker's designs adapted into modular systems.
Rather than producing every installation entirely from scratch, the system uses individually handcrafted components that can be configured for different interiors, from private homes to larger architectural projects.
Founded in 2007 by Leon Jakimič, Lasvit specialises in bespoke lighting, glass installations and architectural glass, combining traditional Bohemian glassmaking with contemporary design.
Other projects by Lasvit featured on Dezeen include its 2025 Soaked in Light exhibition, which featured a splash-shaped installation and glass light imprinted with a tree branch.

Nepal’s leader labels devastating flood a ‘warning to the world’
Unknown

Nepal’s leader labels devastating flood a ‘warning to the world’
Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the UN that world leaders must act on climate change.
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah has appealed for action to combat the rising threat of climate change, calling the flood that devastated his country last month “a warning to the world”.
Shah made the comments during his address to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday night. He told the gathering that the August disaster “was not just a local tragedy”, asking them the question, “Have you really heard that warning?”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3The Nepal floods question: When the Himalayas collapse, who gets warned?
- list 2 of 3Photos: Nepal flood survivors find little trace of former lives
- list 3 of 3‘Orphaned’ by floods, more than 500 Nepali children face uncertain future
Political leaders “have been negligent to translate those warnings in action at the speed and scale that the vulnerable people require,” he said.
At least 1,453 people died when a torrent of mud, rock and water struck northern Nepal and the China-Tibet border on August 26, triggered by a glacial collapse.
According to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 5,500 people were still missing and 13,795 had been rescued.
Researchers from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) group said in a report released last week that the disaster was not caused by a single extreme weather event, but rather a “compound crisis” shaped by long-term warming, glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and geological instability.
Shah said climate change was hurting people not responsible for the crisis but who “are paying a colossal price for it”.
He said Nepal contributed less than one-tenth of 1 percent of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. About 99 percent of the country’s electricity comes from hydropower, and many workers were trapped in tunnels by the flooding.
“Our glaciers are retreating, our mountain slopes are becoming unstable, our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development,” Shah said.
Shah urged the international community to help bear the cost of helping Nepal adapt to climate change.
He proposed to create a ‘Himalaya Climate Resilience Mechanism’ which would include Nepal and neighbours India and China, and would allow them to share satellite data and expertise, monitor glacial lakes and strengthen joint early warning systems.
Nepal has asked the UN’s loss and damage fund for $20m in aid, the maximum allowed, but a tiny fraction of what it needs. A preliminary assessment by the government has placed the cost of the disaster at $5bn.
The fund, established in 2022 in the aftermath of catastrophic floods in Pakistan, has yet to make even its first disbursement, and observers see Nepal as a key test of its credibility.
Earlier this week, the United States pledged an additional $31m in new flood recovery support.

U.S. Air Force expands tests of glider-based spy drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:51:33 UTC
15:51:33 KST

- The U.S. Air Force added $46.1 million to DZYNE Technologies' ULTRA operational assessment contract, raising its total value to $85.6 million.
- ULTRA is a long-endurance surveillance drone that can fly more than 80 hours, with testing planned in the United States and overseas.
The U.S. Air Force has more than doubled the value of its contract with DZYNE Technologies for operational testing of ULTRA, a glider-like surveillance drone that can stay in the air for more than three days, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The $46.1 million modification raises the contract’s total value to $85.6 million, up from $39.6 million. It covers operational assessment of the Uncrewed Long-Endurance Tactical Reconnaissance Aircraft, with work in the United States and at overseas locations through March 26, 2031. The Air Force obligated $12.3 million in fiscal 2025 research and development funds at award. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center in Dayton, Ohio, is managing the contract.
ULTRA is built on the airframe of the Stemme S12, a German two-seat motor glider, fitted for remote operation. The Air Force Research Laboratory’s Center for Rapid Innovation began the project with DZYNE in 2019 and took it from concept to first flight in under 10 months.
The aircraft weighs about 1,360 kg (3,000 pounds) and has a wingspan of 25 m (82 feet). It can fly for more than 80 hours carrying over 180 kg (400 pounds) of cameras, signals-collection gear or other sensors, and it is controlled over satellite links. It cruises at roughly 130 km/h (81 mph) and needs a runway of about 1,500 m (5,000 feet). The laboratory says ULTRA can travel more than 3,200 km (2,000 miles) and still loiter over a target for a full day.
That endurance is what the Air Force is buying. The MQ-9 Reaper, the service’s main surveillance drone since 2008, spends much of its flight time getting to and from distant areas. The research laboratory designed ULTRA for long-range missions, pointing specifically to the Pacific.
ULTRA has already flown operationally. The Air Force deployed it to an undisclosed location in May 2024, and The War Zone reported that it was flying from Al Dhafra Air Base in the United Arab Emirates. Those missions reportedly complemented MQ-9s over the Middle East. The Air Force requested four ULTRA aircraft for $35 million in its fiscal 2025 budget.
DZYNE has since developed ULTRA Turbo, a version with a turbocharged engine for better performance at high altitude. The company said in April that the Air Force Research Laboratory had ordered three ULTRA Turbo aircraft, after a first flight above 5,500 m (18,000 feet). DZYNE has also reported a 60-hour mission-representative flight at 7,600 m (25,000 feet) and 185 km/h (115 mph).
Air Force budget documents cited by The War Zone show ULTRA Turbo is due for an operational assessment within U.S. Central Command’s area, the Middle East, starting in fiscal 2026 and continuing into 2027. The contract announcement does not say whether the new funding supports that effort.
DZYNE says the aircraft can also carry electronic warfare equipment, relay communications and launch other payloads. The company opened a 11,600 square meter (125,000-square-foot) facility in Irvine, California, in 2024 to build ULTRA and its other long-endurance drones.

What Wood Should I Use on the Coast?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

Wood and coastal architecture have always gone together. It's one of the defining materials of coastal structures. But creating that aesthetic in an environment where weather is a constant part of life demands more from the wood you choose.
Rain isn't unique to coastal areas. What makes the coast different is the combination and frequency of exposure. Humidity, ocean winds, salt-laden air, direct sun, and frequent storms repeatedly take wood from wet to dry and back again. In many coastal regions, these aren't occasional weather events. They are simply part of the climate. That makes two characteristics especially important when selecting wood for coastal construction: durability and dimensional stability.
The Coast Demands More From Wood
Wood naturally absorbs and releases moisture as surrounding conditions change. As its moisture content increases, it swells. As it dries, it shrinks.
Repeated over time, that movement can contribute to checking, splitting, cupping, warping, and gaps between boards. It can also place stress on joints, fasteners, and finishes. Prolonged moisture exposure may also create conditions for rot and decay.
Choosing wood for the coast is therefore about more than appearance or even how long it will last. The material needs to be durable enough to withstand the demanding climate and stable enough to perform predictably within it.
Building for the Coast
Builders have been managing these conditions for generations. Successful coastal construction uses smart design and detailing to manage water and allow wood to dry. Siding profiles and spacing can accommodate movement, while ventilation and drainage help prevent moisture from becoming trapped. Corrosion-resistant fasteners withstand salt exposure, and coatings can provide another layer of protection.
Those practices remain important regardless of the wood being used. Material selection, however, can provide another layer of resilience. Choosing wood that resists decay and moves less as moisture conditions change means the building isn't relying entirely on coatings or construction details for protection. The material itself becomes part of the strategy. That matters in an environment where exposure is inevitable.
Changing How Wood Responds to the Environment
Traditionally, builders have selected naturally durable wood species and used careful detailing to manage the movement and weathering that come with wood. Advances in wood technology now provide another approach: changing how the wood itself responds to the environment.
Acetylation does this by permanently modifying wood at the cellular level, changing how it interacts with water. The wood absorbs significantly less moisture, reducing swelling and shrinking while also providing strong resistance to rot and decay.
Because the modification extends throughout the wood, its durability isn't dependent on a coating or surface treatment. The wood can be finished to achieve a particular appearance or left to weather naturally while retaining its underlying performance. For coastal construction, that creates another level of confidence. Good design and building practices still matter, but the wood itself is better prepared for the environment it will face.
Where Accoya Fits
Accoya is wood built for coastal environments, delivering long-term durability with exceptional dimensional stability. Its resistance to rot and decay is backed by a 50-year warranty above ground and a 25-year warranty in ground or in freshwater. Its dimensional stability is also covered by warranty, providing defined limits for swelling and shrinking.
These characteristics have allowed Accoya to be used on coastal projects across siding, decking, windows, doors, and other exposed exterior applications. When a particular appearance is desired, it can be coated or left to weather naturally without sacrificing its durability.
For architects, builders, and homeowners, that opens up more possibilities for using real wood in places where exposure might otherwise influence the design. Coastal construction will always demand thoughtful detailing and good building practices. The difference comes from starting with a material designed to stand up to the environment. When you have confidence in how the wood will perform, you have more freedom in how you use it.

Northrop’s F-16 jammer deal tops $1.9 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:43:26 UTC
15:43:26 KST

- The U.S. Air Force added $87.4 million to Northrop Grumman's F-16 electronic warfare suite contract, bringing its total value to $1.92 billion.
- The funding supports low-rate initial production of the AN/ALQ-257 system, with work in Rolling Meadows, Illinois, through 2029.
The U.S. Air Force has added $87.4 million to Northrop Grumman’s contract for the AN/ALQ-257 Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, a new radar-jamming and threat-warning system for the F-16 fighter, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The modification funds low-rate initial production, the first small production run before full-rate manufacturing. It raises the total value of the contract to $1.92 billion, up from $1.83 billion. Work will take place at Northrop Grumman’s plant in Rolling Meadows, Illinois, and is scheduled to finish by Dec. 31, 2029.
The Air Force obligated $79.4 million at award: $11 million in fiscal 2025 research and development funds and $68.4 million in fiscal 2025 aircraft procurement funds. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, manages the contract. The announcement did not say how many systems the money will buy.
The system, known as IVEWS, warns F-16 pilots when enemy radars are tracking them, jams those radars and helps locate and identify the threats. Northrop Grumman says it covers an ultra-wide frequency range, including millimeter-wave radars, which operate at very high frequencies used by some modern missile seekers and fire-control systems.
IVEWS is built into the aircraft. Earlier F-16 self-protection jammers, such as the ALQ-131 and ALQ-184, hang in pods under the jet’s belly and take up the centerline weapons station.
The Air Force picked Northrop Grumman for the program in 2021. Two F-16 Block 50 jets flew more than 70 sorties and over 100 flight hours during a seven-month operational assessment at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, and Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, which wrapped up in 2025. By July 2026, the system had logged more than 550 flight-test hours across 300 sorties, company officials said.
In September 2025, the Air Force issued an urgent operational need to get IVEWS into service with F-16 units in the Middle East. The next month, Northrop Grumman reported that the suite had been integrated with the APG-83 radar being installed on upgraded F-16s.
The first Air Force production batch will equip 72 F-16 Block 50 jets, Northrop Grumman vice president Jim Conroy told Air & Space Forces Magazine in October 2025. Up to 450 U.S. F-16s are to receive the system in the initial program, Militär Aktuell reported in January. Northrop Grumman is also offering IVEWS to foreign F-16 operators, whose fleets together with the U.S. total more than 2,800 aircraft.
Congress set aside $187 million in last summer’s reconciliation bill to finish development testing and begin initial production, Conroy said at the time. He said the fiscal 2026 appropriations bill, then still pending, included $250 million for the first full-rate production lot.
The F-16 is expected to remain one of the main fighters of the U.S. Air Force and dozens of allied air forces into the 2040s, alongside the F-35. IVEWS is one of several upgrades meant to keep the jet competitive, together with the APG-83 radar and Northrop Grumman’s LITENING targeting pod.

Northrop gets $124 million for delayed F-35 radar parts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:37:41 UTC
15:37:41 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Northrop Grumman up to $123.8 million for long-lead parts for 67 APG-85 radars for U.S. F-35s.
- Delays to the APG-85 have forced U.S. services to accept new F-35s with ballast in place of radars.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Northrop Grumman up to $123.8 million to buy long-lead parts for 67 AN/APG-85 radars, the new radar meant for the F-35 fighter, as brand-new jets continue to reach U.S. squadrons with ballast in their noses instead of radars.
The contract, announced Sept. 24 by the U.S. Department of War, covers materials, parts and components for what it calls APG-85 Lot 7, supporting the delivery schedule for 67 production radars for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Navy. Long-lead items are parts that take years to make and must be ordered well before final assembly.
The U.S. Air Force is paying $66.5 million and the U.S. Navy $57.3 million from fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds, all obligated at award. Northrop Grumman will do the work in Linthicum Heights, Maryland, and is scheduled to finish in February 2031. The fixed-price incentive contract, with a firm target price, was not competed. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, is managing it.
The APG-85 is an active electronically scanned array radar built with gallium nitride components. It is designed to replace the APG-81 that has flown on the F-35 for years and is a core piece of the Block 4 upgrade package. The F-35 Joint Program Office had planned to start fitting it to some jets in Lot 17, the aircraft production batch delivered from 2025 through September 2026.
The radar has not arrived on time. Lockheed Martin redesigned the nose structure of Lot 17 jets to hold the APG-85, and the new mounting cannot accept the older APG-81 without major structural rework. With no radar to install, Lockheed has been delivering jets with ballast in the nose to keep the aircraft balanced. Development problems with cooling and power consumption have contributed to the delay, Avionics International reported.
The first radar-less F-35B flew its acceptance flight in late February 2026. At a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on June 23, Lt. Gen. Gregory Masiello, head of the F-35 Joint Program Office, told lawmakers the U.S. Marine Corps had accepted six F-35Bs without radars. He said he would not count those jets as fully mission capable. The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy were expected to start accepting aircraft in the same configuration later in 2026.
The jets can still fly and use their other sensors, including electro-optical systems, and they can receive data from other aircraft. They cannot search for, track or target aircraft on their own radar.
A fix on the production line is still years away. Lockheed has proposed a nose bulkhead that can take either radar, but it is not expected to be ready until Lot 20, whose deliveries begin in 2028, Breaking Defense reported. Jets delivered before then without radars are due to be retrofitted once APG-85s become available.
Export customers are not affected. F-35s built for foreign buyers, including Poland, still carry the APG-81, because the APG-85 is not being offered abroad.
The Marine Corps said the Block 4 schedule depended on developing several components at the same time and that delays to some of them disrupted the plan. It called that approach a calculated risk the program office needed to take.

AI chiefs press UN for global safety rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:36:11 UTC
15:36:11 KST

CEO of OpenAI Sam Altman speaks during a United Nations Security Council meeting on artificial intelligence (AI) and international security under "Maintenance of International Peace and Security" during the 81st session of the United Nations (U.N.) General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters on Sept. 23, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Alexi J. Rosenfeld / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP)
Leading artificial intelligence developers urged the U.N. Security Council on Sept. 23 to establish international safety standards, warning that increasingly capable systems could escape human control, enable biological weapons development and concentrate power in too few hands.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said AI offered opportunities for creativity and discovery but could outpace institutions and make decisions people could no longer understand or control.
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone,” he said, arguing that governments accountable to the public should help shape those decisions.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei warned that poorly managed AI could pose “a risk to humanity as a whole,” citing its potential misuse to develop biological weapons and the danger of losing control of advanced models.
He called for agreements banning the use of AI to develop biological weapons, common standards for testing models, stronger evaluation and verification systems, and international reporting mechanisms for serious safety incidents.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said protecting the public could not be left to technology companies. Britain would put AI at the center of its G20 presidency next year, he said.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot also called for an international framework to regulate the technology.
The United States opposed a global regulatory body. White House science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios urged governments to develop their own expertise and institutions, with international cooperation focused on sharing best practices.
China’s U.N. ambassador, Fu Cong, called for stronger regulatory frameworks, emergency response mechanisms and cross-border cooperation.
AI was also on the agenda when U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House on Sept. 24 for talks covering trade and security.
Trump said the two countries would hold important discussions on AI and work toward more balanced trade. Xi called for stronger communication and said both countries had a responsibility to ensure the technology remained under human control and served public welfare.
The leaders later attended a White House dinner with technology executives including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos and Altman.

Office for Future Converts Former School Into Housing for Displaced Families in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Office for Future is converting a former school in Stavyshche, Ukraine, into housing for 42 families displaced by the war. Developed for the Charity Foundation Housing for IDP, the project, titled "Dvir – The Shared Courtyard," reuses the approximately 1,900-square-meter building to create 42 apartments and 200 square meters of shared indoor spaces. The intervention combines the existing structure with new timber elements, an energy retrofit, and the transformation of the former asphalt courtyard into a permeable green space.
The school has served as a local landmark for decades and previously accommodated generations of students. Rather than replacing the existing structure, the project retains and reorganizes it around a new residential program, introducing four apartment types ranging from studios to three-bedroom units, alongside fully accessible apartments for people with disabilities. Shared areas, children's play spaces, and meeting rooms are positioned alongside the private units, while some of the communal spaces are planned to accommodate cultural activities and events open to local residents.
The architectural intervention involves a series of targeted changes to the existing building. Strategic demolitions are used to reorganize the interior and improve spatial efficiency, while a freestanding timber walkway provides access to the apartments. A new timber roof is introduced above the existing structure, incorporating approximately 800 square meters of photovoltaic panels, while the building envelope is upgraded as part of the project's energy retrofit.
Related Article
The Ukrainian Pavilion Examines Displacement and Shared Space Through "Pool of Questions" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale
The former schoolyard is also substantially reconfigured. Approximately 850 square meters of existing asphalt will be removed through a process of desealing, allowing the courtyard to become a permeable landscaped area. Portions of the original paving are retained as pedestrian paths through the garden, creating a network of routes between the building and the shared outdoor space. The project is conceived as a residential micro-community that connects the new housing with the wider town. The courtyard and shared interior spaces provide areas for residents to meet, while their planned use for public activities maintains a connection between the former school and the local community.
"Dvir – The Shared Courtyard" is the third intervention in Ukraine promoted by the Charity Foundation Housing for IDP. Designed by the Florence- and Lausanne-based Office for Future, the project brings together adaptive reuse, new timber construction, energy upgrades, and landscape transformation within an existing structure. Its 42 apartments are intended to provide housing for displaced families while retaining the former school's role as a shared place within Stavyshche. For Office for Future, the building's existing presence and collective memory in Stavyshche are therefore part of the project's approach to its conversion.
Other recent projects and initiatives have also explored housing in response to displacement and affordability. At the 20th International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia, Ukraine's pavilion, "Pool of Questions," is presented by CO-HATY, a volunteer initiative established in 2022 by METALAB and relocated members of Ukrainian Urban Curators, which restores abandoned buildings as housing for internally displaced people. The project asks not only where displaced people can live, but when they can begin to rebuild everyday life. In a different context, the 2026 OBEL Award recognized the Balearic Social Housing Model for its changes to social housing administration between 2019 and 2023, while OMA and Y.A. Studio's 730 Stanyan in San Francisco provides 160 permanently affordable homes for low-income and formerly unhoused households and Transitional Age Youth.

Australia pushes tougher AI safeguards after OpenAI agent breaches government portal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:29:54 UTC
15:29:54 KST

A rogue OpenAI agent’s unauthorised access to an Australian government Medicare statistics portal is adding urgency to Canberra’s plans for tougher artificial intelligence safeguards, while potentially testing the country’s already strained technology relationship with Washington.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday that the incident, which occurred in June, was “unacceptable” and that he had expressed his “extreme concern” directly to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The government has launched a forensic investigation with the Australian Signals Directorate.
The agent accessed public and non-public files on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal after being blocked from obtaining certain information.
Australian officials said no individual’s Medicare data was accessed and described the impact as relatively minor, while stressing that the unauthorised access itself was a serious incident.
OpenAI said it discovered the incident in August and notified Services Australia in September. Australian officials have criticised both the delay and the way the notification was made.
Breach could shape Australia’s AI rules
The incident arrives as Australia develops national AI standards and considers broader regulation of the rapidly expanding technology sector.
Experts say the episode could strengthen calls for AI companies to report security incidents promptly, provide greater transparency around autonomous systems and face clearer responsibilities when their products interact with government infrastructure.
The government has already announced that the incident will be examined by a task force, with findings expected to inform its wider work on AI standards.
Australia has also maintained a tougher position on copyright than OpenAI and Anthropic have sought, requiring companies to negotiate with rights holders rather than receive a broad exemption for training on Australian creative content. Both companies recently urged Canberra to reconsider that approach.
Data centres face a new test
The fallout could also influence how Australia assesses the rapidly growing infrastructure needed to support AI.
OpenAI has partnered with Australian data-centre operator NextDC on a planned 612-megawatt facility in Sydney, while Anthropic has partnered on a proposed 2.16-gigawatt facility in Queensland. Both projects require government approvals.
The breach may increase attention on the concept of “social licence” — whether major technology projects provide sufficient benefits and protections for the communities where they operate.
Australia is already considering rules governing data-centre energy use, water consumption and the treatment of Australian content used to train AI systems.
Victoria state this week announced new data-centre rules that include renewable-energy requirements, water restrictions and community investment provisions.
US tensions add another layer
The regulatory debate comes against existing friction between Canberra and Washington over technology policy, including Australia’s restrictions on social media for under-16s and other proposed online-safety measures.
Australia’s decision to maintain its copyright rules has also frustrated OpenAI and Anthropic, which have argued for greater flexibility to train AI models on Australian material.
Technology policy experts say Australia now faces a broader choice over how aggressively it wants to regulate frontier AI while attracting investment in data centres and maintaining close ties with the United States.
For Canberra, the Medicare incident has turned that debate from a question of future safeguards into a more immediate test of how AI systems should be governed when they interact with critical public infrastructure.

Romania gets its first South Korean K9 howitzers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:27:23 UTC
15:27:23 KST

- Romania has received its first K9 howitzers, K10 resupply vehicles and K12 vehicles from Hanwha Aerospace under a nearly $1 billion contract.
- The order covers 54 K9s and 36 K10s, with most future vehicles to be built at Hanwha's new plant in Petrești, Romania.
Romania has received its first K9 self-propelled howitzers, K10 ammunition resupply vehicles and K12 recovery vehicles from South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace under its tracked self-propelled howitzer program.
Romania signed a contract worth nearly $1 billion with Hanwha on July 9, 2024, for 54 K9 howitzers and 36 K10 resupply vehicles, along with ammunition and tracked and wheeled support vehicles. The deal includes 18,000 rounds of 155 mm ammunition. An initial batch of 18 K9s and 12 K10s is being built in South Korea, and the remaining vehicles are due to be produced in Romania.
The contract originally set the first delivery for early 2027. Hanwha said in July that the first vehicles would arrive in the second half of 2026 for testing and evaluation, with the rest of the initial batch following in early 2027. The first Romanian K9, named Tunetul, Romanian for Thunder, rolled off Hanwha’s production line in South Korea in April.
The K9 is a tracked howitzer that fires 155 mm shells from a 52-caliber barrel and can move off quickly after firing to avoid return fire. Romania is the tenth country to buy it and the sixth NATO member, after Türkiye, Poland, Norway, Finland and Estonia. The new guns will replace Soviet-era 152 mm artillery and older 155 mm systems still in Romanian service.
The K10 is built on the same chassis as the K9 and keeps the howitzer supplied in the field. It carries 104 shells and 504 propellant charges and transfers them automatically at up to 12 rounds a minute, reloading a K9 completely in about 37 minutes. Romania is the third K10 operator, after Norway and Australia.
Production is set to move to Romania. On Feb. 11, Hanwha broke ground on the Hanwha Armoured Vehicle Centre of Excellence Europe in Petrești, Dâmbovița County, northwest of Bucharest. It is the company’s first factory in Europe. The site covers about 181,000 square meters (1.9 million square feet) and will include assembly lines, testing facilities and a 1,751 m (5,744-foot) driving track. Hanwha aims to source up to 80% of the work from Romanian industry, with partners including Iveco and Pro Optica.
In July, Hanwha outlined plans to invest €1.3 billion ($1.48 billion) in defense production and technology transfer in Romania. The company says the Petrești plant could later build infantry fighting vehicles, long-range precision strike systems and unmanned ground vehicles, and estimates that expansion tied to an infantry fighting vehicle program could create up to 2,000 jobs.
Under the 2024 contract, all 54 howitzers and 36 resupply vehicles are due within five years of signing.

The shutdown is another blow to Ukraine’s once-mighty steel sector, which previously accounted for 15 per cent of the country’s exports but has come under pressure from Russian attacks and restrictions from the EU, its top trading partner.
Russia has intensified air strikes across Ukraine in recent months, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that have hit businesses, logistics networks, Black Sea port facilities and civilian infrastructure.
The economic impact of the attacks is cutting tax revenue and leaving the government with a widening budget gap as it seeks to finance the war, officials have said.

“It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror.”
Ukraine has also stepped up its attacks on Russia, targeting defence and energy facilities as well as major online retailers, in an effort to undermine revenues and support for Moscow’s war effort.
‘My alarm clock is a Shahed drone’
A drone strike on a high-rise building in central Kyiv early on Sept 25 killed a 14-year-old boy in what Zelensky described as an “absolutely savage and sickening” attack.
Later in the day, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the bodies of four people had been found in a parking lot in a separate daytime strike on an office building. Another seven people were wounded, he said.
Speaking to Reuters, 29-year-old Kyiv resident Anna said the mounting attacks made it feel as though she was “living under a gun”.

Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war, triggered by its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

ArcelorMittal, whose Kryvyi Rih plant produced 1.7 million metric tonnes of steel in 2025, said it expected to book a non-cash impairment charge of around US$1 billion (S$1.27 billion).
“It is with deep regret that we have concluded that we are no longer able to safely operate ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih,” subsidiary chief executive officer Mauro Longobardo said, in a statement.
The plant’s operations also include iron ore mines, which produced 7.6 million tonnes of iron ore in 2025, according to the company’s annual report.
“We are discussing the future of the plant with the Government of Ukraine and will focus on preserving the infrastructure, so when peace finally returns, options for restarting production remain available,” said Longobardo.

It plans to work with employee representatives and local management on measures to support workers, the person said.

A defence pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan could turn into a broader pact "for the Muslim world" that includes Iran, Turkey's parliament speaker said on Friday, adding that it is expected to be submitted for ratification from next month.
The regional powers signed the "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement" in August, weeks before Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis launched attacks against Saudi Arabia, in reaction to the wider Iran war. Similar to NATO's Article 5, the pact stipulates that an attack on one ally constitutes an attack on all. The signatories have been meeting to lay out the parameters of the accord and assess Riyadh's needs.
"For international agreements to come into effect, parliamentary approval is needed. The meetings held as part of the agreement at the moment are preparatory meetings," Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus told reporters in Ankara. Asked whether the pact was against Iran, Kurtulmus repeated Turkey's position that the agreement did not target any specific country but was primarily aimed at ensuring the security of states in the region amid conflicts and Israel's "hostile policies", adding that Tehran could potentially join the pact too.
"We never see the Mecca Agreement as a pact against Iran, it must not be that way. In fact, we hope the Mecca Agreement can turn into a broader agreement for the Muslim world. Iran can join this agreement too, we hope it will become much stronger with the participation of other regional countries," he said.

2026-09-25
06:23:00 UTC

An explosion caused a residential building to collapse in the crowded touristic center of Athens on Friday, injuring three people and damaging houses, shops and cars across a historic neighborhood.
It was not immediately clear what caused the blast in the two-story building in Plaka near some of Athens' most popular sites including the Acropolis and the Temple of Zeus, sending rocks and broken glass as far as three blocks away.
Police spokeswoman Constantina Dimoglidou told public broadcaster ERT that the fire brigade has not yet concluded its site inspection.
Fire crews and ambulances rushed to the scene as smoke billowed above the ancient monuments. The building where the blast took place was reduced to a mess of twisted metal, broken balconies and hanging concrete slabs.
"It was like the whole building, the whole block blew off. That's how strong it was," said local resident Andreas Martzaklis.
At least five trapped in collapsed building
Authorities said a passer-by was injured. Two women who had been trapped in an adjacent building were rescued and being treated in hospital.
The area is home to many hotels and short-term rentals and crowds of tourists stroll its narrow streets lined with cafes and souvenir shops.
A police source said at least five people lodged at the building, part of which was rented out to tourists. It was not immediately clear if others were trapped.

American rapper Macklemore, who was dropped as the opening act for Ed Sheeran over pro-Palestinian remarks, announced on Thursday he would headline his own "Free Palestine" concert tour that will start next month.
The tour will begin in Dublin, Paris and London, Macklemore said in an Instagram post. US dates and additional performers will be announced later, he said, adding that proceeds would be donated to organizations that support the Palestinian people.
"Being apolitical during a genocide doesn't work anymore," he said. "People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it."
The Grammy-winning rapper had been due to perform at eight additional Sheeran shows when he was removed last month from the tour following remarks at a show in New Jersey.
"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine,'" he said on stage.
Macklemore said owners of stadiums where Sheeran was set to play had objected to those remarks.
Israeli officials have strongly denied that their actions in Gaza amount to genocide and say they are justified as self-defense.
Macklemore has been an outspoken critic of Israel's actions in Gaza
Sheeran, an English-born singer-songwriter and one of the world's top-selling recording artists, said the decision to dump Macklemore came from tour organizers, not him, and that he tried to find a resolution. He apologized for his handling of the situation at a performance in Philadelphia and decried Israel's treatment of residents in Gaza as "unjustifiable."
Macklemore has been an outspoken critic of Israel's military actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
"If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it's that something has shifted over the last three years," Macklemore said on Thursday. "There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now."
"What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he added. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."

Activists chant, 'Netanyahu, go to hell'

One by one, officers pulled protesters from the group, tied their hands behind their backs with zip ties, and escorted them to police buses. The activists kept chanting "Netanyahu go to hell" outside the buses.

====================================================================================================

‘Orphan,’ the new film by László Nemes, tells a bleak story of a Jewish boy in 1950s Budapest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:22:14 UTC
15:22:14 KST

László Nemes burst onto the international movie scene with this first feature film, Son of Saul (2015), which told the story of a member of the Sonderkommando at Auschwitz, the unit tasked with disposing the millions of murdered bodies at the death camp.
It subverted every cliché of Holocaust filmmaking up to that point. Where most Holocaust dramas were slow-paced, and some, like Schindler’s List, even featured tasteful black-and-white cinematography and dialogue in English (one of the only European languages not spoken by a sizable percentage of death-camp inmates), Son of Saul went for grueling realism.
The movie is in color, and the Sonderkommando work at breakneck speed, as we know they were required to do from accounts of the few survivors.
But it had a deep emotional core, about a man who is shaken out of the numbness he has used to protect himself when he goes on a doomed quest to give a proper burial to a murdered boy he claims is his son.
It was such a perfectly conceived and realized movie that it won the Best Foreign Language Film Oscar, as well as the Grand Prix at Cannes, and dozens of other awards.
Few have ever made such a great film, and expectations were understandably, perhaps unfairly, high for Nemes’s subsequent movies. His follow-up feature, Sunset, was far more modest, and now he has a new film, Orphan, which opens Thursday in Israel.
'Orphan' is set on the backdrop of a crushed student uprising
Although it is set after the war, Orphan references the war in nearly every disconsolate frame, and captures the melancholy of trying to pick up the pieces after a tragedy of such a grand scale.
Much like Son of Saul, it subverts the cliches of stories about boys searching for their true father and wishing that this father was a great hero. Based on the story of Nemes’s own father, it is about a 12-year-old boy named Andor (Bojtorján Barabás) in Budapest in 1957.
A student uprising against the Stalinist regime was just crushed by the Soviets, and it’s a bleak, hopeless setting, which mirrors the bleakness of Andor’s life.
He is not an actual orphan but is one of the luckier Jewish children who survived the war in an orphanage and was reunited after the war with one parent, his mother, Klára (Andrea Waskovics). His father, Hirsch, whom he has always been told was a brave and brilliant man, perished in a death camp.
Andor treasures every scrap of information about his father, and clings to a vain hope that he might not really have died. He needs this fantasy about his father to help him get through his days.
His mother works in a state-run shop and barely has enough money for food. Just as bad, from her son’s point of view, she is depressed and careworn, with barely any energy for him. Andor spends much of his time avoiding bullies and trying various schemes to make a little money with his one trustworthy friend.
When a crude, obnoxious gentile butcher, Berend (Grégory Gadebois), who turns out to be not only rude but violent, rides up to their building on a motorcycle, acting like he owns Klára, Andor knows that their already struggling family is in even worse trouble.
'Orphan' has stylistic similarties to earlier works
Gradually, what we sense from this butcher’s first appearance becomes clear to Andor. Klára’s first husband may well have been a murdered hero, but it seems likely that Berend is Andor’s real father. It turns out that this married butcher hid Klára during the war and forced her into a sexual relationship.
She managed to escape his clutches once the war ended, but now that he has found her, he still considers her his, and wants her back, along with the boy he thinks of as his son.
Not only does his reappearance shatter Andor’s fantasies about his father, but it presents him with a terrifying problem: He must contend with this violent man who wants to come and live with him and Klára.
In Hungary in this period, there is nowhere for Klára to turn for help, especially since Berend is buddies with many of the local Communist Party functionaries.
The movie has some stylistic similarities with another, very different portrait of a troubled childhood, Francois Truffaut’s The 400 Blows, especially in its refusal to sentimentalize anything. Childhood is a time when children are at the mercy of the adults around them and have no one to turn to if those adults are brutal or neglectful.
Andor is not in a concentration camp, like Saul in Son of Saul, but he lives in a reality where he may be a victim of violence at any moment. Orphan vividly portrays that climate of fear.
Unbearable tension with no hope for anything better
While no movie could be harder to watch than Son of Saul, in some ways, somehow Orphan makes you long to flee the theater more than Son of Saul does. The bleakness of Andor’s life is so relentless, I found myself wishing the movie would end long before it did.
Son of Saul teased us with the promise that Saul would find some small measure of redemption in the end, and showed that he had achieved a kind of grace just by choosing to try to bury his son.
Here, there is absolutely no glimmer of hope, and nearly every scene involving Berend has the unbearable tension of a family gathering ready to explode into brutality, even death.
Cinematographer Mátyás Erdély has done a brilliant job of making the sepia-toned photography mirror the emotional barrenness of the world that Andor inhabits.
The cast is excellent, and Gadebois manages the almost impossible feat of giving us some glimpses of the butcher’s humanity: Despite his flaws, he does care for Klara and wants to raise this boy. But while Truffaut gave us hints that his abused hero would find a way out, Nemes gives us no such comfort.

Sinwar warned Israel of 'earthquake' weeks before October 7, former Fatah official reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:22:09 UTC
15:22:09 KST

Former senior Fatah official Sufian Abu Zaida disclosed more information on the unusual message from Hamas leader in the Gaza Strip Yahya Sinwar that he had relayed to Israel three weeks before the October 7 attack in a documentary aired on Al-Ghad on Thursday.
In the interview, Zaida said that for more than a year he served as an intermediary in a secret channel between Israel and Hamas in an effort to advance a prisoner exchange deal.
The channel was opened in March 2022, after senior Hamas official Ghazi Hamad approached Zaida and asked for his help in advancing the talks. Zaida contacted a former senior Israeli security official and later met with Israeli officials.
According to Zaida, the contacts progressed to discussions over the names and lists of prisoners, but the sides did not reach an agreement.
As part of the talks, Zaida also met with then-Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Ronen Bar. He said he presented Bar with the conditions Hamas had set for a deal. Among other things, Sinwar demanded the release of all female prisoners, prisoners under the age of 18, prisoners released in the Gilad Schalit deal who had subsequently been rearrested, and veteran prisoners, while giving priority to sick prisoners.
According to Zaida, the Israeli side offered extensive measures benefiting the Gaza Strip in exchange for resolving the prisoner issue, including increasing the number of Gazan workers permitted to enter Israel, rehabilitating the electricity grid and other infrastructure, and advancing reconstruction in the Gaza Strip.
Despite progress in the contacts, the sides did not reach an agreement.
Sinwar warns Israel that Hamas would put 'cards' on negotiating table
On September 14, 2023, Zaida met with Sinwar in Gaza. During the meeting, he said Sinwar asked him to relay a message to Israel that before the end of that month, Hamas would place “cards” on the negotiating table that would cause an “earthquake,” and that Israel should prepare for the “emptying of the prisons.”
Zaida said Sinwar dictated the message to him precisely and asked him to deliver it exactly as given.
Zaida transmitted the message to the Israeli side in both Hebrew and Arabic.
According to him, he was contacted less than half an hour later to verify that Sinwar had indeed intended to convey those words, and he was summoned to an urgent meeting the following morning.
At the meeting in Ashkelon, Zaida was asked what Sinwar meant by an “earthquake” and what the “cards” were.
Sinwar's message keeps security officials awake
According to Zaida, the officials he met told him that no one in the security establishment had slept that night because of the message.
Zaida replied that Sinwar had been calm when he conveyed it to him.
That was, he said, the final meeting held through the contact channel. Zaida returned to the Gaza Strip on October 5 and was scheduled to meet Sinwar again on October 8.
The meeting never took place. Twenty-two days after Zaida relayed the message, the October 7 attack occurred.

The festival will take place at Aktopraklik Mound Archaeopark, which sheds light on Bursa’s 8,500-year history.
Arkeofest, a festival dedicated to archaeology and experimental archaeology, will bring history enthusiasts together with 50 hands-on workshops at Aktopraklik Mound Archaeopark in Bursa on Sept. 26-27.
Organized for the fifth time by Bursa Metropolitan Municipality under the coordination of its Department of Urban History and Promotion, the festival will take place at Aktopraklik Mound Archaeopark, which sheds light on Bursa’s 8,500-year history.
Organized by the Bursa Museum under the municipality’s Museums Branch Directorate, the festival will explore the city’s rich cultural heritage and its history as home to different civilizations over thousands of years.
The archaeopark brings together archaeological excavation areas dating to the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods, architectural reconstructions and traditional houses dating from the Ottoman era to the present day.
The site will host archaeology-related activities during the festival from noon to 6 p.m. on both days.
Participants will have the opportunity to experience ancient production techniques through 50 different workshops.
Activities will include making stone tools, dyeing fabric with plants, exploring Neolithic architecture, making pottery on a wheel, learning Hittite cuneiform, minting coins and preparing ancient dishes.
The festival will also support local production through a marketplace featuring handmade products by women entrepreneurs from the region.
The Rafadan Tayfa team will take the stage at 3 p.m. on Sept. 27, the second day of the festival, with a stage show and concert aimed at children and families.
Arkeofest will be open to the public free of charge. Free transportation will also be provided to facilitate access to the festival site.
A shuttle will depart every 30 minutes from three stops at Uludağ University to the Arkeofest site between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m. on festival days.

The festival will spread across different parts of Istanbul. (AA Photo)
Istanbul will host the Türkiye Culture Route Festival from Sept. 26 to Oct. 4, bringing concerts, exhibitions, theater and ballet performances, workshops and gastronomic events to venues in the city.
Organized by the Culture and Tourism Ministry, the festival was first launched in 2021 under the name “Beyoğlu Culture Route Festival” and will be held in Istanbul for the sixth time this year.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said Istanbul was being considered not merely as a festival venue but as a cultural route in its own right, bringing together the traces of different civilizations, beliefs and cultures.
“İstanbul is a unique city that brings together the traces of different civilizations, beliefs and cultures and allows the past and present to coexist,” Ersoy said. “For this reason, we consider Istanbul not only as a festival venue but as a cultural route in its own right.”
He said it was particularly meaningful that the story of the Türkiye Culture Route Festival had begun in Beyoğlu in 2021 and that Istanbul was now hosting the festival as its 20th stop.
“For nine days, we will transform Istanbul’s squares, museums, historic buildings, stages and different neighborhoods into meeting points for culture and art,” Ersoy said, adding that the program aimed to bring the city’s cultural heritage together with different generations through world-renowned orchestras, local artists, exhibitions, performing arts, gastronomy routes and children’s activities.
Royal Philharmonic Orchestra to open festival
The festival’s opening concert will be performed by Britain’s Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at the Turkish Telekom Opera Hall of the Atatürk Cultural Center (AKM).
The program will also feature the National Arab Orchestra, which combines classical and contemporary interpretations of Arab music with orchestral traditions, as well as “Carmina Burana,” the Istanbul State Symphony Orchestra, pianist and composer Büşra Kayıkçı, İncesaz, the Presidential Classical Turkish Music Choir and the eighth Istanbul International Folk Music Festival.
Public concerts at Galataport’s Clock Tower Square will feature Özcan Deniz, Oğuzhan Koç, Murat Boz, Kıraç, Simge, Poizi, Bengü, Ceza and Bayhan.
The AKM Turkish Telekom Open-Air Stage will host performances by Aydilge, Resul Dindar, Poizi, Oğuzhan Koç, Derya Uluğ and Motive.
The performing arts program will include the “Stanislavsky Ballet Gala” at the AKM Theater Hall, under the artistic direction of the team that performed at last year’s Bolshoi Ballet Festival.
Other productions on the program include “Swans,” “Carmen,” “Delirium,” “The Abduction from the Seraglio,” “Cinderella” and “There Is Actually No Spoon.” Musical and opera performances aimed at children will also be staged as part of the festival.
The AKM Gallery will host “Three Painters: Alaettin Aksoy, Mehmet Güleryüz, Komet,” featuring works from the Taviloğlu Collection.
Exhibitions, talks, a FotoMarathon, karaoke sessions, children’s activities and workshops will be held at the Tophane-i Amire Culture and Art Center, Rami Library, Büyük Çamlıca Mosque, Tarık Zafer Tunaya Culture Center, Taksim Mosque Culture and Art Center and museums across Istanbul.
The festival’s gastronomy program will offer routes highlighting Istanbul’s culinary heritage, from centuries-old restaurants to street food. The routes will stretch from Beyoğlu to Moda, the Bosphorus to Şile, and Eminönü to Vefa and Sarıyer.
Programs in Beyoğlu, Galata, Karaköy, the Historic Peninsula, Fatih, Beşiktaş, İstinye, Kanlıca, Beykoz, Şile and Kadıköy Moda will be guided by chefs, academics and content creators including Vedat Başaran, Maksut Aşkar, Emre Şen, Oğuz Yenihayat, Özge Samancı, Aylin Öney Tan and Kübra Yüzüncüyıl.
The festival will thus spread across different parts of Istanbul, bringing together music, stage arts, visual arts, workshops, children’s programs and gastronomy activities at cultural institutions, historic sites, public squares and neighborhoods.

Istanbul’s traffic gridlock costs residents 12 days a year: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:20:23 UTC
15:20:23 KST

(DHA Photo)
Residents of Istanbul lose up to 12 full days a year to traffic congestion, according to a report highlighting the scale and economic impact of the city’s chronic traffic problem.
The Türkiye Traffic Situation Report, prepared by Professor Sadettin Ökten of the City Thought Center under Istanbul’s Esenler Municipality, examines traffic in Türkiye from multiple perspectives, including economic losses, road safety, driver behavior and traffic culture.
The study draws on a nationwide field survey of 3,000 people aged 15 and above, as well as focus group discussions held in Istanbul, Ankara, Eskişehir and Malatya with traffic police officers, drivers, driving-school representatives, municipal enforcement officers and motorcycle couriers.
The report says traffic congestion can result in as much as 288 hours of lost time per person annually in Istanbul — equivalent to approximately 12 full days. It also cites INRIX 2025 data showing that drivers in the city lose an average of 105 hours each year specifically because of traffic bottlenecks.
According to estimates cited in the report, traffic congestion in Istanbul costs the economy around $10 billion annually. The figure includes not only additional fuel consumption but also lost time, labor and productivity, along with other economic impacts associated with congestion.
Additional fuel consumed because of traffic congestion alone is estimated to cost around $760 million a year.
Although the figures are based on different methodologies, the report says both illustrate the significant impact of congestion on time and productivity.
The report also points to the rapid growth in the number of vehicles on Türkiye’s roads. The number of registered vehicles stood at around 20 million in 2015, rising to 33,193,636 by the end of October 2025.
The study also examined the experiences of motorcycle couriers, who have become an increasingly visible part of urban traffic amid the growth of delivery services.
Registered motorcycles surpassed cars in seven provinces across Türkiye, including Istanbul, Manisa, Muğla, Aydın, Kilis, Şanlıurfa and Şırnak, as of August, hitting 7.6 million compared to 18 million cars, according to Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) data.
Couriers participating in focus group discussions said heavy delivery pressures, insecure working conditions and inadequate parking and lane arrangements can sometimes push them toward taking greater risks on the road.

Colombia severs diplomatic ties with Iran
Bogotá cites links to terrorist groups and concerns over human rights and Iran’s nuclear program; consular relations remain in place
Colombia announced Thursday that it had formally severed diplomatic relations with Iran, effective Sept. 19, citing national and hemispheric security concerns and links between Tehran and terrorist and narcoterrorist groups.
The Foreign Ministry said it had also considered human rights violations in Iran, attacks on countries outside the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and what it described as obstruction of International Atomic Energy Agency efforts to assess Iran’s nuclear program.
Together, those issues had eroded Colombia’s trust in the Iranian government, the ministry said. The break does not end consular relations.
The move comes amid a shift in foreign policy under President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in August. His government has restored ties with Israel after his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, broke them in 2024 over Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar welcomed Colombia’s decision in a social media statement provided for this article, praising de la Espriella’s leadership and calling for a united response to Iran. "I commend Colombia 🇨🇴 and the leadership of President @ABDELAESPRIELLA for severing diplomatic relations with the Iranian regime. This is a clear stand against terrorism, narco-terrorism and Iran’s dangerous nuclear ambitions. The free world must stand united against the Iranian regime."

Int’l team to study giant Van Lake microbialites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:20:12 UTC
15:20:12 KST

The microbialites in Van Lake will be studied through a series of advanced analyses as part of a project involving five universities from Türkiye, Italy, Poland, and China. (DHA Photo)
An international team of scientists will launch fieldwork in eastern Türkiye to investigate Van Lake’s massive microbialites starting Sept. 28, seeking clues to how the lake evolved over millennia.
Researchers from five universities in Türkiye, Italy, Poland and China will collect 40 to 50 samples from the lake. The project, supported by the Van Yüzüncü Yıl University (YYÜ) Scientific Research Projects Coordination Unit, includes Pamukkale University alongside international partners.
Reaching sizes up to 40 meters, the coral-like structures contain nanospheres scientists believe are key to their formation. The team will dive off the coasts of Ahlat, Adilcevaz and the Altınsaç region of Gevaş to gather samples. Researchers will hand-carry the materials to Italy to prevent degradation.
Laboratories in Italy will run advanced chemical and imaging tests on the samples, including scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, micro-Raman, X-ray diffraction, inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry.
Associate Professor Çetin Yeşilova, from the YYÜ Engineering Faculty Geological Engineering Department, said the international team previously studied Salda Lake.
“Microbialites up to 40 meters exist in Van Lake, ranking among the largest and most widely distributed examples globally,” he said. “We want to make deductions about their formation conditions and the geological evolution of Van Lake.”
Yeşilova said the project will answer how and why the structures formed, as their exact origins and contributing factors remain unknown.
Türkiye’s largest body of water, Lake Van, is a massive endorheic lake with alkaline waters that support a unique environment for microbialites, which are rock-like underwater structures formed by microorganisms over thousands of years.

In an interview with Ortadoğu Analiz, the journal published by the ORSAM think tank, Kurtulmuş outlined parliament’s three responsibilities in the next phase of the “terror-free Türkiye” initiative.
A planned monitoring commission would follow the law’s implementation, he said.
Parliament would also review security agencies’ assessments of the PKK’s dissolution and disarmament, along with the government’s decisions on individual cases.

Parliament approved the framework law on Aug. 10.
Kurtulmuş said its implementation would require transparency, equal treatment and effective oversight.
He also called for an end to discriminatory and divisive political language, saying disarmament alone was not the final goal.
The process should strengthen democratic participation and citizenship while preserving Türkiye’s unitary structure and official language, he said.
Turning to the region, Kurtulmuş said non-state armed groups should no longer be treated as legitimate political actors.
Respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and equal citizenship of Iraq, Iran, Syria and Lebanon should be shared principles, he added.
Türkiye’s approach could not simply be copied in Iraq and Syria, he said.
“The two countries’ historical and social conditions are different. What can be transferred is the method.”
Türkiye and Iraq agreed on Sept. 23 to restore full state authority in Sinjar and end the presence of banned foreign armed groups, according to a joint statement issued after President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan met Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in New York.

The two countries also agreed to expand trade and investment and accelerate joint projects, including the Development Road.

Feature: Mooncakes bridge Chinese culture with Lao people's Mid-Autumn Festival celebration
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:15:54 CST
15:15:54 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- When the Mid-Autumn Festival is mentioned, mooncakes are often among the first things that come to Lao people's minds. With their sweet, dense and rich flavor, mooncakes offer Lao people a simple yet memorable way to experience Chinese culture through taste.
Kham, a 32-year-old resident of the Lao capital Vientiane, told Xinhua on Friday that although she is neither Chinese nor of Chinese descent, she buys mooncakes every year ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival, often giving them to elders or guests invited to dinner gatherings. For Kham, the festival is closely associated with the taste of mooncakes and the time spent with people close to her.
"Every year I host a small party for my friends and family to gather and have dinner together. After dinner, we eat mooncakes together. So when I think of the festival, the taste of mooncakes shared with the people closest to me always comes to mind first," she said.
For Kham, the mooncake has become more than a seasonal delicacy. Its taste is tied to memories of gathering with family and friends, giving her a personal connection to a Chinese festival despite not having a Chinese background.
Phonethida, a Lao vendor selling mooncakes, said the pastries appeal to customers not only for their taste but also for their distinctive and elegant packaging, which makes them suitable as gifts.
"When the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches, more Lao customers come to buy mooncakes. Some buy them for their families, while others buy them as gifts. I believe many Lao people are already familiar with mooncakes and have tasted them before," she said.
"Even when it is not the festival, some customers still ask for mooncakes. They tell us that they like the taste and want to eat them, especially with tea," Phonethida said.
The popularity of mooncakes among Lao people reflects how a traditional Chinese festival food has become familiar to some in their everyday lives, offering a simple way for people to encounter and exchange culture through taste.
Beyond the taste of mooncakes, the Mid-Autumn Festival also offers Lao people another way to encounter Chinese culture through learning and cultural experiences. For Lao students studying Chinese, traditional festivals provide opportunities to participate in activities that help them gain a deeper understanding of China and its culture beyond what they learn in the classroom.
Xayadeth, a 17-year-old student taking a Chinese language course, said he looks forward to Chinese festivals because they allow him to experience Chinese culture firsthand while learning new words and expressions related to each celebration.
He said his Chinese language institute organizes special activities for students during different Chinese festivals, giving them opportunities to learn about a wider range of Chinese traditions.
"I like learning through activities during festivals because they help us understand more about China and its culture. There are things that we cannot fully imagine just by reading books or studying in the classroom," he said.
The Mid-Autumn Festival, celebrated annually on the 15th day of the eighth month in the Chinese lunar calendar, falls on Sept. 25 this year. ■

traditional emirati patterns and craft frame al maktoum archives’ interiors in dubai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:15:47 UTC
15:15:47 KST

Emirati heritage shapes the layout of Al Maktoum Archives
At Dubai’s Al Maktoum Archives, Kart Group brings the warmth of a traditional majlis into a government workplace. Palm-frond weaving, hand-tufted wool, and CNC-cut marble carry Emirati heritage into the interior, integrating cultural references into the everyday setting of the archive.
Designed by Mustafa Khamash and his team at Kart Group, alongside contractor EMKAY, the 8,000-sqft headquarters occupies Level 2 of Dubai’s Emirates Towers. The working institution safeguards historical records, private manuscripts, and cultural narratives documenting the Maktoum family’s lineage and the emirate’s evolution. The design combines the requirements of a contemporary workplace with references to this history.
The traditional Emirati majlis informs the furniture layout, with a seating suite positioned at the center of the space. Mashrabiya motifs from the Al Shindagha Museum provide another starting point, with their repeating geometry reconstructed from fundamental units and adapted to contemporary surfaces and fabrication methods.
Traditional motifs take on new forms across the interior
Geometric motifs are particularly visible in the custom carpet, hand-tufted from New Zealand wool. Its pattern aligns across the floor, extending the geometric composition beyond an individual furnishing. Al Khoos, the traditional palm-frond weaving craft, introduces another material reference through woven palm fronds, fine metal inlays, and stenciled wall coatings. At the principal feature wall, CNC-cut and engraved marble brings the heritage geometry to an architectural scale, with the pattern digitally redrawn for stone.
Each motif was adapted by Kart Group’s design team to its medium, from hand-tufted wool to furniture inlays and machine-cut marble. This allows the references to remain recognizable while responding to the different qualities and tolerances of each material.
Kart Group brings the traditional Emirati majlis into a government workplace
Wool, palm fronds, and marble anchor the workplace
Material selection balances longevity, texture, and cultural relevance. New Zealand wool provides resilience and softness underfoot, woven palm fronds maintain a connection to traditional making, and marble establishes a sense of permanence. Contemporary textiles from Romo, Dedar, and Kirkby Design sit alongside these materials.
The traditional majlis suite is complemented by an AJZAL Burj Rashid coffee table, while Herman Miller Aeron task chairs and Polflex leather armchairs support the workplace program. These contemporary elements keep the archive grounded in present-day use rather than historical reenactment.
The interior connects the archive’s institutional purpose with the continued use and adaptation of inherited patterns and craft traditions. Heritage extends beyond the collection itself into the materials, furniture, surfaces, and working environment surrounding it.
